titles.name: 30MC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by decree on the promotion's first card out of two dissolved Hard Knocks Wrestling belts, and changed hands twice across its served run -- once on a mystery referee's fast count, once retrieved off a ladder.

titles.name: 30MC Young Gun Championship
titles.epitaph: Unified from two old Young Guns belts on the promotion's first card and changed hands four times across its served run, ending with a champion counted out of the ring in a finish the broadcast itself never explains, and a belt burned on camera the same night.

titles.name: 4 Winds Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt 4 Winds Wrestling crowned last and placed above the four compass titles it had run on since opening. Its own inaugural tournament ran across Maelstrom III: Legacy in March 2004 and finished with Jerms holding a trophy belt he used, minutes later, to club the night's guest referee in the back of the head.
titles.notes: Receipted to the fed's own Maelstrom III: Legacy card and to Jerms' own roster card, which bills him "1st Ever 4 Winds Wrestling Champion (Won the Tourney at M3: Legacy, Current Champ)".

titles.name: East Wind Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: 4 Winds Wrestling's tag titles, crowned at Maelstrom II: Eruption in December 2003 at the end of a gauntlet and a tournament final. The division they were built for kept emptying: in February 2005 the fed put the belts to a members' poll asking whether to keep them as tag titles, suspend them, or turn them into a ladies', pure-wrestling or cruiserweight championship, and its own owner argued to keep them on the ground that killing the tag division would cost 4WW its place in Primetime Central's.
titles.notes: The poll and the argument are in the fed's own East Wind Title Situation thread (promotions/4ww/archive/forum-east-wind-title-situation.html).

titles.name: North Wind Championship
titles.epitaph: 4 Winds Wrestling's own top singles belt from its first night. A gauntlet on the opening StormFront of July 2003 crowned Jay Phoenix as its first champion; the belt then changed hands four times in eight months, through Syxx Figures, Jaime, Todd Dream and Patti Anderson, and every one of those changes turned on outside interference the fed staged deliberately — a coal miner's glove, a run-in, a stablemate with a title belt in his hands, and finally a guest referee counting three.
titles.notes: The awards site's own Hall of Fame ballot names "Jay Phoenix (First Ever NWT Champion)" and "Todd Dream (Longest Ever NWT Reign)"; the reign sequence below is built from the fed's own show scripts and the fed's own Official 4WW Title History thread (promotions/4ww/archive/forum-official-4ww-title-history.html).

titles.name: South Wind Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt 4 Winds Wrestling gave its second division, decided in a ladder match at the end of a two-bracket tournament in July 2003 and held first by Patti Anderson. Its own record is the fed's busiest: a champion in the fed's own count went through it roughly every few weeks, and one holder wrote on the fed's own board that at the rate it moved there would be fifty-four South Wind champions in a year.
titles.notes: Patti Anderson's own roster card bills her "First Ever South Wind Champion"; the later sequence is receipted to the fed's own Official 4WW Title History thread (promotions/4ww/archive/forum-official-4ww-title-history.html).

titles.name: Tempest Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt named for the midweek show 4 Winds Wrestling ran for one month and then dropped. Tempest the programme was cancelled in August 2003 because a midweek deadline did not fit the roster's own schedules; the name came back as a championship, and the fed's own title historian could not find dates for its first two holders.
titles.notes: The cancellation is announced in the fed's own Federation News of 2 August 2003; the missing early dates are stated as missing in the fed's own Official 4WW Title History thread (promotions/4ww/archive/forum-official-4ww-title-history.html).

titles.name: West Wind Championship
titles.epitaph: The fourth compass belt, and the one 4 Winds Wrestling booked for gimmick matches — its recorded changes include a Flaming Cross match and a two-out-of-three-falls bout fought over 220 light tubes and barbed-wire ropes with an I Quit third fall.
titles.notes: The gimmick stipulations are quoted from the fed's own Official 4WW Title History thread (promotions/4ww/archive/forum-official-4ww-title-history.html); the fed's own East Wind poll thread describes the belt's own booking as "the WWT's gimmick stuff".

titles.name: 96 Commonwealth Championship
titles.epitaph: Salim Raj won the Commonwealth Championship in a three-way with Chad Vargas and Makayla Fox on 27 April 2009; Fox took it from him on 17 May and defended it against Brandon Maddox at Screaming For Vengeance and Twilight Rayn at Parental Advisory 11.
titles.notes: The June pages call it 'the WU Commonwealth Championship'.

titles.name: 96 Elite Championship
titles.epitaph: Michael Ahriman won the Elite Championship in a three-way with Jinx and Alex Kent on 27 April 2009; Jinx held it by Screaming For Vengeance, where Requiem beat him for 'the brand new Elite Championship belt' in June, and the pages end with Requiem holding it.
titles.notes: The June pages call it 'the WU Elite Title'; the belt is the one the April eXpose crowned Ahriman with, which is why the company is held as one under both names.

titles.name: 96 Lugar Championship
titles.epitaph: Chad Vargas was 'the new Lugar champion' on 6 May 2009; Drake Daniels beat him for it at Screaming For Vengeance on 7 June, where the commentary says the Lugar championship 'is going to become the One Shot', and Skit-Zo took the renamed belt at Parental Advisory 11.
titles.notes: The previous holder, if any, is not named, and the June pages call the belt the One Shot title in the same breath as the old name; the name recalls the older fed's One Shot title but the lineage is this company's own.

titles.name: 96 Prodigy Championship
titles.epitaph: The Chaotic Cage match of 18 October 2009 gave the Prodigy title to the man pinned in the final fall: Nathan Lancaster, who defended it against Rico Sutton on 26 October and still held it on 9 November.
titles.notes: Created by the rules of the cage match, which hand the Prodigy title to 'the man to get pinned, or submitted'; Nathan was the last man pinned.

titles.name: 96 Revolution World Championship
titles.epitaph: The Chaotic Cage match of 18 October 2009 crowned Johnny Styles the first '96 Revolution World Champion' (the match's own rules call it the Undisputed World Championship); Nathan Lancaster was declared champion after pinning him on 3 November.

titles.name: AAPW Atlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's secondary singles belt and its hottest: five reigns traced across the year (two chained in this delta's own held pages), vacated once when the champion is removed from the fed, and closing 1997 with "The Demon" Damien Lestat as champion after winning the vacant title at Invasion.

titles.name: AAPW Atlantic Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created July 1997; The Suicide Blondes win a four-way dance for the inaugural title (23 July, off-page), retaining through three defenses before The Trailer Park Assassins win it 16 December (chained in this delta's own held pages).

titles.name: AAPW Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created June 1997; "Dashing" Derek Lankford wins the inaugural tournament final (23 July, off-page), turning on his own stable in the same segment; The Crow wins a three-way to close the year (16 December, chained in this delta's own held pages).

titles.name: AAPW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a four-way at Night of Champions II (The Crow; one reign chained in this delta's own held pages); five further reigns traced by the DEDICATED-AAPW digest, closing 1997 with "Cactus" Bubba Steed as champion after a no-DQ-for-the-champion win at the first Invasion.

titles.name: AAPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a tournament from Night of Champions I through Night of Champions II (3 March 1997, Matt "Techman" Sutherland over Wayne Hanson); changed hands three more times across the year (two chained in this delta's own held pages), closing 1997 with Wayne Hanson as champion after a four-way elimination at Madison Square Garden.

titles.name: AAPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in the Double Trouble tournament (27 January, The Stylistics; two reigns chained in this delta's own held pages); three further reigns traced by the DEDICATED-AAPW digest, closing 1997 with The Punishers as two-time champions -- "the first two-time AAPW tag team champions," their own words.

titles.name: AAWA Master of Mayhem Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-flavored second belt already around Miguel Sanchez's waist by this pass's own first sighting of him -- won, per the show's own recap, in a steel cage match against Death Demon and 'Rowdy' Ryan that survives only as backstory, not as a document in this pass's own held corpus.
titles.notes: Do not invent a title match where none was billed.

titles.name: AAWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The AAWA's own top prize, first seen around Rip Daddy Scorpio's waist on the premiere edition of Saturday Night Fight -- a title the fed itself, not a rival's commentary, put into the record.
titles.notes: First attested holder and only reign recorded from this pass's own read; the corpus's own earlier and later dated posts (not read in full) may carry further title history.

titles.name: AAWC Television Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
titles.epitaph: "Lethal" Lex Taylor held the AAWC Television title in what the fed's own broadcast called a vice-grip, broken once by Big Mack and regained in a tag team rematch. It came off him at Oktoberfest '96 in a triangle match against Xavier Virile and Bloodhunt, under a stipulation that the first man to pin anybody won it. Taylor had the match won — he hit the Lex Plex on Virile and raised his own hand — but Bloodhunt had tagged himself in a half-second earlier, put Taylor down with the Headshot, tagged Virile's arm and rolled him, barely conscious, on top of the champion. Dr. Silver's entire group came to the ring afterwards, and Silver handed the belt to Virile himself in exchange for a bottle of water: the night the AAWC's own commentary worked out that Virile had been Silver's from day one. Nine months later it was around Troy Windham's waist, booked into a four corners defence at World War Games 3 and billed on a rival promotion's own card as the belt he carried into a World title match there.

titles.name: AAWC Unified Championship
titles.notes: Attested by a CSWA retrospective on the Hornet/GUNS feud (promotions/cswa/archive/cswa-spotlight-hornet-vs-guns-1998.html), which describes it as "created from a previous merge of three of the AAWC's lesser titles" and records its own end: at WrestleFest '95 it was merged with the AAWC World Title to create the AAWC Universal Championship.
titles.epitaph: A belt built out of three other belts and then folded into a fourth. The AAWC merged three of its own lesser championships into a Unified Championship, and Hornet took it from Mike Randalls at the fed's own World War Games in March 1995 — a win GUNS answered by attacking him, which is where a three-year feud across four promotions started. Two months later the AAWC merged this title with its own World Championship at WrestleFest '95 to crown a single Universal Champion, in a round robin the surviving account describes as GUNS, Hornet, Dr. Silver and Flic Rair, the first man to beat his three opponents in consecutive matches taking the belt. Nobody else is recorded as holding it.

titles.name: AAWC United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
titles.epitaph: The AAWC's secondary singles belt, and the one with the longest memory in the fed's own commentary. Marcus Price held it in the mid-1990s and lost it to Dr. Silver, who "outsmarted Price two years ago to beat him for the very same AAWC United States title"; Mike Randalls held it at some point too, billed as a former champion in his own right on a night the record does not date. Price won it back in Pittsburgh the week before Oktoberfest '96 and was booked to defend it on both of that event's nights — first against Randalls, then against "Marvelous" Mike Chain. The Randalls defence is the one the record holds: a bloodbath in which Randalls jabbed a broken table leg into his own forehead to shake off the Fashion Statement, and Price tried to walk up the aisle and was sent back by the fed's own President. The one surviving copy of the card ends mid-count on a Price small package, so who left New Orleans with the belt is not recorded. Nine months after that, in July 1997, the belt was on Anarky, booked to defend it at Wembley Stadium in a rematch with "Marvelous" Mike Chain.

titles.name: AAWC Universal Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the AAWC's own card of 5 August 1995, AAWC's UNDER NEW OWNERSHIP, served in the CSWA wing (promotions/cswa/archive/aawcs-under-new-ownership-1995-08-05.html), and by the CSWA's own Unified World Heavyweight Championship history (promotions/cswa/archive/unified-world-heavyweight-championship-history-1997.html). It is named on neither of the Oktoberfest '96 card's own three title matches; whether it was still active in October 1996 is not in the record.
titles.epitaph: The belt the AAWC carried through 1995, and the one its own record only ever shows being defended against outsiders. "Mr. Magnificent" Tom Adler won it at WrestleFest, the night the fed's presidency was sold out from under Robert Schmid, and defended it that August at Cameron Indoor Arena in a steel cage against GUNS, with GUNS' own Enterprises World Heavyweight title also on the line — a match decided when Adler dropped down the far side of the cage while a commentator held GUNS off the floor on his shoulders. Adler left with both belts. Three months later, at Thanksgiving Weekend 1995, Hornet beat him and took the Universal title away as well. The AAWC's own Oktoberfest '96 card, thirteen months after that, names four championships and this is not one of them.

titles.name: AAWC Universal Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
titles.epitaph: The AAWC's own tag team championship, held across the fed's two surviving cards by two different teams and never once seen changing hands. In August 1995 it was on THE ARMED FORCES, Battleship and Submarine, led by their manager TTL, who kept it at Cameron Indoor Arena when the referee ruled a double disqualification on a challenge by ARROGANCE — Joey Melton and Peyton Wright, with Teri Melton at ringside — after Steven Flair and GUNS both got involved. By Oktoberfest '96 it was on "Showtime" Shawn Matthews and "Flannel Animal" Kurt Taylor, booked to defend against the Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, a team the broadcast booth spent the first night pretending to be frightened of. The Vegas Connection had come close to the belts earlier that year, and the Untouchables won their way into the second night's match on the first. When and from whom either reign began, and whether either ended, is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: AAWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
titles.epitaph: The AAWC's own top belt, and the one whose record breaks in half. Its earliest trace is its own disappearance: on 24 October 1993, at the CSWA's LAST CALL II, "AAWC World Champion Hot Shot" carried it into a six-man IRONMAN of CHAMPIONS that merged the IWCCW World title, the AAWC World title and a ten-title Unified Championship into one belt, and Hornet won the final. Three years later the AAWC is billing an AAWC World Heavyweight Championship again, and nothing held says how it came back. In that second life Marcus Price held it and lost it weeks before Oktoberfest '96, in a triangle match against Dr. Silver and "Superstar" Scotty Michaels that he went into with his own finisher suspended: Silver had filed a protest with the AAWC offices calling the Fashion Statement a blatant chokehold, the office suspended the hold pending an investigation, and the referee stopped Price using it. Price's answer was to apply it to the fed's President at ringside. Silver walked out of that match with the belt and was still carrying it into the New Orleans SuperDome, where he spent the night filling other people's tag matches with his own men and steering the Television title into the hands of a wrestler he had apparently been running since the man's first night. Whether Silver ever lost it is not recorded, but by the summer of 1997 the belt was moving fast: "Superstar" Scotty Michaels was newly crowned on 9 July, and inside a fortnight Steve Masters — a former champion himself — took it off him at World War Games 3 in Wembley Stadium on a stipulation added mid-match, with the board's own headline wondering whether Michaels could begin a third reign in two months. Masters is still champion at the last word anywhere held.

titles.name: AAWF Network Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own All-American Wrestling Federation territory, attested for 6 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: AAWF Network Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own All-American Wrestling Federation territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record.

titles.name: ABF Continental Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its Continental Title was among the vacant titles put on the line at its first Raw on 8 July 2002 and was defended again at the Raw reported on 16 July. The fed's own champions list names Randy Savage as Continental Champion.

titles.name: ABF Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its post of 30 June 2002 adds a Cruiserweight Title, to be on the line at the first show; its card for the Raw of 29 July bills Rico (c) against La Parka. The fed's own champions list names Rico as Cruiserweight Champion.

titles.name: ABF Euro Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its Euro Title was among the vacant titles put on the line at its first Raw on 8 July 2002; a post of 16 July reports a defense of it and a number-one contender named for it. The fed's own champions list names GoldDust as Euro Champion.

titles.name: ABF Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its card for the Raw of 29 July 2002 bills the Hardcore Title as a Hell in a Cell match, Mick Foley (c) against Rhyno, The Roaddogg and Spike Dudley. The fed's own champions list names Mick Foley as Hardcore Champion.

titles.name: ABF Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its news posts carry a four-corners tag title match added to a Raw on 3 July 2002 and a defense reported on 16 July; its card for the Raw of 29 July bills The Outsiders (c) defending against Raven's team. The fed's own champions list names The Outsiders as Tag Team Champions.

titles.name: ABF Women's Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships. Its post of 30 June 2002 adds a Women's Title, to be on the line at the first show. The fed's own champions list names Stephanie McMahon as Women's Champion.

titles.name: ABF World Title
titles.epitaph: One of the Angle Based Fed's seven championships; a post of 27 June 2002 says that all its titles are vacant at the start of the company. Its own news post of 8 July 2002 puts all of its vacant titles on the line at its first Raw, and a post of 16 July bills a one-on-one world title match against Hulk Hogan. The fed's own champions list names Hulk Hogan as World Champion.

titles.name: ACE North American Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's number-two title, often used as a stepping stone to the World Title.

titles.name: ACE Television Title
titles.epitaph: A weekly-defended title open to any wrestler regardless of ranking.

titles.name: ACE World Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship, defended monthly on television and at every pay-per-view.

titles.name: ACE World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The promotion's sole tag team title, open to any pairing of singles wrestlers.

titles.name: Action Championship
titles.epitaph: Action!'s Action Championship was first won by Chris Fear on 20 March 2002. The fed's own record carries 9 reigns on it, across 8 different champions. The longest is Jeff Garvin's, 143 days from 31 August 2003. One of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder; another changed hands off-page, by the fed's own owner's award rather than a match. Phil Atken held it at the end of the surviving record, his own status left open twice on the fed's own last show.
titles.notes: Pre-history residue, 2002-03-31 ('Resentment' special): see action-001's note -- an overturned title-change finish, not a reign, with no title-log row. Two mechanical conflicts on this belt are resolved by legacy log rows 2538/2539 (action-007/action-008); see their notes. Jeff Garvin's second reign ends off-page: Reed Young hands the belt to Phil Atken on Pressure Point 90 (2004-01-21), no strip shown; Atken's own reign is filed open to the fed's own record's end (Pressure Point 92, 2004-04-07, leaves his status 'unclear' twice, and the fed's own last word follows 9 July 2004) rather than given an invented loss.

titles.name: Bantam Championship
titles.epitaph: Action!'s Bantam Championship was first won by Joey Malone on 10 July 2002. The fed's own record carries 8 reigns on it, across 8 different champions. The longest is Joey Malone's, 81 days from 10 July 2002. Keith Scott Zimmerman held it at the end of the surviving record.
titles.notes: Pre-history residue, 2002-03-31 ('Resentment' special): a ladder match for a Bantam Championship the fed's OWN OWNER character retracts on air minutes later ('it's way too soon to bring out the B Title'), before the belt's real creation by tournament on 2002-07-10 (bantam-001). No reign, no championship existed to change hands; see bantam-001's note. Two mechanical conflicts on this belt are resolved by the legacy log row 2546 (bantam-007); see its note.

titles.name: Carnage Championship
titles.epitaph: Action!'s Carnage Championship was first won by Simon Seaman on 26 May 2002. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 5 different champions. The longest is Max Danger's, 195 days from 17 March 2003. HardCase held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Dyad Championship
titles.epitaph: Action!'s Dyad Championship was first won by Clit 'n Candy on 25 August 2002. The fed's own record carries 7 reigns on it, across 7 different champions. The longest is Arcade & Son's, 126 days from 25 May 2003. The International Workrate Connection held it at the end of the surviving record.
titles.notes: Tag-team style (style_id 2).

titles.name: King of Submission
titles.epitaph: A submission tournament whose final was fought at Blood, Sweat, and Tears in February 2003 for a three-foot trophy. Max Danger won it when Jeff Garvin's corner threw in the towel, and the trophy stood at his table at the fed's own awards night a month later.

titles.name: Action! "Television" Championship
titles.epitaph: Action!'s Action! "Television" Championship's first recorded champion is Keith Scott Zimmerman. The fed's own record carries 5 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is Keith Scott Zimmerman's, 21 days from 2003-01-06. Sweet Aroma held it at the end of the surviving record.
titles.notes: The '(t)' marker on the Pressure Point 59 match Dirk $eller vs. Sweet Aroma (5 May 2003) is the fed's own champion tag for it, exactly as (A!)/(b)/(c)/(D) mark its four filed belts -- treated here as a real lineage the record carries, served as an unfiled belt with its lineage. Keith Scott Zimmerman is billed as already champion ('the newest member of the Action family... also the "Television Champion" of Action!') at his in-fiction DEBUT on the first of the nine matches -- the title is presented as pre-existing his arrival, self-proclaimed/'unsanctioned' (his own word, in the Pressure Point 44 match of 6 January 2003), never sanctioned by the fed's own record. Grade for the whole chain: primary-source (every reign is read from the matches' own texts, at the grade the text supports; two turnovers are undated on-page and bracketed, see action-tv-002/003's conflict fields).

titles.name: End Game Match
titles.epitaph: A match fought at ACW's End Game shows, its finishing places recorded on the fed's own Accolades page down to fourth. Three editions are recorded there, 2005, 2009 and 2010, each with its own winner.

titles.name: ACW Gateway Championship
titles.epitaph: Made for a new division on Courage 131, 20 January 2011, when Jeremy Hunt, ACW's new Overlord, unveiled the belt and awarded it to Billows; Shawn Jessica Hart pinned Billows for it two weeks later and held it through the last card of that run. Ryan Sully submitted champion Dude In Mask for it at ACW's first World Wide Wrestlecide on 3 November 2011, and Chris Hopper held it by mid-2012. The fan board's own account calls it "now-defunct" by February 2013, retired sometime after a match Jack Harris lost for it at that year's End Game -- a card not otherwise recovered in the held record.

titles.name: ACW King of Ages
titles.epitaph: An annual tournament rather than a belt, and by the fed's own Accolades page its marquee one, run at times with sixteen entrants and at times with twenty and settled on its own show. Khristain Keller won the 2003 edition on 7 September 2003, beating Vince Jacobs in the final, and his bio card notes he was still waiting on the title shot it was supposed to carry. The 2004 edition ran its qualifiers through July and August — Lancett, Simian Kade, SilverHAWK, Quinton May and God's Forgotten Son all fought through them — and God's Forgotten Son beat May in the final on 22 August 2004, which also made him United States Champion. The third ran through five Courage cards in 2010, from a qualifying battle royal to a three-man finale at King of Ages on 26 August, in which Jesse Ramey beat Z and Keith Scott Zimmerman, and its prize was new: the King's Choice, which its holder could use for any purpose.
titles.notes: Won in the fed's own tournament, at most once a year (2003, 2004 and 2010), and never defended between editions. Its own characters call it a title (Khristain Keller, 26 August 2004: "I am the reigning King of Ages, never having lost the title in the first place"); no defence of it survives in the fed's own record.

titles.name: Scorpion Fight Night Challenge
titles.epitaph: A one-night points contest fought under Scorpion Fighting rules, its falls scored against targets drawn every ten minutes and its winner the one with most points at the night's end. It ran twice: Alias won the first, in April 2009, which also made him Scorpion Fighting Champion, and Omega the second, in June 2010.

titles.name: ACW Scorpion Fighting Championship
titles.epitaph: ACW's hardcore belt, and the one belt in the fed whose fate a champion got to decide out loud. It entered ACW on 11 May 2003, when Vincent Pembridge won a six-person fight to become its first champion, and Quinton May took it from him at King of Ages that September. Quinton May, Phil Atken, Chris Messiah and Azrael Asesino held it through 2004; Fejona Min held it alongside the Television Championship from Relentless on 30 September, and when Seymour Almasy won the Television title at breakOUT the fed's owner handed him this one too and left it to him whether the two stayed merged. On Courage 72 Almasy announced they would not — “the two titles will REMAIN SEPARATE” — and set his own rule for which belt went up in which kind of match: the Scorpion in anything with a stipulation, the Television title in a straight one. He defended it that same night in a kendo stick match, and lost it at End Game 2005, where Lowell Dot Com pinned him first in a five-way elimination match for both belts. Coral Avalon, Brandon Youngblood, Calypso and Jimmy Cain held it through 2006, and the fed's belt page vacated it that July. Alias won it when the fed came back in 2009, and Iceman, Landon Stevens, Omega, Fejona Min and Tyson XL held it through the 2010 tour, Fejona Min carrying it into the bout at King of Ages 2010 that its own title page says unified it with theAsylum's Black Title as the ACW [Black] Scorpion Title. Khristain Keller won it on 27 January 2011, on a card that is not served, and on the fan board's run Keith Scott Zimmerman and GoldenHAWK, billed as BlackHAWK, carried it into 2013.
titles.notes: The fed's own title page, note *13: at King of Ages 2010 "there was something of unification bout that involved the ACW Scorpion Fighting Title and the infamous Black Title from theAsylum. The result was the birth of the ACW [Black] Scorpion Title"; Fejona Min won it. The Black Title's reigns before that night are theAsylum's.

titles.name: Spirit of ACW Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt ACW claims as its oldest and buried twice. Its own history segment dates it to 2 April 1993 and names four champions before the fed split it into the United States and Television titles; its own belt page lists six reigns from June 1993 to its retirement in March 1995, and the two do not agree on the names. It carries a rule no other belt in the promotion had: whoever holds it picks the stipulation every match it is defended under, match by match or across a whole reign. It came back on 26 January 2006, carried to the ring by the man billed as its first champion, and the Television Championship match already booked to open Legends II became the match that crowned it instead. Andy Sharp won it and held it until the fed's belt page vacated it on 10 July 2006. When ACW came back, Steve Knox won it in a ladder match on the Courage of 9 April 2009, and nine more reigns followed in the next two years; Dean Denton pinned Andy Sharp for it at Dia de los Muertos on 27 February 2011, the last card of that run. On the fan board's run Seymour Almasy, billed as Orphan, came to the Nippon Budokan in January 2012 as its champion and kept it against KIRU, and by February 2013 the fed called him “the longest-reigning Spirit of ACW in history”; Jesse Ramey was billed as its brand-new champion that month.

titles.name: ACW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at Glory on 6 July 2003, when SilverHAWK decreed that the winners of a three-team, sixty-minute Iron Man match would become the first ACW Tag Team Champions: El Janitors won it, defended the belts three times, and were stripped of them on 7 December 2003, when the fed folded. They returned with the 2004 revival — theNormans took them at Relentless on 30 September 2004 and kept them past Splink on Courage 65 by disqualification; Splink took them from theNormans at breakOUT on 6 February 2005 and went missing, and the fed retired the belts that May. The Heirs of Wrestling won them out of vacancy at The Wake on 17 September 2009, and nine more changes followed by February 2011; Big E. Smalls, Orcs and Humans and Team HOSS held them in 2012 and 2013.

events.note: Retired at End Game 2005 by the fed's own title page, the champions Splink having been missing for months; brought back in 2009.

titles.name: ACW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The other half of the split Spirit of ACW, and the belt Seymour Almasy came to the fed to win. Its own belt page carries a staged history of thirteen reigns from January 1999 to July 2002 before ICU won it on the Courage of 13 October 2002. Alias won it on 16 March 2003 and vacated it on 1 June 2003 after an undefeated reign; Quinton May won the battle royal for it at Glory and held it until the fed folded that December, then won it back in a ladder match on 8 April 2004; Fejona Min took it from him on 7 October 2004 in a match that put the Scorpion Fighting Championship on the same shoulder. Almasy beat both her and Kelly Flawless for it at breakOUT, defended it through the spring and summer of 2005, and lost it to Andy Sharp on Courage 79. Sharp was carrying it on 26 January 2006 when ACW announced from the stage that it was being folded back into the returned Spirit of ACW; the show's own text leaves him looking down at it, “the last in a long storied list of champions.” It came back on Courage 106 in Madrid on 11 March 2010, when Trevor Wilson declared himself its owner and SilverHAWK let it stand, and Midnight Cowboy retired it for good at World.Wide.Wrestlecide 001 on 30 April 2010, eight days after winning it at Legends IV.

events.note: Retired from the stage at Legends II and integrated into the reintroduced Spirit of ACW Championship; Andy Sharp is named its last champion.
Retired again at World.Wide.Wrestlecide 001 by its champion, Midnight Cowboy, eight days after he won it; it had been revived on Courage 106.

titles.name: ACW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the two belts ACW's own in-fiction history says was made by splitting the Spirit of ACW in half, and one of the two it retired to put that belt back together. ICU was its first champion of the television age, in September 2002, and it changed hands twice at Relentless that October. Dante Inferno won it inside a steel cage at Glory in July 2003; God's Forgotten Son won it at King of Ages in August 2004 and defended it at breakOUT; Kelly Flawless took it in a battle royal on Courage 71 and lost it to Alias on Courage 81. At Legends II on 26 January 2006 the fed announced from the stage that the title was being retired and that Alias — “the Original Pulp Hero,” whose own card claims a 1997 reign under a different ring name — would be its last champion. It came back in 2010 as the All-Star Academy's top prize and ended with the Academy that December.

events.note: Retired from the stage at Legends II with the Television Championship, when the Spirit of ACW came back; Alias kept the belt.
Retired at the All-Star Academy's SHOWCASE Finale III, when the Academy was declared defunct; Shade is named its last champion.

titles.name: ACW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top of All-Star Championship Wrestling's card, and the belt the fed kept taking away from people. Osyrus was its first champion of the television age, in September 2002, and it changed hands four more times before the fed folded in December 2003. “Superstar” Vince Jacobs won it from Alias at King of Ages in August 2004 in the third and, at the time, final match of a rivalry ACW dated back a decade; Jacobs and Khristain Keller pinned Alias at the same time at breakOUT the following February, and on the next Courage SilverHAWK vacated the belt. Keller took it at End Game, Max Danger took it from Keller on Courage 86, 19 January 2006, and Seymour Almasy took it from both of them in a three-way at Legends II on 26 January 2006. He defended it through the spring, twice in one night at Honor & Glory after being made to qualify for his own main event, and Andy Sharp pinned him for it at Courage 100 on 6 July 2006. When the fed came back in 2009 he won it again, beating Andy Sharp in the final of a tournament for the vacant title on the Courage of 9 April 2009, and never lost it in a match: on the night of Legends III, 4 June 2009, he was found unconscious in a straight jacket, and Max Danger won it in a battle royal. After Max Danger, Andy Sharp, Alias, Trey Vincent and Keith Scott Zimmerman held it through 2010, and Z won it at End Game in Rome on the last night of 2010 and was champion when that run ended. On the fan board's run, Tyson XL, The Amazing Gabriel and Andy Sharp held it into 2013.

titles.name: ACWF Canadian Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Cardiac Kid" Joey Valachi, defended on a UWF broadcast 3 January 1997 and challenged for again at the fed's own Beach Wars '97.

titles.name: ACWF Tag Team Championship (1996 lineage)
titles.epitaph: A separate, disputed 1996 tag lineage: a two-week reign publicly alleged to have been won by bribery, triggering a formal ACWF investigation and a broadcast exoneration.
titles.notes: The holder and the investigation's own outcome are documented in prose rather than as a dated reigns.json row: the accused holder's name and the investigation's own broadcasts are cited from CWAA's own unheld record, not reproduced under this wing.

titles.name: ACWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Iceman" Greg Smith from the fed's own December 1996 launch; Smith later loses it and publicly blames a UWF wrestler on air, and the belt is still seen in an ACWF duffel bag on a UWF card as late as 3 September 1997, days before the fed's own closure.

titles.name: ACWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Three changes across this collection's own holdings: Deadly Intentions (December 1996) lost it to Hellfire and Damnation on the fed's own debut broadcast, which in turn gave way to the New Sensations by mid-1997, who lost it to Lt. Daniel "Lethal" Lawson and Sgt. Mark Sherrick on 23 August 1997 -- the fed's own last recorded title change, won, by the announce team's own admission, on an illegal pinfall.

titles.name: Baja Blast Championship Sponsored by Taco Bell
aka: Baja Blast Champion Sponsored by Taco Bell
titles.epitaph: Its title history opens on a vacancy: Hot Mask held the belt first, then exited the territory suddenly enough that no in-fiction loss was ever staged, the title and a place in ADW's own lineage left open for him before El Triton won it back out of the resulting three-way. Sponsored by Taco Bell — the sponsorship is part of the legal name, said in full every time, without exception.

titles.name: AEW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt. Its Corino roleplay has Steve Corino enter the Wrestle War match for it on 3 May 2015, and the Aries roleplay says Roman Reigns left the TD Garden as the new champion, after a match so large that fifty-eight other men 'came pretty close'. No earlier champion and no later reign survives.

Attested once: The Perfectionist held it as of the site's last update, despite losing his own results-page bout to Undertaker by Tombstone Piledriver days earlier. No earlier champion or title change survives.

titles.notes: Attested only as a current-holder snapshot on the fed's own titles page — no title history or earlier champion survives.

titles.name: AEWA Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Four lineage changes traced through 1997; the belt's own history runs through the AEWA's wholly-owned regional promotion as well as its own flagship shows.
titles.epitaph: Penance opened 1997 as champion, defending against Adam Anderson in January before losing the belt to the Holy Ghost on Saturday Night Slam later that same month. "Cardiac Kid" Joey Valachi took it from the Holy Ghost at the promotion's own Kickoff '97, announced as the show's own mystery challenger, and carried it into the AEWA's regional promotion, where he defended it to a time-limit draw against the regional promotion's own Marc Thomas. By the fed's own 2 October newsletter, Fuse is champion, having already defended the belt against Valachi in September.

titles.name: AEWA National Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Retired into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship on 16 April 1997.
titles.epitaph: Graphic Violence held this belt into 1997 before losing it to the Assassins at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. It stopped existing as its own belt on 16 April 1997, at AEWA Extreme, when the Assassins lost a dedicated unification match to the World Tag Team champions, the Machines, merging the two lineages into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship.

titles.name: AEWA North American Championship
titles.notes: Four lineage changes traced through 1997, ending the corpus's own coverage vacant with a tournament under way.
titles.epitaph: A mid-card belt that moved constantly and then simply stopped: Justin Trouble held it into 1997, lost it to Deathwatch in a triangle match at the promotion's own Kickoff '97, saw the Caretaker take it at AEWA Extreme in April, and won it back himself by the end of August. By the fed's own 2 October newsletter the title is vacant, with a tournament already under way to fill it — the last word this corpus has on the belt.

titles.name: AEWA Television Championship
titles.notes: One lineage change traced through 1997, both reigns defended repeatedly including a steel-cage defense at the promotion's own AEWA Extreme.
titles.epitaph: Sir Gallade carried this belt into 1997 off a December 1996 win over Randall Osbourne and held it through both of the fed's own 1997 pay-per-views, including a steel-cage defense against Osbourne at AEWA Extreme. By the end of August "Bullywug" Glenn Hudson had taken it from him, and Hudson was still defending it as the corpus's own coverage closes out in early October.

titles.name: AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Created 16 April 1997 at AEWA Extreme, merging the World and National Tag Team lineages in a dedicated unification match — the single cleanest structural fact in the wing's own dossier.
titles.epitaph: Born at AEWA Extreme on 16 April 1997, when the Machines beat the Assassins in a match built specifically to merge the fed's own World and National tag lineages into one belt: the referee hands over "the new Unified Tag Team Title belts" and the ring announcer crowns the Machines the first Unified champions on the spot. By the end of August the West Coast Connection held it, and were still defending it in late September as the corpus's own 1997 coverage closes out.

titles.name: AEWA World Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.notes: Six lineage changes traced through 1997 from the fed's own broadcasts and newsletters; the top belt of the promotion, defended on both of its 1997 pay-per-views.
titles.epitaph: The AEWA's own top belt changed hands six times in 1997 alone. Shane Matthews carried it into the year off a battle-royal win the previous November, lost it to Deranged on a chair shot in January, and watched Deranged lose it to "Crimson" Joe Reed at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. Reed's first reign lasted less than two months: Heavy Metal took it off him in a four-way at AEWA Extreme in April, and was himself dethroned within weeks by "Superman" Mike Stewart in a match the AEWA's own record does not carry at all — it survives only as footage replayed on a rival federation's pay-per-view. Reed took the belt back from Stewart at Battle Klash II that summer, in a show that briefly made him champion of two federations at once, and was still champion in the fed's own newsletter as late as 30 November 1997. A rival's own Top 200 write-up records that Randall Osbourne finally ended that reign sometime in 1998, past the edge of the wing's own 1997 record.

titles.name: AEWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Retired into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship on 16 April 1997.
titles.epitaph: The Machines held this belt into 1997 and defended it against the West Coast Connection at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. It stopped existing as its own belt on 16 April 1997, at AEWA Extreme, when the Machines beat the National Tag Team champions, the Assassins, in a dedicated unification match and the two lineages became one — the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship.

titles.name: AeWF Anarchy Championship

titles.name: AeWF King of Extreme Crown

titles.name: AeWF King of the Air Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained by Sean Waltman against Wardancer in a match ruled a double count-out on Thursday Night Whiplash, after which a three-way ladder match was announced for the belt.

titles.name: AeWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained by the Snakes, Viper and Python, against the Dark Side in a double-pin draw on Thursday Night Whiplash.

titles.epitaph: Held by Snake Eyes entering 1998, teaming with fellow champion the Evangelist rather than defending it alone on Thursday Night Whiplash.

titles.name: AeWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Evangelist entering 1998, teaming with fellow champion Snake Eyes rather than defending it alone on Thursday Night Whiplash.

titles.epitaph: AGW's namesake singles championship, first won 15 February 1998 (in a tournament final, footnote 11) and defended through 33 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, E.H. Brawler's reign beginning 30 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. Its footnote 23 reign changed hands in a 4-way Flaming Barbed Wire Baseball Bat Match.

titles.epitaph: AGW's tag championship successor to the discontinued U.S. Tag Team Titles, its first reign the finals of a 16-team tournament (footnote 22) beginning 27 March 1999; 21 recorded reigns follow before the ledger's own last word, New Death Sensation's reign beginning 30 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus.

titles.name: AGW Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: AGW's weight-limited championship (a 240-pound maximum per the ledger's own footnote 19), first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 55 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, Jason Star's reign beginning 30 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. Matt Grendel's own reign (19 January 1999) was struck from a front-office scheduling error that gave the 247-pound Grendel a title shot over the weight limit; President Speed Racer stripped him days later and awarded him a TV Title shot instead, though the ledger still counts Grendel a past champion.

titles.name: AGW Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: AGW's secondary singles championship, first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 37 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, Shawn Michaels's reign beginning 5 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus.

titles.name: AGW Super Heavyweight Title

events.note: the fed's own ledger marks the belt "BELT DISCONTINUED" after Brolly's reign beginning this date, with no further holder recorded.

titles.epitaph: AGW's heavyweight-division championship, first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 10 recorded reigns -- the shortest-lived of AGW's founding titles, discontinued outright after Brolly's final reign began 17 January 1998. Anaconda's own reign (1 November 1997) lasted five minutes: he already held the Intercontinental Title and asked for the belt to be handed back to Brolly (footnote 10).

titles.name: AGW TV Title
titles.epitaph: AGW's television championship, first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 55 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, Jason Star's reign beginning 9 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. Won by Atlas on the fed's own earliest surviving results card, 15 September 1998 -- the one AGW title change this wing holds a served results document for.

titles.name: AGW Unified Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Attested solely by Nelson's own bio card, which names it as one of three belts making up his "AGW Triple Crown Tag Champion" distinction, alongside the World and Anything Goes tag titles. No reign document, no other mention, and no exact date survive in the held record.

titles.epitaph: AGW's secondary tag championship, first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 33 recorded reigns until the fed's own ledger discontinued it 23 March 1999, replacing it with the Anything Goes Tag Team Titles.

titles.name: AGW Women's Title
titles.epitaph: AGW's women's championship, its earliest recorded reign (Tessa, a tournament final) undated in the fed's own ledger; 20 further recorded reigns follow before the ledger's own last word, Goth Chick's reign beginning 26 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. The belt sat vacant from 13 January 2000 "due to injury" -- the only vacancy in this ledger the fed's own text attributes to a wrestler's health rather than a stripping, no-show, or administrative gap.

titles.name: AGW Woman's Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Attested solely by Jessica Dawn's own bio card, which bills her a "Woman's Tag Team Champion." No reign document, no named co-holder, and no other mention survive in the held record.

titles.name: AGW Woman's World Title
titles.epitaph: Attested solely by Jessica Dawn's own bio card, which bills her a three-time "Woman's World Champion" -- a title name distinct from the "AGW Women's Title" the fed's own title-history ledger tracks through early 2000. No reign document for this title survives in the held record; whether it is that earlier belt under a later name, or a wholly separate later title, is not attested either way and is left unresolved rather than assumed.

titles.name: AGW World Title
titles.epitaph: AGW's flagship championship, first won 7 October 1997 at the fed's own founding and defended through 26 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, Mark Payne's reign beginning 30 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. Kid Nitro's own reign ended not by a loss but by his death in a quadrangle Bridge match in the EEMWF, vacating the belt (the fed's own title-history ledger, footnote 2) -- the one reign this ledger records ending in kayfabe death rather than defeat.

titles.name: AGW World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: AGW's flagship tag championship, first won 7 October 1997 and defended through 38 recorded reigns before the ledger's own last word, E.H.B./McKnight's reign beginning 16 January 2000, running into the fed's own hiatus. One reign (Conveyors Of Pain over The Cowboys, 8 August 1998) lasted three hours -- the shortest recorded on this wing.

titles.name: AICW Inoki Cup
titles.epitaph: An eight-man single-elimination tournament staged across the Tokyo Thunder Festival's own two nights, won by "Big D" Devon Burke over Rory Christianson in the final. Burke defended the cup successfully the same event, against Vic Garibaldi, and is still billed champion in the fed's own last-recorded show.
titles.notes: Born from a one-time tournament but billed and defended afterward as an ongoing championship, not a single trophy.

titles.name: AICW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at Apocalypse '97 in the "King of the Hill" battle royal — two simultaneous eleven-man battle royals whose survivors met in a singles final, won by "8-Ball" Vic Garibaldi. The belt passes to Mista Smith and then to "The Ultimate Male" Chris Del Rio off-page, in transitions the surviving record never shows, before Gino Valentini wins it from Del Rio at Steel City Meltdown, the belt's own last recorded change.

titles.name: AICW North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named once in the surviving record: the Asian Assassination Squad, Blackjack Takahashi and Thripaq Nguyen, are billed as champions on AICW's own Survival of the Fittest. No document shows the title being won, defended, or lost.

titles.name: AICW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: AICW's own first title, awarded at a seven-man gauntlet on Fright Night to "Swingin'" Chandler Stone. The belt changes hands repeatedly across the surviving record — to Elvis, to Stephon T. Davis, to "Pretty Boy" Troy Walcott, to "The Convict" Oswald Bates, and, after an off-page saga involving a voided win and a Commissioner's own fiat award, to Legion and then Zeek Monkey — several of its own transitions never shown on any served card.
titles.notes: One document (Steel City Meltdown) names a physical belt "the AICW Extreme title"/"jobber title" in what its own surrounding text treats as this same lineage; not clearly resolved in the surviving record, so recorded here rather than as a separate title.

titles.name: AICW World Championship
aka: American Internet Championship Wrestling World Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man ladder match at Apocalypse '97, where "The Demon" Kyle Bane became the fed's own first-ever World Champion. "Hard Line" Byron Brady dethroned him in a steel cage at New Year's Revolution; a masked debutant billed only as The Saint won it from Bane a second time at the Tokyo Thunder Festival, in a match decided by Byron Brady's own disguised interference as the Demonweb's "Legion"; Brady reclaimed it from The Saint at Steel City Meltdown, the belt's own last recorded change in the surviving record.
titles.notes: The belt's own name drifts between "World Championship" and "World Heavyweight Championship" across the held record without the fed itself ever marking a rename; recorded as one continuous lineage.

titles.name: AICW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at Apocalypse '97 in a tag tournament final won by the Nubian Warriors, Nelson and Muffasa Bukola. The Perfectly Perfect Duo, Lance and Max Studd, dethroned them at Seasons Beatings/Violent Night and held the belts through the whole of the surviving record after — five months and counting by the fed's own last-recorded show.

Every AOWF title, including this one, was declared vacant at the opening of AOWF_2; the held record's only confirmed reign is Tommy Riley's own win of a three-way Ladder Match there, over Chad Hazzard and Stephen "the Monkey" MacDonald.

titles.name: AOWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned once in the held record: a scored four-way contest on the finale of the alliance's first event (AOWF, November 1999) — first to three falls wins — Nightshade defeating Shame, Savage Warrior, and Chaos, each entering as a champion or top contender of one of the alliance's own four founding member federations.

titles.name: AVW Appalachian Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's second singles title, vacant at its launch in January 2001 and held by Dan Debacle by the end of February. His defence against Leevon Parks on 26 February 2001 was broken up by Seth Alexander's chair, and Alexander and Parks were booked to fight for the number-one contendership at Bluegrass Bash.

titles.name: APW Bruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested only on pay-per-view in gimmick matches; held by Smasher through mid-1997, taken by Mumonkan on Wednesday Night Chaos, 15 October 1997, via Smasher's own interference against the defending Psycho.

titles.name: APW Cruiserweight Title (denied)
titles.epitaph: Explicitly and honestly denied by the fed's own founder: "no Cruiserweight title" -- recorded because acronym-cousin feds do carry one, and the fed's own negative is itself a fact worth keeping.

titles.name: APW EXTREME Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a 17-man Battle EXTREME at the fed's own rename event, Anarchy In The UK II; held by Supernova into mid-1997.

titles.name: APW International Championship
titles.epitaph: A new title in the fed's second era; first champion Brandon Charm, named on-air at Christmas Carnage.

titles.name: APW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Added to the fed's slate by August 1997 for wrestlers 210 lb and under; contested in a tournament reaching its later rounds by WrestleStock '97.

titles.name: APW North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Destruction into April 1997; The Syndicate wins the titles on WrestleStock '97 Day 1.

titles.name: APW Six-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Iron Sultan & Cosmic Connection's own trio into mid-1997, defended against Masters of Havoc's Psycho & Scary Nights.

titles.name: APW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Mondo Somatic across 1997; lost and regained across the fed's own late-year cards, most recently on Wednesday Night Chaos, 15 October 1997.

titles.name: APW Unified British Commonwealth-North American Championship
titles.epitaph: A merged title, its constituent belts seen separately in March 1997 and unified by June; held by 62nd Assassin as of Anarchy In The UK III.

titles.name: APW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Brandon Charm through most of 1997, contested repeatedly by American Patriot; vacant for Anarchy In The UK III; won by Mondo Somatic in the WrestleStock '97 Day 3 finale, and Chris Douglas is billed as champion by King Of The Hill II.

titles.name: APW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Unforgiven and later Destroyers across 1997; Dr. Doom & Masked Bulldog billed as champions by King Of The Hill II.

titles.name: APWA Championship
titles.caption: Won by Taylor "The Godfather" Luchinni in the Tourney Smash ladder-match main event, the held record's first attested APWA Championship (World Heavyweight) reign.
titles.epitaph: APWA Championship of APWA: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: APWA National Championship
titles.caption: Pipe Bomb was crowned the first APWA-and-EAPW National Heavyweight Champion at APOW's debut; J.D. "The Bird" Raven won a National Championship tournament match at Tourney Smash a month later -- the title's own path between the two is not recovered in the held record.
titles.epitaph: APWA National Championship of APWA: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: UWF Arena Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the undefeated Powerhouse through the start of 1999, survived even after his first non-title loss.

titles.name: ASWL Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in ASWL's own founding rules post as one of three titles the fed intended to run; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: ASWL United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in ASWL's own founding rules post as one of three titles the fed intended to run; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: ASWL World Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in ASWL's own founding rules post as one of three titles the fed intended to run; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: CWA Alpha Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWA’s own title inside Anarchy Wrestling’s 2006 run, decided by a tournament whose final The Nameless won over Trinity Holmes on 28 May 2006. The Moose won it on 1 July, defended it in a steel cell at Wars of the World and lost it to Rated R in the octagon at Dead By Dawn.

titles.name: AW Championship
titles.epitaph: Anarchy Wrestling’s top singles belt, awarded vacant to The Nameless on 21 December 2005 and carried in turn by Rated R, Gerard Angelo and Tommy Purr before Halloween Jack took it from Tommy in a four-way ladder match at Wars of the World on 30 September 2006. Tommy won it back at Dead By Dawn under a guest referee, and Battle of the Warriors 2007 bills Rated R as champion; the champions page, captured in April 2007, ends with Tommy’s second reign.

titles.name: AW Anarchy Monarchy title
titles.epitaph: A crown created at Battle of the Warriors 2006, in a four-way won by Myst, with Scavenger announcing that once a month someone would challenge the king or queen of AW. Its champions page lists a Monarch for each month through November 2006 and notes no pay-per-view in March, ten holders in all.

titles.name: AW Superior Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at the first Battle of the Warriors, on 18 January 2006, in a five-man battle royal won by Max Cameron. Max walked out with the belt on 12 February when he was let go, Bombshell won it vacant that night, Diego Alvarez and The Moose followed, and the title was dissolved on 1 July 2006 when The Moose won the CWA Alpha title.

events.note: Its champions page says the title was dissolved when The Moose won the Alpha title on 1 July 2006.

titles.name: AW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Anarchy Wrestling’s tag belts, won by Aftermath and Cameron Jacques in a seven-team challenge on 5 February 2006 and vacated a week later when Max Cameron left with his stable’s belts. Air Canada, De’Anton Maybon and Parker Davis, S.E.X., Delirium and the New Age Dogg Pound followed, and Vigilante and The Moose took them in a four-corners match at Wars of the World on 30 September 2006.

titles.name: AW Xtreme Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt for the company’s high-flyers and brawlers alike, awarded vacant to Hoshi Yakamoto on 21 December 2005 and passed through a battle royal, a table-filled rumble, an open challenge and a hardcore main event. Hoshi holds it three times by its own champions page, which dates Frank Merritt’s first reign to 7 October 2006 though the 23 September Insurgence shows him winning it a week earlier.

titles.name: Chaos Theory Championships
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag-team belts, introduced on the night of All Nite Action 2 when Jon Tees handed them to Matt Ward and Suriel N. Crowlie. Vinny Vegas and Maxx Kalifornia are said by the All Nite Action V card to have won them at Cold Fall; the belts were vacant on 1 January 2010, and Scott Owens and Morrigan won them by beating Parental Advisory in the thumbtacks, ladders and wire match at Idus Martias.
titles.notes: The Idus Martias card says Owens and Payne once 'cost Parental Advisory the championships'; no page says whether Parental Advisory ever held them, and the 2010 champions page lists the belts vacant from 1 January 2010 until that match.

titles.name: EWA Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: The EWA's tag belts, listed as Tier IV: Devestation Inc. won them at HalloWicked 2K7, Dog House took them on 12 November 2007 and defended them against Damage Co. on 2 December, and Beauty & the Beast took them on 13 December 2007. No later tag belt carries them on; the Chaos Theory Championships began vacant.

titles.name: AW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt, listed as Tier I. Kaige won it in a three-way at HalloWicked 2K7 and Alexander Caine vacated it on 13 December 2007. The fed calls Morrigan, who won it in the All Nite Action 1 cell on 29 July 2008, its first champion since Kaige; Jason Lovell took it at Cold Fall on 21 September 2008. The 2010 page lists it vacant on 1 January 2010 and Dave Wilson champion from the Rabbithole of Idus Martias.

titles.name: Iron Man Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed as Tier V in 2008 and retired on 1 January 2010: a belt whose holder had to defend it at every event. James Caine, Madison Divera and Spaz Blud held it in November and December 2007; Suriel N. Crowlie won it at Noitcerusser I and The Diablo Slayer took it from him on 12 August 2008. The Iron Man and No Limit belts were combined into the Untamed Championship at Cold Fall on 21 September 2008.
titles.notes: No holder is listed between Spaz Blud in December 2007 and Suriel N. Crowlie in July 2008.

events.note: Its record says it was 'combined to new title' on 21 September 2008.
events.title: aw-anarchy-2008-untamed

titles.name: No Limit Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by Jon Tees after Blunt Trauma for lighter wrestlers, weighing no more than 219 pounds. The Noitcerusser I glass match for it ended in a draw and the belt stayed vacant; Breeze was its first and only champion on 26 August 2008, and it was combined into the Untamed Championship at Cold Fall on 21 September 2008.
titles.notes: The page of 2010 also lists the belt as retired on 1 January 2010.

events.note: Its record says it was 'combined to new title' on 21 September 2008.
events.title: aw-anarchy-2008-untamed

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed as Tier II, open to anyone. Morrigan won it in a three-way at HalloWicked 2K7 and defended it three times in November and December 2007; the fed awarded it to him again on 7 April 2008 and Morgan Call took it from him at Blunt Trauma on 20 April. It was vacated on 29 July 2008, listed vacant again on 1 January 2010 and won by Devlin Raine in the scramble match of 17 January 2010.

titles.name: Untamed Championship
titles.epitaph: Described as the fed's basic hardcore title, with a defence required at every Action. The Diablo Slayer won it when the No Limit and Iron Man belts were combined at Cold Fall on 21 September 2008, and the page of 2010 shows it awarded to him again on 1 January 2010; he defended it against Jesse Williams at All Nite Action IX.

titles.name: Apex Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own namesake title, defended and lost within its earliest served weeks before changing hands again by interference in a three-way.

titles.name: Hard Knocks Championship
titles.epitaph: Renamed live from the Iron Man Championship by the promotion's incoming owner minutes after its first served title change.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice across the promotion's own three served cards.

titles.name: United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned vacant on the promotion's own first served pay-per-view, then held into the promotion's next served card despite a count-out loss.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands by interference on the promotion's own first served pay-per-view and was carried by its new holder through the promotion's next served card.

titles.name: AWA Championship
titles.epitaph: The championship of AWA, SWWE Fed's own developmental territory, whose matches the promotion's own 29 April 2007 card says began that same night. rxnolasco is billed as the new champion, having won "a brutal match," at Unsurrender per the promotion's own October 2007 news post.

titles.name: Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: American Wrestling Alliance's own top belt, described on its own page as the centre piece of the promotion before anyone had worn it. Its first card's main event was announced as a qualifier for the tournament that would crown a champion; no tournament bracket, match or champion survives.
titles.notes: heavyweight.html, the fed's own championship page; no reign is attested anywhere in this deposit.

titles.name: Trios Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: Three belts held together by a team of three, carrying their own rule set: a partner who leaves the ring is replaced without a tag, breaking up a pinfall is legal, and the team that breaks one up then has eight seconds to run a move of its own. American Wrestling Alliance staged a trios match on its first card and planned one on nearly every event; no champion survives.
titles.notes: triostag.html, the fed's own championship page; no reign is attested anywhere in this deposit.

titles.name: Asian Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands after a three-month reign on the promotion's own Battle Royal pay-per-view.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a brawl that spilled into a restaurant and a fishing pool on the promotion's own Battle Royal pay-per-view.

titles.name: AWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dream King for roughly four months before he dropped it to Marvelous Mike at the federation's own pay-per-view, Slaughter in the Hell; no document survives naming when or where Dream King himself won it.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held throughout the promotion's own Battle Royal pay-per-view without being defended there.

titles.name: Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained by disqualification on the promotion's own Battle Royal pay-per-view after an ally's interference.

titles.name: AWA Chaos Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore belt called the Chaos Weight title in one card's script; The Rumbler is announced its champion after beating J Sane at Blood Is Thicker Than Water, and the record names no earlier holder.

titles.name: AWA Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Derek Cantina going into Blood Is Thicker Than Water, where teammate Michael Manson took it; by Adrenaline on 19 November 2005 Johnny Arnette is champion and The Rumbler beats him for it, and the record does not show how it passed between.

titles.name: AWA Fem-X Championship
titles.epitaph: The women's belt, held by Brandi James at Blood Is Thicker Than Water and, from Adrenaline on 19 November 2005, by Skylar Black in the commentary's own words; Jamie Brant's roleplays of 2006 stage her winning it.

titles.name: AWA X/Prime Unified Championship
titles.epitaph: Made by Simon Sensation's win over Prime Time champion Angela Jameson at Blood Is Thicker Than Water, a finisher-only unification of the X and Prime Time belts.

titles.name: AWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles belt, held by Mike Young going into Blood Is Thicker Than Water, where Cody Carson beat him for it in the ladder-billed main event of 25 September 2005; Carson is billed World champion in roleplays after.

titles.name: AWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Jestin Mounts at a pay-per-view the record does not otherwise hold, then defended successfully here against Rae Lyyn through a chaos of outside interference.

titles.name: AWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Marshall Gates going into a non-title main event he wrestled to a no-finish before turning on his own stable; the record does not attest when he won it or what became of the title after.

titles.name: AWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Alan Fiscus, billed by the promotion's own commentary and the owner alike as its World Champion; the record does not attest when he won it.

titles.name: AWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at least once between two of the fed's own wrestlers, captured only in an undated recap montage on a later broadcast.
titles.notes: A recap montage on Wednesday Night Warriors II (7 March 1997) shows Kevin Slater winning this title from Remy Boudreaux; no date for that match survives.

titles.name: AWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, attested from its own digest; no reign is dated from the one document served this pass.

titles.name: AWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag title, attested from its own digest; no reign is dated from the one document served this pass.

titles.name: Alliance Championship
titles.epitaph: AWC's Alliance Championship was first won by Emerald Isle on 1 July 2005. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 5 different champions. The longest is Emerald Isle's, 151 days from 1 July 2005. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. The Coalition held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Countdown Trophy
titles.epitaph: AWC's Countdown Trophy was first won by Teresa Tomas on 23 June 2006. The fed's own record carries 4 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is Vince Jones's, 35 days from 4 July 2006. One of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt. AWC discontinued it on 1 September 2006.

events.note: The fed's own title history ends the trophy at Coast To Coast with the note "end of summer; trophy discontinued".

titles.name: Frontier Championship
titles.epitaph: AWC's Frontier Championship was first won by Tim Shipley on 9 August 2005. The fed's own record carries 12 reigns on it, across 10 different champions. The longest is Ellis Nash's, 91 days from 24 March 2006. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Jack Murphy held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Livewire Championship
titles.epitaph: AWC's Livewire Championship was first won by The Educator on 5 July 2005. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 6 different champions. The longest is The Educator's, 49 days from 5 July 2005. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. AWC disbanded it on 24 December 2005 and reinstated it in September 2006. Scott Taylor held it at the end of the surviving record.

events.note: The fed's own title history disbands the Livewire Championship after Winter Warfare and reinstates it in September 2006, with the first return champion decided at Untouchable.

titles.name: Relentless Championship
titles.epitaph: AWC's Relentless Championship was first won by Crimson O'Malec on 7 June 2005. The fed's own record carries 7 reigns on it, across 7 different champions. The longest is Red Rock's, 178 days from 7 March 2006. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Jack Murphy held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Transatlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: AWC's Transatlantic Championship was first won by Alexander Strider on 6 May 2005. The fed's own record carries 10 reigns on it, across 7 different champions. The longest is Pierce Lavelle's, 140 days from 30 August 2005. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Darcy Crisis held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: AWE America's Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own card schedules; no champion is recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWE Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own card schedules and Rocktober line-up; no champion is recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWE International Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own War of the Worlds unification card; no champion is recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWE North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own War of the Worlds unification card; no champions are recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWE Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the promotion's own rules alongside its singles championship from April 2002; no team is recorded winning or defending it.

titles.name: AWE Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the promotion's own rules as the championship of its federation champion and contested from vacant in an eight-wrestler tournament whose first round was held on 18 May 2002; no final survives.

titles.name: AWE Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own War of the Worlds unification card; no champion is recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Vincenzo Galliano across the fed's surviving 1997 broadcasts, defended against its own founder and operator persona, Creed, in the fed's own build to a year-end unification match with APW.

titles.name: AWE World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested by the Academics and LiveWire on the fed's own Rocktober line-up; no champions are recovered by name in this collection's own served holdings.

titles.name: AWI North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at the AWI Union supercard when War Machine beat the previous UWA-lineage North American champion, Jack Fury -- recapped in exact-dated detail by Mission Control's own courtroom segment.

titles.name: AWI Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Gary White's belt through the held record's two-show window, successfully defended at Explosion against a challenger distracted by a mysterious ringside stranger.

titles.name: AWI World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: D.A. Bookthrower's belt as of the held record's Mission Control -- the “Legal Eagle” never himself appears on screen to defend it in either held document.
titles.notes: Confirms, by primary-source Usenet content, the third of the three AWI-branded titleholders (a World, a World Tag Team and a Television champion) this wing's own registry row already cited from cwfpro's unification ledger.

titles.name: AWI World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Megaton at the AWI Union supercard, a title change this collection knows only by recap, never by its own primary document.

titles.name: AWMC Extremist Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's hardcore title, changing hands eight times across 1999 before being retired and later revived.

titles.name: AWMC Great Lakes Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's second-tier singles title, roughly equivalent to a United States or Intercontinental championship.

titles.name: AWMC Motor City Championship
titles.epitaph: A title created in August 1999 for the federation's less experienced roster, changing hands four times in its first five months.

titles.name: AWMC Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's tag team title, changing hands six times across 1999.

titles.name: AWMC Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top prize, changing hands seven times across 1999 alone, from a Hell in a Cell main event in January through a three-way dance in September.

titles.name: AWP American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top title, meant for its hardest worker and defended at least once a month. "Elite Sensation" Eric Emerson held it in June 2001; Sinister won it by making Andy Madison submit in a cage match, and retained it against his own partner, the Professional, on Breakdown in December 2001.

titles.name: AWP Can-Am Championship
titles.epitaph: A title whose holder stands first in line for a heavyweight title match. Steve Jensen held it in June 2001 and kept it against the Professional on Total Darkness, before the title was merged into the Triple Crown.

titles.name: AWP Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Added in late 2001 to spotlight the federation's cruiserweight division. Ben Tuckwell held it in November 2001 and lost it to Ashlyn Summers on RAGE in December, when the special referee, Brian Taylor, turned on him.

titles.name: AWP Fight Club Championship
titles.epitaph: The title for the federation's street fighters. BIG GUY won it at Spring Riot with the PPD's help and was billed to put it up in an open challenge in June 2001, before the title was merged into the Triple Crown.

titles.name: AWP Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The title for the federation's best two-man team. The PPD, Lance and Max Studd, won it for a second time from the American Renegades and held it in June 2001; after it fell vacant, the Conceptuals were champions by late November 2001 and retained against the Down South Connection on RAGE in December.

titles.name: AWP Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The title for the best of the federation's television wrestling, defended more often than any other. Hiroyoshi Takada held it in June 2001; Vincenzo Sandora came away with it from Ready to Rumble II, though Chris Johnson, the last man standing in that night's battle royal, claimed it was his.

titles.name: AWP Triple Crown Championship
titles.epitaph: Created from a merger of the Fight Club, Can-Am and New Age titles. Steve Jensen held it by November 2001 and retained it against the Motor City Madman on RAGE in December.

titles.name: BAHW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at Hardcore Haven when El Jaguar defeated The Ring Assassin; vacated at some point before a new tournament final is referenced in the held record's May 1997 holdings.
titles.notes: The gap between El Jaguar's win and the May 1997 tournament final referenced in a later show is not receipted -- an honest gap, not a silent thinning.

titles.name: BAHW Television Championship
