titles.epitaph: Crowned for the first time in this collection's own holdings at Hardcore Haven, when "The Perfectionist" Nik Nyce won a lengthy tournament final; defended successfully one week later.

titles.name: BAHW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at the fed's own founding-era supercard, Hardcore Haven, when Chimera dethroned the reigning "Paralizer" Patrick Bordeau.
titles.notes: Bordeau's own prior reign predates this collection's earliest surviving card; no won-date recovered for it.

titles.name: BAHW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top prize, already held by Rick "The Reaper" Erickson at the held record's earliest surviving card and defended by him through every subsequent show this pass has read.
titles.notes: Reign-by-reign lineage before this collection's own earliest card is not recoverable.

titles.name: Big Apple Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top singles title, held through the last held BAWF broadcast by a wrestler whose own long-hidden family history became the story of the promotion's spring.

titles.name: BAWF Manhattan Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional title first attested in the fed's own record by February 1998; the fed's own broadcasts separately bill its reigning Television Champion as a former holder, with no date surviving for that reign.

titles.name: Big Apple Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag championship, defended in three-way and multi-team matches through the last held BAWF broadcast.

titles.name: BAWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A mid-card title already through multiple hands by the spring of 1998; the fed's own broadcasts separately bill two other wrestlers as former holders, with no date or order surviving for either reign.

titles.name: BBW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The only belt Buck Brothers Wrestling could afford: an unaltered WWE replica title, John Cena side plates still on it, hung on a promotion run out of a flea market to bring vendors through the door. The founding pitch says the quiet part itself — calling it a world title is a joke, but the promotion is a joke, so it all works out. No champion was ever named, no match for it ever announced, and no card it might have been defended on was ever run.
titles.notes: Declared in the founding pitch's own CHAMPIONSHIP section, which also describes the physical belt: a WWE replica, bought as-is with no alterations and John Cena side plates. The pitch names no other championship — "[t]hat's all they can afford for now" — and the promotion never launched, so no reign, tournament or contender for it exists.

titles.name: BCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Xero is the only champion this holding attests, retaining the belt against Ace on 25 April 2008; no earlier or later history survives.

titles.name: BCW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Danger Dave is the only champion this holding attests, retaining the belt against Xander on 14 July 2008; no earlier or later history survives.

titles.name: BCW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Killer K is the only champion this holding attests, retaining the belt against Fusion on 14 July 2008 in their fourth billed meeting ("Fusion vs. Killer K IV") — implying at least three earlier, unrecorded defenses against the same challenger; no earlier or later history survives.

titles.name: BCW Triple Crown Championship
titles.epitaph: Total Destruction defeated the defending champion, Eric Hinz, on 14 July 2008 — the only title change this holding attests, and the only one of BCW's five 2008-era titles to actually change hands in the surviving record. No earlier history survives.

titles.name: BCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Commander D is the only champion this holding attests, retaining the belt against Alex Austin in a team lumberjack match on 25 April 2008; no earlier or later history survives.

titles.name: BCW JuniorWeight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Gaslaw Gala broadcast (16 May 1999) and Title History page together attest exactly one reign: Hypnosis won this belt with a Stunner. The two documents disagree on the defeated opponent — the broadcast itself stages the match against The Phantom, while the Title History page names The Purple Haze — both readings stand, neither reconciled. No later change survives.

titles.name: BCW London Territorial Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Title History page and News page together trace three changes of this belt across roughly three months in 1999: Brent Morris won it in a Battle Royale, John Cole beat Morris, Scott Simpson beat Cole (in Canada), and R.J. Draper beat Simpson on 11 July 1999 — the last champion this holding attests. No earlier or later history survives.

titles.name: BCW National Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own 4 April 1999 card bills the newly-crowned champion as "the NEW NeWA European / BCW National Champion" in one breath — the same belt carrying a hub-level name alongside its own promotion name, per the fed's own text, not a separate title and not evidence of any join to another wing.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own 4 April 1999 card and Title History page together trace a long, mostly undated chain: Titan won it in a Four Man Battle Royale at Manchester Colosseum, then Chris Mann, The Wraith, HICAL (twice, the title held up between), and Titan (a second time) each held it in turn, none of it dated. Rowdy Piper then beat Titan in an I Quit Match at Gaslaw Gala, 16 May 1999 — the fed's own broadcast of that night receipts the change directly. Lord Ravager beat Rowdy Piper the following day, 17 May 1999, per the fed's own Title History page alone — the last champion this holding attests.

titles.name: BCW National Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Title History page attests exactly one reign: Angels of the Night won this belt from Bobby Blaze and The Phantom at London Live, Buckingham Palace. No individual member of Angels of the Night is named anywhere in the held record, and no later change survives.

titles.name: BDW Broken Championship
titles.notes: Called the “Platinum” title in Brock RockHard's own roleplays #15–16 (5 Jun 2004), the day before and the same week as BDW's own show text calls the same belt “the Broken title” (7th Static, 6 Jun 2004) — read as the same championship under two names rather than two belts, since both name the same champion defending against the same challenger in the same week.
titles.epitaph: Brock RockHard won BDW's Broken Championship in a five-way match at The Return I (30 May 2004), pinning Rob Zone with a set-up inverted DDT while Methid and Pretty Boy Evans never reached the ring. He retained against Rob Zone on the fed's own 7th Static and was still champion at the held record's last title snapshot.

titles.name: BDW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Arik Caine won BDW's Hardcore Championship at the fed's first pay-per-view, The Return I (30 May 2004), in a Hardcore Elimination Match he closed by pinning Andrew Irving. A week later, on the 7th Static, he refused to defend it against Methid, citing a threatened lawsuit against Co-Owner Jeffery, and the fed's own later title snapshot shows the belt with no listed champion — a title change or vacancy the surviving record doesn't date or explain.

titles.name: BDW Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: No reign survives in the held record — the fed's own title-history ledger and its own later champions snapshot both show the belt without a champion.
titles.epitaph: No Tag Team Championship reign survives in the held record; the belt appears in the fed's own title structure but never with a name against it.

titles.name: BDW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: BDW's own top title changed hands once in the surviving record: “The Irish Bastard” Sean McClancy won the vacant championship in a triple threat over Emilio Dervante and JJ Jarone at the fed's first pay-per-view, The Return I (30 May 2004). A rematch with Dervante was rebooked as a ladder match for 27 June 2004, Anger & Rage; the outcome doesn't survive in the held record, and McClancy was still champion at the fed's own last title snapshot.

titles.name: BEW Atlantic Title
titles.epitaph: Named once, in passing: Night of Armageddon's own broadcast introduces Jaigo as "its former Atlantic Champion." No reign dates, no defense, and no successor survive in the held record — the belt is not defended anywhere on this card.

titles.name: BEW Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own broadcast bills Flesh, entering the Night of Armageddon main event, as "a seven time Hardcore champion" and "its current HARDCORE CHAMPION" — but the belt is never defended on this card; the untitled main event that follows carries no title stakes in either the broadcast's own introduction or the fed's own card page. No reign start survives, and no title change is documented in the held record.
titles.notes: SOURCES DISAGREE with the fed's own card page, which labels the night's Extreme Warrior vs. Jonathan Prophet crucifixion match "BEW Hardcore Title Match" — the broadcast's own repeated, internally consistent dialogue instead calls that same bout a Television Title defense (see bew-television). Flesh's own concurrent Hardcore billing, entering a later match on the same show, is inconsistent with Prophet also holding that same belt that night; both documents are receipted, neither silently resolved.

titles.name: BEW Television Title
titles.epitaph: Defended in a no-time-limit Crucifixion match at Night of Armageddon (20 March 1999): Jonathan Prophet, its billed reigning champion, lost the belt to Extreme Warrior after both men fell through live land mines from the top turnbuckle and Prophet was nailed to a wooden cross mid-match — the belt's own only documented title change in the held record.
titles.notes: SOURCES DISAGREE with the fed's own card page, which labels this same bout "BEW Hardcore Title Match" (see bew-hardcore) — the broadcast's own dialogue names the Television Title three separate times (Hughy's own introduction, Prophet's own billing as "its current Television champion," and the winner's call, "new Television Champion"), the stronger and more internally consistent account, preferred here; the card's own conflicting label is receipted at bew-hardcore rather than silently dropped.

titles.name: BEW United States Title
titles.epitaph: Defended at Night of Armageddon (20 March 1999): Flyin' Bryan Mercy, its billed reigning champion, lost the belt to James Pope's debuting Limo Wreck finisher — the belt's own only documented title change in the held record, and, per the fed's own broadcast commentary, Pope's first match in the BEW.

titles.name: BEW World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: No dated title-history ledger survives for this belt. The fed's own served card billed the Jamie Williams vs. Devastator match as "the BEW World Title Match" and its own broadcast calls it "the header to the main event" — a distinct, earlier match than the Flesh vs. Kevin Merrix bout that actually closes the show untitled. Devastator, its billed reigning champion entering Night of Armageddon (20 March 1999), never appears in person, cutting his own promo by remote screen before losing the belt to Jamie Williams's Northern Lights Elbow — the belt's own only documented title change in the held record.

titles.name: BIWF Internet Heavyweight Champion
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 16 June 1997 founding rules document as the prize of its planned 20 June 1997 debut battle royal. No result of that card survives in the held record, so no bestowal or holder is recorded.

titles.name: USW Blood N Guts Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in the surviving record, ending with a pairing still holding it as of the league's own last dated bulletin.

titles.name: AVW Bluegrass Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, left vacant at its launch and put up in a tournament seeded by a Bluegrass Rumble. The first final, Jake Davids against Chris Collins on 26 February 2001, ended with Davids pinning Collins after outside help, and the co-president at ringside took the belt back and ruled the match a no-contest, ordering a cage-match rematch for Bluegrass Bash.

titles.name: BLWA BLLV Championship
titles.epitaph: A second singles belt whose own list opens on 3 February 2008 with Steve Smith beating Drake Daniels and ends with Dari Wheeler's Rumble win on 30 April 2008; the page does not say what the letters stand for.

titles.name: BLWA Prime Time Championship
titles.epitaph: The champions page lists a Grand Prix belt crowned at GoldRush on 16 June 2007 under the Prime Time heading; the entries from 16 December 2007 name the Prime Time title without a prefix, and the last holder was Dave Johnson on 6 April 2008.
titles.notes: The Grand Prix and the Prime Time entries share one list on the champions page and are filed as one belt.

titles.name: BLWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Team Vendetta were the first Tag Team champions at GoldRush on 16 June 2007; the Ring Generals, Stoner and Dark Wolf, DOA and Shawn Hunt with Jaden Lee or Brian Cady held the belts until DOA's reign when the fed closed.

titles.name: BLWA TVX Championship
titles.epitaph: Desperado was 'first and only TVX Champion' at GoldRush on 16 June 2007, a belt listed under the Prime Time heading.

titles.name: BLWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt, first won by Celeste LaRue at GoldRush on 16 June 2007 and passed through nine reigns in ten months, among them a tournament crowning Hallow Wicked on 12 November 2007; the champions page ends 'Championship Vacant due to BLW Closer'.
titles.notes: Also called 'the Universal Championship' in the eXposed of November 2007 and a World title on the champions page.

titles.name: Blood Money Championship
titles.epitaph: Reaper defended it at Trial And Error (27 Jan 2002) against Dr. Doyle Van Helsing in a two-arena hardcore key hunt; the fed's own Money, Power, Respect II recap (28 Jul 2002) names Violent B the new champion out of a Krisis-and-Violent-B-vs.-Tank-and-J-Man tag match whose own text never actually shows Violent B taking a fall or a pin — a title change the surviving record asserts without fully narrating.
titles.notes: The corpus never shows the title passing from Reaper to Violent B directly — an honest gap between the two recorded reigns.

titles.name: Cash Money Championship
titles.epitaph: Mark Espinosa lost it to The Underlord at Trial And Error (27 Jan 2002); The Underlord — also billed as 'Mafia Man' Mario Ghotti — carried it at least through a non-title FallOut main event before Paranoia won a three-way for it at Money, Power, Respect II (28 Jul 2002), still champion when 'The Violence' Vince Jones and Raymond Mercy debuted by jumping him the same night, and still champion as of the last dated reference the corpus holds (mid-August).

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Chilly K, billed as its own 'first substantial' champion, defended it against The SensationalSal One at Trial And Error (27 Jan 2002) and lost a non-title rematch to Eiji Fujiwara at FallOut without the belt changing hands — the only reign the surviving record evidences.

titles.name: Million Dollar Championship
titles.epitaph: Axel Teflon defended it against Kid Krazie at Trial And Error (27 Jan 2002), ending Krazie's own career; by Money, Power, Respect II (28 Jul 2002) it belonged to ICE, unrecorded in between, and changed hands there to Da Thug when ICE's own ex-girlfriend Kelly set him on fire mid-pinfall — Da Thug still champion at the record's own end.

titles.name: BMW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant entering Money, Power, Respect II (28 Jul 2002) per the fed's own recap; 2GLS (Reality and Jeremiah Wilson) won it there off Big Money Legends (Kid Krazie and Scott Phillips) in an Inferno Tables match, both teams sent through burning tables before the finish.
titles.notes: The vacancy itself — who held it before, and why — is not evidenced anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: Top Dollar Championship
titles.epitaph: Revealed 'back' on air by Da Mab on 2 August 2002 as part of Louis Miranda's new stable's own announced plans — the surviving record names no holder, before or after.
titles.notes: No reign structured; the belt is shown, not awarded, in what this pass read.

titles.name: BMW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Risk won it from Jeremiah Wilson at Trial And Error (27 Jan 2002) with an assist from Axel Teflon; Billy Blaze held it through an unrecorded change somewhere in the following months before Tax pinned Risk in a triple threat at Money, Power, Respect II (28 Jul 2002) to end Blaze's own three-month reign — and carried it, still champion, into a mid-August title defense against 'Tank' Hank Gunyon and Reality whose result the surviving record never shows.
titles.notes: The Blaze-regains-the-title transition between Risk's Trial And Error win and his own reign as champion by Money, Power, Respect II is not evidenced anywhere in the held record — an honest gap, not an inferred date.

titles.name: Warrior Grand Prix Championship
titles.notes: The trophy and belt promised to the winner of BodyCount's own single-elimination Warrior Grand Prix tournament; awarded once, on the corpus's own record, at the close of the first tournament in October 2012. A second tournament was announced in 2015 but never reached a result.
titles.epitaph: A one-off tournament belt, won once and never again defended on the record this pass could recover.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Celestial Championship
titles.epitaph: BRA's own top singles title, changing hands repeatedly across the promotion's run (Sherry Ann, Yvette Malreaux, Evonne Carmikel, Lisa Dream, Tiffany Lane and Lindsay Locke among its recorded holders); a 2001 “Celestial Tournament” closes out the surviving record with a Heaven-and-Hell cage final between Akira Hagawa and Casey Gaines whose result does not survive.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Fallen Angel Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Lesley “Viper” Magnus from Janus on 2 October 2000 in an “I quit” match and defended successfully against Sasha and again against Janus through the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Featherweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-class title whose belt Jennifer Christian won from Angel Dust on 16 October 2000 and lost by the site's own next mention of the division, in December 2000; a 2001 tournament for the vacant title (Jenn Christian, Shea London, Tiffany Lane, Sissy Landers among the entrants) closes out the surviving record unresolved.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A no-rules title contested repeatedly through 2000 among wrestlers including Janus and Sandra “The Tiger” Blake; not confirmed on the belt of any wrestler minted from this pass's own roster.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Women's Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-class belt the fed's own year-end pay-per-view introduced vacant, contested and won in the same broadcast; the surviving record holds no history for it before that night.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Nicknamed “BRATT” by the fed's own commentary, first contested in January 2000 between Jenny Anderson and the team of Simply Divine; by the promotion's final 2001 season the belts were on the line between the site's own British Bombshells and East/West, an outcome the surviving record does not confirm.

titles.name: Battling Ring Angels Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in January 2000 and first won by Tiffany Epitaphine in a ladder match with the belt suspended above the ring, per the fed's own news column; later challengers included Americana and Nina Larue.

titles.name: Mountain Dew Championship
titles.epitaph: A sponsor-named secondary title. champs.php names Jake Keeton champion, and two served BRAND promos — Mary-Lynn Mayweather's "Church Bells Calling" and Steve Solex's "Booked or Not" — both target him over it, the only in-fiction texture surviving for any of the fed's three belts.
titles.notes: champs.php; its own mdc.php title-history page renders nothing beyond a pulled-and-uncaptured news feed.

titles.name: BRAND Name Championship
titles.epitaph: BRAND Wrestling's own top title. Its champs.php page, the only surviving record of its lineage, names SHARC as champion with no history behind the belt — the title-history pages for all three of the fed's championships pulled from a news database this deposit does not carry.
titles.notes: champs.php, the site's own current-champions page; its own bnc.php title-history page renders nothing beyond a pulled-and-uncaptured news feed.

titles.name: BRAND Texas Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: BRAND Wrestling's third championship. champs.php lists it VACANT, with no lineage behind it in the surviving record.
titles.notes: champs.php; its own bthwc.php title-history page renders nothing beyond a pulled-and-uncaptured news feed.

titles.name: SWL World Brawler Title
titles.epitaph: Created and first won by American Heartthrob on the promotion's earliest surviving card; changed hands to Night off-page, then to Chaos Bill at Sharp Turn, who retained it through a technicality after being knocked unconscious at the 1st Anniversary show.

titles.name: BSCW Canadian Championship
titles.epitaph: J.C. Swinger won it while vacant in May 2001 and lost it, with his unbeaten run, to Goo at Detonation. Taurus, already World Champion, made Goo submit for it that August, and by October the fed's roster was saying the title was gone.

titles.name: BSCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: X-Kalibur's reign was cut short by Leo in May 2001, and Leo kept it through a sixty-minute triple threat Iron Man match at Detonation. By August it was "Deadly" Derek Irvin's until John O'Riordan beat him, and that autumn a tournament decided it, won by Shrapnel over Tyson Bryson at The Process of Weeding Out.

titles.name: BSCW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Vic "Tim Dogg" Simmons held it through Detonation 2001 with a splash onto a steel grocery cart. Sykopath kept it through a Detroit Death Match, a Helter Skelter match and a Taipei Death Match before Richard Harris took it from him at The Process of Weeding Out by leaping off the balcony of Viking Hall.

titles.name: BSCW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in an eight-man Royal Rumble at Viking Hall in February 2001 and won by the rookie Matt Maelstrom, who was being called a former champion by May.

titles.name: BSCW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced at Ragnarok in September 2001, where Max C won it first and lost it the same night to Matt Wilson's impromptu rematch. Wilson never came back, the title was held up at Hostile Intentions, and Todd Royal won it in a rumble at The Process of Weeding Out by tying his bootlace to the bottom rope.

titles.name: BSCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Hellz Angelz won it from Da Old Timerz at Viking Hall in February 2001; Gemini held it through Detonation, and the Q's lost it to Debonair in a loser-leaves-town triple threat at Ragnarok. Whiskey Jakk and Derek Irvin became champions by surviving the Thunderdome at Hostile Intentions, and Hell On Earth took it from them at The Process of Weeding Out when Jakk left his partner to be pinned.

titles.name: BSCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Andrew Sampson, a two-time champion, lost it to Max C at Detonation 2001 and left the fed that night. Johnny Spades held it by August, until Greed beat him backstage and Grinnin pinned him with the Gobsmacker.

titles.name: BSCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Philippe LaFleur won it in February 2001 with a referee Rick Sturgis had paid, and Justin Keith was carrying it by May, when Taurus took it from him two falls to one in the Detonation main event. Keith won it back at Ragnarok that September as the first three-time champion the fed had billed, then lost it to "Deadly" Derek Irvin in a ladder match at Ascension, with his late brother's honorary belt hanging beside it.

titles.name: BSWF Lunar Championship
titles.epitaph: Named only as a rankings category on the fed's own undated Rankings page, which gives it no champion, no contenders, and not even the "Vacant" label its Solar counterpart carries.
titles.notes: No reign is registered — the surviving record never names a Lunar Champion.

titles.name: BSWF Solar Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed vacant on the fed's own undated Rankings page, with no ranked contenders and no champion ever named anywhere in the held record.
titles.notes: No reign is registered — the surviving record never names a Solar Champion.

titles.name: BSWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own undated Rankings page names the Made Men (Merchandi$e and Mi$ta) as champions, with Nick Hart and Debo as the #1 contenders — how or when the Made Men won the belts is not recorded. The fed's own Thursday Night Thump-Fest broadcast stages their own only surviving defense, against Kadafi and Scarface, but the referee is pulled from the match before any decision and the text never rules a winner.

titles.name: BSWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own "Super September" Pay Per View, a six-man tournament, is the fullest surviving account of a title change: Ceesalo defeated Nick Hart in the tournament final to become champion. The Clark held the belt next — his own winning of it is unrecorded, but he defended it into the fed's own Monday Mayhem broadcast, where Wrestletech's interference turned the match and Merchandi$e became champion. Merchandi$e still held the belt as of the fed's own undated Rankings page and its own Thursday Night Thump-Fest broadcast, where Debo carried off the physical belt in a post-match angle without a title actually changing hands — the last-attested state of the championship in the held record.

titles.name: CPW Bunkhouse Title
titles.epitaph: Attested for one reign, won at the league's own IWF Birthday Bash event, before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: BWA Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man tournament on the promotion's own debut card, 22 September 1997, with Bishop winning the final over Ace Malone; still held by Bishop at the held record's last BWA broadcast three days later.

titles.name: BWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for a sixteen-man single-elimination Turkey Day tournament and first held by Gravedigger, who beat the Rowdy One in the final after a screwjob interference angle involving the fed's own on-screen President.

titles.name: BWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: Inaugurated in a multi-man War Games match at Hotter Than Hell 2001, won by the Prophet, who carried it through the run.

titles.name: BWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Dennis Windham and Lance Nelson in a five-team elimination match at Hotter Than Hell 2001, then lost to the Deities at Meltdown.

titles.name: BWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice across the promotion's return to television in 2001: the Journeyman Lance Nelson reclaimed it in a three-way dance, then lost it to a returning Attila at Meltdown.

titles.name: BWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested only in retrospect -- AzteK is credited elsewhere as "the former BWF World Champion," but no title match or reign appears in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: BXWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced vacant at the fed's own February 1997 founding, alongside a World Tag Team Championship and an Intercontinental Championship; no reign is recorded anywhere in this collection's own 1997 holdings, and the wing's only surviving show (Thursday Terror) crowned no champion.
titles.notes: The fed's own roster-and-titles bulletin, msg_id UDmYOKIJ55UJ, 5 Feb 1997.

titles.name: Chris Horowitz Memorial Softcore Championship Trophy
titles.notes: Billed as the prize for this wing's own advertised Softcore Invitational, a six-way elimination match its announcement runs 'in the spirit of the IWF in particular'; the trophy is named, in homage, with the board name of the IWF's own booker, a member of the same community who was still posting on that board into January 2006. No result for that match survives anywhere in the held record.
titles.epitaph: A trophy announced for a match that never got a result, the surest single fact this wing's own record leaves behind.

titles.name: CAEW Sheer Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own California Extreme Wrestling territory, attested for 7 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: CAEW Ultimate Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own California Extreme Wrestling territory, attested for 12 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: CAEW Unfiied Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own California Extreme Wrestling territory, attested for 11 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: Can-Am Championship
titles.epitaph: A title built around a standing tournament, crowned for the first time in the held documents (the Trixxster over the Twilight Prince by submission, Danger Zone '98). No further change of hands falls inside the held record.

titles.name: CAWO Atlantic Regional Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: CAWO Atlantic's own top singles title, first awarded in a ladder match at Red Dawn.
titles.epitaph: Won once, in the fed's own only completed show, and never defended again on the surviving record.

titles.name: CAWO Central Regional Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: CAWO Central's own top singles title, first awarded in a two-out-of-three-falls match at Red Dawn.
titles.epitaph: Won once, in the fed's own only completed show, and never defended again on the surviving record.

titles.name: CAWO International Regional Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: CAWO International's own top singles title, first awarded in a cage match at Red Dawn.
titles.epitaph: Won once, in the fed's own only completed show, and never defended again on the surviving record.

titles.name: CAWO Pacific Regional Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: CAWO Pacific's own top singles title, first awarded in a submission match at Red Dawn.
titles.epitaph: Won once, in the fed's own only completed show, and never defended again on the surviving record.

titles.name: CAWO World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: CAWO's own top tag title, first awarded to the winner of a four-team tournament at Red Dawn.
titles.epitaph: Won once, in the fed's own only completed show, and never defended again on the surviving record.

titles.name: CCW Atlantic Championship
titles.notes: Named only in the fed's own rulebook of 7 December 2004, second in a list of five championships. Whether it is the Trans-Atlantic Championship of 2003 under a shortened name or a belt of its own is not something the record answers.
titles.epitaph: A line in a rulebook. The federation's own championships page for it was captured as an empty template, and no champion of it is named anywhere in the surviving record.

titles.name: CCW International Championship
titles.epitaph: First awarded at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, in a tournament final decided when the promotion's own president forced a controversial count.

titles.name: CCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, won by Dazz from Tommy Gunn in a steel cage match at the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: CCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by The Dark Alliance from The Specialists at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, amid the kidnapping of a rival manager.

titles.name: CCW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Axl Blaze against Alex Libido at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, in a match fought above a cage suspending the challenger's own wife.

titles.name: CCW X-Treme Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested inside Hell in a Cell at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, changing hands from Doctor Pain to "The Franchise" Reon Wilson.

titles.name: CCW International Championship
titles.epitaph: "Boardwalk" Bradley Warden became CCW's first-ever International Champion by beating "The Bullet" Ricky Revolution, and was still recognized as champion when the fed's own surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: CCW West Coast Championship
titles.epitaph: "GQ" Geoffrey Quartz won this title at CCW's own "First Night" debut show (18 January 1997); by the fed's first RSPWF broadcast that July his brother "IQ" Ian Quartz held it instead, an unrecorded transition, and Ian was still champion when the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: CCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an 8-man single-elimination tournament at the fed's own "Explosion!!" pay-per-view (30 March 1997), won by Desmond Harrison, its first champion; X.Plosion took the belt from him at FanFest, beat him again in the Slamfest main event of 9 July 1997, and was still champion when the fed's own 1997 record breaks off. When CCW returned in the winter of 2000 the title stood vacant, and a new tournament was begun to fill it.

titles.name: CCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Murder Inc. became CCW's first tag team champions by beating the Devestation Express, and were billed to defend the belts against Fire & Ice at the fed's own "Explosion!!" pay-per-view (30 March 1997). By the fed's first RSPWF broadcast that July, Fire & Ice held them, by a change no surviving document records. When CCW returned in 2001, its own cards called Fire & Ice the last CCW Tag Team Champions.

titles.name: CCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: First awarded in an eight-man tournament at the promotion's own debut supercard, won by Da' J-Man over Retribution.

titles.name: CCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: First awarded in a battle royal on the same night as the promotion's own Heavyweight Championship tournament, won by "The Bruiser" Aaron Stone.

titles.name: CCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced on the federation's first broadcast, 7 January 2001, as the prize of a Royal Rumble to be held the following week and open to anyone entered by the next Friday. No reign survives.

titles.name: CCW Hardcore Championship
titles.notes: Named in the fed's own 2004 rulebook among five championships, two years after the alliance's profile page and one year after the only change of it the record holds.
titles.epitaph: It was fought for with barbed wire. The one title change held is Revolution's opener, where Enigma beat Jack Manson in a match whose props were a trash can wrapped in barbed wire and a board of nails pulled out of a bin bag, and the belt changed hands on a referee's decision Manson spent the rest of the night calling a screw job. Scorpion held it in the spring of 2002 and Brad Douglas was billed the champion in the first week of March 2003; nothing held says how it travelled between any of them.

titles.name: CCW Heavyweight Championship
aka: CCW Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.notes: The alliance's own member profile of the fed calls it the World Heavyweight Championship in its champions block and the CCW Heavyweight Title in its own history on the same page; the fed's own ring announcer reads it out at Revolution as the CCW Heavyweight Championship of the World. Every form is the record's own.
titles.epitaph: Nineteen men are named as having held it, and the fed named them itself: Revolution opens on a montage of nineteen former champions flickering past with the belt, from The Supreme Machine through Ghettodogg, Hardcore Gorilla Mask and El Mierda to Jason McAllister. Almost none of those reigns is recoverable. What the record does hold is the shape of the belt's own crises — a 104-day reign by Phil Burner in 2000 that the fed still called its record, a month in the spring of 2002 when its own rankings listed the title vacant and two men tied at the top, Blayze losing it at Revolution after pulling the referee into a charge, and Legacy taking it off Jason Dread in January 2005 and putting him through a table on his way out of the ring. That is where the record stops.

titles.name: CCW Independent Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own magazine calls it the Independant Title in its own card listing; the ring announcer reads it as the CCW Independent Championship.
titles.epitaph: A belt defended at Revolution with the champion and the challenger tied together at the wrist. The ring announcer read the rules out before the bell — pinfall, submission, or touching all four corners in turn — and Scorpion kept it against Dan Logan, having already been billed the holder of it that same month. Kensuke Suzahara was the champion a year earlier and fourth on the fed's own top ten the week that list was written.

titles.name: CCW International Championship
titles.notes: Named only in the fed's own rulebook of 7 December 2004, third in a list of five championships.
titles.epitaph: The federation listed it third among its own five belts in December 2004 and built a page for it. The page was captured blank, the rulebook line is the whole of the evidence, and no holder of it survives.

titles.name: CCW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by El Mierda heading into a December 1999 defense; no surviving document confirms the outcome.

titles.name: CCW Pacific Championship
titles.notes: Attested once, in the alliance's own member profile of the fed. It is absent from the fed's own 2004 rulebook list and from every 2003 document held.
titles.epitaph: John Jupiter held it in the spring of 2002 and stood third on the federation's own list of its ten best that March. One page names the belt, once; by the time the fed wrote its rules down again it was listing five championships and this was not one of them.

titles.name: CCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: It was vacant in the spring of 2003 and the fed filled it with a tournament: a Tag Team Lethal Lottery drawn by the president, a four-team elimination match that ran forty-three minutes and sent one team forward, and a three-team ladder match at Revolution that Adam Christ and Jack Manson won by pinning Damien Nhyte. Neither man waited to be announced; they took the belts and left through the crowd. A year earlier the Blood Brothers held them, and one of the Blood Brothers was billed the world champion on the same page.

titles.name: CCW Trans-Atlantic Championship
titles.notes: Two years later the fed's own rulebook lists an Atlantic Championship instead, among five belts, with no Trans-Atlantic Championship beside it and no explanation of a rename. That belt is recorded separately, as ccw-atlantic; nothing held joins the two lineages.
titles.epitaph: The second belt on the card, and the one whose own name did not survive the fed's last era intact. Michael "Spitfire" Stevens won it out of a three-way against Gobstopper and Ace Hawk at Revolution; a year earlier the alliance's own profile page named The Valiant One the champion in its champions block and Brad Lamen the champion in its own top ten, on the same page, in the same month. Both readings are kept.

titles.name: CCW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by 2 Cold Scorpio as of 15 November 1995; the title stands untouched when he loses a same-night non-title match to Shawn Michaels, and he is previewed defending it against Bret "Hitman" Hart at Survivor Series '95.

titles.name: CCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Raven, who retains it on 15 November 1995 against Razor Ramon after Ramon's own cornerman, the 123 Kid, turns on him mid-match.

titles.name: CCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Sting, who retains it on 15 November 1995 over Steve Richards under a loser-leaves-CCW stipulation, then is previewed defending it again against Hunter Hearst-Helmsley at Survivor Series '95.

titles.name: CCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The record holds one reign, Ric Flair's, from 1995.

titles.name: CCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Public Enemy as of 15 November 1995, previewed defending it against Harlem Heat at that Sunday's Survivor Series '95 -- the held record's single surviving document never shows the Public Enemy in the ring.

titles.name: CCW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation ran a women's division from 1999 and kept running one to the end of what survives; three women's matches opened the Lockdown before Revolution and two more were on the card the last time it advertised one. Devyl's own card claims four reigns with it and an award for the longest of them. The one change held is Revolution's, where Sheena Ramone took it from Lacey Skye Morris by disqualification — a decision the fed declared and the record keeps as declared.

titles.name: CCWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The shared prize of a three-federation alliance, its first champion crowned in a match that left both finalists unable to stand.
titles.notes: Sanctioned by the three federations' own joint alliance, self-named in its broadcasts' own closing copyright line ('"A World Of Pain" is (C) 1999 of the Coast to Coast Wrestling Alliance') and spelled out by member on a separate contemporaneous newsgroup post the same year ('the Coast to Coast Wrestling Alliance [GLCW/MLW/LWC]') to distinguish it from an unrelated same-acronym startup. Housed under this promotion's own shard because its own on-screen president is the surviving record's one individual production credit ('Day One was produced by "Hollywood" Chris Hebert (MLW)'); crossover-booking edges already link this promotion to both other members, and a frontier row records the alliance itself.

titles.name: Flash Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced 14 March 2005 to replace the retired Television Championship: an eight-man single-elimination tournament, its first-round bracket named in the fed's own news — Justin Warner vs. Dan Blitz, Freezer Burn vs. Mercenary, Painkiller vs. Chris Night, and Randy Taylor vs. Kris Krimzon — with no results captured before the held record ends.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: CCWA's own February 2005 news bills the returning Mercenary as a four-time former Hardcore Champion — the only surviving mention of this belt in the held record. No reign, date, or opponent survives to receipt a ledger entry; its history likely predates the fed's own December 2004 hack, which the fed's own news says cost it roughly twenty results.

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Furious came into the held record already champion; Danielle Northsky took the belt from him at Sensation with her own Spirit Way, and was still champion when the surviving record ends in March 2005, billed against Psyno and, per the fed's own commission-request thread, a new challenger, Sylkk.
titles.notes: Furious's own reign predates the held record; no won-date survives the fed's own December 2004 hack. Billed once as the “Continental Championship” in the fed's own news — an informal restyling of this same belt's own name, not a second title.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Dead won the belts in their own CCWA debut at Sensation, over a last-minute pairing of Pete Hardy and Psyno, and were still champions — having turned back a #1 contenders match between Painkiller/Freezer Burn and Chris Sanchez/Chris West two weeks later — when the surviving record ends in March 2005.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Inaugurated at Sensation: Chris West won the first Television Championship from Wayne "Freezer Burn" Hammond in a barbed-wire match, Chris Sanchez's own interference clearing the way. Two weeks later Tony Stecchino stripped West of the belt on the air, the same night West was fired from the roster, and the fed's own 14 March 2005 news declares the title retired outright, replaced by a new Flash Championship tournament.

events.note: The fed's own news declares the Television Title no longer exists, replaced by the new Flash Championship.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Johnny Dollar came into the held record already champion; Ronnie McNeil took the belt from him at Sensation, reversing a second Bottom Dollar attempt into the fall, and was still champion — having retained it in a No Contest against Tony Stecchino after Eddie B.'s interference — when the surviving record ends in March 2005, billed to defend against Lyger.
titles.notes: Johnny Dollar's own reign predates the held record; no won-date survives the fed's own December 2004 hack.

titles.name: CCWe Underdawg Championship
titles.epitaph: Massacre_sr was stripped of the CCWe Underdawg Championship on 19 January 2001 for violating the fed's own jobbing and padding policies, the vacancy turning a scheduled Triple Threat into a Fatal 4 Way whose own result the surviving record doesn't capture.

titles.name: Chad Dupree Memorial Cup
titles.epitaph: The Chad Dupree Memorial Cup's one roll of winners across both hosts: EUWC's four runnings, 2004 to 2007 (Jordan Lockhart, Rocko Daymon, Nero, STEALTH), and TEAM Wrestling's two, 2006 and 2007 (New Era of Wrestling, The A-List). The hosts number it differently: EUWC's 2006 card is the third annual, TEAM's 2006 final the inaugural, and EUWC's event history heads 2006 and 2007 alike “3rd Annual” against the 2007 card's “4th Annual.” Each stands as its page gives it.

titles.name: CEWF Battle Royal Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by "Deadly" Dirk Venom during the fed's own European Tour angle, one of at least two Battle Royals he won outright.

titles.name: CEWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by "Flashy" Freddy Massey out of the fed's first Battle Royal and held through many defenses before Al Andrewson finally beat him for it after a month-long chase.

titles.name: CEWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Roger DeCarnac from original holder The Gravedigger, then put up (and lost) in a World Title shot against Lightcrest, which DeCarnac was working to regain as of October 1994.

titles.name: CEWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Lightcrest as of the fed's own first surviving retrospective column (October 1994); no title-change document survives.

titles.name: Showtime Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's lower title, named for the network that carries its shows. The Big Bang Theory's chairman says the winner of the tournament's consolation match takes it, and the Whiplash of 13 March 2008 bills a first Showtime Title match for its triple-threat winner after The Ascension. No page names a holder, and no reign is filed.

titles.name: CWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed by the fed's own pages as the title the Championship Tournament crowns at its pay-per-view, The Ascension (4 May 2008, the HP Pavilion, San Jose): 'the crowning of the first CWC World Champion'. No page names a holder, and no reign is filed.

titles.name: CHAOS!!! International World Championship
titles.epitaph: "Stunning" Scott Alexander held this belt before the fed's own summer 1996 shutdown; the fed's broadcast team discloses on-air, during the October 1996 relaunch card, that he was stripped of it without the title changing hands in the ring -- left vacant when this corpus ends, also referred to in the same broadcast as the "International Title" and "International Championship."

titles.name: CHAOS!!! World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A double-elimination tournament opened on the fed's own 6 October 1996 relaunch card: Anarchy and the HammerHeads won their winner's-bracket first-round matches, advancing to face former champions Black Rain and former WEW champions Apocalypse respectively, with the surviving record breaking off before the tournament's own conclusion -- the belt still unclaimed when this corpus ends.

titles.name: CHWE Gimmick Match Championship
titles.epitaph: X-Pac held the CHWE Gimmick Match Championship as of the fed's own champions page.
titles.notes: No dedicated ledger or documented match survives; sourced to the champions page alone.

titles.name: CHWE King of the Ring Championship
titles.epitaph: Archangel won the fed's own King of the Ring Tournament, defeating Viscera in the final.
titles.notes: Dated exactly to the fed's own documented tournament final.

titles.name: CHWE Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Phantom won the CHWE Heavyweight Championship in the final match of the fed's own Ladder Tournament, defeating Rob Van Dam. The fed's own later champions page instead names The Rock as champion, undated and unreconciled against the documented match.
titles.notes: See data/reigns.json's own conflict object on this title's reign row.

titles.name: CHWE World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Undertaker and Viscera held the CHWE World Tag Team Championship as of the fed's own champions page.
titles.notes: No dedicated ledger or documented match survives; sourced to the champions page alone.

titles.name: CHZ Alpha Championship
titles.epitaph: Harry Manback is the Alpha Champion at BreakOut 2002 on 18 December 2002, when Petapaw names a number one contender for the belt. Don Rossi won it on 26 March 2003 and the Darkness took it from him at May HayDay 2 on 14 May, handing it over that night to Rage, whom Keyser Soze named the nBk's Alpha Champion.

titles.name: CHZ Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The Count won the first CHZ Hardcore Championship at Caged Fury 1 on 1 August 1999, in the match since named the Transylvania Hardcore Match, and carried it through the CHZ and FWF mergers. The SWF years passed it among Staz, Freddy Landstrom, the Outlawz and BlaQ Inc.; The Count won it twice more and was kept as a non-fighting champion until the New CHZ held a final, which Diablo won over his partner Fire on 21 September 2001. Extreme Chancelz took it from Diablo in the fed's first barbed wire match, 14 November 2001; Black Dragon, Lucifer and Madd Maxx followed in early 2002, Maxx winning it on 6 March 2002 and billed to defend it against Wild Dog and Lucifer at NBK Pride, with no result surviving. Lucifer beat Mad Max for it on 26 March 2003; Xear was champion by 23 April, and Zen Kyosaku beat him for it in a three-way at May HayDay 2 on 14 May 2003.
titles.notes: The fed's own Hardcore title history (/promotions/chz/archive/hardcore-title-history.html): Black Dragon took it from Extreme Chancelz on 24 January 2002, Lucifer from Black Dragon at No Luv on 27 February, and Madd Maxx from Lucifer on 6 March 2002. The 21 September 2001 Friday Night Wild bills Diablo's win "for the right to be the First Hardcore Champion" and calls him "the first ever CHZ hardcore champion" (/promotions/chz/archive/fnw-2001-09-21.html), where the title history carries the belt back to The Count on 1 August 1999: sources disagree.

titles.name: CHZ Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The CHZ's top belt, first won by Millenium in a four-man elimination battle royal at Caged Fury 1 on 1 August 1999. Its own title history carries it through the fed's years as the FWF and the SWF — Cellrock relinquishing it when the CHZ closed in November 1999, JT Fringe winning the FWF title at that fed's opening, Rufus Blaq becoming the first SWF World Champion — and through a six-month vacancy while the SWF was closed in 2000. Kris Snyder, later Chazzy 2 Cool, won it in the New CHZ on 27 May 2001; Staz took it from him on 4 July and left North America with the belt at the end of August. After five months vacant, Matt "The Franchise" Helms won it at Caged Fury 2 on 30 January 2002, beating Diablo and then Don Rossi, The Count and Chazzy 2 Cool in a two-cage final, and is billed to defend it against Keyser Soze at NBK Pride, with no result surviving. The fed's June 2002 relaunch under a new owner listed a World Heavyweight Championship with no champions and crowned its own first champion (see chz-world-heavyweight). The belt's 2003 shows, after the fed's new era opened at BreakOut 2002: Gus Theo is billed champion on 5 March 2003, Matt Helms holds it again by 26 March after Caged Fury 2, and Harry Manback beat Helms for it at May HayDay 2 on 14 May 2003, keeping it on 21 May when a second referee's count of Drayton MacPhereson was ruled void.
titles.notes: The chain follows the fed's own Heavyweight title history (/promotions/chz/archive/heavyweight-title-history.html), which runs through the fed's FWF and SWF years exactly as the fed kept it; the Hall of Fame, the news archive and the held show scripts corroborate it. The 2003 reigns are filed on this belt, not on the June 2002 relaunch's (chz-world-heavyweight): the new era that opened at BreakOut 2002 carried the fed's 2001-02 belts on (Don Rossi, North American champion since February 2002, defends that title at BreakOut, "A title mind you that Don Rossi held twice before", /promotions/chz/archive/breakout-2002-12-18.html; Mad Max, Hardcore champion since March 2002, defends it on 26 March 2003), and on 26 March 2003 Matt Helms, this belt's champion of January 2002, says "Not only do I once again possess the CHZ World title" (/promotions/chz/archive/wnw-2003-03-26.html).

titles.name: CHZ Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Cellrock was the first CHZ Intercontinental Champion, beating Triple D in a Last Man Standing match at Caged Fury 1 on 1 August 1999 and winning fifteen straight before the CHZ closed. The belt ran on through the FWF and SWF years — Kryptosonic, who retired undefeated; JT Fringe and Jaguar-F trading it in February 2000; Staz ending Jaguar-F's career in a Loser Leaves Town cage match. In the New CHZ, Black Dragon, Don Rossi and Merlin held it through 2001; Chazzy 2 Cool took it from Merlin on 12 December 2001, Brent Brewer from Chazzy 2 Cool on 9 January 2002, and Kaanen Thorne from Brewer on 18 March 2002. Thorne is billed to defend it in a three-way at NBK Pride, with no result surviving.
titles.notes: The fed's own Intercontinental title history (/promotions/chz/archive/intercontinental-title-history.html) dates every change from 1999; Brewer won the title from Chazzy 2 Cool on 9 January 2002.

titles.name: CHZ National Championship
titles.epitaph: The secondary singles title of the CHZ's 2002 run, decided by a tournament that opened on the first Wild in July 2002. Xander Crave won it from Logan Cage on 7 August 2002 and kept it through the summer, against Tyler Van Serio on 21 August and Logan Cage again in a knockout match at Mind Games, until the fed's new owner stripped every champion on 11 September 2002.
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own 2002 champions and title-history pages (/promotions/chz/archive/champions-2002-09.html; /promotions/chz/archive/title-history-2002.html); not one of the belts the fed's 2001-02 site listed.

titles.name: CHZ North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in the New CHZ in 2001: Don Rossi won it on 2 May 2001, beating Chester Park in the final, and lost it three weeks later to Thor. Steve Santos made Thor submit for it in July and kept it through the autumn shows, against Gazz Maybury on 21 September and Matt Helms on 9 November, until he retired; Matt Helms won it from Brian Nash at the 12 December 2001 Wild and lost it to Violent Dave on 9 January 2002; Rossi took it back from Dave on 6 February 2002, the first two-time champion. Rossi retains it against Diablo by disqualification on 22 March 2002 and is billed to defend it again at NBK Pride, with no result surviving. Rob Lewis beat Don Rossi for it at BreakOut 2002 on 18 December 2002; Lucifer is billed its champion on 5 March 2003, when he does not come to work for a defence against Bloodlust, and Keyser Soze was its champion by 26 March 2003 and kept it through a count-out loss to Chris Holler on 9 April.
titles.notes: The fed's own North American title history (/promotions/chz/archive/north-american-title-history.html): Santos lost it to Matt Helms on 21 September 2001; Violent Dave took it from Helms on 11 January 2002 and Rossi from Dave on 6 February 2002.

titles.name: CHZ Omega Championship
titles.epitaph: A title the booth calls one carried over to the CHZ from the LOW, which Inferno won by beating Lucifer in a TLC cage match at BreakOut 2002 on 18 December 2002. Wild Dog was declared Omega Champion after beating Gus Theo on 26 March 2003 and kept it by disqualification against Lucifer on 9 April; with the title vacant, he won it again by beating Chazy 2 Cool in a ladder match at May HayDay 2 on 14 May 2003.

titles.name: CHZ Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Millennium and Canon, the original Outlawz, were its first champions at Caged Fury 1 on 1 August 1999; Sex and Violence — Dirk Diggler and The Crow — won it five times across the CHZ, FWF and SWF years, trading it with the Detroit Boyz in the autumn of 1999 and retiring after their last reign in 2000. Boylan's Boys held it longest, from November 2000 to May 2001. In the New CHZ the Disciples of Thunder held it from May 2001 and Hell's Fury (Diablo and Fire) from July; Son's of Thunder (James and John, managed by Simon) won it from Hell's Fury in the fed's first tables match on 9 November 2001, and by 23 January 2002 the Disciples (Atlas and Mountain) are billed the reigning champions, with no show recording the change. The Disciples were fired and the titles went vacant on 1 March 2002, and the Midnight Wonders won them in a four-corners elimination match on the 13 March 2002 Wild; they are billed to defend against Soul Stormer and 'Psycho' Cody Hawk at NBK Pride, with no result surviving. The fed's June 2002 relaunch under a new owner listed a Tag Team Championship with no champions and crowned its own champions (see chz-tag-team-2002). The titles were reinstated in 2003 after a tournament to crown new winners: the AAOD, Lucifer and Diablo, won them by beating the Reaper and Archangel, billed Heaven and Hell, at May HayDay 2 on 14 May 2003 and kept them on 21 May.
titles.notes: The fed's own Tag Team title history (/promotions/chz/archive/tag-team-title-history.html) gives the Disciples of Thunder (2) one reign, 9 November 2001 to 1 March 2002 ("DOT was fired after a period of inactivity"), and dates the Midnight Wonders' win 18 March 2002; the 9 November 2001 Friday Night Wild crowns the Sons of Thunder and the 13 March 2002 Wild stages the four-corners match. Sources disagree. The 2003 reign is filed on this belt, not on the June 2002 relaunch's (chz-tag-team-2002): the new era that opened at BreakOut 2002 carried the fed's 2001-02 belts on (see chz-heavyweight's notes), and the 14 May 2003 booth calls the titles "reinstated" (/promotions/chz/archive/may-hayday-2-2003-05-14.html).

titles.name: CHZ Tag Team Championship (2002)
titles.epitaph: The Tag Team belt of the CHZ's June 2002 relaunch under its new owner, listed on the fed's title page with no champions and on its champions page as vacant, the contenders to be announced. A tag team title tournament ended on 14 August 2002 with Redemption Song, Jim Surge and Ben Campbell, beating the Flying Vergomovs in a falls count anywhere final; they kept the titles against Gold Rush on 21 August, the Mind Games cage match against the Mystery Assailants ended in a no contest, and the fed declared the titles vacant on 2 September 2002 as Redemption Song moved on.
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own 2002 champions and title-history pages (/promotions/chz/archive/champions-2002-06.html; /promotions/chz/archive/title-history-2002.html); not the belt of the fed's own 2001-02 Tag Team title history (/promotions/chz/archive/tag-team-title-history.html). The Tag Team titles reinstated in 2003 are filed on chz-tag-team, the belt that era carried on (see its notes).

titles.name: CHZ Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Established in 2002 and decided by an eight-man, three-week tournament: Chris Nightly won the final at No Luv on 27 February 2002, and he changed his name to Chris Mathews on 1 March, which the fed's own title history counted as a second reign, "the shortest title rain ever," though the title did not change hands. Rage tapped Mathews out with an ankle lock on 22 March 2002 to take it, and is billed to defend it against Galuda at NBK Pride, with no result surviving.
titles.notes: The fed's own Television title history (/promotions/chz/archive/television-title-history.html) records the tournament win at No Luv, 27 February 2002, as Chris Nightly, and his renaming to Chris Mathews on 1 March 2002 as a second reign.

titles.name: CHZ Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced at BreakOut 2002 on 18 December 2002 as a golden-thong belt made for the event, which Xstacy won by beating Misty Helms with Mad Max's help. Commissioner Inferno stripped her of it on 23 April 2003 after the belt she swung at Sai hit him, and Sai, managed by Dynamo Dragon, won the vacant title by beating Misty Helms at May HayDay 2 on 14 May 2003.

titles.name: CHZ World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt of the CHZ's June 2002 relaunch under its new owner, listed on the fed's title page with no champions and on its champions page as vacant, the contenders to be announced. Jake Schultz was crowned "the first CHZ World Heavyweight Champion" at Mind Games on 31 August 2002, powerbombing Matt Hunt through a table in a barbed wire tables match, and lost it when the fed's new owner stripped every champion on 11 September 2002.
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own 2002 champions and title-history pages (/promotions/chz/archive/champions-2002-06.html; /promotions/chz/archive/title-history-2002.html) and billed "the first CHZ World Heavyweight Champion" on its 11 September 2002 front page (/promotions/chz/archive/front-page-2002-09.html). The 2003 World title is filed on chz-heavyweight (see its notes).

titles.name: CIN Golden State Heritage Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary title, first announced as the Southern (California) Heritage Title and set to be decided in a fifteen-man battle royal at X-Rated in July 2001.

titles.name: CIN Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, vacant at its opening and first won by Mac Rollins in the ladder-match final of a sixteen-man, one-night tournament on 30 June 2001.

titles.name: CIN Hollywood Title
titles.epitaph: A television title the promotion recognised from its opening but kept vacant, pending the size of its roster.

titles.name: CIW International Champion
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own top title, representing Canada and every country the promotion planned to tour; no champion is recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CIW International Tag Team Champions
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own tag titles; no champions are recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CIW North American Champion
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own second-ranked title, representing Mexico, the United States and Canada together; no champion is recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CIW Carribean Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own top prize, to be defended every thirty days; no champion is recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CIW Island Paradise Title
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own secondary title and usual number-one contendership for the heavyweight title; no champion is recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CIW Carribean Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own tag titles; no champions are recorded in the surviving document.

titles.name: CNWL Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by "Sexy" Simon Pretswell in a ladder match at the fed's own Lord of the Ring '98 pay-per-view, per the fed's own closing retrospective.

titles.name: CNWL Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Tower of Power against BJ Mullinax in a no-DQ table match at the fed's own founding card (31 May 1998), per the fed's own closing retrospective.

titles.name: CNWL Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a steel-cage spot at the fed's own founding card (31 May 1998), where interference from a rival fed's own wrestlers cost Stylz the match and let Attrition claim it.

titles.name: CNWL Million Dollar Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands from Axe to Polar Bear at the fed's own founding card (31 May 1998), per the fed's own closing retrospective.

titles.name: CNWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top belt; the fed's closing retrospective recounts Rally Jackson winning it from Dan Johnson at the fed's own founding card (31 May 1998) and Guru's own defense of it in a bloody chair-shot brawl at the fed's Battlezone '98 closing special.

titles.name: CPW Appalachian Valley Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed vacant in the same Update, alongside the East Coast belt.

titles.name: CPW East Coast Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed vacant in the fed's own 14 October 1997 Update, with no reign attested anywhere in this wave's corpus.
titles.notes: Reign start listed by the fed's own Update as "9/21/97 - Today," i.e. vacant since the title's own creation.

titles.name: CPW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed vacant in the same Update, the third of CPW's three unclaimed singles belts.

titles.name: CPW Virginia Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: CPW's only attested title change: won in a three-way on the fed's own surviving show and still listed as held the very next day in the fed's own Update.

titles.name: CRF Can-Am Championship
titles.epitaph: Mr Peak was billed as the reigning CRF Can-Am Champion on the fed's own 3 February 2001 return card, defending against Hell Spawn and Triple C.

titles.name: CRF Enforcer Championship
titles.epitaph: Manowar was billed as the reigning CRF Enforcer Champion on the fed's own 3 February 2001 return card, a hardcore defense against The Monk, Pagan, Carnage and Batman.

titles.name: CRF Rapid Fire Championship
titles.epitaph: Triple C was billed as the reigning CRF Rapid Fire Champion on the fed's own 3 February 2001 return card, defending against Freebird and Baretta.

titles.name: CRF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Manowar and Mr Peak, billed together as "Over & Out," were the reigning CRF Tag Team Champions on the fed's own 3 February 2001 return card, defending against Myth Inc. and the CRF Gods.

titles.name: CRF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: El Jobre was billed as the reigning CRF Television Champion on the fed's own 3 February 2001 return card, defending against The_g_a_m_e and Agent_orange.

titles.name: CRF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Con_victor, promoted up from the iIWF, was billed as the reigning CRF World Champion defending against Juggernaut and Wheelie on the CRF's own 3 February 2001 return card, posted as CyberSlam's own shutdown crisis threatened to end the game.

titles.name: CROW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at Schools Out For Summer after outside interference struck the wrong man, then survived a ladder-match defense a month later.

titles.name: CROW Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a battle royal, stripped during the promotion's mid-1998 reorganization, and reported under a new holder by the promotion's own October ranking sheet.

titles.name: CROW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held since May 1998 by the Gospel Preachers until a ringside stable's interference cost them the belts at Scorch Wave 98.

titles.name: CROW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded vacant at Schools Out For Summer and changed hands again before the promotion's own next pay-per-view.

titles.name: CROW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a 2-out-of-3-falls, falls-count-anywhere main event at Scorch Wave 98.

titles.name: TWL Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Chuckie Martinez entering 1999, who retained it against a recruited heavyweight at the promotion's own 26 January 1999 pay-per-view under the promotion's own rule barring a title change on a count-out. He later lost the title to Anthony Levert, who lost it in turn to El Puerco in a widely questioned finish at the promotion's own Armageddon event; Puerco retained it in a non-title four-corners bout ruled a no-contest on the promotion's own 3 May 1999 broadcast, the last card of the surviving record.

titles.name: CSW Can-Am Tag Champions
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Calgary Stampede Wrestling territory, attested for 2 reigns in its own record. Formed when Rocky Mountain Wrestling's own National Tag Team Titles were unified into this territory's record by its first champions' win.

titles.name: CSW Canadian Pride Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Calgary Stampede Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record. Continues the Georgia Elite Wrestling territory's own Canadian Pride Title after it transferred to Calgary Stampede Wrestling; the record states the title was vacated due to inactivity and rebranded as the Northern Star Champion.

titles.name: CSW Canadian Pride Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Calgary Stampede Wrestling territory, attested for 2 reigns in its own record. The record states the titles were vacated due to inactivity and rebranded; no further reigns survive under either name.

titles.name: CSW National Title
titles.epitaph: CSW's own second-tier singles belt, contested from January 1996, and the deepest of its four lineages at fourteen independent-era reigns — all recorded here. Mercury won it first, eliminating a young Miguel Sanchez in a battle royal, and the feud that opened it ran on: "It was always Sanchez vs Mercury," his own bio says, "They have been in a feud for over 2 years." Sanchez took it twice, and was named the Icon on the second. Bermuda Billy Page's own bio independently confirms the ledger down to the ordinal — "Billy became the 2nd man to win the CSW National title." Tom Cage was on his second reign when the acquisition stripped him of it in February 2004, still trying to get the CSW's own office to sign him a champion-versus-champion match against the TPW. Four further wrestlers — Charlie, Jack Kelly, Prowler and Reefer King — claim this championship on their own bio cards and appear nowhere in its fourteen reigns; those claims are recorded on their own tenures, not here.
titles.notes: Source: csw-title.html/csw-national-title.html/csw-royal-title.html/csw-world-tag-team-title.html's own shared line: "Title is stripped by Pres Burns who has Acquired the CSW Efed".

titles.name: CSW Northern Star Champion
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Calgary Stampede Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record. The rebranded continuation of the CSW Canadian Pride Title.

titles.name: CSW Royal Title
titles.epitaph: CSW's own third singles belt, contested from March 1996 — the only one of the four whose header does not start with the promotion. Kevin McFly won it first, eliminating Miguel Sanchez in a battle royal ("He did become the 1st Royal champion," his own bio agrees, in a career he says he otherwise made no name in). Eight independent-era reigns survive on the fed's own numbered ledger, all recorded here, eight different men — the only CSW belt no one ever won twice. Facing Death's own bio credits the stable rather than the man for his: "The UBH did help him win the CSW Royal title. His only title he ever won." Mike Hart was defending it in February 2004 when the acquisition stripped him of it, though the prose on his own page names a different belt than his own card does.
titles.notes: Source: csw-title.html/csw-national-title.html/csw-royal-title.html/csw-world-tag-team-title.html's own shared line: "Title is stripped by Pres Burns who has Acquired the CSW Efed".

titles.name: CSW Title
titles.epitaph: CSW's own top belt, contested from January 1996 as the "CSW World Title" and renamed the plain "CSW Title" that August. Tank won it first, eliminating Mercury in a battle royal, and said so himself afterwards — "Tank was a rookie when he came too the csw and became the 1st world champion." Nine independent-era reigns survive on the fed's own numbered ledger, all recorded here; six men held it, Mr. Ravishing twice. The Heartbreaker's own bio insists he was the second of them and Tank the man he beat, where the ledger puts Ace Stevens between the two — a disagreement kept rather than settled. Shane Curton was defending it in February 2004 when Pres Burns, having acquired the CSW Efed outright, stripped it from him and folded the lineage into his own CWF-Pro hierarchy; the belt's later CWF-Pro-branded life is recorded on CWF-Pro's own title row.
titles.notes: Source: csw-title.html/csw-national-title.html/csw-royal-title.html/csw-world-tag-team-title.html's own shared line: "Title is stripped by Pres Burns who has Acquired the CSW Efed".

titles.name: CSW World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: CSW's own tag belt, contested from January 1996 as the "CSW Tag Team Title" and renamed "CSW World Tag Team Title" that August. The Raxton Brothers won it first, throwing the Pretty Boys out of a battle royal, and dominated its whole independent-era run — three of nine recorded reigns by the ledger's own count, plus a fourth spell the ledger pointedly does NOT number, restored to them after the CSW itself stripped UBH's disputed house-show win and handed the belts back. (Zamza, one half of that UBH team, tells it differently on his own page: the match never happened, and the promotion closed before the pay-per-view could.) This ledger keeps more of the promotion's texture than any of the other three: the only reign length CSW's entire record preserves — the Kennel Killers' 22 days, its longest, by a team whose members are named nowhere at all — and the note that Crippler, one half of "Rico Suave & Crippler," was the belt's own first Black champion. The Raxton Brothers were still champions in February 2004 when the acquisition stripped the lineage and folded it into CWF-Pro's own tag belt.
titles.notes: Source: csw-title.html/csw-national-title.html/csw-royal-title.html/csw-world-tag-team-title.html's own shared line: "Title is stripped by Pres Burns who has Acquired the CSW Efed".

titles.name: Enterprise World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The superleague belt the CSWA staged as its own top prize between the Unified Championship's tours. Mike Randalls won the sixteen-man founding tournament over Flic Rair at BATTLE OF THE BELTS X in November 1994 and lost it five weeks later to the Muppet Maneuver and a downed referee; Tom Adler escaped a double-title cage with it in August 1995, Randalls took it back on sixty points in the CSWA X-MAS IRONMAN CHALLENGE, GUNS powerslammed him for it in the SuperPRIMETIME triangle on Martin Luther King Day 1996, and Mark Windham left WINTER'S WARRIORS VII with it after Hornet turned on GUNS and a paid-off referee counted the fall.

titles.name: Enterprise World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag championship the CSWA ran alongside its Unified belts for a single documented year. Generation X-Press won the EN World/US tag tournament final over the FORCE at BATTLE OF THE BELTS XIV in July 1996; the Japanese Assault took it from Troy Windham with the Shogun Slam in a unification match at FISH FUND XI that September, and the fed's own record carries nothing further.

titles.name: Greensboro Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A promotion naming a championship after the city it was invented in, and then defending it for thirteen years. Big Wesley Slack won the founding tournament in 1988; Mark Windham took it from him and then retired it when he won the CSWA Heavyweight Championship, and Jay Youngblood was defending it again by 1989. It goes dark for years and comes back: the fed's own newspaper records Aaron Douglas as the first Greensboro Champion since 1997 when he beat Apocalypse in the tournament final at ELVIS LIVES XI in January 1999. From there it moves fast — Randy Harders, Douglas again, Blade, Wicked Sight, Sky Suicide, Evan Aho — and the fed's own Champions page still has a holder for it in April 2001.

titles.name: Greensboro Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fourth belt of 1988 and the shortest-lived in the fed's own record. Strange But True won the founding eight-team tournament, beating Ace In The Hole in the final on the fourth card of the year, and lost it the next year in a belt-against-belt match with the United States Tag Team Champions. Nothing after that survives.

titles.name: CSWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A second singles belt, made in 1988 alongside the World Championship and gone from the fed's own record long before the web. Purple Hayes won a tournament for it on the third card of 1988; Ed Parsons took it from him on the fourth and Mark Windham took it from Parsons on the fifth, retiring the Greensboro Championship when he did. Vladimir Rushevcof beat Berserker for it in 1989. After that the fed's own archive stops carrying it and its Champions pages never list it again.
titles.notes: Distinct from the World Championship, which the same 1988 cards track separately: on the fifth card of 1988 Mark Windham wins this belt while Joey Melton defends the World Championship in the main event.

titles.name: Intracontinental Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding memoir as one of the belts added over the years, and surviving in exactly one document: the CSWA's own Champions and Contenders page on PRODIGY, updated 15 July 1997, which lists it as vacant and to be decided in an eight-man tournament. No champion for it appears on any page held here, before or after.

titles.name: CSWWA Ladies Enterprises World Championship
titles.epitaph: A women's championship crowned once in the surviving record: Queen Sonya beat "Stone Cold" Stephanie Conner in the tournament final at FISH FUND XI in September 1996 to become its first holder.

titles.name: CSWA Presidential Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt tangled up with the office it is named for. The fed's own newspaper describes it as previously retired and revived at THANKSGIVING WEEKEND SPECTACULAR '99, when a returning Co-Commissioner ousted the other one from the commissionership and put the title back on a wrestler. Randy Harders lost it to a returning Alex Wylde in an impromptu match in Philadelphia; Aaron Douglas took it from Cameron Cruise at ANNIVERSARY 2000 on a three-count made by Hornet himself. By April 2001 the fed's own Champions page carries it as vacated, to be filled at ELVIS LIVES XII, and does not say why.

titles.name: ULTRATITLE
titles.epitaph: The tournament trophy the CSWA invented and then leased out across the hobby, first run on PRODIGY in 1992 with sixty-four entrants and by 1995 seeded to two hundred and fifty-six men across four divisions. Dr. Silver beat Timmy Windham with the Suicide Machine in the 1995 final at WINTER'S WARRIORS VI; the 1996 edition put its winner, Paul Pierce, straight into the Unified World Championship.

titles.name: Unified World Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag championship after the merges, carried by two men rather than renamed for each of them.
