Eddy Love and Kevin Powers won it at BATTLE of the BELTS XVI in May 1999; by December 2000 the fed's Champions page has Foreign Exchange holding it, and by April 2001 Simply Stunning, since PRIMETIME in Paducah. The fed's own page writes it plural — Championships, two belts — throughout.
titles.notes: The fed's own Champions page header reads "Unified World Tag Team Championships", plural. Whether and how it descends from the 1988 CSWA World Tag Team Championship is not settled by any page held here.

titles.name: United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the three belts the fed built in its first year, and the one that changed hands most. Jay Youngblood won the founding tournament in 1988 and lost it to Hornet on the very next card; Safari Sakan took it off Mark Windham in 1989 and Windham won it straight back. Eleven years later it was still the belt a run got built on: Kevin Powers won a tournament for it at FISH FUND XII in 1998, Eli Flair took it in a Triangle match in January 1999, and Nemesis won it twice in the same year, the first time out of a Barbed Wire Ladder Match he came into with a concussion. Lawrence Stanley and Havoc carried it through 2000.

titles.name: United States Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Made in 1988 out of an eight-team tournament the Big Connection won, beating Armed and Dangerous in the final. By 1989 the fed was staging it belt-against-belt with the Greensboro Tag Team Championship, and the Overseas Connection beat Strange But True in that match. The fed's own archive carries it no further.

titles.name: CSWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first belt the CSWA made, and the one it kept. Joey Melton is defending it on the second card of 1988 and Hornet takes it from Purple Hayes the year after; a decade later it is still the fed's own main event, won out of an eight-man tournament at FISH FUND XII in August 1998 and carried through steel cages and IRONMAN round-robins until the record thins out. Its 1999 is the year that reads hardest: Hornet wins it in San Antonio in April and is stripped of it by a Co-Commissioner at BATTLE of the BELTS XVI, Eli Flair takes the vacancy out of the ANNIVERSARY IRONMAN, and Deacon takes it from Flair at THANKSGIVING WEEKEND SPECTACULAR and holds it for most of a year. The fed's own Champions page ends that reign with a sentence it does not explain further: the title was relinquished, in November 2000, on a diagnosis. It was still being defended on the board in 2004.
titles.notes: Called the CSWA World Championship on the 1988 and 1989 cards and the CSWA World Heavyweight Championship on the Champions pages from 1998; the same belt throughout.

titles.name: World Six-Man Championship
titles.epitaph: A six-man belt the fed created in its first year and put on its own three lead characters: Joey Melton, Hornet and Mark Windham took it by beating the Big Connection and Purple Hayes on the second card of 1988. The fed's founding memoir lists it among the titles added as the game grew, alongside the Intracontinental, the Pacific and the Eastern States Heritage; of those four, this is the only one the 1988 card archive actually crowns anybody for.
titles.notes: The memoir names Intracontinental, Pacific and Eastern States Heritage championships alongside this one; no card held here crowns a champion for any of the three, and only the Intracontinental turns up again, listed vacant on the fed's own 1997 PRODIGY Champions page.

titles.name: CSWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The first tag championship, and the one act that runs through the whole of the fed's first two years. The C.S. Express beat the Big Connection to become the first champions in 1988 and then defended it on every card the archive lists: a lumberjack two-out-of-three falls against the Dirty Duo, a double bullrope match against the Indian Warriors, a scaffold match against Armed and Dangerous. They were still holding it at the end of 1989.

titles.name: CWA Aerial Championship
titles.epitaph: A cruiserweight belt that begins with 6Pac Dudley’s win in a Cruiserweight Rumble on 17 May 2003, becomes the Aerial title, is dissolved on 5 September and returns in December; the cards of 2004 show Myst holding it by 1 March and Gloria Lavin retiring it at Outrage on 26 April.

titles.name: CWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore belt first awarded to Romeo Salvador at Hardcore Hell on 10 May 2003 and held by Leech and The Moose before it was merged into the Inter-Continental on 5 July. A second hardcore belt appears from 20 October 2003, with Max Cameron and Dante trading it and Leech holding it from 19 January 2004 until Shannon Skanes won it in a three-way on 22 March 2004.

events.title: cwa-association-2003-superior
events.note: Its own title history: the Hardcore belt was dissolved on 5 July when it was merged with the Inter-Continental to form the Superior title.

titles.name: CWA Inter-Continental/Superior Championship
titles.epitaph: The Inter-Continental title of the CWA’s first summer, in 2003, which absorbed the Hardcore title on 5 July to become the Superior belt. Mach, Q, Shannon Skanes and Vigilante are its holders on the title history, and the cards of 2004 show The Moose taking it on 23 February, SinmaN on 26 April and Tommy Air on 24 May.

titles.name: CWA Women’s Championship
titles.epitaph: Floated as a possibility in the owner’s news post of 1 August 2003 and awarded on 11 August to Lickety Split/Scarlet Bitch. Demona Calaway took it on 30 September 2003 and holds it into March 2004.

titles.name: CWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWA’s top belt in 2003 and 2004: Dizz is its first listed champion on 21 June 2003 and wins it three times that year, and the owner’s own character, Shannon Skanes, holds it briefly in October. Vigilante has it from 19 January 2004, the last holder its title history shows; the cards of 2004 then show Max Cameron taking it at Terror in the Aisles on 29 March and losing it to Leech at Outrage on 26 April, and Ash winning it at Blind Rage on 24 May and keeping it on 7 June.

titles.name: CWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWA’s World Tag Team belts in 2003: Eternal Nightmares won a four-team match on 17 May, and the titles passed through BOD twice, Full House, Northern Exposure and Los Especialistos before Dark Forces took them on 1 December and Reality and Dark Ice Symphony followed in January 2004; the cards then show Dark Forces taking the belts back on 22 March 2004 and keeping them on 24 May.

titles.name: CWA Diva Championship
titles.epitaph: A Diva title created on its Battle of the Warriors 2007 CWA Edition, 13 January 2007, where Corina wins the sixteen-woman Diva Gauntlet to be its first champion; she shares it with Kelly Buchanan after a ladder match on 3 February and defends it alone on 17 February 2007.

titles.name: CWA Inter-Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: The Inter-Continental title as the same page lists it, from Shannon Skanes in January 1984 to Adam Eagle, who holds it from October 2009.

titles.name: CWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag titles as the same page lists them, from the Glory Boys in January 1984 to Team SOB’s run dated August 2009 and still running.

titles.name: CWA Women’s Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWA Women’s title on its Originals cards: Myst defends it at Battle of the Warriors 2007 and vacates it at the end of January 2007, and Sammy Jo Johnson wins it in a five-woman elimination match on 10 February 2007.

titles.name: CWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWA World Heavyweight title as the CWA Originals’ own page lists it, from Yuri Jolnecov in January 1984 to Noah Skanes’s eighth reign, dated May 2009 and still running. Its list runs through 2003 to 2005 with different holders from the CWA World belt of those years in the other CWA wing: the two histories cannot both be the same belt.

titles.name: CWA Aerial Championship
titles.epitaph: The cruiserweight belt of the revived CWA, in which 6Pac Dudley, Thibor Dragosani and Hoshi Yakamoto are its holders through 2008, as the cards of that year show.

titles.name: CWA Diva Championship
titles.epitaph: A Diva title on the revived CWA’s 2008 front page, held by Bombshell from 29 June 2008.

titles.name: CWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag belts of the revived CWA: the New Age Dogg Pound won them at Battle of the Warriors 2008 on 15 January 2008 and lost them to Sex and Violence on 11 March.

titles.name: CWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of the CWA of 2007 and 2008. Its own cards open the run with Wren SilverPhoenix on 23 October 2007, and Tommy Purr and Jack Spade trade it into mid-2008. It is a new run of titles: the belt of 2003 and 2004 is another wing’s, and the two lists share no champion.

titles.name: CWAA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by a 16-man tournament in the fed's own first two months, the CWAA's top title changed hands three more times -- twice by decision, once by unmasking -- before the held record ends with its reigning champion revealed as Marc Thomas.
titles.notes: Vacated by AEWA ruling, 22 June 1997 (sJ2Kd6hfi3AJ).

titles.name: CWAA Six Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the CWAA's own Supershow, decided by a single-elimination tournament on the promotion's biggest card of the year.

titles.name: CWAA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by an eight-team tournament, lost to a steel-cage upset, and reclaimed in August by the fed's own first-ever two-time champions.

titles.name: CWAA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a 12-man battle royal and defended by the fed's own house rule every single week thereafter, the Television title changed hands four times across the held record.

titles.name: CWC International People's Championship
titles.epitaph: A second singles title the fed's own president announced by name and bracket (26 May 1998), with its own tournament scheduled to run entirely at First Night; vacant and uncontested when the held record ends.

titles.name: CWC North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for a four-way elimination match at the fed's own first pay-per-view, Prime Time in North America (21 July 1998); Paul Kingstead became its first champion and still held it when the held record ends.

titles.name: CWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, contested through a sixteen-man single-elimination tournament announced at its own founding and scheduled to conclude at its own first pay-per-view, First Night; vacant when the held record ends, with the tournament having reached its semifinals (Havoc, "Blockbuster" Johnny Detson, Crimestarter Jim and Leviathan).

titles.name: CWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested through a tag team tournament run across the fed's own final weeks; the L.A. Wrecking Crew beat the Hardcore Icons for the vacant belts at Prime Time in North America (21 July 1998) and still held them when the held record ends.

titles.name: CWC Chicago Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top singles title, contested in an eight-man single-elimination tournament at the fed's first pay-per-view and won there by Andrew "Flash" Tucker, who beat Jack Vars in the final by submission after outside interference from Outcast by Society.

titles.name: CWC Chicago Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag team championship, named in its own player's guide but never contested in any document this collection holds.

titles.name: CWC Cook County Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary singles title, contested in an eight-man single-elimination tournament at the fed's first pay-per-view; the final was a ladder match, won there by "Flatlander" Duke Putrid over Tommy Grayson.

titles.name: CWC Skyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own cruiserweight title, a 225-pound weight limit, named in its own player's guide but never contested in any document this collection holds.

titles.name: CWC Atlanta City Championship
titles.epitaph: The Georgia region's own secondary singles title, defended by Aaron D'Arby against Neil Finan.

titles.name: CWC Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The council's own alliance-wide cruiserweight title, contested in a tournament across the member regions that had not concluded as of the council's own served national newsletter.

titles.name: CWC Florida Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Mid-Atlantic region's own Florida-branded singles title, held by Richard Richardson.

titles.name: CWC Georgia State Championship
titles.epitaph: The Georgia region's own top singles title, lost by Logan Gunz to Jimmy "Pretty Boy" Floyd through the wreckage of a timekeeper's table.

titles.name: CWC Georgia State Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Georgia region's own tag title, won in a tournament final by Jason Wallace and Ben Mullins with the aid of a mace attack.

titles.name: CWC Mid-Atlantic Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Mid-Atlantic region's own top singles title, won by Rex Stone in a six-man battle royal after the belt sat vacant.

titles.name: CWC Mid-Atlantic Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Mid-Atlantic region's own tag title, held by FREEK and Static Rule.

titles.name: CWC Mid-South Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A new title created for Tommy Lane when the Southern region was renamed Mid-South Wrestling.

titles.name: CWC Mid-South Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A new tag title created for the Electric Mayhem when the Southern region was renamed Mid-South Wrestling.

titles.name: CWC National Championship
titles.epitaph: The council's own alliance-wide title, contested in a tournament across all seven member regions that had not concluded as of the council's own served national newsletter.

titles.name: CWC National Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The council's own alliance-wide tag title, announced for a match between the Overlords of the Dark and the Hot House in the council's own served national newsletter.

titles.name: CWC National TV Championship
titles.epitaph: The council's own alliance-wide television title, announced for a match between Christopher Stonebreaker and an unnamed opponent in the council's own served national newsletter.

titles.name: CWC Southern States Championship
titles.epitaph: The Southern region's own top singles title, held by Tommy Lane before it moved to the Georgia region in the council's own restructuring.

titles.name: CWC Southern States Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Southern region's own tag title, held by the Polo Club before it moved to the Georgia region, and later defended by the Hot House against the New British Lions.

titles.name: CWC Tennessee Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary Southern region singles title, held by the Carolina Crusher.

titles.name: CWF Anarchy Championship
titles.notes: Source: the SeVeN show script, which headers the match "CWF Anarchy Championship — Anarchy Rules" and ring-announces Mr. X the winner (promotions/cwf/archive/seven-2003-02-01.html); the Redz()ne-2 card, which bills Mr. X "(Champ)" defending against Sean Manning in a Dumpster Match (promotions/cwf/archive/redzone-2-card-2003-03-11.html). No dedicated title-history page for this belt survives.
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a three-way at SeVeN — reduced to a two-way mid-match when Starter was written out by an in-story lightning strike — and won by Mr. X, who pinned Hardcore Z with his own legs on the ropes. The Redz()ne-2 card bills him defending it against Sean Manning in a Dumpster Match ten days later; that show's own results were never captured, so the belt's own history ends there, mid-defense, in the surviving record.

titles.name: CWF Chaos Championship
titles.epitaph: An anything-goes, no-holds-barred belt created at the first Aggression of the second run and awarded to Jason Garret, held under a 24/7 rule that let it change hands anywhere; its own About page names Jake Fury, Cenotaph, Faith, Violent A and Priest among its holders.

titles.name: CWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt for men of 225 pounds or under, added in 2003; Michael Machete is champion on both surviving broadcasts and defends it against Ken Sandwave and Carnage and then against Neptune.

titles.name: CWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The last of the first year's belts, added in 2003 after the Cruiserweight title according to the federation's own About page.

titles.name: CWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at the first Aggression of the second run, on 12 September 2004, and first awarded in a battle royal to Ryan Coleman. Dark Rayne's undefeated reign is billed as the longest; the surviving broadcasts show it passing from Fuel to Christian Connolly at Genocide and from X-Factor to The Punk at Ultimate Chaos.

titles.name: CWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Added in the federation's first months in 2003 and held in the second run by Talent Inc among others; the surviving broadcasts have the Hit Squad champions at Genocide and Generation Xtreme champions by Ultimate Chaos.

titles.name: CWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the federation's opening month, January 2003; Violent A is its former champion on the last Ultimate Chaos and Nemesis was the first man to hold it together with the Tag Team title.

titles.name: CWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Added in 2003 after the Television title; Jake Fury's own Hall of Fame page has him battling Souless for it in the federation's first year.

titles.name: CWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Its own title-history page opens with Faith, who beat Roxie Michaels at Shockwave on 15 March 2005, then Dana Morris on 1 May 2005; the surviving broadcasts show Syd Ashley taking it from Faith in a gauntlet at Genocide and Faith holding it again by Ultimate Chaos.

titles.name: CWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles belt, added in its opening months of 2003. Its own pages name Christian Cage the first World champion of the second run and Faith the first woman to hold it, with Priest champion on both surviving broadcasts; its last broadcasts date his hold on it both to May and to September, with X-Factor's win at Bloodbath between.

titles.name: CWF European Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the circuit fed's own five titles in its October 1997 founding document; no reign is decided in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding document (promotions/cwf-circuit-1997/archive/).

titles.name: CWF T.V. Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the circuit fed's own five titles in its October 1997 founding document; no reign is decided in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding document (promotions/cwf-circuit-1997/archive/).

titles.name: CWF U.S. Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the circuit fed's own five titles in its October 1997 founding document; no reign is decided in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding document (promotions/cwf-circuit-1997/archive/).

titles.name: CWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the circuit fed's own five titles in its October 1997 founding document; no reign is decided in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding document (promotions/cwf-circuit-1997/archive/).

titles.name: CWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the circuit fed's own five titles in its October 1997 founding document; no reign is decided in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding document (promotions/cwf-circuit-1997/archive/).

titles.name: CWF Mid-Atlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on its title-history page is Nemesis, from 20 September 1998; 31 reigns are recorded, the last held by Kris Lewis and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its title-history page runs in five blocks of dated reigns, 1997 to 2001 and again from 2005, with 'CWF Closed' standing where the federation shut down and all titles were vacated.

titles.name: CWF National Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on its title-history page is 'Hotshot' Mike Stewart, from 26 October 1997; 43 reigns are recorded, the last held by Angus and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its title-history page runs in five blocks of dated reigns, 1997 to 2001 and again from 2005, with 'CWF Closed' standing where the federation shut down and all titles were vacated.

titles.name: CWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on its title-history page is Just In Credible, from 26 June 1998; 37 reigns are recorded, the last held by Canadian Made and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its title-history page runs in five blocks of dated reigns, 1997 to 2001 and again from 2005, with 'CWF Closed' standing where the federation shut down and all titles were vacated.

titles.name: CWF Unified Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on its title-history page is T-Money, from 26 June 1998; 48 reigns are recorded, the last held by Apocalypticus and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its title-history page runs in five blocks of dated reigns, 1997 to 2001 and again from 2005, with 'CWF Closed' standing where the federation shut down and all titles were vacated.

titles.name: CWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on its title-history page is Huckster, from 26 October 1997; 35 reigns are recorded, the last held by Paul Blair and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its title-history page runs in five blocks of dated reigns, 1997 to 2001 and again from 2005, with 'CWF Closed' standing where the federation shut down and all titles were vacated.

titles.name: CWF Classic World Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Championship Wrestling from Florida territory, attested for 8 reigns in its own record. Its record then stops with the title vacated; the territory's own next surviving line resumes with a new title reign three months later, with no interim champion named.

titles.name: Cold Championship

titles.name: CWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title Histories page records no former Hardcore Champion. Mike Maddness earns the #1 contendership at Friday Night Blitz (18 January 2002), beating Xtreme T through a trash can; by "Babylon" (25 January 2002) he is already champion, successfully defending against eXodus — the title changed hands, off-page and unrecorded, sometime in the week between the two shows. The belt's own founding and only recorded reign in the held record.

titles.name: CWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named among the fed's own five recognized championships on both the Title Histories and Current Champions pages, but no reign was ever recorded — the belt sits Vacant as of the held record's own last snapshot.

titles.name: CWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title Histories page records exactly one former holder against every other title ("n/a"): Kula, 18 January 2002 to 25 January 2002. The fed's own served Current Champions page names Apocalypse as the reigning Television Champion — the belt's own last-attested state. Read together with the two served shows (Kula defeats Apocalypse at Friday Night Blitz, 18 January 2002; Apocalypse defeats Dr. Doom and Kula at "Babylon," 25 January 2002), this is the whole title's own recorded lineage in the held record: two reigns, both structured here.

titles.name: CWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title Histories page records no former United States Champion; the fed's own served Current Champions page names Dr. Doom as the reigning titleholder — read together, the belt's own founding and only recorded reign in the held record, with no document surviving to say when or how he won it.

titles.epitaph: Billed the fed's own first heavyweight champion since 2001, the belt changed hands once in the surviving record: 'The Natural' Mike Diamond outlasted Paco at SeVeN, submitting him to the Midas Touch with a compromised special guest referee counting the fall, then was immediately confronted by a returning, unmasked Kid Gangster, who produced a signed contract forcing a title match against owner Hellfire X. Whether that match was ever wrestled is not attested anywhere in the surviving record.

Hammerman, Wasp and Lost Soul are its only two-time champions across 21 recorded reigns; one reign ended when Machine of War was injured, another when the Icon Miguel Sanchez was suspended. Muhammad Cala closes the ledger's own account in October 2007, defeating the Golden One to unify the Crown with the Royal Title — the ledger records the Crown itself as “no longer used” from that reign on.

titles.name: CWF-Pro Intercontinental Title

Hero (6), Jackson (4) and Billy Lee (3) are its most frequent holders across 106 recorded reigns, and like CWF-Pro's other flagship belts it absorbed a long list of rival promotions' own titles one by one — the EWF United States, CSW National, SCW Internet, BMWF Intercontinental, WWWCW Intercontinental, IWWA Intercontinental, XXX 2nd, EIWZ North American, TDW International, NWO TV, IWF Intercontinental, CWE National and AWI Television Titles among them. The ledger's own last recorded line names OPG as champion, with no closing note; 20 of the 106 recorded champions survive only as bare ledger names.

titles.name: CWF-Pro Mega Wars Winner
titles.epitaph: An annual battle-royal award rather than a standing championship, run every year since November 1997; Mike Powers is the only two-time winner across the 13 recorded years. Miguel Sanchez won the first Mega Wars, eliminating Jackson; Eric Michaels won the most recent recorded one, eliminating Beastman. One winner's own victory, Beastman's, doubled as a unification, folding the DTW Battle Royal Title into the Mega Wars Title the same night.

titles.name: CWF-Pro Royal Title
titles.epitaph: Founded March 1997 as the UBH Royal Title, absorbed into CWF-Pro that April, when Beastman won a battle royal eliminating R@ven to become its 1st UBH Royal Champion; the fed's own ledger restarts its own numbering at “1” from that point, a fresh count for the CWF-Pro-branded belt though the title runs continuous. Hardcore Pimp (5) and Extreme Adam-X (4) are its most frequent CWF-Pro-era holders across 83 recorded reigns — 19 of them bare ledger names — which fold in a long run of rival promotions' own belts, from the EWF Television Title to the SCW Cruiserweight Title. The Golden One closes the ledger's own account in December 2007, unifying the Royal Title together with the Canadian Title into the Intercontinental Title in a 3-way dance.

titles.name: CWF-Pro Title
titles.epitaph: Opened April 1997 as the CWF-Pro World Heavyweight Title (renamed the CWF-Pro Title that December), when the Icon Miguel Sanchez won a battle royal eliminating Gator at the fed's own “2nd TNF” to become its 1st CWF-Pro World Champion, unifying three developmental belts (UBH, AIWA, DBWF) into it the same night. Across 143 recorded reigns Mike Powers (22), Sanchez (18) and Beastman (14) dominate the ledger, and dozens more changes each fold in a rival promotion's own top belt — the EWF, UCWF, WWWWF, IWWA, IWF, NWO and AWI World Titles among many others — as the belt absorbed CWF-Pro's acquired predecessors and in-house developmental leagues one by one. The ledger's own printed numbering carries two genuine irregularities, preserved exactly as the source prints them: two reign changes are marked “X” instead of a sequential number — one restores Major Disorder to the belt while reprinting his own earlier “(2)” reign-count suffix rather than advancing it, the other restores Seven — and two further numbers, 49 and 133, are simply missing from the fed's own printed list. Eric Michaels holds the belt at the ledger's own last recorded line; 16 of the 143 recorded champions survive only as bare ledger names.

Hardcore Pimp towers over its own 220 recorded reigns, holding the belt 45 separate times against R@ven and Buffo's 10 apiece, and its late-life stretch settles into a running Hardcore Pimp/Beer King trade the ledger records dozens of times over with no method given beyond the name change. Like the fed's other flagship belts it absorbed a long run of rival promotions' own hardcore titles one by one — the IWWA, IWF, TDW No Limits, KWF, PWE, XPWA, Phoenix Promotion, BMWF, Fantasy Brawl, EIWZ and UEH Barbwire Titles among them — and the fed's own printed numbering repeats several positions outright (78 four times over, 79 and 94 twice each) rather than being silently corrected here. The ledger's own last recorded line names Hardcore Pimp as champion, with no closing note; 30 of the 220 recorded champions survive only as bare ledger names.

Leah Sanchez holds it at the ledger's own last recorded line, with no closing note.
