titles.epitaph: Founded February 1997 as UBH's own tag title, ahead of CWF-Pro's own April 1997 founding. TGS (Zeke & Deke) won a battle royal eliminating the Insyders to become its 1st UBH World Tag Team Champions; the Insyders reclaimed it twice across the belt's own brief 6-reign life. The Double Dragons close the ledger's own account that April, defeating the Money Men to unify the UBH World Tag Team Titles with the CWF-Pro Tag Team Titles the same night CWF-Pro's own flagship tag title was founded.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 6 reigns in full; all 6 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/ubh-world-tag-team-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: UEH Barbwire Title
titles.epitaph: Opened March 2007 for the UEH brand, when Canadian Bear won a battle royal eliminating M30 to become its 1st Barbwire Champion. Beer King (4) and Jon Wu (3) are its most frequent holders across 16 recorded reigns, well over half of them otherwise bare ledger names. Hardcore Pimp closes the ledger's own account, defeating Razorwire to unify the UEH Barbwire Title with the CWF-Pro Ultra Extreme Hardcore Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 16 reigns in full; all 16 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/ueh-barbwire-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: UEH Hardcore Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Opened March 2007 for the UEH brand, when Beer King & Bob Barns won a battle royal eliminating the Jackson Boys to become its 1st UEH Hardcore Tag Team Champions — the same duo reclaiming it twice more across the belt's own brief 8-reign life, 7 of the 8 recorded champions surviving only as bare team names. The Johnson Boys close the ledger's own account, defeating the Jackson Boys to unify the UEH Hardcore Tag Team Titles with the CWF-Pro World Tag Team Titles.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 8 reigns in full; all 8 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/ueh-hardcore-tag-team-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: UEH Japanese Title
titles.epitaph: Opened March 2007 for the UEH brand, when M30 won a battle royal eliminating Omegadawn to become its 1st Japanese Champion. Ricky Tan is its only two-time champion across 9 recorded reigns, the rest bare ledger names with no bio page behind them. Russian Warrior closes the ledger's own account, defeating the Samurai to unify the UEH Japanese Title with the CWF-Pro Canadian Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 9 reigns in full; all 9 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/ueh-japanese-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: UEH Title
titles.epitaph: Opened March 2007 for the UEH brand, when Crazy MoFo won a battle royal eliminating Razor to become its 1st UEH Champion. Crazy MoFo reclaimed the belt across its own brief 7-reign life — 4 of the 7 recorded champions survive only as bare ledger names — and held it when the federation closed in November 2007, the ledger's own last line recording it vacated outright rather than unified into any surviving belt.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 7 reigns in full; all 7 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/ueh-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: WWW Beauty Title
titles.epitaph: Opened July 2007 for the WWW women's brand, when Jenna X won a battle royal eliminating Easy Girl to become its 1st Beauty Champion. Jenna X, Cavegirl and the Model each hold it twice across the belt's own brief 15-reign life, the majority otherwise bare ledger names. Lola Sanchez closes the ledger's own account, defeating the Beauty Queen to unify the WWW Beauty Title with the CWF-Pro Women's World Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 15 reigns in full; all 15 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/www-beauty-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: WWW Bytch Title
titles.epitaph: Opened July 2007 for the WWW women's brand, when Hot Baby won a battle royal eliminating Shannon Gill to become its 1st Bytch Champion. Beth Nasty (4) and Shannon Gill (3) are its most frequent holders across 19 recorded reigns, nearly three-quarters of them otherwise bare ledger names. Amber Burns closes the ledger's own account, defeating the Domatrix to unify the WWW Bytch Title with the CWF-Pro Women's World Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 19 reigns in full; all 19 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/www-bytch-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: WWW World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Opened July 2007 for the WWW women's brand, when the Davis Girls (Ashley & Amber Davis) won a battle royal eliminating the Spoiled Brats to become its 1st WWW World Tag Team Champions. Nearly its whole brief 7-reign life survives only as bare team names, no bio page behind any but one. The Spoiled Brats held the belt when the federation closed that November, the ledger's own last line recording it vacated outright rather than unified into any surviving belt.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 7 reigns in full; all 7 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/www-world-tag-team-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: WWW World Title
titles.epitaph: Opened July 2007 for the WWW women's brand, when Queen Bee won a battle royal eliminating Slave to become its 1st WWW World Champion — every one of its 7 recorded reigns a distinct holder, no repeat champion across the belt's own brief life. Jenny Love closes the ledger's own account, defeating Easy Girl to unify the WWW World Title with the CWF-Pro Women's World Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 7 reigns in full; all 7 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/www-world-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: XXX 2nd Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Opened January 2006 when the Flash Brothers (Don & Jerry Flash) won a battle royal, eliminating the Unknown (What & Who), to become the belt's own 1st XXX 2nd Tag Team Champions. The fed's own numbered ledger records just 3 reigns start to finish: the Flash Brothers held it through the Unknown's own brief interruption before reclaiming it, and vacated it outright when the federation closed in November 2007 — the ledger's own last line reads “title abandon no longer used.”
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 3 reigns in full; all 3 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/xxx-2nd-tag-team-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: XXX 2nd Title
titles.epitaph: Opened January 2006 for the XXX brand, when Jason Porn won a battle royal eliminating Cold Blood to become its 1st 2nd Champion. Bobby Williams holds it five times across the belt's own 18 recorded reigns, well ahead of Jason Star and Bryan Williams's two apiece. The Punisher closes the ledger's own account, defeating Williams to unify the XXX 2nd Title with the CWF-Pro Intercontinental Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 18 reigns in full; all 18 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/xxx-2nd-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: XXX Television Title
titles.epitaph: Opened January 2006 for the XXX brand, when Pimp Daddy won a battle royal eliminating Jack Wu to become its 1st Television Champion. Jason Porn (3) and Tommy Ventura (2) are its most frequent holders across 12 recorded reigns, well over half of them otherwise bare ledger names. Jason Star held the belt when the federation closed that November, the ledger's own last line recording it vacated outright rather than unified into any surviving belt.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 12 reigns in full; all 12 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/xxx-television-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: XXX Title
titles.epitaph: Opened January 2006 for the XXX brand, when Bryan Williams won a battle royal eliminating Bobby Williams to become its 1st XXX Champion. Bryan Williams (4), Bobby Williams (3) and Jason Porn (2) trade the belt for most of its own 15 recorded reigns, roughly a quarter of which survive only as bare ledger names. Mike Powers closes the ledger's own account, defeating Williams to unify the XXX Title with the CWF-Pro Title.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 15 reigns in full; all 15 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/xxx-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: XXX World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Opened alongside its XXX 2nd counterpart in January 2006, when Jason Porn & Jason Sexton won a battle royal eliminating Tuff Luck to become its 1st XXX World Tag Team Champions. The Flash Brothers dominate the belt's own short life, recorded as champions in 17 of its 38 ledger reigns; the Kelly Boys (5) and Corey Matthews & Shawn Hunter (7) account for most of the rest. Beastie Boys II (Beastman & Weirdo) close the ledger's own account, defeating the Flash Brothers to unify the XXX World Tag Team Titles with the CWF-Pro World Tag Team Titles. Just over half its recorded champions — 21 of 38 — survive only as bare team names, no bio page behind them.
titles.notes: CWF-Pro's own served title-history ledger records 38 reigns in full; all 38 are structured into data/reigns.json — see promotions/cwfpro/archive/xxx-world-tag-team-title.html for the underlying primary source.

titles.name: Chris Williams Memorial Cup
titles.epitaph: A floating interfederation tournament rather than any one promotion's own institution, named for Chris Williams, a community handler killed in an automobile accident on 4 May 1999. The Cup's own roll of past champions (its organiser's own "CWMC 'Hall of Fame'" posting, 16 May 2007) opens by naming Jay Phoenix its first-ever champion, of what the roll calls the Chris Williams Television Title, at PWW — a promotion Chris Williams himself worked for as an executive. Three further reigns follow on the same roll, in order and undated: TimeBomb, Cutthroat Chris Hatchett, and Gurgles. No year survives for any of the four. The roll's fifth name, Saij, is the one the surviving record also dates: PTC's own news of 2 December 2003 reports him "winning the Chris Williams Memorial Cup" that year — the same year Jay Phoenix's own PCW and PRIME biography cards instead claim a Cup championship of his own, and the same claim PRIME's ReVolution 197 and SCCW's own record separately inflate to a two-time championship. None of Jay Phoenix's three claims is dated to a specific staging or corroborated by any other federation's record; all three stand recorded against Saij's own dated win, unsettled. A third running, staged by GIWF in 2001 and billed inconsistently on-air as both its second and third annual, names no surviving winner. The tournament's only staging fully held is 2007's: run in Flagstaff, Arizona and organised in-fiction by Jay Phoenix as "the first ever PTC Indy Event," six rounds and a Second Chance Battle Royal wildcard across thirty-four entrants, decided by The Illustrious Face-Eater over Digital Mortality in the final, three judges to none.

titles.name: CWO Amazons Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWO's own women's title, changing hands from Amy Savage to Ms. Rose in a three-way match on EXTREME, 9 April 2006.

titles.name: CWO Amazons Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A new women's tag title, first contested and won by Shadows of Heaven (Angel and Lita Dumas) in a 5-team battle royal at the CWO's own tenth-anniversary pay-per-view, FOREVER, 30 April 2006.

titles.name: CWO Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Born from a unification match that absorbed the CWO Light Heavyweight Championship in September 1999.

titles.name: EWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The invading EWA's own tag team belts, presented in the ring and not recognised by the CWO.
titles.epitaph: The invading EWA's own tag team championship: its leader presented the belts from a metal briefcase to the Pit Bosses on the FEVER of 1 February 2002, the CWO announcers said it would not be recognised, and the Pit Bosses were billed as its champions through 10 February, saying they meant to unify it with the CWO tag titles. One reign on record.

titles.name: CWO EXTREME Championship
titles.epitaph: A new singles title, introduced vacant and won by Prince David Tita in an 11-man pinfall/submission battle royal at FOREVER, 30 April 2006.

titles.name: CWO FEVER Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title tied to the FEVER broadcast, held by Brad Wheatley after the 2006 MADNESS tournament and then by Surge, who defended it against Flame in April 2006.

titles.name: CWO International Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title held by Rt Savage as of April 2006, defended outside a non-title Tables, Ladders and Chairs match he lost to Marc Meredyth.

titles.name: CWO International Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag title defended alongside the CWO World Tag Team Championship, first attested held by the Falconi Brothers and won from them by South Street Riot in a no-tags hardcore match, 8 May 2006.

titles.name: CWO Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested at 240 lbs. and under; Moses held it three times across the year, a fact the fed's own 9 November 1997 HOTLINE corroborates directly ("the Light Heavyweight Championship, which he held three times during the past year").

titles.name: CWO North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's secondary singles belt, changing hands ten times across 1997 and ending the year on Fergus "Whirling Scottish Devil" McTavish.

titles.name: CWO North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's secondary tag title, closing 1997 on Riders on the Storm.

titles.name: CWO Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWO's television title, vacated once for a ten-man battle royal at ST. VALENTINE'S DAY MASSACRE II and closing 1997 on Wildfire.

titles.name: CWO Trios Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-man title reinstated at the federation's own INFERNO pay-per-view, 25 June 2006, first won by Nightrain, Ryan Welfare and Jimmy Page.

titles.name: CWO United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Wholyevil billed himself, in his own Hammerlock News interview, as the reigning CWO United States Champion — the interview is undated in the source and names no opponent or show.

titles.name: CWO Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Created vacant for the 2001 EXTREME MEASURES relaunch and won in a three-way match on the promotion's own 9 May 2001 broadcast, the first title made for the wing's own newly opened women's division.

titles.name: CWO World 6-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-on-three tag title that drops out of the fed's own Rankings ledger after the period ending 27 July 1997 and is not carried into the fed's 1998 continuity -- an honest gap in the record, not a claimed retirement of the belt.

titles.name: CWO World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The CWO's own top belt, tracked week by week across the fed's self-published Rankings ledger from the moment the 1997 corpus opens (Master of Darkness Damion, carried over from 1996) through Lord Hile Troy's title-changing swerve at the CWO Celebration on 14 December 1997, when the operator's own on-screen persona turned on the man he had spent the match seconding.

titles.name: CWO World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top tag title, opening 1997 with the Creatures of the Night (dated on-air to a September 1996 win) and closing it with the Deadly Sins.

titles.name: CWWF Hemisphere Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the surviving record: Cawthorne pinned defending champion JC Ice at CWWF's first pay-per-view. A companion Hemisphere Tag Team Title is named on the same broadcast but was not defended that night, one half of its scheduled challengers sidelined by injury.

titles.name: CWWF Mutant/Sci-Fi Championship
titles.epitaph: The top title of the promotion's own science-fiction-themed sub-brand, first awarded through a tournament in the spring of 1999.

titles.name: CWWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the surviving record, at CWWF's first pay-per-view: Sy Kopath won it from Earl of Doom in a hangman's match.

titles.name: CWWF Television Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the surviving record: the Balls Brothers submitted the defending champions, More Ice, at CWWF's first pay-per-view — a title win that broke up the losing team on the spot.

titles.name: CWWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Havoc across the only surviving CWWF document to name a champion, defended once on record: against the debuting Godzilla, winner of the fed's own 16-cage 'Haunted Arena' gauntlet, at CWWF's first pay-per-view.

titles.name: CWWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Crusher across the only surviving CWWF document to name a champion, retained on record against MC Masters at the fed's first pay-per-view.

titles.name: CZWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Killer92 is named the reigning CZWF Cruiserweight Champion on the fed's own undated Champions page — the belt's own last-attested holder in the held record.

titles.name: CZWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: "Super Crazy" AJ Warner is named the reigning CZWF Hardcore Champion on the fed's own undated Champions page — the belt's own last-attested holder in the held record, alongside a CZWF Intercontinental Championship he won the same night on Monday Night Adrenaline (11-21).

titles.name: CZWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Iron Bull entered Monday Night Adrenaline (11-21) as reigning champion and lost the belt to the Undertaker in a Double Tables Match — the earliest documented state of this title in the held record, sent through a table to lose it. The fed's own home page recap frames the two men's rivalry as ongoing ("a seesaw gone wrong"), and no further title change survives; the Undertaker's win is the held record's last-attested state of the belt.

titles.name: CZWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Rey Mysterio entered Monday Night Adrenaline (11-21) as reigning champion and tapped out to "Super Crazy" AJ Warner's elbow submission hold — the held record's last-attested state of this title, with no start date preserved for Mysterio's own reign.

titles.name: CZWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Hippies are named the reigning CZWF Tag Team Champions on the fed's own undated Champions page — the belt's own last-attested holders in the held record; no member roster survives.

titles.name: CZWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Trish Stratus entered Monday Night Adrenaline (11-21) as reigning champion and tapped out to Chyna's chicken wing after a chair shot opened the match's closing stretch — the held record's last-attested state of this title, with no start date preserved for Stratus's own reign.

titles.name: CZWF X-Division Championship
titles.epitaph: John Cena is named the reigning CZWF X-Division Champion on the fed's own undated Champions page. Andre the Giant earned a No. 1 contendership over Randy Orton on Monday Night Adrenaline (11-21), and the fed's own home page recap previews a still-pending challenge — no result for it survives in the held record.

titles.name: CZWF X Division Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: the Chain Gang are named the reigning CZWF X Division Tag Team Champions on the fed's own undated Champions page — the belt's own last-attested holders in the held record; no member roster survives.

titles.name: Damage Wrestling Federation Blood Bash Title
titles.epitaph: Created as a prize for the Blood Bash '97 rumble but never awarded: winner General Glove chose to challenge for the World Championship instead.

titles.name: Damage Wrestling Federation World Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed champion Tom E. Gunn lost the title to General Glove in a two-out-of-three-falls match on Damage's own Saturday Night Fever of 4 August 1997, the only change recorded in this record.

titles.name: DCW EC Underground Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Defiance Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 3 reigns in its own record. Its first champion is billed under Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling before the title's record continues in Defiance Championship Wrestling.

titles.name: DCW EC Underground Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Defiance Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 3 reigns in its own record. Its first champions are billed under Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling before the titles' record continues in Defiance Championship Wrestling.

titles.name: DCW EC Underground Trios Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Defiance Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 3 reigns in its own record. Its first champions are billed under Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling before the titles' record continues in Defiance Championship Wrestling.

titles.name: DCWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended once in this collection's own record, on 8 June 1997, when its own first-ever DCWL Heavyweight Champion, Tazmanian Crippler, beat back an open challenge from Bon Scott to remain champion.

titles.name: DCWL Unified Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on 8 June 1997 when its own champion, Stagg, publicly vacated the belt on-air and handed it to El Juapo ahead of a token, pre-arranged pinfall.

titles.name: DECW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside the World Championship as a second belt to be decided by tournament the week after DECW's own December 1997 launch; no result survives in this collection's own 1997 holdings.
titles.notes: DECW Monday Night War Hour #2, 23 December 1997: "tournaments for the World Title and US title."

titles.name: DECW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the fed's own December 1997 launch, the belt was put up in a 32-man single-elimination tournament that ran across four live rounds that same month; the final, billed for DECW New Year's Bash 98, falls outside this collection's own 1997 holdings and is not held.
titles.notes: DECW's own December 1997 cards (promotions/decw/archive/).

titles.name: DEWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: "Outsider" Scott Hall's title through most of the fed's 1997 comeback season: won from The Giant on the season-opening show, retained through a stripping attempt by the fed's own (soon-departed) Commissioner, then declared vacant during a gap this project's own partition does not cover, and reclaimed by Hall in a three-way dance on the night a new Commissioner, "Nature Boy" Ric Flair, was installed.

titles.name: DEWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top prize of the Dream Extreme Wrestling Federation's 1997 comeback season, changing hands three times across nine weeks -- Kevin Nash's opening-night win over "The Franchise" Shane Douglas, a mystery-challenger swerve loss to Phil La Fon three weeks on, and Nash's own rematch win back three weeks after that -- before settling into a run of successful Nash defences that closes out this project's own read of the fed's 1997 corpus.

titles.name: DEWF World Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: "The Shadow" Michael Monroe's title for the whole of this project's own read of the fed's 1997 season, successfully defended against a touring Michinoku Pro rookie in August; no loss is recorded in anything this project holds.

titles.name: DEWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won on the fed's 1997 season-opening show by The Razor Boys (Al Perez & Paul Diamond) over Blondes 3:16, then lost two weeks later to The Road Warriors (Hawk & Animal) in a three-way dance also involving Blondes 3:16 -- a reign the Road Warriors were still defending, successfully, when this project's own read of the corpus closes out in October. A separate DEWF Trios Championship is name-checked as already standing (held jointly by The Razor Boys and Diamond Dallas Page) but no dated change for it survives in anything this project holds.

titles.name: DPW Central Valley Championship
titles.epitaph: Created "to pay homage to the CVWF," the predecessor federation whose name lives on in this belt alone. Drac "The Raven" Dravin was awarded it for outlasting a 92-minute Royal Rumble stand in March 1996; by 1997 it belonged to Mr. Robinson, who carried it through an undefeated run the newsgroup's own year-end poll later ranked #16 in all of e-wrestling.

titles.name: DPW Network Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Hollywood in a 16-man "Rage in the Cage" tournament at Motor City Madness (1996); held by Daemon "The Dragon" Dempsey as of the fed's own next newsletter (31 January 1997); billed on Hollywood again by 8 March 1997, defending against The Boogieman in a match this wing's own record does not follow to a confirmed fall.

titles.name: DPW Skyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-limited belt (under 245 pounds) held by the Hitman as of the fed's Motor City Madness PPV in 1996; by the New Year's Bash it belonged to Dan James, defending against King Cobra in a match this wing's own record does not follow to its finish.

titles.name: DPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by an 8-man tournament in 1996 and defended almost continuously into 1997: Steven "The Edge" Spector gave way, untracked, to "Devastator" Mick Morton by New Year's Day 1997, who lost it in turn to "Superstar" Steve Sampson at the uncaptured Broken Hearts PPV (14 February 1997). Sampson was still champion, having just survived a Captain Midnight attack, when this wing's own served record breaks off (8 March 1997); the fed's own founder later stated it closed its doors the following April, merging into PCW.

titles.name: DPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Hardcore Heaven as of Motor City Madness (1996); by the fed's own late-January 1997 newsletter the belts belonged to The New Negaforce, a team sharing its name — but not its full 1996 roster — with an earlier DPW tag team.

titles.name: DPW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top prize in its earlier run, changing hands when the challenger's own ally pulled the champion's legs from under him mid-move.

titles.name: DPW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in a falls-count-anywhere match the champion's own pet donkey helped him win.

titles.name: DPW U.S. Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained against a debuting challenger left burned in the face by an exploding gift box.

titles.name: DPW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man tournament at the federation's 2003 reopening and defended almost every week through the spring of 2004, until its own Prodigy stable turned on its first champion to take it.

titles.name: DPW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Created to crown the winner of the federation's first Royal Rumble and defended through the spring of 2004, changing hands twice on record and at least once more off the record.

titles.name: DPW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a tag tournament at the federation's first New Year's card and, after an unrecorded change of hands, won again by the Wolfpack3000's own Mongs, who held it through the spring of 2004.

titles.name: DPW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in the winter of 2004-05 for the federation's small but growing women's roster and won outright by its first challenger.

titles.name: DSW Diamond Star Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in five months -- won in a Gauntlet Rumble, forfeited, then won again by pinfall -- before settling on its reigning champion as of July 2003.

titles.name: DSW Gemini Titles
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag-team championship, won in April 2003 and, by its own account, suspended soon after for want of an active tag-team division.

titles.name: DSW Shooting Star Title
titles.epitaph: Won in a ladder match in April 2003 and still held by the same champion as of the promotion's own July 2003 rankings.

titles.name: DUWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's own three founding titles, shown vacant in its own Version 1.1 rulebook's ASCII belt art. No card or roster survives in the held record, and no champion is ever named.

titles.name: DUWA Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Weight-limited to 210 pounds; shown vacant in the fed's own Version 1.1 rulebook belt art. No card or roster survives in the held record, and no champion is ever named.

titles.name: DUWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Shown vacant in the fed's own Version 1.1 rulebook belt art. No card or roster survives in the held record, and no champions are ever named.

titles.name: DW Hardcore Title
titles.notes: Named on the federation's own title-history index; its own page was never captured.
titles.epitaph: The third of the three belts the federation listed for itself. Its own hardcore page was captured as a bare shell with no body text at all, and no holder of the championship survives.

titles.name: DW Tag Team Titles
titles.notes: Named on the federation's own title-history index; its own page was never captured.
titles.epitaph: A federation whose largest roster ran to nine names still kept a set of tag team championships on its own title-history index. No team is recorded as having held them, and neither of its announced cards carries a tag match.

titles.name: DW World Title
titles.notes: Named on the federation's own title-history index, which linked a page for it that was never captured.
titles.epitaph: The federation listed it first of three and built it a page. Nobody ever crawled that page, no champion of it is named anywhere in what survives, and both of the cards the fed announced are ordinary matches with no title on the line.

titles.name: DWF Atlantic Storm Title
titles.epitaph: The DWF's secondary singles title, to be defended on every card under a special stipulation. "Cream of the Crop" Mike Waldrop held it when the federation reopened in August 2001.

titles.name: Master of the Ring
titles.epitaph: An open invitational tournament trophy contested across a dozen federations' own talent; Jason Keening won the first edition, Chris Courtade the third, and Victor Frost the seventh.
titles.notes: This collection holds a full broadcast for the tournament's seventh edition and a deciding sixth-edition title match contested on that same broadcast; the first edition's own champion is billed on-air but the tournament that crowned him does not survive here, so no reign is recorded for it.

titles.name: Pentagon Pain
titles.epitaph: A multi-man specialty match run alongside the main tournament; November won its third edition over five other men.
titles.notes: Earlier editions are referenced (this is billed as the third) but do not survive in the held record, so only this reign is recorded.

titles.name: SuperBout
titles.epitaph: An annual grudge-match attraction bout, fought outside the tournament bracket; "Bad Eye" McBaine's seventh-edition win over Eddie Jacobs made him a two-time champion.
titles.notes: Jason Keening is billed on the seventh broadcast as the third SuperBout's own champion, and McBaine as a two-time champion; the second and third editions now survive, contested on the same July 2000 broadcast as the Master of the Ring III tournament final, so three of the seven editions' reigns are recorded.

titles.name: DWO Eastern Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended once cleanly and once controversially across this collection's holdings, changing hands at Holiday Bash when a returning John Jennings' interference backfired on the champion he meant to help.
titles.notes: Source: DWO Holiday Bash (24 Dec 1996, part 2).

titles.name: DWO Final Fight Tournament
titles.epitaph: A one-time, sixteen-man tournament run across the promotion's own last card, its final round an eight-man Thunderdome elimination match.

titles.name: DWO National Championship
titles.epitaph: The only title on the Holiday Bash card to survive the night unchanged, with Apollo turning back Sick Rick's steel-cage challenge in the held record's longest recorded match.
titles.notes: Source: DWO Holiday Bash (24 Dec 1996, parts 3 and 4).

titles.name: DWO World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in a street fight through the streets of Corona, New York, with Havok's Mr. Pink and Guy Stone outlasting The Merchants of Chaos for the belts at Holiday Bash.
titles.notes: Source: DWO Holiday Bash (24 Dec 1996, part 3).

titles.name: DWO Women's Championship
titles.caption: Billed vacant for years before WrestleKade X, where Tiffany won it wrestling under the ring name Phoenix.
titles.epitaph: Vacant for years by the promotion's own account before Phoenix (Tiffany) won it in a bloody, interference-marred match against Iris Galiver at WrestleKade X.

titles.name: DWO World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title changed hands controversially again and again across this collection's own holdings: won, vacated by presidential decree, won again in a rematch marred by the same interference, won a year later in a battle royal, won again from a returning ex-convict in a riot that collapsed the ring, and taken one last time in the promotion's own final match.
titles.notes: Source: DWO Wrestle Mayhem (30 Nov 1996, part 3) and DWO Holiday Bash (24 Dec 1996, parts 1 and 5).

titles.name: DWO Extreme Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own June 2002 Champions page lists the belt without a contender; the same page lists Lethal against the Heavyweight title and Lana Day against the Women's.
titles.epitaph: The belt the fed sold on what it could do to a body: eight inches of glass table, a thirty foot cage, a pit of acid. Switchblade won it on 23 May 2002 and defended it with both men's hands taped and doused in glass. Luke Lawless is a former champion by that autumn, Chryste holds it in the spring of 2003, and Kuff McSlade takes it in the first week of July and keeps it a week later in the main event, barely. By the end of September it is on Sean Quinn and being put on the line beside a title Callisto Bane has just forced another man to vacate.

titles.name: DWO Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Billed the DWO Heavyweight Championship on the fed's own 2002 Champions page and by Primetime Central's own New Era results, and the DWO World Title in the fed's own show scripts from the autumn of 2002 onwards.
titles.epitaph: The top of the fed, and the belt its own Champions page described as brutal to reach and worth beatings to keep. John Miro won it on 21 April 2002 and the record loses it almost at once: AJ Trinidad is champion by that June, Adam Stryker by the autumn, Jackson Rust by the end of October, and none of the three changes is dated anywhere held. Lexis Bane's shutdown emptied it, and a World Title tournament through December 2002 put it back on Kaiowas at the first Travesty of 2003. He lost it on 20 April 2003 at Primetime Central's own New Era supercard, to Donny Diamond, inside the DWO Asylum — the only change in the whole lineage the record dates to the day — and he had it back by 10 July, when the fed's own commentary calls him the DWO World Champion in the middle of losing a non-title match.

titles.name: DWO Intercontinental Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Champions page spells the belt Intercontiental; its own show scripts spell it Intercontinental and call it the IC Title.
titles.epitaph: Third belt down the line and, by its own page's account, no less wanted for it. Angelus won it on 25 March 2002, the earliest dated reign anywhere in the DWO's record. Chryste held it twice and was offered the chance to be a triple champion with it against Adam Stryker's World title; Noah White carries it into 2003; by that July the fed vacates it and books four men to fill it at the pay-per-view. It ends on Damian, and it ends by decree — Callisto Bane made him choose between the belt and a Heavyweight title shot on the fed's own Relentless of 25 September 2003, and he threw it down.

titles.name: DWO Pride Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt the record catches only at the end. The DWO ran a number one contender's match for it on 10 July 2003, and by 9 October Kaos had won that shot and Regin was the champion, sitting on commentary during the challenger's match with, the card warned, every reason to get involved.

titles.name: DWO Rising Dominance Championship
titles.notes: The last-ever claim is Angelus Sorrow's own LOW bio card (promotions/low/archive/angelus-sorrow-bio-card.html), not a DWO document; the DWO record itself never records the reign.
titles.epitaph: A belt for the fed's own lower divisions, filled by bracket: the second set of brackets to name the last two competitors ran on Travesty of 11 April 2003. Carys held it that May. It is the one DWO title whose end the record actually names, and the naming comes from outside — a Lights Out Wrestling bio card of July 2004 lists its wrestler's other-federation honours and calls him the DWO Rising Dominance Champion, last ever.

titles.name: DWO Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Gina Muniz and Angelus held it from 16 May 2002, and the fed ran a number one contendership tag elimination for it at Shock Syndrome that ended in a no contest. Draven won it at UnStAbLe that September and Callisto Bane counted it among UnHoly's holdings the same week. By the spring of 2003 it is on Chryste and Carys, taken off Tyrone Grace's side; by October it is on Damian and Roulette, defending against Hecate and Arsenic. Christmas Chaos held a segment about the belts' own concept sketches, and a promise that whoever the new champions were would defend them the following Travesty.

titles.name: DWO Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt the fed insisted other federations looked down on and its own women did not. Kristi Kiss won it on 23 May 2002 and lost it three weeks later in a ladder match at Shock Syndrome that the fed's own results page could only score as "Winner by ?: Kristi Kiss.. Lana Day.. Jaslene Myst..." — Lana Day pinned Kristi Kiss for it, Jaslene Myst took it off Lana Day, and Kristi Kiss won it back without a pinfall. The fed's own newsdesk reported three women holding a claim to one belt and its officials stumped. Nothing held says how it was resolved.

titles.name: DYNASTY Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Reserved for wrestlers 227 pounds and under; no champion is ever attested in the surviving record.

titles.name: DYNASTY Icon Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top prize, carried by its only recorded champion into a return that was never confirmed to air.

titles.name: DYNASTY Icon Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Planned around an eight- or sixteen-team tournament that never reached a recorded result.

titles.name: DYNASTY North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's own endurance title; no champion is ever attested in the surviving record.

titles.name: DZW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the promotion's own opening tournament and settled twice across its served run: once by a champion who sold it outright on camera, once by a surprise entrant backflipping away from the floor with a half-second to spare.

titles.name: EAPW Flyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding constitution (245 lb limit); no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: EAPW National Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A combined APWA/EAPW unification belt; TK Maniac defeats the champion, Pipe Bomb, in the fed's own debut match.

titles.name: EAPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding constitution; no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: EAPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding constitution; no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: EAST World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top prize of EAST Wrestling, awarded vacant on the promotion's own rebranded debut broadcast.

titles.name: EAW Australian National Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: EAW crowned its first, and in the surviving record only, Australian National Heavyweight Champion at its own Mayhem supercard on 1 May 2008: John "Mad Dog" Murphy, winning a Four Corners 30 Minute Iron Man Match over Matt Carter, Santino Romano and Bryan Willett. He carried the belt into EAW's own first Lights Out Cage Match two months later, a title defense in all but name against Willett that ended in a double ten-count draw after Dollar's own interference — the last the surviving record shows of the championship or its own champion.

titles.name: EBWF European Championship
titles.epitaph: The Title History opens this belt with “Started W/The Rock” on Smackdown, 18 March 2004 — the same night it retires the Multicontinental US Championship with The Rock holding that one too. Twenty-three reigns follow in two and a half years: Mark Jindrak, Booker T, Ric Flair, Petey Williams, Shane Helms and Kane each take it twice. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the Iron Man Championship, on the same night Kane won it, and his reign carries into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-iron-man
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “European Title renamed Iron Man Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”, printed directly above Kane's own win at the same card.

titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “European Title”, in the rename entry. Whether the Multicontinental US lineage passed into this belt on 18 March 2004, or simply ended as this one began, is not stated anywhere read.

titles.name: EBWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Tommy Dreamer held it first, from 15 April 2002, and took it three times in its opening year. Fifty-seven reigns ran through it in four and a half years, faster than any other EBWF belt changed hands: The Hurricane took it four times across 2004 and 2005, Cactus Jack, Chris Benoit and David Flair three each. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the No Limits Championship, with Raven's own reign running through the change and on into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-no-limits
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Hardcore Title renamed No Limit Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History carries this lineage under the No Limits name, which it writes as “Hardcore Title” only in the rename entry itself; no page read gives the belt a longer name than that.

titles.name: EBWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: HHH opened it on 11 April 2002 and held it five separate times through December 2002, more than anyone else took it. Vampiro's four reigns run from November 2004 to February 2007, the last of them won in a tournament after the belt had been vacated. Christian took it three times and Randy Orton three, and Bret Hart held it twice in 2003. The Miz's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 closes its own record, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

titles.name: EBWF Iron Man Championship
titles.epitaph: The European Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006, the night Kane won it. Triple H took it from him on Aggression that October, and lost it at Survivor Series on 26 November 2006 without wrestling for it: the Title History records Rene Dupree beating Shawn Michaels, who was defending the title on Triple H's behalf. Dupree held it for the rest of its run, until the belt was retired on Aggression on 1 November 2007.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Belt Retired - Aggression - Thursday, November 1, 2007”, the same night it retires the Television Championship.

titles.name: EBWF LHW Championship
titles.epitaph: Christian held it first, from 15 April 2002, and Lita took it from him that May — the one reign a woman holds on this belt's record. Rey Mysterio Jr. and The Hurricane traded it through 2003, three reigns to four, and it was emptied twice in 2002, at Unforgiven that September and on Smackdown that November. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the X-Division Championship, with Syxx's own reign running through the change and on into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-x-division
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “LHW Title renamed X-Divsion Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “LHW Title”, in the rename entry, and no page read spells the abbreviation out.

titles.name: EBWF Multicontinental US Championship
titles.epitaph: The Rock held it first, from 11 April 2002, and last: he took it a third time at Wrestlemania on 14 March 2004 and the Title History retires the belt with him four nights later, on the same Smackdown it opens the European Championship with him. Twenty-one reigns run between: Stone Cold Steve Austin took it three times in 2002 and 2003, Bret Hart and Christian twice each. It is one of three EBWF belts whose whole record ends before the promotion did.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Retired W/The Rock - Smackdown - Thursday, March 18, 2004” — the same entry date on which it opens the European Championship with “Started W/The Rock”.

titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). Two stretches of this belt's own history are printed out of their own date order (August 2002 and June 2003); the rows follow the dates the page itself gives. Its August 2002 entries place two Christian reigns back to back with no loss between them, which the page does not resolve.

titles.name: EBWF No Limits Championship
titles.epitaph: The Hardcore Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 with Raven still holding it. Raven's reign ran on until the belt was emptied over his own inactive status, and Sting won it from the vacancy in a battle royal at Aftermath on 29 April 2007. Triple H took it from him at Death Before Dishonor that July and it was vacated again on Warfare on 15 October 2007. Lacey's win at Survivor Series on 25 November 2007 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names her champion.

titles.name: EBWF People's Championship
titles.epitaph: Kane held it first, from 15 April 2002. John Cena took it five times between 2003 and 2005 and Booker T four in 2002 and 2003; Kurt Angle and Chris Jericho — billed on this belt's record as Y2J Chris Jericho — traded it five times between them across the winter of 2004. Two of its forty-nine reigns began on the same night, 4 October 2004, when Christian and then The Undertaker each held it, and The Undertaker's own retirement emptied it two days later. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the Television Championship, with Alex Shelley's own reign running through the change.

events.title: ebwf-2001-television
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “People's Title renamed Television Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “People's Title”, in the rename entry.

titles.name: EBWF Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: The Hulkamaniacs — The Undertaker and Hulk Hogan — held it first, from 15 April 2002, lost it at Backlash that month and took it back a week later. Team 3:16, The Rock and Stone Cold Steve Austin, took it three times in 2002 alone. Six of its forty-five reigns changed hands on storyline rather than in a match: four between August 2005 and March 2006, as injuries and a retirement moved half the championship between Shannon Moore, Wes Ikeda, Jeff Hardy and Scotty 2 Hotty, and two more in 2007, when Syxx and then Jeff Hardy vacated their own halves and the other holder kept his. D-Generation X's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 is the last change the whole Title History records, of any EBWF belt.
titles.notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). Two reigns are printed with one name on both sides (“Raven & Raven”, 14 December 2003; “Bret Hart & Bret Hart”, 25 May 2003); they are recorded as printed.

titles.name: EBWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The People's Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 while Alex Shelley held it. Randy Orton took it from him at the King of the Ring in June 2007 and Lance Storm took it at Destiny that September. Storm held it until the belt was retired on Aggression on 1 November 2007, the same night as the Iron Man Championship.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Belt Retired - Aggression - Thursday, November 1, 2007”.

titles.name: EBWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Molly Holly held it first, from 15 April 2002. Torrie Wilson took it eight times over four years, Lita and Stacy Keibler five each, across fifty-two reigns. Lita's last ended without a match: the Title History records her retiring with the belt at Backlash on 30 April 2006 and giving it to Kristal, who is listed as champion from that December. The reign before hers ended in the one vacancy the page explains by a handler leaving the promotion. Jillian Hall's win at Aftermath on 27 April 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names her champion.

titles.name: EBWF World Heavy Weight Championship
titles.epitaph: Kurt Angle won it vacant on 15 April 2002, the earliest date the promotion's own record carries, and it changed hands forty-eight times across six years. Raven took it nine times between June 2002 and April 2004, more often than anyone else; Christian took it seven times, once in 2002 and six more across 2005 and 2006. It emptied four times — in June 2002, after the King of the Ring in June 2004, in November 2005, and on 1 September 2006, the day after Chris Jericho won it, when his own retirement ended a reign one day old. Triple H's win at Wrestlemania 7 on 30 March 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

titles.name: EBWF X-Division Championship
titles.epitaph: The LHW Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 with Syxx still holding it. Thirteen reigns follow in under two years, seven of them inside 2008 alone — one of those won by Val Venis at a house show on 8 January, two days after the belt had been vacated at another. Ron Killings and Paul London took it twice each that spring. Rob Van Dam's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

titles.name: ECEW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held jointly by the real-wrestler personas Sting and Hogan as of the wing's own last surviving document; no title-change record survives.

titles.name: ECW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in the promotion's own first parking-lot brawl on 24 June 1999.

titles.name: ECW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on 24 June 1999 when the promotion's own then-champion lost by submission less than a week into his reign.

titles.name: ECW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in an eight-man battle royal on the federation's only surviving broadcast (18 February 1996) and won by Hack Myers, the last man standing.

titles.name: ECW Dudleyville Hardcore Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Dudley Boyz's own belt, which they declare on Blood, Sweat and Beers the night after Summer Assylum in July 2007, when the Dudley family bring out the old World Tag Team Championships, "back from when Bubba and I were dominating anything that stood in our path", and D-Von says they are rechristened the Dudleyville Hardcore Titles, because Paul Heyman will not give them a fair crack at the Whole F**kin' Show's belts; the diary's own title history (PDF p.8, 'ECW/Dudleyville Hardcore Tag Team Championship') does list it, dating the Dudley Boyz's first reign from 28 July 2007. The Dudley Boyz make their first defence on Revolution in August 2007, beating the bWo with a 3D on Hollywood Nova after Chessman and Oz hit the bWo with the belts, and beat Balls & Axl, who beat the Samoan Gangstas to earn the match, with a 3D on Axl on Blood, Sweat and Beers; the Hardcore Innovators challenge for them at Heatwave on 24 August 2007 and Los Guerreros are billed as third challengers, so the Dudleyz are still the holders when the pages of August 2007's first week end. At Heatwave in August 2007 the Hardcore Innovators, Cactus Jack and Tommy Dreamer, win the belts from the Dudley Boyz in the Dudleyville Hardcore Championship Match, the Dudleyz having defended them earlier that month against Los Guerreros, the Samoan Gangstas and the Briscoe Boys; Joey Styles says the Dudleyville Hardcore Championship has become the ECW Hardcore Championship, and the diary's later posts call the belts the ECW Hardcore Tag Team Championship, 'newly rechristened'. The Innovators ask the holders of the World Tag Team Championship for a Champions versus Champions match at Anarchy Rulz and are still the holders when the pages of September 2007's fourth Monday end. At Guilty As Charged in October 2007 the Dudley Boyz win the Three Way Dance for the tag titles and take the Dudleyville belts back from the Hardcore Innovators (26 October); the Innovators leave the arena with all four belts anyway, and the history lists the Dudleyville belt's unification with the World Tag Team Championship on 30 November 2007, still ahead. In November 2007 the Innovators still carry the Dudleyville belts with the others; Paul Heyman announces that they are to be unified with the World Tag Team Championship at November To Remember XV. At November To Remember XV the Dudley Boyz beat the Hardcore Innovators, and the Dudleyville belts are unified with the World Tag Team Championship on 30 November 2007, the date the history gives.

titles.name: ECW International All Action Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt exclusive to Revolution, announced on the first Revolution of August 2006 for a month-long tournament of fast-paced wrestlers; Jushin Lyger, Ultimo Dragon, Yoshihiro Tajiri and Psicosis are the names the commentary gives for it. Tajiri beats Lyger in the final at Heatwave to become the first champion and keeps the belt over Super Dragon on Revolution after Heatwave. Tajiri keeps the belt until Anarchy Rulz, where Jushin Lyger wins the Triangle Match with AJ Styles and him; The Great Sasuke takes it from Lyger at Guilty As Charged and loses it to Vito on F' The Mainstream a week later, and Vito keeps it over Chris Daniels on Revolution. Vito loses the belt to Christopher Daniels at November To Remember in the Stairway To Hell Match with Super Crazy, when Daniels hangs on to the harness as the ladder collapses and drops to the floor with the belt; Daniels keeps it over Michael Shane at Got Blood? and is still champion when the pages of February 2007 end. The diary's own title history omits Daniels's reign and lists Vito as champion until 28 February 2007, so the history and the text of the shows disagree; both are recorded, and the reign dates follow the text. At Living Dangerously on 28 February 2007, the date the history gives for CM Punk's win, Punk takes the belt from Christopher Daniels in the Triangle Match with Michael Shane when Raven hits Daniels with a chair, so on that date the history and the text of the shows agree even though the history leaves Daniels out; Punk pins Daniels again with a low blow on Blood, Sweat and Beers and is champion when the pages of April 2007 end, with Lance Storm, who won an International All Action title shot in the Stairway To Hell match at Baptism Of Fire, set to challenge him at Cyberslam. At Cyberslam CM Punk keeps the belt over Lance Storm in the No Way Out Match with a GTS while the masked man traps Abyss and Vito outside, and at Hardcore Heaven he keeps it over Storm again with a GTS after Monsters Inc chokeslam Storm onto Abyss's knee; Punk is champion when the pages of June 2007's second week end. On Revolution in June 2007 CM Punk knocks out Paul Burchill and Shane Douglas with the belt, and at Wrestlepalooza and Summer Assylum Vito Thomaselli turns on him and powerbombs him through a table; the belt is not defended in the range, and Punk is champion when the pages of August 2007's first week end, with the history's 29 September 2007 end still ahead. At Heatwave in August 2007 CM Punk hits Paul Burchill with the belt and Vito Thomaselli with a GTS; in September he defends the belt for the first time in months, keeping it over Lance Storm, Big Sasuke Cool and Eddie Guerrero, and Vito Thomaselli is booked against him at Anarchy Rulz, with the history's 29 September 2007 end still ahead. At Anarchy Rulz in September 2007 Vito Thomaselli pins CM Punk with a Crucifix Roll-Up (29 September in the history); at Guilty As Charged CM Punk wins the Last Man Standing Match when referee Jim Molineaux stops it, with Monsters Inc. at ringside (26 October), and he keeps the belt over Lance Storm on Blood, Sweat and Beers. On the first Revolution of November 2007 Paul Heyman has about fifteen security guards strip Punk of the belt ('it ain't yours anymore', 3 November in the history) and starts the International All Action Title Tournament, open to 'hard working, respectful talent'. The first-round winners are Ricky Marvin (over Kensuke Sasaki), Teddy Hart (over Psicosis), Slyk Tayshaun Dudley (over Scorpio Sky) and Excalibur (over Paul London); in the semi-finals Slyk beats Teddy Hart and Ricky Marvin beats Excalibur, and the final, Ricky Marvin against Slyk Tayshaun Dudley, is on the card of November To Remember XV. Ricky Marvin beats Slyk Tayshaun Dudley in the final at November To Remember XV (30 November 2007 in the history) after Big Dick Jr. interferes against his own cousin, and is the new champion; the Code of Diminishing Extremes sets the title to lucha libre rules, with a twenty count and two falls out of three.

titles.name: ECW Lioness Championship
titles.epitaph: The first Lioness Championship, crowned at Anarchy Rulz in September 2007 in a Lioness' Den Match between Jazz, Kelly Thomaselli and Alexis Laree: Alexis Laree wins by rolling up Kelly Thomaselli and hooking her tights, and the diary's own title history lists her as the champion, 'present'. She keeps the belt on Revolution and Blood, Sweat and Beers over Daizy Dudley, Beulah McGillicutty, Traci and Mika Akino, and at Guilty As Charged over Jazz when a new member of Raven's Nest, Nattie Neidhart, runs in and the two of them hit a Double DDT; she is still the champion when the pages of October 2007 end. In November 2007 she and Nathalie lose a Lioness Pack Match to Jazz and Kelly Thomaselli, and on the last Revolution before November To Remember XV she pins Jazz in a non-title match after Nathalie hits Jazz with the belt; Kelly Thomaselli challenges her for the title, and the diary's preview of the card bills Kelly Thomaselli against Alexis, the champion. At November To Remember XV Alexis beats Kelly Thomaselli in the Lioness match with Nathalie's belt shot, and on Revolution and the Saturday show of the first week of December over Mika Akino; Kong, back 'from APW' with Prince Nana, flattens her with a Sit-out Powerbomb, and the diary's next preview books Kong and Akino against Alexis and Nathalie.

titles.name: ECW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of the diary's ECW. Its own title history opens on Shane Douglas's second reign, won in March 1994 and running when the game world leaves real events in July 1994, and the shows of the first ten are set inside Raven's reign that ran from 23 November 2005 to 26 September 2006; Raven is the billed champion at Wrestlepalooza, where he keeps it over Goldberg. Raven keeps the belt through the pages of July, August and September 2006: he retains at Summer Assylum when Shawn Michaels interferes against Paul Burchill, and at Heatwave he sides with Charlie Pag and Paul Burchill and keeps it over Goliath with their help. Raven's reign ends at Anarchy Rulz on 26 September 2006 by the diary's title history, when Shawn Michaels superkicks him in a five-on-five brawl and pins him; Michaels loses the belt back to Raven at Guilty As Charged, in the Triangle Match with Rob Van Dam, after Stephanie Mcintosh lowblows him. At Masters Of Pain on 29 December 2006 by the diary's title history Sabu takes the belt from Raven with a Triple Jump Moonsault after Zakk Wylde punches the champion; Sabu keeps it over Cactus Jack at Got Blood? and is still champion when the pages of February 2007 end. At Living Dangerously Sabu keeps the belt over Steve Austin and Raven then hits him with an Evenflow DDT; the next night on Blood, Sweat and Beers Raven beats Sabu for it with Paul Burchill's and Goliath's help (the diary's own history prints Sabu's reign as ending, and Raven's sixth as starting, on "29 February 2007", which is not a calendar date, so the change is filed at month precision), and keeps it over Shane Douglas at Baptism Of Fire on 29 March 2007 with CM Punk's interference; Raven is still champion when the pages of April 2007 end, with Paul Burchill, who won the Baptism Of Fire match, due a title shot at Hardcore Heaven. At Cyberslam Raven keeps the belt over Rhino in the Steel Cage Match when Paul Burchill, the special referee, counts fast and calls a submission Rhino never gave, after which Burchill turns on Raven with a C-4 (on the next Blood, Sweat and Beers Burchill and Shane Douglas, the masked man, tell how the plan ran for seven months); at Hardcore Heaven, in a match that is not for the title, Raven beats Burchill after CM Punk threatens to throw Kelly Thomaselli off the stage, so that Burchill may never challenge for the belt; Raven's sixth reign continues in the diary's history and is still going when the pages of June 2007's second week end, with Owen Hart booked to challenge him at Wrestlepalooza and Bret Hart in a Triangle Match for the belt. At Wrestlepalooza in June 2007 Raven keeps the belt in the elimination Triangle Match with Bret and Owen Hart, then is Chokeslammed by the mystery signing, Mark Calaway; on Blood, Sweat and Beers Paul Heyman forces Raven into a non-title match against Vito Thomaselli, and Calaway's Chokeslam lets Vito pin the champion. At Summer Assylum (Friday, week 4, July 2007) Raven keeps the belt over Calaway when Rhino Gores Calaway; Raven is still champion when the pages of August 2007's first week end, with the history's date for the reign's end, 1 October 2007, still ahead. At Heatwave in August 2007 Vito Thomaselli beats Raven in the Barbed Wire Cage Match and is presented with the belt, but on the next Blood, Sweat and Beers Raven reads out a clause of the contract that voids any title change after outside interference, and says the belt is still his; Rhino wins the first Buck Stops Here Match at Heatwave and is booked against Raven at Anarchy Rulz, with the history's date for the reign's end, 1 October 2007, still ahead. At Anarchy Rulz in September 2007 Raven beats Rhino with Mark Calaway's help and is then chokeslammed by Calaway; on the first Revolution of October Owen Hart makes him tap to the Sharpshooter after Chris Jericho's chair shot and is the champion (1 October). Owen retires after Guilty As Charged, where Chris Jericho wins the Ultimate Submission Match on a ruling that his tap came after the time limit and loses the belt minutes later when Raven, using the Commissioner's right to book one match of his choosing at a pay-per-view, pins him with a Raven Effect (26 October); the company's owner then strips Raven of his powers as Commissioner and books Paul Burchill against him for November To Remember XV. In November 2007 Paul Heyman, back in power, tells Raven on Revolution that nobody in the arena is comfortable seeing him as the champion and that Paul Burchill will beat him at November To Remember; on the third Blood, Sweat and Beers he makes the match a Loser Leaves ECW Match, with anyone outside it who touches either man to be fired, and says that the man who stays will be the Undisputed ECW World Heavyweight Champion. Raven is still the champion when the diary's preview of the card ends. Raven loses the Loser Leaves ECW Match to Paul Burchill at November To Remember XV (30 November 2007 in the history) and leaves ECW; Burchill is the new champion and, on the Saturday show, defends under the Code of Diminishing Extremes' modified British rules (twelve five-minute rounds, two falls out of three); CM Punk, now the leader of Raven's Nest, loses to him in a non-title match, and Rhino, who gores Burchill twice and beats Vito Thomaselli in a number one contendership match, is booked against him at Masters of Pain.

titles.name: ECW World Tag Team Championship
aka: Undisputed ECW World Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: The pair of belts the Dudley Boys hold in the diary's first ten shows, in a reign its own title history dates from 23 May 2006 to 2 August 2006. They beat the Hardy Boys for them on the first show and again on the eighth, and the ring announcer bills both as title matches. The Hardy Boys win the belts in the opening match of the first July post, with Brock Lesnar's help, and the Dudley Boys win them back for what the commentary calls their tenth reign; after Heatwave Raven and Paul Burchill take them, and Big Stevie Cool and Hollywood Nova take them from Raven and Burchill. The Blue World Order keep the belts through the autumn, beating Burchill and Abyss at Anarchy Rulz, until Abyss and Goliath, as Monsters Inc., take them from the bWo at Guilty As Charged. The Whole F**kin' Show, Rob Van Dam and Shawn Michaels, take the belts from Monsters Inc. at November To Remember on 26 November 2006 by the diary's title history, keep them against Monsters Inc. at Got Blood? and on Revolution in February, and are still champions when the pages of February 2007 end. The Iron Saints, Salvatore and Brandon Thomaselli, take the belts from the Whole F**kin' Show at Living Dangerously on 28 February 2007 by the diary's title history, with a Spike Powerbomb on Shawn Michaels after Rob Van Dam steps off the apron, and lose them at Baptism Of Fire on 29 March 2007 in the first Halflife Handicap match, when Rob Van Dam and Shawn Michaels win with a Five Star Frog Splash on Salvatore; the Whole F**kin' Show are champions when the pages of April 2007 end. At Cyberslam the Whole F**kin' Show keep the belts over Los Increibles in the Ladder Match when Rob Van Dam pulls them down; at Hardcore Heaven they keep them over the Canadian Connection, who won the three-way dance for the number one contendership at Cyberslam, when Shawn Michaels, bloodied and alone while Rob Van Dam runs to help Traci, pins Christian with a third Sweet Chin Music; the champions quarrel through June but are still champions when the pages of June 2007's second week end. At Wrestlepalooza in June 2007 the Whole F**kin' Show keep the belts over the Hardcore Innovators with simultaneous covers; the Dudley Boyz, returned to ECW, win the number one contendership, and at Summer Assylum the champions beat them in the Tables Match with Shawn Michaels's Sweet Chin Music through a table; they are still champions when the pages of August 2007's first week end, with the history's 26 October 2007 date for the reign's end still ahead. After Heatwave in August 2007 the Whole F**kin' Show attack the new holders of the Dudleyville Hardcore Titles, the Hardcore Innovators; in September they keep the belts over the Dudley Boyz on Revolution, and the Innovators ask for a Champions versus Champions match at Anarchy Rulz, with the history's 26 October 2007 date for the reign's end still ahead. At Guilty As Charged in October 2007 the Dudley Boyz win the Ladders, Chairs, Canes and Flaming Tables Three Way Dance from the Whole F**kin' Show, whose partners fall out when Shawn Michaels's Super Kick takes down Rob Van Dam, and from the Hardcore Innovators; the history lists the Dudley Boyz's reign, their ninth, from 26 October to 4 November 2007. In November 2007 the Innovators still carry all four belts to the ring; Paul Heyman announces the Undisputed ECW Tag Team belts and a match at November To Remember XV in which the Dudley Boyz and the Hardcore Innovators unify the titles, and the diary's preview of the card bills that match with the Dudley Boyz as the champions. At November To Remember XV (30 November 2007 in the history) the Dudley Boyz beat the Hardcore Innovators and raise the Undisputed ECW Tag Team Titles, the belts the diary calls the first unified ones; on Revolution on the first Monday of December the titles change hands in a restarted Three Way Dance: Slyk Tayshaun Dudley and Big Dick Dudley Jr. win them when Slyk makes Bubba Ray tap to the Boston Crabs, and they keep them over Thomaselli-Thomaselli '08 on the Saturday show. The history lists the Second Generation of Dudleyz as the champions from 4 November 2007, a date that the text does not agree with: the order of the shows is the text's, the dates are the history's.

titles.name: ECW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt Chris Jericho carries through the diary's first ten shows, in a reign that its own title history dates from 23 November 2005 to 8 August 2006. He keeps it over Lance Storm, Doug Williams, Bryan Danielson and Cactus Jack, and again on the tenth show, where the commentary counts his reign as entering its seventh month. Chris Jericho keeps the belt through the pages of July, then loses it to Rhino on 8 August 2006 by the diary's title history, wins it back a week later, and loses it again to Rhino in the Triangle Match with Christian at Heatwave. Rhino keeps the belt until Anarchy Rulz, where the returning Shane Douglas beats him for it; Kensuke Sasaki takes it from Douglas at Guilty As Charged and still holds it when the pages of November 2006 end. Vito Thomaselli takes the belt from Kensuke Sasaki on the debut Blood, Sweat and Beers on 4 December 2006 by the diary's title history, when Francine lowblows Sasaki; Vito keeps it through December and January with Francine's help and then the New Age Enterprise's, until Bret Hart beats him for it with the Sharpshooter on Blood, Sweat and Beers on 6 February 2007; Bret Hart is champion when the pages of February 2007 end. Paul Burchill takes the belt from Bret Hart at Living Dangerously on 28 February 2007 by the diary's title history, with a clean C-4 after he sends the New Age Enterprise away, and loses it back to Bret Hart on Blood, Sweat and Beers on 22 March 2007 when his knee gives way; Bret Hart loses it to Chris Jericho in the Triangle Match with Christian on Blood, Sweat and Beers on 15 April 2007, and Jericho is champion when the pages of April 2007 end, with Rob Van Dam booked to challenge him at Cyberslam. At Cyberslam on 24 April 2007 by the diary's title history Rob Van Dam takes the belt from Chris Jericho in the Lumberjack Match, when Shawn Michaels Superkicks Jericho off the ropes while Christian is held at ringside and a Five Star Frog Splash wins; at Hardcore Heaven on 29 May 2007 AJ Styles, who debuted in May, takes it from Van Dam with the Canadian Connection's hockey sticks and a Styles Clash while Michaels is away from ringside; Styles is champion when the pages of June 2007's second week end, having beaten Rey Mysterio Jr. with a low blow and lost a non-title match to Juventud Guerrera. On Revolution in June 2007 AJ Styles beats Juventud Guerrera with a low blow and the Styles Clash, and at Wrestlepalooza he keeps the belt over Guerrera with another Styles Clash after pushing Guerrera's foot off the rope while the referee does not see it; at Summer Assylum he keeps it a third time when Francine's pretended turn lets Guerrera hit Styles with a low blow and Christopher Daniels hits Guerrera with the belt; Styles is champion when the pages of August 2007's first week end, with Guerrera's challenge for Heatwave still unanswered and Ultimo Dragon billed against him on the next Revolution, so the history's 28 September 2007 end is still ahead. At Heatwave in August 2007 AJ Styles keeps the belt in the Stairway To Hell Match, in which Juventud Guerrera, challenging with his mask at stake, loses the mask; in September Styles beats Jerry Lynn on Blood, Sweat and Beers, and Ultimo Dragon is booked against him at Anarchy Rulz, so the history's 28 September 2007 end is still ahead. At Anarchy Rulz in September 2007 Ultimo Dragon pins AJ Styles with an Asai DDT after Francine's interference (28 September); at Guilty As Charged AJ Styles wins the four-way Stairway To Hell Match by pulling the belt from the strap above the ring (26 October), and Juventud Guerrera storms in with a chair. In November 2007 Styles keeps the belt over Juventud Guerrera on Blood, Sweat and Beers when the referee misses Guerrera's foot on the rope, and over Rey Mysterio Jr. on Revolution, and loses it on Revolution on the last Monday of the month (26 November) when Guerrera rolls through his Spiral Tap into a pin, for his first title in ECW. Paul Heyman has announced a newly designed belt and a title match at November To Remember XV against the winner of a three-way match, Ultimo Dragon, who is hurt in it (an EMT says 'a cracked sternum'); in a backstage scene the company's owner and Heyman ask Rey Mysterio Jr. to wear Dragon's mask and compete as Ultimo Dragon (PDF pp.1654-1655), and the history lists Guerrera as the champion, 'present'. Juventud Guerrera keeps the belt at November To Remember XV over Ultimo Dragon, whom Francine's lowblow and DDT leave open to a 450 Splash, over The Great Sasuke on the Saturday show and over Eddie Guerrero on Revolution on the first Monday of December; Christopher Daniels is booked against him next, and the history lists Guerrera as the champion, 'present'.

titles.name: ECWA Tag Team Championship

titles.notes: ECWA's own founding post, 3 September 1997: "the tag team titles will be decided this weekend on SMASH!"

titles.name: ECWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Tommy Van Dam as of the fed's own September 1997 launch, a reign corroborated the same month by a third-party dream-match card staging him beating SPWA's own World Champion. Two other names are billed elsewhere in the held record as former holders -- Kevin Kage, before moving on to run RCW, and "Madness" Kaine Merson, later a manager in another fed's storyline -- but no document recovered here sequences either against Van Dam's own reign.
titles.notes: ECWA's own founding post, 3 September 1997.

titles.name: EEF European Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: The fed's own top title; won by Josef "The Cavalier" Tadeuscz in a 15-man tournament at The Grand European, vacant by December, then won by "Normal" Klaus Lehman in a twelve-man battle royal at Survival of the Fittest.
titles.epitaph: EEF European Heavyweight Championship of EEF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: EEF German Championship
titles.caption: Held by "Classic" Andrew Archer; a rival claimant bills himself the 'Real GERMAN CHAMPION' by December, a disputed lineage carried not resolved.
titles.epitaph: EEF German Championship of EEF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: EEF Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: First won by The Monarchy, beating the Italian Stallions in the Grand European final.
titles.epitaph: EEF Tag Team Championship of EEF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: EEF Transcontinental Championship
titles.caption: A fourth EEF belt, named in the December PPV's own roll-call; no reign is attested in the held record.
titles.epitaph: EEF Transcontinental Championship of EEF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: EEMW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Declared for himself by the league's own founder, BLAZE, on its first show, unopposed for as long as the corpus survives.

titles.name: EGWF Rocky Mountain Championship
titles.epitaph: Senator Johnson pinned Ares for the title on EGWF Saturday Night, the fed's own build show for its first PPV, Armegedon -- despite Rainman's own interference against Johnson mid-match. A companion sighting on a rival fed's (EHWF's) own results show independently corroborates this title's existence.

titles.name: EGWF Rocky Mountain Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Studly's won the tag title from the Irish Inmates in a No-DQ match on EGWF Saturday Night, a chaotic finish with an uncredited interferer taking out most of both teams before the fall.

titles.name: Extreme Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on camera in March, passed unseen to a wrestler who later quit the federation mid-show, and was awarded a second time to the winner of the federation's own year-end battle royal.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by three different teams across three surviving cards, twice retained by disqualification or restart rather than changing hands cleanly.

titles.name: Extreme Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in the surviving record, once on camera by a fan-supplied chair shot and once by an undocumented transition, and was still held when the collection's own record ends.

titles.name: US Title
titles.epitaph: Created at the federation's own year-end battle royal and awarded, in the same match, alongside the vacant Extreme Internet Championship.

titles.name: Extreme World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the same wrestler for the whole of the surviving record, called "the Internet championship" once and "the Extreme World Title" thereafter by the federation's own inconsistent usage.

titles.name: TNM World Title
titles.epitaph: Decided in a hosted, cross-federation tournament EIWF ran across four December 1997 broadcasts, UPS winning the final over Blueline Basher Lund -- disputed the same night by a rival claimant, "Darkside" Tim Johns, who billed himself the undefeated champion from an earlier, unresolved tournament outside this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: EIWZ European Title
