titles.epitaph: Havok won a tournament final over Pain to claim the belt at Christmas Bash 1998 and retained it against Annihilator five days later — the only two documented moments in this title's own surviving lineage. CWF-Pro's own already-served Canadian Title ledger later records the belt unified into its own, defeating Havok in the process, years after the events held here.

titles.name: EIWZ Extreme Title
titles.epitaph: Pain won the belt in a ten-man Royal Rumble main event at Christmas Bash 1998 and retained it against Jazz five days later — the only two documented moments in this title's own surviving lineage. CWF-Pro's own already-served Ultra Extreme Hardcore Title ledger later records the belt unified into its own, defeating Pain in the process, years after the events held here.

titles.name: EIWZ Light Weight Title
titles.epitaph: Necromancer won an eleven-man Royal Rumble to claim the belt at Christmas Bash 1998 and retained it against The Creep five days later — the only two documented moments in this title's own surviving lineage. CWF-Pro's own already-served Royal Title ledger later records the belt unified into its own, defeating Necromancer in the process, years after the events held here.

titles.name: EIWZ North American Title
titles.epitaph: Flint won the belt via disqualification over Jazz at Christmas Bash 1998 and lost it to Triple X five days later — the only two documented moments in this title's own surviving lineage. CWF-Pro's own already-served Intercontinental Title ledger later records the belt unified into its own, defeating Flint in the process, years after the events held here.

titles.name: EIWZ Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Cool Moe "D" and SCSU Pimpster won the belts in a Royal Rumble-style tag match at Christmas Bash 1998, the only documented moment in this title's own surviving lineage. CWF-Pro's own already-served World Tag Team Titles ledger later records the belts unified into its own, defeating the pair in the process, years after the event held here.

titles.name: EPW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Established for Black Dawn (2004) alongside the World Heavyweight Championship. The title history document itself carries the reign line through a 2013 hiatus; reigns are recorded here only through 14 November 2009.

titles.name: EPW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created April-May 2005 per the fed's own announcement and first awarded by tournament at Black Dawn 2005. The title history document itself carries the reign line through a 2013 hiatus; reigns are recorded here only through 14 November 2009.

titles.name: EPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Established for Black Dawn (2004), the promotion's own first pay-per-view. The title history document itself (fwrestling.com forum 342) carries the reign line through a 2014 hiatus; reigns are recorded here only through 14 November 2009.

titles.name: EPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Established for Black Dawn (2004) alongside the World Heavyweight and Intercontinental Championships. The title history document itself carries the reign line through a 2014 hiatus; reigns are recorded here only through 14 November 2009.

titles.name: EMWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Known only from a single holder: the community's own 1996 Hall of Fame record credits Brewster Cogburn with winning this title during the EMWA's founding-era (1990-94) run, alongside titles he later held in other federations. No ledger of challengers, defenses or an end to the reign survives in anything this project holds.
titles.notes: Sourced entirely from third-party corroboration — the rec.sport.pro-wrestling.fantasy community Hall of Fame's own 1996 nomination and inductee documents (served under promotions/rspwf/archive/) — rather than from any EMWA-original card; no EMWA-own title ledger from the 1990-94 era survives in this project's holdings.

titles.name: EMWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Known from two documents, both of them another federation's. John Girder was billed as its holder when the EMWA put the belt against the FWF's own World Championship at Dreamcard V in April 1992 — "Who is the REAL World Champion in fantasy wrestling?", the card asked — and he lost by disqualification when his opponent threw him a set of brass knuckles behind the referee's back and then acted as though he had been hit with them. By that October the FWF was calling him "at least former" champion. No ledger of the EMWA's own survives, and no other holder is named anywhere this project holds.
titles.notes: The Dreamcard V card (promotions/dreamcard/archive/dreamcard-v-the-rising-sun-final-lineup-1992-04-16.html) and the FWF's own singles ledger (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-singles-record-1993-01-08.html) and its own match report of 3 October 1992 (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-damien-vs-hurricane-1992-10-03.html).

titles.name: EMWC Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Righteous" Richard Blue entering the promotion's own 7 April 1999 broadcast, where Youth Gone Wild won it in a steel cage match after an outside attack left the champion unable to defend himself.

titles.name: EMWC North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dirt Dog Unique Allah, who turned back a challenge from Pietro Sandini in a Double Title Ladder Match at the MGM Grand Garden in January 1998, despite his own tag-team partner turning on him mid-match.

titles.name: EMWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: EMWC's top championship, defended by Gabriel Whitecross against the winner of a twenty-man battle royal on the promotion's own pay-per-view stage at the MGM Grand Garden in Las Vegas.

titles.name: EMWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Zokugun Sangai entering the promotion's own 7 April 1999 broadcast, where The Epitome of Cool won it by pinfall.

titles.name: EMWC World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Precious" Pietro Sandini, who turned back a challenge from Dirt Dog Unique Allah in a Double Title Ladder Match at the MGM Grand Garden in January 1998.

titles.name: EMWO World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Chased through a summer-long tournament but never awarded before the federation closed.
titles.notes: Established in the federation's own outline document as its top singles title, defended at least once a month. A tournament to crown the first champion ran across the federation's own July supercard (Christian York advancing past Destroyer by run-in) toward a scheduled final against Jack Vars at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, Summer Sizzler; no surviving document names a champion crowned.

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Epic Wrestling's North American Championship, won by Jason Winters on 26 November 2001 and taken from him by the Hardcore Isosceles Trapezoid in a Poisoned Pyramid Deathmatch at Epic Warfare VI on 23 December 2001. Sam Potright beat the Trapezoid for it at Vengeful Hearts on 24 February 2002 and holds it at the record's end. The federation's own title history also lists reigns from 1983 to 1995: the invented past of its story, served on its page.
titles.notes: Source: the federation's own title history (/promotions/epic-2001/archive/epic-2001-title-history.html); the champions page of 1 March 2002 (not served: a two-line list) names Ben Archer and Sam Potright. The history prints the last change 'February 24, 2001'; Vengeful Hearts is dated 24 February 2002 by its own 2002 event list and by the Trapezoid's own reign, which began on 23 December 2001.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The World Heavyweight Championship of Epic Wrestling's revival, vacated in its story when Wayne Carter's career ended and won by Seth Anson in a tournament on 3 December 2001. Ben Archer took it from him at Vengeful Hearts on 24 February 2002 and is its last champion in the surviving record. The federation's own title history also lists reigns from 1983 to 1995: the invented past of its story, served on its page.
titles.notes: Source: the federation's own title history (/promotions/epic-2001/archive/epic-2001-title-history.html); the champions page of 1 March 2002 (not served: a two-line list) names Ben Archer and Sam Potright.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: EPW's Hardcore Championship was first won by Blackheart on 1 August 2003. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. The longest is King Hardkore's, 131 days from 24 August 2003. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. The belt was vacated on an unrecorded date after Tom Conway's reign, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: EPW's Intercontinental Championship was first won by Hudman, before 2003-08-15. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 6 different champions. The longest is Chapel's, 168 days from 9 January 2004. Ace held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Legacy Championship
titles.epitaph: EPW's Legacy Championship was first won by Tom Conway on 11 July 2004. Tom Conway held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: EPW's Tag Team Championship was first won by Blackheart and Mephisto on 24 August 2003. The fed's own record carries 4 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is Mike Stryker and Devildriver's, 24 days from 28 August 2003. One of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt. EPW did away with it on 8 June 2004 until a tag team division could be established.

events.note: The fed's news post of 8 June 2004 says officials decided to do away with the gold until a tag team division could be established.

titles.name: World Championship
titles.epitaph: EPW's World Championship was first won by Hudman, before 2003-08-24. The fed's own record carries 4 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is John Adams's, 189 days from 21 September 2003. Chapel held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: EPW Northeastern Title
titles.epitaph: Named as the fed's second singles belt in both surviving editions of its own handbook; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: EPW World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Named as the fed's most prestigious singles belt in both surviving editions of its own handbook; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings (the fed never posted a card).

titles.name: EPW World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named as the fed's only tag belt in both surviving editions of its own handbook; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: ESW Queen of the Ring Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's women's title opens in its table on 13 September 2009, when RC Pride beat Orloc at Pyrophoric, and runs through five reigns in a year: Bombshell, Kira Yakamoto and Bishop Spade between RC Pride's two reigns, the last won at Lethal Lottery on 15 September 2010.

titles.name: ESW Survivor Championship
titles.epitaph: Steve Sinclair created the Survivor title on 10 November 2003, when the NYCW Tag Team titles were dropped, and appointed Kid Krazy its first champion; the fed's rules call it 'a gimmick themed title'. Its table runs through forty-six reigns to Amber LeBeau on 15 September 2010, among them Tommy Purr's 242 days in 2009, the longest run of any belt in the fed, and Steve Sinclair's own reign in September 2008.

titles.name: ESW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Eddie and Kid Krazy won the first Tag Team titles at Kick Ass Inc on 30 June 2003, and Steve Sinclair put the belts on the shelf on 10 November 2003 when the two stopped being partners. They came back as a yearly one-night tournament held at the Bruise Cruise, the way the fed's own history says the King of the Ring is run, and its table lists eight champions from 2003 to the Gary Barber and Shawn Sanders pairing of 2010.

titles.name: ESW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Devo won the first Television title in a fifteen-man over-the-top battle royal at the second Kick Ass Inc on 7 April 2003. Its table runs through forty-two reigns to Vise on 28 September 2010, and the holders include Rayne, the first to hold both the World and Television titles, Exodus, whose 189 days stood as the record, and Kid Krazy, who held it four times.

titles.name: ESW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt. Eddie won it as the NYCW World title at the first Kick Ass Inc on 3 March 2003, and it runs through the change of name to the ESW and forty-one reigns in the fed's table to Craig Williams on 15 September 2010, among them Slipstream's five and Darien Sunn's record 230 days. The table's footnote says it was merged with the CWA and BLPW World titles to become the Triple Crown Championship.
titles.notes: The page's footnote: 'The ESW World title was merged with the CWA World title and the BLPW World title to become the Triple Crown Championship.'

titles.name: Empire State Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top prize, named as the shared goal of several wrestlers in its debut promo pack; no title match survives, and the belt stands vacant in the record.

titles.name: ESWP European Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a 1997 tournament held partly on a sibling federation's own broadcasts, changing hands twice more that year per that federation's own corroborating billing.

titles.name: ESWP European Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held jointly by two of the promotion's own 1997 stars, per a sibling federation's own corroborating billing.

titles.name: ESWP Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for a 1997 tournament staged jointly with a sibling federation, whose own broadcasts crowned and corroborate its first champion.

titles.name: ESWP North American Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional singles title defended twice in the promotion's surviving record, its second reign ending in a title shot broken up before the bell.

titles.name: ESWP North American Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully once by disqualification before its holder gave it up to chase a bigger title, per the promotion's own later billing.

titles.name: ESWP Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated when its holder moved up to the Heavyweight title, then won by tournament in the same broadcast.

titles.name: ESWP Women's Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully once in this record; its own start is not documented.

titles.name: ESWP Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, changing hands twice at its own shows in the spring of 1996 before settling on a champion who carried it into 1997.

titles.name: ESWP World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the promotion's own first pay-per-view and defended once more in this record, with no further change documented.

titles.name: ESWP World Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the promotion's own first pay-per-view and changed hands two weeks later, the only women's singles title recorded changing hands in this run.

titles.name: ESWP World Women's Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, changing hands at least twice more by January 1997 without a surviving document for the middle change.

titles.name: IGA Euro Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced on 7 November 2001, when Estrago outlasted nine other men in an elimination match to become its first champion; he defended it against Nick Hart and Marco Avery.

titles.name: GAWA European Championship
titles.epitaph: Won and lost within the same three-way dance at WrestleKrazy II, then held through a disqualification finish engineered by a jealous former ally.

titles.name: UWF European Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Chaple through at least the middle of 1999, then by Shogun Assassin by the promotion's own 18 November 1999 broadcast.

titles.name: EUWC 52 Wild Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC 52 Wild Championship is attested only through the Uprising, Superiority, Aftershock, Ultra Brawl and Bloodbath event-history pages — no dedicated title-history ledger for it survives. "Brooklyn's Finest" Kai A.
titles.notes: Minted entirely from event-history mentions (no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt).

events.title: euwc-unitedstates
events.note: Samuel Roundtree won a fatal four way over Havoc, "All Business" Eric McRae & "Classy" Mike C (the reigning 52 Wild Champion) at Main Frame, unifying the 52 Wild Championship into the United States Championship.

titles.name: EUWC Championship
titles.epitaph: Blackout's own world title, distinct from Main Frame's EUWC World Heavyweight Championship -- Cuchulain is confirmed champion by Ultra Brawl VIII (24 September 2006) and retains it through a cross-promotional Champion vs. Champion win over Jay Smash at the 2006 Chad Dupree Memorial Cup. How or when Cuchulain won the title is not cleanly attested -- a recap on main-frame-2006-09-29 names an "EUWC Championship Tournament" dated 24 August 2006, but that recap's own text is too fragmentary and reused across clips to confirm the actual final.
titles.notes: Minted from confirmed-champion billing; the title's own founding match is unattested (see epitaph).

titles.name: EUWC European Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC European Championship's own ledger opens in July 2004 with Jack "The Ripper," whose two reigns both came against opponents billed from a partner promotion, RBW — one of the clearest surviving traces of EUWC's own cross-federation booking. The Monster, Jacob Jacobs, Apocalypse, T. Waring and the Odinist cycled the belt through RBW-billed defenses before the Odinist's own retirement, when the RBW itself closed, vacated it in August 2005; T. Waring's second reign, the Monster's second, and John Doe carried it into the fed's short fifth-era hiatus around Blood Bath 2005. Chris Comet's 460-day reign, the longest recorded on the belt, ran from June 2006 to Ultra Brawl IX in September 2007, when Cobris Grayson won it. Grayson's own reign carried the belt to its own unification, into the EUWC International Championship (his own second title), in the Unification Match at Blood Bath, 9 July 2008.

events.title: euwc-international
events.note: Cobris Grayson, the reigning European Champion, won this four-way Unification Match at Blood Bath to become International Champion, folding the European title he already held into the International title he won in the same match.

titles.name: EUWC Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC Hardcore Championship is attested only through the Ultra Brawl, Bloodbath and Aftershock event-history pages — no dedicated title-history ledger for it survives, and several hand-offs between its eight recorded reigns are unrecorded gaps rather than invented continuity. Neighborhood Sniper won it in a Ladder Match at Ultra Brawl III in October 1999; T-Charger, Johnny Hardcore, Kaine, Marshall Snow, Sevyn and Bibyl carried it in turn across the fed's second, third and fourth eras, the title going dark for stretches the surviving record never explains. Bibyl's win over Sevyn at Blood Bath, 30 November 2003, is the last EUWC Hardcore Championship reign attested anywhere in the held record. Distinct from the 1997 EUWC Hardcore Television Championship, a separate, one-match-only belt from the fed's founding era.
titles.notes: Minted entirely from event-history mentions (no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt); several reigns carry an honest gap where the actual title change is unattested.

titles.name: EUWC Hardcore Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Albino won the title’s debut match, a Caribbean Strap Match over the Wraith, at Blood Bath 1997 — the only reign the surviving record attests. Distinct from the plain "Television Championship" John Shaft held the year before, and from the later "Hardcore Championship" that debuts after EUWC’s first hiatus.
titles.notes: Recovered from the Bloodbath/Blood Bath event-history page; no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt.

titles.name: EUWC International Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC International Championship's own history table opens with Ahmed the Powerhouse winning a tournament final the night EUWC opened, 28 July 1996, and changed hands some fifteen times through the fed's founding two years — X.Plosion, Don Hall, The Crow, Consequence, HICAL and Dan Sokolov (twice) among the holders — before Dan Sokolov's own vacating reign carried it into EUWC's first hiatus in April 1998. Mid-lineage, on 28 September 1997, HICAL unified the North American Championship into this belt. Fred Rogers, Dan Sokolov, Triple T, Erik Kelly, Ray Santana, Cuchulain, The Chameleon, Kritical Kondition and STEALTH carried the title through its second era; Sledgehammer, T-Charger, Simon, HICAL, Larry Serson, Triple T, Neighborhood Sniper, Gavin Glass, David Harten and Virus carried it through the third, before a third hiatus vacated it in June 2002. Nick Marshall, Damian Stone, Cole Justice, Sean Taylor, Jim Roberts, Apocalypse, Danny Collins and Lynch Garrisson cycled it through the fourth era — Apocalypse's own loss to Danny Collins staged at a show the Uprising event-history page dates a full year earlier than the title ledger itself, an unresolved discrepancy between the fed's own documents — before Sean Taylor's second reign absorbed a fourth hiatus (230 days deducted) and Tyrone Walker reopened it at Superiority II in July 2005. After a run the fed's own record does not otherwise explain, the ledger resumes in the mid-2000s with Rocko Daymon, Hawkeye (twice), Sevyn, Jonathan Darkstar and Cobris Grayson carrying it through EUWC's final fwrestling.com-hosted years.

titles.name: EUWC International Tag Team Championship
aka: EUWC Unified International Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Killers Inc retained it at Ultra Brawl in August 1996 over the Missouri Connection, then apparently lost it — unrecorded — to Badd Company before that October’s Blood Bath, where Badd Company retained over a team the card spells "Kiillers Incorprated." At Ultra Brawl II the following August the Midnight Massacre won it from Cause & Effect in a "Unification Match," becoming, per the card’s own words, the "Unified International Tag Team Champions."
titles.notes: Every reign recovered from the Ultra Brawl and Bloodbath/Blood Bath event-history pages; no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt. Only reigns with a recorded WIN are structured (Killers Inc’s and Badd Company’s "retain" defenses are recorded as matches, not reign rows, since no won-date survives for either).

titles.name: EUWC North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC North American Championship's own history table opens with STEALTH winning it in EUWC's first-ever 20-man Blood Bath, 27 October 1996, then changed hands seven more times across the fed's founding year before Chet Jenkins carried it into a unification match at And The Winner Is... Part V: War Games on 28 September 1997, where HICAL (as International Champion) absorbed it into the International Championship. The belt itself lay dormant for eight years — the ledger's own "Defunct" — before Lt. Hawkeye's win over Cuchulain and Tony DeLucci at Blood Bath, 20 November 2005, "resurrected thanks to the roster split"; due to a short hiatus that same night, the reign's own active clock is recorded as beginning 9 February 2006. Angel of Death, Cuchulain, Artur Arina and Braden Kincaid carried it into the fed's own final active years. Braden Kincaid's own reign carried the belt to its second and final unification, into the EUWC International Championship, in the Unification Match at Blood Bath, 9 July 2008 -- Kincaid himself was never pinned in the fall.

events.title: euwc-international
events.note: HICAL (International Champion) defeated Chet Jenkins (North American Champion) at And The Winner Is... Part V: War Games to unify the belts. The North American title lay dormant until a November 2005 revival.

events.title: euwc-international
events.note: Cobris Grayson (entering as European Champion) defeated Braden Kincaid (North American Champion, among others) in a four-way Unification Match at Blood Bath to become International Champion and unify the belts.

titles.name: EUWC North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Powers of Destruction won it from Cuttz ’n’ Broozis at EUWC’s first Blood Bath, 27 October 1996 — the only reign the surviving record attests.
titles.notes: Recovered from the Bloodbath/Blood Bath event-history page; no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt.

titles.name: EUWC Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A Main-Frame-exclusive title founded via a Tag Team Turmoil match at Ultra Brawl VIII (24 September 2006), announced by Matt Pickstock as a second tag lineage alongside the existing EUWC World Tag Team Championship -- the Turmoil's own match text does not survive, but the Black Death Gauntlet are confirmed the founding champions by the very next show read.
titles.notes: Minted from a confirmed-champion billing (chad-dupree-memorial-cup-2006-10-15) plus Matt Pickstock's own prior announcement (main-frame-2006-08-20/09-19); the founding match itself is unattested.

titles.name: EUWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: John Shaft retained it against Consequence by disqualification at EUWC’s first Blood Bath, 27 October 1996 — the only appearance the surviving record attests, and no won-date for John Shaft’s own reign survives. Distinct from the "Hardcore Television Championship" Albino wins the following year.
titles.notes: Recovered from the Bloodbath/Blood Bath event-history page; no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt.

titles.name: EUWC United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC United States Championship changed hands more often than any other EUWC belt on record. Its ledger opens with YAHOO winning a tournament final on 25 May 1997 and cycled rapidly through Don Hall, The Crow, Stephon Kardell and Kris Blade before the promotion's first hiatus in April 1998; once EUWC returned it kept the same pace, naming dozens of reigns across every era through the promotion's second hiatus (Angel of Death, Ray Santana and Tony DeLucci among the early holders), its third (Cuchulain, T-Rex, David Harten and Bibyl), its fourth (Larry Serson, Rob Sampson, Gavin Glass, Marshall Snow and Virus), and its fifth (Ryan Baker, Samuel Roundtree, Major Action, T-Charger and Scott Samson) — Samuel Roundtree's second reign, in June 2005, absorbing the EUWC 52 Wild Championship outright in a fatal four way Unification match. Angel of Death carried the belt three separate times; Adam Benjamin lost the belt off-page, exact date unrecorded, to Texas Lightning, who carried it into the title's own final unification, into the EUWC International Championship, in the Unification Match at Blood Bath, 9 July 2008.

events.title: euwc-international
events.note: Cobris Grayson (entering as European Champion) defeated Texas Lightning (United States Champion, among others) in a four-way Unification Match at Blood Bath to become International Champion and unify the belts.

titles.name: EUWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC World Heavyweight Championship is the fed's flagship title, first won by STEALTH at Summer Sizzler on 28 July 1996 — the same week EUWC's own Ultra Brawl series began. The belt changed hands rapidly through its founding two years — Fred Rogers, Don Hall (three times), Genesis Taylor, Dan Sokolov, X.Plosion, HICAL (twice), YAHOO and Chet Jenkins all held it before HICAL's own refusal to defend it at When Worlds Collide helped trigger EUWC's first hiatus in April 1998. HICAL, STEALTH, Dan Sokolov and Erik Kelly kept it moving through the fed's second era, into a run of short reigns (Ray Santana, Triple T and Neighborhood Sniper trading it four times inside two months in 2000) before David Harten's win, at the same show the ledger bills "Caged In!," carried it into a second hiatus that November. Cuchulain, Jordan Lockhart, Buck Naked, STEALTH and Rob Sampson cycled it through a third short era before a third hiatus in June 2002; Jordan Lockhart's second reign reopened it in April 2003, and Paul Doom, Lord Alucard, Angel of Death, Jay Smash, Holocaust (twice), Damian Stone, Danny Collins, Sean Taylor and Stephen Greer carried it across a fourth hiatus the fed's own ledger buries inside Sean Taylor's own 2004–2005 reign, deducting 220 days from its recorded length rather than pretending the promotion never went dark. STEALTH carried it across several further reigns spanning more than a decade, the last coming at the 4th Annual Chad Dupree Memorial Cup on 28 October 2007, a sixteen-man tournament held after the belt was declared vacant amid the chaos that followed Ultra Brawl IX. Through 2006 and 2007 the belt changed hands rapidly among the fed's own later roster — Jay Smash three times, Adam Benjamin, Nero and "Classy" Mike C among them — before STEALTH's own final win closed out the surviving ledger.

titles.name: EUWC World Juniorweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Discovered only through EUWC’s full-card event-history pages rather than any dedicated ledger: the Perfect Pugilest regained it at Ultra Brawl in August 1996, Sweet Daddy Bad Ass regained it again that October at EUWC’s first Blood Bath, Michael Foreman won it fresh at Ultra Brawl II in August 1997, and Ender won a Four Corners match for it at Blood Bath 1997. The fed’s own text names it inconsistently, sometimes "Juniorweight Championship" and sometimes "World Juniorweight Championship" — the same belt, one lineage.
titles.notes: Every reign recovered from the Ultra Brawl and Bloodbath/Blood Bath event-history pages (/promotions/euwc/archive/ultrabrawl9-ultrabrawl-history.html, /promotions/euwc/archive/bloodbath2007-bloodbath-history.html); no dedicated title-history ledger page survives for this belt.

titles.name: EUWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The EUWC World Tag Team Championship's own ledger opens with the Specialists (Nate Augustine & Roger Thorpe) on 28 July 1996, the same Summer Sizzler card that crowned the fed's first World Heavyweight Champion, and changed hands more than a dozen times across the founding two years — the Beantown Bruisers, the Outsiders, the Black Panthers (twice each), the Surf Patrol, the Glamour Boys (twice), the Hellraisers, Team PSD and Harlem Connection among the teams — with three separate vacancies along the way (a controversial finish, the Outsiders' own contract lapsing, the Black Panthers' retirement) before Harlem Connection's reign carried it into EUWC's first hiatus in April 1998. Team PSD's own second reign reopened it in October 1999, and a run of ad hoc pairings and named teams — the Salvation, the Dark Angels, the Kool Klub, American Mafia, the Blood Brothers, Alliance of Violence, the Kings, Extreme Lightning and the Wannabes among them — carried it through EUWC's second era into its second hiatus. New Pimps on the Block reopened it in September 2001; Diabolic Forces, the Enders, the Motley Crew and a returning American Mafia carried it through the third era before a third hiatus. Nero & Big G (billed under Lynch Garrisson's own tag-team nickname "Big G") won it three separate times across the fourth era, trading it with Scott Samson & T-Charger, the Action Faction, Buck Naked & Samuel Roundtree, the Dream Team (twice), Shock Therapy, the Dominion (twice), U.S. Express, the Rebellion and Diabolic Forces, before Team Danger's own reign absorbed a fourth hiatus (240 days deducted).

titles.name: Cell Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's Cell Championship was first won by Jinx on 14 August 2002. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is Damon O'Halloran's, 59 days from 7 August 2003. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt or vacated. eVo retired it on 9 November 2003.

events.note: The write-up has the Cell division retired by decree at Faith on 9 November 2003; the fed's own champions page still lists its last champion.

titles.name: Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's Continental Championship was first won by Erin Christoph on 10 July 2002. The fed's own record carries 10 reigns on it, across 9 different champions. The longest is Asis's, 109 days from 5 February 2003. Three of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt or vacated. eVo unified it into the United Championship on 31 August 2003.

events.note: The fed's own title history records the belt unified with the ULWN Heavyweight Title and renamed the United Title.
events.title: evo-2002-united

titles.name: eVolved Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's eVolved Championship was first won by Seara on 15 January 2003. The fed's own record carries 8 reigns on it, across 8 different champions. The longest is Scott Evans's, 98 days from 29 June 2003. One of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt. eVo unified it into the United Championship on 10 December 2003.

events.note: The fed's own pages for the eVolved, United and retired titles record Matt Hunt defeating Thug roC to unify the eVolved and United titles.
events.title: evo-2002-united

titles.name: High Impact Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's High Impact Championship was first won by Quasar the Great on 14 August 2002. The fed's own record carries 5 reigns on it, across 5 different champions. The longest is Thug roC's, 63 days from 9 October 2002. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt or stripped from the holder. eVo unified it with the Rising Star Championship into the eVolved Championship on 15 January 2003.

events.note: The fed's own title history closes the belt with the line that it was unified with the Rising Star Championship to form the eVolved Championship.
events.title: evo-2002-evolved

titles.name: Rising Star Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's Rising Star Championship was first won by Asis on 14 August 2002. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. The longest is Sean Mason's, 52 days from 24 November 2002. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt or stripped from the holder. eVo unified it with the High Impact Championship into the eVolved Championship on 15 January 2003.

events.note: The fed's own title history closes the belt with the line that it was unified with the High Impact Championship to form the eVolved Championship.
events.title: evo-2002-evolved

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's Tag Team Championship was first won by The Unlimited on 24 November 2002. The fed's own record carries 16 reigns on it, across 11 different champions. The longest is The Syndicate's, 76 days from 3 July 2003. One of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder. St. Violence held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: United Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's United Championship was first won by Thug roC on 31 August 2003. The fed's own record carries 2 reigns on it, across 2 different champions. The longest is Thug roC's, 101 days from 31 August 2003. Matt Hunt held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: eVo's Universal Championship was first won by Sovereign on 14 August 2002. The fed's own record carries 9 reigns on it, across 8 different champions. The longest is Xander's, 98 days from 25 May 2003. James Kimson held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: EWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested under a 230-pound limit. Dean McGrath became the inaugural champion at the 31 October 1998 Devil's Night; the belt passed to 'Maverick' Matt Blanchard, then Tyrant, then Shawn Foster across the captured run, and was vacant again by the fed's own 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA Global Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's hardcore-stipulation belt. Ronny Wonder was announced champion on 22 November 1998, the same broadcast that also announced Richard Riley as champion in what the show's own text plays as a joke rather than a clean handoff; Cyris held the belt clearly from 6 December 1998 through at least the end of that year. It was vacant again on the fed's own 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA Global Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize under two names across its life — the Extreme World Championship at launch in 1998, renamed Global Heavyweight by the 1999 relaunch. JD Freeman won the inaugural Extreme World title in an eight-man tournament at the fed's first pay-per-view and retired from it undefeated soon after; the belt sat vacant through the rest of the captured 1998-99 run and was still listed vacant on the fed's own 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own #2 title, billed as the North American 'Cyber' Championship in its early weeks before the qualifier dropped. It changed hands four times across the captured 1998-99 run — Lonewolf, then The Train (Wayne Rothschild), then The Multinational Rebel, then Johnny Sledge — and was vacant again on the fed's own 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed by the fed's own rules as its 'Ironman' belt, defended weekly. Its captured lineage runs from Ray Simmons through Capital Punishment, Suicide King, Tommy Grayson and Roadkill across the fed's 1998-99 run, and was vacant again by the 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant on the fed's own 3 June 1999 rankings page.

titles.name: EWA Breakthrough Championship
titles.epitaph: The lower-card belt of the 2008 pages. Its champions page gives eighteen reigns in two lists that meet at Dominic Deaver, champion from Shockers December 25th: the past list runs from Scott Acid (Collision 2006) and ends his reign at Ground Zero, where the Calamity list also ends; the current list, under a note that the two titles have been unified, carries him on to Ascension and runs to Daigo Prisken (Ground Zero III).

titles.name: EWA Calamity Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt the 2008 champions page lists only as past: eight Calamity champions from Treize Delacroix (Shockers Jan 30th) to Chris Kane (Wipe Out to Ground Zero), after which its page says the Calamity and Breakthrough Championships were unified.

titles.name: EWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A short lineage of three reigns in 2004: Michael Bendis won it in a Battle Royal at Wipe Out on 26 June 2004, Rage took it in a Ladder Match on 4 August and Joker on 21 August. Mark Fletcher's biography says the Cruiserweight Title was the earlier Rising Star Title renamed.

titles.name: EWA European Championship
titles.epitaph: A mid-card belt held from its first reign on 5 April 2003 (Dragon) through twenty reigns to Crucifix on 30 April 2005. Its page footnotes two events: Richard Bison was stripped on 9 September 2003 for injuring a rival to keep him out of an Elimination Chamber, and the title was unified with the WWO Internet Championship at Collision 2004 under David Boyce's reign.

titles.name: EWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt of 2003 and 2004. Camaro won its title tournament at Kingdom Come on 10 May 2003 and its page counts ten reigns to Brett Cotter on 27 November 2004. The page's sixth row carries a note that the WWO Championship and the EWA Championship were unified into the EWA Undisputed Heavyweight Championship on 27 March 2004, under a reign dated 17 January 2004; the Sinners card of May 2004 bills the title as the EWA Undisputed World Heavyweight Championship.

titles.name: EWA Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's second belt in its 2008 rules, an upper and mid-card title. Its champions page lists fourteen reigns from 'Shockers Jan 30th' to Matt Wolfe, who won it on 7 January 2008 (Monday Night Shockers). The page does not give the years of its earlier changes.

titles.name: EWA Legacy Championship
titles.epitaph: The main-event title of the fed's 2008 pages, whose rules call it the most prestigious title in the EWA. Its champions page lists thirteen reigns, from Scott Acid (Sinners IV) to Richard Bison, who won it on 24 December 2007 (Monday Night Shockers) and is the champion at the page's end. Only the shows are given for most changes; the page dates two.

titles.name: EWA Survival Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt whose first champion, Joker, is dated 5 April 2003, the same day as the European Championship's. Its page lists sixteen reigns to Mark Fletcher on 25 September 2004, including a vacancy before Sense Green's win on 26 June 2004.

titles.name: EWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag belts, with fourteen reigns on its page from a survivor match at the TTTTT2 on 5 July 2003 to Brett Cotter and Michael Bendis, The Regulators, on 14 September 2004. The page numbers two different reigns 6; its date for the last reign sits ten days after the news of 4 September 2004 reports The Regulators winning the titles from Gekido.

titles.name: EWA TV Championship
titles.epitaph: Five reigns in 2004, from a unification of the EWA Rising Star Championship and the WWO TV Championship on 21 February 2004 (Keith, beating Alexander) to Lotus, who won a five-way on Sinners 2 on 23 May 2004. Four of the five champions appear on the page only as pictures and are named from the pictures' file names; the next row's beaten champion, or the Sinners 2 card, bears out each name.

titles.name: EWA European Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from KG's tournament win on 2 March 1998 to Lee Tenn's win on 31 March 1999, ending vacant at the fed's own close with no post-closure revival recorded (unlike the World Heavyweight and Hardcore titles, which both saw one further reign after the fed's own "closed" ledger note). Seven of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the founding and closing anchors through Stevie Richards's, Shawn Copeland's, SmirtDogg's, Erik Draven's, and Haywood Jublome's own reigns; the remaining stretches (Alex Wright, Prodigy, Makaveli, Edge, The Prince, and others' own reigns) still ride the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from E-'Nuff's Triple Threat Steel Cage Weapons match win on 16 January 1999 to Nukeman's Nuclear Hell Match win on 13 October 1999 — like the World Heavyweight title, the belt briefly outlives the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-October revival chain. A third reign, Vendetta's own Junkyard Brawl win between the two anchors, is now also reified; the remaining stretch (Raven's and Reaper's own reigns) still rides the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from The Pessimist's tournament win on 15 January 1998 to Jack Daniels's Triple Threat Ladder Match win on 25 September 1999, the belt briefly outliving the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-September revival. Seven of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the founding and closing anchors through Scott Cummings's, Shawn Michaels's, Haywood Jublome's, Grady Smith's, and Venom's own reigns; the remaining stretches (Scott Hall, Hannibal Manson, Deathstar, Jeff Bunda, Crazy Canuck, Ruger Ice, The Rock, Terry Conklin, Jack Reed, and Tanaka's own reigns) still ride the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from SmirtDogg's tournament win on 12 January 1998 to The Kaze's six-man Four Corners win on 9 October 1999, the belt briefly outliving the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-1999 revival chain. Six of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the founding and closing anchors through Shawn Michaels's, Shawn Copeland's, Philip Donovan's, and Lunatikk Crippler's own reigns; the remaining stretches (Aaron Martin's own several reigns, Thorne Richards, Joe Satre, New Jack, The Prince, Scott Tokage, Terry Conklin, Michael Modest, Max Pins, and Craven Blood's own reigns) still ride the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from Hunter Hearst Helmsley's tournament win on 2 February 1998 to Philip Donovan's Three Way Dance win on 22 September 1999, the belt briefly outliving the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-September revival. Seven of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the founding and closing anchors through KG's two own reigns, Stevie Richards's, Venom's, and Hunter Hearst Helmsley's own second reign; the remaining stretches (Steve Austin, Eclipse, Castor Troy, The Gunslinger, and many others' own reigns) still ride the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from SmirtDogg's Battle Royal win on 15 January 1998 to Bret Hart's win on 13 October 1999, the belt briefly outliving the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-1999 revival chain; the same page's own notes record the title briefly renamed "North American" after a unification with a Canadian belt (note 8) and renamed back to United States when all EWA titles were declared vacant (note 15). Ten of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the founding and closing anchors through Erik Draven's own four reigns, SmirtDogg's second, KG's, Stevie Richards's, Kanyon's, and "Cold" Harding Cash's own reigns; the remaining stretches (Prodigy, The Golden Child, Dallas Page, Raven, Justin Hicks, The Wyldsyde, Vic Deakins, and others' own reigns) still ride the title's own served page, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated fifteen-reign chain from Scott Cummings's tournament win on 12 January 1998 to Mortis's Triple Threat win on 9 October 1999, each change carrying its own stipulation note (a No Holds Barred match, a Steel Cage Death Match, a Ladder Match, a Casket Match) and one stretch — 20 April to a re-run tournament in October 1999 — recorded on the page's own ledger as "Vacant... Federation closed," the belt itself briefly outliving what its own note calls the fed's end. Thirteen of the belt's own reigns are reified here, chaining the two founding/closing anchors through Erik Draven's nine own reigns (the fed's own most-decorated titleholder), Stevie Richards's and Shawn Copeland's own repeated exchanges, and SmirtDogg's own three; the remaining stretches (Kane, Ric Flair, Prodigy, Jeff Bunda, Justin Hicks, Thorne Richards, and The Golden One's own reigns) still ride the title's own served page rather than a separate reigns.json row, pending those wrestlers' own future minting.

titles.name: EWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a dated lineage from Harlem Heat's tournament win on 12 January 1998 to Jack Daniels and Venom's win on 6 October 1999, the belts briefly outliving the fed's own "closed" ledger note (recorded vacant from 20 April 1999) via a late-1999 revival chain. Two reigns are reified here: Jack Daniels and Venom's own closing win, and Shawn Copeland and Erik Draven's own battle-royal win between two vacancies.

titles.name: EWA International Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Hall of Champions index links an International Championship history page (ewaefed.ucoz.com/index/international_championship/0-33) that was never captured.
titles.epitaph: One of the four championships the fed's own Hall of Champions indexes, and one of the three it advertised to applicants alongside the World Heavyweight and Tag Team belts. Buck Evans is the only holder the surviving record names, still champion as of Shatter Point 7/5/11 after Big Nasty's attack put challenger Alexander Slate out of action; Cassandra Avery won a three-way over Thrax and Ruthless Aggression the same night to become his next number-one contender.

titles.name: EWA Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Hall of Champions index links a Tag Team Championship history page (ewaefed.ucoz.com/index/tag_tream_championship/0-35) that was never captured.
titles.epitaph: Advertised to new applicants alongside the World Heavyweight and International belts, and indexed on the fed's own Hall of Champions. The teams the fed signed for it — NeXtreme, the Southern Express — filed with it in mid-2011, but it was the Home Town Heroes (Mark Jackson and Jun Yao) who won it first, at Retaliation, over Total Mayhem and a Sons of Ohio/Wreckers pairing — and spent the rest of the held record fending off the Mayhem brothers, who turned on them the very night they won the belts.

titles.name: EWA Underground Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Hall of Champions index links an Underground Championship history page (ewaefed.ucoz.com/index/underground_championship/0-34) that was never captured.
titles.epitaph: A 24/7 belt with rules of its own: anyone on the roster except the World Champion could challenge for it at any time by sending the word “Challenge” to the front office, first come first served, and it was defended out of a board only its own champion could read. El Pablo won it on Shatter Point in May 2011; the fed's own record shows it changing hands twice more inside two months, to Chris Johnson at Retaliation and then to a surprise-entrant Waylon Krews mid-way through an unrelated tag match on Shatter Point 7/5/11. The fed called it innovative in its own recruiting copy.

titles.name: EWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Hall of Champions index links a World Heavyweight Championship history page (ewaefed.ucoz.com/index/world_heavyweight_championship/0-32) that was never captured.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top belt, and the one it built its newsdesk around: Buzzsaw carried it through the spring of 2011 and booked himself airtime for an announcement the fed spent a fortnight speculating about, and Crimson Blaze chased it until he issued a statement saying he could not get the job done. Justin Marsham beat Buzzsaw for it at Retaliation in a Stairway to Death match, and used his first Shatter Point as champion to promise a title match every week rather than only at pay-per-view — opening with a shot for Crimson Blaze the following week.

titles.name: EWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced by the federation's own president on 30 September 2003 as a new second title, first won four weeks later at the promotion's second pay-per-view.
titles.notes: The federation's president announced the title's creation on 30 September 2003 and named "Crippler" Evan Crowley and Tommy Starr as its first challengers; the surviving record's own next dated document showing the two men fighting for the belt is the 26 October 2003 pay-per-view, which the ring announcer calls for "a NEW" champion.

titles.name: EWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the federation's own debut pay-per-view, an eight-man tournament that crowned its first champion in the tournament final.
titles.notes: Contested in an eight-man single-elimination tournament across the promotion's debut pay-per-view, 28 September 2003.

titles.name: EWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in a three-way Falls Count Anywhere Hardcore Brawl at Royal Demolitions on 10 May 2008, where Red Steel beat the Television champion and the Dark Angel for it. It appears nowhere else in the surviving record.

titles.name: EWA Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in an Ultimate Ladder match at Royal Demolitions on 10 May 2008 — four men, one belt overhead — and won by the Extreme Menace, who was still billed with it three weeks later. Its earlier lineage is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: EWA North American Championship
titles.notes: Board topic 454, “EWA North American”, 12 August 2007 — indexed by title, date and starter on the forum's own listing, never captured.
titles.epitaph: Andy held it through every card the record holds, defending it inside a cage against the Television champion at CAGED and again against “The Real Deal” Jimmy Steele at Royal Demolitions. A topic of its own name was opened on the board's off-topic forum in August 2007, nine months before the first held card.

titles.name: EWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own commentary calls them the “EWA World Tag titles”; its cards bill the match as an “EWA Tag Team Match”.
titles.epitaph: Vacated by order of the fed's own Chairman of the Board, who stripped the champions for refusing to defend the belts together, and settled the same night: a four-team Hell in a Cell at CAGED on 12 April 2008 that X-Rated won. The card's own action text credits the deciding fall to Phoenix, unbilled on any of the four teams -- the announcer's credit to X-Rated stands as the fed's own declared result.

titles.name: EWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The Renagade held it across every card the record holds, defending it against King on 3 April 2008 and against Xero on 21 April. Its last appearance is a contradiction the fed left standing: the 29 May card bills a Television title match, and the ring announcer's own call names the winner Lightweight champion instead.

titles.name: EWA World Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Championship Info board carried four topics in January 2007; none was captured.
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt, and the only one whose lineage the served record actually turns over. Commander D carried it into the Hell in a Cell main event of CAGED on 12 April 2008 and the Model left with it, then kept it four weeks later at Royal Demolitions by climbing a ladder and taking it down himself. Where the belt came from before that, and where it went after 29 May 2008, is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in the fed's own founding post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: North American Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in the fed's own founding post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in the fed's own founding post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in the fed's own founding post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: Extreme Title
titles.epitaph: One of five titles named in the fed's own recruitment post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: IC Title
titles.epitaph: One of five titles named in the fed's own recruitment post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: One of five titles named in the fed's own recruitment post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: US Title
titles.epitaph: One of five titles named in the fed's own recruitment post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: World Title
titles.epitaph: One of five titles named in the fed's own recruitment post, with no champion yet crowned.

titles.name: EWC Elite Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles title, first won in a four-man tournament at the debut supercard and still held at the record's own end.

titles.name: EWC Elite Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by the Natural Born Killaz over two other teams at the federation's first pay-per-view and held through the record's own end.

titles.name: EWC Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's number-two singles title, billed at launch as the Midwest Championship, first won in a ladder match at the debut supercard.

titles.name: EWC Skinnyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's cruiserweight-style title, decided by an eight-man tournament at its second pay-per-view.

titles.name: EWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended weekly on the federation's own house show, first won in a Survival of the Fittest match at its second pay-per-view.

titles.name: EWC North American Title
titles.epitaph: Traced from the federation's own purse table; no reign is recorded within this collection's own held record.

titles.name: EWC Television Title
titles.epitaph: Traced from the federation's own purse table; no reign is recorded within this collection's own held record.

titles.name: EWC World Title
titles.epitaph: Traced from the federation's own purse table; Grim Weibaq is billed elsewhere in the held record (the held Summit of E-Wrestling wing's own Leprecharnage card) as EWC Heavyweight Champion.

titles.name: EWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: The International Championship was decided at WrestleFest 2003, where The Overweighter left with the belt. By the time the fed’s champions page was last captured, six weeks later, it had passed to Super Rob; nothing the fed left records how.

titles.name: EWF International Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Blood Man and J won this belt vacant at WrestleFest 2003, eliminating John Dumas and Chaos in a tag team elimination match — Blood Man pinned Dumas behind the referee’s back with a chair, then the pair finished Chaos with Blood Man’s Bleeding Blood and J’s own J Splash. They were still champions, by the fed’s own commentary and ring announcement called simply the “Tag team championship,” when Jay Krazy, Dumas and Chaos jumped them celebrating the win, and were still holding it six weeks later at the champions page’s last capture, there billed the “International Tag Team” champions. No other holder appears anywhere in what the Elite Wrestling Foundation left.

titles.name: EWF Daemusin Championship
titles.epitaph: A title renamed and revived in EWF in 2009 as the self-described "spiritual continuator" of a 1999-2001 predecessor-federation belt (PCW Stolica); only its one attested EWF-era holder is structured here, from his own roster bio.

titles.name: EWF Evolution Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed by the fed itself as the spiritual successor to a defunct "Konstantynopol" title: 22 structured reign changes from a tournament final (2002) to Oscar Knifer's reign (2007).

titles.name: EWF Fuck the World Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-styled title carrying a profane name the fed used without euphemism on its own site: 28 structured reign changes from a self-awarded first reign (2001) to a vacancy declared at the reactivation show (2007).

titles.name: EWF/PCW Polish Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's longest-running belts by its own record, tracing back to a 1999 predecessor federation (PCW); this collection structures only its EWF-era reign chain (16 changes, 2002-2004), holding the earlier PCW-era ledger as prose on the title's own served page.

titles.name: EWF Puchar Szczęściarza
titles.epitaph: A periodic "Lucky Guy's Cup" battle-royal/tournament trophy, awarded five times across 2004-2009 by the fed's own record; its second edition's scheduled match was cancelled outright and no winner was named.
titles.notes: Its second edition, scheduled for PPV "Kwietniowa Anarchia III" (17 April 2005), was cancelled outright and named no winner.

titles.name: EWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: EWF's own tag championship: 29 structured reign changes from its first holders (2001) through a commissioner-awarded reign at the fed's third PPV (2005).

titles.name: EWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: EWF's own top title from its founding show onward: 16 structured reign changes from Kraven's win of the founding battle royal (2001) to a three-way rights transfer settled at the fed's fourth PPV (2005) and Kraven's third reign (2007).

titles.name: EWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: "Stingray" Steve Fontaine held it through the fed's own 20 April 1995 rankings bulletin; by the last recovered broadcast William the Conqueror held it instead, an unrecorded transition, and he retained it against The Electric Youth by count-out when the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: EWF World Six-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Madhouse Wrestling won it from Graveyard Shift at Ground-Zero (11 April 1995); Asylum held it by the fed's last recovered broadcast, an unrecorded transition, and lost it there to the debuting Beijing Beauties, still champions when the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: EWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: "The Star Spangled Kid" Johnny Banner won it from The Electric Youth at Ground-Zero (11 April 1995); by the fed's last recovered broadcast Dai Kaiju held it instead, an unrecorded transition, and Kaiju was still champion when a run-in stopped his defense against Hulk Hurley cold.

titles.name: EWF Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Elite Wrestling Foundation put its own top belt up as a tournament before it had a champion at all. The first round ran on the fed’s first Immortality, 9 March 2003, and the final closed WrestleFest: Turbulence beat “The Turnbuckle” Jay to be handed the belt and, in the fed’s own commentator’s words, to become “the very first EWF Champion”. He was still carrying it at the last capture of the champions page, six weeks later, and the fed left nothing dated after that.
titles.notes: The fed’s own rules page describes a quite different set of belts — a World Title, an Intercontinental Title, an EWF Title and World Tag Team Titles — which its champions page never uses. Both are held; the rules read as a template the fed never brought into line with what it crowned.

titles.name: AJ Epic Memorial Cup
titles.epitaph: A tournament named for the promotion's own founder after the fed staged his death, and run twice. The first, in 2006, was hosted by px:w rather than by eWo, which was closed at the time; Reno Drake won it at High Impact in August of that year and took a px:w World Championship match out of it, losing to Cody Clark. The second went to Scott Free, a newcomer, in the promotion's own 2007 run. eWo's own titles page claims both.

titles.name: eWo Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top prize, and the belt that opened it: "The Idol" Bill Dynamite beat "The Dealer" Dylan Dunn two falls to one at eWo's first pay-per-view in September 2004, in a tournament final refereed by Erin Jacobs, and the fed's own history calls that night the true start of its success. Dunn is separately recorded as an eWo World Heavyweight Champion, on the same Hall of Fame page. The belt came back with the promotion: Cody Clark pulled it out of a briefcase at BWF Danger Zone 2007 and handed it to The Legend, who put down the BWF Championship to take it. Legend lost it to Czecher in a four-way at Hell & Back, regained it from Czecher at Body Count with a new finisher, then defended it through Supremacy, License to Thrill and Guilty As Charged before Frank Murdoch became the first man ever to pin him in eWo, at The New Black — the reign eWo closed on, in November 2007, with no further word. C.M. Vyrus was reigning by the 2008 return's own sixth of April; Kyle Cross was carrying it into a barbed-wire main event at the record's own last word.
titles.notes: The fed's own Hall of Fame page lists "eWo Champion" and "eWo World Heavyweight Champion" as separate lines for separate men. Whether those are one lineage under two names or two belts is not settled anywhere in the surviving record, and both readings are left standing.

titles.name: eWo Commonwealth Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the promotion's Toronto era and first held by Reno Drake. Ryley Wynters was carrying it into a triple threat against Paul Herring and Juan Ramirez on the 20 April 2008 card; the results page for that show was never captured. By the 18 May 2008 card Erik Dafoe was the champion, and he was billed to defend it against Juan Ramirez at Hell and Back.

titles.name: eWo Freedom Championship
titles.epitaph: The last championship eWo created, first held by Jack Darling. The surviving record shows it fought over in two table matches — an Elimination Tables Match at The Crowning: Epic Homecoming on 23 March 2008, and an Ultimate Tables Match three weeks later where Nijs Landzaat defended it against Nick Toretto — neither with a result that survives. By May 2008 Eryk Adams was the champion, billed to defend it against Eden Turner at Hell and Back.

titles.name: eWo Gutz & Glory Championship
titles.epitaph: A first-run championship recorded once, on Czecher, in the promotion's own Hall of Fame. What it was contested for, and who else held it, is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: eWo National Championship
titles.epitaph: A first-run championship whose only recorded holder is its first: Lawrence Jarvis, on the promotion's own Hall of Fame page. No later reign appears anywhere in the surviving record.

titles.name: eWo Primetime Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship that outlived three of the promotions that carried it. It began in eWo when Johnny Legend won a ladder match at Bound for Glory, and passed through Gabe Shelley, Lawrence Jarvis and Seth Thomas before the promotion closed in December 2004 with nobody left to compete for it. Shelley, its last eWo champion, took it to the Blazenwing Wrestling Federation, which bought the rights to it outright and defended it until spring 2006; px:w's chairman Paul Reynolds then purchased it and activated it there; when px:w closed it went back to BWF for a short while. In the fed's own words it "is one of a select few championships that has gone through many federations," and "many believe it lost it's prestige and it has since been abandoned."

titles.name: eWo Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag titles, defended once a month. Bill Dynamite and Czecher held them in the first run, Dylan Dunn and Scott Royal twice; AJ Donavon and Bobby Dynamite, Xaria Linette and Alexis Sykes, and C.M. Vyrus and Ryley Wynters as Nuclear Wynter all held them afterwards. The Takeover were defending them on the 11 November 2007 card, and Nuclear Wynter had them back by April 2008 — with a shirt of their own in the fed's own store. The Iconoclast were the champions by the Hell and Back card, billed against the former champions The Takeover.

titles.name: eWo Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended every week under the fed's own rules — the fastest clock any eWo belt ran on. Ryley Wynters was its first champion; Nijs Landzaat took it after ending Erin Jacobs' winning streak, and the fed's own account has his manager pushing for a bigger contract on the strength of it and being turned down.

titles.name: eWo Triple Crown Championship
titles.epitaph: Recorded once in the promotion's own Hall of Fame, on Czecher, listed alongside — not instead of — his eWo, United States, Gutz & Glory and Tag Team reigns. Whether it was a physical belt or the fed's own name for holding the other three is not settled in the surviving record.

titles.name: eWo United States Championship
titles.epitaph: eWo's secondary singles belt, defended twice a month under the fed's own rules. Czecher held it in the promotion's first run. In its second, Cody Clark carried it into BWF Danger Zone 2007 in a briefcase and handed it to Chris Roman in the middle of the ring; Roman held it up for the crowd to read, then laid it down and walked out with the rest of them.

titles.name: eWo Valor Championship
titles.epitaph: A second-run singles belt, and the busiest one in the fed's own rulebook: three defences every month, more than any other championship it carried. AJ Donavon and Ryley Wynters both held it.

titles.name: EWP United Kingdom Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own second-ranked title, described as defended on every card; no champion is recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: EWP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top title, planned to be crowned in an eight-man tournament at its own Halloween Brawl '99 pay-per-view; no result survives in the record.

titles.name: EWP World Juniorweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own title for wrestlers under 235 pounds; no champion is recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: EWP World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag title; no champions are recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: EWUK Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by the Duo of Annihilation against the Moral Majority on 27 August 1997; no result survives in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: EWUK Wednesday Night Warriors, 27 August 1997 (promotions/ewuk/archive/).

titles.name: EWUK Warriors Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed for defense on 27 August 1997 alongside the Tag Team Championship; no result survives in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: EWUK Wednesday Night Warriors, 27 August 1997 (promotions/ewuk/archive/).

titles.name: EWUK World Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in the fed's own first-round tournament at its inaugural Wednesday Night Warriors broadcast (24 April 1997); no tournament result survives in this collection's own held record.
titles.notes: EWUK Wednesday Night Warriors, 24 April 1997 (promotions/ewuk/archive/).

titles.name: EWWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Tommy Kain when the surviving record shows it, at Kingdom of the Wicked, where he retained in a triple threat against Ash and David Rheaume. The EWWF office voided the title by decree on 10 October 2002, stripping Kain and voiding Vinnie Cepacelli's own standing as number-one contender, with a successor title promised for the unheld “To Hell and Back.”

titles.name: Surrender Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested champion Despair won the title from Randy Love in a parking-lot ladder match on 16 April 2002. He lost it around 10 July to Homeless Joe Boxcar (shown only in a later recap) and regained it the same night, 17 July, after Trinity interference. Ashlyn Summers held it undocumented by 8 August, retaining in a hardcore match that night and again at Kingdom of the Wicked; Harvester of Sorrow held it undocumented by 5 December, having already assaulted Summers before that broadcast.
titles.notes: The fed's own broadcasts also call this belt the “Surrender Extreme Championship” and, coarsely, the “Sex Championship”/“EWWF SEX Championship” — the same title under three names in the promotion's own words, confirmed explicitly in its own commentary (“she holds the Surrender Extreme Title...the SEX title”); the registry uses its fullest attested name.

titles.name: SEWF Championship
titles.epitaph: A sixteen-man tournament the EWWF ran entirely on its own broadcasts across October 2002 for a title its own ring introductions and commentary call the “SEWF Championship,” “SEWF World Title” and “SEWF Heavyweight Championship.” Tommy Kain won the tournament's final at the unheld “To Hell and Back,” then retained on 5 December against Jimmy Slade after Simon Underwood, the triple threat's third man, was pulled from the match before the bell by Slade's own attack.
titles.notes: This title shares its name and lineage words with the historical, closed sewf promotion's own World Heavyweight Championship (sewf-world) but is never shown as staged, sanctioned or administered by that promotion — the EWWF runs, judges and crowns it on its own shows throughout. Filed as a distinct title belonging to ewwf-surrender-2002; the sewf promotion's own registry row and its own title's reign history are untouched. Flagged for further review given the shared name.

titles.name: EWWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for an eight-team single-elimination tournament at Kingdom of the Wicked, won by Rune Tao and Liam Zen, who retained the same night against Andrew Krumm and Syko. Jersey City Street Machine (Rocky Camarelli and Sammy Paulison) held the belts undocumented by 2 October before losing them to Ryan Delaney and David Rheaume on 5 December, with help from Nick Demola and the debuting Seventh Seal.

titles.name: EWWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Smoove when the surviving record opens, changing hands on 16 April 2002 to Thomas Casey. The title cycled repeatedly across the spring and summer among Casey, Jimmy Slade, Axel Reed and Randy Love before Slade's 8 August win; it later passed undocumented to Randy Love and was ruled to Sammy Paulison by disqualification on 10 October, then passed undocumented again to Larry Spikowski, who retained against Ragnarok on 5 December.

titles.name: EWWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Adam Mitchell when the surviving record opens on 16 April 2002. Simon Solkoff held it undocumented by Redemption in June, retained through a time-limit draw and a three-way C-4 exploding match at Kingdom of the Wicked, and lost it to Despair in a two-on-one handicap match on 2 October, Adam Mitchell counting the pin himself. Despair retained against Simon Underwood on 10 October before losing it to Harvester of Sorrow in a three-way with Ashlyn Summers on 5 December, the last held broadcast in this run.

titles.name: EWWF Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a two-out-of-three-falls scaffold and steel cage match thirty feet above the ring.

titles.name: Extreme Power Championship
titles.epitaph: Extreme Power's own top championship, billed as held by Batista as of the promotion's own 8 December 2006 show. The same document also calls the title the "World Heavyweight Championship" in its own next-week teaser line, without explaining the two names -- both are treated here as the same title as the source itself does. Batista was due to defend it against Undertaker the following week; that show was not captured.

titles.name: EWO Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship during its 1999 revival, won by a wrestler who also carried the promotion's Hardcore title into the same reign.

titles.name: GAWA Extremely Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Always defended in a gimmick match; switched hands at WrestleKrazy II in the same title-vs-title stipulation that cost Striker Phrost the All American belt.

titles.name: FASW World Television Title
titles.epitaph: A first-round tournament bracket is underway as of the promotion's own 10 May 1997 show; no reign is recorded within this collection's own held record.

titles.name: FASW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Psychrobat into Superstar Summit, where a Unification Match against the EWA's own TV Champion folded it into a single belt -- the FASW's own separate lineage ends there, undefeated.

titles.name: FASW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Hellshock into Superstar Summit, April 1996, defending against Gunnar "The Grizzly" Gaines; the surviving 1996 record does not show the outcome, and the FASW's own independent run ends at this same event.

titles.name: FAW Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on FAW's own December 2002 title-history index as one of four belts whose recorded history began on 1 December 2002, and named again in the 2003 list of titles the fed stopped defending. The only holder the surviving record identifies is Dave Tronick, billed as a former Continental Champion on his own return at Diabolical Day 2003; the index page's own linked histories were never captured.
titles.notes: FAW's own Title History index, December 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-title-history-index.html), FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html) and FAW's own Diabolical Day 2003 recap (promotions/faw/archive/diabolical-day-2003-2003-07-13.html).

titles.name: Diabolical Day King
titles.epitaph: The tournament FAW ran on its own Diabolical Day pay-per-view every July, and the title its winner carried for the year: Diabolical Day King. The winner took a World Championship shot with it — in 2001 on the following night's FAW is WAR, in 2003 at Collision Course.

titles.name: FAW European Championship
titles.epitaph: A mid-card singles belt through 2001 and 2002 — Jim ‘JLC’ Phoenix twice, Spawn, Skipster, Baz, Kryptonite, Shensui Yusuki, Shifty and Cyrus Skar all held it, and Joe La Fontaine was champion at the fed's own June 2002 snapshot. It is one of the five titles FAW's own 2003 champions page names as no longer worth keeping.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, June 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-june-2002.html), FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html) and the fed's own roster-database bio cards (faw.projectefed.com/cgi-bin/roster.cgi), workshop-held, never served.

events.note: Champion Cyrus Skar has the title discontinued on-air ("Europe is a waste of space") and replaced with a new FAW United States Championship; Tom "the Bomb" has the physical belt discarded and hands Skar the new US title instead. FAW Breakdown #1, read in full.

titles.name: FAW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: A short-lived belt of the 2003 era. The Meditator was champion going into Diabolical Day on 13 July 2003, where a fatal four-way with Khristian Call, Damien Ryan and Horazon ended with Call sitting on a broken ladder for the three-count. Call was still champion at the fed's own August 2003 snapshot; by December the title was gone from the fed's own list.
titles.notes: FAW's own current-champions page, August 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-current-champions-august-2003.html), FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html) and FAW's own Diabolical Day 2003 recap (promotions/faw/archive/diabolical-day-2003-2003-07-13.html).

titles.name: FAW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt Apocalypse held six times. Skipster held it twice, Jim ‘JLC’ Phoenix twice, Baz twice, and Spider, Bayne and The Omega Fro once each; Violator was champion at the fed's own June 2002 snapshot. It was one of the titles dropped in the 2003 cut.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions snapshot of 6 February 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-february-2003.html) names "Golden Nine" Jeff Harris as Hardcore Champion, narrowing the undocumented transition between Damien Ryan's 29 September 2002 win and Harris's own reign to on-or-before 6 February 2003 -- previously the transition was bounded only by Harris's confirmed title on 30 March 2003. A same-week Panic card (promotions/faw/archive/faw-panic-card-2003-02-02.html) bills a Hardcore Title triple threat, Jeff Harris vs Rzarector vs Skipster, corroborating the same snapshot; no results page for that card survives.

titles.name: FAW International Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's secondary singles belt, and one of the three it kept when it cut its championship list down in 2003.
