Sean Mason defended it in Chris Thunder's own pay-per-view debut at Breakaway 2001; Jim ‘JLC’ Phoenix took it after eight months on the roster and called it the breakthrough of his career; Chris Thunder won it in a triple threat at Taking Hardcore To The Extreme in October 2001, in the match that started the xCw invasion, and lost it inside the month. Shifty held it in the summer of 2002. Sniper beat The British Bomber for it on the 6 July 2003 Panic and was still champion at the fed's last surviving snapshot that December.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, June 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-june-2002.html), FAW's own current-champions page, August 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-current-champions-august-2003.html), FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html) and FAW's own Hall of Fame page (promotions/faw/archive/faw-hall-of-fame.html).

titles.name: FAW Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Chris Thunder was the first champion, in August 2001. No other holder appears anywhere in the surviving record, and the belt is absent from every later list of the fed's own championships.
titles.notes: the fed's own roster-database bio cards (faw.projectefed.com/cgi-bin/roster.cgi), workshop-held, never served — Chris Thunder's own bio card: “became the first FAW Light-Heavyweight Champion”.

titles.name: FAW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Reinstated in the summer of 2001 and held by nearly every stable FAW ran. Dark Generation took the belts and were stripped of them when both champions were injured; Skipster and The Omega Fro, Chris Thunder with three different partners, the Mass Murderers, the Foam World Order and New School all held them across 2002. They were vacant going into Diabolical Day 2003, where a triple threat gave them to the Vice Squad — who were handed the belts and put on the floor with chairs in the same minute.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, June 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-june-2002.html), FAW's own current-champions page, August 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-current-champions-august-2003.html), FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html), FAW's own Hall of Fame page (promotions/faw/archive/faw-hall-of-fame.html) and FAW's own Diabolical Day 2003 recap (promotions/faw/archive/diabolical-day-2003-2003-07-13.html).

titles.name: FAW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: FAW retired this belt in memory of Joe “Soulja” Smallze, who wrestled here and died in April 2002. The fed's own champions page carried the line where a champion's name would go: “Retired in honour of Joe Smallze R.I.P”. It did not stay retired: by SummerSlaughter in August 2002 the fed had brought it back and put it on the line, over the objection of Smallze's own cousin Hardcore Hoefel, who stole the belt from champion Syd and buried it at Smallze's grave hours before Syd defended it anyway, losing it to J.J. Dynasty.

events.note: Retired unfilled in memory of Joe “Soulja” Smallze, who died in April 2002.

titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, June 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-june-2002.html), captured 10 June 2002. The same fact is independently recorded in the Primetime Central corpus already held.

titles.name: FAW Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Sat above the World Championship on FAW's own earliest surviving site. The Olympian held it first, into a March 2001 I Quit Match against Lex Luger; Luger carried it into a four-way battle royal at Extreme Beating and lost it there to British Bulldog, then held it again by the fed's own FAW is War card at month's end. A Tables, Ladders and Chairs rematch against Bulldog for it at May Day Massacre was called off on air for injuries to both men, and FAW's own president scrapped the belt that night — though the fed's own later site still names a champion for it into 2003.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, dated March 2001 and captured 21 April 2001 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-2001-03.html); its own cards page, same snapshot (promotions/faw/archive/faw-cards-2001-03.html); Tuesday Torture, 20 March 2001, Friday Night Fear, 23 March 2001, Extreme Beating, March 2001, FAW is War, 30 April 2001, and May Day Massacre, 5 May 2001 (promotions/faw/archive/tuesday-torture-2001-03-20.html, friday-night-fear-2001-03-23.html, extreme-beating-2001-03.html, faw-is-war-2001-04-30.html, may-day-massacre-2001-05-05.html and may-day-massacre-card-2001-05-05.html). FAW's ten registered titles do not include this belt. This crawl's own full 2003 read (When Worlds Collide 2003, Panic (February and 6 April), Extreme Beating Three) turned up Sean Mason billed champion throughout but found no textual support anywhere for this note's own earlier claim that Xander was separately billed champion -- that claim could not be corroborated and may be an error in this row's own prior research pass.

titles.name: FAW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Created on FAW's own first Breakdown to replace the discontinued European Championship, at reigning European Champion Cyrus Skar's own request; Skar became its first holder without a match.
titles.notes: FAW Breakdown #1 (2002-08), read in full.

titles.name: FAW Woman's Championship
titles.epitaph: One champion survives in the record: Tanya Vigilante, on the fed's own June 2002 champions page. The title is named again only once more, in the 2003 list of belts FAW decided to stop defending.
titles.notes: FAW's own champions page, June 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-june-2002.html) and FAW's own champions page, December 2003 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-december-2003.html).

titles.name: FAW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: FAW's top belt, and the one the fed kept through every rebuild it went through. Its first champion, HaHaKlown, is recorded as never having lost it — he handed it to his own sidekick Deadman and became president instead. Pyro took it at Breakaway 2001, American Psycho took it from Pyro, and from there it moved almost monthly: Spider, Spawn, Jim ‘JLC’ Phoenix, Skipster, The Omega Fro twice, The British Bomber, Chris Thunder for nine days in January 2002, Tony Vigilante, Rzarector through the summer of 2003, and Violator from Deceit on 9 November 2003. The fed's own paperwork survives in snapshots rather than as a ledger, so the order above is what its champions pages and its Hall of Fame between them attest, not a continuous chain.
titles.notes: A separate, earlier champions snapshot of 8 April 2002 (promotions/faw/archive/faw-champions-april-2002.html) names The Omega Fro as World Champion, International Champion EDH, European Champion Shifty, Hardcore Champion Xander, and Tag Team Champions Foam World Order (Neo & 9th Wonder Of Foam); all five corroborate reigns already recorded as open-ended at that date and do not themselves change any recorded date.

titles.name: FCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.caption: One of four titles announced by the fed; no card or title change survives in the held record.
titles.epitaph: FCW Cruiserweight Championship of FCW ENTITY E: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: FCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: One of four titles announced by the fed; no card or title change survives in the held record.
titles.epitaph: FCW Heavyweight Championship of FCW ENTITY E: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: FCW Intercontinental Championship
titles.caption: One of four titles announced by the fed; no card or title change survives in the held record.
titles.epitaph: FCW Intercontinental Championship of FCW ENTITY E: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: FCW Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: One of four titles announced by the fed; no card or title change survives in the held record.
titles.epitaph: FCW Tag Team Championship of FCW ENTITY E: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: FDW Championship
titles.epitaph: Crush!'s own top championship, decided in a ten-man Battle Royal on the brand's own first show (1 November 2007) and won by Rated R, the last man standing after nine eliminations.

titles.name: FDW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Pedro_RKO and Mr.Xtreme Hardcore over Lord and Rated R on Crush!'s own first show (1 November 2007), Pedro_RKO turning on his own partner to secure the win.

titles.name: FEW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Lightning" Levi Ash as of his own 18 October 1997 career retrospective, the wing's only attested title.

titles.name: Flatlined World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Four men held it in four months. Takeo Brown had it on New Year's Day 2003 and Liphe Gonne took it off him on the same card; Javier Garcia took it from Gonne at Pride & Victory that February; and Frank Minio took it from Garcia on fightSHOW: 015 on 23 April, with a right fist thrown to counter a blow that would have won the fight. Garcia stayed on his feet after being knocked out and challenged for it again before he left the cage, for a CLASH in May whose date the fed never announced.

titles.name: Flatlined World Lightweight Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Current Champions page of February 2003 lists the belt with N/A where the champion's name goes (/promotions/ff/archive/current-champions-2003-02.html); its own title history, captured that April, records one holder (/promotions/ff/archive/title-history-2003-04.html).
titles.epitaph: Vacant on the fed's own Current Champions page in February 2003, and won six weeks later by Chester Ramis, a heavyweight who had spent a chapter working out that a week of illness and five lost pounds were about to drop him a weight class. He is the only champion it ever had.

titles.name: FFA/ToC Cup and Belt
titles.epitaph: The prize of an eight-woman one-night tournament announced for 1 June 2002, to be worn for a year alongside a hundred thousand dollars. The tournament was never staged and the belt was never awarded.

titles.name: Heidi Leick Hardcore Cup
titles.epitaph: A hardcore trophy named for the wrestler who was to referee it, open to the wrestlers eliminated from the Super 8 and to three entrants who asked for it alone. It was never contested.

titles.name: FFA/ToC Tag Cup
titles.epitaph: The prize of a seven-team tables, ladders and chairs elimination match announced for 1 June 2002. Applications closed on 28 April 2002 and the match was never staged.

titles.name: IGA Fight Club Championship
titles.epitaph: A bronze belt on a red strap, defended anywhere but the arena: parking lots, bars and locker rooms. Malkav won it at the Last Chance Bar & Grille on Devil's Night, 30 October 2001.

titles.name: Forgotten.LEGENDS Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Never contested, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own champions page throughout the surviving snapshots, with no reign of any kind recorded.
titles.notes: Billed vacant on champions.html as of the fed's own last surviving backup (10 March 2003). No reign is recorded.

titles.name: Forgotten.LEGENDS Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Never contested, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own champions page throughout the surviving snapshots, with no reign of any kind recorded.
titles.notes: Billed vacant on champions.html as of the fed's own last surviving backup (10 March 2003). No reign is recorded.

titles.name: Forgotten.LEGENDS World Championship
titles.epitaph: Never contested, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own champions page throughout the surviving snapshots, with no reign of any kind recorded.
titles.notes: Billed vacant on champions.html as of the fed's own last surviving backup (10 March 2003). No reign is recorded.

titles.name: FoB Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by tournament in December 2003 and won by Jamie Noble over Kraven in the final. It changed hands four times inside six months and twice by vacancy — John Lennex gave it up on a call-up to Revenge, and Chaos won the five-way that replaced him — then stopped dead with Robbie Crockett's reign on 25 May 2004. The fed brought it back sixteen months later and put thirty-one men in a Rebirth match for it; Christopher Daniels won, and was still champion when the record ends.
titles.notes: Transcribed complete from the fed's own published Championship Lineage (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-supercard-schedule-2005-09-29.html), which gives each reign's own length in days.

titles.name: FoB Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by exactly one team in its first life — Chris Harvard with Justin Credible, then with Shelton Benjamin after Credible left mid-reign — sixty-seven days that ran to 25 May 2004 and stopped. It came back with the promotion in September 2005 and moved three times in eighty-one days: The Butlers won a four-team tournament for it, the Detroit Street Thugs took it off them, and The Fear took it off the Thugs on 8 December 2005, the last change the lineage records.
titles.notes: Transcribed complete from the fed's own published Championship Lineage (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-supercard-schedule-2005-09-29.html). The tournament final The Butlers won was a fatal four-way against the Marcello Family, the Sonic Death Monkeys and Alpha Gamma Sigma; none of the three is minted, their names standing in the served ledger itself.

titles.name: FoB Wrath Championship
titles.epitaph: The Foundation of Brutality's second belt, crowned the same night as its first: Ozena beat Tony “The Marvel” Mason for it on 6 December 2003, then quit. Two of its four 2004 reigns started as vacancies and a third was simply handed to the number one contender, and it went dark with Tatewaki Kuno's on 25 May 2004 — the fed's own lineage lists it thereafter as a retired belt whose banner it no longer had. It was reinstated on 8 December 2005 with a division of its own, entered by beating a member of it, and Baxter Baxter beat Gene Snitsky to be its fifth champion.
titles.notes: Transcribed complete from the fed's own published Championship Lineage (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-supercard-schedule-2005-09-29.html), which marks the belt “[Retired Belt, Banner Not Available.]”. The reinstated division's own rules are set out in the Sacrifice of 13 October 2005 (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-sacrifice-2005-10-13.html).

titles.name: fW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: No champion is recorded for the fW Cruiserweight Championship in the surviving record — the fed's own champions page still read the unfilled template's own “Wrestler Name” in every slot, under both the champion and all three contenders, at its last capture, 6 March 2003.
titles.notes: Recovered from the fed's own champions page (promotions/fortune-fwrestling/archive/champions-2003-03.html), captured 6 March 2003.

titles.name: fW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: No champion is recorded for the fW United States Championship in the surviving record — the fed's own champions page still read the unfilled template's own “Wrestler Name” in every slot, under both the champion and all three contenders, at its last capture, 6 March 2003.
titles.notes: Recovered from the fed's own champions page (promotions/fortune-fwrestling/archive/champions-2003-03.html), which bills this championship under the bare header “United States,” captured 6 March 2003.

titles.name: fW World Championship
titles.epitaph: No champion is recorded for the fW World Championship in the surviving record — the fed's own champions page still read the unfilled template's own “Wrestler Name” in every slot, under both the champion and all three contenders, at its last capture, 6 March 2003.
titles.notes: Recovered from the fed's own champions page (promotions/fortune-fwrestling/archive/champions-2003-03.html), captured 6 March 2003.

titles.name: FSW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own tag-team championship, inaugurated in a five-way gauntlet-turned-ladder match on its own debut supercard.
titles.notes: Attested only through a contemporaneous third-party recap of the federation's own debut supercard; the federation's own results page is hosted externally and is not in the held record.

titles.name: FSW Sunshine State Championship
titles.epitaph: A second title introduced by early 2006, contested for across the promotion's own broadcasts through mid-2006 and made official as a supercard match by an on-air contract signing; no result for that match survives in the held record.

titles.name: FSW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Inaugurated by an eight-man tournament that ran across the promotion's own weekly broadcasts in October and November 2005, with its final scheduled for the promotion's own debut supercard; no result for that final survives in the held record. The title's own belt was confirmed on a reigning champion by the promotion's second supercard in May 2006, defended there in a three-way match against two further challengers; the record does not show when or how that reign began.

titles.name: FSW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The first run's hardcore championship. Mike Marvelous, refereeing, awarded it to Jacob Jackson at High Impact on 27 August 2000 when time ran out, though Dysan believed he had won. Jack Miller held it three times; at Final Destination on 26 November 2000 he ran Hardcore Camo over with a car in the parking lot and took the belt on the same night Camo had won it. Jack Brooze won it vacant at Redemption on 26 August 2001. A Paranoia write-up of October 2001 has P.S. Mad pin Brooze for it; at Futile Resistance in November 2001 Brooze is billed champion again and PS Mad wins it from him, together with the Rising Star title, and the fed's champions page still listed him at the end of the year.
titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; the first run's show write-ups, among them an undated Paranoia results page of October 2001; the Futile Resistance preview card ("Jack Brooze(c)"); the champions page captured on 28 December 2001. The October 2001 title history ends with Jack Brooze and carries no line for the Paranoia change.

titles.name: FSW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship of the fed's first run. Cyle Chaos became the first FSW Intercontinental Champion by climbing a ladder for the belt at High Impact on 27 August 2000. Big Daveylicious, Mike Marvelous, Colin Baird, Jacob Jackson, Aggonizer and Johnny Mayhem were among its holders before Painkiller, the boss, made Mayhem lay the belt down on 6 April 2001. Punisher 2000 won it at Hallowed Knights on 7 October 2001, and Jonny Trip pulled it down in a ladder match at Futile Resistance in November 2001; the fed's champions page still listed Trip at the end of that year. The 2002 run did not bring the title back.
titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; the first run's show write-ups; the Futile Resistance preview card ("Punisher 2000(c)"); the champions page captured on 28 December 2001. The October 2001 page names Carlton Carter beaten on 15 May 2001, where its previous row makes neXt the champion.

titles.name: FSW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship of the fed's first run. Shelldog won it first in a four-way at High Impact on 27 August 2000, and Falken and D. Jaxx followed; on 13 October 2000 the fed's title history records it stripped from D. Jaxx and retired. It came back at Love Hurts on 26 February 2001, when Ron Jacobs won it in a three-way, and passed through T.Q. Smooth, who was stripped of it in March, Andy Overdose and Matt Senate to Chris Taylor on 4 May 2001. By the end of October 2001 the title history marked it retired again.

events.note: The fed's own title history, in both its April and October 2001 captures: "Ttile Retired | Stripped from D. Jaxx | 10/13/00 | Maximum Veloicty". The title was contested again from Love Hurts, 26 February 2001.

The fed's own title history, as captured on 31 October 2001, heads the belt's table "Lightweight-Retired" (its April 2001 capture heads it "Lightweight"), and its champions page of December 2001 lists no Lightweight champion; no date is given.

titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; the Love Hurts write-up; the champions pages captured on 8 April and 28 December 2001.

titles.name: FSW Prime Time Championship
titles.epitaph: Mike Marvelous became the first FSW Prime Time champion at High Impact on 27 August 2000. Marc North won it from him in a three-way at Total Annihellation and vacated it at Fallen on 29 October 2000, calling it the Piece of Trash title. It changed hands often after that, through Kay Kash's win in a three-way at Defiance on 15 July 2001, and by the end of October 2001 the fed's title history marked it retired. The 2002 run put it up for grabs again at Genesis on 18 August 2002, as the Primetime Championship, and Angelo Deville won it; he kept it through every defence the surviving record holds, the last on 20 November 2002, when he also won Cassius Deamont's FSW contract.

events.note: The fed's own title history, as captured on 31 October 2001, heads the belt's table "Prime Time-Retired" (its April 2001 capture heads it "Prime Time"), and its champions page of December 2001 lists no Prime Time champion; neither page dates the retirement. The fed brought the title back at Genesis on 18 August 2002.

titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; its 2002 Title Histories page; the show write-ups of both runs. The 2002 Title Histories page numbers Angelo Deville's reign fourteenth, after the thirteen of 2000–01, where the Genesis write-up puts the title up "for the first time".

titles.name: FSW Rising Star Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship of the fed's first run. Its first champion was crowned at High Impact on 27 August 2000: The Riddler in the show's own write-up, Aggonizer in the fed's title history. Red Hurricane won it at Total Annihellation that October, Colin Baird took it in a Hell In A Cell ladder match at Fallen, and neXt, champion from March 2001, handed the belt to Max Danger on 10 April 2001, saying he was moving on to higher things. Jack Brooze won it at Hallowed Knights on 7 October 2001, and PS Mad pinned him for it and the Extreme title together at Futile Resistance in November 2001.
titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; the first run's show write-ups; the Futile Resistance preview card ("Jack Brooze(c)"). The High Impact and Total Annihellation write-ups have The Riddler win the title and lose it to Red Hurricane; both captures of the title history give those two lines to Aggonizer. The 15 July 2001 row names the card Paranoia; the same page's other rows of that date, and the fed's booking, say Defiance.

titles.name: FSW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Five Star Wrestling's tag team championship, in both of its runs. The Psycho Brotherz won it first in a four-corner elimination match at High Impact on 27 August 2000. It was stripped or vacated more than once in the first run, and P.S. Mad and Sound, who won it at Love Hurts on 26 February 2001, declared the belts the Hardcore Tag Titles. At Futile Resistance in November 2001 Human took the title from Blake in a parking lot and then held it alone. In 2002 Ming and Michel Krieg won it vacant at Genesis on 18 August, Bad Frotitude took it in a three-way on 26 September, and at Bad Moon Rising on 20 October the masked Dead Presidents won it from Bad Frotitude in a chain match and unmasked as Politically Incorrect, William S. Powell and Reginald V. Lovecraft. Rites To Pain, Jason McAllister and Neurosis, won it from them on 27 November 2002, the last show the surviving record holds.
titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; its 2002 Title Histories page; the show write-ups of both runs; the champions page captured on 28 December 2001. The 2002 page has Ming and Michel Krieg beat Bad Frotitude at Genesis, where the write-up has them beat A Tag Team; it dates the Jacksons' title 29 November 2000 (Fallen, 29 October, on its own World list) and Bad Moon Rising 21 October 2002.

titles.name: FSW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Five Star Wrestling's top championship, in both of its runs. Steve Johnson won it first, beating Matthew Morrison in the final of a tournament at High Impact on 27 August 2000. It changed hands often over the next year and was stripped from its champion more than once; Chris Fear won it at Hallowed Knights on 7 October 2001, and Blitz pinned Fear for it at Futile Resistance in November 2001. When the fed returned in 2002 the title was vacant: a four-way for it at Genesis on 18 August 2002 was ruled a no contest, and Timo Bolamba won it at Bad Moon Rising on 20 October 2002, pinning Mike Marvelous in the final of the Dead or Alive tournament. Bolamba beat Chris Chase in his first defence on 27 November 2002, the last show the surviving record holds.
titles.notes: Sources: the fed's own title history on thefsw.com, as the Wayback Machine captured it on 8 April and 31 October 2001; its 2002 Title Histories page; the show write-ups of both runs; the August 2000 tournament bracket. The 2002 write-ups bill Bolamba's belt as new and call its first holder the first FSW World Champion, while the 2002 Title Histories page numbers his reign sixteenth, after those of 2000–01, and Bad Moon Rising bills Mike Marvelous a former World Heavyweight Champion. The October 2001 page dates Johnny Mayhem's first win "4/17/02"; its own order, its Intercontinental row and the April 2001 calendar put that Glory on 17 April 2001. The 2002 page dates Bad Moon Rising 21 October 2002; the show and its advertisements give Sunday 20 October.

titles.name: FWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Lionheart" Adam Lash as of the held record's February 1997 holdings; no title change survives.
titles.notes: FWA's own founding roleplayer-recruitment post.

titles.name: FWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Ass Kicker" Adam Anderson as of the held record's February 1997 holdings; no title change survives.
titles.notes: FWA's own founding roleplayer-recruitment post.

titles.name: FWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Malice through the held record's February 1997 holdings, including a bloody barbed-wire successful defense against "Gangsta" Crush's own challenger status turned aside -- Malice retained, though the match ends with a mystery attacker cutting his throat open on the top rope.
titles.notes: FWA's own PPV recap (promotions/fwa-association/archive/).

titles.name: FWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Steve Gunn at the start of 1997's own newsletter profile; changed hands to King 3933540$ Perfect in a three-fall streetfight/Texas Death/I Quit main event refereed by a guest Sandman, inside a four-week window this collection can date no more finely.
titles.notes: FWA's own newsletter and PPV recap (promotions/fwa-association/archive/).

titles.name: FWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Masters of Destruction (Psycho Sabu & Master Blaster) as of the held record's February 1997 holdings; no title change survives.
titles.notes: FWA's own founding roleplayer-recruitment post.

titles.name: FWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: No FWA document of its own survives to say when this title was created or who held it first. Its last champion, The Dehibilitator, lost to Shaman on 28 July 2000, three and a half weeks after the rest of the FWA was absorbed into the WWA, unifying the FWA Hardcore Championship into the WWA Extreme Championship — the whole of this title's surviving record.

events.title: wwa-extreme
events.note: Unified into the WWA Extreme Championship when Shaman defeated defending FWA Hardcore Champion The Dehibilitator on 28 July 2000 (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-28.html).

titles.name: FWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: No FWA document of its own survives to say when this title was created or who held it first. Its last champion, Buck Floyd, defeated WWA United States Champion Shawn Cage at the WWA's own Independence Day Rumble (2 July 2000), unifying the FWA North American Championship into the WWA United States Championship — the whole of this title's surviving record.

events.title: wwa-united-states
events.note: Unified into the WWA United States Championship when Buck Floyd defeated WWA United States Champion Shawn Cage at Independence Day Rumble (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

titles.name: FWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: No FWA document of its own survives to say when this title was created or who held it first. Its last champion, Chad Goodman, lost to Lyle Wile at the WWA's own Independence Day Rumble (2 July 2000), unifying the FWA Television Championship into the WWA Television Championship — the whole of this title's surviving record.

events.title: wwa-television
events.note: Unified into the WWA Television Championship when Lyle Wile defeated defending FWA Television Champion Chad Goodman at Independence Day Rumble (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

titles.name: FWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: No FWA document of its own survives to say when this title was created. Its earliest attested holders, Brody Thunder and King Apples, are recorded from a host promotion's own March 1999 broadcast weekend, which carries a taped-fist ladder match changing the title. Its last champion, Jim Black, arrived at the WWA's own Independence Day Rumble (2 July 2000) and defeated WWA World Heavyweight Champion Nik Segier, unifying the FWA World Championship into the WWA's own belt — an undocumented gap separates the two eras.

events.title: wwa-world-heavyweight
events.note: Unified into the WWA World Heavyweight Championship when Jim Black, arriving from the FWA, defeated WWA World Heavyweight Champion Nik Segier at Independence Day Rumble (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

titles.name: FWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: No FWA document of its own survives to say when this title was created or who held it first. Its last champions, Allied Chaos (Kyle Niker and Connor Pearce), carried the belts into a challenge for the WWA's own Unified World Tag Team Championship on the WWA's own 25 June 2000 card — booked as a scripted title change, refused on-page by the defending WWA champions, Random Acts of Violence, who won the match outright and came out of it holding both sets of belts — the whole of this title's surviving record.

events.title: wwa-world-tag-team
events.note: Random Acts of Violence (Maim and Torture), the defending WWA World Tag Team Champions, defeated Allied Chaos (the FWA World Tag Team Champions) at Friday Fights, 25 June 2000, in a match booked to unify the titles — the champions refused the scripted job on-page and won instead, ending the FWA Tag Team lineage's own separate existence by defeating its champions rather than by a clean transfer (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-06-25.html; wwa-2000-06-25, match 4).

titles.name: FWF Intercontinental Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded, not won: the federation put twelve men in a battle royale on another promotion's card, Dreamcard IV, and gave the last man standing a new championship. Blue Steele was that man, lost the belt to a backroll press with the ropes for leverage, and took it back with the Iron Deathlock. Three reigns across two men is the whole of its ledger, and the federation kept a separate five-man contenders list for it — an undercard division with its own ranking, run by the same hands.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own singles ledger (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-singles-record-1993-01-08.html).

titles.name: FWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided by an eight-match round-robin tournament its own ledger opens with, and won in the final by Storm, who broke one man's back and put another in hospital on the way there. Devastation took the belts off them in November 1992 with a cast to the back of the head, turned back the Chameleons, and then lost them at the Clash of the Masters to the PWA's own champions on a fall taken with a foot on the bottom rope and the referee not seeing it. The federation's own rankings, posted a fortnight later, still list Devastation as champions.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own tag ledger (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-tag-rankings-history-1993-01-07.html). SOURCES DISAGREE on where the championship stood at the end: the same document records the Clash of the Masters loss and heads its own rankings "Champs: Devastation". Both readings are recorded.

titles.name: FWF United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The consolation prize of the founding tournament and the busiest belt on the ledger: six reigns across five men, with a vacancy in the middle when its holder won the World Championship and had to give it up. Damien Flayer held it twice, John Lawless twice, and Joe Reed took it off Flayer with a small package on 9 April 1992. Titan Morgan's win over Lawless on 14 October 1992 is where the ledger leaves it; a month later he defended it to a double countout and then carried it into the Clash of the Masters against the PWA's own United States Champion, and lost by countout.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own singles ledger (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-singles-record-1993-01-08.html).

titles.name: FWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top belt, and the one it opened with: its own ledger's first two matches are a double-elimination tournament, and the winner of the first was awarded the World Championship while the loser took the United States title as consolation. Five reigns follow across the ledger's own sixty-eight matches. Doctor Death took it first and lost it to a man who hit him with a stick; Annihilus won it by submission and lost it to an inside cradle; Titan Morgan held it until Death took it back with the Vulcan Death Grip on 15 April 1992, the one change of it the surviving record holds a report of. By January 1993 the federation was billing its holder as "PWA/FWF World Heavyweight Champion" — the belt had been unified with another federation's at the Clash of the Masters, and Death had won that too.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own singles ledger (promotions/fwf-1992/archive/fwf-singles-record-1993-01-08.html).

titles.name: FWF/ASW Unified Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship unified across two Sister Leagues members, FWF and ASW, held by "Devastating" Daniel Lewis as of December 1997 -- though the Sister Leagues' own weekly ranking the same day records the holder as disputed.
titles.notes: FWF's own 18 December 1997 anniversary bulletin; Sister Leagues Ratings List, 18 December 1997.

titles.notes: FWF's own 18 December 1997 anniversary bulletin.

titles.name: FWF Intercontinental Championship

titles.name: FWG Continental Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's secondary heavyweight belt, named in its first FAQ and folded into the new World Triple Crown Championship when the N.I.W.F. took over FWG at License to Kill.

titles.name: FWG World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's cruiserweight title, won by Lance Dewlock from Primo Destruccion on the 20 August 2001 Rampage; Dewlock treated the belt as his own personal showcase into the fall.

titles.name: FWG Deathmatch Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's hardcore title, won by Darkside from the N.I.W.F.'s Hardcore G at License to Kill, held by Firestarter by early September, and won by Rio Nexan in a four-way brawl through a McDonald's at WrestleSeries.

titles.name: FWG World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's tag championship, held by the N.I.W.F.'s Blast and Psycho Cebo after License to Kill, then by Skull and Hellbound, before Sniper and Inferno won it back in a TLC three-way at WrestleSeries.

titles.name: FWG Television Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's title for up-and-comers, held by Passion until Sheyda won it in a ladder match at WrestleSeries.

titles.name: FWG World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: FWG's top belt, unified at License to Kill into a World Triple Crown when Duke tha Hammer's win over Viper was combined with the N.I.W.F. Heavyweight and FWG Continental titles under the incoming N.I.W.F. ownership. Brick Wall held it into September 2001, when Viper won it back at WrestleSeries.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's Cruiserweight Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 15 May 1998, held by Ultra Violet. The fed's own record carries 67 reigns on it; 48 of them, across 30 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Tempest's, 288 days from 23 February 2002. Five of them ended outside a match (handed over with no match, stripped, vacated).

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's Hardcore Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 12 June 1998, held by Falcon. The fed's own record carries 86 reigns on it; 69 of them, across 41 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Eli Flair's, 187 days from 27 April 2002. Three of them ended outside a match (handed over with no match, vacated).

titles.name: International Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's International Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 19 February 1999, held by Black Panther. The fed's own record carries 24 reigns on it; 24 of them, across 15 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Eron the Relentless's, 94 days from 31 October 1999. One of them ended outside a match (retired).

titles.name: Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's Internet Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 8 May 1998, held by Austin Davis. The fed's own record carries 50 reigns on it; 38 of them, across 26 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Scott Slugger's, 277 days from 23 February 2002. Five of them ended outside a match (retired, stripped, vacated). The Flying Frenchie held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's Tag Team Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 26 June 1998, held by Punisher Squad (Jim Dudley & Chris Kidman Jr.). The fed's own record carries 68 reigns on it; 46 of them, across 31 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Austin Davis & Boston Strangler's, 358 days from 30 December 2001. Two of them ended outside a match (vacated). The Entourage held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: United States Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's United States Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 8 December 2002, held by Borst. The fed's own record carries 12 reigns on it; 3 of them, across 3 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Borst's, 134 days from 8 December 2002.

titles.name: Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's Women's Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 29 October 1998, held by Briana. The fed's own record carries 18 reigns on it; 17 of them, across 10 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Briana's, 268 days from 24 December 1999. One of them ended outside a match (handed over with no match). James Armstrong held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: World Championship
titles.epitaph: fWo's World Championship: the earliest reign served here begins on 24 April 1998, held by Jim Dudley. The fed's own record carries 66 reigns on it; 50 of them, across 24 different champions, are served here so far. The longest of those is Erik Kelly's, 187 days from 27 April 2002. Five of them ended outside a match (stripped, vacated).

titles.name: UWF Gang Warfare Championship
titles.epitaph: A stable-vs-stable title first won by Fates Warning in 1998; the promotion's own records name more than one concurrent champion in early 1999, not reconciled here.

titles.name: GCW Austral-Asian Championship
titles.epitaph: The singles belt of the Austral-Asian division, the third of the federation's three regional titles.
titles.notes: Declared in the hobby's own directory of the five e-mail wrestling leagues, 13 June 1993: “This league recognises four singles and four tag team titles in the following divisions: World, Pan American, Euro-African, and Austral-Asian” (promotions/rspw/archive/a-comprehensive-guide-to-e-mail-wrestling-1993-06-13.html). That sentence is the whole of what is known about the belt. NO REIGN IS RECORDED, and none is owed: no document in the held record names a holder of it, on any date. The federation's own posts do not survive anywhere in the held record, so nothing further about this belt is likely to.

titles.notes: Declared in the hobby's own directory of the five e-mail wrestling leagues, 13 June 1993: “This league recognises four singles and four tag team titles in the following divisions: World, Pan American, Euro-African, and Austral-Asian” (promotions/rspw/archive/a-comprehensive-guide-to-e-mail-wrestling-1993-06-13.html). titles.name: GCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of a federation that changed it six times in eight months without a repeat champion, and did not leave the name of one of them behind.
titles.notes: Declared in the hobby's own directory of the five e-mail wrestling leagues, 13 June 1993: “This league recognises four singles and four tag team titles in the following divisions: World, Pan American, Euro-African, and Austral-Asian” (promotions/rspw/archive/a-comprehensive-guide-to-e-mail-wrestling-1993-06-13.html). That sentence is the whole of what is known about the belt. NO REIGN IS RECORDED, and none is owed: no document in the held record names a holder of it, on any date. The federation's own posts do not survive anywhere in the held record, so nothing further about this belt is likely to. The same entry counts the singles scene as the less stable of the two: “there have been six World champions in eight months with no repeats.” Six reigns are therefore known to have happened, and not one of the six champions is named.

titles.name: GCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's senior tag belts, and by its own writer's account the most stable thing in it: one team held them for all but seven days of the first six months. Which team is not recorded anywhere.
titles.notes: Declared in the hobby's own directory of the five e-mail wrestling leagues, 13 June 1993: “This league recognises four singles and four tag team titles in the following divisions: World, Pan American, Euro-African, and Austral-Asian” (promotions/rspw/archive/a-comprehensive-guide-to-e-mail-wrestling-1993-06-13.html). That sentence is the whole of what is known about the belt. NO REIGN IS RECORDED, and none is owed: no document in the held record names a holder of it, on any date. The federation's own posts do not survive anywhere in the held record, so nothing further about this belt is likely to. The same entry counts the tag scene as “VERY stable”: “one team held the World tag title for all of the first six months, with the brief exception of seven days.” That reign, and the seven-day one inside it, are known to have happened, and neither team is named.

titles.name: GCW Missouri Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Gateway City Wrestling's top prize, open to any wrestler regardless of weight and slated for defense every three to four weeks -- announced in the fed's own founding guide before any match was ever held.

titles.name: GCW Television Title
titles.epitaph: Gateway City Wrestling's secondary title, restricted to wrestlers under 290 pounds and slated for defense every other week -- announced in the fed's own founding guide before any match was ever held.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's Cruiserweight Championship was first won by Chameleon on 22 April 2001. The fed's own record carries 11 reigns on it, across 10 different champions. One of its reigns ended outside a match (retired with the belt). Tessa Windsor held it when the record ends; a card of March 2007 calls the belt retired.

events.note: The federation's own words, in the closing line of the Vanguard Championship's first title defence: "Vetra has the retired Cruiserweight and Hardcore titles on his form like a gold vest while he holds his Vanguard Title up in the air." The Cruiserweight Championship's last reign in the record begins 9 Jul 2006 (Tessa Windsor) and the belt appears in no later title match, so the retirement falls between that night and 9 Mar 2007. Corroborated by the federation's own Record Book, whose 'Defunct Titles' section carries exactly three headings — GCW Cruiserweight Title Records, GCW Vanguard Title Records, GCW Women's Title Records — while the Hardcore title keeps its records among the live belts. Source: the fed's own card, WorldWide of 9 Mar 2007.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's Hardcore Championship was first won by Toad on 21 March 2001. The fed's own record carries 41 reigns on it, across 26 different champions. The longest is Trey Tremendous's, 1693 days from about 28 July 2005, a span that takes in the belt's retirement and reinstatement. Twice in 2005 the belt left him and came back the same night, at Warpath and at Dangerous Games. One of its reigns ended outside a match (vacated). GCW unified it into the Television Championship on 10 January 2012, at WorldWide, in a three-way match won by Sexton Hardon. A card of March 2007 calls the belt retired, and a news column of March 2010 speaks of the 'REINSTATED' Hardcore Title.

events.note: The federation unified the Hardcore Championship into the Television Championship in a three-way match between the two champions and a challenger. Its own voice, before the bell: "Bryan: As per the higher ups, the Television and Hardcore title are being unified and, albeit for a short time, one person will leave here as the first double champion since Triumph Frost." And after: "Andrews: Your winner...and the NEW GCW Unified Television and Hardcore champion.....SEXXXXXXXXX-TONNNNNNN......HARRRRRRRRRRRDDDDDD-ONNNNNNNNNNNNN!!!!!" / "Bryan: Hardon pulled through to become the first ever Unified Hardcore and Television champ in GCW history". The direction is the Television title's: the fed's own title log files this match and the belt's next and last match (Dangerous Games of 17 Mar 2012, 'Television Championship Match') under the Television title, and the fed's own title list carries the champion of record. The federation's own name for the belt from this night is the Unified Television and Hardcore Championship; Yale spends the entrance segment failing to coin a shorter one and Bryan settles it — "Let's just stick with the Unified Television and Hardcore title for now". Source: the fed's own card, WorldWide of 10 Jan 2012 (billed 'TELEVISION & HARDCORE/VANGUARD CHAMPIONSHIP UNIFICATION MATCH').
events.title: gcw-gcwonline-2001-hdtv

events.note: The federation's own words, in the closing line of the Vanguard Championship's first title defence: "Vetra has the retired Cruiserweight and Hardcore titles on his form like a gold vest while he holds his Vanguard Title up in the air." The last Hardcore reign the page carries begins 19 May 2005, so the retirement falls between that date and this card. The reversal has the federation's own word too: a news column of 17 Mar 2010 ('The WorldWide Web #1') says "We knew after GCW Radio that the Tag Team Titles had been suspended, which drew the ire of Bryan Mayhem. But Mayhem was satisfied; he gets credit for a Tag Title reign, and now he's the sole holder of the REINSTATED GCW Hardcore Title." Source: the fed's own card, WorldWide of 9 Mar 2007, and the fed's own news post of 17 Mar 2010.

titles.name: HDTV Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's HDTV Championship was first won by Capo on 20 May 2001. The fed's own record carries 48 reigns on it, across 42 different champions. The longest of known length is Jay Terror's, 157 days from 10 May 2007. Sexton Hardon held it at the end of the surviving record, as the Unified Television and Hardcore Champion after the Hardcore Championship was unified into it on 10 January 2012.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's Tag Team Championship was first won by Wallstreet Hustlers on 3 April 2001. The fed's own record carries 29 reigns on it, across 28 different champions. The longest is Blood Games's, 1113 days from 21 March 2002. Four of its reigns ended outside a match (two vacated, one departed, one retired). Bryan Mayhem held it at the end of the surviving record.

events.note: The federation's own card, Devil's Night 2005 (30 Oct 2005), in the words of the champion Joshua Curtis: "It has been explained to me that the Tag Team Division here in GCW has flat lined and there is no way to revive it and that effective immediately the tag division has died with myself and Ami being the last champions of record." WorldWide 31 (6 Nov 2005) confirms it ("when the tag division got shut down"). The belt was later revived: the federation's own Tag Team Title History gives its reign No. 16 (21 Mar 2006) as won from 'Vacant'.

titles.name: United States Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's United States Championship was first won by Thirteen on 22 April 2001. The fed's own record carries 39 reigns on it, across 33 different champions. The longest of known length is Karina Wolfenden's, 314 days from 20 November 2010. Two of its reigns ended outside a match (vacated, forfeited). Aimz held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Vanguard Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's Vanguard Championship's first recorded champion is 'The Silent Assassin' Peter Vetra. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. GCW unified it with the Television Championship at Warpath 2007, on 3 June 2007, when Jay Terror beat Katie O'Clare, and Shaman reinstated it in 2011. The federation unified it into the Hardcore Championship on 11 October 2011.

events.title: gcw-gcwonline-2001-hdtv
events.note: At Warpath 2007 the federation staged the Television and Vanguard Championship unification match, "contested under Vanguard Rules... which means the winner of this match can be declared only by 5 second knock-out or submission": Jay Terror beat Vanguard Champion Katie O'Clare, and the timekeeper tossed both belts into the ring for him. Source: the fed's own card, Warpath 2007 (3 Jun 2007).

At Rampage on 11 Oct 2011 the federation staged a one-title-leaves match between Vanguard Champion Shaman — "the last remnant of the Hardcore division, save for the current Hardcore Champion" who "brought back The Vanguard title" — and the Hardcore Champion, Brad Cruz, who won it on the Cruzifix Slam: "Andrews: Here is your winner...the GCW Hardcore Champion...The SoCal Prophet...BRAAAAAAD! CRUUUUUUUUUUUUZZZZZZZ!!!" and "Bryan: What a war that was, and we've got a SOLIDIFIED Hardcore Champion!" The Vanguard title is named nowhere after this night; the card of 10 Jan 2012 still calls the belt 'HARDCORE/VANGUARD' in its billing and its commentary corrects that on air to the Hardcore title. Source: the fed's own card, Rampage of 11 Oct 2011.
events.title: gcw-gcwonline-2001-hardcore

titles.name: Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's Women's Championship's first recorded champion is Icebabe. The fed's own record carries 6 reigns on it, across 5 different champions. One of its reigns ended outside a match (stripped from the holder). The federation's own Record Book lists it among the defunct titles.

events.note: The federation's own Record Book carries a 'GCW Women's Title Records' heading under 'Defunct Titles', so the federation itself records the belt as defunct. The heading is empty of records, which is its own honest fact about how little of this belt the federation kept. Source: the fed's own Record Book.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: GCW's World Heavyweight Championship was first won by Octavian on 22 April 2001. The fed's own record carries 34 reigns on it, across 22 different champions. The longest of known length is Andy Murray's, 269 days from 21 June 2009. Three of its reigns ended outside a match (two vacated, one ended when the holder departed). Johnny Borealis held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: GCW Glory Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's showcase singles title, contested across a months-long "Rise to Glory" tournament run.

titles.name: GCW Southern Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional title tied to the promotion's own southern identity, defended outside the ring as often as in it.

titles.name: GCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on-air by commentator Tommy Flynn during the 2004 revival's own second broadcast, with a promised update on its status the following week; no update, holder, or further mention survives in this wing's own held record.

titles.name: GCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated by two-time former champion Brandon Simpson before the 2004 revival's own broadcast record opens; commissioner James Oslo ordered a four-way match at the 1 August 2004 pay-per-view WE ALL FALL DOWN to crown a new champion, with Heath Starr and Aroku Murakami claiming the first two of the four match slots across this wing's own surviving broadcasts.

titles.name: American Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: One champion, one night, and a lineage that is entirely its own crowning. The fed created it at Founder's Day Tradition II on 30 August 1998 out of the Western Heritage and Intercontinental championships at once, when Daisy Butterfly beat Sarah Summers by submission and was crowned its inaugural holder. Nothing held records a defence, and the fed filed it among its retired heavyweight championships.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own current Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html).

titles.name: GDWA Extreme Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created out of thin air on the fed's own December 1998 return broadcast and handed to Heidi Leick without a match, over the announce table's own open disbelief; she made her first defense the same night.
titles.notes: First and, in the held record, only recorded reign: awarded to Heidi Leick on the Tease and Catfight of 30 December 1998 (msg_id e7ZLH3O5EXIJ; promotions/gdwa/archive/gdwa-tease-and-catfight-1998-12-30.html). Not to be confused with the American Heritage or Intercontinental championships, which the same broadcast announces will merge into a new North American Heritage Championship at a Valentine's Day 1999 PPV -- that title and event are not minted here for want of a document past the announcement.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship

events.title: gdwa-american-heritage
events.note: Unified with the Western Heritage Championship at Founder's Day Tradition II, Municipal Stadium, Cleveland, Ohio; the fed crowned the winner its inaugural American Heritage Champion.

titles.epitaph: The Internet Heavyweight Championship under a new name, from 18 January 1998, and the shortest-lived lineage the fed kept: one holder, seven months, and an ending that was also a beginning. Daisy Butterfly carried it out of Sendai and into Founder's Day Tradition II that August, where she beat the Western Heritage champion by submission and the two belts became one. The fed filed it thereafter among its retired heavyweight championships.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own current Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html).

titles.name: Internet Heavyweight Championship

events.title: gdwa-intercontinental
events.note: "The title is formally changed from the Internet Heavyweight Championship to the Intercontinental Championship" — the fed's own Lineages page, dating the change to the Miyagi-ken Sports Center in Sendai, Japan.

titles.epitaph: The fed's second singles belt, crowned in a tournament final at the first Summer Supercard in May 1996 and contested eight times over the twenty months after — a stripping for breach of contract, a Royal Rumble win, a three way dance at Fall Moonsault 1997. Its lineage did not end so much as change names: on 18 January 1998 in Sendai the fed formally renamed it the Intercontinental Championship, with Daisy Butterfly holding it throughout.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own 1997 Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-1997.html); the rename is recorded on the fed's own current Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html).

titles.name: Ironwoman Square Dance Tournament
titles.epitaph: Not a belt but a crowning, contested once a year at Fall Moonsault. Daisy Butterfly took the first at the Carolinas Stadium in September 1996; Andrea Chandler took the second at the Sky Dome in Toronto in November 1997, and the fed named her Wrestler of the Month for it. The pay-per-view calendar bills Ironwoman Square Dance Matches as a headline attraction of the show.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own current Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html); billed on its own pay-per-view calendar (promotions/gdwa/archive/pay-per-views.html).

titles.name: Ladies Extreme Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A second tag belt stood up as the fed absorbed the LEWA promotion's own tag division, decided in an off-panel tournament the held record never shows -- only its champions, billed in passing on their way out the door.
titles.notes: Announced with an opening tournament bracket on the Monday Night Tease of 7 July 1997. By the Tuesday Night Catfight billed 22 July 1997, the Misfits (Godiva, Dalbello Rage) are introduced on air as champions; the deciding tournament match itself is not in this held record.

titles.name: Transnational Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt with a rulebook of its own: defended every four weeks, open to any cruiserweight, and any contender above.500 who challenged had to be given a shot. It was crowned in a tournament final at the US Air Arena in Baltimore in July 1997, and its only recorded champion held it for more than a year while adding two other titles to it — the first wrestler in the fed to hold two belts at once, then three. It was vacated at Founder's Day Tradition II in August 1998. In January 2000 the fed announced a tournament to crown a new one.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own Lineages pages (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html, promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-1997.html); its defence rules are set out in the fed's own FAQ sheet (promotions/gdwa/archive/faq-sheet.html) and the new tournament announced on the Dragon's Lair marquee (promotions/gdwa/archive/dragons-lair.html).

titles.name: Western Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt decided twice by Royal Rumble and defended, at the end, three times in six weeks. It was crowned at the first Summer Supercard in May 1996 when Sachie Yokoyama last-eliminated Radhi Ananda, and changed hands eleven times over the two years after: knocked away at a Fall Moonsault, vacated in October 1997 by a champion who had just won a second belt, won again out of a Rumble, and finally taken by Daisy Butterfly in the match that unified it with the Intercontinental title. The fed's own handler's page of 21 October 2000 has it live again, three days out from crowning a brand new champion on its first card out of Tacoma.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own Lineages pages (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html, promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-1997.html); the 2000 revival is on its own handler's page (promotions/gdwa/archive/handlers-page-2000-10-21.html).

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of the line, and the one the fed dated its own founding by: its ledger opens with a tournament final on 5 April 1996, held under the two federations GDWA grew out of, and then records the same wrestler being inaugurated GDWA World Champion at the same building on 21 April. Seven reigns follow it across two and a half years — one ended by a stripping for breach of contract, one won in a three way dance decided by a pinfall and a disqualification at once, one settled by a tournament final in the Fukuoka Dome. The last change the fed recorded put it on Black Lotus at Founder's Day Tradition II in August 1998. Its own site announced in January 2000 that a pay per view called Glory Days would crown a new and undisputed champion; nothing held says it did.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own Lineages pages (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-current.html, promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-1997.html); the Glory Days announcement is the scrolling marquee on its own Dragon's Lair page (promotions/gdwa/archive/dragons-lair.html).

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Two reigns and a held-up division. The Misfits beat Lady Luck in Osaka Castle Hall in October 1996 to become the inaugural champions and held the belts eight months, until the Hyena Queens climbed out of a steel cage with them in Madison Square Garden. On 26 September 1997 the fed held its own tag division up and stripped the champions; nothing held records the belts being crowned again.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own 1997 Lineages page (promotions/gdwa/archive/lineages-1997.html); neither team's own roster survives.

titles.name: GEW Canadian Pride Title
titles.epitaph: An explicit in-universe spin-off of the defunct CPW World Heavyweight Title from the earlier, unrelated IWF play-by-mail game; held three times before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEW Elite Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Georgia Elite Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEW Global Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Georgia Elite Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEW National Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Georgia Elite Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEW National Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Georgia Elite Wrestling territory, held three times before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEW USW Title
titles.epitaph: Billed alongside an explicit spin-off of a defunct IWF league title, and sharing its own name with the unrelated IWF league of the same acronym; held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: GEWA Americas Championship
titles.epitaph: Named only by a former champion's own billing (Red Raven, "a former GEWA Americas champion"); no title-change document survives in this collection's holdings.
titles.notes: Honest gap; no reign recorded.

titles.name: GEWA Global Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize; its only complete, dated 1997 defence in this collection's holdings was written inside another alliance's own shared broadcast rather than the fed's own card.
titles.notes: Champion Dr.

titles.name: GEWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Named only by an outside billing; no title-change document survives.
titles.notes: Honest gap; no reign recorded.

titles.name: GEWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by an explicit Neo-Nazi-gimmick stable, The Fourth Reich, as of December 1997 -- content note carried on the wing's own face per the no-taste-rulings gavel.
titles.notes: No won-date recovered; the team is billed as champions in the 11 Dec 1997 broadcast with no earlier title-change document surviving.

titles.name: Affliction Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-legacy
events.note: Unified with the Hardcore Championship in a match on the card of Blackout, 22 August 2010, which made the GIW Legacy Championship (the fed's own Hardcore history: "Unified with Affliction Championship Becomes GIW Legacy Championship"). The fed's own North Beach table carries this belt's one reign as its first line and then "VACATED".

titles.epitaph: GIW's Affliction Championship: 1 reign is served here, across 1 different champion, the first beginning on 18 July 2010 with Damon Synn. Of these, 1 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). The fed's own North Beach table opens with this belt; it was unified into the Legacy Championship on 22 August 2010.

titles.name: GIW Deep South Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-undisputed
events.note: Unified with the Galveston Island Championship to become the GIW Undisputed Championship (the fed's own history: "Unified with 'Galveston Island Championship' to become 'GIW Undisputed Championship'"; the card of Revolt, 17 February 2011).

Retired when the fed closed in August 2013 and brought back when it returned (the fed's own history: "Belt Retired when Company momentarily closes, brought back when company returns"). The date is that of the last card before the closure, 4 August 2013; no card names the retirement itself.

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-undisputed
events.note: Unified with the Undisputed Championship on the card of 29 October 2014 (the fed's own history places it at On Hallowed Ground IV, its Undisputed history at On Hallowed Ground III; the card is headed On Hallowed Ground). The belt was brought back by Aspen Chaud on 15 March 2015.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Deep South Championship: 16 reigns are served here, across 15 different champions, the first beginning on 24 January 2011 with Madison Seton and the last on 30 August 2015 with Geneva Lost. The longest of those is Christopher Darren Erns's, 99 days from 22 July 2014. Of these, 5 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was unified into the Undisputed Championship on 17 February 2011, retired at the 2013 closure, brought back in 2014, unified again on 29 October 2014 and brought back once more on 15 March 2015.

titles.name: EPW Evolve Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-evolve
events.note: Renamed the GIW Evolve Championship: the fed's own Deep South history reads "Title Vacated Due to Injury, Renamed 'GIW Evolve'"; the card of Revolt, 11 November 2010 has the champion not showing up and qualifiers for the GIW Evolve title following. History and card give different reasons for the vacancy; both stand.

titles.epitaph: GIW's EPW Evolve Championship: 2 reigns are served here, across 2 different champions, the first beginning on 5 October 2010 with Christopher Darren Erns and the last on 19 October 2010 with Chris Armstrong. The longest is Chris Armstrong's, from 19 October 2010 to about 11 November 2010 (24 days in the fed's own history); of the reigns with both dates exact, the longest is Christopher Darren Erns's, 14 days from 5 October 2010. Of these, 1 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It took this name on 31 August 2010 and became the GIW Evolve Championship on 11 November 2010.

titles.name: GIW Evolve Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-deep-south
events.note: Renamed the Deep South Championship: the fed's own Deep South history reads "Title Changed To 'Deep South Championship'", on the card of Monday Night Affliction, 24 January 2011.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Evolve Championship: 2 reigns are served here, across 2 different champions, the first beginning on 28 November 2010 with Eric Sparrow and the last on 9 January 2011 with Christopher Darren Erns. The longest of those is Eric Sparrow's, 42 days from 28 November 2010. Of these, 1 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It became the Deep South Championship on 24 January 2011.

titles.name: Galveston Island Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-undisputed
events.note: The belt the fed's cards called the Galveston Island Championship became the GIW Undisputed Championship when it was unified with the Deep South title in the Eric Sparrow and Chris Jericho match of the card of Revolt, 17 February 2011; the fed's own Undisputed history carries the one run of reigns under both names.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Galveston Island Championship: 5 reigns are served here, across 4 different champions, the first beginning on 3 June 2010 with Aspen Chaud and the last on 13 February 2011 with Chris Jericho. The longest of those is Wake Walker's, 98 days from 22 August 2010. Of these, 2 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). The fed's own Undisputed history carries it as the first seven lines of one belt; on 17 February 2011 it became the GIW Undisputed Championship.

titles.name: GIW Hardcore Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-legacy
events.note: Unified with the Affliction Championship into the GIW Legacy Championship on the card of Blackout, 22 August 2010.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Hardcore Championship: 4 reigns are served here, across 4 different champions, the first beginning on 18 July 2010 with Billy Spizatoni and the last on 21 September 2015 with George Stark. The longest of those is Jamie Vaccaro's, 32 days from 21 July 2010. Of these, 3 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was unified into the Legacy Championship in 2010; the fed's own history then has it retired, reinstated by David Sinclair and vacated at the 2015 hiatus.

titles.name: ION Television Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-television
events.note: Billed as the GIW Television Championship from the card of Revolt, 20 January 2011; no card or history line announces a change of name.

titles.epitaph: GIW's ION Television Championship: 5 reigns are served here, across 5 different champions, the first beginning on 22 August 2010 with Megathreat and the last on 31 October 2010 with Joshua Acquin. The longest is Joshua Acquin's, from 31 October 2010 to about 9 January 2011 (71 days in the fed's own history); of the reigns with both dates exact, the longest is Tony Miranda's, 24 days from 2 September 2010. Of these, 2 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was billed the GIW Television Championship from 20 January 2011.

titles.name: GIW Legacy Championship

events.note: Retired when Aspen Chaud became owner of the fed (the fed's own history: "Belt Retired when Aspen becomes Owner"); the card of 24 November 2012 introduces her as the new owner, and no card names the belt's retirement itself.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Legacy Championship: 8 reigns are served here, across 7 different champions, the first beginning on 22 August 2010 with Jamie Vaccaro and the last on 15 August 2012 with Aspen Chaud. The longest of those is Alexis Terry's, 105 days from 15 January 2012. Of these, 1 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was made at Blackout on 22 August 2010 by the unification of the Hardcore and Affliction belts, and retired in November 2012.

titles.name: Lightweight Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-ion-television
events.note: Renamed the ION Television Championship on the night of Revolt, 22 July 2010: that card says David Sinclair will announce a new name for the championship later that night (no announcement is on the card), and the card of 29 July 2010 says Jake Kennedy "won the ION Television title" the week before.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Lightweight Championship: 2 reigns are served here, across 2 different champions, the first beginning on 15 July 2010 with Nitro and the last on 22 July 2010 with Jake Kennedy. The longest of those is Jake Kennedy's, 31 days from 22 July 2010. The first two lines of the fed's own Television history; renamed the ION Television Championship on 22 July 2010.

titles.name: GIW North Beach Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-undisputed
events.note: Unified with the Undisputed Championship on the card of Revolt, 7 March 2014, when Michael Lynch beat Alexis Terry (the fed's own North Beach table ends the belt with "VACATED"; the card has Lynch carry both). The belt came back in 2019.

titles.epitaph: GIW's North Beach Championship: 11 reigns are served here, across 10 different champions, the first beginning on 20 March 2011 with Alioth Starre and the last on 25 August 2019 with Agustin Gates. By the dates served here the longest is Michael Lynch's, 257 days from 23 June 2013, which the fed's own table counts as 54 days; of the reigns whose dates fit the table's own lengths, the longest is Alex Castellanos's, 59 days from 9 June 2011. Of these, 3 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It carries the fed's own North Beach table from 2011; the Affliction and NOX belts before it are listed beside it. It was unified into the Undisputed Championship on 7 March 2014 and crowned a new champion in August 2019.

titles.name: GIW North Beach Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-epw-evolve
events.note: The 2010 North Beach belt was renamed the EPW Evolve Championship; the fed's own Deep South history records "Title Changed from GIW North Beach to EPW Evolve", and the card of Tuesday Night Evolve, 31 August 2010 has the champion called the Evolve champion rather than the North Beach champion. The fed's own history places the note before Chris Armstrong's win of 22 August 2010; the cards place the change of name after it.

titles.epitaph: GIW's North Beach Championship: 3 reigns are served here, across 3 different champions, the first beginning on 17 June 2010 with Apollo Calix and the last on 22 August 2010 with Chris Armstrong. The longest of those is Chris Armstrong's, 44 days from 22 August 2010. This is the 2010 belt, not the North Beach Championship of 2011 to 2019 (a separate belt that shares the name); it became the EPW Evolve Championship on 31 August 2010.

titles.name: GIW NOX Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-north-beach
events.note: Became the GIW North Beach Championship at the unification bout of 17 February 2011 (the fed's own Television history: "Unified with 'GIW NOX Championship' to become 'GIW North Beach Championship'"); the unification bout ended in a double count-out and no champion was named that night.

titles.epitaph: GIW's NOX Championship: 3 reigns are served here, across 3 different champions, the first beginning on 17 January 2011 with Mike Bryant and the last on 13 February 2011 with Madison Seton. The longest of those is Mike Bryant's, 14 days from 17 January 2011. Of these, 1 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It became the GIW North Beach Championship on 17 February 2011.

titles.name: GIW Tag Team Championship

events.note: Retired with Matt Kluge on the card of Blackout II, 11 September 2011 ("all the belts will be retired with him"); reinstated by Blake Beckett on 5 January 2012.
Retired with the division on the card of 9 February 2012 after Seth Ramsey was hurt (the fed's own history: "Seth Ramsey Injured, Belts Momentarily Retired"); brought back in April 2015.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Tag Team Championship: 12 reigns are served here, across 10 different champions, the first beginning on 28 November 2010 with Technical Mechanica and the last on 19 July 2015 with The Setons. The longest of those is Perfect Combination's, 77 days from 3 May 2015. Of these, 6 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was retired by the fed in September 2011 and February 2012 and brought back in April 2015.

titles.name: GIW Television Championship

events.title: giw-galveston-2010-north-beach
events.note: On the card of Exile (13 February 2011) a match was announced for the next week to merge it with the GIW NOX Championship into the GIW North Beach Championship; the unification bout of 17 February 2011 ended in a double count-out and the belt was active again in May 2011 (the fed's own history: "Activated Again by La'Sarah Audric").

Retired by Joshua Acquin, the winner of the opening match of Final Solution, 4 December 2011, under that match's terms, and returned to Joshua Acquin on 9 February 2012 (the fed's own history: "Belt Momentarily Retired, Then Returned Acquin Still Champion").
Thrown away by Chairman Matt Kluge on the card of Category 5, 1 July 2012 (the fed's own history: "Title Disposed of by Chairman Kluge"); reinstated by Aspen Chaud on 15 March 2015.

titles.epitaph: GIW's Television Championship: 28 reigns are served here, across 23 different champions, the first beginning on 13 February 2011 with Joshua Acquin and the last on 7 September 2015 with Alexis Terry. By the dates served here the longest is Joshua Acquin's, 77 days from 4 December 2011, which the fed's own history counts as 11 days; of the reigns whose dates fit the history's own lengths, the longest is Henry Malkin's, 70 days from 19 February 2012. Of these, 7 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It was retired twice by the fed, in December 2011 and July 2012, and reinstated on 15 March 2015.

titles.name: GIW Undisputed Championship
titles.epitaph: GIW's Undisputed Championship: 18 reigns are served here, across 14 different champions, the first beginning on 17 February 2011 with Eric Sparrow and the last on 18 August 2019 with Bronx Valescence. By the dates served here the longest is Alexis Terry's, 257 days from 23 June 2013, which the fed's own history counts as 54 days; of the reigns whose dates fit the history's own lengths, the longest is Alioth Starre's, 155 days from 29 May 2011. Of these, 4 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). It is the Galveston Island Championship under the name it took on 17 February 2011; it took in the Deep South belt on that date and again on 29 October 2014, and the North Beach belt on 7 March 2014.

titles.name: GIW Women's Championship

events.note: Retired on the card of Revolt, 11 November 2010, with the fed's own history reading "Title Retired" ("the GIW Women's Championship will be RETIRED once and for all").

titles.epitaph: GIW's Women's Championship: 5 reigns are served here, across 5 different champions, the first beginning on 11 July 2010 with Violet Vanity and the last on 26 August 2010 with Kacie Church. The longest is Kacie Church's, from 26 August 2010 to about 11 November 2010 (78 days in the fed's own history); of the reigns with both dates exact, the longest is Alexii Ravynova's, 18 days from 4 August 2010. Of these, 2 ended outside a match (stripped, vacated or retired). Its cards call it the Divas title and the Galveston Island Women's title side by side in 2010; it was retired on 11 November 2010.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Twenty-eight reigns, headlined by Corporal Punishment's own three separate runs and Lyle Wile's 113-day reign, the longest in the belt's history; Jay Phoenix held it 53 days in 2001, between Celest's two reigns. Jaxx's own second reign is the final Intercontinental Championship the GIWF's own record names. Restarts as the UWF's own Intercontinental Championship.

titles.name: North American Championship
