titles.epitaph: Briefly renamed the “Native American Title” during Jay Phoenix's own reign — the fed's own Quick Facts crediting its creation to “Jay Phoenix's overwhelming egoti—*shot*” — and, in an earlier stretch, the belt Lew Spectre vacated by throwing it in a trash can, only for Daneel McCord to retrieve it three days later; also carried, in later use, as the “European Title.” Restarts as the UWF's own North American Championship.

titles.name: North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Added September 1999, briefly disbanded after The Dark Lords' own reign and revived by tournament seven months later. The Phenomenons held it three times, the second a 112-day reign, the belt's own longest; Street Science's own win over the Phenomenons and the Bringers of Darkness, 4 July 2001, is the fed's own last recorded change of this title.

titles.name: Regal Rumble
titles.epitaph: An annual over-the-top-rope elimination match, crowning an individual rather than a stable. Two champions are on the surviving record: Blaze on 30 January 2000, and Ricky Ketsu-Eki at the Regal Rumble 2001 PPV, over runner-up Craig Wright.

titles.name: Stable Wars
titles.epitaph: A four-team elimination tournament crowning a stable rather than a single champion, run every May from the fed's own founding year. Three champions are on the surviving record: the Youngbloods in 1999, the Order of the Hammer in 2000, and the Faux-Youngbloods in 2001. The format outlived the fed that invented it — the UWF picked the honor up whole and ran it all the way to a sixth edition.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's hot-potato belt — 68 changes of hands across the run, more than any other GIWF title. Jay Phoenix held it 13 days in 2000 under the ring name Inferno. Blade's own final reign, the fed's last recorded TV Championship change, closes on a vacancy: he “vacated the title before it was retired.” Restarts as the UWF's own Television Championship.

titles.name: (T)he (H)ardcore (C)hampionship
titles.epitaph: Added January 2000 and, by the fed's own admission, “never officially recognized by the GIWF” — its shortest reign lasted roughly seven minutes (Lew Spectre's tournament win, immediately “defeated” by Ace Thunder), its longest 95 days (Gurgles), and its last GIWF holder, L.U.C.A.B.O.T., “to this day has never been able to rid himself of the title.” Restarts as the UWF's own THC, later salvaged as a physical belt by Gurgles after the UWF's own hardcore title was banned.

titles.name: GIWF National Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created alongside the World Heavyweight Championship at this run's own 'Title Tyranny' relaunch battle royal, awarded to the battle royal's own last-eliminated entrant.

titles.name: GIWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at this run's own 'Title Tyranny' relaunch battle royal, alongside a companion National Championship; not to be confused with the same-named title on either held GIWF wing.

titles.name: GIWF Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at Turkey Day Titles and still in David "Death Sentence" Stevens's hands at Gold Rush II, the record's last dated card.

titles.name: GIWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the fed's own Turkey Day Titles PPV and defended in a steel cage before Steve Latini escaped ahead of Jacob McDonahey to take it in April 1996.

titles.name: GIWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned at Turkey Day Titles and still in Mean Man-Mama's hands at Gold Rush II, the record's last dated card.

titles.name: GIWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: GIWF's top prize, changing hands four times across this record from a gold-belted Lonestar through to Desert Storm's ladder-match win at Wrestle Wrath.

titles.name: GIWF World Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Pressure Point in the fed's own inaugural Gold Rush tournament and held for a full year before the three-man Jingoist dethroned them at Wrestle Wrath.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Twenty-four reigns across the promotion's own run, opening on Akira's tournament win and closing on Gurgles's second, 89-day reign — the longest of the belt's GIWF life and its final one on record. The lineage restarts as the UWF's own World Heavyweight Championship at the September 2001 tournament that opened the new fed.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Phenomenons' own first tag title — three reigns across the fed's run, the last an 89-day hold — in a lineage that also crowned the Dragoons, the Fomorians (won in what the record calls “the Dublin pub brawl”), and, at the close, Street Science's own 89-day final reign. Restarts as the UWF's own World Tag Team Championship.

titles.name: GLCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created from a battle-royal-tested trophy division, its first champion crowned with a little outside help he never admitted to needing.

titles.name: GLCW Great Lakes Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a Texas death match settled only after a rival promotion's own president interfered against the defending champion.

titles.name: GLCW Iron Crown
titles.epitaph: Settled twice across a single year in two-out-of-three-falls contests between the same two men, the second changing hands only when the challenger turned the champion's own finishing hold back on him.

titles.name: GLCW Legacy Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended once on the record against the very challenger who had already lost it, the champion's night saved only because the promotion's own rules refuse a title change on a count-out.

titles.name: GLCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a grueling defense settled by a single backdrop driver in the match's closing seconds.

titles.name: GLCW World Crown
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a six-way elimination match its own promotion called the biggest night in its history, decided only after a fallen champion rose from a stretcher to reclaim the ring and finish what a title match had already tried to settle without him.

titles.name: GLHW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own first Extreme Champion was crowned in a Hell in a Cell match on its own 5 October 1999 retrospective broadcast.

titles.name: GLHW Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles belt, billed on PSiKNYTE entering the federation's own 5 October 1999 broadcast.

titles.name: HBW Global World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands three times before the promotion's own final champion carried it into HBW's 2000 closure.

titles.name: GLOW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top title, defended twice in a matter of weeks against three separate challengers without changing hands.

titles.name: GLOW Northeast Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional secondary title whose holder weathered a string of number-one contenders across the promotion's early summer.

titles.name: GLOW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag-team title, held into midyear behind a manager who ran interference on its champions' behalf.

Three reigns across seven weeks: Doc Dean won it in a ten-man battle royal, lost it seven days after the ledger's own next entry to Mark Schrader (who beat an injury-replacement Brian Adias, not Dean himself, by the fed's own footnote), then reclaimed it thirteen days later and was still champion when the record ends.
titles.name: GLW Midwestern Title
titles.notes: From the fed's own title-history ledger, current through 31 March 2001.

titles.epitaph: Four reigns, one of them lasting a single day: Colorado Kid won a 30-minute, three-falls-to-two Iron Man Match for the belt and lost it the very next night to Flash Flanagan, who was still champion when the record ends.
titles.name: GLW Television Title
titles.notes: From the fed's own title-history ledger, current through 31 March 2001.

titles.epitaph: The belt changed hands exactly once in the surviving record: Masato Tanaka won it outright in a 30-man Deadly Draw match at Deadly Draw 2001 (26 January), lastly eliminating Indiana Kidd Jr., and was still champion when the fed's own last title snapshot was taken. No earlier holder or later title change survives.
titles.name: GLW World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: From the fed's own title-history ledger, current through 31 March 2001.

titles.epitaph: The busiest belt on file: four reigns in twelve weeks, changing hands between The Headhunters, the Armstrong brothers, The Extremists, and finally Jesse James Armstrong and Ken Shamrock. The title-history ledger has that pairing still champion as of 31 March; the fed's own separate Current Champions page, dated the same day, calls the titles vacant instead — both readings survive, and nothing resolves which is right.
titles.name: GLW World Tag Team Titles
titles.notes: From the fed's own title-history ledger, current through 31 March 2001.

titles.name: GNW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested vacant and contested in a 13 January 1999 over-the-top-rope battle royal, with its winner billed as the promotion's own representative to an EWWF-wide tournament.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Asia Pacific Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Jason Storm over Frazer Fury in the tournament final at the federation's first full supercard.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Combative Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A new tag division's first championship, won by a two-man pairing of two-thirds of the promotion's own Daimyo trio.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Jisatsu Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in a five-man scaffold battle royal fought over a barbwire-roped scaffold above tables, won by “Demon Boy” Ishrinku.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Super-Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Kashan Akuma over The Banshee in the tournament final at the federation's first full supercard.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Trios Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Zokugun Sangai in a twelve-man, four-team cage war at the federation's first title-crowning supercard.

titles.name: Gunryo Pro Triple Crown Championship
titles.epitaph: A unified championship whose first defense survived a challenge from the promotion's own Jisatsu champion, and whose own legitimacy was disputed on-air by a rival citing manager interference.

titles.name: GPW American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a ladder match at Genesis; the notch below the World Heavyweight title.

titles.name: GPW American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named vacant in the promotion's own first newsletter (28 October 1999); no holder is recorded anywhere in the held record.

events.title: gpw-unified-world-tag-team-gpw-global-1999
events.note: Merged with the World Tag Team Championship at Blazing Glory 2000, in the promotion's own first title-for-title unification match, won by the reigning American champions, The Coast to Coast Connection.

titles.name: GPW Brass Knux Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a no-disqualification, falls-count-anywhere match at Genesis.

events.note: The promotion's own on-air ownership dissolved the division at Blazing Glory 2000 after both the reigning champion, Oyabun, and his own scheduled challenger, Barry Gradwell, left the company.

titles.name: GPW Regional Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own proving ground for younger talent, contested best two-of-three falls at Genesis.

titles.name: GPW Unified World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at Blazing Glory 2000 in a title-for-title unification match, merging the promotion's own World and American Tag Team Championships into one lineage; The Coast to Coast Connection defeated the reigning World champions, XtremeCharisma, to become the first Unified champions.

titles.name: GPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned via a two-pool tournament culminating in an enclosed steel-cage final at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, Genesis (24 October 1999); defended at least once every 30 days.

titles.name: GPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned via a three-pool elimination tournament at Genesis.

events.title: gpw-unified-world-tag-team-gpw-global-1999
events.note: Merged with the American Tag Team Championship at Blazing Glory 2000, in the promotion's own first title-for-title unification match, won by The Coast to Coast Connection over the reigning World champions, XtremeCharisma.

titles.name: GPW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in an enclosed-cage match at Genesis; defended weekly on the promotion's own television programs.

titles.name: Gr8 wwf Fed Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Steve Blackman regained it from Goldust on the first Saturday Night RAW, 7 December 2002, pinning him after D-Von Dudley's return put Goldust through a table.

titles.name: GRW Atlanta City Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional singles title, defended in a bloody, weapon-aided main event that the champion retained by turning the challenger's own blinding powder back on him.

titles.name: CWC Southern States Championship
titles.epitaph: A cross-promotional title shared under the Continental Wrestling Council's own Southern States banner; this pass's own holdings find it already established and defended, not created.

titles.name: GSWP Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: A weapons-based title created to settle a three-way grudge, its inaugural winner still carrying it at the promotion's own summer Pay-Per-View after turning back a hardcore challenger.

titles.name: GSWP Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own "endurance belt," billed as defended nearly every week, changing hands twice across this record before settling on a champion who carried it through the rest of the promotion's surviving broadcasts.

titles.name: GSWP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, first decided by a single-elimination tournament, changing hands only once in this record when a returning ally's outside interference cost the champion his title at the promotion's own summer Pay-Per-View.

titles.name: GVWL Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Sabu over Chris Benoit in the Cruiserweight Title Tournament final, then lost back to Benoit in a cage-match rematch at Hot Summer Battle.

titles.name: GVWL Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Reached its semifinal round (Mr. Perfect vs. Vader, DDP vs.

titles.name: GVWL Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by The Outsiders (Hall & Nash) over L.O.D. in the Tag Team Title Tournament final; still champions as of the wing's own last surviving record, having beaten The Headbangers in defense.

titles.name: GVWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Reached its semifinal round (Sting vs. Bret Hart, Psycho Sid vs.

titles.name: GVWL World Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by The Undertaker over Stone Cold Steve Austin in the World Title Tournament final at Hot Summer Battle.

titles.name: GW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Jay Robson held it into the spring of 2003 and lost it to Sage Sabbot in a ladder match in the last week of March, which is the whole of what the record says about how it moved. Sabbot was still carrying it at WrestleCade III five weeks later, using it as a weapon on the man who had just taken the Platinum title off Kullypso, and the ring announcer introduced him for the International title match with it in his hands. Roz Blayze won the right to challenge him on the same night, in a four-way ladder match for a replica of the belt.

titles.name: GW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a tournament whose final the record never resolves: the fed's own Clash of the Titans card of 28 February 2003 stages the final as its main event under two silhouettes, and its own newsdesk reports a fortnight later that an International Champion was crowned there. Derek Frost is carrying it a month afterwards, tagging with Jay Robson as ColdBlood and booked to defend it against Roz Blayze on 7 April. By WrestleCade III it is Tragic Hero's, and he keeps it in a four-way elimination match that Quartz walks into to spear the last man standing so that Tragic Hero can put him in the Perfect Circle.

titles.name: Iron Fist Championship
titles.epitaph: Global's Iron Fist Championship's first recorded champion is Pete Hardy. The fed's own record carries 2 reigns on it, across 2 different champions.
titles.notes: One line in the whole record: the four-man gauntlet on the oldest write-up, the Evolution of 19 February 2003, whose winner is hailed the new Iron Fist Champion.

titles.name: Unsanctioned King of the Death Match
titles.epitaph: Global Wrestling's King of the Death Match, billed unsanctioned. One crowning is recorded, 2005's, won across four Devil's Night death matches.

titles.name: GW Platinum Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt that spent the spring of 2003 being taken rather than won. Venom Alexander was carrying it on 31 March when the arena screen cut to Leviathan going through his locker room and walking out with it, which Venom watched from the ring in the middle of a tag match. Mark Kullypso has it by WrestleCade III five weeks later, with nothing held saying how, and loses it there to Jay Robson and The Next Element — after which four Nevermore men lock the new champion in the ropes with a stack of chairs and Derek Frost comes down the ramp with a skateboard.

titles.name: GW PrimeStar Championship
titles.notes: Vacant before the tournament: the front page's own championship row shows the PrimeStar belt paired with the site's own mysteryman silhouette rather than a champion's headshot. The fed's own front page hangs its six championships in a row as belt graphics that swap, on hover, for the current champion's own headshot; three of the six pairings are independently corroborated by the fed's own show text of the same week, which is what makes the mechanism readable at all.
titles.epitaph: Won in one night, by one man, in the only tournament the fed's record holds end to end. Six men were bracketed for it at WrestleCade III on 2 May 2003; Deacon Holmes came through a triple threat and Leviathan through a triangle match, and Leviathan took the final by refusing to let go of an octopus hold until Holmes passed out inside it. Its own name had been in the fed's rumour mill a season earlier — a match for it between Johnny Dollar and the Enigma was supposed to have happened at the previous pay-per-view and does not appear on that card.

titles.name: Rising Sun Championship
titles.epitaph: Global's Rising Sun Championship was first won by Cady Coleman on 2 December 2007. Cady Coleman held it at the end of the surviving record.
titles.notes: Global Underground's belt, created at its first champion's crowning at the Underground of 2 December 2007, the last Underground show in the record.

titles.name: GW Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own front page hangs its six championships in a row as belt graphics that swap, on hover, for the current champion's own headshot; three of the six pairings are independently corroborated by the fed's own show text of the same week, which is what makes the mechanism readable at all.
titles.epitaph: The United Kings — the English Gent and Pete Hardy, billed together out of the land of warm beer and bad weather — are the only team the record ever places with it. They were booked to defend it against the Tragic Kingdom at Clash of the Titans in February 2003, and the fed's own front page was still pairing the tag belts with their photograph in April. The night that page was captured they had wrestled Venom and Cobra in a non-title match, and lost it by disqualification with the English Gent bleeding through a bandage at ringside.

titles.name: GW Television Championship
titles.notes: THE CHAIN OF THIS BELT IS NOT BUILT. Global Wrestling's own show texts carry at least twelve further changes and defences of this championship between 2004 and 2006 — among them a champion stripped for not defending it weekly, the vacancy that filled, and six other holders — every one receipted line by line in the federation's own scripts and none of them yet minted. What this record holds is one recovered reign inside a longer history, not the belt's lineage.
titles.epitaph: A weekly television championship the federation defended almost every show, and one night of it survives in this record: 21 August 2005 at Evolution, in Las Vegas, where the masked Emoticon rolled the champion Dawn McFarlane up and the referee — the federation's own word for him is stunned — handed the belt over. He was still carrying it when the record runs out. The rest of the belt's life is in Global's own scripts and not yet chained here.

titles.name: GW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own newsdesk of 30 March 2003 separately calls Lance Daniels "the GW Heavyweight Champion" in the same week its own news post of 28 March calls Silent Wind the new World Champion. Both readings stand; no seventh belt is recorded anywhere in the fed's own front-page championship row, which lists six.
titles.epitaph: The belt the fed built its own last spring around, and it changed hands three times in six weeks without a single one of those changes happening in a GW ring. Maverick Reno lost it because Salaok fired him, and the co-owner handed it to Silent Wind, who said publicly that he felt cheated of it. Silent Wind carried it out of Global Wrestling altogether on 20 April 2003 and defended it on Primetime Central's own New Era supercard against Christopher Camero, in a traditional square ring the commentary said its own wrestlers had stopped being used to; Camero beat him with a superplex DDT and was still carrying it a fortnight later, when Jason Dynasty asked him for a shot and was told he was not at that level. Salaok is billed a five-time holder of it and Ben J. Pailthorpe a two-time one; neither reign is anywhere in the surviving record.

titles.name: GWA USA Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dustin Haas (4-6) at the league's own Week 11 count; attested only on the rankings sheet itself.

titles.name: GWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Tim Croft (7-5) at the league's own Week 11 count; never seen defended anywhere in this collection's own holdings, though the Tournament of Bruises' own winner is promised a shot at it within seven days.

titles.name: GWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Power Force, Warrior816 and Ahmed Johnson (5-1) at Week 11, and still billed as reigning champions a month later on the Halloween in Hollywood card against a challenging team, Raging Heat, whose own members this collection cannot name.

titles.name: GWA World TV Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dread Saxon (6-6) at the league's own Week 11 count; like the USA title, attested only on the rankings sheet itself.

titles.name: GWC Global Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested on the promotion's first broadcast as a round-robin, won by Crossbones at Quake of Fire and defended in a steel cage at Extreme Challenge I.

titles.name: GWC Global Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Its inaugural champions, Inclement Weather, were crowned at Extreme Challenge I.

titles.name: GWC Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Its inaugural champion, Joey Terrell, was crowned in a three-way match at Extreme Challenge I.

titles.name: GWC Trans-Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Hypnosis in a ladder match at Quake of Fire and defended by Brian Taylor against Jeff Floyd at Extreme Challenge I.

titles.name: GWC Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Messiah in an eight-man tournament in October 2001, changing hands four more times by December.

titles.name: GWC Regional Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested from the promotion's first Titans broadcast, changing hands repeatedly through FightFest and into December 2001.

titles.name: GWE Atlantic Champion
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 4 November 1997 founding pitch (five titles: World, Pacific, Atlantic, Middle Crown, and Tag Team) alongside a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly card structure. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives.

titles.name: GWE Middle Crown Champion
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 4 November 1997 founding pitch (five titles: World, Pacific, Atlantic, Middle Crown, and Tag Team) alongside a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly card structure. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives.

titles.name: GWE Pacific Champion
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 4 November 1997 founding pitch (five titles: World, Pacific, Atlantic, Middle Crown, and Tag Team) alongside a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly card structure. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives.

titles.name: GWE Tag Team Champions
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 4 November 1997 founding pitch (five titles: World, Pacific, Atlantic, Middle Crown, and Tag Team) alongside a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly card structure. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives.

titles.name: GWE World Champion
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 4 November 1997 founding pitch (five titles: World, Pacific, Atlantic, Middle Crown, and Tag Team) alongside a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly card structure. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives.

titles.name: GWF Breakthrough Championship
titles.epitaph: A brand-new belt minted for one night only: the closing show's own single-elimination Breakthrough Tournament, its winner promised a GWF Championship match in the same evening's main event. Robert "Badger" Garland outlasted Chris Williams in the final to become the only man ever to hold it.
titles.notes: `nature: self-awarded` reflects that this belt was created and awarded within a single night's own tournament rather than defended on any ordinary schedule, not that it was uncontested — eight men fought across two rounds and a final for it.

titles.name: GWF Champion of Champions
titles.epitaph: A one-night-only elimination gauntlet at the fed's own closing show, open to every titleholder in the building. Michael Smart, entering on a technicality with a lower-card belt few in the room even remembered, outlasted them all to become GWF's only Champion of Champions.

titles.name: GWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Toast Hogan's own belt during the 2006 Food Division craze the fed's own Hall of Shame remembers fondly. Retired by Alex Storm ahead of the 2013 closing show and fought for one last time between Debolt Dragonsbane and XO Malone, a match Baron Trotter interrupted before either man could win it outright — Storm declared the two Co-Champions on the spot. The lineage ended that same night, unified into the International Xtreme Championship.
titles.notes: Toast Hogan is Michael Toaster's own retired early gimmick (see michael-toaster's tenure); his 2006 reign is remembered only in retrospective, no date or result recovered.

events.title: gwf-2006-international-xtreme
events.note: Baron Trotter's win over the Co-Champions in a triple threat for the "Undisputed GWF International Xtreme Championship" folded this lineage into that title.

titles.name: GWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Lodis3 held it three times in GWF's earliest days, per the fed's own Hall of Shame retrospective. The Reprobate's own March 2009 bio card lists a further, undated reign already ended by that point. By the January 2013 closing show the belt sat vacant after holder Jay Ramirez's arrest, until SheltonSplash handed it back to Reprobate backstage and made his very next tournament bout a title defense — which Reprobate won, retaining the belt through the fed's own last night.

titles.name: GWF Interbrand Championship
titles.epitaph: The only reign the surviving record recovers for the GWF Interbrand Championship is The Reprobate's own eight-month run, closing 22 March 2009 — who he won it from, and who took it from him, went uncaptured.

titles.name: GWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Chris O'Malley's own long-held prize — he defended it as recently as 2013's reunion-tour build — forfeited voluntarily at 20113 in exchange for a slot in the closing show's own GWF Championship match. Five men (SheltonSplash, Ken Davidson, Nitro Nick, Jeff Maximus and Chris Williams) fought to fill the vacancy that same night in a five-way elimination match; Chris Williams outlasted them all to become the belt's own final champion.

titles.name: GWF International Xtreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Falcon McKenzie retained it against Michael Smart in a bloody hardcore defense on 27 April 2008; by the 2009 reunion tour it belonged to Baron Trotter, who fended off a returning Mark Madison in a billed-but-uncaptured defense and carried it to the fed's own last night. At 20113, Baron unified it with the Co-Cruiserweight Championship in a triple threat against XO Malone and Debolt Dragonsbane, becoming the Undisputed GWF International Xtreme Champion for GWF's own final record.

titles.name: Sunday Brunch Heavyweight-Interbrand Championship
titles.epitaph: A title of GWF's own lower-card Brunch program, distinct from the main-roster Interbrand Championship despite the shared name. Michael Smart held it into the fed's own last night, entering the closing show's Champion of Champions match on the strength of it.
titles.notes: No won-date or prior result survives — Michael Smart names himself the holder from the ring at 20113, on a technicality, to force his own way into the Champion of Champions match.

titles.name: GWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A well-traveled belt: SheltonSplash and Kevin McAuliffe lost it to XO Malone and Damian DeNiro's own Movement in a match the record keeps only as a flashback; by April 2008 The Number 4 and Michael Toaster's own Numbered Toast held it, walking out on their own title defense at that month's War Games rather than lose it clean; by 2013 it belonged to Dave Shadow and Kevin McAuliffe's own Neo-Evolution, who lost it in the fed's own last hours to Danny Mainer and Bryan Daniels — the final GWF Tag Team Champions.
titles.notes: The Billionaires Club (Wolfenstein and John Beanshaw Wrathfield)'s own reign, named only in a 28 July 2008 Hall of Shame retrospective with no result or date recovered, likely precedes all five dated/flashback reigns above; recorded on this same title id rather than split, given no evidence of a distinct belt.

titles.name: GWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man reunion-tour tournament on 27 March 2009, the United States title went to Star-Man, the field's own least-experienced entrant, over The Reprobate in the final. Star-Man held it through the fed's own last night, retaining against Reprobate one final time at 20113 in January 2013.

titles.name: GWF Championship
titles.epitaph: GWF's own top prize, worn by Wolfenstein as the fed's first Undisputed Champion in its earliest days, then by James Murphy, then Michael Toaster, then Chris O'Malley after Locked N' Loaded 2007, then SheltonSplash after Valentine's Vengeance 2008, then Don Cicinni after three Omerta superkicks in a match recovered only as a flashback. The belt's own last night is the fed's own last night: on 20 January 2013's closing show, "20113," Chris O'Malley pinned Robert Garland in a four-way lumberjack match to become GWF's final champion — the title, like the promotion around it, going dark undefeated.
titles.notes: "GWF Global Championship" is the name a single flashback promo gives the belt Don Cicinni won from SheltonSplash (promotions/gwf-2006/archive/rp-the-living-fairytale.html); every other surviving reference calls it the GWF Championship or GWF World Championship. Recorded as one title under the more common name rather than split, per THE REBIRTH DOCTRINE's own default-to-one-record posture, absent evidence of two distinct belts.

titles.name: GWF Cruiserweight Title
titles.notes: The fed's own cruiserweight-division title, restricted in its founding document to wrestlers under 235 pounds and defended weekly.
titles.epitaph: Introduced as the GWF's own cruiserweight title, restricted to wrestlers under 235 pounds and defended weekly by its founding document's own rule; no title match is attested.

titles.name: GWF Extreme Title
titles.notes: The fed's own third-ranked singles title, pitched in its founding document for extreme wrestlers.
titles.epitaph: Introduced as the GWF's own third-ranked singles title, pitched in its founding document for extreme wrestlers; no title match is attested.

titles.name: GWF Television Title
titles.notes: The fed's own weekly-defended television title, billed in its founding document as a launching pad for younger wrestlers.
titles.epitaph: Introduced as a weekly-defended launching pad for younger wrestlers in the GWF's own founding document; no title match is attested.

titles.name: GWF US Title
titles.notes: The fed's own second-ranked singles title, introduced in its founding document as mandatory-defense at least three times a month.
titles.epitaph: Introduced as the GWF's own second-ranked singles title, requiring three defenses a month by its founding document's own rule; no title match is attested.

titles.name: GWF World Title
titles.notes: The fed's own top singles title, introduced in its founding document as mandatory-defense at least twice a month.
titles.epitaph: Introduced as the GWF's own top singles title, reserved in its founding document for "the best of the best"; no title match is attested.

titles.name: GWL Imperial Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Vice-President and on-screen wrestler Johnny Dice through this collection's own holdings, retained against Killer Ken Wilson at the fed's own first pay-per-view.
titles.notes: The title's own founding is recorded only as a tournament-in-progress (Wednesday Night WAR, 11 Apr 1997); its final round does not survive in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: GWL World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at Mother's Day Massacre when Roadkill's Outsiders won by countout over the reigning Angels of Death.
titles.notes: The Angels of Death's own prior reign predates this collection's earliest surviving card; no won-date recovered for it.

titles.name: GWNW Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Tigerheart" Rally Jackson through the promotion's own last held document.

titles.name: GWO Canadian Championship
titles.epitaph: The Canadian title, won by Slim Pickens on the CWO’s card of 2 August 2004 and carried in turn by Devo, Austin Fierro and Rated R, with Austin Fierro billed as champion on the last card in the mirror.

titles.name: GWO Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore belt created at Maximum Impact on 1 November 2004 in a four-way won by Slim Pickens, then won by Jack Spade at Bloodshed on 29 November.

titles.name: GWO Pacific Championship
titles.epitaph: The Pacific title of the GWO, first held in these pages by Soul Reaver on 2 August 2004, with Tex Murrphy, Radd Matthews, Rated R, Stevie James, Kosmic Kitty and Parker Davis among its holders.

titles.name: GWO Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The GWO’s tag belts, won by the Regulators on 2 August 2004 and passed to Thunder and Marla Storme, to the Smooth Kriminals, vacated after a double pin on 8 November, awarded to Beyond Control in an open match on 29 November and won by Thunder Storme in January 2005.

titles.name: GWO TV Championship
titles.epitaph: The company’s television belt, first held in these pages by Johnny K-9 in August 2004 and re-issued as a new belt in September, with Hellfire Jack, The Moose, Gerard Angelo and Slim Pickens trading it through the winter.

titles.name: GWO Championship
titles.epitaph: The GWO Championship, first awarded to Myst in a three-way at Security Breach on 4 October 2004, then to Max Cameron in a steel cage a month later and to Lethal Weapon at Bloodshed on 29 November. Sal Clemenzo is the champion on the last card in the mirror, in February 2005.

titles.name: GWO Gotham City Championship
titles.epitaph: Named by the same in-fiction title-count promo (30 December 1997) as the second wrestler's own belt; not one document of GWO's own survives to carry a reign.

titles.name: GWO World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Named alongside the GWO World Title by the same in-fiction title-count promo (30 December 1997); not one document of GWO's own survives to carry a reign.

titles.name: GWO World Title
titles.epitaph: Named, with a co-held GWO World Tag Team Title, by an in-fiction wrestler's own title-count promo inside another federation's broadcast (30 December 1997); not one document of GWO's own survives to carry a reign.

titles.name: GXW Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles championship held across this corpus's own record by two wrestlers, the second still attested as champion when this pass's own reading ends.

titles.name: GXW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship contested at least three times in this promotion's own show lineups with no marked incumbent surviving among them; the promotion's own year-end staff retrospective separately names its earliest attested champion, Inferno, in 2002.

titles.name: GXW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team championship, held by three different teams across this corpus's own record and still live in its final attested defense.

titles.name: GXW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own most actively defended championship in the held record, changing hands at least four times in its first year alone before settling into a reign this corpus never sees end.

titles.name: GXW Television Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A second, short-lived tag championship the promotion ran alongside its main World Tag Team title for at least the two months this wing's own Front Office record attests, never mentioned again after December 2001.

titles.name: GXW Unified World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship, changing hands at least three times across the held record's three-year record and carried into its renamed 'GWE' era by the same wrestler who was still defending it when this pass's own reading ends.

titles.name: GXW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own women's championship, attested by name across this corpus's own record with a single marked champion surviving in the pages read this pass.

titles.name: GXW X-treme Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship contested in gimmick and multi-man matches throughout this corpus's own record, held by at least three different wrestlers across the run this pass read.

titles.name: GZW Deathmatch Championship
titles.epitaph: Jake Smith wins the title's opening reign by first blood over Gargoyle at Friday Night Fury #1; Griz holds it by Autumn of Armageddon, retaining it there over Furykainne and again over DevilTress in a casket match at Dead Zone, with no surviving document recording how the title passed from Smith to Griz. The fed's own separately served "GZW Champions" snapshot page instead credits the title to "The Griffin" rather than Griz — a contradiction that page's own provenance note already records.

titles.name: GZW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Three reigns chain across the held record's three structured shows: Sadistic Sam wins the opening reign in a triple-threat submission match at Friday Night Fury #1; Jake Smith dethrones him at Autumn of Armageddon; Blackbird, of the heel stable Black Sunshine, wins it from Jake Smith in a table match at Dead Zone. The fed's own separately served "GZW Champions" snapshot page instead credits the title to The Hammer, who never appears in the held record's structured title matches — a further, undocumented change this record cannot chase and does not invent, preserved as an open contradiction rather than a fourth reign.

titles.name: GZW People's Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested only by the fed's own separately served "GZW Champions" snapshot page, which lists Anarkyst as holder — no title match, reign start, or reign length survives the held record's three structured shows. Held here results-free rather than invented.

titles.name: GZW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crucyfix and The Fro win the title's opening reign at Friday Night Fury #1 over Madd Dogg and Geno; Gargoyle and Hydro, of the heel stable Black Sunshine, hold it by Autumn of Armageddon and retain it again at Dead Zone, with no surviving document recording how the title passed between the two reigns.

titles.name: GZW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Big Earl holds the title through Autumn of Armageddon, retaining it there over Madd Dogg, before losing it to Thane Blackout in a five-way ladder match at Dead Zone — the fed's own separately served "GZW Champions" snapshot page independently corroborates Thane Blackout as the reigning champion.

titles.name: GZW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs an unbroken chain of twelve champions from "The First" Paul Spartan through a late-era Kage — Zachary Sharp, "The Wrestling Franchise" Monarch, "Career Killer" Maxx Pain, Zac Sharp, "Smooth Operator" Billy Bond, Deacon Kane, Magic, Sincere, T-Rex (carried over from the fed's own predecessor, EWO), Firefly, T-Rex again, and Kage among them — none of it dated on the page itself. Two reigns anchor the ledger here: Paul Spartan's founding reign, per that page's own opening entry, and Zion's win over Above Average Josh Reetz at Autumn of Armageddon, the fullest dated PPV card the corpus preserves. A separate roster page elsewhere in the corpus calls Josh Reetz, not Paul Spartan, the promotion's "first-ever GZW World Champion" — a contradiction the surviving record itself does not resolve, recorded here rather than silently picked. A third reign is now structured from the corpus's own Dead Zone PPV card: Crucyfix defeats Zion in the corpus's own first Crucyfixion Match, strapping him to a burning cross after Black Sunshine's own interference. The fed's own separately served "GZW Champions" snapshot page instead lists Zion, not Crucyfix, as the reigning champion at the time of that page's own writing — a further, unresolved contradiction against the corpus's own record, preserved rather than reconciled.

titles.name: Hammer Championship Title
titles.caption: Hammer Wrestling's top singles title, vacant throughout the surviving run while an eight-man tournament to crown a champion began.
titles.epitaph: Hammer Wrestling's top singles title, vacant from its introduction in 2001. An eight-man tournament to crown its first champion began, and no champion is named in any of the promotion's own posts.

titles.name: Hammer Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: Hammer Wrestling's tag team title, vacant throughout the surviving run.
titles.epitaph: Hammer Wrestling's tag team title, introduced in 2001 and vacant in every one of the promotion's own posts; no team is ever named its champions.

titles.name: SWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Won for the first time on the promotion's own opening card.

titles.name: HCW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Won on the federation's earliest cards and called its longest-reigning championship by the federation's own award show before changing hands to the wrestler who would later hold the World title alongside it.

titles.name: HCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in a tournament, vacated once when its first champions were fired for disrupting a pay-per-view, and held twice over by the same team before the federation closed.

titles.name: HCW Triangle Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at the federation's largest surviving card, with a tournament to crown a new champion announced that October whose outcome does not survive in the held record.

titles.name: HCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in an eight-man tournament at British Invasion to succeed the retired United States Championship, and still held when the federation closed.

titles.name: HCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in a 32-entrant tournament and formally retired by the federation's own broadcast in July 1997, replaced by the Television Championship.

titles.name: HCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in a 30-man battle royal at the federation's first pay-per-view and fought to a one-hour draw at its last, with the champion of record still holding it when the promotion closed.

titles.name: HCW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's most actively defended secondary title.

titles.name: MWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided for the first time on the promotion's own inaugural card, its merchandise reportedly outselling every other wrestler's on the tour.

titles.name: SWL World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Won by Mr. Justice from Insanity at Sharp Turn; billed held by Mass Destruction by mid-1998, per the fed's own newsletter, after Mass Destruction's own turn on the promotion at its Pay Per View, Warzone.

titles.name: UWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in early 1999 and was left unsettled after a Blackout upset, pending the promotion's own Battle for the Belt tournament.

titles.name: HFWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Docta Devistate wins a same-card tournament (over King Thunder, then the Great Muta in the final) on the fed's own 17 July 1997 card.

titles.name: HFWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Mr. Nice Guy crowned the first named champion, defeating the Great Muta on the fed's own 17 July 1997 card.

titles.name: HHWO North American Title
titles.epitaph: A title introduced for the fed's second-era Rebirth show (15 November 1998), contested there in its own four-corners match.

titles.name: HHWO Skyweight Title
titles.epitaph: A title introduced after the fed's founding Handbook; held by "The Headliner" Scott Wright entering the Rocktober 98 card (18 October 1998), defended there in a Rabid Goat Death Match.

titles.name: HHWO TV Title
titles.epitaph: A title first seen at the Rocktober 98 card (18 October 1998) as a Barbed Wire Ladder Match, then defended in a three-way cage match at the fed's Rebirth show (15 November 1998).

titles.name: HHWO United States Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary singles belt, contested in a three-way match at the fed's first pay-per-view, Legends 98 (30 August 1998); its later lineage is not established in the documents read this pass.

titles.name: HHWO World Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top prize, created for its first pay-per-view, Legends 98 (30 August 1998), where a three-way match determined the first HHWO World Champion; by the fed's second-era Rebirth show (15 November 1998) the World Title had become a four-man tag-team ladder match and an eight-man tournament, a schema change this record notes without a traced lineage between the two.

titles.name: HIWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested by tournament from the wing's own inaugural card in March 1997 -- a fifteen-man battle royal decided the first bye into the second round -- but no further round of the tournament survives in this collection's holdings, and no champion is ever crowned on the surviving record.
titles.notes: The battle royal's own broadcast text, msg_ids z1qE35RHxL0J and vwBm7H-iK5kJ.

titles.name: HIWF World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A lighter-weight singles title contested through 1998, with one four-time champion by his own count.

titles.name: HIWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in September 2001 as an eight-man single-elimination tournament to crown its first champion, still underway when this record ends.

titles.name: HIWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag team title held by The Predators through the summer of 1998 and, after an untracked gap, by the Insano Boys in the promotion's reopened 2001 run.

titles.name: HIWF World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A gauntlet-contested singles title, changing hands repeatedly through 1998 and once decided by a sixteen-man single-elimination tournament after its own champion was stripped for holding two titles at once.

titles.name: HIWF United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title contested through 1998, twice changing hands by weapon-assisted or foreign-object finishes.

titles.name: HIWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top singles title, changing hands five times across 1998 including a masked-challenger swerve and a title-versus-title stripping.

titles.name: HIWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in the steel-cage final of the fed's own World Title Tournament, both men going off the top of the cage through three tables, awarded to "Mr. Universe" Tommy Drummond on the technicality that his feet touched the floor first; still on his chest as of the fed's own last-attested card, and later carried by him, unclaimed by any HIWF authority, into a promo staged inside a different federation entirely.

titles.name: HIWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a Tag Team Title Death Match won by the L.A. Mafia over the Hate Machine on a last-second pinfall at 59:59 of a sixty-minute limit; lost by the Mafia to the Nobles, also over the Hate Machine's own return challenge, within a month.

titles.name: HKW Texas Outlaw Championship
titles.epitaph: Hung above the ring and crowned in a No Disqualification handicap ladder match, held by Jake Morgan for the rest of the promotion's served run, alongside a rival promotion's own Junior Heavyweight belt he took from its champion.

titles.name: HWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested twice on the same December afternoon in 1997 by an entity that claimed a five-year history nobody in the newsgroup believed: a 16-man battle royal crowned Stonecold, and the same day's DEATHMANIA — billed as the fed's first pay-per-view — staged an entirely separate match for the same championship, won by Emortal Soldier, with no acknowledgment that Stonecold had just won it hours earlier. Neither the announcer nor either script explains the discontinuity; both results stand as the fed's own text gives them.
titles.notes: Entity-scoped title, not shared with any other HWA-lettered entity in this cluster.

titles.name: HWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Ken Davidson, challenged for a "Boston Brawl" three weeks out that falls outside this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: Attested by promo claim only, not a results document.

titles.name: HWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Bad Ass John, and separately billed to Sir Johnathan in another promo this wing's own holdings do not reconcile.
titles.notes: Attested by promo claim only, not a results document; a rival promo also bills Sir Johnathan as champion, restated as found, not resolved.

titles.name: HWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, held by Blade against a promo-only challenge from Malibu Mike Donovan for a Sunday pay-per-view this collection's holdings do not carry past the challenge itself.
titles.notes: Attested by promo claim only, not a results document.

titles.name: HWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Contended by the Duo of Death and the Odds in a promo billed as "the last stepping stone to a shot at tag team gold"; this collection's own holdings never recover a champion.
titles.notes: GAP REGISTERED: no holder survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: hWo National Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's first title, crowned at Scarred For Life on 17 July 2005; its owner congratulated the player of The Butcher on winning it three days later. The fed's own results page for that night is not held.

titles.name: IAWF International Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested from the fed's own charter and announced card; no reign holder confirmed in the document served this pass.

titles.name: IAWF World Iron Man Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, only defended in one of four stipulated no-countout match types; announced for a three-way defense at the fed's own second Free-per-View.

titles.name: IAWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A newly-opened division per the fed's own charter; no reign holder confirmed in the document served this pass.

titles.name: GPWA E-Mail Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Jordan Stone by the site index's own later, undated snapshot; no document in the held record shows a title match, or even names the title outright anywhere but that one ranking table.

titles.name: GPWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A tournament staged across two 1998 On The Road cards (3 February, 19 March) reached its own final round -- Angry Chef against Jack Emerald -- which the held record never shows being contested; by the 5 October 1998 Topeka show Chef is billed the reigning champion, retaining the belt twice in one night against Commander Cody and then Emerald himself, still billed the #1 contender. He also defended it against Dane Thompson at an untranscribed "GPWA Slim Pickens" show, breaking Thompson's ribs. By the site index's own later, undated snapshot the belt had changed hands again, to "Sideshow" Tad Detmer -- another of the wrestlers the fed's own news names for a different, September 1998 tournament draw (the vacant ICBINR U.S. Heavyweight Championship's own 4-Corners) -- with no document in the held record showing how.
titles.notes: The tournament final's own result (Chef over Emerald, presumably, per the bracket the 19 March 1998 card sets up) is never shown on the page; Chef's own reign is receipted from the Topeka Tabloid's "ANGRY CHEF RETAINS TITLE" headline treating the reign as already standing, not from a documented title-winning match.

titles.name: GPWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Thunder & Lightning won a four-way match against The Cutting Edge, Ron Baxter & Hiroki Date, and the Princes of Darkness at "Small Package" (28 February 1998), then successfully defended against Date & Baxter in the held record's latest dated card result (24 May 1998). By the site index's own later, undated snapshot the belt had changed hands to The Man & The Myth, ranked in the GPWA's own tag-team rankings alongside three other pairings the held record never shows in the ring -- how or when the title changed hands is not documented.
titles.notes: Corrected 2026-08-31: the tier-1 mint dated the title-winning match 27 April 1998, conflating the two 1998 "Small Package" cards; the held record's text places the four-way win at the 28 February 1998 Small Package, with the 27 April Small Package instead staging the match that earned Date & Baxter their own title shot.

titles.name: IOWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Junior Mafia by the site index's own later, undated snapshot; no other document in the held record names the title or a champion.

titles.name: IOWA Onslaught Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Jacob McDonahey by the site index's own later, undated snapshot; no other document in the held record names the title or a champion.

titles.name: IOWA Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Fire & Ice by the site index's own later, undated snapshot; no other document in the held record names the title or a champion.

titles.name: ICBINR United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Declared vacant 28 September 1998, when the GPWA's own four entrants for a 4-Corners qualifier were announced by blind draw (Reginald Parkhurst III, Jack Emerald, Kai A. Lewis, "Sideshow" Tad Detmer) -- the qualifier's own result is not documented. Parkhurst went on to face an IOWA representative, Nate McManus, at End of the Beginning (31 December 1998), winning the inaugural reign; still champion by the held record's latest dated mention (29 March 1999) and the site index's own later snapshot alike.

titles.name: ICBINR United States Heavyweight Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named "Vacant" by the site index, the held record's only mention of the title anywhere -- no reign, champion or title match survives in the held corpus.

titles.name: ICEW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Created and awarded in a single ten-man battle royal that outlasted a mid-match unmasking — ICEW's third and last title crowned in this wave's own record.
titles.notes: Contested by Dylan Dice, Poe, Killa, Jason Starr, Mike Madland (as the masked "Deathbringer," unmasked mid-match), the Executioner, Joel Gutman, Vile Vince Viper, LOCO and Matt Howard.

titles.name: ICEW World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a same-night tournament final and defended once before this wave's own record runs out — the lighter of ICEW's two weight-class belts, held throughout by the same man.
titles.notes: No reign before Jeff "Madfox" Matthews' own survives; none is attested.

titles.name: ICEW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: ICEW's top title, crowned the same night as the Cruiserweight belt and defended once, via a rematch the fed's own broadcast staged as a screwy-finish restart after a manager's ringside protest.
titles.notes: The 31 August defense restarted the same match against the same challenger (Glenn Skiba) after an in-fiction referee-and-manager controversy; this is read as one continuous title defense, not two.

titles.name: ICPW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own secondary title, twice defended without a fall on one October 1999 broadcast after both challengers were removed before the bell.

titles.name: ICPW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top title, won in a best-of-three-falls match voted Match of the Year against the man who was voted the promotion's most hated wrestler.

titles.name: ICW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Established as the promotion's primary singles title and put up in a sixteen-man tournament on its debut card; no champion is crowned within this record.

titles.name: ICW International Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Ordered into being by the promotion's own commissioner after a post-match ambush on its debut card; the first match to crown a champion is scheduled for the following week, past the end of this record.

titles.name: ICW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Established as the promotion's secondary singles title in its founding handbook; no contest for it survives in this record.

titles.name: ICW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded without a match on the debut Adrenaline broadcast of 21 November 2002 to Jade Evans, the one woman to answer the call for a women's battle royal. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: ICW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top title, first contested on its debut Adrenaline broadcast of 21 November 2002, where the Canadian Crippler pinned Jared Hart to become its first champion. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: ICW International Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top singles title.

titles.name: ICW Juniorweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-limited singles title, open to any wrestler regardless of gender.

titles.name: ICW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's second-ranked singles title.

titles.name: ICW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team title, also billed the International Tag Team Championship.

titles.name: ICW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A midcard singles title, defended most weeks on the promotion's own Friday Night Fallout broadcast.

titles.name: ICW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's women's singles title.

titles.name: FJPW Asian Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed by the fed's own FAQ as the Icon Heavyweight Championship's own top contender's prize, nicknamed "Mr. Endurance" for its stated near-nightly defense schedule. No reign was ever recorded in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: FJPW's own FAQ v2.5 (9 November 1997); not named in the earlier handbooks.

titles.name: FJPW Icon Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced as FJPW's own top prize from the fed's own founding handbook onward, meant to be crowned by a 32-man single-elimination tournament (named, across three successive announcements, the E-1 Invitational's own "Chamber of Horrors," a "Torture Chamber" match, and finally a "Deathdome" cage) at the fed's own mid-November 1997 pay-per-view. No result for that event survives in this collection's own holdings, and no reign was ever recorded under either name the tournament was billed under.
titles.notes: FJPW's own founding handbook (27 September 1997) and FAQ v2.5 (9 November 1997); the tournament's own successive announcements of 1, 15, 24 and 26 October 1997.

titles.name: FJPW Icon Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: Announced across three successive card previews to be decided by a multi-team inverted cage battle royal -- first at the fed's own mid-November pay-per-view, then again on a separate proposed weekly card -- naming the Lion's Den among the intended entrants each time. No result for either event survives in this collection's own holdings, and no reign was ever recorded.
titles.notes: FJPW's own founding handbook (27 September 1997), card previews of 15, 24 and 26 October 1997, and the RAGE weekly-show announcement of 10 November 1997.

titles.name: FJPW Juniorweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced as the top prize of FJPW's own J-Crown/Juniorweight division (220 lbs and under). No reign was ever recorded in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: FJPW's own founding handbook (27 September 1997) and FAQ v2.5 (9 November 1997).

titles.name: ICW Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the fed's own Season Beating's line-up as the Light-Heavyweight Championship but called the "Cruiserweight" title twice in the same broadcast's own commentary -- an in-house naming inconsistency, recorded rather than resolved. Held by "ShotGun" Chris Scott going into a defence against Curt Crane whose result does not survive in the recovered text.

titles.name: ICW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at the fed's own Season Beating's PPV (17 January 1997) to replace a vacated ICW International Championship: the broadcast announces the International belt vacated ahead of the match and its winner crowned with a new North American belt. Peter Bell, the reigning International/North American champion introduced pre-match, retained by disqualification over Brian Anthony.

titles.name: ICW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Magus at the fed's one surviving complete pay-per-view, defended successfully against Royal Rumble winner Todd Newkirk. "Bad Boy" Mark Bagwell is billed as the belt's first-ever champion and Curt Crane recounts winning it at the fed's own "ICW Blood Bowl" tournament in 1996; no document in the held record narrates how the title passed from Crane to Magus.

titles.name: ICW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned for the first time in this collection's own holdings at Season Beating's, the finals of a tournament: Boxoffice Bound over Damage Incorporated, decided by Zulu Nation's interference.

titles.name: ICWC Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Ultimate Warrior at the January 2008 launch, carried over from the discontinued UWF Intercontinental Championship. British Bulldog and Ricky Steamboat traded it before Edge won it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: ICWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Established when the Nasty Boys won a six-team elimination bout over Nikita Koloff & Jim Duggan, Alex Shelley & Chris Sabin, Sean Waltman & Justin Credible, Christopher Daniels & Elix Skipper and the Samoan Swat Team. Chris Sabin & Alex Shelley, Sean Waltman & Justin Credible, Doom and finally the Powers of Pain held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: ICWC United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Established when Alpha Male won a tournament final over Ricky Steamboat. The served ledger's own table continues past that final with an unlabeled name sequence (Steamboat, Rey Mysterio, Tank Abbott, Steamboat, Finlay, Finlay, Chavo Guerrero Jr., Chavo Guerrero Jr., Alpha Male, Alpha Male, Rhyno, Alpha Male, X-Pac) whose WON BY/WON FROM/WHEN columns did not survive extraction cleanly and are not structured into reigns here.
titles.notes: The served title-history page's own United States Championship table breaks down after the tournament-final reign — a run of names with no surviving column structure. Left unstructured rather than guessed; see the epitaph.

titles.name: ICWC World Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the January 2008 launch, filled when Gail Kim won a five-woman elimination match. Awesome Kong, Mickie James and Awesome Kong again held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: ICWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the January 2008 launch, filled when Dean Malenko won an eight-man tournament final over Owen Hart. Hulk Hogan, Jeff Jarrett and Kurt Angle held it in turn, before Edge defeated champion Kurt Angle, Sid Vicious and Jeff Jarrett in a Fatal Four Way. Edge's second reign unified in the XWF World Heavyweight Championship, defeating XWF Champion Brock Lesnar and Hulk Hogan in a Triple Threat at ICWC Capital Combat (2009).

titles.name: ICWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The ICWF Cruiserweight Championship changed hands at the Sixth Birthday Bash in September 2002, when Syd Barrett pinned a rival trio member to win a six-way Pyramid Match.

titles.name: ICWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced in the federation's own January 2006 Revised Information Packet to be awarded through a "Spin the Wheel" deathmatch tournament and defended every two to three weeks; no reign was ever recorded against it.

titles.name: ICWF World Tag-Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the federation's own January 2006 Revised Information Packet as its tag-team championship, required to be defended once a month; no reign was ever recorded against it.

titles.name: ICWF Television Title
titles.epitaph: Pitched in the federation's own January 2006 Revised Information Packet as a stepping stone toward the World Title, defended weekly; no reign was ever recorded against it.

titles.name: ICWF World Title
titles.epitaph: Declared the federation's top prize in its own January 2006 Revised Information Packet, required to be defended at least once a month; no reign was ever recorded against it.

titles.name: ICWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The ICWF Tag Team Championship changed hands at the Sixth Birthday Bash in September 2002, when the challenging Mob Squad, a three-man unit, won the titles from Brother & Brother in a Borneo Cage Match.

titles.name: IEW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: An IEW title fought under extreme rules, won by 'The Extremist' Adam Richardz in a three-way dance at Awakening, 17 March 2002. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: IEW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary IEW title, vacant at its 2002 return, won by 'Simply Electric' Eli Johnson in a battle royal on Monday Metal, 25 February 2002, and kept by him in a three-way Hell in the Cell at Awakening. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: IEW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: IEW's women's title, long vacant before Little Buff beat Christina Mazing for it on Monday Metal, 25 February 2002; she kept it in a three-way at Awakening. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: IEW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Vacant at the promotion's 2002 return and decided by a fourteen-man tournament.
titles.epitaph: The top title of IEW, vacant at its 2002 return and decided by a fourteen-man tournament whose final at Awakening, 17 March 2002, Tom Tombstone won over Jared Sengir. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: IEW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: IEW's tag team title, won single-handed by Jason Craven over the Jekel Brothers at Awakening, 17 March 2002. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: IEWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own weekly-broadcast title, defended twice in a row against former champion Richard Starr without a clean finish either time.

titles.name: IEWA Women's Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A title Jessica Starbird calls her first true win, distinguishing it from an earlier, amnesia-clouded match she does not fully remember for a since-vacated television title.

titles.name: IEWA Women's Skyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-class title for the fed's own lighter women's division, carried by Jun Shiratori into a locker-room-clearing brawl and swung as a weapon rather than defended on camera.

titles.name: IEWA Women's Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A title held through the fed's own spring 1998 hiatus by the Prima Donnas, who spent the layoff at a Formula One race rather than in the ring.

titles.name: IEWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A title that changed hands between Japan Connection and Hysteria before the Disciples of Rage's own debut season, then drew a cage-match challenge on the strength of that history.

titles.name: IEWA World Women's Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top women's title, defended in ten-woman and ten-man tag gauntlets as freely as in singles matches; Napualokelani carried it through a disqualification win over Jessica Starbird that ended with a run-in from GDWA's own World Champion. Created for an open cross-fed battle royal announced on 21 October 1997, to which SJPW, GDWA and the Modern-Day Wrestling Alliance all sent wrestlers.

titles.name: IEWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested only in a hardcore-rules match, added to the fed's slate by mid-January 1997; retained by "Kryokiller" Ken Wilson over Thunder Rider in a 60-minute Iron Man match, 9 falls to 8, on 22 September 1997.

titles.name: IEWA Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man battle royal on the promotion's third weekly broadcast, decided by a ringside run-in that shoved the last challenger from the top rope.

titles.name: IEWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Briefly held by Fast Eddie alongside the World Heavyweight Title at the fed's own founding and vacated under its one-title rule; no successor survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: IEWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: First held by Fast Eddie at the fed's own founding; held by the Vulture entering 22 September 1997 undefeated since March, and lost that night to Leeb in sixteen seconds after an Armageddon ambush, the shortest title match on the fed's own record.

titles.name: IEWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First held by Skull & Dave Douglas at the fed's own founding; held by Damage (Kain & Die Maschine) entering 22 September 1997, and lost that night to the Horsemen (Rig & Lord Nightmare).

titles.name: IEWA World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: First held by Dave Scar at the fed's own founding; held by the Vulture alongside the World Heavyweight belt as of 22 September 1997, with this collection's holdings not tracing the lineage between the two or showing it change hands after.

titles.name: IeWC Juniorweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A lighter-weight division title whose tournament opened with Jeff Dallas's win over the veteran favorite Cobra on Wednesday Night WarZone; held by Jinsei Shakanuzi by early summer 1998.

titles.name: IeWC National Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in an eight-man tournament in spring 1998, with two first-round matches carried on Wednesday Night WarZone before a champion held it by early summer.

titles.name: IeWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded in April 1998 when the National Title Tournament's own roster cuts left two teams facing off for the vacant belt; changed hands once more before the promotion's own last surviving broadcast.

titles.name: IeWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, contested in a spring 1998 tournament; two of its first-round matches aired on Wednesday Night WarZone, with the final billed for Spring Fest 98 that May.

titles.name: IEWF Extreme Heritage Title
titles.epitaph: Defended in a 1997 Match-of-the-Year-nominated bout (Billy Sexton vs. Biff McGriff) per the community's own year-end ballot; no result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: IEWF Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: Held at some point by "The Perfectionist" Nik Nyce, per a rival federation's own sig-block billing; no dated reign survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: LWC Rio Grande Championship
titles.epitaph: A title fought over in extreme-rules gimmick matches, changing hands at the promotion's own South Laredo Rodeogrounds. Steve Spector held it through the autumn of 1998 and beat Adam Craig in two out of three falls at Last Tangle In Texarkana; Thantasia and Johnny Rage held it in early 1999.

titles.name: LWC Silver City Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own post-rename regional title. Dallas "Perfection" Reed held it in 1997 and Alex Wallace, a two-time champion, lost it in the four corners main event of Last Tangle In Texarkana on 15 November 1998 to Tex Violence, who still held it in February 1999.

titles.name: LWC Six Gun Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title on the promotion's own LWC side. Mark Cutter lost it to Mark Wugger (Glenn Hudson) by 18 October 1998, and Rob James took it from his partner at Last Tangle In Texarkana on 15 November 1998; he was billed as its champion in April 1999. Past holders named on air include Casey James, Brody Thunder and J.W. Hardin.

titles.name: LWC Twin Pistol Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag team title on the promotion's own LWC side, held by the Nine Inch Males from the Pinfall Bunkhouse Battle Royal of 19 July 1998 and still on their shoulders at a three-day interfederation pay-per-view in April 1999, where they turned back a challenge from Black Sun Rising. The Blaze Brothers disputed the reign in the autumn of 1998.

titles.name: IEWF World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Won by Bishop in a Royal Rumble battle royal and defended into the fed's own September 1997 rename; a second, unreconciled claimant is billed elsewhere in this same census's own corpus, and the conflict is carried rather than resolved.

titles.name: IEWF World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Held by Prophets of Rage as of September 1997, the community's own #1-ranked tag team that year.

titles.name: Intergalactic Championship
titles.epitaph: An open championship the Commission built its whole promotion around, won for the first time in a four-way dream match at the ULTRATITLE finale and changing hands for the first time in a bloodied main event that ended its inaugural champion's 146-day reign.

titles.name: Intergalactic Team Championships of the Universe
titles.notes: Introduced for the Unlucky For Some 2013 tour and contested through a series of qualifying matches; no reign is recorded in the held record.
titles.epitaph: A team championship introduced for IGC's own Unlucky For Some 2013 tour, its qualifying series still underway when the record read this pass goes quiet.

titles.name: iGWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Hak dethroned Dysturbed for the iGWF World Heavyweight Championship with help from stablemate TripleXXX, reported only in the winner's own newly-crowned-champion interview on 16 August 2000, no date or show captured beyond it.

titles.name: iHEL Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: iHEL's top singles belt: a four-way elimination on 16 August 2000, staged as a double-stakes match with the Television title in the same ring, cost Big_Daddy the Heavyweight belt and handed it to British_Kid in the same night.

titles.name: iHEL Pitfighter Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore belt decided inside a local convenience store: Drater walked out of a four-way "Jiffy Store Brawl" on 16 August 2000 as the new Pitfighter Champion, no prior holder named in the surviving record.

titles.name: iHEL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: iHEL's television belt changed hands in the very match that cost its own outgoing Heavyweight Champion his title: a four-way elimination on 16 August 2000 sent Jay_Biess's TV reign to Big_Daddy, the same man just dethroned as Heavyweight Champion.

titles.name: IHWA Bloody Sunday Championship
titles.epitaph: The one singles title defended every Sunday, Bloody Sunday broadcast rather than at every pay-per-view.

titles.name: IHWA Bloody Sunday Tag Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag title defended every Sunday, Bloody Sunday broadcast rather than at every pay-per-view.

titles.name: IHWA Multi-National Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary singles title, defended at every pay-per-view and at least once a month.

titles.name: IHWA World Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested only in gimmick matches, defended at every pay-per-view and at least every other month.

titles.name: IHWA World Hardcore Tag Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested only in gimmick matches, defended at every pay-per-view and at least every other month.

titles.name: IHWA World Wrestling Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, defended at every pay-per-view and at least every other month.

titles.name: IHWA World Wrestling Tag Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top tag title, defended at every pay-per-view and at least every other month.

titles.name: IHWF Associate Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page runs a fully dated three-reign chain from its own vacant start: Enforcer's founding reign (27 January 2001, pinning Mullet in a four-way over Blaze and Enigma), Max Powers's reign ("Beginning of an Era," 18 February 2001, a Bat Match win over Enforcer and Mayhem), and Hellraisin Holly's own closing reign (17 March 2001, defeating Max Powers at SNS in Peoria, Illinois) -- marked "Close" on the fed's own ledger.

titles.name: IHWF Extreme Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page runs a fully dated three-reign chain from its own vacant start: Mercenary's founding reign (27 January 2001, pinning Max Powers in a three-way over Killer K), Impulse's reign ("Beginning of an Era," 18 February 2001, a submission win over Mercenary), and Outcast's own closing reign (25 March 2001, surviving a nine-man Sanitarium Match at Reckless Behavior that included the reigning champion, Impulse) -- marked "Close" on the fed's own ledger.

titles.name: IHWF Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page runs a fully dated three-reign chain from its own vacant start: Stevie Greene's founding reign (3 February 2001, pinning the Godfather after a Game Over), Chaos's reign ("Beginning of an Era," 18 February 2001, defeating Stevie Greene), and Trent Ulrich's own closing reign (17 March 2001, pinning Vaughn in a triple threat at SNS in Peoria) -- marked "Close" on the fed's own ledger.

titles.name: IHWF Tag Team Title
