titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page runs a fully dated three-reign chain from its own vacant start: 187/Max Powers's founding reign ("Beginning of an Era," 18 February 2001, a three-way win over Slade/Apocalypse and Black Gunn/Godfather, with Killer K/Strife also contesting), Black Gunn/Mercenary's reign (Reckless Behavior, 25 March 2001, defeating the former champions with a Gunsmoke), and Plop & Splash's own closing reign, billed under a joined team name rather than an individually-named pairing -- the page's own two dates for that reign (25-31 March 2001) are the only reign on this belt's ledger given a full range instead of "Close," read here as the page's own last-updated snapshot rather than a declared handoff.

titles.name: IHWF World Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page runs a fully dated three-reign chain from its own vacant start: Apocalypse's founding reign ("Beginning of an Era," 18 February 2001, defeating the Godfather with the Bloody Mary), Vaughn's reign ("Reckless Behavior," 25 March 2001, a Triple Threat win over Apocalypse and the Godfather), and the Godfather's own closing reign (31 March 2001, defeating Vaughn one on one at Saturday Night Slaughter) — marked "Close" on the fed's own ledger. All three reigns are structured on this ledger, chained founding to closing.

titles.name: IICW Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A named tournament title, contested on the fed's own Monday Night Showdown; this collection's holdings do not recover a champion.
titles.notes: GAP REGISTERED: the fed's own text uses "Lightweight" and "Light-Heavyweight" for what may be one tournament; recorded as found, not reconciled, per the source wave digest.

titles.name: IICW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by an eight-man tournament run across the fed's own first three shows; its only recovered champion is attested by two later, third-party résumé mentions rather than by the fed's own results page.

titles.name: IICW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Chased on air by four wrestlers across the fed's own held shows; this collection's holdings never recover a champion.
titles.notes: GAP REGISTERED: no holder, no tournament, no result survives.

titles.name: IICW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Zulu Nation billed themselves the number-one contenders without ever having wrestled for it; this collection's holdings never recover a champion.
titles.notes: GAP REGISTERED: no holder survives.

titles.name: Deschenes Cup
titles.epitaph: An eight-man invitational tournament trophy contested once, across both nights of the event, and never revived within the held documents.

titles.name: IIWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top prize of the International Internet Wrestling Association's first 1998 incarnation, billed for monthly defense against a top-five contender -- announced in the fed's own founding handbook.

titles.name: IIWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag team title of the International Internet Wrestling Association's first 1998 incarnation -- announced in the fed's own founding handbook.

titles.name: IIWA World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The secondary singles title of the International Internet Wrestling Association's first 1998 incarnation, billed for weekly defense -- announced in the fed's own founding handbook.

titles.name: IIWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own weight-class belt, changing hands across nine recoverable reigns through 1996 and 1997 with one late-1997 forfeiture line left unresolved by the fed's own surviving record.
titles.notes: A forfeiture line to Richard "Moxy" Blue (29 November 1997) stands beside a Derek Mota reclamation the same December; the collection's own holdings do not resolve which is the title's own last word for the year.

titles.name: IIWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by battle royal one week after the promotion's own first pay-per-view, this belt changed hands at least nine times across 1996 and 1997 with two of its later changes recorded only as bare announcement lines.
titles.notes: Two 1997 changes (18 August, 24 September) survive only as announcement lines inside show bodies this pass did not read in full; the winners' names are not recovered here.

titles.name: IIWF United States Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created on air in February 1997 because the fed's own Executive Committee judged its rivals were winning the tag-team wars, crowned at that spring's Ring Wars III, and billed as defunct by that same November — a complete founding-to-abolition arc inside a single year.
titles.notes: The fed's own Golden Grapple Awards stage direction (22 November 1997) calls the belt "defunct" as a prop description; no formal retirement announcement survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: IIWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top prize, crowned in a 24-man tournament at the fed's own first pay-per-view and carried, across eight recoverable reigns, into a title still live at the end of this collection's own 1998 holdings.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from the fed's own weekly rankings-table markers and ring-announcer receipts; two changes (mid-1996, the vacancy-tournament result of July 1997) are dated only to a bounded window.

titles.name: IIWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a ten-team, two-ring clash at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, this title's lineage runs clean through early 1997 and tangles across August to November, where this collection's own holdings carry two teams both claiming it at once.
titles.notes: The August-November 1997 stretch (a Midsummer Madness change to the Syndicate, a Golden Grapple lyric crediting Cold Spell) is the messiest run in the fed's own record and is registered here as partially unresolved rather than silently picking one line.

titles.name: IL Tsunawoharu Championship
titles.notes: Isamu League's own top championship, unveiled at a press conference on 31 January 2010. The fed's own promoter announced on Lesson 2 (23 March 2010) that the first champion would be crowned by a one-night tournament, open to the whole roster, at the fed's planned debut pay-per-view, National Threat I, in June 2010.
titles.epitaph: A championship belt unveiled with fanfare and never contested: Isamu League's own planned coronation tournament never got a card, and no document in the held record ever names a Tsunawoharu Champion.

titles.name: International League Pro Wrestling Death-Match Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of the federation's own first newsletter; its own founding bulletin bills a twelve-man Bring-Your-Own-Weapon Royal Rumble to crown a first champion.

titles.name: International League Pro Wrestling World Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of the federation's own first newsletter; its opening round, Will Shelton against Malice, was announced for the federation's debut card.

titles.name: International League Wrestling International Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of Thursday Night Ringside; ILW's own founding document bills a tournament already under way to crown its first champion.

titles.name: International League Wrestling North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of Thursday Night Ringside; ILW's own founding document bills an eight-way ladder match to crown its first champion.

titles.name: International League Wrestling Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of Thursday Night Ringside; no tournament or match to crown a first champion is described in the documents read.

titles.name: International League Wrestling World Championship
titles.epitaph: Unclaimed as of Thursday Night Ringside; ILW's own founding document bills its first champion to be crowned in a Bring Your Own Weapon Royal Rumble.

The March 1999 snapshot bills Christopher Savage the reigning Atlantic Champion; his own bio card separately bills him a three-time Atlantic Champion in total, the other two reigns undated and unordered against this one.

titles.notes: The current reign is receipted to the fed's own final champions snapshot; the two additional reigns are receipted to Christopher Savage's own bio card ("Atlantic Champ (three time)"), which gives no date or order.

titles.notes: Attested only as a current-holder snapshot, "as of March 1999" by the fed's own page — no title history or earlier champion survives.

titles.name: iMWA Holy Scripture Championship
titles.epitaph: A one-off tournament belt: Damion won a final billed only as "winner of match one vs winner of match two" to become the new Holy Scripture Champion on the Saturday of Road to CWZ, 30 September 2000 — his own final opponent unnamed in the surviving text.

titles.name: iMWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The_Crew "regained" the iMWA Tag Team Championship from Sickness 2K in a no-holds-barred cage match on the Friday of Road to CWZ, 29 September 2000 — Sickness 2K splitting up in the match's own aftermath.

titles.name: iMWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: A title that moved three times across one week in the surviving record: Amundson beat a seven-time champion, Bolt, for the belt; Mr Arse took it from Amundson on the Friday of the two-night Road to CWZ card; and the very next night Mr Arse lost a separate Loser Leaves iMWA match and left the belt vacant on his way out the door to the CWZ.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Jeff Hardy from the promotion's own 8 December 2006 show onward. A title defence against Carlito and AJ Styles was announced for the following week, but the next captured show swapped in CM Punk as a non-title opponent instead; no title defence survives in the documents held here.

titles.name: MEW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Already active by March 2002, it changed hands twice inside three weeks: Baphomet took it from Mr. Satan, then lost it to Justin Tyme.

titles.name: NAWC Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Restarted after a disqualification finish so the promotion's own first titleholder could be crowned in the same match.

titles.name: TWL Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Palimetius the Historian at the promotion's own Helloween event by catching a dropped title belt off a ladder. He lost it to Sandman at the promotion's own 26 January 1999 pay-per-view; Sandman in turn lost it to XeRo at the promotion's own Armageddon event, the last title change recorded before the surviving record ends.

titles.name: UWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands three times across 1999, from Rockin' Rebel to a two-time former champion, Deathstalker, and on to Mike "Showtime" Bradshaw, who denied Deathstalker a third reign.

titles.name: STW Intercontinental Women's Title
titles.epitaph: Awarded at its creation, then changed hands some three times before its own last attested champion.

titles.name: IGA International Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for a single night: a battle royal earned the shot, and Mark Davenport, already half of the IGA World Tag Team Championship, beat Donovan Keltrane for it after a rival promotion's wrestler ran in against the challenger.

titles.name: International Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary singles title, already active when the held documents begin and still changing hands as they end. Read directly at Spring Slams (Tommy Rifles over James Pillow) and Danger Zone '98 (Drew Mahony retains over Tommy Rifles); several further changes (EMT, Destructo, Johnny Glamour, Drew Mahony, Scottie Extreme) are attested only by the fed's own title-history sheet, off-panel.

titles.name: STW International Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands five times before its own last champion was stripped for failing to defend it and attacking officials, the belt then unifying with the vacant National Television title.

titles.name: CPW International Television Title
titles.epitaph: Began as the CPW Provincial Title and was renamed International partway through, changing hands fourteen times before an irregular final defense posted after the IWF's own closure.

titles.name: IEWC Americas Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's second-ranked singles title, first awarded on the strength of a screwjob finish.

titles.name: IEWC World Featherweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-limited singles title instituted alongside the promotion's expansion into a full federation; its own tournament was left undecided.

titles.name: IEWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's most frequently defended title; its own tournament was left undecided.

titles.name: IEWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, first awarded to the winner of its own sixteen-man founding tournament.

titles.name: EWWF Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in three weeks, from a barbed-wire-bat gimmick match to a surprise rollup.

titles.name: FWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A second world-level belt contested on the promotion's own closing weekend under different branding from the promotion's own name; its own promotional origin is not explained in the surviving text. Mr. Apples defended it against Brody Thunder in a taped-fist ladder match on the promotion's first closing night, 19 March 1999, and lost it.

titles.name: INWI Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded from the founding tournament's own final on 23 March 1997 (Pimp Daddy Brown over John Stillwater), the top prize churned through four champions across the year -- Brown to Brody Thunder at SuperCard I's Steel Cage main event, Thunder to the Springer in the 1997 Ringmaster PPV main event, and the Springer to Tony Houston by the following show, Houston still champion at Winter Storm '97.

titles.name: INWI Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced mid-year and awarded by its own tournament final at Heat Wave '97 (Sam Adams over David McCarter), the belt passed through Awesome X and McCarter again before a late-year stretch (James Pillow, Bill Bob Woijicowski) ended with Michael Bane holding it into December.

titles.name: INWI New York Championship
titles.notes: The United States Championship, renamed on-air in October 1997; the reign ledger continues unbroken under Sam Adams.
titles.epitaph: The United States Championship's own lineage continues here under its on-air rename (see inwi-united-states); Sam Adams carried it through the autumn before Mr. Cherry won it at Winter Storm '97.

titles.name: INWI Northeast Championship
titles.epitaph: The other Northeast-branded belt from the founding weekend (Jonathan Sunset), its lineage is the wing's most volatile: it passed through Brody Thunder, a vacancy-filling battle royal (Mr. Ed Rogers), Dell Pickle, Zack Sharp, the Springer (twice, trading with Sharp), Rogers again, King Apples, and finally Bill Bob Woijicowski, who won it at Winter Storm '97 wrestling in disguise as a mystery entrant.

titles.name: INWI Northeast Television Championship
titles.epitaph: One of two Northeast-branded belts awarded the same tournament weekend (23 March), crowned on Brody Thunder before a run of short reigns -- the Springer, Mike Garvey, Firestar, Vito Rizzotto, Bill Bob Woijicowski -- settled with Tony Houston from mid-August on.

titles.name: INWI Ringmaster
titles.epitaph: A summer-long single-elimination tournament with its own belt, trophy and kayfabe cash purse, culminating in a PPV final; "Cold and Calculating" Tony Houston beat Jason Chandler to become the first-ever Ringmaster at the fed's own 1997 Ringmaster PPV. The '1997' in its own name implies annual intent, though no second edition survives in this wing's own holdings.

titles.name: INWI Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The founding tournament's tag final (23 March) crowned the MacDaddies as the first Heavyweight Tag Team Champions; the Big Brothers, the Terminators, the Comforters and, at year's end, the ad hoc pairing of James Pillow and Vinny Vitrone all held it before the returning Friendship Express -- disguised as 'the Masks' -- won it at Winter Storm '97.

titles.name: INWI Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in the founding tournament final by Vito Rizzotto, the belt changed hands to Mr. Apples within days and stayed with him for the bulk of the spring and summer before a fast rotation through Harvey Thunder, Ultimate Perversion, Pig Pen and Jason Chandler carried it to year's end.

titles.name: INWI Trans-Atlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced by 1999 as a successor to an earlier, unheld "Can-Am" belt; Jeffrey Drake held it into the promotion's own closing weekend before losing it to Kris Klepan on the second night, 20 March 1999.

titles.name: INWI TV Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The consolation half of the founding tag final (the Peeler Brothers), this belt bounced hardest of all -- the Friendship Express and Solid Gold traded it repeatedly across the spring and summer before Solid Gold's own reign from mid-July ran uninterrupted through the rest of the wing's own served record.

titles.name: INWI United States Championship

events.title: inwi-new-york
events.note: Renamed on-air to the New York Championship; same belt, same lineage (Sam Adams was champion through the rename).

titles.epitaph: Crowned in the same 23 March tournament final (Jason Starr over PO Box), the belt passed through John Stillwater and PO Box before Mike Garvey took it at Heat Wave '97; renamed on-air to the New York Championship around mid-October under its reigning champion, Sam Adams, with the lineage carried unbroken under its new name (see inwi-new-york).

titles.name: IPW Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists five reigns of the IPW Championship, from 1 July 2005 to 9 April 2008, with the title twice retired for the fed's closings and once more on its last night, and a footnote saying it was renamed the UCW Championship while UCW held it in 2005.
titles.notes: The page's footnotes record that the title was retired three times: when UCW closed in 2005, when IPW closed in November 2006, and on the last night in April 2008.

titles.name: IPW Pure Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists one reign of the Pure Championship, won on 9 April 2008, the fed's last night, when the title was retired; its About page gives the title's own rules: three five-minute rounds, no pinfalls, a win by submission or a ten count, and a title change allowed on a disqualification.
titles.notes: The fed's own rules page for it sets out three five-minute rounds, no pinfalls and a win by submission or a ten count.

titles.name: IPW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists three reigns of the tag titles, all between 25 July and 7 November 2006, ending with the belts retired when IPW closed in November 2006.
titles.notes: The page does not number a team's members beyond the parenthetical in its holder cell; two holders are named as pairs without a team name.

titles.name: IPW-XFWL E-Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended through the fall of 2003, the belt changed hands at Hardcore Holiday when Bouncer pinned the champion in a three-way Triangle Turbulence match with its own unusual pinning rules.

titles.name: IPW-XFWL Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in the record that survives: Bouncer lost it to Mark Prohibition in mid-2003, and Mark lost it to Venom in the deciding fall of a two-out-of-three-falls match at Hardcore Holiday.

titles.name: IPW-XFWL Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Future's reign ended not in the ring but in an office: after their chain match against The Russians at Hardcore Holiday drew two referees to two different pinfall calls, the promotion's own authority figure declared the title vacant and promised a tournament in January.

titles.name: IPW-XFWL Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Mistress Of Light held the belt into the fall of 2003 before Peaches won it at an untelevised event; Amanda Clark then won it from Peaches in a ladder match at Hardcore Holiday.

titles.name: IPW-XFWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Tyrant's reign ended at Hardcore Holiday, pinned by 411 in a triple-threat Bring Your Own Weapon match against JuggaØ, a former owner of the promotion's own predecessor.

titles.name: IPWA International Title
titles.epitaph: Per the fed's own Handler's Handbook (26 August 1998), reserved for wrestlers billed from outside the United States, defended at least twice monthly; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: IPWA Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's only tag team title, per the Handler's Handbook (26 August 1998), defended at least monthly; no titleholders or title match survive in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: IPWA Television Title
titles.epitaph: Per the fed's own Handler's Handbook (26 August 1998), reserved for "hard workers, mid carders or even, some times, low carders," defended weekly; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: IPWA United States Title
titles.epitaph: Per the fed's own Handler's Handbook (26 August 1998), reserved for American wrestlers, of equal value to the International Title; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: IPWA World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Per the fed's own Handler's Handbook (26 August 1998), reserved for "main eventers and superstars only" and defended at least monthly; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: iQFWC Blood and Guts Championship
titles.epitaph: Mikey_ripper became the new iQFWC Blood and Guts Champion at Thursday Terror, 20 January 2001, judged on rewrite quality after Wendell failed to make the card and Randy came up short.

titles.name: iQFWC Contenders Championship
titles.epitaph: An unusual belt awarded inside its own contendership match: Hex beat Lordy on points, 15-13, in a Hell in a Cell contenders final at Thursday Terror, 20 January 2001, to "take home the contenders Title."

titles.name: iQFWC United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Deth dethroned Mad_hatter for the iQFWC United States Championship at Thursday Terror, 20 January 2001, winning 6-2.

titles.name: iQFWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Last Rites (Cripler and Deth), who won the belts from Psychotic Tendancies at a show the surviving record doesn't capture, turned back a challenge from Black Magic (Voodoo_death and Voodoo_lord) at Thursday Terror, 20 January 2001.

titles.name: IRCCW Continental Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at IRCCWMania II, 20 May 1997, and won there in its first-ever match by Kronus & Saturn (the Eliminators) over Deadly Force (Big Bubba Rogers & Bam Bam Bigelow) in a Philadelphia street fight.

titles.name: IRCCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained by Hakushi in a three-ladder match at IRCCWMania II, 20 May 1997 -- his second reign by his own broadcast team's count.

titles.name: IRCCW North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Scott Hall until IRCCWMania II, 20 May 1997, where Chris Benoit won it from him in a steel-cage War Match.

titles.name: IRCCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: First held by Triple H, won in a battle royal at the fed's own inaugural PPV, Fight For The Titles '96; held by Stone Cold Steve Austin by IRCCWMania II, 20 May 1997, who retained it against Hollywood Hulk Hogan there.

titles.name: IRCCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Harlem Heat (Stevie Ray & Booker T) at IRCCWMania II, 20 May 1997, retaining there against The Gangstas.

titles.name: EWWF Ironman Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended twice, including a bloody Taipei Fist submission match against a three-time former World Champion.

titles.name: iTFA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Freezer and Pimp_man won the iTFA Tag Team Championship on 15 August 2000, billed by the fed's own report as becoming the "OFFICIAL" champions — language that reads as the title's own first sanctioned decision rather than a change of hands.

titles.name: iTFA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Arrow lost the iTFA Television title to Vapor in a three-way on 15 August 2000, only for the belt to sit vacant again within two days as Vapor chased the People's Championship instead — the next card's own preview reports the vacancy without a captured replacement match.

titles.name: iUIWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Carrion became the iUIWA Heavyweight title holder by beating Way, reported in the same undated post as the Showstoppa change and bounded the same way by a 4 March 2000 Wayback capture.

titles.name: iUIWA Showstoppa Championship
titles.epitaph: Slobberknock beat Anarky to regain the Showstoppa title, only for the belt to go vacant in the same report on his own promotion out of the iUIWA — undated in the source itself, bounded by a 4 March 2000 Wayback capture.

titles.name: iUWA SkullCrusher Championship
titles.epitaph: Sabit was billed as the iUWA's reigning SkullCrusher Champion in the fed's own 16 August 2000 column, which frames the belt as "more of a tradition" than an ordinary championship.

titles.name: iUWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Zabingu was billed as the iUWA's reigning Television Champion in the fed's own 16 August 2000 column naming every current titleholder.

titles.name: iUWA Underdogg Championship
titles.epitaph: Tomango was billed as the iUWA's reigning Underdogg Champion in the fed's own 16 August 2000 column naming every current titleholder, no captured match establishing when the reign began.

titles.name: iUWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Slammin Stu was billed as the iUWA's reigning World Champion in the fed's own 16 August 2000 column; a later preview (30 August) frames a World title match between two other slammers without naming a champion, a possible untracked change the surviving record doesn't resolve.

titles.name: IWA Featherweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-class singles title of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for defense every other card -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Global Championship
titles.epitaph: The top singles prize of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for defense on every card -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Global Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The top tag team prize of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for defense on every card -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for weekly defense -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Superstar Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles title of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for defense every other card -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Superstar Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary tag team title proposed for this April 1998 e-federation, contingent on enough tag teams joining -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The women's singles title of this April 1998 e-federation, billed for defense every other card -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: X-Pac won the belt in a four-corners match at Sweet Surrender over HBK, Chaos and Mr. Fro Chuck Brown. By Saturday Night Massacre, Chaos is billed the "current Cruiserweight Champ" — an unstaged change of hands — and retains it at Barbed Wire when both challengers no-show, the held record's last-attested champion.

titles.name: IWA European Title
titles.epitaph: X-Pac is the earliest-attested champion, defending against Raven at Sweet Surrender in a Ravens Rules match — Raven wins there, an Evenflow through a table. By Saturday Night Massacre, Chaos is billed the "current... European Champion," an unstaged change of hands, and loses the belt that same night to a masked arrival revealed as Raditz. Freebird Michael Hayes is the attested champion by Barbed Wire, retaining when his own challenger no-shows — a further unstaged transition, and the held record's last-attested champion.

titles.name: IWA Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: Mankind is the fed's own earliest-attested champion, winning the vacant title from Mad Stoner in a dumpster brawl at "Survivor Series" (18 April 1999). By "Saturday Night Massacre" (14 August 1999) the title had passed to O.G. Chunk, who won it in a four-corners scramble aided by a mystery masked man later revealed as Raditz — Raditz himself takes the belt from Chunk at the fed's next served PPV, "Barbed Wire." The Mankind-to-Chunk handoff is not staged anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: IWA Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: DoggFather won the belt vacant in a ladder match at Survivor Series (Badd Ass Billy Gunn and Roaddogg Jesse James running in to help him). Billed a two-time champion by Sweet Surrender — an unstaged loss and regain in between — he loses it there to Steel. By Saturday Night Massacre, Raven is the attested champion, retaining over Ringmaster (Ravens Rules, Sycho Sid and Raditz both factoring into the finish) in an unstaged change of hands from Steel. Sycho Sid wins the title new at Barbed Wire, pinning Chaos after O.G. Chunk is pulled from the scheduled three-way by injury — Raven's own loss of the belt is never itself staged.

titles.name: IWA Stables Title
titles.epitaph: Degeneration-X won the belts vacant from the Dungeon of Doom in a Hell in a Cell at Survivor Series, then lost them to Corporate-SDH at Sweet Surrender in a three-way cell match against House of Pain — President NateDogg fast-counting the pin himself. By Barbed Wire, nWo Turney holds the titles, an unstaged change of hands from Corporate-SDH, and retains them there against a Degeneration-X rematch, Turney elevating Triple H with the Turney Bomb — the held record's last-attested champions.

titles.name: IWA Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Mr. Fro Chuck Brown and Mad Stoner won the belts vacant at Survivor Series (a masked figure staged with Sting's own moveset factoring into the finish) and lost them to Shawn Michaels and Orge Lambart at Sweet Surrender off a fan's ringside interference. Turney and Stone Cold Steve Austin are billed "former champions" walking into Barbed Wire, an unstaged reign between the two — Freebird Michael Hayes and Triple H win the vacant titles there, the held record's last-attested champions.

titles.name: IWA World Title
titles.epitaph: Triple H is the earliest-attested champion, defending against Sting at "Sweet Surrender" (27 June 1999) in a steel-cage main event with President NateDogg as special guest referee — Sting dethrones him there, Scorpion Death Drop and a NateDogg fast count. By the fed's own next served broadcast, "Saturday Night Massacre" (14 August 1999), Shawn Michaels is billed as champion against Turney, an undocumented change; Turney in turn is dethroned by Canyon at "Barbed Wire" after a masked-man run-in (revealed as Chaos and Shawn Michaels) let Canyon steal the pin. Three reigns are structured here on staged evidence; the two intervening changes of hands ride the record as unstructured, attested-but-undocumented gaps.

titles.name: IWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The lighter-weight singles title of this September 1998 e-federation's Cruiserweight Division -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag team prize of this September 1998 e-federation -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles title of this September 1998 e-federation -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: IWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: The top prize of this September 1998 e-federation's World Division -- announced in the fed's own founding rules packet, never contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: AeWF Television Championship
titles.caption: A championship billed under a rival promotion's own initials but defended and held exclusively on IWE's own broadcasts in this collection's holdings.
titles.epitaph: A career-vs-title match settled its only documented change of hands, ending the defending champion's own in-ring career on the promotion's comeback special.
titles.notes: Billed throughout this document as the "AeWF Television Championship"; no document in this collection's holdings ties it to the wholly unrelated held federation carrying the same initials (a 1990s European promotion). Recorded here, under the promotion whose own card is the only one in this collection to defend it, exactly as billed.

titles.name: IWE Intercontinental Championship
titles.caption: Abolished for four years before the promotion's comeback special crowned a new champion in a bloody two-out-of-three-falls match.
titles.epitaph: Vacant for four years, the title was finally awarded after a cage match climax that saw one combatant deliberately set his own opponent's face on fire.
titles.notes: The broadcast's own commentary states the title "had been abolished for the past four years" before this card; no prior holder is named in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: IWE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: The promotion's top title, vacant since a 1999 closure the broadcast itself declines to elaborate on, awarded in a three-way main event marred by hired interference.
titles.epitaph: Vacant since the federation's own prior closure in 1999, the title was awarded in a three-way main event decided by a betrayed betrayal.
titles.notes: The broadcast's own commentary states "the IWE was last held in 1999," without naming the prior champion, before cutting itself off ("Names aren't necessary"). A wholly unrelated held federation's own wrestler biography independently attests an earlier IWE World Title reign for a wrestler named Chris Hopper, won from a wrestler named Kame at a card called "Survival of the Fittest," with Hopper still champion when the league closed — the flashback footage on this card's own broadcast replays that exact same title-winning sequence. That reign is not structured in this record: its own event is not a document held in the held record, only a third-party mention in another wing's biography page, so no show record exists here to anchor it.

titles.name: IWE World Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: The promotion's own tag team championship, billed as newly reinstated for a four-way elimination match on the comeback special.
titles.epitaph: Its own former champions fell in the very tournament that crowned their successors, on the promotion's comeback special.
titles.notes: Billed as "newly reinstated" ahead of the four-way match that crowned Enemies of the State; the previous champions, God's Justice, are named only in the broadcast's own commentary, with no document surviving in the held record to date their own reign.

titles.name: IWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Created mid-run when Fear betrayed his own manager, Max Rakkus, to crown himself its first champion, before losing it to The Grim Rapper the same night he also lost the Heavyweight title.

titles.name: IWF Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Rage across the site's earliest surviving record, lost to Fear in a manager's screwjob the same night Rage was fired, and finally won by Nemesis, who choke-slammed Fear through a table to become the last champion on the surviving record.

titles.name: IWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Neil Down and Bob Ondis before The Afrolites won it by forfeit after months spent chasing a title shot; the site's own record leaves an earlier, undated claim by The Afrolites to already holding the belts unresolved against this captured title change.

titles.name: IWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Silicon Sally before CalcGirl, a debuting rookie, won it in a match settled by a guest referee's fast count.

titles.name: IWF Emerald City Championship
titles.epitaph: IWF's top championship, born of an eight-man tournament at the fed's own debut pay-per-view and changing hands once, at the promotion's own supershow, before its own record goes quiet with the title still around its second champion's waist.

titles.name: IWF Mount Rainier Championship
titles.notes: Introduced for the fed's own Season 2 relaunch and awarded in a five-man "King of the Mountain" rumble rather than a conventional tournament.
titles.epitaph: A second championship introduced for IWF's own Season 2 relaunch, awarded in a five-man rumble decided as much by faction interference as by the ring itself.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Declared “a legit title” from the ring mid-show by the fed's president at Christmas Clash '98 — a beat the crew repeated almost exactly when the UWF later legitimized its own THC — and won on the spot by Hades over Crow, the mentor of the recently-deceased Carnage. The site's own homepage, captured early the following year, names Freak the reigning champion by then.

titles.name: IWF North American Championship
titles.epitaph: A newly created title, put on the line for the first time ever between Eric Draven and Sinister at the promotion's own Hostile Takeover pay-per-view.

titles.name: IWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Fast & Furious against the Rotten Bastards at the promotion's own Hostile Takeover pay-per-view.

titles.name: IWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Taken by Jackson Phillips from Eric Draven, then defended against Ron Nasty at the promotion's own Hostile Takeover pay-per-view.

titles.name: IWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Xtreme Limits against Rob Cole inside an Ultimate X Cage at the promotion's own Hostile Takeover pay-per-view.

titles.name: IWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Butterball as of 13 February 1997, filling the vacancy the fed's own December 1996 broadcast had announced pending a sealed steel-cage match; defending it that same night against Darlock and again six days later against Sao at the War of the Alliances.

titles.name: IWF Television Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The record holds 3 reigns, from Brain Busters in November 1996 to Assault & Battery in 1997.

titles.name: IWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Amish Warrior as of 12 December 1996, previewed defending it against Sonar that Sunday.

titles.name: IWF Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by American Ninja as of 12 December 1996; the same broadcast previews Amish Warrior chasing the title away from him.

titles.name: IWF Universal Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Soul Takers as of 12 December 1996, previewed defending it against Death & Destruction that Sunday.

titles.name: IWF US Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Death & Destruction as of 13 February 1997, the fed's own newest tag title; a non-title outing against Flying Thunder is previewed for that same night.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-man chain across the fed's one surviving window: Cerberus of the stable FX, Bob “Monkey” Charlie of the Youngbloods, and Jack “Big Six” Henderson, who no-showed the year-end Slammy Awards and vanished from the story before defending the belt again at Christmas Clash '98.

titles.name: Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Todd “Ratboy” Prentiss, crowned when the division began at the In Your Computer PPV, held it through the longest uninterrupted reign the fed's recovered 1998 show recaps hold, contested against the Youngblood Psycho. The site's own homepage, captured early the following year, names Black Dragon the reigning champion by then.

titles.name: IWF National Championship
titles.epitaph: Taken from Johnny Rage by Crusher at WrestleFest '97, in Rage's first defense in weeks.

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Coma's own belt before he carried the Commissioner name Joseph Rosso into the GIWF — credited a four- or five-time North American Champion as leader of the stable Crash Team, the belt's defining figure through the fed's recovered 1998 recaps, defended against Rob Williams in the Christmas Clash '98 main event billed as “two of the biggest egos going at it for North American gold.” The site's own homepage, captured early the following year, names Cage the reigning champion by then — consistent with an independent, undated title-history source whose own holder list ends at the same name.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Opens with the Warrior Clan — Akira, Tenzan, Black Dragon and company, a demonic/martial-arts stable said to have gone undefeated through seven defenses before Halloween Hell '98 — and the recovered 1998 recaps pick back up with “Omega,” Curt Raines and Scott Maestol, champions into the window until Maestol's storyline knee injury vacated the belts, the same device the GIWF and UWF would each reuse. The site's own homepage, captured early the following year, names the Hellraisers the reigning champions by then.

titles.name: IWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully by "King" Kevin Payne against Destroyer at WrestleFest '97.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of the founding fed, passing through three men across the fed's recovered 1998 show recaps: Rob Williams's early two-time reign under his “Real Deal” ex-Navy-SEAL gimmick, a five-minute reign for Grim Reaper that ended on a simple clothesline, and Alien (kayfabe Chris Phillips of the Insane Crew) carrying it into a Buried Alive match at Christmas Clash '98, the year-end story those recaps close on. The site's own homepage, captured early the following year, names Lew Spectre the reigning champion by then — the last title change the surviving record shows before the fed handed over to the GIWF.

titles.name: IWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Taken from AJ "Black Ice" Stanson by Derrick DaMann in the main event of WrestleFest '97.

titles.name: IWF/WOW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested in the promotion's own 1999 bulletins, contested in handicap and special-stipulation matches alongside the World Heavyweight title.

titles.name: IWF/WOW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully by "Trouble Man" Martin Richards against the Desert Scorpion at WrestleFest '97, when both men were counted out.

titles.name: IWF/WOW North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded for the first time at WrestleFest '97, when Helter Skelter won a tournament final over Horror.

titles.name: IWF/WOW US National Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested in the promotion's own 1999 bulletins, defended on its weekly cards.

titles.name: IWF/WOW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A single unified world title billed by the promotion's own 1999 bulletins, standing where the 1997 supercard had crowned two separate, parallel World Heavyweight lineages; no document in the held record records the unification itself.

titles.name: IWF/WOW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully by Body Count against America's Least Wanted at WrestleFest '97.

titles.name: IWL Internet Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: One of the IWL's own six championships per the fed's own September 2004 tournament announcement, which names its three most recent past holders in order but gives no dates for any reign.
titles.epitaph: One of the federation's six prestigious championships, left vacant as of September 2004 so that year's King of the CyberRing tournament winner could claim it outright.

titles.name: IWL World Championship
titles.notes: Named as one of the IWL's own six championships in its September 2004 King of the CyberRing tournament announcement; no holder is named in the surviving record.
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top championship, named in passing in its 2004 tournament announcement as the prize the King of the CyberRing winner had previously contended for; no holder survives on the record.

titles.name: IWL United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Dean Malenko's own title more than any other wrestler's, held by him at least twice across the surviving record and voted the fed's own Best US Champion two years running, before ending the surviving record on Tracy Smothers.

titles.name: IWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Walked from Sid, the tournament winner on the fed's own founding card, through a dozen real-wrestler-persona reigns across 1996-97, ending the surviving record still around Ken Shamrock's waist after Balance of Power '97.

titles.name: IWL World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Public Enemy at the fed's own founding tag tournament and changed hands often enough that the fed's own Top Ten list joked about weekly title changes; Public Enemy alone reclaimed it a fourth time before it moved on twice more in the surviving record's final months.

titles.name: IWL Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated by Deathcall in the fall of 1997 and picked up by Fire Mexica in December, who held it through the surviving record's end.

titles.name: IWL Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dale D'Amico into late October 1997 -- who refused the fed's own Most Hated Wrestler award on-air rather than accept it -- before moving to The Capitol at the BarbWire Blitz supercard and staying there through the surviving record's end.

titles.name: IWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice across the surviving record's final months, from Estrago through Savage Steele to Terrier Tim Larson, and stood vacant at the record's own end.

titles.name: IWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Made history in September 1997 when the Empress of Darkness became the fed's own first-ever female World Champion, and closed the surviving record on Spazzz after a December title change at the Winter Washout.

titles.name: IWL World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Traded twice across the surviving record between the same two teams, The Merry Men and The Super Powers, with The Merry Men back on top by the record's own end.

titles.name: Japan National Women's Junior Championship
titles.notes: Decided by a single match between Keiko Sakura and DARIA Wakizawa at Virgin's Brawl.
titles.epitaph: A junior women's title of the JIWWA, decided at Virgin's Brawl on 15 December 2001, where Keiko Sakura beat DARIA Wakizawa for it in 21 minutes 46 seconds. One reign is recorded.

titles.name: Jersey Jack Badass Tag Straps
titles.epitaph: Jersey Jack Grappling's own tag team championship, still waiting for its first champions when the held record ends.

titles.name: Jersey Jack Big Badass Strap
titles.epitaph: Jersey Jack Grappling's own top championship, a fifty-pound steel strap, still waiting for a first titleholder when the held record ends.

titles.name: Jersey Jack Big Beermug of Doom
titles.epitaph: A secondary championship built as a steel beer mug on a wooden base, meant to be defended in periodic open tournaments, still unclaimed when the held record ends.

titles.name: Jolt Ambassador Championship
titles.epitaph: The 2005 site's second belt ('The 2nd belt in this company'), to be defended at least every thirty days and carried by its champion as Jolt's ambassador whenever another federation asked for a wrestler. Kenjiro Ito won it at WrestleSault I on 27 February 2005, beating Chris Mezz in the match the pay-per-view gave the Triple Crown semi-finals' runners-up, and took it outside Jolt within three weeks, beating Aimz on PRIME Wrestling's ReVolution 58 of 16 March; the night before, his main-event defence against Carson Nash had ended in a no contest.
titles.notes: The rules: the 2005 information page (/promotions/jolt-2001/archive/jolt-2001-information-faq-2005.html). The title match: the site's own WrestleSault I review (/promotions/jolt-2001/archive/jolt-2001-column-6-2005-03-01.html).

titles.name: Flyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Avispa Ultima was the Flyweight Champion on Warriors 01, where he faced Sanchez Cano and Cordova; a member asks in the review whether the belt is to be called the LoC Flyweight Championship.

titles.name: jOlt International Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt Erik Rave won at iNtense 10, which passed to Bane Loneheart, Azrael Ravenell, Reno Davis, who vacated it the night he won it at Thieves Honour, and Rush before Azrael Ravenell took it again at Rise of the Legends on 28 October 2001. He defended it into 2002; J-Con won the title from Trey Vincent by submission at Unwanted on 28 May 2002. The revival of 2012 opened with Rush as its champion; Jonathan Conspiracy beat him for it on Warriors 02, whose first review is dated 28 June 2012, and lost it to The Nashvillain at Divide & Conquer, where it was absorbed into the Relentless title.

titles.name: Moral Championship
titles.epitaph: LLB's own belt: he wore a 'Morally the jOlt World Champion' shirt on 16 December 2001, and the card of 20 January 2002 shows him defending the Moral Title, which Wippit Guud calls not a real jOlt title. He retained it in a ladder match against Wippit Guud on 3 February 2002.

titles.name: Relentless Championship
titles.epitaph: The Nashvillain was the Relentless Champion when the revival opened and kept the belt against Jonathan Conspiracy on iNtense 35; the board's reviews note that the champion cannot turn down a match. Reno Davis took it from him on Warriors 05, and at Divide & Conquer the review says the International title was absorbed into it.

titles.name: Revolutionary Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for jOlt's second season: Dave Gibson won the first Revolutionary Championship at Unwanted on 28 May 2002 when the referee disqualified Sam Potright for a foreign object.

titles.name: jOlt World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Total Conquest, Sepiroth Du Luc and Persephone, won the vacant belts at iNtense 22 and lost them at Thieves Honour to Fueled by V.I.A.G.R.A., who lost them at Rise of the Legends to V.I.A.G.R.A., High Flyer and Tony Davis. Chris Titan and Mike Extreme won them at Cataclysm by the fed's own title history; Team V.I.A.G.R.A. took them back on 3 February 2002, and Derecho and Blazer won them in the Tag Team Turmoil Gauntlet at Unwanted on 28 May 2002. In the 2012 revival the Heirs of Wrestling won the belts in a four-corners match at Divide & Conquer and kept them against Sylo and Ray Chavez on Warriors 05.

titles.name: Jolt Triple Crown Championship
titles.epitaph: The 2005 site's top singles prize: three belts, the 2001 jOlt World Heavyweight Title, the 2002 jOlt World Championship and the new Triple Crown Title, decided by a tournament through February 2005. Brandon Youngblood won its final from Jeff Garvin at WrestleSault I on 27 February after fifty-four minutes; on the 15 March Tuesday Night Intense he threw the belt down to save Melissa Garvin from Garvin's Hammer Jammer, and the page ends asking whether he had forfeited it. Kenjiro Ito's own later biography cards say he won it on Jolt's last show.
titles.notes: Sources disagree on the last champion: Kenjiro Ito's PRIME card (/promotions/prime-2003/archive/kenjiro-ito-bio.html) and GCW card (/promotions/gcw-gcwonline-2001/archive/kenjiro-ito-bio.html) name him; fWo's own text of 21 September 2005 (/promotions/fwo-fans-1998/archive/fwo-fans-1998-disney-s-wednesday-warfare-2005-09-21.html) bills Carson Nash 'the last Jolt Triple Crown Champion'.

titles.name: Underground Championship
titles.epitaph: Derecho was the Underground Champion when the revival opened. He defended it against Rune Winters on iNtense 35 and BIG Little Italy on Warriors 01 and met Citizen for it at Divide & Conquer; the board's reviews call him its champion through iNtense 38.

titles.name: jOlt World Championship
titles.epitaph: jOlt's top belt, first won by Brandon Blade at a2o: Alpha To Omega on 24 June 2001. The fed's own title history carries it through Blade, HaVoK, Blade again and erØn, who left holding it and had it vacated at Rise of the Legends on 28 October 2001, and gives it to The Don at Cataclysm on 30 December. The fed's other accounts also name Kodiak Vic Creed its champion: Unwanted's opening video of 2002 shows him among the past champions, the 2005 site replays the Cataclysm match among its 'jOlt Vintage Classics' and ends it with 'new jOlt World Heavyweight Champion: Kodiak Vic Creed', and its Mardi Gras write-up says the re-make of the belt served 'for Kodiak Vic Creed and The Don’s reigns'. The second season began in May 2002 by putting the belt up again: at Unwanted on 28 May 2002 Erik Rave won a thirty-man battle royale and with it 'a NEW jOlt World Championship'. The revival of 2012 opened with Brandon Blade as the jOlt Champion on iNtense 35; Damien Lee fired him on iNtense 36, and the belt was contested at Divide & Conquer, whose first review is dated 30 July 2012: Sylo beat Superstar Vince Jacobs there for it, in a main event that also ended the Legacy title. Derecho won it at Power Struggle in June 2013 and lost it to Aran Thompson at Thieves' Honor that August; Jeremy Ryan was its champion in 2015, and Death Wish, the final show, books him against Omega in a steel cage for it and the Fearless belt.

titles.name: jOlt X-Treme Championship
titles.epitaph: Graphic Violence won the vacant belt at Rise of the Legends on 28 October 2001 and vacated it at Cataclysm on 30 December, where KroW won it from the Extremist. The card of 20 January 2002 still calls KroW 'the X-Treme champion'.

titles.name: J1 Rikidozan/Neo Japan Pro Wrestling Unified Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Two belts carried together, the J1 Rikidozan title and the Neo Japan Pro Wrestling Heavyweight Championship, reactivated with the blessing of Neo Japan's former head. MASSIVE Akita won them in the CORONATION tournament final at Ryogoku on 3 February 2001 and made his first defense there against Rick Taylor on 24 March, still champion when the record ends.

titles.name: Pan Asia Juniorheavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A junior heavyweight championship to be decided by the round-robin Junior Struggle League of May and June 2001, with a final set for Tokyo Budokan on 16 June. Tasogare no Prince led the league when the last results were posted on 21 May; no champion appears in the surviving record.

titles.name: IGA Jr. Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's title for wrestlers under 225 pounds, decided by a tournament in the autumn of 2001. Ryan Arnott was its first champion and kept it through a five-man ladder match at Devil's Night.

titles.name: JWA Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the fed's own debut PPV, "And Justice For All" (22 August 1999) per Biff Wellington's own opening line, and billed for that night between Faith and Mass Carnage ("the Angel") — Leon Wallace is billed to present the belt to its winner. No document in the held record stages or resolves the match; no reign survives to structure.

titles.name: JWA Trans-Atlantic Title
titles.epitaph: Crowned at the fed's own debut PPV, "And Justice For All" (22 August 1999) — Biff Wellington's own opening line promises "the World, the Trans-Atlantic, and the Hardcore Titles will all find homes tonight" — but the title match itself falls in one of the five unserved parts of that broadcast, so its first champion is not attested by any held document. By "Dark Justice" (14 November 1999, the held record's last-attested show), Matt Attict holds the title and defends it successfully against Preacher, with M.o.A. interference and a run-in from the masked "Mysterio."

titles.name: JWA World Television Title
titles.epitaph: Already a defended title when the held record opens: Oasis is billed defending it against Gangrene at "And Justice For All" (22 August 1999), a match the served part does not itself capture. Jose Gonzalez is billed at "Dark Justice" as "a former two-time JWA TV champion," meaning the belt changed hands at least twice more off-page between the two held shows. By "Dark Justice" (14 November 1999, the held record's last-attested show), Chad Hazzard holds the title and defends it successfully against Gonzalez, with the M.o.A. beating him down after the bell.

titles.name: JWA World Title
titles.epitaph: Keith Wildwing won the title in the fed's own debut PPV, "And Justice For All" (22 August 1999) — a twenty-man battle royal feeding into a ladder match, its own closing pinfall lost to the surviving transcript, but confirmed by "Blind Justice"'s own opening recap package, which shows Wildwing "his body tired and worn" holding the belt. That same recap frames Jon Clark as having then taken the title from Wildwing off-page — a reign this ledger does not structure, since no document dates or stages it directly. At "Blind Justice" itself, Bryan Mercy outlasted Clark in a Triple Threat Ladder Match to become champion, and successfully defended the belt against War at "Dark Justice" (14 November 1999) — the held record's last-attested title change. Two reigns anchor the ledger here: the founding and the last-attested.

titles.name: KAWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A new lightweight championship the federation introduced after its own first pay-per-view, decided in a bracketed tournament won by Sammy Griffin on Fever in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, 7 August 2004.
titles.notes: The federation's own news bulletins name the tournament's first-round pairings (Sammy Griffin vs. Colt Montana, Tommy Flames vs. Peter Hilo, "Playboy" Tyler Rose vs. DJ Hawthorne, Ceaser Risley vs. Shadow of Style); no card transcript for the tournament final survives in this collection's own holdings, but KAWF Update #17 (6 December 2004) confirms Sammy Griffin as champion, crowned on Fever in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, 7 August 2004.

titles.name: KAWF Global Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own original top championship; vacant entering its 2004 comeback season and left unresolved after interference ended a grudge match for it on the comeback broadcast. Discontinued by the time of the federation's own 2006 second comeback, whose own recruitment document states plainly: "Were not going Global this time around so that title was axed."
titles.notes: The federation's own recruitment document (8 April 2004) calls it the heavyweight championship, defended at least every two months; a news bulletin the same week as the comeback broadcast lists the title vacant.

titles.name: KAWF Mason Dixon Championship
titles.epitaph: A new championship introduced for the federation's own December 2006 supercard, decided in a four-man tournament.
titles.notes: The tournament's own semifinals (Cyn Bailus vs. Red Hood; Johnny Pain vs.

titles.name: KAWF Promotional Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own second-tier singles prize, described in its own recruitment document as the one fans see most often; crowned vacant on the 2004 comeback broadcast.
titles.notes: The federation's own recruitment document (8 April 2004) describes it as defended at least every 30 days and, on overseas tours, every other show.

titles.name: KAWF Streetlife Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own hardcore prize -- no-disqualification, falls count anywhere -- changing hands in a ladder-and-tables tag match on the 2004 comeback broadcast.
titles.notes: The federation's own recruitment document (8 April 2004) describes it as defended at least every 30 days.

titles.name: KAWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own tag-team prize, left vacant entering the 2004 comeback season and decided in a four-way elimination match at the federation's own first pay-per-view.
titles.notes: Attested as vacant from the federation's own earliest 2004 news bulletins onward; the four teams that filled its own inaugural four-way match were Youth Gone Wrong, the Boys Next Door, the Natural Criminals and the True All Stars.

titles.name: KAWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own first women's championship, introduced for its 2006 second comeback and decided in a triple-threat match at the promotion's own December supercard.
titles.notes: The federation's own first-ever women's match, a non-title bout between Josie Saito and Nikki Glass, was held at 'Welcome Home' (30 September 2006) three months before this title was contested.

titles.name: Knoxville City Championship
titles.epitaph: Its own record opens with the belt already around Sinister's waist, and both of its two surviving defenses end the same way: Sinister's arm raised. The first came in a three-way against Mark Thomas and Chi Chi LeVaughn, settled by the Chi-Town Massacre; the second, weeks later, against the Amazing Wigga.

titles.name: Smokey Mountain Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: McCloud Valentine and Chi Chi LeVaughn held it into a 29 May 2001 defense against Southern Uprising, last-minute replacement challengers standing in for an injured team, who left with the titles.

titles.name: Volunteer Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Stevie Scott held it through both of the belt's surviving defenses, first against Matt Donovan, then against Brian Storm three weeks on, the second win coming only after Michelle Bailey's interference turned the finish.

titles.name: The Kozak Cup
titles.epitaph: Awarded to the winner of each edition of the tournament, declaring him the year's best newcomer; two editions crowned a champion within this record's own window.
titles.notes: A third edition's field was seated by 22 December 1999, but its own result falls after this record's year boundary.

titles.name: KP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced by K-PRO's own president ahead of the promotion's first show as the prize of an 8-man tournament; billed as held by Shinsuke Nakamura by the time of the promotion's Desperado tour.

titles.name: KP World Jr. Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside K-PRO's other titles ahead of the promotion's first show; KENTA defended it successfully against Shuji Kondo on 6 July 2009 for his second defense.

titles.name: KP World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside K-PRO's other titles ahead of the promotion's first show; billed as held by Masato Tanaka and Tatsuhito Takaiwa ahead of a defense on 19 July 2009.

titles.name: KP World Trios Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the visiting No Remorse Corps, who defended it successfully against Team FTW's Tomohiro Ishii, Jado and Gedo on 6 July 2009 for their second defense.

titles.name: L.A.W Heavyweight Belt
titles.epitaph: Billed in the fed's own founding handbook (11 August 1998) as "the most important [belt] in L.A.W," to be awarded by record and roleplay performance rather than an immediate tournament; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: L.A.W. Skyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title the champion escaped defending rather than risk losing outright, provoking a rematch challenge that the surviving record does not resolve.

titles.name: L.A.W Universal Tag Team Belts
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag team title, per the founding handbook (11 August 1998), to be won by "the best recorded tag team in L.A.W"; no titleholders or title match survive in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: L.A.W Western States Belt
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary singles title, per the founding handbook (11 August 1998), representing "the Western state, including California"; no titleholder or title match survives in the record read for this pass.

titles.name: LCW World Cruiserweight Title
titles.notes: Named in the fed's own rulebook (promotions/lcw-1997/archive/rulebook.html) but carries no dedicated ledger; the one reign structured here is drawn from two dated snapshots (the Champions and Rankings page, 6 Jan 2000 capture; the Upcoming Events page's own billed title match, 7 Mar 2000 capture) rather than a won/lost chain.
titles.epitaph: The LCW World Cruiserweight Title survives only as a snapshot: Angel of Death held it by 6 January 2000 and was still billed defending it seven weeks later, against Trevor Kidd on a card whose own result was never captured — no ledger names an earlier champion or records how Angel of Death himself won it.

The LCW World Hardcore Title (billed the World Extreme Title in the fed's own rulebook) survives from a pre-history holder, "The Stalker" Steve Caslu, whose own reign predates the ledger's own 4 August 1998 opening entry, through 17 more recorded reigns to "The King of Slack" Chris Egerton's own 16 April 2000 win over Cuchulain, its own final entry in the surviving record.
titles.name: LCW World Hardcore Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (17 title changes, plus the ledger's own pre-history holder, 4 Aug 1998 – 16 Apr 2000) structured from the fed's own served ledger (promotions/lcw-1997/archive/hardcore-title.html).

titles.epitaph: The LCW Heavyweight Title changed hands across 29 recorded reigns, from a 14 February 1997 inaugural tournament — won by Tower — through Johnny Hardcore's own 14 May 2000 tournament win over a vacant title, its own final entry in the surviving record; HICAL alone held it four separate times.
titles.name: LCW Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (29 title changes across 30 recorded holders, 14 Feb 1997 – 14 May 2000) structured from the fed's own served ledger (promotions/lcw-1997/archive/heavyweight-title.html).

titles.epitaph: The LCW Tag Team Title changed hands across 35 recorded reigns, from an inaugural tournament won by the Travellers on 14 February 1997 through Blood Brothers' own 16 April 2000 win over the Wannabes, its own final entry in the surviving record — including one team tracked continuously across four billed names (the Insiders, then Pain, then the Sylvania Brothers, then the Outlaw Enforcers) and two vacancies.
titles.name: LCW Tag Team Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (30 entries, including two vacancies and one team's own four-name rename chain tracked continuously by the ledger's own numbering, Feb 1997 – Apr 2000) structured from the fed's own served ledger (promotions/lcw-1997/archive/tag-team-title.html).

titles.epitaph: The LCW Television Title changed hands seven times across the fed's own surviving ledger, from a 24 October 1999 debut tournament through Johnny Wannabe's own second reign, won from "IRA" Sean Fein on 14 May 2000, its own final entry in the surviving record.
titles.name: LCW Television Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (7 entries, 24 Oct 1999 – 14 May 2000) structured from the fed's own served ledger (promotions/lcw-1997/archive/television-title.html).

titles.name: LCW Evo Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded as the "neo Title" the day LCW split in two, and renamed for the wing's own name change from neo to Evo. Rook Black carried it from the split itself through the winter, until Duel choked him out — the Dawning video package's own words call it an "Evo Title match," oddly, rather than naming the belt outright, which is quoted rather than resolved. By Dawning, Doctor David Chambers held it, and kept it there through the wing's own last captured shows, surviving Dean Wallace's grudge and fending off a fresh challenge from Michael Gabrielle before the record runs out.

titles.name: LCW Evo Madhouse Championship
titles.notes: LCW's own Hardcore Championship, retitled the Madhouse Championship the moment Evo (then neo) split off with it — see the sibling lcw-mercury wing's own tier-3 pass, which independently confirms Mercury kept the tag titles while Evo took the Hardcore/Madhouse lineage.
titles.epitaph: LCW's own Hardcore Championship, carried into the split and renamed the moment neo opened. Duel held it from the very first day, defending it through the winter of 2001-02 against Gryfon and, on a card whose own results were never captured, Frank Heimdal — until Heimdal finally took it off him in a cage at Dawning, the wing's own second Madhouse Champion.

titles.name: LTD Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man tournament at LTD's own first show, New Blood Rising, where Bob Yobbo Jr. beat Barabbas, Scott Royal and Myrddin across a single night. Venom took it from Yobbo between shows and held it through Winter's Wrath before Myrddin — billed under the aka Robert Tical — won it back, presumed at the uncaptured Steel City Carnage PPV. Myrddin was still champion, and still defending it in a six-man that also carried the tag titles, when the surviving record runs out.

titles.name: LTD Lethal Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested already held by Barabbas as of the 19 March 2002 Progression show, where he retained it against Sloan Malice inside a Hardcore Steel Cage. Still champion, against an opponent the surviving record never names, when it runs out.

titles.name: LTD Progressive Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested already held by Headbuster as of LTD's own December 2001 front page, and defended clean through Winter's Wrath. Headbuster lost it to Scott Royal at an uncaptured show sometime before 19 March 2002, and Royal was still champion — and still defending it, in a three-way against Humpy and Poltergeist that both men earned by eliminator wins the same night — when the surviving record runs out.

titles.name: LTD Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a tournament seeded at Winter's Wrath from eight teams; the final is never captured, and HaVoC (billed Ruthless Inc. once Maxx Vain joined) are the first attested champions, holding the belts into 19 March 2002. Baine and Parker Louis, wrestling as Global Warning, won them off Ruthless Inc. that night in the same six-man that kept Myrddin's LTD Championship, and were still champions — billed back down to a two-man HaVoC challenge for Genesis — when the surviving record runs out.

titles.name: LCW Mercury North American Championship
titles.notes: Called the "Platinum Title" once, in the federation's own December 2001 newsdesk recap of a card whose own results survive only in that basic-form summary (promotions/lcw-mercury/archive/mercury-front-page-2001-12.html); every other served document, including the federation's own champions.html and every show text from November 2001 forward, calls the same lineage the North American Championship. Recorded as a naming variant from a single dated source, not resolved either way.
titles.epitaph: Founded to replace two retired belts in the promotion's own post-split reshuffle, and awarded to whoever climbed a bloodied ladder highest at Mercury Rising. Memosarks, Magnum Wolf and Geoffrey Slate traded it through the winter, Slate's own reign beginning with a cage-match escape at Silent Nightmare; Gol took it from Slate in the spring, and Dirge took it from Gol the week after, still holding it when the record runs out.

titles.name: LCW Mercury Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded on the belts stripped from Evo's own Dean Wallace and Frank Heimdal in the split that made Mercury, and put up in a first-Fusion match the Trent Brothers won. The titles changed hands eight times across the promotion's own run — twice on Sloan's own turns, twice inside EEI's own shifting membership, once when Beaumont simply reassigned a vacated half without a match — before settling on Vincent Picasso and Johnny Glamour as the Elite, still champions when the record runs out.

titles.name: LCW Mercury World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded with a fourteen-man single-elimination tournament in the promotion's own opening weeks, closed on a bloody "I Quit" match at Mercury Rising. Harbinger held it as the promotion's flagship champion into the winter, lost it to Pariah in a double-down shootfight the referee himself had to call, and Pariah carried it into Oblivion's own opening assault at Suicide, where Gol pinned him to become the group's first champion. Geoffrey Slate took it from Gol on an uncaptured show days later — the shortest reign in the belt's own short life, by the roster's own reckoning — and was still defending it when the surviving record runs out.

titles.name: LCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: The federation's own Title Holders and Title Histories index (promotions/lcw/archive/lcw-title-histories-index.html) linked this belt's own ledger to a pop-up window that was never captured anywhere in the surviving record. The two reigns held here are cross-referenced from the served show corpus itself — a card and two characters' own already-registered tenures — not from any ledger.
titles.epitaph: LCW's flagship singles title survives in the record at exactly one hinge point: Pheonyx held it into the Thursday Tempest card of 9 August 2001, defending it against Gravity with a special guest referee, and lost it to Rook Black on the Torn pay-per-view of 3 September 2001 — the same show that split the federation into Mercury and Evo. Both men were fired from LCW the same night, and Rook Black carried the belt with him into the angle half. No earlier or later reign survives in the held record; who Pheonyx beat for it, and how long he held it, is not recoverable.

titles.name: LoC Elite Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists 4 reigns of the LoC Elite Championship, from Randy Orton (21 April 2007) to Tyler Black. Its page says the title was vacated or deactivated on 24 June 2007 when the league shut down, and that at the restart of 6 December 2008 Ricky Steamboat gave previous champions their titles back as if the reigns had never ended.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LOC Elite Championship (2010)
titles.epitaph: Chapter One promised a tournament for 'the first-ever LOC Elite Champion'. Edge won it in a four-way over Austin Starr, Desmond Wolfe and Christopher Daniels at the end of the one-night tournament on Chapter Three, 7 May 2010; the champions page, dated before that night, still lists the title as vacant.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LOC Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Chapter One of 23 April 2010 billed the next week's main event as the match that would crown 'the first LOC Heavyweight Champion'. CM Punk won it over Samoa Joe on Chapter Two, 30 April 2010, with Ricky Steamboat as special guest referee, and kept it over Samoa Joe and AJ Styles on Chapter Three, 7 May 2010, the last held card.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: Sweet N' Sour International Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists one reign of the Sweet N' Sour International Tag Team Championship: KENTA/Marufuji, from 31 January 2009. The page lists it under the Sweet N' Sour name rather than LoC's; on the 28 February 2009 card it is billed as the International Tag Team Championship.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LoC Pure Wrestling Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists 2 reigns of the LoC Pure Wrestling Championship, from Colt Cabana (31 March 2007) to Lance Storm. It was vacated or deactivated when the league shut down on 24 June 2007. The page lists it among its inactive championships; its last champion was Lance Storm.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LOC Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Kings of Wrestling won the first LOC Tag Team Championship on Chapter One, 23 April 2010, in a four-team elimination over the American Wolves, the Briscoe Brothers and the Latin American Exchange; the champions page lists them as champions from that night.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LoC United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists one reign of the LoC United States Championship: Takeshi Morishima, from 6 December 2008.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LoC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists 3 reigns of the LoC World Heavyweight Championship, from Bryan Danielson (31 March 2007) to Chris Jericho. Its page says the title was vacated or deactivated on 24 June 2007 when the league shut down, and that at the restart of 6 December 2008 Ricky Steamboat gave previous champions their titles back as if the reigns had never ended.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LoC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own champions page lists 5 reigns of the LoC World Tag Team Championship, from The Hardy Boyz (10 March 2007) to Rated RKO. It was vacated or deactivated when the league shut down on 24 June 2007.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its champions page lists it, never a real company's belt.

titles.name: LEGENDS Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned for the first time in an eight-man single-elimination tournament on the promotion's own opening broadcast.

titles.name: LEGENDS Worcester County Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned for the first time in a chaotic three-way match on the promotion's own opening broadcast.

titles.name: CPW Lethal Ladies Title
titles.epitaph: Attested for two reigns, both held by the same wrestler, before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: MWA Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won for the first time on the promotion's own inaugural card and defended successfully a week later.

titles.name: UWF Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Recorded vacant in the promotion's own 21 July 1999 report.

titles.name: NAWC Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Opened the promotion's own Lightweight division in a six-man Last Man Standing match.

titles.name: SWL World Lightweight Title
titles.epitaph: Defended by Prodigy at Sharp Turn against Mr. Mainevent, then billed held by Hyper Man before Gene Hoffman won it on an uncollected episode of Friday Night Raw, per the fed's own mid-1998 newsletter.

titles.name: UWF Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by The Scissor, of the stable Zombies Unlimited, through early 1999.

titles.name: LOL Galactic Title
titles.epitaph: Billed in the fed's own founding FAQ (21 July 1998) as "the big one; the most prestigious title offered by the LOL," reserved for the very best.
