Won by Van Halent at the fed's own SantaSlam '98 season finale in November 1998, per its own later recap; Van Halent carried the belt through the fed's 1999 return, retaining it against every challenger the surviving record shows.

titles.name: LOL Orange Grove Texas Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary singles title, named after the birthplace of LOL boss Ronald Adonis per the founding FAQ (21 July 1998). Held by G.I. Slow entering the fed's 1999 return before he lost it on the fed's own 6 June 1999 broadcast to "The Loose Screw" Dmitri Damian Maku Stalin, who successfully defended it at the fed's own 20 June 1999 broadcast, the last of the surviving record.

titles.name: LOL World Tag Teem Titties
titles.epitaph: The fed's only tag team title, per the founding FAQ (21 July 1998), which notes a third title may be added later "should we develop a big enough roster." Unclaimed in every document held before the fed's 1999 return, it was finally awarded on 3 June 1999 to the Real American Zeroes by tournament; they lost it eleven days later to a pairing of Bubbolicious Bob and Van Halent, whose own partnership then broke up, and the fed's on-screen Chancellor held the belts up rather than let them be defended by a team that could not work together. A rematch to crown new champions, announced for 28 June 1999, falls after the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: LOW Aftermath Championship
titles.epitaph: The championship of Aftermath, the midweek show Lights Out Wrestling ran alongside Realm. Iron Lung, Pax, Jason Warrior, Tyrone Johnson and Kimi Aikohana are the champions the fed's own record names; Jason Warrior's own bio card dates his reign precisely, from the In The End pay-per-view of 11 June 2003 to Wakeup Call on 31 August 2003, and says he relinquished it rather than lost it. Pax's own bio card lists "LOW Aftermath Champ[Creator]" among the LOW titles it gives, a claim to the belt's creation, and Iron Lung's own manager came back at Shellshock for a belt he said he had won himself.

titles.name: LOW King of the Death Match
titles.epitaph: An annual crown rather than a defended belt, and the one honour Lights Out Wrestling carried in its masthead banner alongside its five championships. Adam Stryker is recorded as the 2004 King of the Death Match and Donny Diamond as the 2005; no other year survives in the fed's own record.
titles.notes: Won once a year in the fed's own tournament — a bracket entered by invitation, run over rounds with byes and a final, and settled on the night — and never defended between crownings. Its own masthead banner carried the reigning king in the same strip of champion portraits as its five championships, and one of its own bio cards lists the crown among a wrestler's LOW titles. No defence of it survives anywhere in the fed's own record.

titles.name: LOW Realm Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Realm, the weekly show it was defended on, this was Lights Out Wrestling's own mid-card championship and the one its record tracks most closely: Eric Russo, Jason Ortiz, Cyrus Skar, Malik Katsuya, The Demond, Ron Diamond and Brody Dahmer all held it. Cyrus Skar's own bio card records him as Realm Champion "until LOW closed for the 1st time" — the belt outlasting the fed's own first run — and he lost it on the fiftieth Realm without being pinned, stripped mid-match by the fed's own president for attacking his valet.

titles.name: LOW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Lights Out Wrestling's own tag team championship, held for long stretches by one pairing under two names: Eric Russo and Jason Kage won it in August 2002 and held it again from August 2003 as the Metallo Zords, and The Gold Ranger and The Silver Ranger — the Zords' own two members, named as such on the team's own bio card — record the same reigns on their own cards. The Saikyo System took the belts off them up a ladder on the fiftieth Realm, and Delta Upsilon Iota, a fraternity act of Colby Korver and Hank Cobb, held them through CATASTROPHIC.
titles.notes: SOURCES DISAGREE on who the Metallo Zords were. Jason Kage's and Eric Russo's own bio cards each record a Tag Team Championship reign "as the Metallo Zords" from 18 August 2003; The Gold Ranger's and The Silver Ranger's own cards record a Tag Team Championship reign of their own across the same period. Both readings are recorded rather than resolved. The team's own bio card settles who the Metallo Zords were even where it does not settle whose reign this was: its kayfabe Real Name field reads "Gold Ranger and Silver Ranger".

titles.name: LOW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Lights Out Wrestling's own top prize, and the belt its whole first year of storyline ran through: CADE was billed as the first man to hold it, Mike Meyhu took it and the presidency together after turning on Trigger, and Tristan Belmont, Jason Ortiz, Jason Kage and Donny Diamond carried it across the fed's second run. Annihilation won it in an Asylum Match at CATASTROPHIC in October 2004 and hanged himself on the wire that lowered it to him in the same segment; the fed's own masthead banner shows the belt vacant six weeks later. No title ledger of LOW's own survives; what is known of the lineage comes from the fed's own bio cards, its served shows and the champion banner it stamped into the masthead of every page.

titles.name: LOW Xtreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt that carried the fed's own tagline — Lights Out Wrestling billed itself "Xtreme Has Returned" and named a championship after the word. Annihilation, Reality/Mayhem, Iron Lung, Angelus Sorrow, Psymon, Juvian Ramorez, Dark Haze and Eric Russo all held it across three years. Iron Lung defended it on Realm 48 in a thirty-count Warrior Match and lost it three weeks later to Angelus Sorrow in an Ultimate Taipei Match with broken glass glued to the ropes; Ramorez took it off Psymon at CATASTROPHIC in a two-out-of-three-falls match the fed's own commentary called stolen.

titles.name: LPW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A five-man tournament that began on 22 March 2002 was meant to crown the first Lightweight champion of Legend Pro Wrestling's relaunch. Rock And Roll Rebel was champion by 9 April, when he kept the belt against Dragon Ninja after both men's finishers landed at once, and Dead Skull held it by 3 May.

titles.name: LPW National Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant through Legend Pro Wrestling's 2002 relaunch until Wesley Potter beat Johnny Ziro for it at Clash of the Champions on 13 April 2002, helped by the Assassin, who pulled the referee from the ring and clubbed Ziro. Its name follows its champion's nationality, so Potter's reign was billed as the United States National title. He held it on the last card.

titles.name: LPW Superfight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant when Legend Pro Wrestling reopened in March 2002 and decided in a career-ending steel cage match on 15 March, when Kobra Khan threw Hurricane Wild Child through the cage wall and ended his career in the promotion. Khan kept the belt past Devastator on 19 April after Andrew Dixon and Paul Setzer shocked Devastator with a defibrillator, and Dead Skull carried it by 3 May.

titles.name: LPW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant when Legend Pro Wrestling reopened in March 2002 and filled within two weeks: the Shadowlords won it on 12 March, the Oriental Assassins took it from them on 9 April after an unseen figure's darts, and the Puerto Rican Slayers won it from the Assassins on 13 April in a Final Confrontation superfight that sent the Assassins out of the promotion. The Slayers still held it on 3 May 2002.

titles.name: Undisputed Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: The Undisputed Universal title was defended by Adam Simon on 3 May 2002 in a best-of-three-falls superfight with Zodiac, who beat him two falls to one with the Big Bang off the top rope onto the commentary table after twelve years away from the ring.

titles.name: LPW Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of Legend Pro Wrestling's 2002 relaunch, vacant for two years after the first run closed and decided by a single-elimination tournament. Jake MacKenna, billed as a rookie sensation, won it at Clash of the Champions on 13 April 2002 after Devastator wrecked Kobra Khan in the final. Andrew Dixon held it by 3 May, and he vacated it on 5 May, leaving the belt without a champion.

titles.name: LRW Pit Fight Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Lucha Revolution Wrestling territory, attested for 12 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: LRW Southern Star Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Lucha Revolution Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record. The territory's own record shows the title moving to Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling for its next reign.

titles.name: LRW Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Lucha Revolution Wrestling territory, attested for 12 reigns in its own record. The record's own live day-count formula was not updated on this title's ninth reign when the tenth began; this record follows the later reign the sheet itself goes on to list.

titles.name: LRW World Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Lucha Revolution Wrestling territory, attested for 14 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: LSW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by the time of the wing's own Monday Massacre broadcasts, contested between 'Deadly' Dave Morgan and Dangerous D-Vo Wilson -- the crowd's own signage at the broadcast's opening ('Morgan was screwed out of the belt!') implicates a contested decision in Wilson's favor, and Wilson is repeatedly billed the promotion's own Heavyweight Champion from that night forward. The deciding match itself does not survive in this collection's holdings, so no reign is logged. A cage-match defense against Kiwi Justice is announced for the promotion's first supercard, Disturbance In Dallas, outcome not held.
titles.notes: An earlier tournament semifinal (Morgan defeats Trevor McWade) is held on the wing's own Monday Massacre Highlight page; the final itself is not held.

titles.name: LSW Regional Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Trevor McWade as of the wing's own Monday Massacre broadcasts; a defense against number-one contender 'Deadly' Dave Morgan is announced for the promotion's first supercard, Disturbance In Dallas, outcome not held in the held record.
titles.notes: Named only in the Commissioner's own announcement, msg_id F_BuUx28X3oJ.

titles.name: LSW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced vacant as of the wing's own Monday Massacre broadcasts, to be decided in a Four Way Bunkhouse Dance at the promotion's first supercard, Disturbance In Dallas, among The Ukrainian Brothers, The Desperados, Too Hot To Handle and Pain and Agony -- outcome not held in the held record.
titles.notes: Named only in the Commissioner's own announcement, msg_id F_BuUx28X3oJ.

titles.name: LSWU Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded to the promotion's first champion by presidential decree at its debut broadcast, rather than won in the ring.

titles.name: LSWU Southwestern Championship
titles.epitaph: First awarded in a battle royal on the promotion's second broadcast, immediately contested again by a debuting newcomer.

titles.name: LVPWA Featherweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Open to wrestlers weighing 235 pounds and under.

titles.name: Las Vegas Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's weekly-defended television title.

titles.name: LVPWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's number-two title, declared vacant if not defended within thirty days.

titles.name: LVPWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, defended at least once a month.

titles.name: LVPWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top tag team title.

titles.name: Las Vegas Championship
titles.notes: El Gordo Grande won the first Las Vegas Championship, a bracelet, in the Final Table Match at Supershow On The Strip I and lost it to Erik Mateo (billed there as Eric Mateo) at Hard 8 (17 June 2006). No later card shows it change hands; in August 2009 Mateo says he left LVW still holding it. The bracelet The Captain holds in LVW's own "4:18" (posted 4 August 2009) is the separate Strip Championship he won from Olvir Arsvinnar at Snake Eyes (1 June 2009).
titles.epitaph: A secondary title decided for the first time by a bracket of poker-table gimmick spots, awarded to whoever could put an opponent through the right table.

titles.name: Strip Championship
titles.notes: Created by The Floor in May 2009 as a bracelet 'and a ticket to the top': three successful defenses earn a shot at the LVW Champion on the next show, five earn the right to name the stipulation (the booker's announcement of 2 May 2009). The Captain beat Olvir Arsvinnar for the first bracelet at Snake Eyes (1 June 2009), after Aaron Roddick broke a bat over Olvir's head.
titles.epitaph: A white-gold bracelet created in 2009 as a stepping-stone to the World title, first won on the strength of a run-in.

titles.name: LVW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Later referred to in the fed's own text simply as the "LVW Championship" and "LVW Title."
titles.epitaph: LVW's top championship, crowned for the first time in a 60-minute Ironman match and, after an interval of untracked reigns, fought over again in a 30-man battle royal.

titles.name: LVWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in a ten-way dance on LVWF's first Era 3 broadcast (19 August 1996) and won by The Stud Muffin, who pinned The Terminator with a top-rope clothesline.

titles.name: LWWA Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: Held by "Lightning" Levi Ash per his own career retrospective, corroborated by his own later free-agent ad; no title-change document survives.
titles.notes: Attested by the holder's own promo claim only, not a results document.

titles.name: LWWA Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Held by the Bright Brothers per a fellow wrestler's own career retrospective; no title-change document survives.
titles.notes: Attested by a third party's promo claim only, not a results document.

titles.name: MACW Bunk House Champion
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Mid-Atlantic Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 7 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: MACW Great American Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Mid-Atlantic Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record. The territory's own record states this title was rebranded as the MACW World Title with Zero Dragon still champion, on 7 August 2023; no further reigns survive under either name, and its final reign is later cited as one of two titles unified into the MACW UDC Title.

titles.name: MACW Great American Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Mid-Atlantic Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 5 reigns in its own record. Its final reign is recorded on the Georgia Elite Wrestling territory's own record as won by the End of Days in a unification match, forming the GEW-recorded Unified Tag Team Titles.

titles.name: MACW UDC Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Mid-Atlantic Championship Wrestling territory, attested for 2 reigns in its own record. Its first reign unified the Great American Heavyweight Title (by then renamed the MACW World Title) with a second title held by a wrestler billed under the same name as the Georgia Elite Wrestling territory's own Doom-Head.

titles.name: MASW Deathmatch Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Midwest All-Star Wrestling territory, held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: MASW National Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Midwest All-Star Wrestling territory, held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: MASW North American Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Midwest All-Star Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: MASW United States Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Midwest All-Star Wrestling territory, held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: MAW All Action Championship
titles.epitaph: MAW's newest belt, announced by Rip Chord at Eleventh Hour on 12th November 2011 as the replacement for the Trios titles he has just retired: held by the man best able to adapt to changing conditions, it is to be defended in randomly selected matches whose stipulation the champion learns only just before the bell. JD Morgan wins it that night in a ten-man battle royal (the diary's own title records say "Won in a Battle Royal") and keeps it against Ernest Youngman in a submission match at Farewell Tour on 22nd November. At Remember November on 26th November the belt is up for grabs all night, a pin or submission anywhere being enough, and it passes through Kid Arachnid, Black Eagle, Wanda Fish (the first woman to hold it), Knuckles and Amazing Fire Fly before JD Morgan wins it back with a chair. He keeps it against Jonnie Perez and Providence at End Of Days and Riley McManus at New Year, Old Rivalries, Bradford Peverell at Leap Into The Unknown on 5th February 2012, in a straight wrestling match, Wanda Fish and Fumihiro Ota in a Triple Threat at All Or Nothing on 12th February, Kashmir Singh at Third Time's The Charm on 5th March and Kirk Jameson in a submission match at March Madness on 12th March, and at April Showers on 5th April survives the six-champion Gold Rush match and takes the Traditional title from Primus Allen as well. Donnie J takes the All Action belt from him in a ladder match at South East Crisis on 8th April; Aaron Andrews wins it from Donnie J in a title-versus-title match at May The Force Be With You on 5th May and loses it back to him at Great Lakes Madness on 9th May in a two-out-of-three-falls match, and Donnie J keeps it in the diary's pages from June to August 2012 against Father Johan in a pole match at High Noon on 5th June, Firebird in a submission match at South East Madness on 9th June, Eddie Powell and Citizen X at Summer Showdown on 12th June, Firebird again at Hotter Than Hot on 5th July, JD Morgan in a thirty-minute draw for this and the Traditional title at Great Lakes Grand Parade on 9th July, Powell and Rudy Velasquez at Summernova on 5th August and Providence in a ladder match at South East Grand Parade on 9th August. At Iron on 12th August Rip Chord says the title can change hands anywhere, and Black Eagle, helped by Firebird, pins Donnie backstage for the belt; Firebird turns on Eagle in a corridor and Donnie, after hitting Firebird with a metal briefcase, pins Eagle to take it back the same night. The diary's own title records list "Black Eagle (2) August 2012 3" and "Donnie J (3) August 2012 0". Donnie J is still the champion in the diary's pages for September 2012. The diary's own title records list "JD Morgan (2) November 2011 7".

titles.name: MAW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: MAW's top belt. Erik Strong holds it when the diary opens and defends it at nine of the first ten shows (Spring Fever's main event is a tag match), against Jean Cattley, Findlay O'Farraday, Citizen X, Ricky Douglas, Raphael, Antonio, Davis Wayne Newton and Jacob Jett, before losing it to Jean Cattley in a three-way with Black Eagle at Where It All Begins Again in October 2008. Jean Cattley keeps it against Erik Strong in a best-of-three-falls rematch at Remember November, then against Black Eagle, Ultimate Phoenix twice, Fumihiro Ota, the Masked Patriot, Stevie Grayson, Jacob Jett and Trent Shaffer, and fights Steven Parker to a time-limit draw at Iron in August 2009; the diary's own title records give the reign twelve defences. Cattley and Steven Parker draw again at Fall Of The King in September 2009; Parker then beats him for it in a thirty-minute Iron Man match at Where It All Begins Again in October 2009, keeps it against Darryl Devine and Cameron Vessey, and loses it at The Rip Chord Invitational in January 2010 to Jay Chord, who cashes in the title shot guaranteed to the previous year's Invitational winner; Jay keeps it against Thom Morgan, Stevie Grayson, Amazing Fire Fly and Kirk Jameson and fights Aaron Andrews to a time-limit draw at April Showers. The diary's own title records give Parker's second reign ten defences and Jay Chord's sixteen. Jay Chord keeps the belt through the summer of 2010 against Erik Strong, the Masked Patriot, Fumihiro Ota and Firebird in a three-way, Brandon Smith, Steve Flash and Trent Shaffer, until Aaron Andrews beats him in a thirty-minute Iron Man match at Where It All Begins Again on 26th October 2010, by two falls to one, after Rip Chord's bell and a referee's reversal of the last fall; Andrews keeps the belt against Joey Poison (Toxin) at Eleventh Hour in November. The diary's own title records list Andrews's reign as "Aaron Andrews October 2010 41". Aaron Andrews keeps the belt against Hugh de Aske at Remember November, Matthew Gauge at Season's Beatings, Jay Chord in a street fight at New Year, Old Rivalries on 12th January 2011 (the match the narrator calls MAW's best ever), Primus Allen at The Rip Chord Invitational, Firebird at March Madness and JD Morgan at April Showers; Tommy Cornell's threat to pull him back to TCW fails when he signs a new deal for a full year. In the diary's pages to September 2011 he keeps the belt against Black Eagle on 12th May, Erik Strong on 26th May, Kirk Jameson, Hugh de Aske, JD Morgan, Firebird and Jay Chord in a six-man Gold Rush match on 12th June, in which he turns on Jameson with a Standing Hot Shot onto an exposed turnbuckle, Fumihiro Ota on 12th July, Hugh de Aske on 26th July, Steve Flash on 12th August, Chance Fortune on 26th August and Ernest Youngman on 12th September. In the diary's pages to January 2012 he keeps the belt against Brandon Smith on 26th September, Randy Bumfhole in a time-limit draw on 12th October, Kirk Jameson, who cashes in the guaranteed shot of the Invitational title, on 26th October, Chance Fortune, Steve Flash and Fumihiro Ota, having written into a new contract the right to refuse challengers, and Randy Bumfhole again at The Rip Chord Invitational on 12th January 2012. In the diary's pages from February to May 2012 he keeps the belt against Jared Johnson at Leap Into The Unknown on 5th February, Kashmir Singh at All Or Nothing on 12th February, Wanda Fish on 2nd March, in her last match, Brandon Smith on 5th March and Jim Force on 12th March; at April Showers on 5th April, one of the six champions in the Gold Rush match, he gets Randy Bumfhole thrown out of the field by using his right to refuse a challenger and comes through without being pinned. He keeps it against Steve Gumble on 8th April, Randy Bumfhole in a steel cage match on 12th April, which the narrator counts as his thirtieth title defence, and Donnie J in a title-versus-title match on 5th May, which wins him the All Action belt as well, and again in a thirty-minute Iron Man match on 12th May, which he wins by two falls to one, by the skin of his teeth. In the diary's pages from June to September 2012 he keeps the belt against Lassana Makutsi at High Noon on 5th June, which he chooses to open the show, Fumihiro Ota at South East Madness on 9th June, in a thirty-minute match the narrator counts as his thirty-fourth defence, KC Glenn at Summer Showdown on 12th June, who cashes in a guaranteed title shot, Bradford Peverell at Hotter Than Hot on 5th July, in what the narrator calls the worst main event in years, Kid Toma at Beach Blast on 12th July and Rich Money at Summernova on 5th August, in a thirty-minute draw. At Summer Showdown he swings the belt into Kirk Jameson's head and joins The Fallen, and at Back To School on 5th September he loses a non-title steel cage match to Money. He is still the champion in the diary's pages for September 2012.

titles.name: Rip Chord Invitational
titles.epitaph: MAW's annual tournament, whose winner the diary's own title records list under "Rip Chord Invitational" and whose champion the text treats as guaranteed a title shot. Antonio is the 2008 winner; at The Rip Chord Invitational in January 2009 Kid Arachnid beats Fumihiro Ota in the final and is unmasked as Rip Chord's son Jay (the record line reads "Kid Arachnid (Jay Chord)"). Jay Chord, the 2009 winner, cashes in the title shot the Invitational guaranteed him at The Rip Chord Invitational in January 2010, after losing his quarter-final to Erik Strong. Primus Allen beats Strong in the 2010 final with the Running Powerslam and becomes the champion; the diary's own title records list him as "Primus Allen" under January 2010. Primus Allen says at Eleventh Hour in November 2010 that he will not defend the Invitational crown at the 2011 tournament but cash in the guaranteed title shot it carries, a year after his win, against Aaron Andrews. Kirk Jameson wins the 2011 tournament on 21st January 2011 by beating Antonio, Firebird and Hugh de Aske on the one night, after a field that took in qualifiers at Remember November, Season's Beatings, End Of Days and New Year, Old Rivalries and a quarter-final on a tour show; Primus Allen, the holder, has by then spent his crown's title shot on Aaron Andrews. The diary's own title records list Jameson under January 2011. Kirk Jameson spends the guaranteed title shot of his crown on Aaron Andrews at Where It All Begins Again on 26th October 2011 and loses. The 2012 tournament is a field of eight, with qualifiers at Season's Beatings, End Of Days and New Year, Old Rivalries and the rest on 12th January 2012, when Kid Arachnid beats Jared Johnson, Firebird and JD Morgan on the one night and is unmasked as KC Glenn; the diary's own title records list him as "Kid Arachnid (KC Glenn)" under January 2012, and the narrator notes that tew.com now rates the show of Above Average importance, the company's first. In the diary's pages from June to July 2012 KC Glenn, the holder, cashes in a guaranteed title shot against Aaron Andrews at Summer Showdown on 12th June and loses; after Beach Blast on 12th July he leaves MAW.

titles.name: MAW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: MAW's tag belts. The Canadian Blondes hold them when the diary opens, Perez & Shaffer win them in the Beach Blast ladder match in July 2008, and Trent Shaffer carries them into the autumn with a new partner, Stevie Grayson. The Gauge Brothers take the belts from Shaffer & Grayson at The Rip Chord Invitational in January 2009, Morgan & Benning take them at All Or Nothing in February and keep them against C-V-2 and the Canadian Blondes, and C-V-2 win them at Iron in August 2009. C-V-2 keep the belts against the Internet Favourites, the Masked Patriot and Kashmir Singh, Riley McManus and Shane Nelson, and Ultimate Phoenix and Kashmir Singh; Cameron Vessey leaves for USPW in March 2010, and Casey Valentine and Jared Johnson carry the belts on, keeping them in the April Showers three-way, against Morgan & Benning at Spring Fever and against Shaffer & Grayson at Mother, May I?. The diary's own title records list the whole reign as "Valentine & Johnson", with nine defences. Casey Valentine and Jared Johnson keep the belts against the Internet Favourites, Morgan & Benning and, in a three-way, the Internet Favourites and Ricochet & Sharp, until the Canadian Blondes beat them in a three-way at Fall Of The King in September 2010 for a record third reign; the Blondes keep them in a four-team ladder match at Where It All Begins Again in October and against Brandon Smith and Joe Benning on a November tour show. The diary's own title records list the Blondes' reign as "The Canadian Blondes (3) September 2010". The Canadian Blondes keep the belts against Smith & Singh at Remember November, the Internet Favourites on 11th December, the Bailey Boys at Season's Beatings and Smith & Singh on 25th December, until Kashmir Singh and Jean Cattley, a pair thrown together when the Blondes injure Brandon Smith, beat them at New Year, Old Rivalries on 12th January 2011. Cattley and Singh keep the belts against Antonio & Raphael, the Blondes and Thrash and Firebird, until the Canadian Blondes beat them at Spring Fever on 23rd April 2011 and Jean Cattley loses a Loser Leaves Town match to Casey Valentine and leaves for the SWF. The diary's own title records list the reign as "Cattley & Singh January 2011 3". The Blondes keep the belts against the Young Americans, Smith & Singh with the Dark Raptors, Kid Arachnid and Amazing Fire Fly, the West Texas Peacekeepers, Smith & Singh with Ford & Speed, Leftie Wilkes and Ben Williams, The Quest and the Young Americans again,, the Young Americans and Smith & Singh in a three-way on 26th September, the Young Americans again and the Internet Favourites, until Smith & Singh take the belts from them at Where It All Begins Again on 26th October 2011, ending the fourth reign at six months. Smith & Singh keep them against the Second Sons, in a three-way with the Dark Raptors and Ford & Speed, against Ford & Speed, Firebird and Citizen X and, at The Rip Chord Invitational on 12th January 2012, in a three-way with Ford & Speed and Lockdown, and then beat the Canadian Blondes, who cash in their rematch four months after losing the belts, at Great Lakes Crisis on 2nd March 2012, and keep the belts against the Second Sons at March Madness on 12th March and May The Force Be With You on 5th May. The Second Sons earn their shot by winning a four-team match at April Showers on 5th April. At High Noon on 5th June 2012 Smith & Singh keep the belts in a three-way against the Second Sons and Ford & Speed, and a week later, at Summer Showdown on 12th June, they lose them to Firebird and Black Eagle, The Dark Raptors, when Firebird pins Singh with the Phoenix Firebird Splash. The Dark Raptors keep them against the West Texas Peacekeepers at Great Lakes Grand Parade on 9th July, the XX Factor at Summernova on 5th August and Spectrum Infinity at Iron on 12th August, and lose them at Back To School on 5th September to Team Honor, Jared Johnson and Lassana Makutsi, when Black Eagle taps out to the Carolina Crossface. The diary's own title records list The Dark Raptors as "June 2012 3" and Team Honor as "September 2012 4". The diary's own title records list their reign as "The Canadian Blondes (4) April 2011 11".

titles.name: MAW Traditional Championship
titles.epitaph: MAW's second singles belt, announced by the narrator at All Or Nothing in February 2009 "in honour of the great success stories of the past". Stevie Grayson wins it in the ten-man Mayhem Battle Royal at March Madness, keeps it against Jay Chord at Spring Fever and Curtis Jenkins at Summer Showdown, and loses it to Darryl Devine at Beach Blast; Devine keeps it from Ultimate Phoenix at Iron. Stevie Grayson regains it from Darryl Devine at Where It All Begins Again in October 2009 and loses it to Hugh de Aske at End Of Days in December; de Aske keeps it against Fumihiro Ota, Hugh Lee, "Bulldozer" Brandon Smith (a time-limit draw) and Kirk Jameson until Aaron Andrews wins it at Spring Fever in April 2010, and Andrews keeps it against Antonio at Mother, May I?. Aaron Andrews keeps it against Casey Valentine and Jared Johnson in a triangle match, Firebird and Toxin until Primus Allen beats him at Iron in August 2010; Allen keeps it against Kirk Jameson and Joe Benning and loses it at Where It All Begins Again in October to Jonnie Perez, who keeps it on the November tour shows. The diary's own title records list Allen under August 2010 and Perez under October 2010. Jonnie Perez keeps it on the December and early January tour shows and against Matthew Gauge at End Of Days, until Gauge wins it at The Rip Chord Invitational on 21st January 2011; Gauge, leaving for Japan, loses it to Hugh de Aske in a three-way with Perez at Leap Into The Unknown on 12th February, and de Aske keeps it against Perez, Jean Cattley and "Regular" Joe Benning. The diary's own title records list Gauge under January 2011 with no defence and "Hugh de Aske (2)" under February 2011. Hugh de Aske keeps it against Fumihiro Ota, Providence, Black Eagle and, in a fifteen-minute draw, Jay Chord, until Primus Allen beats him at Summernova on 12th August 2011 with a Sitout Spinebuster; Allen keeps it against Ernest Youngman and, in a three-way, Steve Flash and Erik Strong. The diary's own title records list "Primus Allen (2)" under August 2011. Primus Allen keeps it against Bradford Peverell at Where It All Begins Again on 26th October 2011, Riley McManus at Season's Beatings, Jared Johnson in a fifteen-minute draw at End Of Days, Kid Arachnid on 5th January 2012 and Kirk Jameson at The Rip Chord Invitational on 12th January, KC Glenn, the Invitational champion, in a time-limit draw at Leap Into The Unknown on 5th February 2012, Randy Bumfhole at Third Time's The Charm on 5th March and Lassana Makutsi at March Madness on 12th March, and loses it at April Showers on 5th April to JD Morgan, who pins him in the six-champion Gold Rush match. JD Morgan keeps it against Bradford Peverell and Lord Geoffrey Windameer in a three-way at Mother, May I? on 12th May, and keeps it in the diary's pages from June to September 2012 against Steve Gumble in a draw at High Noon on 5th June, Amazing Fire Fly at Summer Showdown on 12th June, Gumble at Hotter Than Hot on 5th July, Donnie J in a thirty-minute draw for the Traditional and All Action titles at Great Lakes Grand Parade on 9th July, Black Eagle at Beach Blast on 12th July, Sean Deeley at South East Grand Parade on 9th August and Rudy Velasquez at Iron on 12th August; he is pinned by Deeley in a six-man match at Back To School on 5th September, a non-title match, and is still the champion in the diary's pages for September 2012. The diary's own title records list "JD Morgan April 2012 12 Won in a Gold Rush match".

titles.name: MAW Trios Championship
titles.epitaph: MAW's trios belts, announced by Rip Chord at All Or Nothing in February 2010 after Ultimate Phoenix's lucha experience and his trouble with The Firm. The Watch meet The Firm at March Madness to decide the first champions, and The Firm (Jean Cattley, Darryl Devine and Ryan Powell) win; they keep the belts against the Internet Favourites and Fumihiro Ota at April Showers. The diary's own title records list the first reign as "Cattley, Allen & Powell". The Firm keeps the belts against Shane Nelson, Amazing Fire Fly and Riley McManus at Summer Showdown in June 2010, with Primus Allen standing in for Darryl Devine, and loses them to Fumihiro Ota, Brandon Smith and Kashmir Singh at Hotter Than Hot in July; the new champions keep them against Ricochet, Sharp and Toxin at Summernova and against Jared Johnson, Nelson Callum and Roderick Remus at Eleventh Hour in November 2010. The diary's own title records list the two reigns as "Cattley, Allen & Powell March 2010" and "Smith, Ota & Singh July 2010". Fumihiro Ota, Brandon Smith and Kashmir Singh lose the belts to The Triple Threat (Jared Johnson, Roderick Remus and Nelson Callum) at Season's Beatings on 12th December 2010, when Firebird distracts Ota; the new champions keep them at End Of Days and on four tour shows. The diary's own title records list the reign as "Johnson, Remus & Callum December 2010 7". The Triple Threat keep the belts on the May and early July tour shows until Kid Arachnid, Chance Fortune and Randy Bumfhole, billed as The Firm, take them at Summernova on 12th August 2011; The Firm keep them against The Fallen at Back To School. The diary's own title records list the new champions as "Arachnid, Fortune & Bumfhole August 2011 1". The Second Sons, Casey Valentine, Cameron Vessey (on loan from USPW) and Antonio, take the belts from The Firm at Where It All Begins Again on 26th October 2011, Valentine pinning Kid Arachnid; at Eleventh Hour on 12th November Rip Chord says he does not like championships that let two men rely on a third and retires the Trios titles, creating the All Action title in their place. The diary's own title records list the last champions as "Vessey, Valentine & Antonio October 2011 - Retired November 2011".

titles.name: MAWA North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on-air during the fed's own Bell Time debut broadcast (2 July 1997), where commentary anticipates Dutch McNeely as a future titleholder. No bestowal is shown on-screen in the surviving script, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: MBE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: MBE's own top championship, defended and retained through every fwrestling.com-era show read this pass.
titles.epitaph: MBE's own big gold belt, held through the whole of its fwrestling.com relaunch without once changing hands on the shows this pass could read.

titles.name: MBE World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: MBE's own tag title, successfully defended in a ladder match on the first show of the fwrestling.com relaunch.
titles.epitaph: MBE's own tag straps, kept by the Thrillbillies through a ladder match against a trio of their own hooligan rivals.

titles.name: MBWF Air Wave Championship
titles.epitaph: A men's belt first won by the Electric Youth at the league's Winter Bash of 1992, with a defence due within 28 days; he was still champion when he beat Scourge at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993.
titles.notes: "Air Wave Champion............. Men Only" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF All-Comers Championship
titles.epitaph: Open to men and ladies and decided by a sixteen-man tournament that was set to open on 23 April 1993. Colossus won its final from Noose Lupack at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993 and was its first champion.
titles.notes: "All-Comers Champion........... Men and Ladies" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF Ladies World Championship
titles.epitaph: The ladies' league's singles belt. The Countess, the first woman to enter the league, was champion by default until Angel Pit Bull beat her at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993.
titles.notes: "Ladies World Champion......... Ladies Only" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF Master of the Ring Championship
titles.epitaph: A men's belt that the Gross Gladiator took from Scourge on 30 November 1992 on a Monday Madness show, with a defence due within 14 days, and kept until the Great Tadaka pinned him at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993.
titles.notes: "Master of the Ring............ Men Only" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF Princess of the Ring Championship
titles.epitaph: A ladies' belt named in the league's write-up of December 1993. No holder is named.
titles.notes: "Princess of the Ring.......... Ladies Only" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Open to men's and ladies' teams. Tempest, the first team entered, were the first champions; the Slammers held the belts by 14 June 1993 and lost them to Pain Unbound at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993 after one of their own stopped fighting for the other.
titles.notes: "World Tag Team Champions...... Mens teams and Ladies Teams" in the league's write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: The league's top belt, open to men, and vacant when the league opened on 10 October 1992; Death Croc was champion by 19 October. Wolverine took it from him at Friday Ferocity #2 on 26 February 1993 and lost it back to him at Grapple Wars on 18 June 1993.
titles.notes: Named in the league's founding post ("M.B.W.F. World Champion"), its update of 19 October 1992, the newsletter of 18 March 1993 and Grapple Wars 1; "World Heavyweight Champion.... Men Only" in its write-up of 14 December 1993.

titles.name: MBWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in MBWF's own founding recruitment post as one of three titles on offer; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: MBWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in MBWF's own founding recruitment post as one of three titles on offer; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: MBWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in MBWF's own founding recruitment post as one of three titles on offer; no holder or result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: MCMW Midwest Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the federation's own title list; no holder or title match survives in the held documents.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own title list; no holder or title match survives in the held documents.

titles.name: MCMW Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the federation's own title list, with an August 1995 tag tournament announced to crown the first champions; no completed tournament result or holder survives in the held documents.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own title list, with an August 1995 tag tournament announced to crown the first champions; no completed tournament result or holder survives in the held documents.

titles.name: MCMW Title
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles championship, first won by Fortress in a twenty-man battle royal at the promotion's debut Usenet pay-per-view, MatWar, and still held by him as of the last surviving records.
titles.notes: The federation's top singles championship, first won by Fortress in a twenty-man battle royal at the promotion's debut Usenet pay-per-view, MatWar, and still held by him as of the last surviving records.

titles.name: MCMW TV Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the federation's own title list as the belt defended weekly on its TV program; no holder or title match survives in the held documents.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own title list as the belt defended weekly on its TV program; no holder or title match survives in the held documents.

titles.name: MCRW 8-Mile Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Motor City Roughneck Wrestling territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record.

titles.name: MCRW American-Made OC Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Motor City Roughneck Wrestling territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record.

titles.name: MCRW American-Made OC Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Motor City Roughneck Wrestling territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record.

titles.name: MCRW American-Made OC Trios Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Motor City Roughneck Wrestling territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record.

titles.name: MCW Gladiator Title
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-styled title whose every defense is a gimmick match; the record picks it up already in progress by August 1999.

titles.name: MCW Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A title held by an Australian, second-generation wrestler whose April 1999 defense ended in an interference-marred finish with no result declared on air.

titles.name: MCW Midwestern Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top singles title, decided by an eight-man tournament that crowned its first champion at the promotion's own April 1999 pay-per-view.

titles.name: MCW Midwestern Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag title, awarded to the winner of a round-robin tournament settled at its own April 1999 pay-per-view.

titles.name: MCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A title the record picks up already in progress, its holder wagering his own freedom on a title defense before the belt later resurfaces on a different champion.

titles.name: MCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: MCW's top championship, first awarded at the fed's own debut pay-per-view and left vacant seven months later when its holder turned on the promotion on air; a battle royal crowned its next champion the following January.

titles.name: Michael Hegstrand Cup
titles.notes: The fed's own Title History document labels this a "Tag Team Tournament" trophy rather than a defended championship.
titles.epitaph: A tag team tournament trophy MCW's own Title History document names for Michael Hegstrand, first awarded to New & Improved D-X after a four-team bracket in the fed's own final months.

titles.name: MCW Legend
titles.notes: The fed's own Title History document describes this as "a special championship belt presented on a special occasion" rather than a standing, defended title.
titles.epitaph: A one-off belt MCW's own Title History document calls "a special championship belt presented on a special occasion," contested in a single sixty-minute Ironman match that ended in a draw, with both competitors awarded the title.

titles.name: Missouri Champion
titles.notes: The fed's own Title History document (last edited 29 January 2007) states this regional title was "Never Awarded."
titles.epitaph: MCW's own designated "Main Regional Title," left unawarded through the whole of the fed's Title History document's own record.

titles.name: MCW North American Championship
titles.notes: Retired by the fed 28 January 2007 with no further reign; the fed's own Title History document does not say why.
titles.epitaph: A secondary title decided by an eight-man tournament at MCW's own debut pay-per-view and retired outright a little over seven months later, with no second reign ever recorded.

titles.name: King Goofy Stip - Lord of the Pants
titles.epitaph: A novelty title whose matches carry a stipulation drawn at random; it changed hands on a split judges' decision at the promotion's own January 1999 pay-per-view.

titles.name: Pipsa© "Special" Chimpionchip
titles.epitaph: A title that changed hands when the reigning champion failed to appear for a title defense and a stand-in was pinned in under a minute.

titles.name: MCW Super Dooper Keen Team Things
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag title, won at its January 1999 pay-per-view by two members of a three-man stable after their opponents' own manager interfered and drew a double disqualification the previous month.

titles.name: MCW Big Chrome Wurld Chimpionchip
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top singles title, changing hands at its own January 1999 pay-per-view when a short in a mount's control harness sent the challenger crashing down for the pin.

titles.name: MCW Brutality Championship
titles.epitaph: Priest held it from All Hallows Annihilation on 19 November 2007, when he beat Whitecloud for it, until Annie Alvarez took it from him and Jonas Griffin at Mayhem on 28 January 2008; a ladder match on 7 April 2008 named a number one contender for her.

titles.name: MCW Global Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt of the Livewire brand, introduced with its debut on 21 January 2010: Dazz is its first champion by his own account and keeps it past Jay Williams that night.

titles.name: MCW Millenium Championship
titles.epitaph: A Livewire belt, spelled Millenium in the roleplays: Segador is its first and current champion by Dazz's account of 4 February 2010, and keeps it against Aerik Walker on the first Livewire.

titles.name: MCW Motor City Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt named for the city: Dazz's roleplays make Angelica Jones its champion in September 2009, with a Motor City contender match on 7 September 2009; it was stripped from her on 2 November 2009 in a title-versus-title match and was contested again at Nightmare Before Christmas.

titles.name: MCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Kaplan James and Shitface McKee held it from 3 November 2007 until BROS beat them and three other men at Purgatory on 25 February 2008; Dazz's roleplays show Southern Blood holding it in 2009 and Vitriol and Ambrosia taking it two weeks before Nightmare Before Christmas.

titles.name: MCW TV Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles belt shown on its champions page by a TV Champ plate: Rayne Young is champion on the capture of 7 January 2008, over Eric Moreland, and the title stands vacated from Mayhem on 28 January 2008.

titles.name: MCW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Annie Alvarez is billed its champion on the Mayhem card of 7 April 2008, defending against Angelica Jones; the fed's news of 26 February 2008 says its Women's title information was being revamped.

titles.name: MCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top singles belt, shown on its champions page as the World title: Rayne Young held it from All Hallows Annihilation on 19 November 2007, Annie Alvarez took it at Purgatory on 25 February 2008, and Dazz's roleplays carry it from Rayne Young to Dazz, Angelica Jones and back to Dazz between July and December 2009.
titles.notes: The champions page's plate is a World Championship image; Dazz's roleplays call the belt the World Heavyweight title.

titles.name: MECW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant when the promotion returned from its hiatus, first won by Corey Irons on 2 May 2001 with no opponent named, then taken from him by Johnny Eastland on a later Main Event broadcast; no further change survives.

titles.name: MECW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First won by the Misfits on the same broadcast where Johnny Eastland took the Hardcore title; the promotion's own report names neither their opponents nor the title's founding date, and no further change survives.

titles.name: MECW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Left vacant, first won by Corey Irons over the Iron Predator on 9 May 2001, then, once vacant again, won by Johnny Eastland over Jaguar by 7 June 2001; no further change survives.

titles.name: MECW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned for the first time in a tournament at MECW's debut pay-per-view, Hell Night, on 26 May 2001, when Corey Irons beat Johnny Eastland in the final; a rematch was promised for early June but no result survives.

titles.name: Memphis Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt that stands for 'respect, honor and pride'; its champions box says n/a and its concept page lists Joe Average and Ein on one line and C.D. Justice on the next, without saying what the lists mean.

titles.name: Memphis PRO Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top-tier title, 'the big prize'; its champions box says n/a and its concept page lists Chris Storm and Cleveland Paige on one line and Markus Tobin on the next, without saying what the lists mean.

titles.name: Memphis PRO Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag belt, 'gold plated straps'; its champions box says n/a and its concept page lists three teams (Justice and Nash; Laguna and Reno; Deacon and Abraham) without saying what the lists mean.

titles.name: MFF Heavy Weight Title
titles.epitaph: Midevil Spawn, already the reigning champion entering Clash of the Champions '99, retained the Heavy Weight Championship against Destroyer — a Robo Destroyer interference set up a Destroyer near-fall before Terrax speared and Tiger Bombed Destroyer, letting Spawn finish the match — the only documented moment in this title's own surviving lineage. Dead Pool's own served bio card separately counts one undated past Heavy Weight reign of his own, not structured here for lack of dates.

titles.name: MFF International Title
titles.epitaph: Black Bolt, the reigning champion, lost the International Championship to Weapon-X, a mystery special opponent, at Clash of the Champions '99 — the only title change in this belt's own surviving lineage. Dead Pool's own served bio card separately counts one undated past International reign of his own, not structured here for lack of dates.

titles.name: MFF Light Weight Title
titles.epitaph: Night Crawler, the reigning champion, lost the Light Weight Championship to Blizzard at Clash of the Champions '99, aided by a Cannonball run-in — the only title change in this belt's own surviving lineage.

titles.name: MFF World Title
titles.epitaph: Deathlok, the reigning champion, lost the World Championship to Spawn in a special-referee match at Clash of the Champions '99 that ended with the referee, GW Bridge, attacked after the pin — the only title change in this belt's own surviving lineage. Dead Pool's own served bio card separately counts four undated past World reigns of his own, not structured here for lack of dates.

titles.name: MLW Northern Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended with no rules in a baseball stadium's own equipment rooms.

titles.name: MLW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship, changing hands three times by screwjob or scaffold across its first seven months.

titles.name: MLW Canadian Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: A mid-card championship the promotion's own broadcasts named inconsistently across the year, but tracked as a single lineage here for want of any document splitting it in two.

titles.name: MLW Maple Leaf Championship
titles.epitaph: Unveiled by the promotion's executive vice president as the prize of the Maplemania 2 opener, and won there by Takisuma Ogama after red mist blinded his opponent.

titles.name: MLW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded from vacancy to the winner of a five-team hotel-bar brawl.

titles.name: MLW True North Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled from vacancy in a Royal Rumble and changed hands again inside a fortnight.

titles.name: MLW True North Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Taken from DT Richman and Ron Rivers by Ryan Winters and Nemo Chan-El, who kept it by disqualification at Maplemania 2.
titles.notes: Billed as the True North Tag Team titles on the promotion's 2001 broadcast; no document shows whether it continues the 1999 World Tag Team Championship or the 1999 True North Championship.

titles.name: MLW Iron Man
titles.epitaph: A singles belt won only via the annual Yukon Eric Memorial Cup tournament and held for one year, named in the fed's own rules document; no champion survives in this collection's holdings (the tournament itself is never attested as having been held).

titles.name: MLW Northern Heavyweight
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top singles belt, named in its own rules document; a third-party federation's own broadcast bills a wrestler as "Former MLW Northern Champion" (cited, not reproduced, per the canonical-copy rule) -- the held record's only reign attestation, unminted below.

titles.name: MLW Northern Tag Team
titles.epitaph: The fed's own only tag belt, named in its own rules document and coveted on-camera by the debuting Judgment Night; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: MLW Provincial
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary singles belt, named in its own rules document; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: MLWO HardCore Championship
titles.epitaph: A weapons-match title carried in the autumn of 1996 by Marcus Renge, who is later introduced as the fed's longest reigning HardCore champion, and by Justin B in January 1997.

titles.name: MLWO Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title decided in a tournament that Matt Harris won over Sean Torrington, then billed Sean Stevens. Harris defended it against Steve Spector in a dog collar chain cage match on Slam Supercard 2 on 26 April 1997, and a 1998 introduction calls him the former and only MLWO Lightweight Champion.

titles.name: MLWO Mini World Championship
titles.epitaph: A title for the fed's smaller wrestlers, which Jakito Martin kept against Mini-Dog on Battle Brawl II.

titles.name: MLWO North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's second singles title. Angel of Pain lost it to Jim Mongol on the Wednesday Washout of 6 November 1996. Jak Martin, Sean Torrington and Danny Ice followed; Steve Sampson won it from Ice at Ground Zero on 28 June 1997, and the runner-up of the Torture Cage at Torture Chamber 2 took it under the match's own stipulation. Steve Spector won it from Matt Harris at Winter Inferno 97, and Tommy Marauder, the Man From Heck and Kevin Legend held it in 1998.

titles.name: MLWO North American Tag Team Championship
aka: VPWF North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag team title that Da Ghetto Blasters lost to the Two Dudes With Attitude on the Wednesday Washout of 6 November 1996. ER, Michael Jeffries and Andrew Saunders, carried it in December 1996 and January 1997, and the fed's president announced in January 1997 that it would be unified with the world tag belts.

titles.name: MLWO Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A title created in January 1998 from the former PCW Northwestern belt, with its first champion, Matt Harris, crowned in a torture cage match on the Saturday Slam of 24 January 1998. Vince Valor says Harris handed it to him, and Kevin Legend was later billed as the final MLWO Television champion.

titles.name: MLWO Unified Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag title, billed as the World Tag Team Championship in 1996 and unified with the North American tag belts in 1997. The Mobb and Da Ghetto Blasters held it in the autumn of 1996 and the Rednecks and the Vegas Fighters in 1997; the Rednecks won it from the Vegas Fighters in a ladder match on May Madness: The Anniversary on 25 May 1997. The Good Knights defended it at Torture Chamber 2 on 26 October 1997 and lost it to the Rich and Infamous at Winter Inferno 97, whose retirement from the titles on the Saturday Slam of 28 March 1998 was a hoax. The Natural Born Annihilators, masked as Team LWC, won it in a three-way at May Madness 98 on 25 May 1998.

titles.name: MLWO United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's third singles title. Joe Patrinne carried it in November 1996 and kept it against Venom on the Wednesday Washout of 6 November; Deathwatch was introduced as champion at Deadly Games on 22 March 1997. Mister Robinson defended it against Marcus Renge at Ground Zero on 28 June 1997, and Paradox won it from Jason Knight in a Texas Death Match at Torture Chamber 2 on 26 October 1997. Victor Vance and then Bishop held it in early 1998.

titles.name: MLWO World Heavyweight Championship
aka: MLWO Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.epitaph: The fed's top singles title. It was billed as the VPWF World Heavyweight Championship in the autumn of 1996, when Mauler carried it and Guy LaChance won it and lost it back. Marcus Renge and Jak Martin held it before Steve Sampson pinned Martin at Deadly Games on 22 March 1997; Martin won it back in a steel cage on 26 April, the first man to hold it twice. Marcus Renge won the five-man Torture Cage of Torture Chamber 2 on 26 October 1997, and Mister Robinson took it from Martin in the ladder match of Winter Inferno 97. Captain Midnight held it after February 1998 until it was handed to Steve Spector and dropped, leaving it vacant; Midnight won it back in a ladder match at May Madness 98 on 25 May 1998.

titles.name: MPW Des Moines City Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in an eleven-man battle royale on the promotion's first broadcast, 5 July 2001, won by Stone Harris; Nick Hart dethroned him a week later in the main event of the second broadcast.

titles.name: MSW World Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Mid-South Wrestling territory, held once before it was left vacant in the surviving record.

titles.name: MSW World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Mid-South Wrestling territory, held twice before it was left vacant in the surviving record.

titles.name: MVW Empire State Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in early 2001 and won by Donovan Keltrane, who kept it through a non-title loss to Dick LeBaron weeks later.

titles.name: MVW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided by a pole-climb Capture the Flag hardcore brawl on the fed's own "Power Hour" pilot episode (21 May 1998), the first title established under that show's own name.

titles.name: MVW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated ahead of the promotion's 2001 return and settled by a sixteen-man, two-night tournament, The Ascension, that Owen Neo won by beating Rage in the final.

titles.name: MVW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Legacy" Paul Kiljoy in a 1998 unification match with a rival promotion's own Television title, and won by Snow from a champion and one other challenger in a 2001 three-way.

titles.name: MWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Kevin Frost as of the promotion's own 50th episode of Turmoil in June 2006, non-title against Scorpio; the record does not attest when or how he won it.

titles.name: X Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by NoMaD across the two April 2006 episodes served this pass, contested for by Scorpio; the record does not attest when or how the title changed hands before or after.

titles.name: MWC Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own sanctioned singles title; Terry "Shotgun" Storm held it into the fed's own early-July 1996 schedule, entering a submission-match defense against Magus whose outcome does not survive in the held record.

titles.name: MWE Havoc Championship
titles.notes: Named in the fed's own Adrenaline Rush results (board topic 7556801, "Havok Title Match"), in the pre-match roleplays for it (board topics 7553106 and 7554081) and across the roleplays of early 2009. The championship ledger, board topic 7550985, covers five other belts and not this one.
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-division belt the fed's own championship ledger never covered. It was decided in an Inferno match between JJ Executioner and Milenko at Adrenaline Rush on 28 December 2008, with Executioner promising in his own roleplay to be the first Havoc Champion. By the following January it was in Eric Derf's hands alongside the X-Television title, and Alex Bowen spent the spring of 2009 saying in public that he intended to reclaim a belt he refused to see laid to rest. No ledger of its reigns survives.

titles.name: MWE Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt whose whole recorded lineage runs across four months. Sonny Williams beat Vega Knight for it on 12 December 2008, on the final edition of Friday Night Genesis. Zak Warner took it from him on the 26 January 2009 Monday Night Mayhem, and Paige beat Warner for it at Highway to Hell on 29 March 2009. The ledger then listed it vacant, to be decided at Tribulation — and at Tribulation on 24 May 2009 it was: Sinc Mercier won a Scavenger Hunt match to unify it with the United States Championship under his own name, and this title's own reign ledger ends there. See the United States Championship's own epitaph for the unified lineage onward.

titles.name: MWE Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt MWE crowded most: its first recorded champions, Project Revolution, won it at Turmoil in a six-team match, and the pair who took it from them, Maxxamillion Mustafa and the Grand Mystique, won it the same way. Darius and Boyd beat the Hollywood Hooligans for it on the 24 November 2008 Genesis, lost it to Project Revolution on the 12 January 2009 Monday Night Mayhem — a match the fed booked as a unification with a separate World Tag Team Championship — and the belts passed to Tex-Mex that March and to the Black List Mafia at Highway to Hell on 29 March 2009. The fed billed them the Undisputed MWE Tag Team Championships from the unification onward. Black List Mafia never lost the belts in the ring: Leon Roberts vacated them himself on 22 June 2009 to chase the vacant United States Championship instead, and no further reign is held in the held record.

titles.name: MWE Undisputed Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own championship ledger (board topic 7550985, "Championship Histories") heads this lineage "MWE Undisputed Championship History" while its show scripts bill the same belt as the MWE World Heavyweight Championship, the MWE World Championship and the MWE Championship interchangeably; both billings are recorded rather than one resolved into the other. Between the November 2008 brand draft and the Adrenaline Rush II unification the fed staged a second, Genesis-exclusive world title, won by D.C. on the 12 December 2008 Genesis and absorbed into this one — the ledger records no separate reign history for it.
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top belt. David Whitman won it in a ten-man battle royal at Crowning Glory II on 10 August 2008 and lost it, reclaimed it and lost it again across the next four months, to Sonny Williams at Turmoil and to Brian Michaels on a December Monday Night Mayhem. At Adrenaline Rush II on 28 December 2008, in a Three Stages of Hell match at Madison Square Garden, D.C. beat Michaels to unify the MWE Championship and the World Championship into a single Undisputed Championship. Whitman took it back in a triple threat two weeks later and held it into the summer of 2009, billed at Tribulation that May the longest-reigning champion in MWE history — two apparent losses along the way, to Ace Cannon in March and to Joseph Sharpman in May, both controversial finishes the fed's own text and its own on-air ruling declined to recognize as title changes. His real, final loss came on 8 June 2009, to Sinc Mercier in a Triple Threat also involving Kevin Hardaway. Mercier held it at least into that August, retaining at Independence Day and, after an overturned double-DQ, at Crowning Glory.

titles.name: MWE United States Championship
titles.epitaph: MWE's secondary singles belt, and the one its ledger records changing hands most often. Sinc Mercier beat James Sullivan for it at MWE Turmoil on 14 September 2008. Alejandro Rodriguez took it from him at Wrestle Wars II that October in a three-way with Mason Resoan and was stripped of it once the fed reviewed the tape of the finish. Mercier won it back that November, lost it to Resoan at Adrenaline Rush II and beat him for it again at Friday Night Overdrive on 13 February 2009 in a Ladder Match. The ledger then recorded it vacant, to be decided at Tribulation; the belt was still being defended in Shattered Glass and Iron Man Table matches through the year, Mason Resoan and Leon Roberts fighting for the vacant title at Independence Day that July. At Tribulation on 24 May 2009, Sinc Mercier won a Scavenger Hunt match to unify this belt with the Intercontinental Championship under his own name — his fourth US title, his first IC title, both at once.

titles.name: MWE Women's Championship
titles.notes: Named in the fed's own Crowning Glory II Hall of Fame segment (board topic 574107), its Tribulation 2009 induction segment (board topic 7631072) and Paige's own roster card (board topic 7550706). The championship ledger, board topic 7550985, does not cover it.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own women's belt, remembered on screen rather than recorded in its ledger. Katherine Tenaud was its first champion, named as such in the Hall of Fame ceremony that opened MWE's relaunch in August 2008 and again at Tribulation the following May, where the fed called her the only woman in its history to win a title that was not this one. Paige is billed a former holder on her own roster card. No ledger of its reigns survives.

titles.name: X-Television Championship
titles.epitaph: MWE's own junior-division belt, and the only one in its ledger to pass through a mask. Aeron Beowulf beat J.K. Valentino for it at Crowning Glory II on 10 August 2008; Vega Knight took it that October and was stripped of it on being drafted to Genesis. A tournament final at Adrenaline Rush II settled it as a Mask vs Career match between the masked Mysterious G and Samuel Steele, and the winner pulled his own mask off afterwards to reveal Eric Derf. Anderson surrendered the belt on air that May rather than defend it, and the fed's own text records no result for the "NEW, and PROPER Champion" match Dick Malibu promised in its place. The belt was still being defended at the October 2009 Turmoil.

titles.name: MWWA Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Announced in the fed's own founding FAQ and put up for grabs in a sixteen-man single-elimination tournament whose format DDT unveiled on 20 August 1997, running toward the promotion's own first Supercard, Windy City Showdown, 20 September 1997; no reign is recorded within this collection's own held record, which ends before the bracket completes.

titles.name: MWWA Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Announced in the fed's own founding FAQ; the community's own on-air commentary names Team Canada, the Ministry of Justice and Heavy Metal as contenders. No reign or tournament format is recorded within this collection's own held record.

titles.name: MWWA Television Title
titles.epitaph: Announced in the fed's own founding FAQ; the four Title Tournament entrants eliminated short of the semifinal are diverted into a separate four-man tournament for this belt. No reign is recorded within this collection's own held record.

titles.name: NAAW American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary title, contested weekly.

titles.name: NAAW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship, defended at every supercard and roughly every three to four weeks otherwise.

titles.name: NAAW Lightheavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's weight-limited title, its lineage disputed on-air by two rival challengers in mid-1999.

titles.name: NACW Light Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.epitaph: A title that changed hands four times across the promotion's own surviving record, once inside two minutes and once handed over outright before a match could begin.

titles.name: NACW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag title decided in a four-way match at the promotion's own debut pay-per-view and contested by shifting duos through its own surviving record.

titles.name: NACW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's midcard singles title, which changed hands four times across its own surviving record, once by a forfeit after a champion's real-world arrest.

titles.name: NACW Toughman Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-styled title defended on a burning scaffold at the promotion's own second World Tour pay-per-view, its own record ending with the belt itself stolen from the winner.

titles.name: NACW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: A frequently-contested singles title that changed hands three times in five months, ending its own surviving record around the waist of a rising young star.

titles.name: NACW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top singles title, changing hands three times across its own surviving 1999 record, twice by pinfall and once by an interference-marred Royal Rumble.

titles.name: NAPW Canadian Heritage Championship
titles.notes: A "NAPW Heritage Championship" is also named once in the classic-era served corpus (Stone Zellor, Anniversary Assault II, 31 Oct 2007); whether it shares a lineage with this belt is unresolved.
titles.epitaph: The revived era's own third championship, restarted vacant in a May 2014 five-way melee that Sammy Devine won. Changed hands between Devine and Bruiser Breton twice across the Phenomenons' own touring season, then again to a name the fed's own title-history ledger never recorded a transition for — the ledger's own last word (28 Dec 2014, Devine) and the 2014 Year End Awards' own later snapshot (Feb 2015, Prince Wadjethotep) simply disagree, a gap in the surviving record, not a resolved handoff.

titles.name: NAPW Extreme Jobber Championship
titles.epitaph: NAPW's own joke belt played straight — an Extreme Jobber Championship whose first holder, "Bad Boy" Joey Malone, is credited by his own bio card, which also records him losing the honor to Nightmare.

titles.name: NAPW Provincial Championship
titles.epitaph: NAPW's own second singles title, crowned the same debut night as the World Championship — Ravager beat "The Moose" Mark Millar for it, 31 Oct 2005 — and changed hands repeatedly through the classic era's own first two years.

titles.name: NAPW Pure Honor Championship
titles.epitaph: A classic-era NAPW belt contested on technical-wrestling terms — its own roster bios name holders and contenders, though no dated lineage survives in the recovered record.

titles.name: NAPW Television Championship
titles.notes: Reigns here are a partial reconstruction from title-change callouts across the served show corpus, not a single ledger.
titles.epitaph: A classic-era-only mid-card title (2005-2010), never revived after the 2010 closure as far as the surviving record shows. "Dirty" Don Travelli held it across at least two separate reigns per the served corpus, trading it with Lobo; the fed's own Sept 2010 rankings sidebar confirms Chris Casino as champion at the classic era's own close, though the hand-off from Travelli's own last confirmed reign (Apr 2006) isn't in the held corpus — years of real, unreconstructed gap.

titles.name: NAPW World Championship
titles.epitaph: NAPW's own top title from its first night on — The Plague won it in a match at the very debut show, 31 Oct 2005 — through a densely-chained run of classic-era champions (Patrick Bickle, "Perfection" Evan Cartwright, and two Ravager reigns, the second a ten-defense run ended by Donovan Astros on a date the fed's own broadcast called live, 31 Jul 2007) into an overseas ECFW/REBEL tour and a three-plus-year Astros reign confirmed still standing by the fed's own Sept 2010 rankings, the classic era's own last word. Into the promotion's 2010 closure and 2013 revival, the title restarted vacant and ran through five more champions — Anton Petrov, Clancy King, Abbey Graves, Jay Deschain, and Declan Black, the revived era's own last-recorded champion — a chain the fed's own title-history ledger keeps complete from Nov 2013 on. One real, named gap remains in the classic-era chain: exactly when and to whom Ravager first lost the title, sometime between his Feb 2006 win and Bickle's Oct 2006 win, isn't in the held record.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The revived era's own tag belt, carrying a four-month reign by the touring outside act the Phenomenons — a four-way at Tagstravaganza to Flavour Explosion — before Those That Would Inflict Ill took it over and were still champions as of the January 2015 roster snapshot the record ends on.

titles.name: National Championship
titles.epitaph: A vacant title contested on Crush!'s own first show (1 November 2007); Mr.X.Division won it over Ricardo_619 with a reversal into a Stunner.

titles.name: STW National Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands six times before its own last champion was stripped for holding two World Heavyweight titles at once, the belt then unifying with the vacant International title.

titles.name: N.A.W. Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Jeff "The Machine" Keenan's belt until a chair shot from Bill Bob Woijicowski put it on Mad Goat instead.

titles.name: N.A.W. East Coast Championship
titles.epitaph: "Human Torture Rack" Ian Walsh's own regional belt until Dennis Windham took it from him with a low blow and the Texas Death Drop.

titles.name: N.A.W. Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Bladeliners' own prize, successfully defended against the Widow Makers on Tuesday Night Tango.
titles.notes: A separately billed tag title from the later Tuesday Night Tango era, distinct in this record from the earlier World Tag Team Championship; no document ties the two lineages together.

titles.name: N.A.W. World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Deathwish's own belt, taken from him by a debuting "Mr. Muscle" Jim Vickens the night his own ally Jade "The Blade" turned on him at ringside.

titles.name: N.A.W. World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice inside eight days in the spring of 1998, landing on the Midnight Strikers by way of a folding chair.

titles.name: NAW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: New Age Wrestling built its first month around a belt it never got to award. A battle royal on the opening Anarchy made Cereal the number one contender; the two-out-of-three-falls match against TraV that followed a week later is the last thing on the only copy of that show that survives, and it stops mid-fall. Five days later the fed’s own title histories page still read Vacant, and the card for the following Saturday billed a match for the number one contendership all over again.
titles.notes: Named on the fed’s own title histories page of 8 April 2003 as vacant; the surviving copy of the 3 April Anarchy breaks off during the match that was to fill it.

titles.name: NAW Pacific Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Pacific Lightweight Championship was billed for the fed’s second Anarchy — Destiny against Krissi in a Cat Fight in a Cell — and the match never happened: Destiny couldn’t reach Detroit and Krissi was attacked backstage before the bell. It stood vacant on the fed’s own title histories page five days later. Nothing else about it survives.

titles.name: NAW Rising Star Championship
titles.epitaph: The Rising Star Championship was the first belt New Age Wrestling actually awarded. Mystic J — billed at seven feet ten and 410 pounds, with a finisher called The 747 — beat Weaponary for it on 3 April 2003 and walked out to a backstage interview with the belt over his shoulder, the fed’s own ring announcer handing it to him in the ring first.

titles.name: NAW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Hitmen — Renegade and Nightmare — are the only Tag Team Champions New Age Wrestling ever names. They were billed as champions defending against Lightning and Satan’s Wrath on 3 April 2003, and the surviving copy of that show carries the announcement of the match and no result for it.

titles.name: NAW Xtreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The Redeemer became the first Xtreme Champion on 3 April 2003, a half-inch away from losing it to Xtra Ordinary by the commentary team’s own account. The card the fed posted for 12 April billed a rematch against Phil, and there the record stops — no results page for that date survives, and the card’s own stipulation labels don’t resolve cleanly enough to say under what rules.

titles.name: NAWA European Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four singles titles named in the wing's own March 1998 recruitment ad; no reign or holder survives in this pass's own holdings.
titles.notes: Named, not structured with a reign, in the fed's own recruitment post (4 March 1998).

titles.name: NAWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four singles titles named in the wing's own March 1998 recruitment ad; no reign or holder survives in this pass's own holdings.
titles.notes: Named, not structured with a reign, in the fed's own recruitment post (4 March 1998).

titles.name: NAWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four singles titles named in the wing's own March 1998 recruitment ad; no reign or holder survives in this pass's own holdings.
titles.notes: Named, not structured with a reign, in the fed's own recruitment post (4 March 1998).

titles.name: NAWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The wing's top singles title, one of four named in its own March 1998 recruitment ad; no reign or holder survives in this pass's own holdings.
titles.notes: Named, not structured with a reign, in the fed's own recruitment post (4 March 1998).

titles.name: NAWC J.R. Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant as of 14 March 1997, per the fed's own tournament-bracket document; no result survives.

titles.name: NAWC North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant as of 14 March 1997, per the fed's own tournament-bracket document; no result survives.
