titles.name: NAWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tournament for the vacant title began 14 March 1997; no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: NAWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant as of 14 March 1997, per the fed's own tournament-bracket document; no result survives.

titles.name: NAWC World Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned via a 31-man tournament beginning 9-10 March 1997; Rick Steiner holds the title by 14 March, the fed's own record end.

titles.name: NAWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Newly crowned by forfeit ahead of March Madness, won by Chaos.

titles.name: NAWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated ahead of March Madness and reclaimed there by a former holder, "Chicken Hawking" Hustler.

titles.name: NAWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended successfully by Lasher and Mystikal against Overpower and Marcus Millenium at March Madness.

titles.name: NAWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Tony Morris, who went on to win the Best of the Best battle royal at March Madness.

titles.name: NAWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Skye Daniels through the fed's sole surviving pay-per-view.

titles.name: NAWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize, held by Lasher through its sole surviving pay-per-view.

titles.name: NaWF/AeWF Dangerzone Championship
titles.epitaph: First contested in a twenty-man battle royal on 21 September 1998 that ended with no champion crowned after a masked faction attacked the final two entrants.

titles.name: NaWF/AeWF North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First contested in a four-team elimination match on 2 October 1998, won by the Mongolian Assassins.

titles.name: Blitzkrieg Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title of the hardcore style, held by Judasbleek (2013 and 2014), Benjamin Jones, Eric Yulan, Brock Newbludd, Jake Tockwell, Ohiyama, Chris Smith, VIP, Big Rick Strongbern and Jonny Bedlam.

titles.name: Dynasty Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag titles, whose first holders in the held posts are the Dynasty Cup's champions of 2013; later holders include Sons of Evolution, A-List, Clan Strongbern and The House.

titles.name: Infamy Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title held by Techno Dragon, Son of Malta, Benjamin Jones and Eric Yulan in the held posts.

titles.name: Keystone Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title, defended on SLAM and at the pay-per-views and 'open challenged' by its holders; its holders include Derecho (2013), Judasbleek (2014), Ali Amore (2016 and 2017), Max Hopper (2017), Alex Reyn (2018 and 2019), Rey de los Diamantes (2019) and Jake Tockwell (2019).

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top singles title, held in the held posts by Vic Gravender, Saphire, Chris Moliano, Derecho, Warren Spade, Jake Tockwell, Brock Newbludd, Pat Gordon Jr and Jonny Bedlam.

titles.name: NCCW International Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary heavyweight title, defended more often than the World Titles: "GQ" Geoffrey Quartz won it at the fed's own first dated show, and Purple Pride is its own last recorded champion, winning it eight days before the fed's own record breaks off.

titles.name: NCCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: NCCW's mid-card belt, defended most weeks on the fed's own Saturday Matinee per its 1998 recruitment ad, changing hands eight times (two by forced vacancy) before "Strictly Business" Lew Spectre won it, defended it once on pay-per-view, and held it for over eighteen months without a single loss, forfeiting it only when the promotion folded around him.

titles.name: NCCW World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Limited to wrestlers under 230 pounds and rated by the fed's own FAQ a close second to the World Title: changed hands eight times in fifteen months, twice by forced vacancy (an injury, a departure) and the rest inside the ring, with Superstar's own three separate reigns the title's own throughline.

titles.name: NCCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: NCCW's top title from the fed's own 1998 opening bell: "Dominator" Don Cameron became its first-ever World Heavyweight Champion and held it twice more inside the fed's own first year, the belt passing through six further champions across the fed's own dated record before Cameron reclaimed it a final time, undated, and spent the fed's final stretch defending it against a mounting challenge from Lew Spectre.

titles.name: NCCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands nine times across the fed's own opening fifteen months, including one team discarding the belts on the same night they won them and a masked team's own mid-reign unmasking, before Coast-to-Coast Connection's second reign closes the fed's own dated record.

titles.name: NCCW Southern Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: Won and lost twice across the promotion's own five-week run: the Crippler took it in the vacant first-card main event and lost it to Bobby "Bad Apple" Durango at the fed's first pay-per-view, and Durango was still champion when he folded it into the promotion's first double title two cards later.

titles.name: NCCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, where "Cajun" Huey Armstrong became its first champion; Bobby "Bad Apple" Durango won it from him ten days later in a winner-take-all match that also carried the Southern Heritage belt, becoming the fed's first double champion. A fellow Usenet participant's own later signature line names a different wrestler as the reigning, undefeated champion at the promotion's own fold, a claim no card in this record corroborates.

titles.name: NCCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, where "The Natural Wonder" Max Maxwell won a tournament final over the Mad Goat to become the fed's first-ever World Heavyweight Champion, successfully defending it against "Lucky" Lambert at the next and last card this record holds. A fellow Usenet participant's own signature line, five weeks later, names Bobby "Bad Apple" Durango as champion instead; no card documenting how the title changed hands survives.

titles.name: NCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced on air 18 March 1997 alongside three sister belts, left vacant until the fed's own inaugural supercard crowned "The King of Desire" Ray Kinge -- the wrestler this fed also carried to #105 in the 1997 RSPWF Top 200.
titles.notes: 1 September 1997), a card not held in the held record. Not structured here; see the digest for the fuller chain.

titles.name: NCW World Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's own four inaugural titles, open to the whole roster regardless of division or sex; "Violent" Victor Frost won it first, at the fed's own inaugural supercard.
titles.notes: The lineage continues past this pass's own served record, including a disputed second claimant later in 1997; not structured here -- see the accession digest (workshop record).

titles.name: NCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced on air 18 March 1997; won by Bad Company at the fed's own first supercard, in a match its beaten opponents ended by handing the belts over themselves.
titles.notes: The lineage continues past this pass's own served record; not structured here -- see the accession digest (workshop record).

titles.name: NCW World Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced on air 18 March 1997, the only one of the fed's four inaugural belts closed to men; left vacant until Lupa won it at the fed's own first supercard.
titles.notes: The lineage continues past this pass's own served record, including a champion's-own-choosing Gauntlet storyline that fall; not structured here -- see the accession digest (workshop record).

titles.name: NCWA National Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's own five title lineages; this collection's holdings do not yet trace its reign-by-reign lineage.
titles.notes: Reign ledger not reconstructed.

titles.name: NCWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's own five title lineages, defended on the Spring Slamfest 97 supercard; this collection's holdings do not yet trace its reign-by-reign lineage.
titles.notes: Reign ledger not reconstructed.

titles.name: NCWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own most active belt, changing hands twice in three days per the source wave's own reading of the cards; this collection's holdings do not yet trace its reign-by-reign lineage.
titles.notes: Reign ledger not reconstructed.

titles.name: NCWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the fed's own five title lineages; this collection's holdings do not yet trace its reign-by-reign lineage.
titles.notes: Reign ledger not reconstructed.

titles.name: NCWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, defended on its Spring Slamfest 97 supercard alongside four others; this collection's holdings do not yet trace its reign-by-reign lineage.
titles.notes: Reign ledger not reconstructed; see the wing's own tier_source.

titles.name: NECW World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's weight-limited title.

titles.name: NECW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship, its lineage disputed on-air by a rival claimant in early 1999.

titles.name: NEFW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The NEFW's cruiserweight championship. Raptor held it across February 2002, turning back Rasco Raines by count-out and Speedy Irons by pinfall.

titles.name: NEFW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The NEFW's hardcore championship. Christian Cable held it into late February 2002 and beat Vigilante to keep it.

titles.name: NEFW New England State Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional NEFW singles championship. Butcher Ben held it into a Boiler Room match against Scourge at Body Count and kept it, both men carried from the arena.

titles.name: NEFW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The NEFW's second singles championship. Corona turned back Chris Rogers and Inferno in February 2002 before losing the belt to Scourge on the Sanitarium of that month; Scourge held it past the Senator three days later.

titles.name: NEFW Rage Championship
titles.epitaph: A new NEFW championship geared toward the cruiserweight division, announced in the federation's own September handbook. Its first match was set for Day of the Dead, Ripper and Xara against the Goth and a tag partner chosen by lottery, the winning team then facing off for the belt.

titles.name: NEFW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The NEFW's tag team championship. The New Broncos, London Tower and Lightning Kid, held it through February 2002, beating Joey Steroidz and a masked partner and keeping it on a disqualification against the Senator and Hannibal.

titles.name: NEFW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended on every televised programme. Senton kept it on a forfeit in February 2002 and lost it inside a steel cage to White Lightning Chris Rogers on the Sanitarium of that month; Rogers kept it on a double count-out against Rude Dude.

titles.name: NEFW Unified Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: An old NEFW championship restored to active competition. Tommy McKnight beat the reigning Butcher Ben in a two-out-of-three-falls match to take the belt on the federation's last card before scaling back its operation, and kept it against the Crimson Christian on Impact two and a half weeks later.

titles.name: NEFW Title
titles.epitaph: NEFW's top championship. Tommy McKnight took it from Blade on the February 2002 Nemesis, drew with him at State of Shock, and lost it back to Blade six days later, Blade's fourth reign by the broadcast's own count. Senton held it by the Body Count pay-per-view of June, keeping it against his own brother Corona. The federation's own September handbook renamed the belt the NEFW Title, calling it representative of the Champion of the Federation rather than a claim to world status, and that October's tournament for it ran through a Doctor Melancholy-Hannibal final the served cards do not carry the result of.

titles.name: NEHW Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Northeast Hardcore Wrestling territory, attested for 6 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: NEHW Tag Team Titles

titles.name: NEO Alberta Television Championship
titles.notes: The promotion's own television title, long vacant before a royal rumble filled it at the Crimson Glory supercard in 2002; defended on every broadcast thereafter by its own rule.
titles.epitaph: New Era Old School Wrestling's television title, defended on every episode of "The Show" by the promotion's own rule. It had been vacant for some time when a royal rumble at Crimson Glory crowned "Vicious" Vic Valiant in 2002; Valiant retained it against Red Dragon on 23 August and drew with Jayson Graham on 8 September, and Kristoff St. Livingstone took it from him on 24 October, still champion when the record ends.

titles.name: NEO Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: The promotion's own top title, first awarded at its December 2000 year-end supercard (already served).
titles.epitaph: New Era Old School Wrestling's top title. Steve Dumars won it at the promotion's year-end supercard in December 2000, retained it against Matthew Reason at Snowed In on 18 February 2001 and again at Storm Warning on 7 May 2001, and was still champion in the promotion's report of 26 June 2001.

titles.name: NEO Pacific Championship
titles.notes: The promotion's own second-tier title, crowned by a four-man tournament that ran across this record's own January-February 2001 shows.
titles.epitaph: New Era Old School Wrestling's second-tier title, created through a four-man tournament across its January and February 2001 shows. Amuro Balsa won that tournament on 18 February 2001; Messiah held the title by 11 April; Matt Saunders beat Messiah at Storm Warning on 7 May 2001 and was still champion on 26 June.

titles.name: NEO Skyweight Championship
titles.notes: The promotion's own weight-restricted (under 215 lbs) title; already held when this record's own January 2001 preshow opens.
titles.epitaph: New Era Old School Wrestling's title for wrestlers under 215 pounds. Sushi Tsunami held it when the promotion's January 2001 preshow opened, and Psicopa won it from Sushi Tsunami in a ladder match at Storm Warning on 7 May 2001, still champion on 26 June.

titles.name: NEO Rocky Mountain Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The promotion's own tag title, first awarded in a four-way elimination match at Storm Warning, 7 May 2001.
titles.epitaph: New Era Old School Wrestling's Rocky Mountain Tag Team Championship, first awarded to Monkey You in a four-way elimination match at Storm Warning on 7 May 2001. The new champions were attacked after the match by the Forces of Chaos and were still champions on 26 June 2001.

titles.name: J1 Rikidozan/NJPW Unified Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship, which changed hands in the main event of a two-night tag league supercard.

titles.name: J1 Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles championship, reclaimed in an American title match and honored with a ring ceremony back home.

titles.name: New ERA PRODIGY Classic Xtreme Championship
titles.notes: First seen contested at a tournament final on the federation's own International Intrigue pay-per-view (9 June 2005, Chaos vs. Dallas Carter), with no result recorded. Jason Payne is billed champion on two 2009 cards, the Almost Live special (26 June) and Unplugged (18 July); nothing in the held record's text connects his reign back to the 2005 tournament. The title is vacated and recontested in a new single-night tournament on the federation's own Destrucity II card (23 January 2010, John Doe, Ashe Corvin, Trevor Cane and Chaos), again with no result recorded; recorded as an honest gap rather than a guessed chain throughout.
titles.epitaph: A cross-promotional hardcore title, crowned and re-crowned across the federation's own run in tournaments whose own outcomes this corpus never directly records.

titles.name: New ERA of Wrestling Television Championship
titles.notes: MWG is billed champion by the federation's own 17 September 2005 RAPTURE card, defending against Mr. Entertainment; the immediately preceding International Intrigue pay-per-view (9 June 2005) put him against the title's own prior #1 contender, Jason Payne, with no titleholder marked on either man, suggesting the title changed hands at that show, though no results document confirms it directly. A later champion, Cameron Cruise, is billed against Erik Black on the federation's own Destrucity II card (23 January 2010), more than four years later, with nothing in the held record's text bridging the two reigns; recorded as an honest gap rather than a guessed chain.
titles.epitaph: New ERA of Wrestling's second-tier singles title, contested across the federation's whole run from an ambiguous 2005 change through a merger-era reign four years later, with no results document ever confirming a change of hands directly.

titles.name: New ERA of Wrestling Women's Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The one championship of New ERA of Wrestling's women's division, won by Karla Starr at the first BattleBRAWL in December 2004 and held by her for two years until Juliet Marceau announced it over on RAUCOUS of 19 December 2006 and Starr took off its faceplate to reveal the VENUS World Heavyweight Championship underneath.

titles.name: New ERA of Wrestling World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Jean Rabesque was billed champion by January 2005; the Phantom Republican's own reign, begun around 12 January 2006, is now structured (see reigns) and independently corroborated by an 18 April 2006 cross-federation posting naming him champion and Jean Rabesque his immediate predecessor. A co-championship split with Rocko Daymon by mid-2009 after a merger with WFW is attested only by billing on cards served elsewhere in the held record. New ERA's own rules document, dated 15 January 2011 in its own text, states that when the federation switched to a season-based format its reigning World Heavyweight Champion "became" the first champion of a renamed New ERA Championship -- the same title continuing under a new name, not a new belt -- and eliminated the Television and PRODIGY Classic Xtreme Championships, folding their own champions into the new title's bankable-shot system. The corpus does not capture who held the belt at that exact transition, though its own next captured card already bills a champion (see reigns r004) who names, in his own promo, the rival he took the belt from. The title changed hands at least three more times across 2011 (see reigns r004-r007), with a final open challenge left unresolved when the held record's last captured card ends without a results document.
titles.epitaph: New ERA of Wrestling's own top championship, first crowned in a Fatal Fourway Battle Royal at the federation's founding show, carried through a 2009 merger and unification with a second promotion's own world title, and renamed the New ERA Championship when the federation switched to a season-based format in 2011 -- the held record's last captured card, in 2015, still finds it standing at the center of an unresolved open challenge.

titles.name: New ERA of Wrestling World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Attested only by a single card's own billing (WFW:NE's Destrucity II, 23 January 2010): Cameron Cruise and Problem Child are named champions, defending against Jack n' Hoff. No earlier title history or results document survives in this corpus's own read slice.
titles.epitaph: New ERA of Wrestling's tag title, attested only once in the held record, at a 2010 pay-per-view defense by Cameron Cruise and Problem Child.

titles.name: N.E.W. Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top prize of New Extreme Wrestling, won in a Four Way Dance at Friday Night Slam Dance after the reigning champion suffered a knee injury mid-match.

titles.name: N.E.W. Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a Crucifix Match at King of the Mat 2, the loser tied to a crucifix suspended above the ring.

titles.name: N.E.W. North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended at King of the Mat 2 in a match twice interrupted before a masked ally settled it.

titles.name: N.E.W. Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by newcomers the Crash Test Dummies in a tournament final at King of the Mat 2, over two members of a top singles stable.

titles.name: ECW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's ECW Heavyweight Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 6 reigns, from The Sandman's (December 1995) to Justin Credible's (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Justin Credible as champion.

titles.name: ECW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's ECW Tag Team Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 5 reigns, from Mikey Whipwreck & Cactus Jack's (December 1995) to The Brood (The Fallen Angel & The Vampire Warrior)'s (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves The Brood (The Fallen Angel & The Vampire Warrior) as champion.

titles.name: ECW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's ECW Television Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 7 reigns, from Mikey Whipwreck's (December 1995) to Shane Douglas's (January 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Shane Douglas as champion.

titles.name: WCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's WCW Cruiserweight Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 2 reigns, from Jeff Hardy's (December 1997) to Hayabusa's (January 1998); created by a tournament whose final is at Starrcade in December 1997. The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Hayabusa as champion.

titles.name: WCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's WCW Heavyweight Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 7 reigns, from Randy Savage's (November 1995) to Shawn Michaels's (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Shawn Michaels as champion.

titles.name: WCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's WCW Tag Team Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 8 reigns, from Lord Steven Regal & Squire David Taylor's (June 1996) to The Forgotten (Bam Bam Bigelow & Big Van Vader)'s (January 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves The Forgotten (Bam Bam Bigelow & Big Van Vader) as champion.

titles.name: WCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's WCW Television Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 9 reigns, from One Man Gang's (November 1996) to Chris Benoit's (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Chris Benoit as champion.

titles.name: WCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's WCW United States Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 6 reigns, from Kensuke Sasaki's (November 1995) to Bill Goldberg's (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Bill Goldberg as champion.

titles.name: World Wrestling Federation Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's World Wrestling Federation Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 8 reigns, from Diesel's (November 1994) to Steve Austin's (March 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Steve Austin as champion.

titles.name: World Wrestling Federation European Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's World Wrestling Federation European Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 7 reigns, from The British Bulldog's (March 1997) to Booker T's (February 1998). The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Booker T as champion.

titles.name: World Wrestling Federation Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's World Wrestling Federation Intercontinental Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 11 reigns, from Goldust's (February 1996) to Dean Malenko's (March 1998). Before them the list names Razor Ramon's reign, his fourth by its count, without a date; the diary's first shows have him as champion until Goldust wins the belt in February 1996. The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Dean Malenko as champion.

titles.name: World Wrestling Federation Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's World Wrestling Federation Light Heavyweight Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 8 reigns, from Scorpio's (January 1996) to Chris Jericho's (August 1997); created in January 1996 and retired at SummerSlam in August 1997 (the diary's own list ends it "Championship Retired").

titles.name: World Wrestling Federation Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The diary's World Wrestling Federation Tag Team Championship: its own title history in the diary's posts dates 13 reigns, from Owen Hart & The British Bulldog's (January 1996) to Al Snow & Chris Candido's (March 1998). Before them the list names The Smoking Gunn's reign, their second by its count, without a date; they lose the belts at the Royal Rumble of January 1996. The last post, in March 1998 on the diary's calendar, leaves Al Snow & Chris Candido as champion.

titles.name: NeWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by the Weasel from Thor "a while back," per the federation's own first weekly report, and defended against Katana the same week the report went out -- Thor's own vignette that week renewed the challenge, calling the Weasel out by name for a rematch the surviving record never shows happening.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own first weekly report, 27 September 1991 (promotions/newa-1992/archive/newa-first-week-results-1991-09-27.html).

titles.name: NeWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Passed from the Vikings to the Holy Rollers to the Imperial Storm (Bushi and Samurai), by the federation's own account, with the Imperial Storm turning back the Fists of Death in the first week's own results.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own first weekly report, 27 September 1991 (promotions/newa-1992/archive/newa-first-week-results-1991-09-27.html). The two accounts are not reconciled in the surviving record; "Kamakaze" is left unminted rather than guessed onto the chain.

titles.name: NeWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Sumo, the master-of-merchandising gimmick behind the federation's own Little Sumo doll and cartoon tie-in, who turned back Kawasaki Godzilla in a title defense during the first week's own card -- Nerdmaster, Kataklysma, Wakizashi, Thor and Wilbur were the week's own ranked contenders.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own first weekly report, 27 September 1991 (promotions/newa-1992/archive/newa-first-week-results-1991-09-27.html).

titles.name: NeWA World Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Odin when the federation's own first weekly report went out, and never shown changing hands again in the surviving record -- the self-declared "only true champion of the world" turned back a challenge from Intruder in the same week's own card, with Tub O'Lard, Randy "The Count" Lawler, Bushi, Lord Roderick and Sledge the Carpender named as the week's own ranked contenders.
titles.notes: Transcribed from the federation's own first weekly report, 27 September 1991 (promotions/newa-1992/archive/newa-first-week-results-1991-09-27.html).

titles.name: NeWA North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Source: the hub's own title-history page. Unlike this hub's own flagship World Heavyweight title (held under the wccw wing), this title's own document claims no real-world ancestor lineage -- its first reign (Roddy Piper, 8 Mar 1998) is billed on the page's own terms as "the first board recognized champion." A 1999 unification (footnote on this title's own page) folds two other retired titles -- United States Heavyweight and Canadian Heavyweight, both also named as retired on the hub's own "Roll Call of Champions" -- into this one via Adam Fierce's win. Eight reigns are structured, the record ending mid-chain (Agent Mandell, still champion per the hub's own latest-held document, the Rankings page dated 4 March 2000).
titles.epitaph: A hub-wide championship of the National eWrestling Alliance, contested by wrestlers drawn from its member territories from March 1998 onward and, per the title's own account, absorbing two retired regional heavyweight lineages (United States and Canadian) into itself in 1999. Eight reigns survive in this collection's own record, Roddy Piper through Agent Mandell, the last still champion as of the hub's own latest surviving document.

titles.name: NeWA World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.notes: Source: the hub's own title-history page. No claimed real-world lineage.
titles.epitaph: A hub-wide cruiserweight championship of the National eWrestling Alliance, defended continuously from January 1999. Twelve reigns survive in this collection's own record, changing hands rapidly through late 1999; the last (El Scorcho, from February 2000) carries an unresolved later complication in the hub's own record rather than a clean end.

titles.name: NeWA World Hardcore Championship
titles.notes: Source: the hub's own title-history page. No claimed real-world lineage. Six reigns are structured; unlike the hub's other four non-flagship titles, no later hub document (the Championship Calendar or the Rankings page) mentions this title again after the title-history page's own last word, so the record ends cleanly with its last attested champion.
titles.epitaph: A hub-wide hardcore championship of the National eWrestling Alliance, defended from February 1999. Six reigns survive in this collection's own record; the last, Frag Sinister from October 1999, is this title's own final attested champion -- also the hub's own "Roll Call of Champions" naming him current as of November 1999, with no later document naming a successor.

titles.name: NWA/NeWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Source: the hub's own title-history page. The page's own table opens with a claimed real-world lineage borrowed from the real NWA/WCW World Tag Team Championship (Terry Gordy & Steve Williams, 12 Jul 1992, through Pat Anderson & C.W. Anderson, 14 Sep 1996-"1997," vacated "due to inactivity") -- consistent with this hub's own convention, seen on the flagship World Heavyweight title (held under the wccw wing), of claiming a real historical lineage before diverging into the fed's own invented continuity. That claimed real lineage is described here, not structured reign-by-reign; only the fed's own post-divergence reigns (Fear & Adam Riggs, 24 Mar 1998, onward) are structured in reigns.json, the same discipline the wccw wing's own flagship title applies. Eleven reigns are structured, the record ending mid-chain (a fourth reign for "The Crazy Ones," attested only by the hub's own Rankings page, 4 March 2000 -- not itself numbered by the title's own page, whose own table ends at a third, bracketed reign).
titles.epitaph: A hub-wide tag-team championship of the National eWrestling Alliance, claiming descent from the real NWA/WCW World Tag Team Championship before diverging into the alliance's own invented continuity from March 1998. Eleven reigns of that continuity survive in this collection's own record -- "The Crazy Ones" the title's single most frequent titleholder, across four separate reigns -- the last still held as of the hub's own latest surviving document.

titles.name: NWA/NeWA World Television Title
titles.notes: Source: the hub's own title-history page. No claimed real-world lineage; the page's own footnote numbering continues directly from the World Heavyweight and World Tag Team pages' own footnotes, confirming the three documents were maintained as one continuous site.
titles.epitaph: A hub-wide television championship of the National eWrestling Alliance, defended continuously from April 1998. Nineteen reigns survive in this collection's own record, several lasting only days; the last (Harbeneth Rookens, from February 2000) carries an unresolved later complication in the hub's own record rather than a clean end.

titles.name: NeWA Mid-Atlantic Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Three reigns survive, none from the fed's own Title History page alone: Mac Michaels was already champion by 17 January 1999, when Lycos took the title from him by pinfall with a foreign object (a "slap jack"); the fed's own News page (27 January 1999) still bills Lycos as reigning "Mid-Atlantic Champion," submitted for a unification match at the NeWA PPV Lord of the Rings; no document says how or when that reign ended.

titles.name: Mid-Atlantic Light-Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Ryan Carling won this title vacant in a Triangle Match, 15 January 1999, and retained it in a Four Corners Match two nights later — the only reign this holding attests. The fed's own Title History page names no title of this exact name, only an empty "Mid-Atlantic Light-Weight Title" row with no entries; almost certainly the same belt under a variant spelling, not reconciled here.

titles.name: Mid-Atlantic Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Title History page attests one reign: Angels of the Night won this belt in a Four Corners Match, 10 February 1999. The same team name holds the BCW National Tag Team Championship on the NeWA hub's own British sister territory; the two are read together as the same touring team rather than a coincidence (see this wing's own Affiliations). The fed's own News page (27 January 1999) implies an earlier reign this holding does not otherwise attest, asking rhetorically whether the champions have defended "even once since Crowing Event" [sic] — no date, match, or result survives for that named event, an honest gap, not resolved here. No later change survives.

titles.name: Mid-Atlantic Television Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own News page (27 January 1999) has Jim Crockett, Jr. Fred Rogers is next attested champion by 10 February 1999, per the fed's own Title History page, via a Three Way Elimination Match rather than any resolution of the ordered series — no document says who else stood in that match, or how or when the vacancy the strip created was filled before it.

titles.name: NEWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands from Mr. Irrestible to "Shotgun" Sammy Cooper on 22 March 1997; also claimed by a rival tag-title claimant from an outside promotion, WNWA, an angle the fed's own newsletter treats as live but does not resolve in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: NEWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Psycho Stud through the fed's own attested run; this collection's holdings do not trace the lineage before or after.

titles.name: NEWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Hate Machine through the fed's own attested run, with the Nobles as the chief challengers; the fed's own December retrospective narrates the belts later changing hands to Jack Diamond and a tag partner, and finally to Midnight Rampage, ahead of the fed's own closure.

titles.name: NEWC Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: The promotion's top singles championship, announced at its debut show and left vacant through a qualifying tournament.
titles.epitaph: Announced at the promotion's own debut show as its top singles title, to be crowned in a Four Corners match at the federation's first supercard, and still vacant through a qualifying tournament in every broadcast this collection preserves.

titles.name: NEWC Television Championship
titles.caption: The promotion's secondary singles championship, crowned in a ten-man battle royal at the federation's second show.
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a ten-man main-event battle royal at the promotion's second broadcast, won by Sabbath, who carried it through both defenses this collection preserves.

titles.name: NEWC Tri-State Championship
titles.caption: A regional championship created for the promotion's own New Jersey, New York and Connecticut roster, announced with a tournament still underway.
titles.epitaph: Created to represent the New Jersey, New York and Connecticut area the promotion's own roster is drawn from, announced with a tournament to crown its first champion that remains underway when this collection's own record ends.

titles.name: NEWCOWF Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: First won by the debuting Eliminators, John Kronus and Perry Saturn, over Doug Furnas and Philip LaFon in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals; a later, uncollected card already bills different champions.
titles.notes: First won by the debuting Eliminators, John Kronus and Perry Saturn, over Doug Furnas and Philip LaFon in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals; a later, uncollected card already bills different champions.

titles.name: NEWCOWF TV Title
titles.epitaph: First won by Ric Flair over Ahmed Johnson in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals; a later, uncollected card already bills a different champion.
titles.notes: First won by Ric Flair over Ahmed Johnson in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals; a later, uncollected card already bills a different champion.

titles.name: NEWCOWF World Title
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles championship, first won by Stone Cold Steve Austin over The Giant in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals, and still billed as his through the federation's last surviving records.
titles.notes: The federation's top singles championship, first won by Stone Cold Steve Austin over The Giant in a tournament final at the promotion's Tournament Finals, and still billed as his through the federation's last surviving records.

titles.name: NEWF Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated 10-reign chain for this belt, from Speed Racer's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) onward. Present holder per the title-history page's own last entry; the fed's own served Pandemonium PPV recap independently confirms the reign, retaining against Assassin.

titles.name: NEWF Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated 8-reign chain for this belt, from Sabu's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) onward. The last recorded Hardcore Champion in the held record.

titles.name: NEWF T.V. Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated 16-reign chain for this belt, from Genesis's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) onward.

titles.caption: Named in the fed's own 9 September 1996 recruitment post as one of five titles; no contender, defence, or result of any kind survives.
titles.epitaph: NEWF United States Tag Team Titles: named in the fed's own recruitment post, never attested as contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: NEWF U.S. Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated 15-reign chain for this belt, from Bolo Yeung's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) onward. The title-history page's own footnote records the belt vacated the same day, "when Speed Racer dumped it to pursue the World Title." The fed's own served Pandemonium PPV recap, dated the same day, does not itself narrate a vacating — it shows Speed Racer defending and retaining the U.S. Title in a straight match against Sinister Sean Blake that same night (Commissioner Clayton's own on-air announcement calls him "the U.S. Champ" going into it), and its own introduction for the later World Title main event billed Most Holy — not Speed Racer — as "The U.S. Champion," a discrepancy between the two served primary sources the held record does not otherwise resolve.

titles.name: NEWF U.S. Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated 9-reign chain for this belt, from Soldiers of Fortune's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) onward. Present holders per the title-history page's own last entry; the fed's own served Pandemonium PPV recap independently confirms them still champions a week later, retaining against Blood Runs Cold.

titles.name: NEWF World Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated seven-reign chain from Dirt's founding win at NEWF: The Beginning (21 June 1998) to Most Holy's win over Alex Star on 1 December 1998, each entry dated to both winning and losing sides. Two reigns anchor the ledger here: the founding reign, and Most Holy's win, independently confirmed by the fed's own served Pandemonium PPV recap — the same Iron Man Match the title-history page's own final entry records.

titles.caption: Named in the fed's own 9 September 1996 recruitment post as one of five titles; no contender, defence, or result of any kind survives.

Present holders per the title-history page's own last entry; the fed's own served Pandemonium PPV recap independently confirms them still champions three weeks later, retaining against Conveyors Of Pain.

titles.name: NEWF World Tag Team Titles
titles.caption: Named in the fed's own 9 September 1996 recruitment post as one of five titles; no contender, defence, or result of any kind survives.
titles.epitaph: NEWF World Tag Team Titles: named in the fed's own recruitment post, never attested as contested in the surviving record.

titles.epitaph: NEWF World Television Title: named in the fed's own recruitment post, never attested as contested in the surviving record.

titles.name: NFW Conference Regular Season Championship
titles.epitaph: The crown for finishing first in an NFW conference's regular season, won by clinching the conference's first seed for the Ultratitle playoffs. The fed's own shows name the East, North and South champions of Season One in 2004, and the Eastern champion of Season Two.

titles.name: NFW Eastern Conference Championship
titles.notes: Crowned once in the surviving record, on NFW's own served card of 15 March 2007, feeding the Ultratitle Final at Wrestlebowl II.
titles.epitaph: The prize for winning NFW's own Eastern half of the 2007 Ultratitle playoffs, crowned by the ring announcer on the spot rather than staged as a title with a history behind it — the fed's own text does not say whether the belt existed before this show or who, if anyone, held it previously. Yori Yakamo Jr. no-sold a second Kooter Cruise chokeslam, bodyslammed him onto Felix Red, and pinned Red with the Yori=Awesome to become the first and, in the surviving record, only NFW Eastern Conference Champion, earning the berth against the Western Conference's own champion at Wrestlebowl.

titles.name: NFW Elite Championship
titles.notes: Named by the fed's own championship ledger only in passing, in the National Championship's own closing note; the belt has no lineage of its own on that page, and what survives of its custody comes from the fed's own served show documents.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: Folded into the new Triple Crown Championship at Reloaded 11, having sat vacant since a 2010 tournament the record never finishes.

titles.epitaph: An interfed belt whose whole custody the record can only half account for. Steve Knox is already carrying it when NFW's own cameras first find it, at Crash TV 46 in August 2008; the show's own account of how he got it has him beating three other promotions' champions to do it, none of it staged on an NFW card. Wyatt Connors took it off him at Supercrash II two months later, in a segment the broadcast reported rather than showed. After that the belt goes quiet: by July 2010 the fed is describing it as vacated and crediting the vacancy back to Knox rather than to Connors, and running an interfed tournament to fill it whose first round is the only round that survives. It was revived on paper in January 2012 for the sole purpose of being merged into the Triple Crown Championship three months later. Where the chain breaks, it breaks in the fed's own record, not in this one.

titles.name: NFW Grand Prix
titles.epitaph: A tournament NFW ran three times. Doctor Curiosity won the first, a three-way elimination bout at Supercrash II in October 2008, Legion the 2011 edition at its Monaco final, and Jack Harmen the 2013 edition, which earned him a shot at the NFW World Heavyweight Championship.

titles.name: Great American Smokeout Bunkhouse Championship
titles.epitaph: A one-night Bunkhouse Stampede eliminator, closed by a War Games segment among its final three, which the fed itself named a championship. Captain Justice won it at Crash TV 50 on 29 August 2009, its one recorded winner.

titles.name: NFW Hulk-a-Thon
titles.epitaph: NFW's Hulk-A-Thon, billed as the first annual: a fifteen-entrant tournament of triple-threat elimination rounds whose five winners met in a War Games-style cage. Yori Yakamo, Jr. won it at Midnight Madness 8, Venice Beach, on 18 March 2006; the next one planned was cancelled.
titles.notes: Billed on the night as "THE FIRST ANNUAL SYMPOSIUM OF THE IMMORTAL HULKAMANIA"; the next Hulk-A-Thon, announced for 2007, was cancelled on air at Crash TV 42 (28 November 2007).

titles.name: NFW Mid-Atlantic Championship
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
titles.epitaph: A regional championship that lasted nine months. Alex Wylde beat Armando Montezuma in the final of a sixteen-man tournament to win it at Banned 4 Life in June 2001; Pat Black took it that November. The ledger records the end as an act of the fed's own authority rather than a match: Commissioner Michael Manson fired Black and discontinued the title on 17 March 2002, at Impact 2.

events.note: Commissioner Michael Manson fired Pat Black and discontinued the title at Impact 2, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

titles.name: NFW National Championship
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
titles.epitaph: A second singles championship the fed introduced at Supercrash I in February 2008, decided in a double-elimination tournament that Teresa Quaranta won over Rook Black. Steve Knox took it that August and Rook Black got it back at Supercrash II, holding it 923 days. Supercrash III in San Antonio put three reigns on it in one night: Thirteen won it and was unmasked on the spot as High Flyer, Doc Curiosity took it from him, and Rook Black took it back. The ledger closes on that second Rook Black reign with a note that the belt became the Triple Crown Championship, merged with the Pure and Elite Championships, after he beat Deacon and Stalker at Reloaded 11 in April 2012.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: The fed's own ledger, in this title's own closing note: the National Championship "became Triple Crown Championship (Merged with Pure & Elite Championship) after Rook Black defeated Deacon & Stalker at Reloaded 11 (04/20/12)."

titles.name: NFW Pure Championship
titles.notes: Named by the fed's own championship ledger only in passing, in the National Championship's own closing note; the belt has no lineage of its own on that page, and the reigns below come from the fed's own served show documents instead.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: Folded into the new Triple Crown Championship at Reloaded 11, on a presidential order announced three months earlier at Supercrash IV.

titles.epitaph: A championship NFW's own ledger never gave a lineage to. Bloodhunt unveiled the belt at the 2010 opening night in Philadelphia after losing to Sean Stevens, crowned Stevens its first champion on the spot, called him drug-free and demanded Olympic-style testing of anyone who wanted it — an argument aimed squarely at the World Champion of the day. Stevens held it into 2011 and was suspended with it; Troy Windham then had Bobby Jack Windham named champion as one of the terms of the Supercrash III deal, on the grounds that no Windham was purer. Legion won it in a four-corners match at Reloaded X by falling on an unconscious champion, and Stalker took it from him at Supercrash IV in a chain match while Legion's own valet worked against him. Three months later it stopped existing, merged into the Triple Crown. The fed's own championship history lists none of that: the belt appears there once, in another title's closing note.

titles.name: NFW Television Championship
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
titles.epitaph: The fed's own working belt, twice discontinued and twice brought back. Tempesta Del Fuerte won it out of a one-night sixteen-man tournament at Impact 4 in July 2002; Steel Viper took it at Futureshock the following month and the title was retired at the end of that same night. It returned at Wrestlebowl II in May 2007 with co-champions — Shawn Jessica Hart and Joe The Plumber simultaneously won the battle royal that decided it, Hart disappeared the next night, and Joe was declared sole champion. Impulse won the vacancy in a Sears Tower match, Castor Strife gave it up to enter the World Title tournament, and Jack Bryant won the vacancy in a five-man ladder match. Its last chapter is a best-of-five series against Dorchester Stratton that the ledger tracks match by match and leaves with Stratton holding it.

events.note: Discontinued at the end of Futureshock and not reinstated until 16 May 2007, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

titles.name: NFW Triple Crown Championship
titles.notes: Created by presidential order inside the fed's own fiction, announced at Supercrash IV and first awarded at Reloaded 11; the fed's own championship ledger records it only as the name the National Championship became.
titles.epitaph: The last singles championship NFW made, and it was made by consolidation rather than by tournament: President Eddie Mayfield ordered the Pure, National and Elite Championships merged into one belt at Supercrash IV in January 2012, and Rook Black won it at Reloaded 11 that April by pinning Deacon in a three-way that also had the reigning Pure Champion in it. He carried it through the promotion's last touring year — Portland, the Gorge, Sydney, Helsinki — turning back the Mighty Impala, Akita and Leyenda de Ocho, and was still holding it at the last card the archive keeps.

titles.name: NFW Ultratitle
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html). SOURCES DISAGREE about how long the Ultratitle ran. The fed's own championship ledger records two seasons and stops after Wrestlebowl II in May 2007; its own show text at Reloaded 13 and Reloaded 14 in 2012 twice refers to Castor Strife holding a 2012 Ultratitle Championship. Both readings are recorded; no third reign is written, because nothing in the served record stages one.
titles.epitaph: Not a championship NFW made. The ULTRATITLE — an eight-tier trophy out of CSWA folklore — was donated to the fed when it rebuilt itself as a fantasy-sports league in 2003, and it was contested across a whole season rather than defended match to match: a draft lottery, two conferences, a sixteen-week regular season on a points table, wild cards, single-elimination playoffs and a Wrestlebowl. Michael Manson beat Shane Southern for Season One at Wrestlebowl I in North Charleston in January 2005. Nova beat Yori Yakamo Jr. for Season Two at Wrestlebowl II in Dallas in May 2007. The fed's own ledger heads the section "NFW Ultratitle Championship (2003-2007)" and records no third season.

titles.name: UWA Women's World Championship
titles.notes: Attested entirely inside NFW's own served corpus, which stages the UWA as a hub-adjacent outside promotion rather than holding it directly; a news article on the same corpus says the belt was renamed after Lucky Seven won an “inaugural SLICE-USA Grand Prix,” a predecessor lineage this collection holds no document for. Filed under NFW rather than the real (1992–1997) UWA: unlike the men's World title, no document here ties this belt to that promotion's own record or its known 1990s roster, and it may or may not be the same in-fiction “resurrected UWA” NFW staged for the men's title (nfw-uwa-world) — the record does not say either way.
titles.epitaph: Lucky Seven is the only champion this record ever names, and she is already carrying the belt the one time it surfaces: an NFW-billed unification bout at Brawl 62 in Berlin, her own in-ring NFW debut, where she defeats Pan-Euro Women's Champion Dani “Alpha” Engel to fold that title into hers. No document held here stages how or when she won it, or whether the “UWA” it names is the same 1990s Philadelphia promotion or NFW's own later storyline revival of it.

titles.name: UWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Staged inside NFW's own continuity as a revival of the real UWA's own vacant, never-resolved World Championship (see that title's own record, uwa-world) — an in-fiction storyline device, not a claim that the real 1992–1997 Philadelphia UWA continued operating. Crowned across two of NFW's own served cards, Wrestlebowl I (31 Jan 2005) and Midnight Madness 5 (18 Nov 2005).
titles.epitaph:
At Wrestlebowl I (31 January 2005), Avery Prosser — fresh off seizing NFW's own North division with his “Seven Deadly Sins” — produced the real UWA's own vacant World Championship belt on air and declared he would “RESURRECT this title” in the name of the man he called its rightful champion, presenting it to Troy Windham as “your DIVINE RIGHT.” Windham, taking the mic, claimed sole credit for having “MADE the UWA” seven years earlier. It was a political gift, not the result of a contest, and it did not survive the night: in the brawl that followed, Craig Miles pulled the belt off the fallen Windham and handed it to Tom Adler, and NFW's own text leaves the title “held up/vacant” for the rest of the season.

It came to a decision at Midnight Madness 5 (18 November 2005): Adler won the vacant title from Windham by disqualification, after Zoltan and August De La Rossi interfered and Windham sprayed him with an unspecified liquid — and Adler surrendered it within minutes, in the very next segment, picking up a microphone and saying only “I Quit” before handing it to Eddie Mayfield without further contest. Mayfield held it through two more defenses in the surviving record without it changing hands again: a no-contest against Eli Flair at UWA Pirate TV (24 December 2005), and a no-decision against Adler at Wrestlestock I (20 April 2006). No later NFW document shows the belt again.

The prop is staged throughout as the same belt the real UWA left vacant in 1997, not a new one — commentary calls it a title “resurrected... for this season,” and Windham's own promo reaches back to that history directly. The real UWA's own ledger (uwa-world) records only what its own 1992–1997-era evidence supports; this row holds NFW's later fiction about it.

titles.name: NFW Western Conference Championship
titles.notes: Crowned once in the surviving record, on NFW's own served card of 15 March 2007, feeding the Ultratitle Final at Wrestlebowl II.
titles.epitaph: The prize for winning NFW's own Western half of the 2007 Ultratitle playoffs, run the same day as its Eastern counterpart. After a double count-out through a ringside table tied the match at a fall apiece, a barbed-wire cage went up for the decisive third fall; Nova came out of it the first-ever NFW Western Conference Champion, earning the berth against Eastern Conference Champion Yori Yakamo Jr. at Wrestlebowl. The same card's undercard staged a separate, unrelated Asylum Immortal Championship prize on a hook above the ring — recorded on that outside promotion's own frontier row, not here.

titles.name: NFW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
titles.epitaph: NFW's own top belt for the whole of its run, and the one prize the Ultratitle never replaced. Bloodhunt was the inaugural champion, beating Ricky Zane at Crash 3 in Baltimore in October 2000 after both men won a thirty-man Random Rumble. Zane took it off him at Banned 4 Life in an angle the ledger records in one word — "Zanegate!" — and the belt then went through the fed's own messiest stretch: Rick Ryconik held it for nothing at all, beaten on the night by Armando Montezuma in a pin Commissioner Michael Manson ruled questionable enough to hold the title up, and Shane Southern won the vacancy in a fourway at Crash 8. Bloodhunt's second reign ended with the title defunct from August 2003 until Manson reinstated it in April 2004 and then won it himself. After that it settled: Doc Silver, Felix Red, Kin Hiroshi — who forfeited it by walking out of a threeway at Crash 43 — Dan Ryan, Nova, and Joe The Plumber, whose 860 days are the longest reign on the ledger, ended when President Eddie Mayfield suspended him for refusing a drug test. Castor Strife won the vacancy in a four-man tournament and lost it to Impulse in a scaffold match billed as The Cutting Room Floor. The ledger's own last word leaves Impulse reigning.

events.note: The ledger records the title defunct from 15 August 2003 until NFW East Commissioner Michael Manson reinstated it on 1 April 2004. (The ledger's own dates disagree with themselves here: the reign it attaches the note to opens 15 August 2002. Both readings are recorded rather than smoothed.) Per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

titles.name: NFW World Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
titles.epitaph: NFW's tag championship, renamed the Everette Memorial Tag Team Championship when it returned in 2008 — for Avery Everette, the figure the fed's own history names as the first owner of the UWA, the Prodigy-era federation NFW says it grew out of. The Showstoppers were the inaugural champions, beating The Oblivion Express and Hellmachine in a three-way dance at Crash 5 on Christmas Day 2000. Hellmachine took the belts at Banned 4 Life and held them 440 days; The Original Showstoppers won a six-team playoff at Futureshock in August 2002 and the titles were retired at the end of that night, unreinstated until Supercrash I in February 2008. The Hollywood Wrecking Crew won the renamed belts in a tournament, and the ledger's own last reign is the Superfly Express, who beat Jack Bryant and Malik Anderson in the final of the Avery Cup.

events.note: Discontinued at the end of Futureshock and not reinstated until 15 February 2008, when they returned renamed the Everette Memorial Tag Team Championships, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

titles.name: BAD World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: The fed's list of its champions of 20 January 2010 says the BAD World Heavyweight Title "will be kept under its current name and defended at the first NGEN PPV"; the fed's own B.A.D. title history post lists Jared Wells' win over Steve Johnson at Unplugged on 31 December 2009 as the latest change before it.
titles.epitaph: Kept under its name when the fed relaunched as NGEN: the fed's list of 20 January 2010 names Jared Wells the BAD World Heavyweight Champion and says he would defend it at the first NGEN pay-per-view. At Cherry Blossom Chaos he kept it against Jesse Ramey, who replaced Steve Johnson, after Wells pinned Ramey when both men were out cold following a Rage Bomb off the top rope.

titles.name: NGEN North American Title
titles.notes: The fed's list of its champions of 20 January 2010 says the WFW North American Title, last held by Dan Ryan, would be decided by a four-way match and renamed under the NGEN banner, and that the WFW title would be sealed.
titles.epitaph: Created for Cherry Blossom Chaos, where Psycho, HAL, Just 1 Dude and JGX fought a Falls Count Anywhere on the Mall elimination match for the vacant title. Its founder, in a post of 12 January 2011, says HAL won when he pinned Psycho.

titles.name: NGEN World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: The fed's list of its champions of 20 January 2010 seals the WFW World Heavyweight Title for this one; no reign of the 1990s NGEN World Heavyweight Title is carried onto it. Sources disagree: an Empire Pro Wrestling page of 8 March 2011 has Donovan Astros call himself the "uncrowned NGEN World Champion"; this title follows its founder's post of 12 January 2011.
titles.epitaph: Created for Cherry Blossom Chaos, the fed's first pay-per-view, where the WFW World Heavyweight Champion Felix Red, whose own title was to be sealed, met the number one contender Shawn Hart for it. Its founder, in a post of 12 January 2011, says Hart won and became the first NGEN World Heavyweight Champion; he retired from running leagues the day before.

titles.name: NGEN World Tag Titles
titles.notes: The fed's list of its champions of 20 January 2010 says the WFW World Tag Champions, Problem Child and Cameron Cruise, would face a team for the NGEN World Tag Titles and that the WFW tag titles would be sealed.
titles.epitaph: Created for Cherry Blossom Chaos, where the WFW World Tag Champions Cameron Cruise and Problem Child met King Krusher and Striker for the vacant titles. Its founder, in a post of 12 January 2011, says Krusher and Striker won when Striker pinned Cruise after Problem Child screwed Cruise.

titles.name: NGOWF Television Championship
titles.caption: Won by Lucien Champion in a twenty-man battle royal; retained once by disqualification against Bradley Fine.
titles.epitaph: NGOWF Television Championship of NGOWF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: NGOWF World Heavyweight Championship

titles.epitaph: NGOWF World Tag Team Championship of NGOWF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.epitaph: Won first out of a seven-man battle royal by one of the fed's own founders four days after it opened, vacated a week later, and carried through thirty-five more reigns. It was vacated again in August 2003 after John Hitchin was written into a limo accident, and Pr0t0typ3 — later fired and put on the fed's own public blacklist — was holding it when the last title page went up.

titles.name: NGW Battle Dome Title
titles.notes: The reign ledger is served at /promotions/ngw/archive/battle-dome-title-history.html; it is not yet transcribed into this registry.
titles.epitaph: The belt the fed's own thirty-man Battle Dome match played for, and Time Bomb was carrying it at the last title page. Border Line 2004 ended with the referee handing it to John Hitchin on the turnbuckles.

titles.name: NGW Cruiserweight Title
titles.notes: The reign ledger, built from /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html (no dedicated ledger page survives), is transcribed into this registry. Named on the fed's own retired-titles page (/promotions/ngw/archive/retired-titles-2004-09.html); the one surviving show-served defence is in /promotions/ngw/archive/results-tns142.html.
titles.epitaph: Retired by the time the fed published a list of what it had retired. It survives in one show script, where Jester walks out with it over his shoulder and the match for it is proclaimed a no contest with one man unconscious.

titles.notes: The reign ledger, built from /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html (no dedicated ledger page survives), is transcribed into this registry. Named on the fed's own retired-titles page (/promotions/ngw/archive/retired-titles-2004-09.html).
titles.epitaph: One of six belts on NGW's own retired-titles page, and counted among Calvin Riley's championships on his own bio card.

titles.notes: The reign ledger, built from /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html (no dedicated ledger page survives), is transcribed into this registry. titles.epitaph: Created by Brian Hardy on 15 May 2000 and awarded to Brian Hardy by Brian Hardy the same day, and defended in hardcore matches almost exclusively for the rest of its life. Fifty-seven numbered reigns, one of them vacated with the note "Title Vacated when the site was deleted"; the fed retired the belt.

titles.name: NGW Women’s Title
titles.notes: The reign ledger, built from /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html (no dedicated ledger page survives), is transcribed into this registry. Named on the fed's own retired-titles page (/promotions/ngw/archive/retired-titles-2004-09.html); most of its lineage is real-WWE-Divas-cast and withheld per the privacy convention.

titles.name: NGW World Title
titles.notes: The full reign ledger is served at /promotions/ngw/archive/world-title-history.html and /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html; it is not yet transcribed into this registry.
titles.epitaph: Crowned at NGW's first pay-per-view, Out Cold I on 25 February 2000, when Excalibur beat Chris Jericho in a no-disqualification steel cage match, and vacated four days later when the man who took it off him quit. The fed's own ledger runs the belt through thirty-six numbered reigns; Scottywood's own is the longest thing on it, seven defences deep through the spring of 2000, and Scott King was carrying it when the fed last published a title page in November 2004.

titles.name: NGW Xtreme Title
titles.notes: The full reign ledger, built from /promotions/ngw/archive/xtreme-title-history.html and cross-checked against /promotions/ngw/archive/champions-and-title-history-2004-11.html, is transcribed into this registry.
titles.epitaph: Made as the NGW Cage Title and renamed on 6 April 2000, and it kept the shape of the first name: its own ledger is a run of Hell in a Cell, graveyard, buried alive, anarchy and mega mall brawl matches, fifty numbered reigns deep. Perry Saturn won the first one out of a triple Hell in a Cell with the belt hung from the roof of the third cage; John Hitchin broke the fed's own title-reign record holding it in July 2004, and it was vacant when the last title page went up that November.
