titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Brenton Cyrus, from 17 April 2009; 2 reigns are recorded, the last held by Death Angel and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF Freedom Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Chuck Matthews, from 13 June 2009; 3 reigns are recorded, the last held by Kaos and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Brenton Cyrus, from 1 March 2009; 4 reigns are recorded, the last held by Alex Mark, ending 9 May 2009.

titles.name: NLWF No Limit Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Death Angel, from 10 March 2009; 4 reigns are recorded, the last held by Swan Lee and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its champions page also lists an Alex Mark reign from 06/09/09, defeating 'Frank Hart/Unified Title', with the same 22 days as his North American row; no recovered card shows it, and Simple Survival calls Swan Lee the current champion, so it is not recorded as a reign.

titles.name: NLWF North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Jackson, from 1 February 2009; 7 reigns are recorded, the last held by Frank Hart and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: The Junior Heavyweight Championship was unified into it on 9 May 2009.

titles.name: NLWF Proving Grounds Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Conor O'Sullivan, from 25 April 2009; 2 reigns are recorded, the last held by Aaron O'Shea and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF Undisputed Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Nick Ridicule and Chuck Matthews; 2 reigns are recorded, the last held by Ryan Apollo and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF Undisputed Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Steven Angel; 3 reigns are recorded, the last held by Jason Hawk and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF Universal Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Havoc, from about 8 March 2009; 8 reigns are recorded, the last held by Frank Hart and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: Its champions page lists the same history under both brands; the shows give two belts only after 28 June 2009.

titles.name: NLWF Universal Heavyweight Championship (Legacy, from 28 June 2009)
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Demetrius Randall, from 28 June 2009; 1 reign are recorded, the last held by Demetrius Randall and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: A second belt from the draw at Simple Survival, which un-unified the Undisputed Universal Championship; its history before 28 June 2009 is the Universal Heavyweight Championship's.

titles.name: NLWF Universal Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is DX Affliction, from 7 March 2009; 4 reigns are recorded, the last held by 25 to Life and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: The Direct Hit tag belts, called Universal Tag Team Titles and Undisputed Tag Team Titles on the pages; on Direct Hit 12 the World Tag Team Titles were unified into them.

titles.name: NLWF Women's World Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Tiffany Starr, from 7 June 2009; 1 reign are recorded, the last held by Tiffany Starr and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is Tails, from 1 February 2009; 4 reigns are recorded, the last held by Brenton Cyrus and still running when the record ends.
titles.notes: The one-year show of 18 January 2010 bills The Notorious K.I.D as 'Heavyweight and Undisputed Champion'; which heavyweight belt that is, and when he won it, is not on the recovered pages.

titles.name: NLWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The first champion on the recovered pages is The Heart Attacks, from 1 February 2009; 4 reigns are recorded, the last held by The Mexican Samurai and Shadow Demon and still running when the record ends.

titles.name: NLWP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Left vacant by the promotion's own Commissioner ahead of a joint pay-per-view with two allied federations, the title was won by a member of the promotion's own roster in a twenty-man Royal Rumble.

titles.name: NMSEWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded in a fourteen-man battle royal on the fed's own Tuesday Night's Main Event, the only title this pass's own holdings attest.

titles.name: CPW North Continental Title
titles.epitaph: Attested for one reign before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: North Eastern Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional title crowned in the held documents' own first supercard (a tournament final, the Highway Star over Sandy Fields, Spring Slams) and defended twice on-panel (Nevermind over the Candyman at Brawl For It All; the Candyman over Al Robertson at Danger Zone '98, also ending Al Robertson's own Hardcore Championship as a stipulation). Several further changes (to Nevermind, the Candyman, Al Robertson, Magnus Colby) are attested only by the fed's own title-history sheet, off-panel.

titles.name: NOW Midwest Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in an upset tiger suplex, the challenger avenging a loss to the same champion two months earlier.

titles.name: NOW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in a brutal outside brawl settled by countout after a chair shot and a concrete powerbomb.

titles.name: NOW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands when a challenger ended the champion's own undefeated streak with a top-rope leg drop, both men left unconscious.

titles.name: NPW Cabin Boy Championship
titles.epitaph: Named once, years after the fact, in a bath-time conversation between a UWF champion and his girlfriend two federations away — Tsunami Oni, explaining why a young opponent had impressed him in the first round of a cruiserweight tournament, remembers that the kid had been Cabin Boy Champion for No Pirates Wrestling. It is the only championship the promotion is ever recorded as having, and the joke of it is the whole promotion's joke: a fed founded on hating pirates named its bottom-rung belt after the lowest rank on a pirate ship.
titles.notes: The sole receipt is one line in PTC's own Cruiserweight Tournament 2 roleplay board, 24 April 2005: "I guess that's why he was Cabin Boy Champion for No Pirates Wrestling." No date, no match, no defence and no second holder survives; the one holder it names, Mickey D, is a PTC/CW2 competitor who has no registry row of his own yet, so the reign below carries him as an honest unminted holder.

titles.name: NPWA Cruiserweight Championship of the World
titles.epitaph: Held throughout the 1998 run by an undefeated Atticus "The Jester" Payne, criticized on-air for rarely putting the belt on the line.

titles.name: NPWA Millennium Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the NPWA's own Millennium Division sometime before the held record's June-August 1998 gap, first held by "Untouchable" Randy Gant before "Superstar" Steve Sampson took it in a chaotic Coal Miner's Glove three-way at Mayhem, 29 Sep 1998.

titles.name: NPWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for 1997 exactly as the fed's own 1996 FAQ had promised ('a third singles belt on the way early in '97'), first won by 'Sadistic' Steve Stone in a 15-man King of the Hill gauntlet at the fed's own Valentine's Day Massacre '97, and defended in turn by 'Breakfast' Bobby Toast and Mustafa before the Cougar carried it into 1998.

titles.name: NPWA North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A second NPWA tag championship, first held by The Cult (Doctor Death & Father Armageddon, with Locutus wrestling in Armageddon's stead) before changing hands twice in three weeks -- to Assault and Battery at the fed's 5th Anniversary Special, then to the Masters of Disaster at Hell On Earth.

titles.name: NPWA World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by a 16-man tournament in late 1996, the title changed hands six times across 1997 -- the Southern Rocker to Jurisprudence to the Mighty Boss to 'Bad Boy' Mark Bagwell to 'Blackheart' Brian Masters to the Silent Striker to Dark Justice, who carried it into 1998's own Death Row Match.

titles.name: NPWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Traced back to the fed's own 1993 founding (Bash, its first champion), the belt changed hands six times across 1997 alone -- Amoral to Locutus to Col. Buddy Lee Jarrett to 'Superstar' Steve Sampson to 'Blackheart' Brian Masters, a November vacancy, and finally 'Hollywood Heartthrob' Dave Diamond's win in a 14-man Pinfall Royale at the fed's own year-end Xmas Gory '97 -- along the way surviving a stolen-belt cliffhanger left unresolved on a satellite cut-off.

titles.name: NPWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A lineage reaching back to the NWC era, the belts changed hands four times across 1997 alone -- the New Cadavre Connection to the Muslim Massacre (their challengers flying Vegas to London on the Concorde mid-show to turn) to the Lords of the Ring to the Asian Triad -- before a further change and a forfeiture carried the title to Drama by year's end.

titles.name: NRG World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top singles prize, defended in a ladder match rematch of the two men's first encounter six years earlier.
titles.notes: The reign recorded here is confirmed defended in NRG's own show-recap post (31 July 2006), which frames the match as a rematch of a first encounter shown in the night's own video package as taking place in 2000.

titles.name: NRG World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team title, shown held in the night's own video recap package rather than defended on the card itself.
titles.notes: No document in the held record shows this title defended; the reign recorded here rests on the show's own pre-taped video package, which shows the champions holding the belts aloft.

titles.name: Stealth Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once in NSW's own surviving record: Chris Crosse lost it to Spawn in a cage match at Bone Bash 2003, the ENDCAP off the top of the cage ending both the match and the reign.
titles.notes: Sourced entirely from Spawn's own April 2003 bio card (promotions/nsw/archive/spawn-bio-card.html), including its embedded "Flash Back" full match script.

titles.name: Tag Titles
titles.epitaph: Won and vacated in the same stretch of the record: Brad Douglas took it alone in a battle royal at Bone Bash, then gave it up chasing the World Title — a push the fed's own closure cut off before it paid out.
titles.notes: Sourced entirely from Brad Douglas's own April 2003 bio card (promotions/nsw/archive/brad-douglas-bio-card.html); no card or results page for the battle royal itself survives.

titles.name: NWA US Championship
titles.epitaph: Recalled only because a rival federation's own preview commentary happened to list it among Nic Nyce's credentials on his way to an SJPW main event -- the NWA itself left no title match, card or roster of its own for this belt.
titles.notes: No document from the NWA's own record names this title directly; it is recovered entirely from a third federation's commentary.

titles.name: NWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt a community reminiscence remembers only as "the belt" still held by initials-only "BT" the day the promotion folded -- the last trace of a federation nobody thought to write down while it still existed.
titles.notes: Named as "World" only by inference from the promotion's own registry caption; the held record's closure post calls it just "the belt." No title match, card or roster of the NWA's own survives for this title.

titles.name: NWC World Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance's own top prize, changing hands at an allied promotion's supercard through a corrupt referee's fast count and an outside faction's interference.

titles.name: All Asian Championship
titles.epitaph: Unveiled on-air before a single champion was named, then contested through a same-night battle royal seeding an eight-man tournament and a best-of-five final series, so that no single night's luck alone could crown a champion.

titles.name: NWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Davy Airborne through the record's own July cards; Hilton Flames is champion by 18 August, the title change itself not attested.

titles.name: NWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Captain America Rick Dorry throughout this record, last defended against the Arabic Animal at Super Challenge 1.

titles.name: NWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated, then won by the Brotherhood in a five-team elimination match, last defended successfully on 4 August 1995.

titles.name: NWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: Explicitly modelled by the fed's own rules on Lou Thesz and Buddy Rogers' two-out-of-three-falls championship matches, and designed to feud with the NWF Championship; no holder survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: NWF Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: Governed by the same top-5-ranking rule as the NWF Championship; no holder survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: NWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended at every TV taping per the fed's own rules; no holder survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: NWF Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, contested by its own written rules (top-5 ranked contenders only); no card reaches Usenet, so no reign, holder or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: NWL International Title
titles.epitaph: A secondary title meant to elevate its holder toward a Triple Crown shot; never contested in the record read.

titles.name: NWL Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's planned tag-team championship; never contested in the record read.

titles.name: NWL Triple Crown
titles.epitaph: Formed by combining the main championships of three defunct predecessor federations; never contested in the record read.

titles.name: NWL International Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own roster document names its holder as of 13 May 2004; no reign start or end date survives in the held record.
titles.epitaph: A championship the National Wrestling League's own roster document confirms was live and defended during the fed's active months.

titles.name: NWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The National Wrestling League's own secondary championship, worn openly by its holder in a served title-defense promo naming the belt by name.

titles.name: NWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The National Wrestling League's own top championship, held by an early signing turned in-fiction front-office boss for as long as this corpus's own record runs.

titles.name: NWWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed on the fed's own roster of six championships, restricted by its own rules to wrestlers under 230 pounds. Its own dedicated title-history page is a blank, never-filled template, and no reign for it survives anywhere in the captured record.

titles.name: NWWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Listed on the fed's own roster of six championships; its own dedicated title-history page is a blank, never-filled template, and no reign for it survives anywhere in the captured record.

titles.name: NWWA International Championship
titles.epitaph: Named inconsistently by the fed's own hand — "International" on its dedicated title-history page and in the 25 June 2000 "Slamfest" script that crowned Gorilla its new champion, "Intercontinental" in the two 1999 pay-per-views that billed Kirk as its holder. Both readings are recorded rather than picking one. How and when Kirk's own reign ended and the title was declared vacant before Gorilla's win is likewise not in the surviving record.

titles.name: NWWA Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: The one title whose own dedicated history page was actually filled in: Scott Credible, crowned its first champion in a six-man battle royal at the 25 June 2000 "Slamfest." The same card's own script separately bills a Killerwolf-vs.-Scott Durden ladder match for the same belt, a contradiction the fed's own text never resolves.

titles.name: NWWA National Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed the “United States Title” in the one pay-per-view script that shows it defended — Buff Bagwell retaining against Dale Hill at the 30 May 1999 “Slamfest” — against the “National Heavyweight” name its own dedicated (and otherwise blank) title-history page carries. The surviving record never shows how Bagwell became champion; his reign is registered from the earliest point he is shown holding the title.

titles.name: NWWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Triple H is billed “one half of the NWWA Tag Team Champions” at the 29 August 1999 “Fall Classic: War Games” — the only trace of this title anywhere in the surviving record. His reign is registered from that earliest, and only, point the record shows him holding it, with neither his partner's name nor how the team won the belt ever recorded.

titles.name: NWWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top belt, portrayed under real WWF names at every turn the surviving record captures it: the Rock lost it to Buff Tortoise in a ladder match at the 30 May 1999 “Slamfest,” regained it by an unrecorded route before the 29 August 1999 “Fall Classic: War Games” (where he retained against Kirk with Chris Jericho's help), and Hellwolf was defending it by the 25 June 2000 “Slamfest” — a second title change the record also never shows. The fed's own dedicated title-history page, dated 2 July 2000, lists it Vacant, a blank template never updated to match its own pay-per-view results.

titles.name: NWWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-limited singles title contested for two months in early 1998 before its own record shows it retired.

titles.name: NWWF Global Championship
titles.epitaph: A fourth singles title that changed hands twice, sat retired for four months, then returned for one further reign.

titles.name: NWWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A no-disqualification, pin-anywhere title the federation's own title-belt page calls new to the promotion; no reign survives in any captured document.

titles.name: NWWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own secondary singles title through its first year, superseded by a renamed United States Championship per the federation's own later description.

titles.name: NWWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own standing tag team title, still listed on its own current title-belt page; the current holder is not attested in any captured document.

titles.name: NWWF Television/Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: A third singles title contested through the federation's own first year, absent from its own later title-belt page.

titles.name: NWWF 3-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-man tag title contested for less than a year before its own record shows it retired.

titles.name: NWWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own current secondary singles title, described on its own title page as the Intercontinental Championship's successor; no title change survives in any captured document.

titles.name: NWWF United States Championship (1997)
titles.epitaph: A short-lived singles title retired less than three months after it was first awarded.

titles.name: NWWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top title from its first card, held eight times across fourteen changes before its own captured record runs out.

titles.name: NYWA State Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced as the prize of a one-off singles tournament at NYWA's sole advertised card, a Nassau Coliseum tryout show; no result survives in this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: OBW Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/obw/archive/obw-champions.html; reign chain also drawn from promotions/obw/archive/chad-bowens.html and promotions/obw/archive/james-parker.html.
titles.epitaph: OBW's own men's flagship singles title, tracked only through incidental mentions on other wrestlers' bios and the federation's own last-touched champions list rather than a dedicated title-history page. Sidster is the earliest attested holder, backed by the newly formed stable the Flock to a defense at Rebirth (30 April 2012); the record does not say when his reign began or ended. Super Krmi held the belt next, by the time Chad Bowens dethroned him on the Storm episode after Storm's 54th — a reign Bowens's own bio credits him with holding twice in total, though only this one surfaces by name in the surviving record. Bowens lost the title the same night to a Money in the Bank-style cash-in by Ice, whose own caption calls it his only reign. How or when Ice lost the belt is not recorded; the corpus resumes the men's title story in early 2013 with Punisher already the Storm-side rival of Execution's own M-Star, and the wiki's own champions list, last touched 21 February 2014, still names Punisher, leader of the stable the Prophecy, as champion.

titles.name: OBW Vixen Tag Team Championships
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/obw/archive/obw-vixen-tag-team-championships.html.
titles.epitaph: The oldest belt the federation's own record dates, crowned 2 July 2011 on Friday Night Storm and defended almost entirely on that brand. Ashanti and Paisley held it three separate times across five months. The Lace Twins took it in a three-way in April 2012 and held it 122 days, the longest reign on the ledger — and lost it not in a match but to a firing, the belt handed to Snickers and Jade Mystique at Violent Voting once the twins were gone.

titles.name: OBW Vixen's Television Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/obw/archive/vixen-television-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: Debuted 28 February 2012 at the federation's own Big Shot pay-per-view, where Kitten beat three others in a sudden-death four-way to become the first champion. Its own article and its own ledger disagree about the belt's size — the prose says six reigns shared between five wrestlers, the table lists ten across nine — and both are recorded here rather than resolved. Leda's 82 days is the longest reign on it; Mahlia won hers in what the ledger calls the first ever Vixens Lockdown.

titles.name: OBW Vixen's World Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/obw/archive/obw-vixen-world-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: Debuted 1 February 2012 on the first night of Wednesday Night Catfight, the federation's own Vixens-only brand, when Cream Stylez beat Jade Mystique in a match its ledger records as merging the OBW Divas Championship and the Execution Woman's Championship into one belt. Ten reigns follow in fourteen months, none of them longer than Mystique's own 92 days, and the belt travels through pay-per-views the federation named Heart of Wrestling, Alcatraz Aggression, Wheel of Torture, Last Man Standing and Xtreme Xmas. The ledger's last word is Ayden Starr-Malice's second reign, won in a falls-count-anywhere five-way at Heart of Wrestling 2013 and still running at 63 days when the record stops.

titles.name: OBW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/obw/archive/obw-champions.html; reign chain also drawn from promotions/obw/archive/chad-bowens.html and promotions/obw/archive/mvp-lux.html. Distinct from the wing's other men's flagship, the OBW Championship (Sidster/Krmi/Bowens/Ice/Punisher lineage), which is reconstructed separately.
titles.epitaph: OBW's second men's flagship singles title, attested only through incidental mentions on other wrestlers' own bios and the federation's own last-touched champions list; no dedicated title-history page survives for it, unlike the Vixens belts. MVP Lux is the earliest attested holder, named only as the champion Chad Bowens dethroned; the record does not say how or when Lux won it, though it does record him earning an open-ended championship opportunity in an Elimination Chamber match at Death Trap (30 July 2012). Bowens won the title from Lux at an Execution television taping ("Execution 86", by his own account 25 June 2013), with help from an outside beatdown of Lux by four other wrestlers, but was forced to vacate it after an in-storyline injury. How or when the vacancy was filled is not recorded; the wiki's own champions list, last touched 21 February 2014, names M-Star as champion by then.

titles.name: OLWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a ladder match on the fed's own served Witch Hunt card.

titles.name: OSF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: OSF's top belt began on a Sunday Night Slam, when OSW's owner made the International Championship the OSF World Title and named its holder, the 500-pound Kimbusa, its first champion. Tempest was champion by May 2003 and retained against Akage Kitagami on 4 June; Inphino Blitz was champion by October and defended against Kenyatta Jackson at B3.
titles.notes: Dated from OSF's own Title History and Champions pages and its news, columns and recaps; the title-change nights between the three reigns are not recorded.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Corg became its first champion at Ascension on 23 June 2002 and lost it to Kid Wonder on 19 October 2002. On the 9 Feb 2003 Slam! Kid Wonder said he was no longer the Cruiserweight champion, kept the belt as his own and lifted its weight restriction; the fed's own title history says he renamed it the Soy Boy Memorial Title. Tyler Nelson won it from him at Crowning Glory 2 on 16 March 2003 and renamed it the United States Title a week later.

events.title: osw-united-states
events.note: Tyler Nelson, who had won the belt as the Soy Boy Memorial Title at Crowning Glory 2 on 16 March 2003, renamed it the United States Title on Sunday Night Slam (the fed's own title history, /promotions/osw/archive/ose-title-history-wrestling-site-july-2003-2003-07-21.html).

titles.name: Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Sebastian "Switchblade" Toomes won OSW's own first Heavyweight Championship in March 2002, at the fed's debut PPV, Crowning Glory. Doug Troy won it from him on Slam 16, 22 May 2002 -- and was immediately Polish Powerbombed through a table by Tom Walczak in the title's own aftermath. Howard Porter held the belt by a September 2002 champions snapshot; a later ledger (per the mining digest) records him as a corrupt Commissioner who won the title through office rather than the ring.

titles.name: International Championship
titles.epitaph: Rhett Locke won OSW's first International Championship at Crowning Glory, the fed's debut PPV, pinning Drew Hostyle on 10 March 2002, and defended it against Tom Walczak and Corg before Propaganda beat him for it at Slam! 14 on 4 May 2002. Propaganda was defending it through June and July until 'Angeldust' Nick Casey won a four-way over him, Lilith and Vampir Nosferatu at Slam! 26 on 27 July 2002. Casey beat Propaganda to keep the belt at By Any Means Necessary on 1 September and held it until 7 September, when the Jane Says segment at Slam! 32 announced Frankie Bones as the new champion; Bones held it at the end of the surviving record. The fed's results archive index tells the July stretch differently, listing Tom Walczak and Rhett Locke as champions with no Casey reign, but the fed's own write-ups of those two cards read both bouts as World Heavyweight title matches and have Propaganda defending the International on both nights.

titles.name: OSW Old-School Championship
titles.epitaph: OSW Online's top championship, vacant through the fed's first seven months: Def Bellows won it in the final of an eight-man tournament at the Field Trip of 3 September 2002 and still held it at the end of the year.

titles.name: OSW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Claimed for months by self-declared champions, the title was made official at the Field Trip of 3 September 2002, when Sexual Energy won it; they still held it at the end of the year.

titles.name: OSW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: OSW Online's first title, won by Chris Colton over Dark Soul in the final of a four-man tournament on 2 April 2002; he held it through the rest of 2002.

titles.name: Queen of Extreme
titles.epitaph: OSW's own women's-division tournament format, not a defended belt but a points-based elimination competition run across several weeks of Slam! and settled at a PPV. The inaugural 2002 field ran eight entrants (Brandi Wilson, Danniella Jones, Anna Keyson, Faith Paris, Bethany Yamato, "Primetime" Laura Wilson, Lillith, and Amanda) through four scored rounds -- promos, a battle royal, a six-woman tag, and a four-corners match -- before Lillith and Yamato met in a Japanese Death Match at Head on Collision, 28 Apr 2002. Lillith won, crowned the first-ever Queen of Extreme.

titles.name: United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The Cruiserweight belt under a new name. Kid Wonder had called it the Soy Boy Memorial Title; Tyler Nelson won it from him at Crowning Glory 2 on 16 March 2003 and renamed it the United States Title a week later, and Jane Reagan had him vacate it on 4 May 2003, after he won the World Heavyweight Title. The Chaos In The Cage match of 25 May 2003 ended in a simultaneous pin on D-Kay Calyx by Politically Incorrect, William S. Powell and Reginald V. Lovecraft, and the fed named both men co-holders; its lawyers found no way to void it, and the pair were allowed to defend the belt as a tag team. Azala Zameer won it from them, billed on that card as the OSW American Championship, in a Contract versus Contract match at Ascension on 29 June 2003. Ivan Stanislav's roster card gives him the American Championship from 24 August to 14 September 2003. Who held it after him is not recorded; the fed was still keeping a contenders list for the American Title on 28 October 2003.
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own title history (/promotions/osw/archive/ose-title-history-wrestling-site-july-2003-2003-07-21.html): the Cruiserweight Title, which Kid Wonder, champion from 19 October 2002, renamed the Soy Boy Memorial Title, and which Tyler Nelson renamed the United States Title on 23 March 2003. The pages name it three ways: the United States Title or Championship (the title history; Tyler Nelson's and Politically Incorrect's cards; the 27 and 28 May 2003 news posts), the OSW or OSE American Championship (Ascension; the Powell, Zameer and Stanislav cards) and the American Title (/promotions/osw/archive/osw-expands-contender-lists-2003-10-28.html).

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Civil Disobedience (Seth Masters & Trevor Hawke) won OSW's own first Tag Team Championship at Crowning Glory, OSW's debut PPV, and lost it the same night three weeks later, 30 March 2002, to Heresian Bloodlust (Hessian & Azrael Cain) — who beat back two challenges from Riptah & Short Circuit before dropping the belts to that same team on 23 June 2002, closing the chain across the fed's own first three reigns. Riptah and Short Circuit then held the belts for a month that summer. The Throwbacks ('Old School' Dave Gibson & Clay Vendetta) held the titles by a September 2002 champions snapshot. By early 2003 the champions were Heaven & Hell (Hessian & Propaganda — Hessian's second tag reign with a second partner), who retained against a crossover challenge from PCW's own Politically Incorrect in a Falls Count Anywhere match, 9 Feb 2003.

titles.name: Ohio Valley Champion
titles.epitaph: Planned as the promotion's own top singles title, to be crowned in an eight-man tournament once the federation reached television; no champion is recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: Ohio Valley Tag Team Champions
titles.epitaph: Planned as the promotion's own tag title, to be introduced once its tag division grew large enough to support one; no champions are recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: Syndication Championship
titles.epitaph: Planned as a title defended only on the promotion's own syndicated television broadcast, once that syndication arrived; no champion is recorded in the surviving documents.

titles.name: OWA Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/owa-orlando/archive/owa-heavyweight-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: OWA's top belt, created February 2016 and won on the federation's own first night: Tyler Chandler took an open battle royal on the 2 March 2016 Anarchy to become the inaugural champion. Its own ledger records exactly one reign, still running at 327 days when the record stops, and its own article calls it “the top-tier championship title in Orlando Wrestling Alliance.” Chandler defended it against Alex Madsen on the January 2017 return show and was billed to defend it against Hunter Gage inside a cage at Rage in the Cage.

titles.name: OWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/owa-orlando/archive/owa-intercontinental-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: Created 18 January 2017 and won the same night by the federation's own owner: Mason Wolfe took a fatal five-way at an OWA live event to become the inaugural and only champion its ledger records. Its own article files it as OWA's third-tier title.

titles.name: INN Championship
titles.epitaph: The singles title of the OWA's INN branch, billed on Nightmare through the winter of 1995.

titles.name: InterNet Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man tournament to launch the OWA's InterNet division, changing hands between Colt and Ricky Blood across December 1995.

titles.name: OWA Championship
titles.epitaph: The OWA's own world title, defended by Amazon Woman through the winter of 1995 against Dangerous Dunk, Traci Lane, and Ricky Blood.

titles.name: OWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The OWA's tag title, changing hands three times across December 1995 before Freddy Fever and Major Threat won it at WinterTime Massacre.

titles.name: OWA Trio Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-man tag championship held by the stable The Crew, first seen defended at Crime Spree.

titles.name: OWA TV Championship
titles.epitaph: The OWA's television title, changing hands repeatedly across 1996 between Amazon Woman, Mariko, Masked Mayhem, Johnny Fate, and Asian Invasion.

titles.name: OWA Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The belt's own championship page is a placeholder the wiki never filled in; the reign source is promotions/owa-orlando/archive/brett-edgar.html and the match is carded at promotions/owa-orlando/archive/rage-in-the-cage-2017.html.
titles.epitaph: Its own championship page never got past the words “coming soon,” but the belt is real in the federation's own record: Brett Edgar's bio card names him and Shane Miller, as Made in Detroit, beating Jake Anderson & Duke Knight and the Connolly brothers in a triple-threat tornado steel-cage match on the Rage in the Cage kickoff to become the first-ever OWA Tag Team Champions. That is the only reign the record carries, and it is the only Rage in the Cage result the record carries at all.

titles.name: OWA United Kingdom Championship
titles.notes: The belt's own championship page is a placeholder the wiki never filled in; it is named and unveiled in promotions/owa-orlando/archive/thursday-night-anarchy.html and listed among the federation's championships in promotions/owa-orlando/archive/orlando-wrestling-alliance.html.
titles.epitaph: Unveiled on the 23 January 2017 Anarchy by the general managers, alongside the announcement of a thirty-two-man tournament to fill it. No champion is recorded, no tournament bracket survives, and the belt's own page never got past the words “coming soon.”

titles.name: OWA Universal Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/owa-orlando/archive/owa-universal-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: Created October 2016 and first contested at the January 2017 live event, where Owen Grady beat Mitch McGillicutty for it. Its own article files it as OWA's second-tier title and describes a belt built as the reverse of the World Championship's — red strap, black lettering inside the die-cut W. Grady was carded to defend it against Adam Dunn inside a cage at Rage in the Cage.

titles.name: OWA Women's Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/owa-orlando/archive/owa-women-s-championship.html.
titles.epitaph: Crowned the same night as the Heavyweight title — Clarissa Evans won a fatal four-way on the 2 March 2016 Anarchy — and held by her for 322 days, the longest reign anywhere in OWA's own record. Erin Spencer-Wolfe took it in a six-pack challenge at the live event that restarted the federation in January 2017, then lost it 39 days later to Angelita Henderson inside a steel cage at Rage in the Cage. The federation's own championship ledger was never revised past that January live event and still names Spencer-Wolfe champion; Henderson's own bio, written after the fact, is the source for the title's actual outcome.

titles.name: OWE World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: First decided in an eleven-man battle royal, then changing hands in its own first defense at the promotion's inaugural pay-per-view.

titles.name: OWE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top title, left vacant through its debut broadcast and decided for the first time in a three-way ladder match at its own inaugural pay-per-view.

titles.name: OWF Akron City Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own hometown title, defended in the opening match of the fed's first-ever card, Sunday Inferno (1 November 1998), between "Flashy" Michael Robinson and Red Raider -- billed on the fed's own Buckeye Buzz newsletter as a clash of former EMWO champions.

titles.name: OWF Buckeye Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own flagship singles title, held by "Mr. Charisma" Christian York into the fed's first card, Sunday Inferno (1 November 1998), where he defended it against "The Disciple" Eric Wayne in the main event.

titles.name: OWF Cincinnati Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team championship, run out of Cincinnati; Cold Justice won it at the promotion's own Christmas Carnage and were billed defending it in a four-way match at the promotion's own closing SnowScraps: Termination card, whose own outcome does not survive the record.

titles.name: OWF Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A tournament title whose semi-finals ran on the fed's first card, Sunday Inferno (1 November 1998); its own newsletter previewed "Sudden Death" Shane Matthews as the promotion's own pick to win the inaugural tournament.

titles.name: OWO World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Meanstreak took the belt from the Crow in a First Blood match, then turned back a non-title grudge match against "Iceman" Josh Cagle days later — the only title change this wing's surviving record shows.

titles.name: OWO Xtreme Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Raven across this wing's surviving record; retained against Terminator when a countout finish denied the challenger the title under the fed's own titles-don't-change-on-a-countout rule.

titles.name: OWWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own lightweight championship, reassigned at a single pay-per-view battle royal after its first champion fell short of the final four.

titles.name: OWWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded to the last man standing from the promotion's own four-way Battle of the Best stipulation after the other three titles were claimed.

titles.name: OWWA Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship, first awarded in a match tainted by its own management faction's interference.

titles.name: OWWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded to the runner-up of a Heavyweight title decider under the promotion's own Battle of the Best stipulation.

titles.name: SCW Pennsylvania State Championship
titles.epitaph: Opened a first-round tournament on the promotion's own debut broadcast before its own president cancelled the tournament the same night; no champion was ever crowned in the surviving record.

titles.name: PAW National Championship
titles.epitaph: Named as the promotion's own top singles prize in its founding FAQ; no champion or title match is recorded here.

titles.name: PAW National Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named alongside the National Championship as one of the promotion's own two founding titles; no champion or title match is recorded here.

titles.name: PAW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named as one of the fed's three singles belts in its own founding post; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: PAW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Named as one of the fed's three singles belts in its own founding post; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: PAW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named as the fed's top singles belt in its own founding post; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: PAW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding post and coveted on-camera by the debuting Darknight Express; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: PCCW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The Aerial Marauder is already champion entering this wing's own served corpus -- how or when he won the title does not survive in this collection's holdings -- and retains it against Raven at Jersey Jams with a staged assist from the World Heavyweight Champion.

titles.name: PCCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Jack Cole won it in an angle recapped rather than shown in this wing's own served corpus; Shane Douglas held it entering CaliQuake '97, where Tony Marconi dethroned him in the same segment that wrote Douglas out of PCCW; Marconi held it into December, surviving both a JUSTICE beatdown and his own staged double-cross of that same stable.

titles.name: PCCW World Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A comedy-billed lineage that changed hands repeatedly across 1997: Syxx lost it to Al Snow (wrestling as "Leif Cassidy"), who was upset by El Jobbo Grande within a week, who in turn lost it to Sean Southward -- the CaliQuake '97 commentary's own recap of "two former PCCW World light heavyweight champions" meeting in a non-title match. El Jobbo Grande is billed a 'former' champion again by Jersey Jams, where a first-round Light Heavyweight tournament match (Ultimo Warrior vs. an unminted opponent) runs toward a vacant or re-claimed title this collection's own holdings do not resolve.

titles.name: PCCW World Six-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held throughout this wing's own served corpus by JUSTICE's own "Law & Order" pairing and the Machine; no challenge for it resolves within this collection's holdings.

titles.name: PCCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: New Jack and John Kronus lost the titles to Pain & Suffering (Sabre and Sledge Hammer of the Danger Zone Alliance) at CaliQuake '97; Pain & Suffering retained in a tables-strewn brawl at Jersey Jams, "our first title defense ever."

titles.name: PCCW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: "Bad Attitude" Blade Dryden held it before CaliQuake '97's own four-way steel cage match crowned Ajax Shiva; Shiva lost it to the fWo's Paul-Dog on 7 December 1997 after interference from the Aerial Marauder.

titles.name: PCW World Title
titles.notes: The promotion's own top singles title, held by Big Elwood through the one defense this corpus records.
titles.epitaph: Defended once on the surviving record, successfully, before the fed's own takeover and rebrand as PCW.

titles.name: PCW Coastal Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed the fed's own "working man's title," defended most often of its four belts. Colossus won it in a battle royal at "One Night in Hollywood," 16 August 1998; the fed's own rankings page a month later billed Boche as champion instead, a change the surviving record never shows happening.

titles.name: PCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Restricted by the fed's own rule to wrestlers under 235 pounds, first decided in an eight-man gauntlet at "One Night in Hollywood," 16 August 1998, won by Daft Vader — the only reign the surviving record holds.

titles.name: PCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top belt, contested for the first time in an eight-man tournament at "One Night in Hollywood," 16 August 1998 — Hale's win is the only reign the surviving record holds.

titles.name: PCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by the stable the Westside Connection in a four-team ladder match at "One Night in Hollywood," 16 August 1998 — the only reign the surviving record holds. The fed's own schedule page bills a challenge from a team called the Stone Crushers on the "Monday Night Special," 21 September 1998; no result survives.

titles.name: Continental Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Continental Championship was first won by Alan Kriegman on 22 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 36 reigns on it, across 31 different champions. The longest is Totally Tubular Tommy's, 84 days from 22 December 2002. Four of its reigns ended outside a match — handed over, stripped from the holder or vacated. Skitzo held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Cruiserweight Championship was first won by Nick Taylor on 22 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 44 reigns on it, across 30 different champions. The longest is Chris Chase's, 56 days from 9 January 2002. Three of its reigns ended outside a match — handed over, stripped from the holder or vacated. Miss Moonlight held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: European Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's European Championship was first won by The Chef on 9 March 2001. PCW retired it on 8 April 2001, under its only champion.

events.note: Alan Kriegman, on the fed's own authority: "by order of Commissioner Naket, I am pleased to announce that effective immediately, the European Belt is retired, and the Rising Star Title has been reinstated in PCW!" — said in the same segment as The Chef's own successful defence that night, so the belt is retired under its only champion rather than lost. The fed's own title log has no row for the belt at all, let alone for its retirement. Source: PCW's own results page for Spring Fling 2001, 8 Apr 2001.

titles.notes: A belt PCW ran for thirty days in the spring of 2001 and that his database holds no row for anywhere: PCW's own title list lists the other seven and nothing else, and all three of its matches carry title_id 0 on their own match record. Created when the fed scrapped the Rising Star Championship for it and retired when the fed brought the Rising Star Championship back, so its lineage is recorded as restarted from title 13. Receipts: PCW's own results pages for March Madness 2001 (4 Mar 2001), Turmoil 24 (6 Mar 2001, 442.txt), Fusion 25 (9 Mar 2001, 375.txt), Sabotage 1 (11 Mar 2001, 305.txt), Fusion 26 (16 Mar 2001, 376.txt), Turmoil 26 (20 Mar 2001, 444.txt), Sabotage 3 (25 Mar 2001, 299.txt) and Spring Fling 2001 (8 Apr 2001, 511.txt).

titles.name: Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Extreme Championship was first won by Scott Naket on 6 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 72 reigns on it, across 54 different champions. The longest is Skitzo's, 65 days from 14 February 2003. Shaun Styles held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: PCW Columbia Valley Championship
titles.epitaph: A regional secondary title the promotion's own broadcasters called the toughest belt to hold in PCW.

titles.name: PCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag championship, briefly unified with DPW's own belts before that promotion closed.

titles.name: PCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's television title, defended on its weekly broadcasts and its pay-per-view cards alike.

titles.name: PCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, contested through four holders and a vacancy in 1997 before the promotion closed with no further title update on record.

titles.name: J-Paradise Championship
titles.epitaph: A junior division declared open to male and female characters weighing 200 pounds or less in the federation's own May 2005 F.A.Q.; no reign was ever recorded against it.

titles.name: Rising Star Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Rising Star Championship was first won by Dan Hollywood on 26 November 2000. The fed's own record carries 36 reigns on it, across 35 different champions. The longest is Dorn Tracer's, 58 days from 21 February 2003. Six of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. PCW scrapped it for the European Championship on 6 March 2001 and brought it back a month afterwards. PCW merged it into the Cruiserweight Championship on 17 September 2002, and revived it four months later. James 'Lunar' Edwards held it at the end of the surviving record.

events.note: PCW scrapped the Rising Star Championship for the European Championship, in its own on-air voice: Tyler Nelson — "the Rising Star Title was caught in a numbers game. With our addition to the Euro TV Satellite Networks, it only seemed natural to create a European title, so the decision was made to scrap the Rising Star strap." The belt came back thirty-three days later, at Spring Fling 2001 of 8 Apr 2001: "the European Belt is retired, and the Rising Star Title has been reinstated in PCW!" TWO READINGS, recorded both (#sources-disagree): in period the fed staged a SCRAP-AND-CREATE (two belts, the Rising Star champion Slade still billed "the current PCW Rising Star Champion" on Turmoil 27 of 3 Apr 2001 while The Chef carried the European belt), while the fed's own later newsdesk trivia line — carried on its site from 2002 on — calls it a RENAME: "That PCW once renamed it's Rising Star title to the European title, and was mostly held by Hall of Famer, the Chef?" The event is filed as the later voice names it and the in-period staging is recorded here; the European Championship carries its one reign either way, and the Rising Star reigns are unchanged. Source: PCW's own results page for Turmoil 24, 6 Mar 2001.
events.title: pcw-european

events.note: PCW merged the Rising Star Championship into the Cruiserweight Championship on this night and said so in its own voice: "the Cruiserweight and Rising Star titles are merged", "This is the last match ever where the Rising Star title will be seen", and "The following match is scheduled for one fall! And will crown the undisputed Primetime Championship Wrestling Cruiserweight Champion!". Anarchy (Rising Star) beat Brandi (Cruiserweight) and left with one belt. The fed's own title log carries no row for the merge. PCW REVIVED the Rising Star Championship four months later — Shanghaied 2003 of 26 Jan 2003 crowns "the first Rising Star Champion in a very long time" and Fusion 108 of 7 Feb 2003 calls it "the newly revived Rising Star division" — so this records a dated event, not a final state. Source: PCW's own results page for Turmoil 96, 17 Sep 2002.
events.title: pcw-cruiserweight

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Tag Team Championship was first won by Goovil on 22 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 51 reigns on it, across 35 different champions. The longest is E2's, 274 days from 25 May 2003. Three of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. Mega Soaring Arrows held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's Television Championship was first won by Revenant on 22 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 46 reigns on it, across 38 different champions. The longest is Teresa Tomas's, 84 days from 22 December 2002. Four of its reigns ended outside a match — handed over or vacated. Tessa Windsor held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: World Championship
titles.epitaph: PCW's World Championship was first won by Kremmen on 22 October 2000. The fed's own record carries 35 reigns on it, across 28 different champions. The longest is Skylar Green's, 265 days from 25 May 2003. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. The belt left Inphino Blitz on 23 February 2004, stripped from the holder, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: PFW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: A stepping-stone title noted for changing hands often.

titles.name: PFW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own most prestigious title, its own flyer noting few handlers have ever held it.

titles.name: PFWL Jr Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by "Dirty" Dan Fuller over Ted Rayden at the founding-era PPV; defends successfully at RoughHouse 96.

titles.name: PFWL North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Titan Team named first champions at the founding-era PPV.

titles.name: PFWL Pro Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Volcano across the recorded cards; Kinkos earns a title shot by defeating Johnny Dingo.

titles.name: PFWL World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Petty Officer Pain at the founding-era PPV; "Badd Boy" Derrick Stardom challenges by RoughHouse 96.

titles.name: PFWL World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "P&P" per the RSPWF awards-ballot sig-block bycatch record (dated 10-27-96 through 03-30-97).

titles.name: PIWA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a barb-wire cage match on the fed's own served March Madness card, its title-picture centerpiece.

titles.name: PIWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on the fed's own served March Madness card, the match that touched off a multi-stable brawl.

titles.name: PPWO Arizona State Championship
titles.epitaph: The PPWO's regional secondary title found its first and, in this collection's holdings, only champion in J'ster, whose reign the fed's own newsletter still carried unbroken as of its last surviving issue.
titles.notes: Source: PPWO Matchwatch Newsletter, Vol.1 Iss.4 (eIYX69HId2IJ), 11 Dec 1997: "Arizona State Champion: J'ster, Record: 2-0-0, Title Reign: 11/23/97 - Today."

titles.name: PPWO Grand Canyon Championship
titles.epitaph: A cruiserweight title created sometime before the held record's mid-December snapshot, and vacant every time the fed's own newsletter reported on it.
titles.notes: Source: PPWO Matchwatch Newsletter, Vol.1 Iss.4 (eIYX69HId2IJ), 11 Dec 1997: "Grand Canyon Champion: Vacant." Not mentioned in Handbook v1.0 (23 Nov); present by the newsletter's own 11 Dec issue -- created sometime in that window, not otherwise dated.

titles.name: PPWO Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The PPWO's top singles title sat vacant throughout this collection's own holdings window, named in the fed's own Handbook and newsletter but never once billed with a challenger or a match.
titles.notes: Source: PPWO Matchwatch Newsletter, Vol.1 Iss.4 (eIYX69HId2IJ), 11 Dec 1997: "PPWO Heavyweight Champion: Vacant."

titles.name: PPWO Tucson Heavyweight Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The PPWO's tag championship, held by Money and Power from their crowning in early November 1997 through the end of this collection's own holdings, undefeated across the three defenses the fed's own newsletter records.
titles.notes: Source: PPWO Matchwatch Newsletter, Vol.1 Iss.4 (eIYX69HId2IJ), 11 Dec 1997: "Tucson Tag Team Champions: Money and Power, Record: 3-0-0, Title Reign: 11/8/97 - Today."

titles.name: 5 Star Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's 5 Star Title was first won by Mark Blaze on 23 June 2003. The fed's own record carries 31 reigns on it, across 25 different champions. The longest is Tyler Rayne's, 275 days from 30 January 2008. Three of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder. Roxy Phoenix held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Alias Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's Alias Title was first won by JTF on 3 March 2004, who became its Xposure Champion; its first four champions carried it under names of their own — Xposure, roC-TV, PRIMEal Rage and PRIMEtime — and the fed's own cards and title log also bill it the Pulse Title and the Internet Title. The fed's own record carries 14 reigns on it, across 14 different champions. The longest is The Illustrious Face-Eater's, 189 days from 16 November 2005. Three of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt or vacated. PRIME merged it into the 5 Star Title on 30 May 2007.

events.note: The fed's own page, closing the 'ALIAS TITLE (DEFUNCT)' section: 'At ReVolution 129, in the "Champions Collide" match, The Supreme Machine (5-Star Champion) defeated Easton Hall (Alias Champion) and Dusk (Intense Champion) in a triple threat match. Sirrajin was declared the final Alias Champion and then the title was merged with the 5-Star Title.' The fed's own title log carries the change but no row for the merge itself. Source: The fed's own card, ReVolution of 30 May 2007, 'Champions Collide: Killean Sirrajin (5-Star) vs. Dusk (Intense) vs. Easton Hall (Alias)', and PRIME's own Title Histories page.

titles.name: Dual Halo
titles.epitaph: PRIME's annual two-ring elimination match at Culture Shock, whose winner took a guaranteed wish, the Golden Ticket. The fed's own Records & Superlatives page lists seven winners, one a year from 2004 to 2010.

titles.name: Global Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's Global Title was first won by Alex Caine on 6 July 2003. The fed's own record carries 10 reigns on it, across 8 different champions. The longest is Ignatius Lisieux's, 152 days from 23 February 2004. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. PRIME renamed it the Universal Title on 26 September 2004.

events.note: PRIME's own title history: 'At this point in time, the Global title ceased to be, and the top prize in PRIME was declared the Universal Championship.' The Universal section opens 'Black Angel declared inaugural champion after vacation of Global Title at King of Kings 2 (9/26/04)' and continues the Global's own numbering. Source: PRIME's own Title Histories page.

titles.notes: PRIME's own Title Histories page, its 'GLOBAL TITLE (DEFUNCT)' section: ten numbered reigns, 6 July 2003 – 26 September 2004; the Universal section continues its numbering from '1. (11.)'.

titles.name: Intense Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's Intense Title was first won by Rock Startling on 6 July 2003. The fed's own record carries 31 reigns on it, across 28 different champions. The longest is Vangelus Olsig's, 361 days from 24 July 2005. Five of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. Its last champion, Seymour Almasy, vacated it on 1 August 2011.

titles.name: Internet Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's own title log files four reigns under the Internet Title between May and September 2006 — The Illustrious Face-Eater's, then Tony Gamble's from 24 May, Jonathon Winters' from 8 July and Adam's from 19 September — and its own title history lists the same changes, on the same nights, as reigns of the Alias Title.
titles.notes: The fed's own title log, five rows under the Internet Title, 24 May – 19 September 2006; its own title history, Alias Title entries 8–11.

titles.name: Jewel in the Crown
titles.epitaph: A tournament PRIME ran once a year from 2003 to 2009, its seven winners listed on the fed's own Records & Superlatives page. By its Hall of Fame page, the first, Ian English, took an automatic Global Title shot from it, at ReVolution 18.

titles.name: Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's Tag Team Title was first won by Mark Blaze & Andy Magnum on 14 September 2003. The fed's own record carries 34 reigns on it, across 31 different champions. The longest is Crudely Civilized's, 134 days from 12 March 2004. Four of its reigns ended outside a match — handed over or vacated. Change in Spades held it at the end of the surviving record. PRIME suspended its tag division after Culture Shock 2010.

titles.name: Universal Title
titles.epitaph: PRIME's Universal Title was first won by Black Angel on 26 September 2004. The fed's own record carries 22 reigns on it, across 17 different champions. The longest is Jason Snow's, 401 days from 13 March 2009. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Hessian held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: PRMW Latin Kings Tag Team Champions
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling territory, attested for 3 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: PRMW Southern Star Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling territory, attested for 1 reign in its own record. Continues Lucha Revolution Wrestling's own Southern Star Title after it transferred to this territory.

titles.name: PRMW WBC Maya Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Puerto Rico Monsoon Wrestling territory, attested for 3 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: PRODIGY Unified World Championship
titles.epitaph: Not one federation's belt but the whole board's, and the CSWA is where its record survives. It began as the CSWA's own Unified Championship, built up across 1992 by Hornet challenging the champions of the other leagues in the Enterprise Superleague, and on 24 October 1993 the IRONMAN of CHAMPIONS at the CSWA's LAST CALL II merged the IWCCW World, the AAWC World and that ten-title CSWA belt into one. Over the next three months Hornet added the UWL Superleague's half and the AR Superleague's title to it. It was retired and re-won twice — a sixteen-man tournament in 1994 that ended with a masked man unmasking himself as Mark Windham, a 128-man ULTRATITLE in 1996 that made Paul Pierce champion — and by 1997 the fed's own page describes it as more than forty championships merged into one and sanctioned by PRODIGY. A five-member committee decided its matches on votes for roleplay quality. Mike Randalls won the last of it on 21 January 1997, the last reign the CSWA's own ledger records. A different fed's broadcast, New Frontier Wrestling's own Wrestlebowl II a decade later, separately bills the same-named belt in a comedic "Monkey Championship Wrestling" interlude — Professor Tremendous, already champion, pinning the last of three billed monkey challengers and unifying it with three more belts. No document joins the two readings; both stand.
titles.notes: Filed under the CSWA because the CSWA is where it started and where its ledger survives; the belt itself was contested across the PRODIGY Wrestling BB's own federations and administered by the Unified Championship Committee, not by the CSWA alone.

titles.name: Pennsylvania State Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: PSW's top singles title, first awarded on the promotion's second broadcast when Lance Hawkins defeated Eric VanGlory.

titles.name: Keystone Championship
titles.epitaph: One of PSW's founding singles titles, named in the promotion's opening announcement; no title match survives in the read record.

titles.name: New England Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: One of PSW's founding singles titles, named in the promotion's opening announcement; no title match survives in the read record.

titles.name: Prime Time Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles title added after PSW's opening announcement, changing hands when Platinum Ro defeated Halo in an impromptu main event.

titles.name: Pennsylvania State Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: PSW's tag title, named in the promotion's opening announcement; the read record's own tag match does not contest it.

titles.name: PTC Cruiserweight Tournament
titles.epitaph: Open to cruiserweights only, run twice: CW1 in 2004 (forty-two entrants across four brackets, free agents permitted alongside PTC and member-fed competitors) and CW2 in 2005, the smallest tournament in the alliance's history at thirty-two entrants. Seymour Almasy's CW1 win extended a run that reached fourteen straight tournament victories across the PIT, CW1 and GTT4 before ending in GTT4's fourth round.

titles.name: PTC Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance's hardcore championship, first won on 21 July 2002 by Menace of the XCWF, who beat Jackson Rust in the final of the R.E.B.E.L. tournament the XCWF ran with PTC's backing and lost it in August to Rust; Rust was stripped of it when he spoke of retiring. The record then reaches the New Era card of 20 April 2003, where the belt already had a history — the results page calls that night only the second defence in the title's own life. Terry Woods came out of semi-retirement to defend it inside the Death Trap, a suspended ring strung with barbed wire over a burning pit, and lost it to Maelgrim in Maelgrim's own debut match. The title was later vacated when Maelgrim and his challenger Kai Shinobi both failed to show for a title match. Tristan Belmont was champion by 27 September 2003 and lost it to Fathom in a hide and seek match on 5 December; Mike Marvelous took it from Fathom in the Lion's Den at WWA's Fiesta on 19 January 2004, Sean McClancy from Marvelous in the Irish Pub Brawl on 21 April, and Moraless from McClancy on UWF's Sunday Afternoon Supremacy on 23 May, before giving it up in July. Joey Vendetti won the vacant title in the Elimination Chamber at PTC Survival on 22 August 2004, Shadow took it from him in a three-way on 22 February 2005, and Nova took it from Shadow in a scaffold match at PRIME's Overkill on 15 May; Nova vacated it on 31 August. Hoyt Williams won the vacant title, while Rich “The Renegade” Rollins took the vacant PTC Global Championship, in a Scavenger Hunt Match at PTC's Super Series I on 6 November 2005. Archibald MacGregor, a free agent, took it from him in a judged title match (the forum's own results are dated 4 June 2006; the fed's later write-up says March) and held it until 29 December 2006, when he dropped out of his next defence and the title went to Nova, the first man to hold it twice. Dusk won the last Extreme Title match, an eight-way, on 15 February 2007, and lost the belt to Jason Snow on 30 April 2007, when it was folded into the PTC Unified Championship. PTC's own title log dates three of these wins differently from the hosts' own cards and PTC's own records of the matches — Marvelous's to 21 January 2004, McClancy's to 20 April and Vendetti's to 9 November 2004, the day the results were posted — and puts MacGregor's win on an AWC card of 30 May 2006; the dates above are the cards' and records' own. Who held it before Woods, and how Woods won it, the record does not settle.
titles.notes: The belt's first two reigns are recorded: Menace won it on 21 July 2002 in the final of the R.E.B.E.L. tournament, and lost it about two weeks later to Jackson Rust, who was stripped of it when he spoke of retiring. Which held record Jackson Rust is has not been settled, so his reign carries the name as PTC's own title log bills him. Nothing survives about who held the title, or how, between his reign and Terry Woods's, which begins at a date nobody has located. At New Era, the results page has Rust at ringside helping Maelgrim, taking revenge for "his title loss, which he didn't actually lose".

titles.name: PTC Global Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance's top prize, defended in an open 128-competitor tournament (eighty signed in the first seventy-two hours) and, by the record's own count, held by sixteen different superstars whose reigns the record places before it was unified with the PTC Extreme Championship on 30 April 2007. Its lineage runs from Vampir Nosferatu's tournament win over Jay Phoenix at PCW's Friday Fusion, through Obsidian, Donny Diamond, three reigns for Seymour Almasy, Chris Storm, Jesse Jamester (who won it from Storm in a four-way crossover title match XUW's own Reborn 2004 show hosted, representing Global Wrestling against Apocalypse and Patti Anderson of Furiously Addictive Wrestling and Four Winds Wrestling), Hessian, Saij, the Latch Key Kid, Emilio Rage, Karina Wolfenden (who vacated it the night she won it), Rich “The Renegade” Rollins, Uber Judge, Shadow and Kimbusa, to Clinton Sage, whose reign ended when Jason Snow won the match that unified the belt with the PTC Extreme Championship. That unified belt, the PTC Unified Championship, now has a record of its own. The sources do not agree on everything: PTC's own title log and PTCpedia date Vampir Nosferatu's win to the final shown on 23 November 2001, where the alliance's news places his reign in February 2002, and the log dates Almasy's win of the title at PTC Survival to 9 November 2004, the day the results were posted, where the show's own billed date is 22 August. The news also has Ignatius Lisieux, who “defeated the dreaded Global Title Curse”, as champion by April 2004, and speaks of a second, unnamed Global Title Tourney winner; PTC's own title log lists neither, so those two reigns stand as the news gives them. Jay Phoenix reached this title's own tournament final once more and lost the judged decision by three points — the closest he came to the biggest prize the whole alliance offered.

titles.name: PTC Infinite Gauntlet Championship
titles.epitaph: The prize of PTC's Infinite Gauntlet, the forum's perpetual roleplay competition, in which each round's winner stayed on as champion. The Uber Judge took it in the first round on 4 June 2005; twenty-six more reigns followed, twenty-five champions in all, until the last round on 20 December 2010, when the host's replies named James von Doom the last champion. Alcaeus was stripped of it in May 2006, and two champions vacated it.
titles.notes: The fed's own table of champions counts 26 reigns by 24 champions and ends with Eegor; the twenty-seventh reign here is read from the host's replies of 20 December 2010 and is graded presumed.

titles.name: PTC Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance's tag team championship, first won at the end of a tournament that ran across its member feds for the better part of a year and finished at New Era on 20 April 2003 — Shane Stone and the Bum Boozler, billed as Homo/Phobic, over the Shadow Riders of Lights Out Wrestling. They held it until 3 February 2004, when the Bum Boozler withdrew from tag team competition and the titles were declared vacant. Souls of the Black Lotus won the vacant titles in a three-way on 19 May 2004 and vacated them on 9 July, when the team retired; the Shadow Riders won them at PTC Survival on 22 August 2004 and lost them around 21 December to Clique Clique BOOM~! in a steel cage match decided on the roleplays. The Masked Monkeys of UWF won them on 24 March 2005 and lost them on 26 April to Unholy Matrimony, Seymour Almasy and Aerith Almasy of UWF, in a three-way decided on the judges' scores for the roleplays, which no federation would host and which was never written; the Killer Pirates of the Outer Caribbean took them from Unholy Matrimony uncontested on 28 May, when the champions did not roleplay, and held them until 4 September, when they were vacated because the team was no longer active in PRIME. The record's last word on the belt is the opening match of PTC vs Archibald MacGregor on 15 September 2006, where Unite, billed as the current GCW Tag Team Champions, won the vacant title over the Killer Pirates of the Outer Caribbean; they were the last champions, and the title was retired on 6 January 2007. PTC's own title log dates the Shadow Riders' win to 9 November 2004, the day the results were posted, where the show's own billed date is 22 August.
titles.notes: The fed's own pages style the belt three ways on one night — "PTC Tag Team Titles Match" on the card, "PTC World Tag Team Title Match" as the results' own match header, and "PTC Tag Team Champions" in the commentary that crowned them. Recorded under the shortest form, with the others as aka.

titles.name: PTC Tag Team Tournament
titles.epitaph: A tag-team tournament the alliance ran on an earlier board of its own, whose brackets and final do not survive; what survives of it is the team it crowned, attested by a contributor who wrestled it and by a beaten opponent answering him in the alliance's own forum two years later. The alliance's own board carries a further tag-team tournament, whose final was judged in April 2004, so this was not the only one it ran.

titles.name: PTC Unified Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt PTC made on 30 April 2007 by unifying its Global and Extreme Titles, in a match decided by judges on the roleplays. Jason Snow won it that day; Clinton Sage, Tchu and Lindsay Troy held it after him, each winning it on another federation's card. Lindsay Troy was the last champion: the title was retired in May 2008.
titles.notes: PTC's own title log dates the retirement to a forum post of 13 May 2008; PTCpedia gives 14 May.

titles.name: PTC Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Made for Angelo Deville after he won GTT3, PTC's third Golden Turnbuckle Tournament, in 2002. PCW's Alliances card of 24 November 2002 bills it as the WT Universal Championship; Deville kept it there against Xavier Kannon, then against Syko Arsonist on a DWO special event, and lost it to Alan Kriegman on OSW's Saturday Night Slam, four judges' votes to three. A round robin to find Kriegman a challenger was called off unfinished. PTC's history of its Global Championship leaves this belt out.
titles.notes: Angelo Deville's PRIME biography card; PCW's Alliances 2002 card; PTCpedia's GTT history; PTC forum posts 132383, 141903, 170608 and 120404 (Deville's own account), 297925 (Syko Arsonist: "the only PTC vs WT match for the Universal Title") and 241787 (the PTCpedia editor: the Universal and Global titles "were separate belts").

titles.name: PWC Puerto Rican Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles title, decided for the first time in an eleven-part tournament that crowned the promotion's own first champion.

titles.name: PURE All-Asia Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship PURE ran through the last three months of its record, and the one belt it moved between its two touring brands. Senji Yulav was its first champion, billed as such from the fed's own January 2003 shows onward. Kohana took it from him at Final Destinies in the Tokyo Dome on 2 March 2003, by submission. A week later at Budokan Hall, Raizo Tenzan beat Kohana for it in ten minutes and thirty-nine seconds, in a match PURE booked to settle which of its two brands the belt would follow; Tenzan took it from the referee's hands rather than be presented with it. The surviving record carries no later change.
titles.notes: Attested by PURE's own show scripts for Final Destinies (2 March 2003) and the Budokan Ikusa (9 March 2003), by its own news rows of 7 and 18 February 2003, and by the roster cards for Senji Yuvlav ("First Ever Pure All Asia Champion") and Raizo Tenzan. Whether this belt is the same championship as the PURE Asian National Title the fed ran a tournament for in May 2002 is not settled by the record: the names differ, the eras do not overlap, and Yuvlav's own card calls him the first ever holder. Filed as a distinct title, and the question is recorded rather than answered.

titles.name: PURE Asian National Title
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html) and by its own news page, which reports a first-round tournament match at Ikusa III (/promotions/pure/archive/news.html). PURE ran a separately-named PURE All-Asia Championship through the first three months of 2003, whose own first holder is billed on his own roster card as "First Ever Pure All Asia Champion"; whether that belt is this one renamed or a second championship is not settled by the record, and the two are held as distinct titles. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
titles.epitaph: A belt PURE ran a tournament for and never crowned inside the surviving record. Its own columnist argued the division belonged to Inphino Blitz on three counts and then argued against himself, calling it a bit of an oxymoron to have a gaijin as Asian National Champion; three of the four other men he ranked in it — Shirata Rinjiro, Masanobu Ozaki and Steven Windsor — were released within three weeks. The fed's own pay-per-view announcement of 21 May 2002 promised the first Asian Champion would be named at Future Destinies, alongside the first World Champion. The held record stops before either.

titles.name: PURE Jr. Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Ikusa IV card, which bills a defence (/promotions/pure/archive/ikusa-4-card.html), and by its own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html). Its whole lineage is the fed's own: a complete Junior Heavyweight Championship history of six numbered reigns, served at /promotions/pure/archive/junior-heavyweight-championship-history.html. Its champions page carries only the holder of the moment — "Champion: El Romantico" in its January 2003 state, "Champion: Radiant" in its last — and Radiant's own roster card carries the only dated list of defences any PURE belt has. The history and the show scripts disagree twice, and both stand each time: the history names Ikusa III for the change of 16 June 2002 that the Ikusa V script carries, and it has Charlie Loc pin The End for the belt on 28 July 2002 where PCW's own Wrestle Vessel script has him pin Alexander Miyagawa for it. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
titles.epitaph: The first belt PURE awarded, and the only one it carried through both of its runs. The End won it on 28 April 2002 at Ikusa II in Matsumoto, beating The H.I.T. and Kensuke Suzahara in a three-way the fed billed as the crowning of its first ever champion. He lost it seven weeks later at Ikusa V in the Sapporo Dome, pinned by The H.I.T. in a tag match the fed put his title on, with The H.I.T. announced in the ring as the new champion, and won it back that summer in a fatal four-way over Inphino Blitz that PURE's own title history places on a show called Ikusa 6 and does not date. It left him for good on 28 July 2002, in another federation's ring: Charlie Loc took it in the first fall of a two-fall match at PCW's Wrestle Vessel that carried the PURE Junior Heavyweight and PCW Cruiserweight titles at once, and was billed afterwards as the first man to win a PURE title outside a PURE ring. He lost it on 13 October 2002 to a masked DJ Nygma, unmasked in the ring that night as El Romantico, who was still champion and under contract to another federation when PURE re-opened. PURE decided the belt again by tournament in January 2003, and Radiant won it on the 26th at Hakatanomori Football Stadium, beating Isao Asai in thirty minutes and fifteen seconds. He beat Asai twice more, then wrestled El Mesias to a draw at Budokan Hall on 9 March 2003, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: PURE Tag Team Titles
