titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own division rankings, which name a PURE Tag Team Title Tournament as forthcoming (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html), and by its own title-history page, rendered from newsdata board 52's neighbour board 78: "#1 - Mang-A-Hero and Inphino Blitz. Defeated the team of Ebola III and Alexander Miyagawa to win the belts at Ikusa V." Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
titles.epitaph: PURE's original tag team titles, awarded once and never defended. Inphino Blitz and Mang-A-Hero won them on 16 June 2002 at Ikusa V in the Sapporo Dome, beating Ebola III and the fed's own owner Alexander Miyagawa in a match booked on air as the first awarding of the belts. No other team held them: PURE retired them when it re-opened in January 2003 and declared a three-man Trinity Tag Team Championship in their place. Mang-A-Hero, on commentary a year later, called himself and his partner the first and last PURE Tag Team Champions.

events.note: PURE's own title-history page, in its own words: "#2 - Titles retired. Retired belts upon the reopening of PURE." Its own show commentary says the same from the other side — "We were the FIRST AND LAST PURE TAG TEAM CHAMPIONS!" / "That's only because Mina retired that spot for the Trinity!" The Trinity Tag Team Titles declared in their place are their own title row, not a continuation of this lineage.

titles.name: PURE Trinity Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The three-man tag team championship PURE instated when it re-opened in January 2003, in place of the two-man tag titles it retired at the same time. Shaun Styles and the Sushi Crew were its first champions, beating the Black Dragons for the belts. The Suburban Ninja Clan took them at Budokan Hall on 9 March 2003, and eight days later answered with an open challenge to any three-man team in the federations PURE shared a host with, offering to defend the belts on those feds' own shows. The surviving record carries no later change.
titles.notes: Instated on PURE's own studio show Axcess, in the fed's own words: "PURE has now instated the brand new PURE Trinity Tag Team titles. Puro wrestling is quite famous for their 6 man tag team action and it was only a matter of time before we embraced that staple of the culture." Its lineage sits at the tail of the same title-history page that carries the two-man tag titles' (newsdata board 78, the page world.shtml renders): "#3 - Trinity Tag Team Championship declared. Sushi Crew / Shaun Styles become new champions over Black Dragons." Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).

titles.name: PURE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own title-history page (/promotions/pure/archive/world-heavyweight-championship-history.html) and by its own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html). That page is rendered from newsdata board 78 and was rewritten in place three times: the held copy reads "#1 - To be determined at 'Future Destinies' (8/14/02)"; the deposit's January 2003 layer reads "#1 - To be determined at a later date (???)"; and the deposit's last layer no longer carries this belt at all, having been overwritten with the tag titles' own history. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
titles.epitaph: PURE announced a World Heavyweight Championship in 2002 and did not award it. The fed built a championship-history page for the belt and filled it with a single line — a first champion to be determined at a pay-per-view in the Tokyo Dome — and rewrote that line twice without ever naming a holder; the belt was still vacant when PURE re-opened in January 2003. It was decided on 2 March 2003 at Final Destinies, in the Tokyo Dome after all, by a four-man tournament Jesse Ramey won over Eddie Mandrake. Ramey defended it a week later at Budokan Hall against Jason Marah, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: PVWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Billy Dahl across both surviving shows; the fed's own 29 December broadcast credits him as "the second two-time PVWF Intercontinental champion," implying an off-page title change and reclaim at the unheld X-Mas Explosion PPV.

titles.name: PVWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant as of 22 December, contested in a match that show; Slim & Elle win the vacant title at the unheld X-Mas Explosion PPV and defend twice on 29 December, both matches ending without a finish.

titles.name: PVWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Big Dave on 22 December; by 29 December the champion is Pearl, the title having changed at the unheld X-Mas Explosion PPV. Pearl's title defense against former champion Stephen McCoy ends without a finish, interrupted by a backstage angle.

titles.name: PVWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Referenced only as discontinued ("whatever happened to the PVWF Woman's title") on the 22 December show; no holder or discontinuation date survives.

titles.name: PVWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Aaron Bolles across both surviving December 1997 shows; defends in a non-title match against Tonzee.

titles.name: PWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won on the same June tournament card as the singles belts and defended through a summer of run-ins and DQ finishes, changing hands only once on camera — an upset by the Dogs of War — before it reached Crime & Punishment, its last PWA-billed holders, in time for the Clash of the Masters.

titles.name: PWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded as the June tournament's own consolation prize and defended more often, and more cleanly, than either of the PWA's other two belts across the whole recorded summer.

titles.name: PWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a June 1992 tournament final between two 600-pound-class monsters and defended almost every week the recap's own record covers, changing hands four times before the promotion's own summer ended — and a fifth time, for good, when its last PWA-billed holder lost it to the FWF's own Doctor Death at the Clash of the Masters.

titles.name: PWA World Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title History page runs one of the richest dated chains in this collection's own holdings, fully chained here across fifty-nine recorded reigns from Tundra (EMT)'s tournament win at "Chaos" (30 March 1999) through Aura's win over Jamie Havoc at "Thriller" (14 November 2002), the corpus's own last-attested change. Sirus Moran alone holds it five separate times, and Showtime five more; the belt is vacated and re-tournamented on several occasions, including once when its own champion (Ashram) "leaves for personal reasons," and splits into a two-holder belt three times running in the summer of 2002 before Fallen Angel unifies it. A handful of holders survive only as bare names on the fed's own page (King Agony, Kevin Cool, Jamie Havoc) with nothing else in the held record to build a fuller character record from.

titles.name: Tempest's Coming Storm Championship
aka: the soon to be renamed PWA Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by exactly one man in the surviving record, defended once on the academy's own February 2003 card, and renamed in a June 2003 tournament announcement the surviving record does not carry a result for.
titles.note: The academy's own record disagrees with itself about whether it had a belt at all: its February 2003 rules page says "no titles," while the 9 Feb 2003 card stages a singles match for this title with a champion already billed, and a June 2003 news post runs a tournament for "the soon to be renamed PWA Championship." Both readings stand (#sources-disagree); no result for the June tournament survives.

titles.name: The Legends (the white jacket)
titles.epitaph: The trophy of the first major of The Circuit, a round robin of 2011 decided in a tie-break final; SJH won it by beating Alex Austin.

titles.name: Prodigy Classic Championship
titles.epitaph: The title of the one-off sixteen-man Prodigy Classic of summer 2011, run for the old Prodigy characters and won by Hornet at Madison Square Garden.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: PWC's Tag Team Championship was first won by Penance on 8 February 2003. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. The longest is Penance's, 56 days from 8 February 2003. Chandler Tsonda held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: PWC's Television Championship was first won by Hoyt Williams on 3 May 2003. Hoyt Williams held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: PWC's World Heavyweight Championship was first won by Jim Axtell on 13 April 2003. Jim Axtell held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: PWE Dream Championship
titles.epitaph: Chaos held it through the spring of 2005 and kept it against Kurt Angle in a Weapon of Choice match at Annihilation. By Deadly Game that November the fed's own results page was calling the same belt the UCW Dream Championship, defended in a cage of weapons by Jarrell Young against three challengers; both names are the fed's own and neither is treated as a correction of the other.

titles.name: PWE Hardcore Championship
titles.notes: The only appearance of the belt in the held record is the segment heading "Seg 9 – Hardcore Champion?!" and the sentence under it (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/underground-network-oct-10-milw-wi-2005-10-09.html).
titles.epitaph: Named once in the surviving record, in the ninth segment of an Underground broadcast from the Bradley Center on 10 October 2005 that opens on a man holding the belt and a question mark in the segment's own title.

titles.name: PWE Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt at the top of PWE's Revenge brand, and the one its own paperwork keeps changing the name of: the front page called it the PWE World Championship in the spring of 2005 and the Heavyweight Championship by the autumn. Ryan Styles carried it out of Saga III in May and lost it in the main event of Deadly Game at Madison Square Garden on 27 November 2005, to Nicholas Pryde, by submission. Eddy Guerrero had challenged for it a month earlier and Sting a year before that; the fed's own record of who held it before Styles is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: PWE's own front-page results bill this belt, verbatim, as the “WWE Intercontinental Championship” — the fed's own paperwork borrowing a real promotion's real title name rather than inventing one of its own. It ends the only way the surviving record shows it: unified into the PWE Silver Crown when Postal Maniac grabbed both belts at once in a Three Way Asylum Match at Deadly Game 2005, beating co-champion Christian and DisasterPiece.
titles.notes: Named exactly as the fed's own front page billed it — “WWE Intercontinental Championship” — kept here without the real-brand prefix per this registry's own title-naming convention; no other served document names it, and its own prior lineage is not in the surviving record.

events.title: pwe-inc-silver-crown
events.note: Postal Maniac grabbed both belts at once in a Three Way Asylum Match at Deadly Game 2005, unifying them (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/front-page-news-2005-12-05.html).

titles.name: PWE Iron Man Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended, at least once, in the match it is named for: Lee Nolan took it off The Prototype three falls to nothing in a thirty-minute Iron Man match at Deadly Game 2005. Before that The Elite defended it in an Ultimate X match against three challengers at Saga III and lost it to one of them, Clarke "The X" Andrews, at The Reckoning that July.

titles.name: PWE Pure Championship
titles.epitaph: Jeff Jarrett beat Crunch for it at Annihilation in the spring of 2005, which is the only thing PWE's surviving paperwork says about the belt at all.

titles.name: PWE Silver Crown
titles.epitaph: Unified out of two belts and into one at Deadly Game 2005: Postal Maniac defended it against Christian and DisasterPiece in a three-way asylum match, won by grabbing both the Silver Crown and the WWE Intercontinental Championship at once, and the fed's own results say the two titles were unified there.

titles.name: PWE Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt PWE's own records call the longest-held in its history: The Regulator carried it 308 days, longer than any championship reign the fed ever counted. It was held by two men at once for a stretch of 2005, after Revenge's own authority figure named The Regulator and Alex Hoffman co-champions when both made the same opponent tap out in the same match. Homicide had it by the autumn and kept it against The Amityville Horror at Deadly Game.

titles.name: PWE Undisputed Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned out of a tournament whose final the Prodigal Sons reached at Last Man Standing on 28 August 2005, and defended in a tables, ladders and chairs match against Fight Against Prejudice at Deadly Game that November.

titles.name: PWE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: PWE Underground's own top belt — a second, brand-specific championship the surviving record never once shows crossing paths with Revenge's own Heavyweight/World Championship. Chaos carried it into Underground Network on 10 October 2005 and lost it there to Bulldozer, who won it with a sledgehammer shot once the referee was knocked cold; a community wrap-up column the next day corroborated the same result while airing a dispute over the two writers' own RP agreement. A departing champion's own promo names Kurt Angle, ZerO and Tex Graham himself among its past holders, alongside Deuce Jackson before Chaos — spoken evidence only, no dates or documents behind any of it.
titles.notes: Distinct from pwe-inc-heavyweight (Revenge's own belt, Ryan Styles to Nicholas Pryde): the corpus stages what read as two parallel Heavyweight/World title lineages, one per brand, never shown unifying or resolving against each other in any served document. Kept separate rather than merged on guesswork — see the wing's own tier_source note.

titles.name: PWE Entertainment Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a Tables, Ladders and Chairs match at New Years Resolution by the fed's own president, against a man who had jumped him in a backstage room before the bell and was fired on the microphone for it while still lying in the ring. The president defended it on the Shockwave card of 13 February 2003 against Micheal Flash; whether he kept it is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: PWE Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The third of the three belts PWE crowned in one night. Andre' Sanders beat Justice Paine for it at New Years Resolution on 25 January 2003 and was still listed its champion on the fed's own Champions page a fortnight later, with Walter Parker named his first contender.

titles.name: PWE Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own Champions page of 13 February 2003 lists the belt with VACANT in the champion's row and a dash in both contender slots (/promotions/pwe-projectefed/archive/champions-2003-02.html); its own Tag Teams page, captured in July, is an empty table (tagteams.html). No reign of it survives.
titles.epitaph: PWE hung a tag team championship on its own Champions page, put VACANT where the champions' names go, wrote a dash in both contender slots, and awarded it +7 points on its own point system for a win that the surviving record never records anybody having. Its own Tag Teams page was still empty in July 2003.

titles.name: PWE Undisputed Championship
titles.epitaph: PWE's own top belt, and the only one it ever crowned in a ladder match. Four men climbed for it at New Years Resolution on 25 January 2003 and Scott Curtis came down with it, helped up the ramp afterwards by the president who had just knocked one of the other three through the ropes. Five days later Lynx put the champion's head through a vending machine backstage and asked for an inferno match for it at the next pay-per-view; the fed was still running a tournament for shots at it in April, and the answer to Lynx's question is not in the surviving record.

titles.name: PWF North American Championship
titles.epitaph: One of three titles announced at the fed's own founding, to be awarded through a tournament at its first PPV, 'In Search of a Champion' -- never posted in the held record. No champion is ever named.

titles.name: PWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: One of three titles announced at the fed's own founding, to be awarded through a tournament at its first PPV, 'In Search of a Champion' -- never posted in the held record. No champion is ever named.

titles.name: PWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: One of three titles announced at the fed's own founding, to be awarded through a tournament at its first PPV, 'In Search of a Champion' -- never posted in the held record. No champions are ever named.

The PWF Challenge Title's own dated ledger runs three reigns deep and closes mid-chain: Crusader Chrome won the title's own first-ever match — a fatal four-way over Theros Macalvia, The Fro, and Maxwell Powers — at Saturday Night Havoc, 24 March 2001; Power G won it from him on 7 April; Rye Hazwaki won it from Power G on 18 April, the ledger's own last entry.
titles.name: PWF Challenge Title
titles.notes: The fed's own four remaining named titles (European, Hardcore, Extreme, Tag Team) are named on the Records page but no ledger, reign, or dated mention survives for any of them in this capture. The World and US Titles are also unledgered here, but their own reigns are independently documented from other primary sources — see pwf-powersite-world and pwf-powersite-us.

titles.name: PWF US Title
titles.epitaph: The PWF US Title's only documented reign in this capture is Rye Hazwaki's, won in the same Double Jeopardy Ladder Match that crowned Crusader Chrome World Champion at War Games, 27 May 2001, with Havok's interference — the same assist that formed the OutKasts.
titles.notes: Several wrestlers' own bio cards claim further, undated US Title reigns from the pre-hibernation "old PWF" era (Crusader Chrome among them) — bio-attested only, not entered as reign rows for the same reason as the World Title above.

titles.name: PWF World Title
titles.epitaph: The PWF World Title's own surviving record is a two-reign, seven-month fragment either side of a gap the capture never closes: Jason "The Goat" Doods won it in a Trio Ladder Match at THE PWF REBIRTH, the fed's own 1 October 2000 relaunch, and Crusader Chrome won it from an unnamed prior holder in a Double Jeopardy Ladder Match at War Games, 27 May 2001, with Bloodbath's interference — the assist that formed the OutKasts. No document in this capture records how the title moved between those two nights; by 24 March 2001, Michael Pellington is announcing a fresh tournament to crown a new champion, and Antonio Gambino is publicly demanding the belt back as the fed's own pre-hibernation titleholder "the first time around."
titles.notes: Several wrestlers' own bio cards claim further, undated World Title reigns from the pre-hibernation "old PWF" era (Gambino, Eraser, DeMoN, Blackbird, Firestorm among them) — bio-attested only, with no date surviving to sequence any of them against each other or against this ledger, so none are entered as reign rows. See each character's own tenure note.

titles.name: PWF Title
titles.epitaph: Introduced as PWF's own top title with no champion; a battle royal to crown the first PWF Champion was announced for the promotion's next show, which does not survive in the documents read.

titles.name: PWF XTag Titles
titles.epitaph: Introduced as PWF's own tag team title, announced vacant alongside the promotion's roster growth; no reign survives in the documents read.

titles.name: PWH Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Pro Wrestling Honor's own tag title, changing hands twelve times before it was left vacant at the federation's own close.
titles.notes: Structured from the federation's own complete title-history page.

titles.name: PWH World Championship
titles.epitaph: Pro Wrestling Honor's own top singles title, changing hands seven times before it was left vacant at the federation's own close.
titles.notes: Structured from the federation's own complete title-history page.

titles.name: Chris Williams Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The PWW's television title, named for Chris Williams, a PWW executive killed in a road accident on 4 May 1999. It is the belt the community's own Chris Williams Memorial Cup grew out of: the Cup's own roll of winners dates the tournament "right back to the first ever tournament to crown what was then called the Chris Williams Television Title (over at PWW)." Jay Phoenix held it among the five.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own account of its own history on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), which lists the five titles of the 1997-2001 run. The revival's four divisions are filed as their own rows; nothing held states whether they continued these belts. The CWTV abbreviation is the staff page's own; the expansion and the tournament origin are the Chris Williams Memorial Cup roll's own words, from the Primetime Central forum (post 230294, workshop-held). Chris Williams is on the memorial register.

titles.name: PWW Eternal Championship
titles.epitaph: The main title of the PWW's 2004 reopening — "the pinnacle of a wrestler's achievement," in the federation's own words, defended once a month. The reopening never staged a show, and the belt has no recorded holder.
titles.notes: Named as the Eternal division (world) on the federation's own 2004 rulebook (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/rules-2004.html) and listed as a championship on its own front page of 25 November 2003 (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/front-page-2003-11-25.html). Whether it continued the PWW World Championship of the 1997-2001 run is not stated anywhere held.

titles.name: PWW European Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the five titles of the PWW's 1997-2001 run. Nothing held records a single reign of it beyond the federation's own statement that Jay Phoenix held it.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own account of its own history on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), which lists the five titles of the 1997-2001 run. The revival's four divisions are filed as their own rows; nothing held states whether they continued these belts.

titles.name: PWW Gemini Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag title of the PWW's 2004 reopening, open both to two singles wrestlers pairing up and to a handler running a team of his own, and defended every two weeks. It has no recorded holder.
titles.notes: Named as the Gemini division (tag) on the federation's own 2004 rulebook (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/rules-2004.html) and listed on the front page of 25 November 2003. Whether it continued the PWW Tag Team Championship of the 1997-2001 run is not stated anywhere held.

titles.name: PWW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the five titles of the PWW's 1997-2001 run. Nothing held records a single reign of it beyond the federation's own statement that Jay Phoenix held it, and most of them more than once.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own account of its own history on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), which lists the five titles of the 1997-2001 run. The revival's four divisions are filed as their own rows; nothing held states whether they continued these belts.

titles.name: Master of the Mat
titles.epitaph: The PWW's own annual single-elimination tournament, open to the whole roster, whose winner claimed the title of Master of the Mat — an accolade rather than a belt, never defended. Its second annual running was the federation's pay-per-view of 14 November 1999, and the reopening of 2004 kept it on the calendar. Jay Phoenix is the one winner the surviving record names.
titles.notes: Set out in the federation's own 2004 rulebook (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/rules-2004.html): "Once a year, there will also be a single elimination style tournament, open to the whole roster, the winner of which will be able to claim the title of 'Master of the Mat'. This is not an official belt, but is rather an accolade, and will not be defended." The 1999 running is the federation's own second annual, held as a pay-per-view broadcast from the Sky Dome, Toronto — collected, not served. Jay Phoenix's win is named on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), without a year.

titles.name: PWW Nightmare Championship
titles.epitaph: The hardcore title of the PWW's 2004 reopening — tables, falls count anywhere, no disqualification — defendable, in the federation's own words, anytime, anyplace. It has no recorded holder.
titles.notes: Named as the Nightmare division (hardcore / extreme) on the federation's own 2004 rulebook (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/rules-2004.html) and listed on the front page of 25 November 2003.

titles.name: PWW Shooting Star Championship
titles.epitaph: The PWW's starting title at the 2004 reopening, open to the whole roster and defended every week — "the first title on the road to the World title," and no less important for it, the federation said. It has no recorded holder.
titles.notes: Named as the Shooting Star division (television) on the federation's own 2004 rulebook (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/rules-2004.html), which describes it as similar to a television title in other federations, and listed on the front page of 25 November 2003. Whether it continued the Chris Williams Television Championship is not stated anywhere held.

titles.name: PWW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag title of the PWW's 1997-2001 run. Nothing held records a reign of it beyond the federation's own statement that Jay Phoenix held it.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own account of its own history on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), which lists the five titles of the 1997-2001 run. The revival's four divisions are filed as their own rows; nothing held states whether they continued these belts.

titles.name: PWW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The PWW's main title through the 1997-2001 run. Its January 1999 broadcast has Johnny Blaze carrying it as champion after taking it from Congo, with a rematch set for Winter Warzone on 7 February, and the federation's own later account names Jay Phoenix as a two-time holder and the only man ever to hold every PWW title.
titles.notes: Named in the federation's own account of its own history on the 2004 staff page (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/staff-2004.html), which lists the five titles of the 1997-2001 run. The revival's four divisions are filed as their own rows; nothing held states whether they continued these belts. The 1999 broadcast is the only held document that stages a reign of it (/promotions/pww-worldwide-1999/archive/pww-wednesday-night-wildfire-1999-01-21.html).

titles.name: PWX Hybrid Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists 24 reigns of the Hybrid Championship, from John Pariah on 2 September 2005 to Terrell Odom, who won it on 7 December 2009 and was stripped of it for injury on 18 January 2010. The page says it can be contested under any rules and by wrestlers of any style.
titles.notes: The page calls it the fed's most unique title: contested under any rules and fought for by wrestlers of any style, hence "Hybrid" wrestling.

titles.name: PWX Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists 21 numbered reigns of its tag titles, from Shocker and Mark O'Neal on 16 December 2005 to Corey Gein and Micheal Norcia on 28 October 2007, with the numbers 16 and 18 missing from the page. The last row records the titles vacated when PWX announced its closure in December 2007.
titles.notes: The page says only the top tag teams in the world compete for these titles. Its heading reads "Campeones de Parejas".

titles.name: PWX Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title history lists 19 reigns of the PWX Championship, from Michael Norcia on 30 September 2005 to Brian Hollywood's second, read as 25 January 2010. The title was vacated when PWX announced its closure in December 2007 and was next decided on 18 October 2009, at Never Say Die 2009, when Ness won it from Jackson.
titles.notes: The page calls it the one title every wrestler strives for, PWX's equivalent of a world title though PWX does not recognize it as a world championship.

titles.name: All-Pro Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's champions page of 29 November 2004 lists this belt as vacant, with no champion, venue or date; no holder is recorded.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's champions page of 29 November 2004 lists this belt as vacant, with no champion, venue or date; no holder is recorded.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's champions page of 29 November 2004 lists this belt as vacant, with no champion, venue or date; no holder is recorded.

titles.name: X-Division Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's champions page of 29 November 2004 lists this belt as vacant, with no champion, venue or date; no holder is recorded.

titles.name: Carolina Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, defended at every big event. Marc Tower, Scott Studd, Eddie Cutlass and Ric Beauty all held it during 2002; Christian Demonstone finally won it from Beauty at Ghosts of RAW on Halloween night.

titles.name: Carolina Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Terry Jacobs and Justin Harper took the belts from Kirk Maclean and Stevie Ray Murdoch at Super Sunday, Bloody Sunday in February 2002 and kept them through the winter; by June Jacobs held them with Kevin Simmons, and The Blood Brothers won them in a three-way at Grand Strand Slam.

titles.name: Piedmont Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Carolina title for young contenders, formerly the Carolina TV Title. On 3 February 2002 the masked Estoque won it from Dave Pitrelli inside a steel cage and unmasked as Eddie Cutlass; Christian Demonstone was defending it by June.

titles.name: RAW Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding handbook as its top title, due to be defended every thirty days and first awarded through a sixteen-man tournament announced for 6 December 1998. No result of that tournament survives in the held record.

titles.name: RAW Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding handbook, due to be defended every fifteen days, with a first defense announced for 6 December 1998 between two teams neither otherwise recorded on this wing. No result survives.

titles.name: RAW TV Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding handbook as its weekly-defended title, with a first defense announced for 6 December 1998 between two entrants neither otherwise recorded on this wing. No result survives.

titles.name: RAW United States Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding handbook as its second-ranked title. No holder or defense survives on the record.

The RAWF Hardcore Title changed hands dozens of times across the fed's own surviving ledger, from Victor Synn's own 29 November 1998 debut reign through David Wilson's own win on 27 November 2002, its own final entry in the surviving record.
titles.name: RAWF Hardcore Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (29 Nov 1998 – 27 Nov 2002) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/title-histories.html); only the ledger's own final reign is structured here.

titles.name: RAWF Hardcore Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF Hardcore Tag Team Title's own surviving ledger runs seven reigns, the New Icons' own 30 April 2000 debut through Sabbath and Xtreme One's own reign, vacated 10 September 2000 — per the fed's own ledger heading, "Vacated Due to Unification of Tag Titles" — and never revived.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (30 Apr 2000 – 10 Sep 2000) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/retired-titles.html), entirely before the served show corpus's own 24 May 2002 opening — no reign structured here. The ledger's own vacancy note is ambiguous on which title absorbed which; recorded as read, not resolved.

titles.name: RAWF Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF Intercontinental Title changed hands repeatedly across the fed's own surviving ledger, from T.A. Tony Gunn's own 14 November 1998 debut reign through Spawn's own win at Wednesday Wargames on 18 December 2002, the fed's own three-year-anniversary show, in his second match in the promotion — the title's own last recorded change before the promotion closed five weeks later.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (14 Nov 1998 – 18 Dec 2002) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/title-histories.html); this registry structures every reign from the fed's own 10 May 2002 changeover through the promotion's close.

titles.name: RAWF Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF Tag Team Title changed hands repeatedly across the fed's own surviving ledger, running from the Misfits' own 14 November 1998 debut reign through Ice Cold and Mandy's own win at Friday Fights on 14 July 2002 — the belt's own last held reign before it sat vacant for the promotion's final four months, per the fed's own ledger.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (14 Nov 1998 – 18 Sep 2002) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/retired-titles.html); this registry structures every reign from the fed's own 3 May 2002 changeover onward. The 18 September 2002 vacancy is ledger-sourced only — the served show that date carries no tag title match, an honest gap rather than an inferred one.

titles.name: RAWF Television Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF Television Title's own surviving ledger runs six reigns, Grave Digger's own 18 December 2000 debut through Jaguar Khan's own win on 20 March 2001 — unified into the United States Title one week later, per the fed's own ledger, and never revived.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (18 Dec 2000 – 27 Mar 2001) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/retired-titles.html), entirely before the served show corpus's own 24 May 2002 opening — no reign structured here.

events.title: rawf-united-states
events.note: Jaguar Khan defeated Brandy Sangria to unite the US and TV titles, per the fed's own retired-titles ledger.

titles.name: RAWF United States Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF United States Title changed hands repeatedly across the fed's own surviving ledger, running from Crippler's own 16 January 1999 tournament win through Tony Rocky Horror's own 26 July 2002 win against a vacancy — the belt's own last held reign before it sat vacant for the promotion's final four and a half months, per the fed's own ledger.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (16 Jan 1999 – 11 Sep 2002) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/retired-titles.html); this registry structures every reign from the fed's own 25 January 2002 changeover onward.

titles.name: RAWF Women's Title
titles.epitaph: The RAWF Women's Title's own surviving ledger runs sixteen reigns, Tonya Brosi's own 26 September 1999 debut through Lynn's own reign, vacated by President Chaos on 27 November 2000, per the fed's own ledger, and never revived.
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (26 Sep 1999 – 27 Nov 2000) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/retired-titles.html), entirely before the served show corpus's own 24 May 2002 opening — no reign structured here.

titles.epitaph: The RAWF World Title changed hands dozens of times across the fed's own surviving ledger, from Dray Dogg's own 8 November 1998 debut reign through Darksider's own win at November Nightmares on 27 November 2002 — a Death Cube, Two Out of Three Falls match against Matt Vandal for the belt Brandy Sangria's own three-way elimination defense had left vacant — the title's own last recorded change before the promotion closed nine weeks later.
titles.name: RAWF World Title
titles.notes: Full reign-by-reign chain (8 Nov 1998 – 27 Nov 2002) survives verbatim on the fed's own served ledger (promotions/rawf/archive/title-histories.html); this registry structures every reign from the fed's own 27 April 2002 changeover through the promotion's close, the window the served show corpus itself covers.

titles.name: RCCW European Championship
titles.epitaph: Left the federation when its own champion, Octane, announced his retirement in the ring and walked out with the belt rather than defend it.

titles.name: RCCW Women's World Championship
titles.epitaph: Retired by the federation's own president the same night its last defense — a double countout between Heroine and Freefall — left its lineage unresolved.

titles.name: RCCW World Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Left the federation with its own champion, Piston, who attacked his challenger before the bell of its one surviving defense and walked out of the promotion with the belt.

titles.name: RCCW World Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on the federation's one surviving pay-per-view when Jason Creed pinned the reigning champion, Quezzy, with a standing corkscrew leg whip; a fellow wrestler's own later tally credits a third holder within weeks, though no card documenting that change survives.

titles.name: RCCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top singles title, held by Clutch into its one surviving pay-per-view main event — a bloody Taipei Death Match against the promotion's Hardcore-billed champion, Maverick, that ended without a fall when both men left the cage and traded belts instead.

titles.name: RCCW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended once in this record, in a match between L-Mo and Carnage that a outside interference cut short as a no contest, leaving the title's holder unchanged.

titles.name: RCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Royal Rampage V recap catches this belt mid-lineage: "Sensational" Johnny Lee defends it in a Triple Threat Table Match against Kerry "Carnage" Carter and Raven Midknight on 18 June 2000, eliminated first by Carter, who is in turn eliminated by Midknight for the title. The surviving record opens with Lee already champion and gives no earlier reign.

titles.name: RCW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Royal Rampage V recap catches Adam Adonis as champion, retaining the belt over Nick Fury in a Ladder Match on 18 June 2000 by gouging Fury's eyes to grab it first. The surviving record neither dates his own win nor shows any further defense. A separate, distinct belt from the RCW World Championship, whose own tournament-win notes elsewhere in the held record use the compound name "World/North American Championship" for that title alone -- this belt's own concurrent, separately-defended existence at Royal Rampage V is the receipt that the two titles do not share one lineage.

titles.name: RCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Royal Rampage V recap catches The Commission (Victor Shade & Donald Blake) as champions, retaining the belts over Strictly Business (Warren Knight & Jesse Bishop) by disqualification on 18 June 2000, when Dominion and Minions of Darkness ran in — the losing faction then threw the belts back down at the champions rather than raise them. The surviving record neither dates the champions' own win nor shows any further defense.

titles.name: RCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Royal Rampage V recap catches Jake Rockwell as champion, successfully defending the belt against The Boog-man in a Crowbar-On-A-Pole Match on 18 June 2000. The surviving record neither dates his own win nor shows any further defense.

titles.name: RCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated chain of 17 reigns from K.C. Colossus's tournament win on 8 November 1997 through Rob Holiday's tournament win on 21 October 2001 -- both tournament finals billed on the page itself for the "World/North American Championship," a compound name used only at those two bracket notes and nowhere else in the lineage, distinct from the fed's own separately-defended RCW North American Championship. The Executive holds the belt four separate times, K.C. Colossus three. The page's own ledger records the title vacant from 6 October to 21 October 2000, the last entry before that stretch carrying its own note "Federation closed," and then vacant again for a full year before Rob Holiday's own win -- an unexplained year-long gap in the source's own stated dates, recorded as it stands. The fed's own served Royal Rampage V recap (18 June 2000) corroborates one reign mid-chain, with The Executive successfully defending against Jack McGriff in a nine-fall main event.

titles.name: Re-RAW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Unveiled on Re-RAW's second broadcast as the prize of a fan-voted tournament ahead of the promotion's first pay-per-view; no champion is crowned within this collection's own holdings.

titles.name: REWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by The Patriot via an eight-man battle royal at WrestleMania 1997, the wing's only attested title change.

titles.name: RFHW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in barbed-wire deathmatches from the wing's own founding; Hayabusa won it from Rick Taylor in a Barbed Wire Thumbtack Deathmatch at the wing's only held show, Clash Of The Champions, with the broadcast's own commentary crediting Taylor as the belt's first-ever holder. No further reign survives.
titles.notes: A companion TV Championship and World Championship are also named on this show's own card but neither title change is asserted -- see this wing's own show notes.

titles.name: Red Crown Championship
titles.notes: RLW's own top championship, crowned via a twelve-entrant, multi-round tournament run across the fed's first six broadcasts and decided at its own first internet pay-per-view, Rush Hour.
titles.epitaph: A red iron crown paired with a title belt, first awarded to the winner of RLW's own inaugural Red Crown Tournament and never seen to change hands again in the record this pass could read.

titles.name: RMW National Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Rocky Mountain Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record. Generated as a spin-off from the AAWF Network Title in 2021; its record notes the title was later rebranded as the Summit Championship, with no further reigns surviving under the new name.

titles.name: RMW National Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own Rocky Mountain Wrestling territory, attested for 9 reigns in its own record. Generated as a spin-off from the AAWF Network Tag Team Titles in 2021; its final reign ended in a unification loss to a Calgary Stampede Wrestling team, and the unified title continued in that territory's own record as the Can-Am Tag Champions.

titles.name: ROC European Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Guilty Pleasure on ROC's own champions list of 3 August 2008; no defence survives in this wing's own captures.

titles.name: ROC Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Edge and Diogo X_Day through this wing's own captures; a Summer Bash defence against 619 Tritur and Jesus of Suburbia was set up on ROC #3 after X_Day lost a title-eliminator to 619 Tritur.

titles.name: ROC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Ring Of Champions' own top title, held by MoonPlague through this wing's own captures; a Summer Bash Triple Threat against Sabão and JakerTombstone was set up on ROC #3 after their own number-one-contender match ended in a double count-out.

titles.name: Eclipse Title
titles.epitaph: RPW's Eclipse Title was first won by Karina Wolfenden on 9 November 2003. The fed's own record carries 5 reigns on it, across 4 different champions. The longest is Ilan Levin's, 28 days from 23 November 2003. Gideon Poe held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: RPW's World Heavyweight Title was first won by Gideon Poe on 11 January 2004. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. The longest is Gideon Poe's, 98 days from 11 January 2004. Karina Wolfenden held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Mid South Title
titles.epitaph: RPW's Mid South Title was first won by Chris Storm, before 2004-03-21. The fed's own record carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions. Shawn Stewart held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: RPW's Tag Team Title was first won by Invincible Gabe and Rampage, between 2004-03-14 and 2004-03-21. The fed's own record carries 2 reigns on it, across 2 different champions. The Forsaken held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: RSP Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Handed to its first champion outright by promotion president Sean Christopher rather than contested for, the title changed hands within weeks to a wrestler who insists to this day that his own shoulders were never pinned.

titles.name: RSP Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First won by a beatdown finish the broadcast's own commentary called into question, the belts were held up entirely by the promotion's own vice president after a three-way defense at Dangerous Games ended too confused to call.

titles.name: RSP Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for whichever sponsor could afford the promotion's own public-access airtime in a given week, the belt was first won in a four-corners match and changed hands at the same Dangerous Games pay-per-view that turned over the promotion's own top title.

titles.name: RSP Western States Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own main championship, first won in a triple threat that closed its debut pay-per-view after an eight-man battle royal and a sudden-death match narrowed the field. Its first two reigns both ended at the same event, the promotion's own Dangerous Games, the first inside the ring and the second outside every document the newsgroup itself preserves.

titles.name: RSPCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's secondary singles title, changing hands twice more within its first six months on this wing's own textual record.

titles.name: RSPCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a one-night Iron Man tournament at the fed's own debut supercard and renamed within its first year for the champion whose kayfabe injury ended his career.

titles.name: RSPCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a cage match at the fed's own debut supercard; the winning pair is withheld under the privacy rule.

titles.name: RSPWF North American Bandwidth Championship
titles.epitaph: Dreamcard's own joke belt, billed at Dreamcard V with one of the newsgroup’s own regulars, under a joke persona, defending against another. Neither name is minted as a character here: the card's own roster policy bills this title's own contenders as “the newsgroup's own regulars,” and the record does not resolve whether the names are real off-newsgroup identities or invented ring personas, so no reign is registered for this belt.

titles.name: RSPWF World Bandwidth Championship
titles.epitaph: Dreamcard's own joke belt, billed at Dreamcard V as the card's own “main event for Part I” — one of the newsgroup’s own regulars under a joke persona defending against another of the newsgroup’s own regulars under a joke persona. Neither name is minted as a character here: the card's own roster policy bills this title's own contenders as “the newsgroup's own regulars,” and the record does not resolve whether the names are real off-newsgroup identities or invented ring personas, so no reign is registered for this belt.

titles.name: RSPWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed at Dreamcard V as “the REAL World Championship” — a joke aimed at Ric Flair losing the WWF's own title at WrestleMania the week before — with Flair the reigning champion and Jushin “Thunder” Liger the challenger; the challenge's own result never survives.

titles.name: RSPWF World Jobber Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed at Dreamcard V with Ronnie Garvin the reigning champion against Steve Armstrong's own challenge — a billing one newsgroup reader's own reply to the card protested outright (“Ronnie Garvin is NOT a jobber!!!”). The challenge's own result never survives.

titles.name: RSPWWCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by four-man tournament at the fed's own January 1997 pay-per-view and defended across at least eight reigns through the rest of the year.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from dated ring-announcer receipts.

titles.name: RSPWWCW European Championship
titles.epitaph: First attested at the 2001 Regal Rumble, already the sitting Television-style provincial title, changing hands once in the held record: Tehawk to Alex Cain, both reigns dated within the same broadcast.
titles.notes: No document earlier than 29 June 2001 attests this title in the held record; how or when Tehawk won it is not recorded.

titles.name: RSPWWCW Extreme Bandwidth Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own invention and best joke, created inside the dossier year and named for the very thing its critics accused the fed of wasting.
titles.notes: This pass's own slice finds the shorter "Extreme Championship"/"Extreme Title" name used consistently and exclusively for the remainder of 1997: John Henry calls it "the World champion and the Extreme Champion" at World War IV (23 Nov, msg_id EmGIN266LyQJ); John Henry again congratulates Alex Demchuk "for winning the oldest belt in internet wrestling, the EXTREME Championship" at RawNitro Is War from St. Louis (15 Dec, msg_id 5NeVMCaqTSAJ); and the Boorcade preview at RawNitro Is War from North Pole previews "The Extreme Title... up for grabs as Alex the Hitman Demchuk defends" (22 Dec, msg_id WVqfpmzKrtEJ).

titles.name: RSPWWCW Intergender Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own signature belt: men and women compete for it on equal terms, and across 1997 it changed hands more often than the world title.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from dated ring-announcer receipts.

titles.name: RSPWWCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended across at least five reigns in 1997, including the fed's best-documented single angle -- a staged forfeiture press conference complete with a 1-900 hotline teaser -- and ending the collection's own holdings in a genuinely unresolved chain.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from dated ring-announcer receipts; the August-December 1997 stretch is registered as partially unresolved rather than guessed, per the dossier digest's own finding.

titles.name: RSPWWCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Inherited from the 1996 predecessor "RSPW Television Title" and defended through the end of this collection's own 1997 holdings, with its belt still referenced by a sibling fed a year later.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from dated ring-announcer receipts.

titles.name: RSPWWCW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended across at least six reigns through 1997, its own storylines tied closely to the fed's founding heel stable, the Creatures Of The Night.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from dated ring-announcer receipts; one change carries no recoverable holder name and is not recorded as a row -- see the wing's accession digest.

titles.name: RSPWWCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top prize, contested across at least nine reigns through 1997 and carried by the fed's own operator across both the opening and closing reigns this collection's holdings attest.
titles.notes: Reconstructed from 138 dated ring-announcer receipts extracted from the fed's own shows.

titles.name: Red Star Wrestling Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title: its 7 April 2009 news ties the Red Star Wrestling Championship to 100% ownership of the company in a Scaffold Ladder Match, and records it vacated the same day; its champions page reads Vacant. Its title-history page holds only a heading.

titles.name: Red Star Wrestling Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag title, held by Team Ego on its champions page, with a 7 April 2009 statement from the new owner that he would decide whether their win stood. Its tag title-history page holds only a heading.

titles.name: RSWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Sat, by the fed's own founding conceit, above every real federation's own world title — the WWF's, the NWA's, the USWA's — as the one belt every organization agreed to recognize. Bruno Sammartino held it from before the surviving record begins through its own end, turning back Andre the Giant in the Memphis card's triple main event and standing billed to defend it again against Curt Hennig on a Tampa card whose own results never survive.

titles.name: RSWA World Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Valiant Brothers from before the surviving record begins, sidelined from the Memphis card by an injury angle — a beatdown from the Road Warriors, with their own manager left "serious but out of danger" — and billed to defend the belts in a cage against Stan Hansen and Terry Gordy on a Tampa card whose own results never survive.

titles.name: Rumble Pro Wrestling Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag prize, first won by Real Xtreme in the final of a one-night, nine-team tournament at Initiation Rites, 10 April 2004.

titles.name: Rumble Pro Wrestling World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top prize, first won by Justin Kell in a match the surviving broadcasts only recall, and held by him through the last card the newsgroup carries.

titles.name: Network Championship
titles.epitaph: RUSH's Network Championship was first won by Marvin Harris on 2 May 2002. The fed's own title log carries 4 reigns on it, across 4 different champions, and ends with Livewire's, from 12 September 2002; PCW's cards of December 2002 and January 2003 carry a fifth, Matt Hunt's, won about 10 December 2002 and still held at Shanghaied III on 26 January 2003. Livewire's, of about three months, is the longest; Scott Cage's, 63 days from 16 June 2002, is the longest with both dates exact. Matt Hunt held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Syndicate Championship
titles.epitaph: RUSH's Syndicate Championship was first won by Statuz Quo on 23 May 2002. The fed's own title log carries 2 reigns on it, across 2 different champions, and ends with El Spiffy!'s, from 18 August 2002; PCW's cards of December 2002 and January 2003 carry three more: Stimpo's (about 1 December 2002), Ebola III's (about 8 December 2002) and The Masked Mullet's, won from Ebola III at Shanghaied III on 26 January 2003. El Spiffy!'s is the longest, from 18 August to about 1 December 2002, which Decimation 2002's commentary counts as 107 days; Statuz Quo's, 87 days from 23 May 2002, is the longest with both dates exact. The Masked Mullet held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: World Championship
titles.epitaph: RUSH's World Championship was first won by Cassius Deamont on 16 June 2002. The fed's own title log carries 3 reigns on it, across 3 different champions, and ends when the belt was vacated on 18 October 2002; the card of Decimation 2002 (22 December 2002), the pay-per-view RUSH and PCW staged together, crowns a fourth champion, Tyler Valentine, in the match for the vacant title. The longest reign with both dates on record is Cassius Deamont's, 63 days from 16 June 2002. One of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Valentine was still billed champion at Shanghaied III on 26 January 2003, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: RVRL Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man tournament at RVRL's 2006 revival opener, won on a foreign-object shot in the final.

titles.name: RVRL Missouri Valley Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: RVRL's secondary title, revived alongside the Heavyweight Championship and won in the same 2006 tournament by a competitor who used a handful of powder and a fistful of tights.

titles.name: RWA World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Pleasure & Paine held the title entering the fed's own served corpus, its own start not recorded. Body Count (Sammie Curr and RIP) won it from them at Friday Night Fury (1/31) and stand as the fed's own last-attested champions on its served Rankings page.

titles.name: RWA World Television Title
titles.epitaph: Chronos swept a four-man-plus tournament for the vacant title, beating Canadian Homeboy in the final. Axon Blade stands as the fed's own last-attested champion on its served Rankings page — an off-page title change the corpus does not otherwise record.

titles.name: RWA U.S. Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Drake Martel won the vacant title in a short-notice tournament final against Death Jester, sabotaged by BeefCarver and the Crow's own revenge attack, and retained it against Deadpool. Bishop stands as the fed's own last-attested champion on its served Rankings page — an off-page title change the corpus does not otherwise record.

titles.name: RWA World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Nuke and Trent Malady fought the vacant title to a 30-minute draw in the fed's own tournament final; Malady won it outright the following week in a Triple Threat, and retained it by DQ against Axon Blade before Da Messiah's own interference handed it to Nuke off-page. Kontra took it from Nuke in a Scaffold Match staged as payback for that same interference, and stands as the fed's own last-attested champion on its served Rankings page.

titles.name: RWF National Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a ten-man battle royal won by a wrestler fired from the roster days earlier, wrestling in disguise as his own "mystery man" replacement.

titles.name: RWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a sixteen-man tournament whose semifinal and final are not attested in the surviving record.

titles.name: Sacred Heart Championship
titles.epitaph: The singles title announced on 25 July 2008 as the prize of the Rainbow Bridge Tournament and 'the highest award the federation offers for singles competitors'; its first winner was to defend it at least once a month at the fed's events. No match for it and no holder are known.

titles.name: European Championship
titles.epitaph: Named as vacant ("Ainda não há") on Sacrifice's own 8 November 2007 champions list; no contest for it survives in the documents held here.

titles.name: Sacrifice Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Kajo and Spartan over Manu Original Punk and Great One on Sacrifice's own first show (2 November 2007).

titles.name: World Championship
titles.epitaph: Sacrifice's own top championship, vacant as of the brand's own first show (2 November 2007), which staged two qualifying matches (Jead over Blackthorn; Kurte$ over Brunovsky) for a title match the following week between Jead and Kurte$; the promotion's own 8 November 2007 champions list still records it as vacant ("Ainda não há"), so this title match's own outcome is not established by any document read.

titles.name: Pride & Honor Championship
titles.epitaph: Saints Haven's own second singles title, won exactly once in the surviving record.
titles.notes: Its own records page: first champion Tony Johnson, one week, zero defenses.

titles.name: Southern Regional Championship
titles.notes: Introduced as the second of the promotion's three founding titles, filled by an eight-man tournament run across its first two broadcasts.
titles.epitaph: Southern Alliance Wrestling's second-ranked title, contested in an eight-man tournament from the promotion's first broadcast; Tommy Flames won it from Bungle on the second broadcast to become its first champion.

titles.name: SBS Television Championship
titles.caption: A secondary singles title.
titles.epitaph: SBS Television Championship of SBS: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: SBS World Championship
titles.caption: The fed's own top title.
titles.epitaph: SBS World Championship of SBS: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: SBS World Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: The fed's own tag title, stripped from its first-recorded holders by presidential decree.
titles.epitaph: SBS World Tag Team Championship of SBS: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: Fuse Custom Chaos Champion
titles.epitaph: The Fuse Custom Chaos Champion was first won by The Animal on 6 November 2005. The fed's own record carries 12 reigns on it, across 12 different champions. The longest is Evan 'Damage' Jackson's, 73 days from 6 September 2006. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — vacated. Jonathan Rhine held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: Fuse Fatal Faction
titles.epitaph: The Fuse Fatal Faction was first won by Critical Error on 18 November 2006. The fed's own record carries 8 reigns on it, across 6 different champions. The longest is Cowboys From Hell's, 78 days from 19 July 2007. One of its reigns ended outside a match — retired with the belt. SCCW retired it on 5 October 2007.

events.note: the federation's own authority figure suspended the reigning Fatal Faction Champions and retired the championship. Recorded outside the booking system: the log row carries no card link and the fields 'Uproar 10/05' / 'Segment: The Last Stand', dated 5 Oct 2007. The belt's own last reign ends `retired` on the same day. Source: The fed's own title log, the fed's own legacy record line.

titles.name: Fuse Fusion Championship
titles.epitaph: The Fuse Fusion Championship's first recorded champion is Ethan Frost, who was already carrying it when the fed's own record opens on him. Its Fusion Rumble of 10 February 2007 ended with Frost and Fred Fusion eliminated together and the two of them declared co-holders. The fed's own record carries four reigns on it, across three champions: Frost alone, Frost and Fusion twice, and The Legacy. Frost and Fusion held it at the end of the surviving record, by then billed under a name its own authority figure refused to recognise.
titles.notes: Self-awarded on the federation's own word: FUSE's own commentary opens the double-title ladder match of Afflicted Glory 2007 (31 May 2007) with "It's time for our first title match of the night! True, both belts up for grabs are unsanctioned, but both of these teams feel passionately about their belts". The same broadcast stages the FUSION straps as belts hung above the ring that the fed itself had not sanctioned for two months and puts them up against the Fatal Affliction straps the reigning team had made for itself, the losing set "banned" from FUSE; the preceding segment, "FUSION Wrestling: RIP", bills the pair as "the Fatal Affliction or FUSION Wrestling titles" and shows the Reeds wearing their own custom straps.

titles.name: SCCW Gateway Championship
titles.epitaph: The SCCW Gateway Championship's first recorded champion is Jonathan Rhine. The fed's own record carries 14 reigns on it, across 14 different champions. The longest is Phillip Kennedy's, 195 days from 11 January 2009. Baron von Blackberry held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: SCCW LiveWire Championship
titles.epitaph: The SCCW LiveWire Championship was first won by Evan 'Damage' Jackson on 12 November 2005. The fed's own record carries 34 reigns on it, across 31 different champions. The longest is Jadian Bridden's, 161 days from 27 September 2009. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. Mitchell Quinlan held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: SCCW SIN Championships
titles.epitaph: The SCCW SIN Championships' first recorded champion is Cowboys From Hell. The fed's own record carries 9 reigns on it, across 9 different champions. The longest is Lance Marshall and Desade's, 141 days from 25 July 2009. Daddy Daughter Day held it at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: SCCW Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: The SCCW Universal Championship's first recorded champion is Evan 'Damage' Jackson. The fed's own record carries 21 reigns on it, across 12 different champions. The longest is Aimz's, 421 days from 2 August 2008. Two of its reigns ended outside a match — stripped from the holder or vacated. The belt left Lane Stevens on 13 June 2010, stripped from the holder, and the surviving record carries no later change.

titles.name: Barrie District Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles prize contested among the promotion's own ranked top three challengers, changing hands in a three-way match on the promotion's 27 February 2005 show.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); the title change recorded here is from SCCW's own 'Lightning Strikes' show-results post (27 February 2005 event date).

titles.name: Barrie District Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team title, described in its own rules but not contested on any show surviving in the held record.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); no reign is attested by any document held here.

titles.name: Innercity Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own television title, defended in a title unification match against the Young Guns Championship on its 27 February 2005 show.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); the reign recorded here is confirmed defended in SCCW's own 'Lightning Strikes' show-results post (27 February 2005 event date).

titles.name: Legacy Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles prize defended under its own 'Legacy Rules' stipulation, retained in a grudge match on the promotion's 27 February 2005 show.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); the reign recorded here is confirmed defended in SCCW's own 'Lightning Strikes' show-results post (27 February 2005 event date).

titles.name: All Barrie Championship
titles.epitaph: Riflewilly was listed as champion on 22 July 2009; Sydney LaRoux took the title from him on 27 July and was still champion on 12 August.

titles.name: All Barrie Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: War Machine were the All Barrie tag champions on 10 August 2009, and the 12 August news calls its announced main event the first match since they won the titles.

titles.name: BARBARIC Championship
titles.epitaph: Jay Jerzey held the Barbaric title on 10 August 2009 after what the fed called the most bloody and brutal match in its history, and was announced to defend it against Rex Masters on 17 August.

titles.name: SCCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's rankings of 22 July 2009 list this title as To Be Determined; Myke Adams, the Bunkhouse Brawl winner, was its newly crowned champion by 10 August and stood first in the ten of 12 August.

titles.name: Simcoe County Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top singles prize, required by its own rules to be defended at least once a month.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); the reign recorded here is confirmed defended in SCCW's own 'Lightning Strikes' show-results post (27 February 2005 event date).

titles.name: Young Guns Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles prize that changed hands in a title unification match against the Innercity Television Championship on the promotion's 27 February 2005 show.
titles.notes: Rules stated in the federation's own rules and handbook post (3 February 2005); the title change recorded here is from SCCW's own 'Lightning Strikes' show-results post (27 February 2005 event date).

titles.name: SCW Brass Knux Championship
titles.epitaph: Created to replace a retired Cruiserweight title; its own first defense at the Continental Cup ended with both men knocked out through a table, and the belt was held up before changing hands again by the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: SCW Deuces Wild Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: SCW Florida Heavyweight Title
titles.caption: Vacant as of the CWF branch show, where a match to fill it (Billy Joe Pherris vs. Adrian 'Tiger' Lee) was set up going into a commercial break; no Part II survives to show the result.
titles.epitaph: SCW Florida Heavyweight Title of SCW ENTITY A: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: SCW Florida Tag-Team Titles
titles.caption: Retained by Hearts of Darkness (Matt Moyer and Rex Stone) against The Warlords on the CWF branch show; the fed's own record does not survive to show when they were won.
titles.epitaph: SCW Florida Tag-Team Titles of SCW ENTITY A: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: SCW Lone Star Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, attested for a single reign in the surviving record.

titles.name: SCW National Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated after a chaotic four-way cage match, refilled in an eight-man Tower of Doom cage match at the Continental Cup, defended to a time-limit draw, then changed hands in a rematch billed "Chapman/Spencer II."

titles.name: SCW National Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created as the Continental Cup tag tournament's own prize, and retained by disqualification against Domination at the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: SCW Royal Flush Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: SCW Show Time Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, held once before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: SCW Southern States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at the Continental Cup in a title-for-title Dog Collar match against a rival promotion's own Florida title.

titles.name: SCW Southern States Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by two different teams across 1999 before falling vacant and being refilled in a three-way scaffold match at the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: SCW Lonestar Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The federation's top singles championship, its vacant tournament won by Pat Gordon, Jr. on 8 December 2019 at the Showdown I iPPV; "Celtic Crippler" Caleb Foley took it from him on the following Rampage, 28 January 2020, in a Triangle Match also involving Alfie Button. Foley's win is the last change the federation's own title history recorded.
titles.source: The federation's own Lonestar Heavyweight Title History page, served as /promotions/scw-southwestern-2019/archive/lonestartitlehistory.html

titles.name: SCW Lonestar Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The federation's tag championship, opened on Las Preguntas at the federation's own first show, 18 June 2019, in a Fatal 4-Way over the Rich Family, the Health Fanatics and the Prague Drinking Team. Davey-Boy O'Brien and Keegan took it from them on 8 December 2019 at Showdown I in a Texas Tornado match, the last change the federation's own title history recorded.
titles.source: The federation's own Lonestar Tag Team Title History page, served as /promotions/scw-southwestern-2019/archive/lonestartagtitlehistory.html

titles.name: SCW Commissioner Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Belts and Champions page names Viper — the roster page's own billed Co-CEO — as Commissioner Champion, the only one of the fed's six titles not recorded vacant on the same page. One reign anchors the ledger here: the only one attested.

titles.name: SCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Never held, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own Belts and Champions page, one of five of the fed's six titles recorded that way on the same document.
titles.notes: Billed "(VACANT)" on the fed's own Belts and Champions page. No reign is recorded anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: SCW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Never held, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own Belts and Champions page, one of five of the fed's six titles recorded that way on the same document.
titles.notes: Billed "(VACANT)" on the fed's own Belts and Champions page. No reign is recorded anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: SCW National Championship
titles.epitaph: Never held, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own Belts and Champions page, one of five of the fed's six titles recorded that way on the same document.
titles.notes: Billed "(VACANT)" on the fed's own Belts and Champions page. No reign is recorded anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: SCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Never held, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own Belts and Champions page, one of five of the fed's six titles recorded that way on the same document.
titles.notes: Billed "(VACANT)" (plural, "SCW Tag Team Champions") on the fed's own Belts and Champions page. No reign is recorded anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: SCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Never held, on the record that survives — billed vacant on the fed's own Belts and Champions page, one of five of the fed's six titles recorded that way on the same document.
titles.notes: Billed "(VACANT)" on the fed's own Belts and Champions page. No reign is recorded anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: SCW Television Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on the promotion's own season-opening broadcast, then again at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, where the winning team included a masked returnee revealed after the bell.

titles.name: SCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on the promotion's own season-opening broadcast, later stripped from a champion whose own path to the belt the promotion judged illegitimate, and refilled in a bloody three-way Dog Collar match at the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: SCW Tennessee Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands on the promotion's own season-opening broadcast with an assist from a masked-off ally at ringside.

titles.name: SCW Tornado Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, attested for a single reign in the surviving record.

titles.name: SCW True Grit Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Sin City Wrestling territory, held twice before it was left vacant in the surviving record.

titles.name: SCW World Championship
titles.caption: The fed's own top title, decided by a Triangle Match at its first card.
titles.epitaph: SCW World Championship of SCW ENTITY B: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: SEEW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in commentary during the fed's own last card (12 July 1997) as the stakes of a match between Mike 'the Mechanic' Malone and Polecat that the surviving record does not carry; no bestowal is recorded.

titles.name: SEEW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended on the fed's own last card (12 July 1997), where champion Polecat retained by double-disqualification against Killer Kenny before vacating the title in a post-match promo to pursue a Heavyweight Championship match instead.

titles.name: SEWF Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled at the end of October 2000 by Phah Q. Dickshine in a three-way, the Extreme Championship was held by eleven champions in turn by the fed's own title histories before the summer of 2001, three of them in March and April alone as Twisted Chaos and Ian Blade traded it. Renamed the Extreme Television Championship by the autumn, it was defended in a Hardcore Hell match of barbed-wire ropes and light bulbs and in a handicapped weapons match, and Smoove won it back at End Game in December 2001.

titles.name: SEWF World Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced by President Thomas Casey on 12 November 2001 and contested by four teams of four in elimination matches, the World Junior Heavyweight Championship was first won by Simon Solkoff in the four-way final at End Game on 10 December 2001, the same night he lost the World Heavyweight tournament final.

titles.name: SEWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled at ShawCade 3 in September 2000 by the Invisibles, the Tag Team Championship ran through nine reigns by the fed's own title histories between September 2000 and May 2001, three of them Tommy Kain and Burt Clifton's, then passed to Sex Stable 2001 at the June relaunch and to the Flaming Jet Planes for a second time on 1 July. The Kasai Contingent won it in Tag Team Turmoil at End Game in December 2001.

titles.name: SEWF World United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled at ShawCade 3 in September 2000 by Simon Southward, the United States Championship went on to Wyatt Wallace, Tommy Grayson, Adam Mitchell, Grayson again and Art Blake, whose 119-day reign from January 2001 the fed called its longest, before Tom Collins, Mitchell again, Mike Bright and Simon Solkoff held it through the summer. Blake held it again at Octoberfest and gave it up in November to a five-way Thunderdome brawl, won at End Game by Trineo Del Abanico, who unmasked as Johnny Sledge.

titles.name: SEWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant through the 2000 relaunch's own tournament, the World Heavyweight Championship was first won by Jay Lange on 3 September 2000. By the fed's own title histories it passed through Johnny Sledge, Ray Hagan, Jarred Matthews and four reigns of Phah Q. Dickshine, two of which ended with Dickshine handing the belt backstage to Jeff Kane and to Archangel for an hour, before Mike Masters took it in May 2001. Art Blake held it with the United States title after a sixty-minute Iron Man Hell in a Cell at Octoberfest, gave it up, and Burt Clifton won the sixteen-man tournament for it at End Game in December 2001.
titles.notes: No reign is registered: the held record stages no title change. See data/shards/sewf/shows.json for the tournament's own Round 2 results and Round 3 announced pairings.

titles.name: SFW NorthWest Title
titles.epitaph: Announced by the SFW's president at its debut as the prize of a four-man tournament the following week, its entrants drawn from a hat at the close of the show: Konrad against Jeff Kane, Jacob Sawyer against Vengence. No result of the tournament survives.

titles.name: STW Sheer Hardcore Title
