titles.epitaph: Changed hands some thirteen times before its own last, official reign.

titles.name: SPW Diamond Title
titles.epitaph: Held jointly by Eric Henry and Andrew Davis, who had won it from Dylan Dice at Endgame, until Todd Lucchesi took it from both in a House of Anarchy three-way at Legacy in March 2002.

titles.name: SPW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Flaming" Bob Muretic as of the federation's own late-1999 record, won in an eight-man free-for-all and defended against a growing line of contenders.

titles.name: SPW Platinum Title
titles.epitaph: Billed as the purists' title; AsH held it into Legacy in March 2002, where Gregory Brians won it five falls to four in a half-hour Ironman match.

titles.name: SJPW All-Asian Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: SJPW's own top singles title, styled "All-Asian" rather than "World" to match the fed's regional self-presentation; the fed's own December 1997 record finds it vacant, with Nik Nyce and Shinji Hamada lined up to fill it following an unnamed former champion's forced retirement.
titles.notes: No reign is dated from the two documents served this pass; the vacancy and the planned Nyce-Hamada match are the only holder information the surviving record gives (promotions/sjpw/archive/year-end-review-dec1997.html).

titles.name: SJPW All-Asian Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the end of 1997 by Black Sun Rising, the pairing of the underrated Blackline and the rookie Alex Akira -- the fed's own record gives no earlier holder or date for the belt.

titles.name: SJPW Battle Arts Championship
titles.epitaph: The title of SJPW's own smallest but hottest-drawing division, held by Steel Serpent as of the surviving record's end -- the fed's own account gives no earlier holder or date.

titles.name: SJPW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won and lost twice across 1997 in a story the fed's own record tells almost entirely after the fact: Super Tengu took it from his rival Shinji Hamada in a pre-arranged finish at the fed's first pay-per-view, then dropped it to Ace Killcannon at the Super J Crown Tournament that September, with Derek Mota lined up for a cage-match challenge as the year closed.

titles.name: Grand Prix Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: A new singles championship first attested held by Kentaro "H-Bomb" Kawasaki in the documents immediately following the revival's own unread Zenmen Sensou supershow (26 June 2004), where a press conference had advance-announced a new title of this name; no document this pass could read records the title match itself.

titles.name: Gunryo Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Despair across the revival era's documented run, defended under its own named rules variant; no surviving document names an earlier holder or a title change.

titles.name: SJPW Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Settled by an SJPW-run tournament in which the favored rookie Jet Jaguar was upset in the finals by the underdog Ishikawa, per the fed's own account.

titles.name: NCWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held for years by Masashi 'Lightning' Lanther before passing to Super Bakemono, who defended it successfully against El Santa Azteca in Okinawa in May 2004; no surviving document names the exact transition.

titles.name: LEGEND! Cup (L-Cup)
titles.epitaph: An eight-man tournament trophy announced for the first night of Spring Classic '02: LEGEND!, meant to name wrestling's first real undisputed legend; the event was called off before the tournament began, and the cup was never awarded.

titles.name: SRW Champion
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Cristiano from SRW's own founding roster list; no document read this pass records how the title was won.

titles.name: SRW Heavyweight Champion
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Carona from SRW's own founding roster list; no document read this pass records how the title was won.

titles.name: SRW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Miguel and Zé Miguel from SRW's own founding roster list; no document read this pass records how the title was won.

titles.name: SSCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the promotion's founding handbook, with an announcement about the title teased for the debut Saturday Night Survival card; no champion is recorded before the record ends.

titles.name: SSCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the promotion's founding handbook as its top prize; no champion is recorded before the record ends.

titles.name: SSCW World Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the promotion's founding handbook; no champions are recorded before the record ends.

titles.name: STW Lonestar State Championship
titles.epitaph: A hybrid style title open to wrestlers of any discipline, introduced in the promotion's founding handbook; no champion is recorded before the record ends.

titles.name: STW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced as the promotion's top title in its founding handbook; no champion is recorded before the record ends.

titles.name: MEW Suicidal Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended by Jack against Nightmare in a street fight that spilled through a parking lot and a staff office before Nightmare won it with an office desk.

titles.name: The Road Warrior's Cup
titles.epitaph: The Summit's own tag-team tournament: sixteen teams at the first Summit in Montreal in July 1991, won by the Soviets, and the seventh Summit's in June 1995, won by Death Warmed Over.

titles.name: The Summit Royal Rumble
titles.epitaph: The Summit's own Royal Rumble, won twice in 1991: by Fury, thirty men over the top rope in Buffalo in July, and by Klingon Phaser, from the fortieth entry of forty, that December.

titles.name: Ultimate Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt made for one match. Its sponsor's own explanation, read out in the ring on the second Summit's last night, was that the two men it had been made for were the only two in e-wrestling who had held major titles in two separate federations at the same time — and that both had since lost those belts, which did not diminish what they had done. Four federation presidents sat at a table at ringside and let the match stand. It is the only championship the Summit ever held of its own, and no defence of it survives anywhere in the held record.
titles.notes: Introduced and explained in the ring by its own sponsor on the second Summit's fourth night, 30 December 1991 (promotions/summit-of-e-wrestling/archive/the-summit-of-e-wrestling-day-4-1991-12-30.html): "This is not a title that can be taken away by normal means. This title denotes supremacy in the ring, which is something only time can efface." Sponsored by TNT Enterprises and sanctioned, per that speech, under the aegis of the four e-federation presidents seated at ringside. Contested once in the surviving record and never defended in it.

titles.name: The Von Erich/Freebird Memorial Trophy
titles.epitaph: A six-man tag tournament of fourteen trios, run once, on the second Summit's third night, 29 December 1991. The Big Three won it in four matches in the one night.

titles.name: SHVF Super-Middleweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Reserved by the promotion's own rules for fighters 240 pounds and under; no titleholder is recorded in the surviving record.

titles.name: UWF Superheavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated in February 1999 after the promotion severed ties with a champion's handler over his conduct toward its president.

titles.name: STW Supreme/World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Known first as the Supreme Tag Team title, renamed World Tag Team during a later reign; changed hands some sixteen times before its own last champions.

titles.name: The Supremer Strap
titles.epitaph: Held by Kraze across the whole of this record, retaining it through a restarted, disqualification-ending challenge from Anthony Mislan at Warzone.

titles.name: SVW Alabama Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's regional singles title, its first champion crowned when a missed top-rope splash cost the round's best-worked wrestler the fall.

titles.name: SVW Alabama Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced in the federation's own founding title list alongside its four sister championships; no tournament or title change for it survives in the held record.

titles.name: SVW Bunkhouse Championship
titles.epitaph: A no-disqualification, specialty-matches-only title, its inaugural tournament run back-to-back with the Heavyweight tournament inside the same week.

titles.name: SVW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a sixteen-man Inaugural Tournament across three rounds in a single week, decided when a distracted referee let a set of brass knuckles change hands mid-match.

titles.name: SVW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won when a distraction from the losing team's own manager let a handful of tights decide the inaugural final.

titles.name: SWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a hard-fought submission match, with the challenger overcoming three kickouts before forcing a stoppage.

titles.name: SWA Canadian Title
titles.epitaph: Never mentioned in the fed's own 27 August 2000 Wrestler Records page, the Canadian Title is live by the time of a later, undated in-fiction predictions column (circa December 2000), which bills Warren Peace as champion and has him defending against Fury; the column separately names a number-one-contender match for the title between Justin Case and Gangsta. No document records a result for either match, or names the title's own first champion.

titles.name: SWA Intercontinental Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Wrestler Records page (27 August 2000) credits two wrestlers with one Intercontinental Title reign apiece — John Rotten and Hendrickson Tyler — a cumulative tally with no dates or order recoverable between them. No further document in the held record names the title again.

titles.name: SWA Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Wrestler Records page (27 August 2000) credits two wrestlers with one Tag Team Title reign apiece — Hendrickson Tyler and Stevie Paginello, each with an unnamed partner — a cumulative tally with no dates, order, or pairings recoverable. The tag team Secret Service (Matt Cross and Will James) is billed "(c)" — current champions — on the fed's own served 27 May 2001 card, roughly nine months later, the title's own last documented reign in the held record.

titles.name: SWA Television Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Wrestler Records page (27 August 2000) credits seven different wrestlers with one Television Title reign apiece — Donny “The Dragon” Chacho, Omega, Rave, The Brock, Barbwire, Hunter, and White Fire — a cumulative tally with no dates or order recoverable among them. A later, undated Fall 2000 in-fiction magazine names Fury as “the new TV champion,” risen through the fed’s own Hardcore ranks. A further undated predictions column (circa December 2000) has Beorn challenging Joseph for the same title; no document survives naming a winner or dating either change.

titles.name: SWA World Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Wrestler Records page (27 August 2000) credits two wrestlers with one World Title reign apiece — Judge and Will Anselm — a cumulative tally with no dates or order recoverable between them. By the time of a later, undated in-fiction predictions column (circa December 2000), the belt is billed as the "SWA/AWA unified championship," held by OutKast — the same title, rebranded once the fed's own SWA/AWA partnership deepened, per that column's own words.

titles.name: SCW North American Championship
titles.notes: Named in the promotion's own info packets of June to September 2001.
titles.epitaph: Held by Heavy Metal Van Hammer through the summer and autumn of 2001, a reign his challenger put at seven months, and by Eric Draven by the end of November.

titles.name: SCW World Television Championship
titles.notes: Named SCW World Television Champion in the promotion's own info packets; called the Television Title on its broadcasts.
titles.epitaph: A secondary title first held, in the Superior Wrestling Alliance days, by the Freek. Iron Man Jordan Jones carried it for some six months into mid-2001; it passed through Charles Purnell and Kevin Candido before Kyren Knight held it that November, defended, in the commentators' words, twice a week.

titles.name: SCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Named in the promotion's own info packets of June to September 2001 as the SCW World Heavyweight Champion's title.
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title. Maverick held it longer than anyone before him, until his partner Viper won it from him with a lead-pipe betrayal behind it in June 2001; by November it had passed to Mike Powers, with Van Hammer next in line at Holiday Havok.

titles.name: SWC Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Sooner Wrestling Council's top title, billed to go to the winner of a twenty-entrant Royal Rumble at the promotion's own debut supercard. No result of that show survives.
titles.notes: The promotion's own 26 January 1999 newsletter previews the Royal Rumble main event for the 31 January 1999 debut card; no result survives.

titles.name: SWC Heavyweight Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Sooner Wrestling Council's tag team title, set out in the promotion's own founding handbook. No champions or title match are recorded in any document read.
titles.notes: Named in the founding handbook's own titles section; no holder survives in any document read.

titles.name: SWC Skyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The Sooner Wrestling Council's cruiserweight-style title, weight-limited to 225 pounds, set out in the promotion's own founding handbook alongside its Television, Heavyweight and Heavyweight Tag Team titles. No champion is recorded before the promotion's trail runs cold.
titles.notes: Named in the founding handbook's own titles section; no holder or title match survives in any document read.

titles.name: SWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The Sooner Wrestling Council's number-two title, billed as defended every week. A first-round tournament to crown its inaugural holder was previewed for the promotion's own debut supercard, but no result survives.
titles.notes: The promotion's own 26 January 1999 newsletter previews a three-match first-round tournament and an unrevealed-stipulation finals bout to crown the first champion at the 31 January 1999 debut card; no result of that card survives.

titles.name: SWF American Championship
titles.epitaph: A founding-era singles title Pagan held three times across the wing's run; the site's own final-season roster page no longer lists a current holder.

titles.name: SWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The wing's lighter-weight singles title, held by El Viento de Muerta on the site's own final-season roster page and by El Cid on its last-dated (21 June 2000) champions page.

titles.name: SWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the wing's own recurring singles titles across its run, changing hands among wrestlers including Pagan and Black Jack; held by E-Klipse on the site's own last-dated (21 June 2000) champions page.

titles.name: SWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: A founding-era singles title changing hands among wrestlers including The Judge, Sean "The Duke" McKenzie and Equalizer; the site's own final-season roster page no longer lists a current holder.

titles.name: SWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands repeatedly among the wing's own late-era teams (The Kold Blooded Killaz, The Living Dead, The Sanitarium of Fear); held by The Union of Former Owners on the site's own last-dated (21 June 2000) rankings page.

titles.name: SWF Toughman Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a battle-royal format at the fed's own Birthday Blast anniversary show in 1998; held by Mark Adams on the site's own last-dated (21 June 2000) champions page.

titles.name: SWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A recurring midcard singles title first awarded during the wing's own first year; held by Steven Braver on the site's own last-dated (21 June 2000) champions page.

titles.name: SWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in a giant double-elimination tournament at the SWF's own first pay-per-view in May 1997; carried by Mr. Shhh during his run through Trinity, The Gangstas and The Church of Pain, and by Fatal Fury on the site's own last-dated (21 June 2000) champions page.

titles.name: SWF Generations Championship
titles.epitaph: A new belt for Generation Supreme, shown off by Richard Eisen and Jack Bruce on the second Friday show of the diary and won by Ace Newton in a ten-man battle royal at The World is Watching. Robbie Retro takes it from Newton on Supreme TV in June 2008. Retro keeps it against Sean Deeley on Supreme TV in Week 1 of July 2008, while he and Newton each claim to be the face of Generation Supreme and both are left off the card of The Supreme Challenge 28. Retro keeps it against Ash Campbell on Supreme TV in Week 3 of July 2008 but loses it to Ace Newton in a Threefold Threat with Jay Chord a week later, Newton pinning Retro with his feet on the ropes; in Week 1 of August the Four Kings and Playboy Jake Sawyer give Newton a new belt, which Richard Eisen calls the new official Generations Championship. Newton keeps it against Kirk Jameson on Supreme TV in Week 3 of August 2008 and, in the SWF.com recaps of Generation Supreme, against El Leon and Swoop McCarthy, and is billed against Gino Montero for it in Week 2 of September.

titles.name: SWF Legends Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt Phil Vibert, the general manager of SWF Legends, unveils on Supreme TV in May 2008 for the hard-brawling veterans who do not compete for the world title, first shown as a tattered old belt. Chris Caufield wins it in a four-way elimination match over John McClean, Runaway Train and Enforcer Roberts on the first SWF Legends in June 2008, and Vibert then hands him the finished belt. Caufield keeps it against Enygma on SWF Legends in June 2008, against Texas Pete by count-out in Week 4 of June, when the Golden Faction's Rocky Golden berates Pete for failing, and against Enforcer Roberts in Week 2 of July, a match the diary says would have moved Roberts to the Legends brand; Bloodstone of the Golden Faction is booked to challenge him at The Supreme Challenge 28. Caufield loses it at The Supreme Challenge 28 to Bloodstone, whose camel clutch ends the match by referee stoppage while Caufield insists he never submitted; Bloodstone keeps it against Brett Biggz and Pistol Pete Hall, and Robbie Retro says Phil Vibert has put him into the match with Caufield at Welcome to the Jungle 2008. Bloodstone keeps it at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 in a Threefold Threat against Robbie Retro and Chris Caufield, pinning Caufield, and against Robbie Retro on SWF Legends in Week 4 of August, when the referee stops the match in the Bloodstone Mutilation.

titles.name: SWF North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt Rich Money holds in Big Money Incorporated when the diary opens, defended against Eric Tyler, Randy Bumfhole and Christian Faith before Steve Frehley takes it at The World is Watching and then refuses to defend it on Supreme TV, leaving Richard Eisen to announce its future. Eisen then sets up an eight-man Grand Prix for it, which Marc DuBois wins over Eric Eisen at Master of Puppets 2008, and DuBois defends it into June 2008. He keeps it in a three-way against Runaway Train and Antonio Marquez at Times of Trouble 2008, against Valiant on Supreme TV in Week 4 of June and, when Chris Morrisette wins by disqualification after DuBois hits him with the belt, in Week 1 of July 2008; the card of The Supreme Challenge 28 puts the title in a Threefold Threat against Zimmy Bumfhole and Antonio Marquez. DuBois keeps it at The Supreme Challenge 28 in a Threefold Threat against Zimmy Bumfhole and Antonio Marquez, when Darryl Devine's interference lets him throw the referee in front of Marquez's shooting star press; Welcome to the Jungle 2008 is set as another Threefold Threat, with Devine, who has complained to Richard Eisen, and Marquez, who wins the Supreme TV three-way against Zimmy Bumfhole and Sean Deeley for the place. DuBois keeps it in the Threefold Threat at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 when Darryl Devine taps to the Model Solution sleeper, beats Zimmy Bumfhole on Supreme TV in Week 4 of August and Scout of The New Wave in Week 1 of September, and is billed against Art Reed in Week 2.

titles.name: SWF Shooting Star Championship
titles.epitaph: The lowest-ranked singles belt, which the diary's characters call the least important in the promotion. Marc DuBois holds it through ladder matches against Enygma and Antonio Marquez until Darryl Devine wins it at The World is Watching. Darryl Devine keeps it through the ladder match with Enygma at Master of Puppets 2008 and on SWF Legends in June 2008, when Phil Vibert names it the title of a new Sky Club Division for the high-fliers. Devine keeps it in the three-way ladder match at Times of Trouble 2008 but loses it to Kid Toma on SWF Legends in June 2008, after the Samoan Family's interference; Toma keeps it against Brett Biggz and American Elemental and then against Jacob Jett, and the belt is not on the card of The Supreme Challenge 28. Toma keeps it against Remmy Skye on SWF Legends in Week 4 of July 2008, the night Eric Tyler hands him a redesigned belt, and Bart Biggz earns a shot for Welcome to the Jungle 2008 by beating Akima Brave by disqualification in Week 1 of August. Acid, a masked high-flier new to the SWF, pins Kid Toma in a Threefold Threat with Bart Biggz at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 and takes the belt; he keeps it against El Leon and Mainstream Hernandez on SWF Legends in Week 3 of August, Remmy Skye in Week 4 and John Greed and Mainstream Hernandez in Week 1 of September, while Bart Biggz asks for a singles match.

titles.name: SWF Sky Club Tag Team Championship
aka: SWF Sky Club Tag Team Titles
SWF Sky Club Division Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: A pair of tag belts Eric Tyler, the new General Manager of SWF Legends, unveils on SWF Legends in July 2008 in his first 'Mr. Tyler Says' segment, so that the Sky Club division's tag teams, tied to the Legends brand, have belts of their own instead of the World Tag Team Championships of the Supreme brand. Tyler sets a four-team tournament with its deciding match at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 among The Upper Class, High Concept, The Tokyo Underground and Pure Energy; High Concept and The Tokyo Underground qualify on SWF Legends in Week 2 of August 2008 by beating The Upper Class and Pure Energy, and High Concept, Elmo Benson and Groucho Bling, beat The Tokyo Underground at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 to become the first champions. They keep the belts against Double Deuce on SWF Legends in Week 4 of August and lose a non-title match to Rocky Golden and Bloodstone in Week 1 of September.

titles.name: SWF Supreme Championship
titles.epitaph: A second top championship Phil Vibert announces on SWF Legends in June 2008, after the terms Richard Eisen put into the brand split attach every singles title to one brand and so tie the World Heavyweight Championship to Supreme TV. Vibert unveils the gold-and-platinum belt on SWF Legends in Week 4 of June 2008, calls it the most expensive in professional wrestling history, and sets the first champion to be decided at The Supreme Challenge 28, where the card puts Christian Faith against Brandon James for it. Christian Faith wins it at The Supreme Challenge 28, beating Brandon James with the Test of Faith sleeper, and Phil Vibert takes the belt from the referee to present it. Faith keeps it against Bloodstone and Eric Eisen on SWF Legends in Week 3 of July 2008, Troy Tornado in Week 4 and Texas Pete in Week 1 of August; Vengeance is booked against him for Welcome to the Jungle 2008, and Brandon James and Steve Frehley meet there for a shot at the belt at Under Control 2008. Faith keeps it against Vengeance at Welcome to the Jungle 2008, after which Vengeance puts him through the timekeeper's table, and against Bryan Holmes on SWF Legends in Week 3 of August; in Week 4 he keeps it by disqualification in a Threefold Threat with Steve Frehley and Rocky Golden, and Under Control 2008 is billed as a Threefold Threat for it among Faith, Brandon James and Steve Frehley.

titles.name: SWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top belt of the diary's SWF. Jack Bruce holds it when the diary opens, a reign the diary's later posts date from last August, and he keeps it through Brandon James at Awesome Impact and Remo at The World is Watching, where Vengeance's interference ends the second match by disqualification. At Master of Puppets 2008 he beats Vengeance in a Supreme Cell match, and the diary's June posts book him against Eric Eisen for it at Times of Trouble 2008. Bruce beats Eric Eisen at Times of Trouble 2008, keeps the belt against Antonio Marquez and John McClean on Supreme TV in Week 3 of June and against Jay Chord in Week 2 of July, and sees Richard Eisen pick him in the brand split, which ties the title to the Supreme brand even if he loses it. Eisen then announces Supreme Double Jeopardy for The Supreme Challenge 28, in which Bruce must defend the belt twice in one night, first against Vengeance, with Eric Tyler added to that first match by Phil Vibert and the second opponent left for Eisen to choose on the night. Bruce beats Eric Tyler and Vengeance in the first Supreme Double Jeopardy match at The Supreme Challenge 28, then loses the belt to Rich Money in the second after Richard Eisen's indecision lets Money into it, ending a reign the SWF.com review puts at some eleven months. Money refuses to defend the belt anywhere but pay-per-view, makes Bruce and Randy Bumfhole each beat Remo for a shot, swaps the belt for a black one set with diamonds on Supreme TV in Week 4 of July 2008, and, when Bruce and Bumfhole fight to a double disqualification in Week 2 of August, sees Richard Eisen make Welcome to the Jungle 2008 a Threefold Threat among the three. Money keeps the belt at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 in a Threefold Threat against Jack Bruce and Randy Bumfhole, pinning Bruce with Bruce's own New York Minute, and Remo hands him his custom belt. He beats Guide on Supreme TV in Week 3 of August with Bruce watching from the ramp and, on a video from the Las Vegas casino he part owns, turns down Bruce's challenge for Under Control 2008; Pistol Pete Hall, who has asked for a match, is billed against him for the belt on Supreme TV in Week 2 of September.

titles.name: SWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The pair of belts held by Sexual Aggression, who took them from The Amazing Bumfholes at Nothing to Lose in February 2008 and defend them on Supreme TV, at Awesome Impact and at The World is Watching. They keep them against The Amazing Bumfholes at Master of Puppets 2008, and Valiant & Giedroyc take them from Sexual Aggression on the first SWF Legends in June 2008, after Joe Sexy walks out on Angry Gilmore mid-match. Valiant & Giedroyc keep the belts when Giedroyc's stoppage win ends the four-way at Times of Trouble 2008, then against The Heartbreakers on Supreme TV in Week 1 of July and The Upper Class in Week 2; the card of The Supreme Challenge 28 sets them against The New Wave and Badd Kompany in a Threefold Threat. Valiant & Giedroyc keep the belts at The Supreme Challenge 28 when Valiant pins Joss Thompson in a Threefold Threat against The New Wave and Badd Kompany, and are booked against Sin Inc for Welcome to the Jungle 2008. Valiant & Giedroyc keep the belts at Welcome to the Jungle 2008 against Sin Inc when Giedroyc rolls up John McClean, beat The Upper Class in Week 3 of August and The Heartbreakers in Week 1 of September, and Richard Eisen names The New Wave the next challengers, for Under Control 2008.

titles.name: SWIFT Championship
titles.notes: Contested for the first time at the promotion's own first (and only documented) pay-per-view, One Shot at Glory, as the prize of a round-robin tournament run across three Retaliation cards.
titles.epitaph: SWIFT MMA's own top prize, crowned once, at the promotion's only pay-per-view, and never recorded changing hands again.

titles.name: SWP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Set to be crowned in a four-way match at Back to Skool Brawl, 20 September 1998, among representatives billed from the IeWC, EMWO, EWO and CROW; the segment served this pass previews the match but does not report its result, so no reign is recorded here.

titles.name: SWWE World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: SWWE Fed's own top championship. Billed as previously held by Underdeath, then by Blaise as of the promotion's own 29 April 2007 card; by Unsurrender it was Salvador defending alongside Felix619 when Mr. Xtreme won it in a Hell in a Cell, per the promotion's own October 2007 news post.

titles.name: TAEWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Rude Dog" Alex Reed entering Summer Blast 1996; lost that night to "Flashfire" Dean Ferris. The surviving 1997 Usenet record does not trace the belt's lineage forward from there.

titles.name: TAEWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: TAEWF World Heavyweight Championship of TAEWF: the surviving 1997 Usenet record shows the reigns listed here and nothing of how the belt ended.

titles.name: Tag Team Champions of Portugal
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Dráculo and Rigo from the federation's own founding roster; no document read this pass records how the title was won.

titles.name: AVW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First awarded on 5 February 2001, when the Board of Education beat Drake and Justice with the K-12 Dropout and were handed newly made belts, only for Southern Tradition to storm the ring. The two teams' feud brought the titles to Bluegrass Bash.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by D-Generation X (Shawn Michaels & Triple H) from Edge and Randy Orton on 8 December 2006, and defended successfully the following night against Chris Jericho and Bubba Ray Dudley.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag title, already active when the held documents begin. Defended once on-panel (Shwag over With Authority, Spring Slams) before changing hands twice on-panel across the record (the Best of the Best over Team Elite, Brawl For It All; the Goths over the Best of the Best, Danger Zone '98) and once more at the one-year Anniversary Special's own eight-team tournament (Teen Angst over the Goths and the Best of the Best in turn). Two further changes (the Lethal Leaders to Shwag; Shwag's retirement handing the belts to Team Elite) are attested only by the fed's own title-history sheet, off-panel.

titles.name: SWL World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Held by the kick Ass order's Mean Man and Basic Killer across the whole of this record, successfully defended in a three-way on the promotion's earliest surviving card.

titles.name: UWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Death's Claw entering 1999, the promotion's all-time top-ranked tag team.

titles.name: UWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Hoodlam, of the stable Dungeon of Devestation, through the middle of 1999.

titles.name: Attitude Tag Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag belts, named 'Tag Team (Attitude Tag Titles)' on its application form; its champions page, stamped 12 January 2009, lists two tag-team champions and two tag-team #1 contenders, all 'None'. No champion is recorded.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its pages name it, never a real company's belt; no reign of it is recorded.

titles.name: BioHazard Title
titles.epitaph: The first singles belt on the fed's champions page, beside the Demon Seed title. That page, stamped 12 January 2009, lists its champion and #1 contender as 'None'. On the first card (11 August 2008) Alexander Loveless unveils it from under a cover in the ring and the announcers hope for 'our first Bio Hazard Champion'; on 3 February 2009 he names Nos and Thomas Evans co-number-one contenders for it at Vengeance for Valentines. No champion is recorded.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its pages name it, never a real company's belt; no reign of it is recorded.

titles.name: ChaosBlood Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's hardcore belt: its application form offers 'Hardcore (Chaosblood Title)' as a division, and Thomas Evans and Brian Larsen apply for it. Its champions page, stamped 12 January 2009, lists the ChaosBlood Champion and its #1 contender as 'None'. No champion is recorded.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its pages name it, never a real company's belt; no reign of it is recorded.

titles.name: Demon Seed Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's second singles belt, named on its champions page and in its wrestler applications ('Singles (BioHazard Title and Demon Seed Title)'). The champions page, stamped 12 January 2009, lists the Demon Seed Champion and its #1 contender as 'None'. No champion is recorded.
titles.notes: The fed's own belt as its pages name it, never a real company's belt; no reign of it is recorded.

titles.name: TCPW North Star Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Twin City Pro Wrestling territory, held three times before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: TCPW Spotlight Title
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Twin City Pro Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: TCPW Spotlight Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A commissioner-created title in the FWA's own Twin City Pro Wrestling territory, held twice before its permanent retirement.

titles.name: TCW All Action Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt the narrator wants to turn into a test of a rising wrestler, with the weight limit removed. Sammy Bach holds it when the diary opens and loses it at Total Mayhem 13 to the Syndicate's Edd Stone. Edd Stone defends it at Excessive Force in June 2008 in the Hangtime Match of his own devising, against Sammy Bach and Acid, and keeps it. Edd Stone keeps it through July 2008, beating Hell Monkey at Summer Showdown with the Party's Over; Hell Monkey won the shot in a three-way ladder match on Badge of Honor. Edd Stone keeps it through August 2008: Art Reed, the fans' choice in a web poll, beats him at Hotter Than Hell only by count out, so the title stays with Stone. Edd Stone keeps it through September 2008: he beats the Cannonball Kid on Badge of Honor, when the Kid tries a powerbomb, and Art Reed in the rematch at Destructive Energy. Edd Stone loses it at Crunch Time in October 2008: Frankie Perez, who won the number one contendership in a three-way match on Badge of Honor, beats him with the P-Clutch after a mule kick to the head, taking his first TCW gold. Frankie Perez keeps it in his first month with it: at A Little South Of Sanity, after entrants chosen on Badge of Honor, he beats Art Reed, Greg Keith and Freddy Huggins in a four-way match, Greg Keith tapping to the P-Clutch. Frankie Perez keeps it through December 2008, beating Hell Monkey, who wins the ladder match for the contract, with the P-Clutch at Psycho Circus after Perez has abandoned Chris Rockwell and allied with Remo Richardson and Phil Vibert.

titles.name: TCW Hard Hitting Championship
titles.epitaph: TCW's newest belt: Mayhem Midden unveils it on Total Wrestling in Week 2 June 2008 and makes every match for it No Holds Barred (no run-ins, no weapons, no disqualification for using only your body). Eddie Peak, Sam Keith, Tyson Baine (who beats American Buffalo in a Strap Match) and Ricky Dale Johnson (who beats Frankie Perez on Badge of Honor) qualify, and Sam Keith wins the first championship in a four-way match at Excessive Force. Sam Keith keeps it through July 2008: he wins by disqualification over Tyson Baine on Total Wrestling, after Tommy Cornell's chair, and beats Ricky Dale Johnson at Summer Showdown with the Proton Lock. Sam Keith keeps it through August 2008: he beats Sammy Bach on Total Wrestling and, in a No Holds Barred match at Hotter Than Hell, Tommy Cornell. Sam Keith keeps it through September 2008: he draws with Chris Rockwell on Total Wrestling when the time limit runs out and, in a No Holds Barred match at Destructive Energy, beats Jeremy Stone with the Proton Lock. Sam Keith keeps it through November 2008, beating JD Morgan with the Proton Lock on Total Wrestling before Sammy Bach, who has taken Wolf Hawkins' contendership as a favour, hits him with a chair; at A Little South Of Sanity he beats Bach with the NeutronPlex. Sam Keith keeps it through December 2008: at Psycho Circus, in a No Holds Barred match, Sammy Bach wins by disqualification when Texas Pete hits him with a chair, a result the diary does not treat as a title change.

titles.name: TCW International Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt of the middle of the card. Wolf Hawkins holds it when the diary opens, keeps it against Koshiro Ino at Where Angels Fear To Tread by interference, and loses it to Ino in a no-disqualification match at Total Mayhem 13. Ino keeps it through June 2008, beating Sam Keith on Total Wrestling in Week 2 and, at Excessive Force, losing to Chris Rockwell only by disqualification. Ino keeps it through July 2008: Tommy Cornell's win on Total Wrestling comes only by disqualification, and at Summer Showdown Ino beats Sammy Bach with the Kobra's Bite. Ino keeps it through August 2008 until Hotter Than Hell, where John Anderson beats him with the Ammo Dump and the diary says TCW has a new International Champion. Anderson keeps it through September 2008: Wolf Hawkins beats him only by count out, and he beats Frankie Perez, Acid and, at Destructive Energy, Eric Tyler, each with the Ammo Dump. Anderson keeps it through October 2008: he draws with Sean Deeley on Total Wrestling when time runs out and beats Jack Marlowe with the Ammo Dump. At Crunch Time he makes an open challenge and Sean Deeley beats him by count-out, a result the diary does not treat as a change of champion. Anderson keeps it through November 2008: he beats Texas Pete on Total Wrestling after Wolf Hawkins interferes, and at A Little South Of Sanity he beats Pete and Hawkins in a three-way match, pinning Hawkins with the Ammo Dump after the Enforcers have beaten him down. Anderson keeps it through December 2008: he beats American Buffalo after Wolf Hawkins's Full Moon Rising lands on the Buffalo, draws with Hawkins at the time limit on Total Wrestling and at Psycho Circus beats Hawkins in a match the diary rates an A, with the Ammo Dump after fifteen minutes.

titles.name: TCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The pair of belts the Machines hold when the diary opens, for a full year by May 2008. They retain against Painful Procedure at Where Angels Fear To Tread and against the Young Guns at Total Mayhem 13. The Machines lose the belts to the New Wave at Excessive Force in June 2008. The New Wave keep the belts through July 2008, beating the Young Guns at Summer Showdown with the Special Force, after losing a non-title match to the School of Tradition on Badge of Honor. The New Wave keep the belts through August 2008, beating the Easy Riders, the British Lions and, at Hotter Than Hell, the School of Tradition. The New Wave keep the belts through September 2008: a disqualification loss to Freddy Huggins and Sammy Bach does not cost them the titles, and they beat the Keith Brothers on Total Wrestling, the Enforcers on Badge of Honor and, at Destructive Energy, the School of Tradition with Scout's Special Force. The New Wave keep the belts through October 2008, the Stone Brothers drawing with them in a non-title match on Total Wrestling; at Crunch Time they beat the Easy Riders, the tournament winners, only by disqualification. The New Wave keep the belts through November 2008, beating the Elite Express and the British Lions and drawing with the Keith Brothers on Total Wrestling when the Easy Riders interfere; at A Little South Of Sanity they beat the Easy Riders and the Stone Brothers in a three-team elimination match. The New Wave keep the belts through December 2008 until Psycho Circus, where they lose them in a hardcore match to the Easy Riders: Billy Fonda and Peter Hopper beat down Scout, take him to the corner and loop a chain, which Carl Batch holds, round his neck to anchor him to the turnbuckle, and finish Guide with the Emergency Stop onto a steel chair. The diary's closing notes call the fall of the New Wave a long reign ended and doubt that the Easy Riders will hold the belts as long.

titles.name: TCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: TCW's top belt, 'a prettier piece of gold the industry doesn't have', defended last on the card. Tommy Cornell holds it when the diary opens and through the first ten shows, beating Troy Tornado at Where Angels Fear To Tread and losing to him only by disqualification at Total Mayhem 13. Troy Tornado takes it from Cornell at Excessive Force in June 2008 with the Star Maker, ending Cornell's reign. Troy Tornado keeps it through July 2008, beating Chris Rockwell and Wolf Hawkins in a three-way match at Summer Showdown with the Star Maker. Troy Tornado keeps it through August 2008: at Hotter Than Hell he beats Brent Hill and Wolf Hawkins in a three-way match, pinning Hawkins after the Star Maker. Troy Tornado is still champion at the end of September 2008: he beats Tyson Baine, Sammy Bach in a ladder match and Chris Rockwell and Eddie Peak, and at Destructive Energy, in a three-way match with Johnny Bloodstone and Tommy Cornell, he and Bloodstone together make Cornell submit; the match ends with both men celebrating, Mayhem Midden saying he will have to talk to the Board, and the commentary saying only that Cornell is not the World Heavyweight Champion. The diary now shows two belts in October 2008: Tommy Cornell walks off with the belt Mayhem Midden is carrying, the Board bars him from title matches for six months, and Troy Tornado and Johnny Bloodstone each appear with a new custom belt, the prediction key billing Tornado as the Standing Champion and Bloodstone as champion of the Canadian Belt. At Crunch Time Tornado keeps his belt, beating Jeremy Stone and Remo Richardson in a three-way match with the Star Maker, and Bloodstone keeps the Canadian Belt, beating Brent Hill with the Bloodstone Mutilation. The Board recognises both belts as championships in November 2008: Mayhem Midden announces that Troy Tornado's and Johnny Bloodstone's belts are recognised, with the proviso that TCW cannot have two World Heavyweight Champions, and orders the two men, or whoever has beaten them for a belt in the meantime, to meet in the Malice in Wonderland main event in January to unify the belts. At A Little South Of Sanity Tornado, barring Tommy Cornell from a title shot, beats him in a non-title match with the Star Maker, and Bloodstone keeps the Canadian Belt, beating Chris Rockwell in a half-hour match. The two belts stay apart through December 2008, the Board's edict that they be unified at Malice in Wonderland in January standing: Johnny Bloodstone keeps the Canadian Belt, beating Edd Stone and, in a non-title match, Merle O'Curle, and Troy Tornado, as Triple-Threat Champion, picks the men for a six-man match whose winner takes the third place in his defence. At Psycho Circus, after Tommy Cornell hits Tornado and Eddie Peak with the retired TCW belt, Tornado beats Peak and Jeremy Stone in a three-way match with the Star Maker, and the diary's preview makes the winner of that match the man who goes on to face Bloodstone at Malice in Wonderland to unify the belts.

titles.name: TCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned by default at TCW's own first house show when tournament finalist Masked Bulldog was written out with an in-fiction injury, leaving Dr. Doom the fed's first-ever World Champion.

titles.name: Harvard Avalon Memorial Trophy
titles.epitaph: The trophy for TEAM's 2008 Tournament of Champions, won by Tyler Rayne; the one winner the record holds.

titles.name: TEAM Challenge Championship
titles.notes: Contested under a different gimmick match each time it changes hands (a steel cage at its debut, later falls-count-anywhere and lumberjack matches).
titles.epitaph: A prize purpose-built to test its holders under a new gimmick every time it's on the line, held throughout its first year by one man.

titles.name: TEAM Championship of Champions
titles.notes: Established between this wing's own first and second eras (the era map's own title-history document dates it to shortly after the first TEAM Invitational Tournament); the title's own establishment and its first champion's own coronation are not captured in this era's own page set, only D!'s standing reign by the time of SuperShow I. Declared vacant at the 2006 Dupree Cup Finals after D! was fired by New Alberta Professional Wrestling for backstage conduct; a vacant-title match (Mr. Amazing! vs. Jake Hix) was set for SuperShow II, outside this era's own window.
titles.epitaph: TEAM's own top prize, held for most of its first year by an underdog Canadian one-night-tournament winner before a real-world firing forced the league to strip it and start over.

titles.name: TEAM FREE FOR ALL~! Championship
titles.notes: An open-invitational title with no rankings or banked shots; any battle royal or gauntlet TEAM books for it crowns the next champion.
titles.epitaph: TEAM's own no-rules prize, open to any comer bold enough to enter the ring, changing hands three times in its first year.

titles.name: TEAM Lethal Lottery Championship
titles.notes: A tag title contested by randomly-paired wrestlers in a gauntlet format; no rankings or banked shots.
titles.epitaph: TEAM's own randomizer of a tag title, first claimed by two men drawn together only for the night.

titles.name: Chad Merritt Trophy
titles.notes: Introduced at the tournament's own preview show as originally designed to be TEAM's own Most Valuable Wrestler award before being repurposed, that same broadcast, as the Invitational Tournament's own prize; named for Chad Merritt, a CSWA authority figure.
titles.epitaph: The prize of TEAM's own first Invitational Tournament, a three-tiered trophy named for one of the circuit's own founding figures and first held by an Englishman who beat five other men from five different federations to claim it.

titles.name: ACW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded by forfeit at the promotion's own debut pay-per-view when the scheduled challenger failed to appear, then defended immediately against a replacement.

titles.name: ACWA Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded to the winner of an eight-man tournament final at the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: MEW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A title already active by March 2002, its own broadcasts announcing Morbid Wolf as the reigning champion before his first served defence, which he won.

titles.name: NAWC Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a Royal Rumble on the promotion's second card, then taken in the ring from its own thief at the first pay-per-view.

titles.name: SWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won for the first time on the promotion's own opening card.

titles.name: TWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed the promotion's longest-held title under Adrian Blades, who retained it against Exodus at the promotion's own 26 January 1999 pay-per-view and against Prince Geatar on its own 21 February 1999 broadcast before a multi-man conspiracy cost him the belt to Dave Davidson at the promotion's own Armageddon event.

titles.name: thReat Aggression Championship
titles.epitaph: The most travelled of thReat's belts. Riot won it from Lennox Dawson on Sunday Night Flaw 04 and handed it to Lawrence Clementia six weeks later; Rejection beat Clementia for it and held it to the company's closure on 23 June 2002, when the belt was retired. In the 2003 run Steve Solex won it at Malevolence, Wolf took it from him at Payback, and Ernie French took it from Wolf at Double Or Nothing and was still champion when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

events.note: "Belt was retired, due to closure of company on 06/23/02" — the title history's own line; the belt returned with the company in 2003.

titles.name: thReat Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A title of thReat's 2003 run. Vertigo won it from Phil Atken on Sunday Night Flaw 16; Phil Atken took it back at Malevolence 2003 over Vertigo and Tyler Davidson, and Tyler Davidson won it from Atken at Payback 2003 and was still champion when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

titles.name: thReat Fighting Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship thReat ran in both of its runs. Quincy Brown won it from Amp Canon at ReLoad 2002 and held it until the belt was retired with the company's closure on 23 June 2002. Vincent Pembridge won it from Jason Semps in a cage on Sunday Night Flaw 18 in 2003 (the fed's title history dates the win to Flaw 17 and counts ninety days), Jere Casarella took it from him on Sunday Night Flaw 25, and psycho-Rio won it from Casarella in a Fight To The Death at Double Or Nothing 2003, still champion when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

events.note: "Belt was retired, due to closure of company on 06/23/02" — the title history's own line; the belt returned with the company in 2003.

titles.name: thReat International Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship thReat ran in both of its runs. Takisuma Ogama won it from Noah Krone at ReLoad 2002 and held it until the belt was retired with the company's closure on 23 June 2002. Chris McCluskey beat blind for it at Double Or Nothing 2003 and was still champion when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

events.note: "Belt was retired, due to closure of company on 06/23/02" — the title history's own line; the belt returned with the company in 2003.

titles.name: thReat Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: thReat's tag team title, first recorded at Payback 2003, where the brothers of Born To Die beat three other teams for it; they were still champions when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

titles.name: thReat World Championship
titles.epitaph: thReat's top championship, held across both of its runs. Xaxon won it at ReLoad 2002 from Disciple X and held it until the company closed on 23 June 2002, when the belt was retired. When thReat reopened, General David Sanders beat Xaxon for it at Payback 2003, and was still champion when the title history ends.
titles.notes: thReat's title history (threat.theewe.net/cgi-bin/superstars.cgi?titlehistory), served at /promotions/threat/archive/threat-title-history.html.

events.note: "Belt was retired, due to closure of company on 06/23/02" — the title history's own line; the belt returned with the company in 2003.

titles.name: TNA Women's Knockout Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the Against All Odds card (a #1 contenders match), in the news of 17 July 2008 (Karen Angle against Kelly Kelly for it) and at Hard Justice, where, vacant, it is decided in a three-way that Angelina Love and Velvet Skye win together as the Beautiful People. 3 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder or, where marked, from the fed's champions page.

titles.name: TNA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as 'Robert Roode Inc. (c)' against the Motor City Machine Guns on the Against All Odds card; the fed's champions page then shows Alex Shelley and Chris Sabin, and by 22 July 2008 the New D-X, Big Show and Rikishi, who keep it at Hard Justice in a steel cage three-way. 3 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder or, where marked, from the fed's champions page.

titles.name: TNA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt. Christian Cage is its champion from the inaugural weeks, in the fed's news of 10 February 2008 ('Christian Cage's championship gold') and on its cards of 13 July and 10 August 2008, where Tomko stands at his side; Hard Justice (10 August 2008) has him keep it against Sting in a Last Man Standing match. 1 reign is filed, each from a page that bills its holder or, where marked, from the fed's champions page.

titles.name: TNA X Division Championship
titles.epitaph: Named on the Victory Road card of 13 July 2008 and on Hard Justice, where, vacant, it is decided in a four-man gauntlet that Jeff Hardy wins. Two earlier holders are known from the fed's champions page only, by the file names of its portrait images. 3 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder or, where marked, from the fed's champions page.

titles.name: TPG Diva Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Trish Stratus for as long as the belt had existed, in the fed's own commentary's words, and lost in three minutes and fifty-seven seconds to a flapjack slam from So Cal Val at Madison Square Garden on 17 December 2005. Two months earlier its champion had stood in the ring and demanded a match putting both of the fed's women's titles on the line at once.
titles.notes: The fed staged two women's champions at the same time — this belt and a Women's Championship held by Lacey — and its own segment calls them collectively “both TPG Diva Titles” (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/tpg-uncensored-results-2005-10-10.html).

titles.name: TPG Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Randy Walker walked out of The Proving Grounds still holding it and onto PWE Underground, where he told a camera that being hardcore champion was what had held him back and offered the belt to anyone who had a use for it. That is the whole of the record.

titles.name: TPG International Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own second belt and, by its own commentary, the one both of its last two champions won out of a tournament — each of them going through David D to get there. Wil the Thrill retained it in a main event against Carlito Caribbean Cool in the spring of 2005; Edge held it after him; JC Sinn carried it into December. On 9 October 2005 the fed ran three first-round matches for it in one night, and its founder came back at Christmas to demand it be dropped for the Pride Title instead.
titles.notes: No title history survives: the pinned TPG: Title History thread is listed on the fed's own roleplay forum, posted 4 December 2005, and was never captured (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/forum-tpg-aggression-132.html). An unresolved claim sits between this belt and the other: FoB's own Rebirth of 20 September 2005 has its commentary announce an interfering wrestler as “THAT'S MORTIS! THE TPG CHAMPION!!” (FoB's own Rebirth of 20 September 2005 (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-rebirth-2005-09-20-9684.html)), and the fed's own record names no belt he could have been carrying. Both of this promotion's singles championships are candidates and no document names one; the claim is recorded on both rows and settled on neither.

titles.name: TPG North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Named once, in a member's own reply to a December 2005 roleplay thread endorsing a contender for it. No champion, no match and no other mention of the belt survives.
titles.notes: The sole receipt is one line in the fed's own Aggression roleplay thread of 9 December 2005 (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/kick-in-the-door-wavin-the-four-four-2005-12-09.html). A second, in-fiction mention survives beside it: David D's own manager asks in a roleplay of 11 December 2005 “why would you want to just champion of North America when you can be the intercontinental champion”, and John Bradshaw Layfield's roleplay of the same week lists “North American Champion, International Champion, and especially The Proving Ground's Heavyweight Championship” as the three belts his opponent might chase (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/1-in-cont-s-match-2005-12-10.html; /promotions/pwe-inc/archive/standard-match-2005-12-10.html).

titles.name: TPG Pride Title
titles.epitaph: AJ Styles held it seventy-nine days and was still arguing about it in August 2004, by which point the fed had taken it away — “the TPG Pride Title is dead now,” one of his own opponents told him, “demolished; taken away.” Sixteen months later the fed's founder came back to Madison Square Garden asking why an International Championship was being paraded around with the Pride Title sitting on the sidelines, and the chairman offered to burn the International belt in front of him and bring this one back instead. It came back: the last line the record ever writes about the promotion has Montel Vontavious Porter defending it in May 2007.

events.note: The fed's own roleplay text of August 2004 has the belt already gone — “Only the Pride Title has been demolished; taken away” — with no date and no closing match recorded. It was defended again by 2007, so the event records what happened, not a permanent state.

titles.notes: Both the reign and the retirement come from one served document: AJ Styles's own signature record and the promo exchange around it (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/iron-man-battle-royal-2004-08-16.html). The board's own last capture, of 27 May 2007, carries a news line reading “TPG Showcase: Pride Title: Montel Vontavious Porter © d. The Mask”, which is held in the workshop and not served and is registered here as a second reign. The belt the fed's own chairman offered to bring back at Madison Square Garden in December 2005 was defended again, under the same name, eighteen months later.

titles.name: TPG Tag Team Championship
aka: TPG Inter promotional Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Patriots — Joey Legend and Daniel Justice — are the only champions the record names, and it names them in the past tense, in a news line about a match they were losing somewhere else.

titles.name: TPG Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced on 9 October 2005 with its champion, Lacey, showing it off to a crowd chanting that she sucked. The fed's own commentary calls her “one of two women's champions”, and its own segment that night has the other one demand a match to put both belts on the line. Nothing in the record says whether that match happened.
titles.notes: Named only by the ring announcer's introduction and the commentary around it (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/tpg-uncensored-results-2005-10-10.html); no other document in the held record mentions the belt.

titles.name: TPG World Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt the fed's own commentary said had returned to The Proving Grounds when Kris Adams won it at Madison Square Garden on 17 December 2005, beating JC Sinn with a frog splash thrown as a tribute. Before that the record is thin and out of order: PWE's own roster records name Chris Watts a former TPG World Champion without a date, and the chairman who had it carried to the ring that night, Mikel Sweeten, is never called champion in words. The fed billed the same belt as its Heavyweight Championship in the weeks either side.
titles.notes: Sources disagree on who held it going into End of an Era III: the show's own announcer crowns a NEW World Champion, and the show's own staging has Mikel Sweeten walk out with the belt over his shoulder without ever being introduced as its holder. Both readings are recorded; no reign is written for Sweeten. An unresolved claim sits between this belt and the other: FoB's own Rebirth of 20 September 2005 has its commentary announce an interfering wrestler as “THAT'S MORTIS! THE TPG CHAMPION!!” (FoB's own Rebirth of 20 September 2005 (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/fob-rebirth-2005-09-20-9684.html)), and the fed's own record names no belt he could have been carrying. Both of this promotion's singles championships are candidates and no document names one; the claim is recorded on both rows and settled on neither. The fed's own booking blurb of 10 December 2005 calls it “the returning 'TPG Heavyweight Championship'” a week before it was won (/promotions/pwe-inc/archive/standard-match-2005-12-10.html).

titles.name: TPW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in an eight-man bracket printed on the fed's own premiere show; also called “World Champion” on air.

titles.name: TPW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a tournament open to the whole roster, its final a Triangle match.

titles.name: TPW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a tournament whose final became a Triangle Tag Team Cage Championship match.

titles.name: TPW X-Treme Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided in the “Xtreme Scramble,” a battle royale open to the entire roster.

titles.name: TRW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced as the prize of a single-elimination tournament in the fed's own 14 February 1998 founding notice; no winner is named in this pull.

titles.name: TTW Impact Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced in October 2002 to be settled by the winning team of a six-man tag qualifier, contested in a triple-threat match the promotion's own text never confirms a result for.

titles.name: TTW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a single-elimination tournament across four September 2002 cards, its championship was settled in a two-out-of-three-falls final.

titles.name: IGA TV Championship
titles.epitaph: A silver belt on a white strap, defended at least three times a month. Maxime St. Jean won the first title match, a six-man elimination at The Battle for Fort Knox, and held it through the rest of 2001.

titles.name: TWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the American Patriot throughout the surviving 1996 record, retained by submission over Tywon on 16 October 1996; no closure or further title change survives.

titles.name: TWW Troy Windham Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top belt, named for its owner, who is stripped of it in the opening angle of 8 September 2008: PowerMaster takes it from Troy Windham and gives it to Cameron Cruise, who defends it at Barre and Newington. No loss of it is held.

titles.name: Dual Combat Championship
titles.epitaph: The last of the four belts on the fed's own Champions page, and the only one it gives plural holders ("Current Holders: [none]"): a tag-team belt. The page, captured 14 February 2003, reads "[none]" for its current and its previous holders, and no match on the fed's three Jurisdiction shows (7, 14 and 21 December 2002) puts it on the line: no holder is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: the fed's own Champions page (ubc.wrestleonline.org/champions.php, Wayback capture of 14 February 2003). The fed's own news of 1 January 2003 books this belt for that Saturday's Jurisdiction card (a three-way tag-team match, Krisis and Violent B, the Kingz of Africa and the Heart Throbs); no surviving record shows that card was held. The relaunch posts of 23 January 2003 (captured on the fed's front page, 14 February 2003) announce a 64-man Dual Combat tournament for it, of which only the qualifying brackets survive.

titles.name: Iron Brawler Championship
titles.epitaph: The third of the four belts on the fed's own Champions page. The page, captured 14 February 2003, reads "[none]" for its current and its previous holder, and no match on the fed's three Jurisdiction shows (7, 14 and 21 December 2002) puts it on the line: no holder is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: the fed's own Champions page (ubc.wrestleonline.org/champions.php, Wayback capture of 14 February 2003). The fed's own news of 1 January 2003 books this belt for that Saturday's Jurisdiction card (Brad Douglas against Johnny NightMare, after a battle royal for a number-one contendership); no surviving record shows that card was held.

titles.name: Superior Brawler Championship
titles.epitaph: The second of the four belts on the fed's own Champions page. The page, captured 14 February 2003, reads "[none]" for its current and its previous holder, and no match on the fed's three Jurisdiction shows (7, 14 and 21 December 2002) puts it on the line: no holder is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: the fed's own Champions page (ubc.wrestleonline.org/champions.php, Wayback capture of 14 February 2003). The fed's own news of 1 January 2003 books this belt for that Saturday's Jurisdiction card (MrSynnerster against Red Vizionz); no surviving record shows that card was held.

titles.name: Ultimate Brawler Championship
titles.epitaph: The first of the four belts on the fed's own Champions page, which lists them from the most important to the least. The page, captured 14 February 2003, reads "[none]" for its current and its previous holder, and no match on the fed's three Jurisdiction shows (7, 14 and 21 December 2002) puts it on the line: no holder is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: the fed's own Champions page (ubc.wrestleonline.org/champions.php, Wayback capture of 14 February 2003). The trophy Brett Wayne lifts at the close of the last Jurisdiction card (21 December 2002) is the fed's "Future Brawler Trophy Award" ("FBA Trophy"), which its own news of that day says the match was for; it is not this belt. The fed's own news of 1 January 2003 books this belt for that Saturday's Jurisdiction card (a three-way elimination match, Chris "AK" Carter, Tommy Grady and Brett Wayne); no surviving record shows that card was held.

titles.name: Bloodfest Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page names Chaos as the sole, current Bloodfest Hardcore Champion; no earlier reign or challenger survives in the held record, and the corpus never calls his own Fridaynight Warfare win over D-Strange a title defense.

titles.name: Bloodfest Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page names Heywood Jablowme as the sole, current Bloodfest Heavyweight Champion -- no earlier reign or challenger survives in the held record, and the belt's own United States counterpart sits vacant on the same page, "To Be Determined @ Bloodfest Dec.1,2000." One reign anchors the ledger here: the only one attested.

titles.name: Bloodfest Tagteam Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page names "The Jablowme Brothers" -- Heywood and Sherwood Jablowme, per the fed's own served Roster page -- as the sole, current Bloodfest Tagteam Champions; no earlier reign or challenger survives in the held record.

titles.name: Bloodfest United States Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Champions page lists the Bloodfest United States Title vacant, with a title match "To Be Determined @ Bloodfest Dec.1,2000" -- no held document records that match ever taking place, and no earlier reign survives in the held record.

titles.name: UCW King Of HaRdCoRe
titles.notes: Awarded to the winner of a tournament at Havoc.
titles.epitaph: Awarded once on the surviving record; no defense recorded.

titles.name: UCW North Atlantic Champion
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own title-history page with no reign history recorded there.
titles.epitaph: No holder survives on the record.

titles.name: UCW South Pacific Champion
titles.notes: A regional title.
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the surviving record.

titles.name: UCW Tag Champions
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own title-history page with no reign history recorded there.
titles.epitaph: No holder survives on the record.

titles.name: UCW Total Champion
titles.notes: The promotion's own top singles title.
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the surviving record.

titles.name: LVW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The title of Las Vegas Wrestling, which UCW bought in August 2006; its holder, Jimmy Donovan, is 'the only LVW champion ever'. Irishred won it at Night of the Legends II and spray-painted it into the B4B Championship, the 'Blood for Blood' belt, won by making an opponent bleed.

titles.name: UCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at Civil War in June 2006 with a four-way match won by Adam Benjamin; Bryan Storms took it at Scars and Stripes and Dakota Smith from him in November 2006.

titles.name: UCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top singles title: its first holder in the owner's title history is The First, followed by Irishred; The First won it back at Scars and Stripes in September 2006 and still held it at Night of the Legends II.

titles.name: UCW Dream Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in a cage of weapons at Madison Square Garden on 27 November 2005 against three challengers at once and retained by pinfall — the only complete UCW title match anywhere in the surviving record, and it was fought on another promotion's pay-per-view.

titles.name: UCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Trent Hawk's, and the belt Ultimate Championship Wrestling was going to put into an Elimination Chamber against its World Title the last time it ran a show. He was still carrying it in August, walking a red carpet into a Foundation of Brutality building where the headmaster took it off him at the door.
titles.notes: The unification match is named only in The Mask's own recollection: “The last time I was in a UCW ring, it was announced that there would be an Elimination Chamber match to unify my World Title, and Trent Hawk's Heavyweight Title.”

titles.name: UCW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by The Mask off Trent Hawk on 15 July 2005 and the only UCW belt that kept being defended after the promotion stopped existing: he retained it against Holden Gilmour on a PWE pay-per-view, then unified it with the IPW Impact Title, and was defending it again against the Prophet when the record ends.

titles.name: UCW US Championship
titles.epitaph: The first belt The Mask ever challenged for and the only one he failed to win: Mike Smith beat him for it in the weeks before the North American Title changed hands, and not one other match for it survives anywhere.
titles.notes: The championship is named once, as “US Title match”, inside a run of match lines the same ledger heads with the promotion's own acronym for its other two belts. The full name it was billed under is not recorded; the short form is kept as written.

titles.name: UCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: The Mask beat BG Bomb for it on 5 August 2005 and had it three weeks when the promotion announced an Elimination Chamber to unify it with the Heavyweight Title, then closed its doors instead. He carried the belt to PWE, where Michael Hopkins was introduced as its champion and he introduced himself as the man it had belonged to — an argument about a company nobody in the room had heard of, conducted with a belt that had its holder's name engraved on it.
titles.notes: Sources disagree on who held it after August 2005: The Mask calls it “my World Title” in the same promo that has Hopkins holding it, and PWE's own Underground introduces Hopkins as the UCW World Champion. Both readings are recorded.

titles.name: UCWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A four-man first-round bracket (Undertaker over Arn Anderson, Ultimate Warrior over Ron Simmons, Lord Steven Regal over Mr. Perfect, Sabu over Chris Benoit) opens the fed's own launch PPV; no further round survives in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: Source: UCWF 'Bash for the Belts' (15 Jul 1996), part 2.

titles.name: UCWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: An eight-team tournament opens the fed's own launch PPV (Road Warriors, Sting and Razor Ramon, Harlem Heat and others all advance past the first round); this collection's own holdings end before a final is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: UCWF 'Bash for the Belts' (15 Jul 1996), part 1.

titles.name: UCWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in an eight-man tournament of real-wrestler-billed first-round matches (Sid vs. Flair, Vader vs. Hart, Diesel vs. Hogan, Luger vs. Michaels) at the fed's own launch PPV; this collection's own holdings end before any semifinal or final is recorded.
titles.notes: Source: UCWF 'Bash for the Belts' (15 Jul 1996), part 3.

titles.name: UCWF Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-stipulation title from the start — a Thumbtacks Match, a Flaming Hell In A Cell, a Deathmatch, a Barbwire Beat Down — that “QBz Finest” Blaze loses to Wes Easton in the first of those at Fury 2002-09-08. Flashing Thunder holds it through an unrecorded turnover into a draw against The Fox at Wrestle Insanity, then loses it, also unrecorded, to Kevin Murray by the time Bryon Wade Osbourne makes his own UCWF debut at Fury 2003-06-20 and wins the title in a Deathmatch with his first opponent. Osbourne survives a draw against Sean Johnson (and a mid-match elimination of Flashing Thunder) at Breakout — the last the surviving record shows of the belt.

titles.name: UCWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Mr. Wacko takes this title from The Fox at Immortality 2002 with a backslide and defends it days later at Fury 2002-09-08 in a fatal four-way against Crazy Hayze, Bobby Linken and Crusher — the last the surviving record shows of the belt, Wacko still champion when the record ends.

titles.name: UCWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Scorpion, of the stable American Bad Boyz, opens the surviving record's own account of this title by taking it from Crash Paradise at Immortality 2002 and defending it at Fury 2002-09-08 — Johnny Johnson steals the belt off him afterward with a kendo stick, an angle beat the record never turns into an actual title change. The lineage that follows shows three more unrecorded turnovers before landing on Notorious, then “QBz Finest” Blaze, who takes it from him at Wrestle Insanity, then “The Reality” A.J. Simmons, who loses it to Rich Bitch at Resurrection — the last champion the surviving record shows.

titles.name: UCWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: A tournament for a third singles title, its own bracket shown only in first-round action at Fury 2003-06-20: Mr. Wacko advances past Jason Compton and Bobby Linken, and The Krazy Kid advances past Santa Claus. No further round survives in the record, and no champion is ever named.

titles.name: UCWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Krazy-Wacko Connection is this belt's own constant, winning and losing it three separate times across the surviving record without ever being shown regaining it on-page: from Dark Carnival at Immortality 2002, lost by disqualification to The G's at Fury 2002-09-08 days later, regained unrecorded by Wrestle Insanity only to lose it there to A.C.E. (Ace Of Spades and Crash Paradise), then regained again unrecorded in time to defend it, “STILL” champions, against Italian Organized Crime at Resurrection — the last the surviving record shows of the belt.

titles.name: UCWF Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: The record's own account of this belt opens on a finish nobody could call: Ace Of Spades and challenger Jinx both have their shoulders down for referee Gangsta Mac's own three-count at Immortality 2002, and the announce team simply refuses to name a winner. The lineage that follows is a chain of retains broken by unrecorded turnovers — CM2, The Krazy Kid and Mr. Wacko each hold it into a show where the record shows someone else already champion — until “QBz Finest” Blaze takes it from Wacko at Resurrection and The Fox wins it off Blaze in a six-man Six Pack Challenge at Breakout, the last title change the surviving record shows for this belt.

titles.name: UCWF Vamped Championship
titles.epitaph: Absent from the fed's own two 2002 shows, first attested with The Krazy Kid already champion at Wrestle Insanity. The Fox takes it from him at Resurrection, loses it to “Prime Time” The Vine at Fury 2003-06-20, and Vine — billed at Breakout as having “just won the title last week” — retains it there against Santa Claus, the last the surviving record shows of the belt.

titles.name: UCWF World Championship
titles.notes: Billed once as the “Heavyweight Championship” at Wrestle Insanity's own finish (promotions/ucwf/archive/wrestle-insanity-2003.html); every other appearance calls it the World Championship.
titles.epitaph: UCWF's own top title changed hands six times across the surviving record, twice on the strength of a bare rollup rather than a clean finish: Johnny Johnson loses it to Bobby Linken at Wrestle Insanity while distracted by a fabricated news report naming him alongside a dying convicted murderer, and The Notorious Don Joe Giovanni takes it from Johnson at Resurrection on a quick count by special guest referee Mumrat, the fed's own owner. Giovanni's own reign is the longest the record shows in outline: he survives a 60-minute Hell In A Cell Ironman against Ace Of Spades at Fury 2003-06-20, three falls to two, only to lose the belt to the same man weeks later in a Breakout dome-cage match, kicked off a 20-foot ladder short of the roof hatch Ace pulls himself through alone. Ace Of Spades is the last champion the surviving record shows.

titles.name: UCWP Canadian Heritage Championship
titles.epitaph: No title-change document survives in the held record.

titles.epitaph: No title-change document survives in the held record.
