titles.epitaph: No title-change document survives in the held record.

titles.name: UCWP World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship; no title-change document survives in the held record.

titles.name: UEA Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance-wide singles title the United E-Wrestling Alliance's own member federations built its one surviving super-card around, settled in a six-match-deep single-elimination bracket drawing entrants from LAW, UCW and the by-then-closed ILOC.
titles.notes: Crowned in the singles half of the alliance's own joint singles-and-tag-team tournament, staged 24 Aug 1996 across a six-part card (uea-uea-tournament-part-1-of-6 through -6-of-6).

titles.name: UEA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The alliance-wide tag-team title crowned in the tag half of the United E-Wrestling Alliance's own joint tournament, settled in a three-round eight-team bracket drawing entrants from LAW and UCW.
titles.notes: Crowned in the tag-team half of the same 24 Aug 1996 six-part super-card that crowned the UEA Championship (uea-uea-tournament-part-1-of-6 through -6-of-6). Both titles came out of the tournament's own opening division listing (part 1 of 6): eight teams, three rounds.

titles.name: UeMW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A second championship, contested only under no-disqualification rules, set out in Underground e-Mail Wrestling's own founding handbook; no card was ever posted to crown a first holder.

titles.name: UeMW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The top championship set out in Underground e-Mail Wrestling's own founding handbook; no card was ever posted to crown a first holder.

titles.name: UeMW Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A weight-limited championship set out in Underground e-Mail Wrestling's own founding handbook; no card was ever posted to crown a first holder.

titles.name: UEW American Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own second-ranked singles title; billed the "North American Title" in 1996 before the 1997 rename.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's own second singles belt, twice held by the same wrestler across the fed's run -- lost to a cage-match challenger at the first Holiday Horror, then reclaimed and defended in a Triple Threat at the second.

titles.name: UEW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.notes: Introduced as an international invitational battle royal at the fed's own 1999 New Year's supercard; billed at its introduction as the European Cruiserweight Grand Prix Invitational Championship before settling into everyday use as the Cruiserweight title.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's newest belt, born out of a fifteen-man international battle royal and successfully defended twice inside its first three months by the man who won it.

titles.name: UEW Internet Championship
titles.notes: Retired 15 March 1997, unified into the UEW Television Championship in a ladder match.
titles.epitaph: A short-lived UEW singles belt with one recorded holder, retired into the Television Championship in a ladder match at the fed's own Ides of March PPV.

titles.name: UEW Television Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own third-ranked singles title.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's own third singles belt, absorbing the retired Internet Championship in a 1997 ladder match before settling, by year's end, into the hands of the fed's own self-billed longest-reigning Television champion.

titles.name: UEW Television Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own second-ranked tag title, decided by an eight-team tournament in April 1997.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's own second tag straps, settled by an eight-team April 1997 tournament and last seen changing hands in the same Holiday Horror 2 scaffold match that also crowned new Ultimate Tag Team Champions.

titles.name: UEW Ultimate Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own top singles title throughout its attested run, 1996-1997.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's own top singles belt, changing hands at least eight times across 1996-97 -- most memorably three separate reigns for one wrestler, ended when a challenger dethroned him with the finisher "Southern Comfort" at the fed's own Holiday Horror 2.

titles.name: UEW Ultimate Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own top tag title throughout its attested run.
titles.epitaph: The UEW's own top tag straps, held four times running by one team before a multi-team scaffold match at Holiday Horror 2 handed them to a pair of challengers on the same night the fed's Television Tag belts changed hands too.

titles.name: Lord of The Underground
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own highest belted honor, its FAQ says, contested only among the holders of its other belts and defended at every pay-per-view; offered vacant to new sign-ups in its November 2005 recruiting drive, with no holder attested in the held record.

titles.name: UeWA Cruiser Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding post; no result survives.

titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own rules and recruitment posts; no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: UEWA World Tag Team Championship Belts
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own rules and recruitment posts; no result survives in the held record.

titles.name: UeWF Atlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: One of a matched pair of regional belts, defended against any challenger of the champion's own choosing who stood inside the top tenth of the rankings. Pain held it into the 1992 hiatus. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. The belt is VACANT in the newsdesk's own standings of 15 February 1992 — Admiral Ax had left it to take the Intercontinental Championship. Biff “the Terror” Jones fills the vacancy on 19 February (“Biff ‘the Terror’ Jones eeked a pin out over Mosh to become the new Atlantic Champion”) and Pain takes it off him on 25 February. A whole reign and a vacancy stood between this ledger's own first two reigns and are now registered between them.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holder transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. The federation's own World Championship semi-final of 28 December 1991 was announced in advance as crowning a champion either way — “the winner to move on to the finals of this tournament and the loser to be named the UEWF's first Atlantic Champion” — and Admiral Ax lost it. Pain's reign is renumbered r002 accordingly; how the belt passed from one to the other is not something any held document says. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: The chain between the two reigns on this ledger is partly recoverable and is not one step. The table of 15 February 1992 reads "Atlantic Champion: vacant"; the same broadcast has Mosh promising to take the belt from Biff "the Terror" Jones "next week"; the roundup of 19 February has "Biff 'the Terror' Jones eeked a pin out over Mosh to become the new Atlantic Champion"; and the roundup of 25 February has "Pain succeeded in dethroning new Atlantic Champion Biff 'The Terror' Jone[s]." So: Admiral Ax (28 December 1991, r001 here) … vacancy … Biff "the Terror" Jones (c. 19 February 1992) … Pain (c. 25 February 1992, r002 here). At least one whole reign and one vacancy sit between the two rows this ledger carries.

titles.name: UeWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own second singles belt, defended weekly against the second-ranked contender. Admiral Ax held it into the 1992 hiatus and was still recognised as champion at the relaunch. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. Mr. B holds this belt at 10-1-1 in the newsdesk's own standings of 30 January 1992; by 15 February he has the World Championship and Admiral Ax has this one at 10-0-0. Ax then defends it twice on the record — over Lord Plunder on 19 February and over Rage on 25 February — and is 14-1 in the last standings the newsdesk printed.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holder transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. Where this belt's own first reign began is still not on the record. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: Admiral Ax holds it throughout — 10-0-0 in the table of 15 February 1992, beating Lord Plunder to retain on the 19th, beating Rage to retain on the 25th, and 14-1-0 in the table that week. His single loss in that span is the World Championship match he lost to Mr. B, not a defence of this belt. Nothing in the held record says when the reign began.

titles.name: UeWF Intercontinental Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The junior tag belts, held by Carnage into the 1992 hiatus and still recognised at the relaunch. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. The Armed Forces hold this belt at 10-1-0 in the newsdesk's own standings of 30 January 1992, with Carnage ranked first behind them; Carnage hold it at 8-2-0 by 15 February and defend it twice on the record, over the Annihilation Alliance on 19 February and over the Ruffians on 25 February. An earlier reign this ledger did not carry is now registered.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holders transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. Nothing in the Summit's own record bears on when this reign began. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: Carnage hold it throughout — defending against the Annihilation Alliance on 19 February 1992 and against the Ruffians on the 25th — and the WeWF's own TTTTTT tournament of 24 March 1992 still bills them into its ring as "the UeWF InterContinental Tag Team Champions, CARNAGE!" Nothing in the held record says when the reign began.

titles.name: UeWF Ladies Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The HellKats and the Valkyries are the only two teams ever recorded holding these belts — the HellKats from around 30 January 1992 until the Valkyries beat them for the titles on 19 February 1992 — and the division closed with the federation's 1992 relaunch with no further holder on record.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. The discontinuation is stated in the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. That is the only sighting of this belt being contested anywhere in the record, and it is a sighting of a card that does not survive. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: A holder does survive, in a document this collection holds and does not serve. The roundup of 19 February 1992 reads "The Valkyries defeated the Hellkats to become the new UeWF ladies tag team champions," and the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March 1992 has two TWIW women watching tapes of UeWF cards and calling the HellKats "one hell of a team." So the division ran, the belts were contested, and at least two teams held or challenged for them — none of which is minted here, because neither document is served and neither team has a row anywhere in the registry.

titles.name: UeWF Ladies World Championship
titles.epitaph: Declared with the federation itself and defended, by its own rules, against the highest-ranked woman who had not had a shot that month. The division was not run again after the spring of 1992 — the president's own relaunch call says so outright. Its first champion was crowned in a ladies' battle royal on the second night of the Summit of E-Wrestling, 28 December 1991: eight women, elimination over the top rope only, and Laurie Liberty, who drew last, threw the Angel of Death out to win it. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. Laurie Liberty is champion at 5-0-0 on 30 January and 6-0-0 on 15 February 1992. On 19 February the newsdesk rolls the finish as tape: Sarah Jackson heaves her over the top rope, Rhonda Rhodes gets in cheapshots on the outside, and “JAckson covers......ONE!....TWO.....THREEEE!!!! We've got a new champion”. Jackson keeps it on 25 February when Rhodes interferes again. The row that said “the reign is left open” is corrected.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. The discontinuation is stated in the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992: "I will not be running a ladies division." Eight women, two starting and six entering at one-minute intervals, elimination over the top rope only; Laurie Liberty drew last and won it. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: This reign ended, and the held record both dates and stages it. The roundup of 19 February 1992 cuts to a clip of the ladies title match and closes it on "JAckson covers......ONE!....TWO.....THREEEE!!!! We've got a new champion"; the roundup of 25 February has "Sarah Jackson kept her Women's belt, when Rhonda Rhodes interfered saving Ms. Jackson from a pinfall at the hands of Laurie Liberty." Sarah Jackson — one of the eight women of the battle royal this belt's first reign came out of — took it from Laurie Liberty in the third week of February 1992 and was still holding it a week later. No reign is minted from an unserved document; the row is corrected instead.

titles.name: UeWF Pacific Championship
titles.epitaph: The Atlantic Championship's opposite number, defended on the same terms. Lord Plunder held it into the 1992 hiatus. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. T'ien “the Master” Lung holds the belt in the newsdesk's own standings of 30 January, 15 February and 19 February 1992, and defends it over the Shropshire Slasher; Lord Plunder takes it back on 25 February with an international object. The first reign on this ledger DID NOT run unbroken to May 1992, and the row that said so is corrected.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holder transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. The federation's own other World Championship semi-final, on the same night, carried the same double purpose — “The Winner will advance to face in the Championship round and the loser will be be awarded the Pacific Championship Title” — and Lord Plunder lost it to Lucifer on 28 December 1991. The reign the relaunch call recognised five months later begins there. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: This belt changed hands twice inside the reign this ledger carries as one. The table of 15 February 1992 has T'ien "Master" Lung as Pacific Champion at 12-1-1, with Lord Plunder first among the contenders; the roundup of 19 February has T'ien beating the Shropshire Slasher to hold it; and the roundup of 25 February has "Lord Pluder beat Pacific Champion T'ien 'The Master' Lung by hitting him with an internation object," with the table that week reading "Pacific Champion: Lord Plunder (12-4-0)." The reign this ledger dates to 28 December 1991 therefore did NOT run unbroken to the May 1992 relaunch: T'ien Lung held the belt in between, and Lord Plunder's second reign begins in the last week of February 1992.

titles.name: UEWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced at the fed's own August 1997 founding, alongside an Americas Title and World Tag Team Titles; no reign is recorded in this collection's own 1997 holdings, and no further trace of the fed survives.
titles.notes: The fed's own founding post, 31 August 1997.

titles.name: UeWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top belt, defended every week against the highest-ranked contender who had not already had a shot that month. The Ultimate Lanny held it when the federation went dark in the spring of 1992, and was still recognised as champion when it reopened that May; no match for the start or the end of that reign survives. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. The belt's own winter is now dated end to end. Lord Plunder is champion in the newsdesk's own standings of 30 January 1992, at 11-2 — and the same issue's rumour mill says why: “The recent ‘administrative errors’ in the UeWF which allowed Lord Plunder to obtain the World Championship were a direct result of the bribing of the UeWFs chief officer - Harvey Wallbanger.” Mr. B is champion by 15 February at 11-2-1; he hands Admiral Ax the first loss of his career to retain it on 19 February; and on 25 February the Ultimate Lanny beats him with a superplex, called move for move — “ONE! TWO!!.........THREEEEE!!!!!! We've got a new World Champion!!!!!” Three reigns are registered here on that record.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holder transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. The federation's own inaugural World Championship tournament ran two rounds on 27 December 1991 and both semi-finals on the 28th, and its final — Mr. B against Lucifer — was advertised for a fifth night that no held document carries. The Ultimate Lanny went out of it in the FIRST ROUND, beaten by Lucifer. Whoever won that final, this reign did not begin at the Summit, and the record still does not say when it did. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: the standings table of 15 February 1992 has Mr. B as World Champion at 11-2-1; the roundup of 19 February has Mr. B beating Admiral Ax to retain it, handing Ax the first loss of his career; and the broadcast of 25 February stages the title change itself, play-by-play — The Ultimate Lanny beating Mr. B with a superplex, "We've got a new World Champion!!!!!" — and prints the new table, "World Champion: The Ultimate Lanny (15-3-1) 89". The reign the May 1992 relaunch call recognises therefore begins in the last week of February 1992, and at least two earlier reigns exist that this ledger does not carry: Mr. B's, and whatever Lord Plunder held when the newsdesk's own rumour mill of 30 January 1992 reported "the recent 'administrative errors' in the UeWF which allowed Lord Plunder to obtain the World Championship."

titles.name: UeWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own senior tag belts, held by the Dangerous Emotions into the 1992 hiatus and still recognised at the relaunch. Carried back from the WeWF wing, whose own newsdesk This Week in Wrestling printed this federation's weekly title results and full rankings through the winter of 1992. The Dangerous Emotions' own manager settles the question of whether theirs is the first reign, on camera at the Boston Garden on 15 February 1992: “Now that my Emotions are the first UeWF tag-team champions, I want you to know that they will be the ONLY tag-team champions.” They are champions in the standings of 30 January and 15 February, retain by disqualification on 19 February and win by disqualification on 25 February.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own founding document, 19 November 1991 (promotions/uewf/archive/new-pbem-the-uewf-1991-11-19.html), which sets out how it was to be defended. Holders transcribed from the federation's own relaunch call, 14 May 1992. It reached a final between the Armed Forces and the Dangerous Emotions — announced for a fifth night that no held document carries — so the tournament narrows this reign's start without dating it. The only surviving trace of the federation's own weekly cards rides on this belt, recorded here: the Summit's own fourth night bills the two teams contesting that semi-final as this federation's own number three and number one ranked tag teams "after three weeks of action," and has the challengers there to avenge "last week's loss to Carnage which almost knocked them out of first place." Three weeks of cards, a running ranking and at least one result between these two teams therefore existed by 30 December 1991. Not one of those cards survives anywhere in the held record, and none is structured here. The weekly record survives second-hand, in another federation's own newsdesk, not yet served here. Nine editions of the WeWF's own This Week in Wrestling and its TTTTTT tag tournament, 30 January to 31 March 1992, plus the EMWA's own Kings Of The Ring of 25 March, are held in this project's own Google Groups dumps and are unserved. Between them they carry this federation's own weekly title results week by week, its full ranking tables with win-loss records and points, and two of its own matches staged play-by-play. What they say about THIS belt: the Dangerous Emotions' own manager, interviewed on the broadcast of 15 February 1992, calls them "the first UeWF tag-team champions" — which would put the Summit's own unstaged fifth-night final their way — and the roundup of 19 February has them losing by disqualification to the Armed Forces and keeping the belts. The roundup of 25 February then has it the other way round, "The Armed forces barely held onto their title, losing to the Dangerous Emotions by DQ," which is either a title change nobody reported or the newsdesk transposing its own two teams. The contradiction is recorded rather than resolved; both documents are held and unserved.

titles.name: UFW Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: A weight-class championship opened on Dream Master at the federation's first pay-per-view, 24 December 1999. Jaguar held it three times and Degenerate twice across a January-to-March run of short reigns. Professor Herbert D. Dorkiman's win of 20 August 2000 is the last change it recorded.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: A no-rules championship opened on Slasher on 24 December 1999 and passed twenty more times, Raker taking it twice in the first two months. Hex's win of 20 August 2000 is the last change it recorded, and he is the belt's holder on the federation's own final Champions page.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW Rising Star Title
titles.epitaph: A championship for the federation's newer members, opened on The Gimp on 26 March 2000 — four months into the run — and traded fifteen more times in five months, The Gimp and Havok each holding it twice. "The Scholar" Howard Porter's win of 19 July 2000 is the last change it recorded for it; the federation's own final Champions page bills him as holding this belt and the US Title at once.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW Stables Title
titles.epitaph: A six-man championship contested between the federation's stables, opened on The Showtakers on 25 February 2000 and carried by The Legion, The Forsaken Brotherhood and The Congregation in turn. Two of its six recorded changes leave the holder undisclosed on the federation's own record, and the federation's own final Champions page lists the belt the same way.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The federation's two-man championship, opened on CHAOS INC. on 24 December 1999. Fifteen reigns are recorded across fourteen teams, The Isolators, CHAOS INC., The Avator & Biohazard and Iceman & Myst each taking two. The Brainiacs' win of 18 August 2000 is the last it recorded, and they are the champions on the federation's own final Champions page.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW TV Title
titles.epitaph: The federation's most-traded championship: twenty-three reigns in eight months, opened on The Body on 24 December 1999. Iceman held it three times and B.A. Bruiser three, Bloodshed, JiN and Anguish twice each. Nemesis' win of 22 August 2000 is the last title change of any kind the federation's own record records.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW US Title
titles.epitaph: A secondary singles championship, opened on Myst on 10 December 1999 and changing hands eighteen more times. Myst took it three times in its first five months and JD Stalker and The Total Package twice each. "The Scholar" Howard Porter's win of 20 August 2000 is the last change it recorded, and he is the belt's holder on the federation's own final Champions page.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW Woman's Title
titles.epitaph: A championship for the federation's women's division, opened on Mystic on 24 December 1999. Pandora and Fury traded it twice each through the spring. The federation recorded Thunder winning it on 28 May 2000 and, on the same date and as the belt's own final line, that the division was discontinued.

events.note: The federation's own Titleholder History page: the belt's final line reads "Division Discontinued", dated 28 May 2000.

titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFW World Title
titles.epitaph: The federation's top championship, first won by Executioner on 19 November 1999 and changing hands seventeen more times over the nine months the fed ran. Layeth the Smack Down held it three times and Myst three times, the two of them trading it across January and again in the closing summer; Roody Poo, the fed's own house jobber, held it for two days in April after counting his own pinfall as the match's referee. Myst's third win, 20 August 2000, is the last reign it recorded.
titles.source: UFW's own Titleholder History page, served as /promotions/ufw-ultra-2000/archive/ufw-title-history.html

titles.name: UFWS All-Jobber (Junior Heavyweight) Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship for the bottom of the card, restricted by the federation's own rules to wrestlers built on 145 power points or fewer, and the first belt it ever awarded — Baron Von Klaw won the All-Jobber final before either of the other tournaments reached its own. It changed hands seven times, was held for one week by a man who was North American Champion at the same time, and ended the record on a Soviet technician the standings had classed a jobber all summer.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own recruitment announcement of 8 April 1991 — “the PWGA All-Jobber champion, a title restricted to wrestlers with 145 power points or less (not counting the 25 free power points for class moves)” — and filled by a six-man tournament on 22 April. The belt is called both the All-Jobber and the Junior Heavyweight title in the federation's own text, sometimes in the same issue. One reign begins inside the unheld Report #11 and is chained across that gap at month precision.

titles.name: UFWS North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's second singles belt, and the only one filled by losing: the runner-up in the opening night's World title tournament took it as a consolation. Its own announcement said the champion would defend against any of the top five contenders, chosen by the president himself so that different people got shots — and it changed hands seven times in four months, including once at the Summit of E-Wrestling and once inside an issue that does not survive.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own recruitment announcement of 8 April 1991 — “the PWGA North American champ, who will defend against any one of the top 5 contenders (I will make the choice myself, so as to give different people title shots)” — and filled on 22 April by the tournament final's losing side. One change happened at the Summit of E-Wrestling (its own wing, id `summit-of-e-wrestling`) and one inside the unheld Report #11; both are chained at month precision with the reason given on the reign.

titles.name: UFWS North American Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's fifth and last championship, announced in July 1991 alongside the founding of the All-Jobber Confederation and filled by a nine-team tournament whose final closed the second SuperCard. The New Mystics won it and were still champions three days later, when the record ends.
titles.notes: Announced in the federation's own Report #10 of 18 July 1991 and filled at the second SuperCard on 26 August 1991 (promotions/ufws/archive/ufws-supercard-2-1991-08-26.html). The federation's own text is the authority and it says five.

titles.name: UFWS World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled on the federation's opening night, 22 April 1991, by a twelve-man tournament whose final also decided the North American belt: the winner took the world title, the loser the second. Sargent Sledge Hammer won it and held it for seven weeks, and the record's last word is that he holds it still. Between those two facts it changed hands five times in ten weeks, once when a whole stable beat the champion unconscious behind the referee's back.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own recruitment announcement of 8 April 1991 — “The PWGA World Champion, who will defend against the No.1 Contender each week” — and filled by tournament on 22 April (promotions/ufws/archive/pwga-by-e-mail-1991-04-08.html, promotions/ufws/archive/pwgea-report-1-1991-04-22.html). One reign begins inside the unheld Report #11 and is chained across that gap at month precision.

titles.name: UFWS World Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Filled by a six-team tournament on the opening night and defended almost every week after it. Seven reigns in four months, two of them by the same team twice over, and the belts finished the record on the team that lost the very first final.
titles.notes: Declared in the federation's own recruitment announcement of 8 April 1991 — “the PWGA Tag-Team champions, who will defend against the No.1 contenders” — and filled by tournament on 22 April. One reign begins inside the unheld Report #11 and is chained across that gap at month precision.

titles.name: UGA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own title page names one champion: Chainsaw Charlie, crowned in the promotion's own "Ultimate Quest" tournament at Summer Breakout 2001 — the only reign the held record attests under the UGA name itself, distinct from the fed's own earlier WWC-era Heavyweight lineage (see the WWC World Heavyweight Championship's own separate record).
titles.notes: This reign's own source (title.html, geocities.com, YAHOOIDS/C/o/Colosseum/Park/8978) is an UNSERVED raw file in this accession's own vault mirror, not one of this wing's four served documents — a prior tier-1 pass's own citation named a served page that does not exist, corrected 2026-08-31 after verifying the claim directly against the raw file (see the reign's own won.source). The same raw page also carries this wing's own UGA Television and Super J-Crown Cup title lineages and two then-vacant titles (International, King of Hardcore), none of which are registered — a pending-enrichment lead for a future formal serving pass.

titles.name: WWC Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a Triple Hardcore Challenge culminating in a bloody four-way dance at Carnacage 99, where Street Punk pinned Joe Snow to become the fed's own only attested WWC Hardcore Champion. No prior champion or title history is named in the held record.

titles.name: WWC International Championship
titles.epitaph: Larry Gionet held the WWC International Championship into Carnacage 99, retaining it by disqualification against The Jester after Jago Ripley and The Beast ran in. No document held records when or how Gionet won the title.

titles.name: WWC World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Mad Dog Mortimer's own defense against Mighty Ryan Kelly at Carnacage 99 ended in controversy: a suspended referee, Frat Boy, came out uninvited and counted the pinfall for Kelly, "apparently" — the fed's own recap's own hedge — making him champion. No prior reign data survives for Mortimer's own title win.

titles.name: WWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a full eighteen-champion chain across the promotion's WWC era (1997-2001), before the WWC name itself gave way to UGA — seventeen of the eighteen reigns are structured here, the page's own numbering skipping from a 14th to a 16th champion, an archival gap in the source itself, never filled. "The Franchise" Shane Stud held the title five times, more than any other champion the ledger names; the chain closes on his own fifth and final recorded reign, won at Carnacage III (31 December 1999, billed the last-ever Carnacage) over Disturbed Youth, the man who had beaten him for the belt eleven days earlier in the WWC's own first-ever Canadian title change.

titles.name: UIW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed for the loser's slot out of UIW's planned Championship Weekend battle royal, then re-announced as its own October tournament with a Madison Square Garden final; no result survives in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: UIW's own September and October 1997 announcements (promotions/uiw/archive/).

titles.name: UIW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced for a 30-man battle royal at UIW's planned September 1997 Championship Weekend, then again for an October 1 Championship Coronation after the September date fell through; no result of either survives in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: UIW's own September and October 1997 announcements (promotions/uiw/archive/).

titles.name: UIW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed for a first-round tournament at UIW's planned Championship Weekend and again at its October relaunch, with a final scheduled for 18 October 1997 at Madison Square Garden; no result survives in this collection's own holdings.
titles.notes: UIW's own September and October 1997 announcements (promotions/uiw/archive/).

titles.name: UIWA Universal Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Sinacle upset four-time, seven-month champion Whipple_jr for the Universal Heavyweight Championship at Stormfront on 11 August 2000 — one reign inside a much longer Whipple_jr lineage the surviving record never fully recovers.

titles.name: UIWA World-Class Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: High Intelligence (Pennance and Jordanzombie) lost the World-Class Tag Team Championship to Murder Inc. (Sinacle and Marley) under hardcore rules at Stormfront, 11 August 2000.

titles.name: UKCW FWA European Title
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own United Kingdom Chaos Wrestling territory, attested for 4 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: UKCW FWA Intercontinental Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: A championship of the alliance's own United Kingdom Chaos Wrestling territory, attested for 7 reigns in its own record.

titles.name: UKWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The prize the promotion's own Champions League tournament was built to crown; no challenger had yet earned a shot as of the last card in this record.
titles.notes: Named inconsistently across the promotion's own text ("UKWA Heavyweight Title" and "UKWA World Title"); treated as one title. No reign is recorded in the held record.

titles.name: UWF Ultimate Championship
titles.epitaph: First won by Archangel at the promotion's own inaugural pay-per-view, "Championship Mania," and held by "Big D" Devestation by the promotion's own 18 November 1999 broadcast.

titles.name: Underaction Championship
titles.epitaph: SWWE Fed's own Underaction brand championship. Salvador is billed as champion on the promotion's own 29 April 2007 card; by Unsurrender, Rayden held it and lost it to Boy Killer, per the promotion's own October 2007 news post.

titles.name: STW Unified Double Crown Title
titles.epitaph: Formed by unifying the vacant International and National Television titles in Bulletin #35; changed hands some fourteen times before its own last champion unified it with two other titles at once.

titles.name: EWWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in a ladder match against a top contender, saved only by a returning ally's brass knuckles.

titles.name: GAWA United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a ten-man battle royale at WrestleKrazy II; its first champion retained it a week later with a hidden pair of brass knuckles.

titles.name: SWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Won for the first time on the promotion's own opening card, by referee stoppage.

titles.name: STW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested for a single reign before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: UPW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Dark since TTW's own closure in November 2015, the North American Championship sat vacant until UPW filled it in a single-night, eight-man tournament on Showdown; "Legionarius" Antonio De Luca beat Glenn Chambers in the final and held the belt through the rest of the promotion's own life.
titles.notes: The served ledger (north-american-title-history.html) also carries an unbroken TTW-era reign chain back to Slamfest II, May 2012; those reigns are not individually registered, for the same reason given on the World Heavyweight Championship's own row.

titles.name: UPW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant since TTW's own closure, the Television Championship was filled by Felix Sandoval in a ladder match on Showdown; he held it through a controversial time-limit-draw defense against Brandon Franklin before losing it to Franklin at Survival, and Franklin lost it in turn to Windham Brody on UPW's own last served Showdown.
titles.notes: The served ledger (television-title-history.html) also carries an unbroken TTW-era reign chain back to Showdown, May 2011; those reigns are not individually registered, for the same reason given on the World Heavyweight Championship's own row.

titles.name: UPW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: UPW's own World Heavyweight Championship continued an older title lineage from a predecessor league the corpus names only as "TTW," whose reign ledger runs back to Slamfest I in May 2011 before recording that TTW itself "closed down" 30 November 2015. The belt sat dark through UPW's own founding until a Fatal Four-Way on the promotion's fifth Showdown crowned Aaron "All Day" Lewis its first UPW-era champion; Derek Rage took it from him at Survival, UPW's own first pay-per-view, and held it through the rest of the promotion's own life.
titles.notes: The served ledger (world-heavyweight-title-history.html) also carries an unbroken TTW-era reign chain back to May 2011; those reigns are not individually registered — their holders wrestled for a promotion this museum does not hold (a predecessor never expanded beyond the initials "TTW" anywhere in the held record), and no UPW tenure could honestly be dated that early.

titles.name: UPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Continued the same TTW-era lineage as UPW's other belts, dark since TTW's own 30 November 2015 closure until the Warriors — DeAwn Carter and Kel Robertson — won it in the main event of UPW's very first Showdown. Soldiers of the Sun took it from them in a Fatal Four-Way at Survival and held it through the rest of the promotion's own life.
titles.notes: The served ledger (world-tag-team-title-history.html) also carries an unbroken TTW-era reign chain back to Slamfest I, May 2011; those reigns are not individually registered, for the same reason given on the World Heavyweight Championship's own row.

titles.name: URW International Title
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast as its secondary championship, to be decided in a four-way ladder match not held in the held record.

titles.name: URW Suicide Title
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast as a hardcore-styled championship for its most extreme competitors; no tournament or match toward it survives in the held record.

titles.name: URW World Tag-Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast; no tournament or match toward them survives in the held record.

titles.name: URW Television Title
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast, with an eight-man tournament toward it beginning the following week, not held in the held record.

titles.name: URW United States Title
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast as its third singles championship; no tournament or match toward it survives in the held record.

titles.name: URW Universal Title
titles.epitaph: Announced on the promotion's opening broadcast as its top championship, to be decided the following week in a 25-man battle royale not held in the held record.

titles.name: USCW Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Crowned at Battle Bowl '98 in a tournament final decided by a stablemate's interference, its new champion ambushed by an old rival within the hour.

titles.name: USCW Light Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands in a three-way match settled by a run-in blow rather than a fall between the two wrestlers left standing.

titles.name: USCW North American Title
titles.epitaph: Ended an undefeated champion's own six-match streak at Midweek Madness.

titles.name: USCW Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Won at Battle Bowl '98 by a team whose own second member never set foot in the ring for the title match.

titles.name: USCW Television Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in three months during the fed's own busiest 1998 stretch, first in the fed's inaugural Weapons and Cage match and then by submission at Midweek Madness.

titles.name: USeW Light-Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt the federation's own smaller men fought over, and the one whose defences the record catches at their least ordinary: a champion branded with a hot iron before his own title match and saved by a magician, and, a year later, a rookie who asked for a match with one of the sport's best high flyers to prove something to himself and shook hands with him afterwards.

titles.name: USeW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Abolished in its own champion's hands. He was stripped of it in February 1996 for two reasons the federation gave at once — that he had begun calling it the Native American Title, and that the federation wanted to be more competitive — and the president then announced the championship would no longer exist, replacing it with a four-way match for a new Television title. Its former holders wrestled on for months billed as former North American champions.
titles.notes: Justice D. Nyde is separately named on the same broadcast as another former North American champion.

events.note: Abolished by the federation's own president in the announcement that stripped Comanche War Dog and opened a four-way match for the new World Television Title. Dated from the Leprecharnage broadcast of 17 March 1996, which places it “three weeks ago.”

titles.name: USeW United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: One reign survives, and it was new when the record catches it: a newly crowned champion in May 1995, already booked into the World Heavyweight title match that was to close the card.

titles.name: USeW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own top belt, and one a returning legend claimed on air had only been renamed: the JCWF's own world title, he said, carried under new letters since the merger that swallowed his federation. It changed hands twice in twenty-two days in the spring of 1996 — taken off 187 at Leprecharnage with a chair slid in by that same returning legend, and taken back on the next Blow-Out in a match the federation's own president cleared both entourages out of, to see who the better man was. Its earlier line is only partly recoverable: a 600-pound champion in May 1995, and a masked former champion out of Guadalajara still being billed as one a year later.
titles.notes: The claim that it was formerly the JCWF's own championship is made on air by Freddy Flame at Leprecharnage and is not corroborated elsewhere in the held record: “you can change the name of the title, but that doesn't mean a two bit thug can still wear it.” Recorded as the fed's own on-air claim, not as an established lineage.

titles.name: USeW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's own senior tag championship. Two reigns survive and neither of their beginnings does: brothers holding it in May 1995 with a mini-tournament booked to decide their next challengers, and an undefeated pair out of London holding it a year later and finishing their Leprecharnage defence in three minutes thirty-six.

titles.name: USeW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Made in early 1996 out of the North American title's own abolition — a four-way match for a new belt, on a night the federation said it wanted to be more competitive — and then the most-travelled championship in the surviving record: three changes in thirty-six days, to a visiting EWF light heavyweight at Leprecharnage, to a masked former world champion three weeks later in three minutes, and to a trumpet-carrying former light heavyweight champion three weeks after that.
titles.notes: The federation's own account of the four-way that created the belt contradicts itself inside a single sentence — it names Haplo as the reigning Television champion at the time AND Justice D. Nyde as the current World Television champion, then says Haplo retained — while every other document bills Nyde as the champion going into Leprecharnage. The contradiction is recorded rather than resolved, and no reign is written for that match.

titles.name: USeW World Television Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A second set of tag belts below the World Tag Team titles, and the busiest pair in the federation's own spring: held by a card-sharp team whose manager kept them at Leprecharnage by getting his own men disqualified, taken three weeks later by two masked giants in a twenty-nine-minute match, and kept a fortnight after that by exactly the same trick in reverse.
aka: USeW World TV Tag Team Championship

titles.name: USPW National Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt Jim Force holds when the diary opens and loses to Citizen X in January 2007. Citizen X keeps it through five defenses by the end of the range, two of them against Force. Steve Flash takes the belt from Citizen X on the third show of March 2007 and keeps it through the April and May shows against Fumihiro Ota, Corporal Doom and William Hayes, with a defense against Hayes set for the first Family Night. William Hayes takes the belt from Steve Flash in a two out of three falls match at the first Family Night, Friday of Week 1, June 2007, and keeps it in June against Art Reed, Freddie Datsun, Muffin and Wanda Fish. William Hayes keeps the belt against Jacob Jett in July 2007 and against Wanda Fish in August. William Hayes keeps the belt against Bulldozer Brandon Smith and Art Reed in August 2007 and against Rudy Velasquez in September; Wanda Fish is set to challenge him at Blaze of Glory. William Hayes loses the belt to Wanda Fish at Blaze of Glory in September 2007, by disqualification when Triple D hits Fish with it; Fish is champion at the end of the range, with Jacob Jett set to challenge her at A Haunting in America. Wanda Fish keeps the belt against Jacob Jett at A Haunting in America in October 2007; Fish, Jett and Art Reed are booked into a three-way for Pilgrimage. Wanda Fish keeps the belt at Pilgrimage in November 2007 by pinning Art Reed in the three-way with Reed and Jacob Jett; she is champion at the end of the range. In December 2007 Wanda Fish is still champion; Phlex, her new boyfriend, is booked as her challenger for Winter Epiphany.

titles.name: USPW Unappreciated Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt the card for Blaze of Glory bills in September 2007 as the "USPW Unappreciated Championship", fought for in a four-way between Bulldozer Brandon Smith, Brett Hall, "The Trademark" Thomas Morgan and Insane Machine, the lower-card wrestlers the narrator says the crowd could not care less about. Bulldozer Brandon Smith wins the match in the first half of the show, and the diary names no earlier holder. Bulldozer Brandon Smith draws with Brett Hall by double disqualification in September 2007 and beats Brendan Idol in October; Hall is set to challenge him at A Haunting in America. Bulldozer Brandon Smith keeps the belt against Brendan Idol and Insane Machine and against Brett Hall in a street fight at A Haunting in America in October 2007; Idol earns a Pilgrimage challenge by beating Hall on the Monday of Week 3. Bulldozer Brandon Smith keeps the belt against Brendan Idol at Pilgrimage in November 2007 with a Backdrop Driver; he is champion at the end of the range. Bulldozer Brandon Smith beats Mean Jean Cattley in November 2007 and has his belt stolen by the Mantis in December, who is booked against him at Winter Epiphany.

titles.name: USPW World Championship
titles.epitaph: USPW's top belt. Bruce the Giant holds it when the diary opens and loses it to Freddie Datsun at Stars, Stripes and Slams in January 2007; Datsun defends it against William Hayes, Peter Valentine and Umaga into March, with a burst appendix after Bruce's chokeslam off the stage keeping him out for part of February. Umaga takes the belt from Datsun in a steel cage match on the third show of March 2007, keeps it against Datsun, Trent Shaffer, Muffin and Datsun again through the end of May, and is set to defend it against Triple D at the diary's first Family Night. Umaga beats Muffin on the fourth Saturday of May 2007 and keeps the belt in June against Triple D at the first Family Night, Freddie Datsun and Triple D again on the fourth Family Night, still champion at the end of June 2007. Umaga keeps the belt against William Hayes at the Family Night of Thursday, Week 4, July 2007 and loses it to Darryl Devine in a steel cage match at the Family Night of Friday, Week 1, August 2007; Devine is champion at the end of the diary's second week of August. Darryl Devine keeps the belt against Bruce the Giant in August 2007, against William Hayes at Summer of Love, which the narrator calls the best match in his history, and against Freddie Datsun and Jim Force in September; he is champion in the first half of Blaze of Glory, where Muffin is set to challenge him. Darryl Devine keeps the belt against Muffin at Blaze of Glory in September 2007, in a match restarted after the referee counted her pin, and beats her down in a cage match on the Monday of Week 4; he is champion at the end of the range, set to defend it against Sam Strong at A Haunting in America. In October 2007 Darryl Devine keeps the belt against Frankie Perez, Bruce the Giant, Sam Strong, back from retirement at A Haunting in America, and Davey Wayne; Freddie Datsun wins the number one contendership and takes the belt away from him in a brawl on the Thursday of Week 3, and the two are set to meet at Pilgrimage on 22 November 2007. In November 2007 Darryl Devine keeps the belt against Umaga on the Monday of Week 1, in a match the narrator rates an A*, and against Freddie Datsun at Pilgrimage, when the Masked Man hits Datsun and Danny Jillefski counts the pin; he is champion at the end of the range. Through December 2007 Darryl Devine is still champion with no title match booked; the Masked Man is revealed as Jack Giedroyc on the Thursday of Week 2 and is booked against him at Winter Epiphany.

titles.name: USPW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The pair of belts The Towers of Power hold until the third show of the diary. They pass to The Dudez!!!1! in January 2007, then to the Canadian Crusties a week later, who defend them against the Lords of War in March. The Dudez!!!1! win the belts back in a three-way match on the third show of March 2007 and keep them against The Demons of Rage and Veteran Mentality, with another defense against the Demons of Rage set for the first Family Night. The Dudez!!!1! keep the belts in June 2007 against the Demons of Rage at the first Family Night and Veteran Mentality at the fourth; Trent Shaffer then carries the belts off after a chair attack, and the diary records no change of champions. The Dudez!!!1! beat Trent Shaffer and Chance Fortune, billed as the dudes, at the Family Night of Thursday, Week 3, July 2007 and take the belts back from the pair, and beat them again in August. Team Seduction, Human Arsenal and Fumihiro Ota with Seduction, take the belts from The Dudez!!!1! at Summer of Love in August 2007; the Dudez are given a rematch, set as a ladder match for Blaze of Glory. Team Seduction keep the belts against The Dudez!!!1! in a ladder match at Blaze of Glory in September 2007; Veteran Mentality are named the #1 contenders for A Haunting in America. Team Seduction keep the belts against Veteran Mentality at A Haunting in America in October 2007. The Valentines take the belts from Team Seduction at Pilgrimage in November 2007 when Triple D turns on Human Arsenal, and lose them minutes later to Divinity's new members The Hotshots, who keep them against The Valentines on the Monday of Week 3. The Hotshots keep the belts against Veteran Mentality on the Thursday of Week 4, November 2007 and against The Dudez!!!1!!! on the Thursday of Week 1, December 2007; Maxmillion Productions are booked against them at Winter Epiphany.

titles.name: SWL United States Television Title
titles.epitaph: Won by Night from a previously undefeated Manhunter with the Nightfall powerbomb on the promotion's earliest surviving card.

titles.name: USWF Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize, first awarded on a controversial triangle-match finish involving a lookalike twin swap.

titles.name: USWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag-team prize, first awarded at its own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: USWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own secondary prize, first decided in a 27-man battle royal and immediately stolen by a wrestler who had hidden under the ring for the whole match.

titles.name: USWF Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own first, undisputed championship, crowned in a one-night, eight-man tournament at its debut pay-per-view.

titles.name: USWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own tag-team prize, first awarded at its debut pay-per-view after a tournament final that ran past its own time limit.

titles.name: UVWA Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: The second-ranked title of the fed's own five-title set, named in its own sole founding document (30 December 1997). No bestowal survives, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: UVWA Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The lightweight division title of the fed's own five-title set, named in its own sole founding document (30 December 1997). No bestowal survives, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: UVWA Ultimate Championship
titles.epitaph: The top title of the fed's own five-title set, named in its own sole founding document (30 December 1997) as 'the big cheese' only the very best in the fed can compete for. No bestowal survives, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: UVWA Ultimate Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The tag-team title of the fed's own five-title set, named in its own sole founding document (30 December 1997). No bestowal survives, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: UVWA Viscious Championship
titles.epitaph: A specialty-match title of the fed's own five-title set, named in its own sole founding document (30 December 1997) for 'the master of special matches.' No bestowal survives, so no holder is recorded.

titles.name: UWA World Championship
titles.notes: Attested by the fed's own Random Rumble card of 24 February 1997 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1997-02-24-uwa-2-0-random-rumble.html); no winner survives in the record. NFW's own later continuity stages a “resurrected” revival of this same belt as one of its own storylines — see nfw-uwa-world, a separate title under NFW's own promotion, not a continuation of this ledger.
titles.epitaph: The UWA's own top prize, and the reason the promotion staged the Random Rumble at all. The belt was vacant going into 24 February 1997 — the card bills it as “up for grabs” and its own commentary calls it “one of the MOST prestigious World titles in wrestling history” — and thirty entrants were called to a Royal Rumble-style match to decide it, with the last two standing set to meet in a ladder match. Commissioner Sullivan tore that up when the final four hit the floor at the same time, ruling instead for a four-way King of the Hill ladder match: the first man to pull the belt off a hoop fifteen feet above the ring. Winston Steele, Nathan Storm, Carlos Canyeta and Javid Dones went back for it. Who came out with the belt is not in the surviving record — the one held copy of the card ends during the entrances, and no later UWA document survives to say. Eight years on, NFW's own continuity stages a revival of this same physical belt as a storyline of its own — see nfw-uwa-world for that record; it is NFW's fiction about this title, not a continuation of the real UWA's own, unresolved history.

titles.name: UWC World Anarky Cup
titles.epitaph: A monthly six-man single-elimination tournament title, with its holder automatically re-entering the next month's field.

titles.name: UWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, defended monthly or stripped for inactivity, with challengers drawn from the top three contenders.

titles.name: UWC World Ironman Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in twenty-minute matches scored by most falls, three times a month and at every pay-per-view.

titles.name: UWC World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag team title, left largely inactive by a shortage of teams.

titles.name: UWF Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Jeff Hardy from Summer Party (28 September 2008), where he retained against Edge. By the Sacrifice brand's own launch (February 2009), John Cena is the billed champion instead; no surviving document records how the title passed from Hardy to Cena. Edge earned the next challenge for it by winning Sacrifice #1's own Elimination Fatal-4-Way, aided by Randy Orton's interference; that match's own result closed with Cena, Orton, Mr. Kiz and Edge in open conflict, setting up a promised BlockDown title match not captured.

titles.name: Contest of Champions
titles.epitaph: An annual December tournament, run four times on the surviving record: Tsunami Oni won the inaugural in 2002 over runner-up Lacuna Debris, Ruff Ryder the second in 2003 over runner-up Ezra Kazee, Hot Mask the third in January 2005 over runner-up Kenny Mercury, and Clyde the fourth in January 2006 over runner-up Chris Storm.

titles.name: UWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Jimmy Wang Yang at the promotion's own founding (20 June 2008). A Sacrifice #1 (24 February 2009) dialogue exchange between Gregory Helms and Kofi Kingston states Helms later held this title on WAR and then lost it back to Jimmy Wang Yang, but no surviving documents carries either of those matches; Jimmy Wang Yang is the billed champion entering WAR #16 (5 April 2009), where he loses the title to Shannon Moore.

titles.name: UWF Divas Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Melina at the promotion's own founding (20 June 2008); still billed as her title on WAR #16 (5 April 2009), where Natalya challenges her for a match "next week", not captured. No document read records Melina ever losing this specific title, though a separately-named "UWF Women's Championship" changes hands twice in the meantime (see that title's own record) -- whether the two are the same title under two different names at different points, or genuinely two parallel women's titles, is not resolved by any document read.

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's Hardcore Championship, held by Ravi Moon on its about January 2010 home page; the about March 2009 page prints the words 'Held Up' where a champion's name would go.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's second singles title, held by Bucky Skyler on its about March 2009 home page and by Tyrone Kidd on its about January 2010 page.

titles.name: Prime Time Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles title the fed calls the Prime Time Championship, held by Edward Stiles on its about March 2009 home page and by Zoey Swan on its about January 2010 page.

titles.name: Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's tag titles, held by the Horsemen on its about March 2009 home page and by Serena and Darren Revel on its about January 2010 page.

titles.name: Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's top title, with two holders on its two held home pages: Blair Kivisto in about March 2009, who had just held it against Gage Gannon at Numbered Days, and Tyler Havoc in about January 2010. The January 2010 page says Andy Titsuhiro has held it twice and Ricky Stanton three times; no date of any of those reigns survives.

titles.name: UWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Finlay on WAR #7 (8 September 2008), where he retains in a Six-Way match. By the Sacrifice brand's own launch (February 2009), King Booker is the billed champion instead; no surviving document records how the title passed from Finlay to Booker.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The number-two belt, and the one the North American Championship was twice folded into and pulled back out of — merged 18 January 2004, separated again that August. Its own 2004 Quick Facts credit Joshua Dunn with the longest reign (140 days) and Digital Mortality with the most (three); Seymour Almasy won it once, in a 3-Title/3-Ladder match, and was stripped immediately. Past the fed's own ledger, Richard Hayes renamed it the “Insert-Name-Here Championship” in January 2005, leaving each champion to name the belt and set its rules; Kenny Mercury held it first, then Ruff Ryder and Jamie Shock in the spring, and Clyde from June until James von Doom took it from him in an August unification match with the North American belt, Clyde winning it back in October. Tessa Windsor's own win over Chris Storm at Sins of the Past (2006) is staged in-show as unifying it with the North American belt, though the fed's own site kept tracking both lineages separately afterward.

titles.name: UWF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Rey Mysterio from at least WAR #7 (8 September 2008), where Randy Orton attacks him ahead of a title match; Mysterio retains against Orton at Summer Party in an I Quit match built on both men's own history with the late Eddie Guerrero. By the Sacrifice brand's own launch (February 2009), Randy Orton is the billed champion instead; no surviving document records how the title passed from Mysterio to Orton. Sacrifice #1 (24 February 2009) sets up an Orton-Mysterio rematch for the following week, not captured.

titles.name: UWF Cruiserweight Championship of the World
titles.caption: A singles championship for the wing's lighter-weight division, changing hands twice inside three weeks in the wing's own 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Won by Uriah Hawkins at Gold Rush 2003 and lost in his first defense two and a half weeks later to a same-night replacement challenger, Chris O'Brien, after Hawkins broke his arm on a botched moonsault fall.

titles.name: UWF Eurasian Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: A singles championship for the UWF-Eurasia roster, defended on the flagship Meltdown card for the first time by Colby Greene.
titles.epitaph: Colby Greene, already champion, retained over "The Hero" Marcus Johnson by pinfall (the Bayou Bomb) on the belt's own first defense on the flagship Meltdown card, 20 October 2004.

titles.name: UWF Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.caption: The wing's top singles championship, held by Edmond Winston IV entering this pass's own October 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Retained by Edmond Winston IV over "Doctor EMS" Eric Matthew Somers on 4 October 2003 under a stipulation that ended Somers's own UWF career.

titles.name: UWF Meltdown Championship
titles.caption: A singles championship for the wing's own midweek program, crowned in a fifteen-man battle royal and two-match tournament on the show's first-ever title edition.
titles.epitaph: Commissioner Becky Byers announced the title the week before, framing it as ending Meltdown's own status as a secondary program; Papa Legba won the inaugural tournament on 17 December 2003, beating Paul Wong in the finals with the Black Magic superbomb.

titles.name: UWF North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: A singles championship held by Eugene Robinson entering this pass's own August 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Defended to a draw by Eugene Robinson against Tragedy on 30 August 2003 after Derek Irvin's outside interference forced a double stoppage.

titles.name: UWF North American Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: A tag team championship held by Team Canada entering this pass's own October 2003 record, until the Ghost Dancers exploited a fine-print contract clause to win it alone.
titles.epitaph: Won by the Ghost Dancers from Team Canada with stereo scorpion deathlocks on 25 October 2003, after a contract clause meant only this title, not the World Tag Team Championship, was actually on the line in the match.

titles.name: UWF Rampage Championship
titles.caption: A singles championship contested on the wing's own weekly broadcasts, held by Paul Wong entering this pass's own August 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Defended nearly every week on Saturday Night Rampage, with Paul Wong retaining it against Tom Landis on 9 August 2003 after Team Canada's interference disqualified the challenger.

titles.name: UWF Unified Television Championship
titles.caption: A singles championship created by unifying the Meltdown and Rampage Championships, held by Marcus Nuit as its first champion.
titles.epitaph: Marcus Nuit, the reigning Rampage Champion, beat Meltdown Champion Tigress by pinfall (the 51st Drop) in a title unification match on 22 June 2005 to become the belt's first champion, then retained it by disqualification over "Violent" Victor Frost in its own first defense on 6 July 2005 after Sabbath's own interference.

titles.name: UWF Women's Heavyweight Championship of the World
titles.caption: The wing's women's championship, won by Stephanie Harper at Gold Rush 2003 and defended against three different challengers within this pass's own record.
titles.epitaph: Won by Stephanie Harper at Gold Rush 2003 and retained against Bliss on 30 August 2003, with a three-way defense against Nina Grimsson and Myra Benedict promised for the following week after their own title-eliminator ended in a draw.

titles.name: UWF Women's North American Championship
titles.caption: A second women's title alongside the long-running Women's Heavyweight Championship of the World, its first champion already crowned by the time of this record.
titles.epitaph: Instituted as a second tier for the women's division, with Sonya Benedict billed as its first champion and a twenty-second countout rule set for her own title defenses.

titles.name: UWF Women's Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: A women's tag team championship billed as held by the Love Sisters, Leanna and Lolita Love, entering this pass's own October 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Held by the Love Sisters, Leanna and Lolita, whom the promotion's own broadcast names as champions; not defended in their 22 October 2003 six-person loss to the Coven, a three-on-three match with no title match of its own.

titles.name: UWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: The wing's top tag team championship, held by the Ghost Dancers entering this pass's own August 2003 record.
titles.epitaph: Held by the Ghost Dancers, Jason and Michael Keening, who retained it by default on 9 August 2003 when a three-way defense against Team Canada and Alex Extreme and Quinn Brown was thrown out as a no-contest.

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Restarted from the GIWF, and blank on the earlier-recovered 2003 title-history page under the note “Title Brought Back From the GIWF Abyss & Restarted by New UWF Owner Al Crud” — a fuller 2004 copy fills it in, and a later rpcommunity.com continuation, captured 2007, carries it a further year past that. Seymour Almasy held it twice inside a single day (won, stripped, won back); James von Doom's own reign is credited 265 days by the source's own count, though its own dates only support 224 — recorded as printed, unreconciled. Merged into the Intercontinental belt in January 2004, pulled back out that August, and unified with it in-show by Tessa Windsor's own win over Chris Storm at Sins of the Past (2006), the fed's own champions overview afterward listing her holding both.

titles.name: Regal Rumble
titles.epitaph: The GIWF's own annual Rumble, continued under the UWF banner: Shawn Eclipse won it at the Zero Tolerance PPV in January 2002, Kevin Starr at the Coronation PPV in July 2003 over runner-up Misfit, and Tsunami Oni at the Terror in Tokyo PPV in August 2004 over runner-up Jamie Shock.

titles.name: Shoot Wrestling Championship
titles.epitaph: The THC's own shadow belt, created when hardcore wrestling was banned in December 2001 and the THC itself briefly went dark; ran independently until 16 February 2003, when it was absorbed back into the reunified THC. Seymour Almasy is among its recorded holders.

events.title: uwf-thc
events.note: Absorbed back into the reunified THC — Jamie Shock's own reign row is marked "final Shoot Champion; title merged into the THC, 16 Feb 2003" in the fed's own ledger.

titles.name: Stable Wars
titles.epitaph: The GIWF's own annual stable tournament, continued under the UWF banner starting with a fourth edition: Generic Faces of Doom in 2002, WACC Mark 4 Stroke 9 in 2003, and Mike Montgomery's own Player's Club at a sixth edition run from Madison Square Garden in 2004.

titles.name: UWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the promotion's own founding (20 June 2008, there named the "World Tag Team Championship"). Billed as held by Paul London & Brian Kendrick by Summer Party (28 September 2008), where they retain against Cade & Murdoch. By the Sacrifice brand's own launch (February 2009), John Morrison & The Miz are the billed champions instead, said in-story to have won the titles at the promotion's own New Years Party (January 2009, not independently captured); no surviving document records how the titles passed from London & Kendrick to Morrison & The Miz. A separate WAR #16 (5 April 2009) dialogue line refers to a "UWF World Tag Team Championship" as a future UW Mania stake, using the founding's own older name; whether this is the same title under its original name, still tracked separately on the WAR brand, or a slip of the promotion's own writing, is not resolved by any document read.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The hot-potato belt of the UWF era, exactly as it had been in the GIWF — the 2004 revision's own Quick Facts credit Shadow Blade with the most reigns (four) and, by its last update, Hot Mask with the longest (79 days). Seymour Almasy held it three times across the run. Several rows carry names the crew would not perform today, marked under the Bum Boozler rule; State Trooper Roger Rogers's own reign ends with him vacating the title and throwing it into a river rather than face Ruff Ryder. After the 2004 revision the belt passed from Silvio Rochelli to James von Doom in the Clash's Television Title Jubilee on 6 March 2005, then to Red Rock, whose reign was the fed's longest to that point, and on through James Mason to Sledge at the Regal Rumble in September.

events.note: The belt was put up in a unification match against the World Heavyweight Championship and went dark when its holder won that match and left with the World title instead. The card of that night calls the match on its way to the ring — “One way or the other, the UWF TV Title’s dead after this match” — and the fed's own 2004 title-history revision carries “Title Suspended.” in the holder's place. A battle royal on 25 Apr 2004 brought the belt back.

titles.name: UWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the promotion's own founding (20 June 2008) and still without a champion as of WAR #16 (5 April 2009), whose own preview text bills a Kennedy-Bourne match to determine a new champion; that match itself was not captured.

titles.name: THC — (T)he (H)ardcore (C)hampionship
titles.notes: Source: uwf.org.uk's own title-history page (three versions, May–Oct 2002, predating the 2004-revision ledger this record otherwise draws on) — “Title taken over by the THC championship belt Gurgles salvaged from the GIWF. UWF refuses to sanction title... Gary Clark officially sanctions title during his reign.”
titles.epitaph: Spelled out letter by letter, always — the weed-abbreviation gag deliberate. Born at Ground Zero 2001, retired weeks later when hardcore wrestling was banned, then carried back to life by Gurgles on the physical belt he had personally salvaged from the GIWF's own hardcore lineage, re-sanctioned under Gary Clark, and merged with the Shoot Wrestling Championship on 16 February 2003. The Hardcore Isosceles Trapezoid — Sean's own creation alongside Almasy — held it four times, more than anyone else on record; Seymour Almasy held it twice. The 2004 Quick Facts credit Nick Persia with the longest reign, 103 days. After the fed's 2004 title-history revision, Misfit took it from Clyde on 13 February 2005; Clyde had it back by July, lost it to Nick Persia at the Regal Rumble in September, and won it again in the Live and Loud 5 Foundry match, where it was unified with the Insert-Name-Here title.

events.note: Hardcore wrestling itself was banned; the belt went dark, with the Shoot Wrestling Championship standing in, per the fed's own 2004 title-history revision.

titles.name: UWF Canadian Heavyweight Championship (discontinued)
titles.epitaph: Held by Bad News Allen Coage at the September 2006 restart, then Bobby Rude, Sean Morley, Bad News Allen again, and finally Lance Storm. The fed's own ledger says Lance Storm carried the belt with him to XWF, but no XWF title on the surviving record continues this specific lineage — an unresolved gap.

titles.name: UWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "American Dragon" Bryan Danielson at the September 2006 restart, then Yoshihiro Tajiri and Dean Malenko, before AJ Styles won a Cruiserweight Gauntlet Battle Royal, pinning Billy Kidman in the finale, on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: UWF Intercontinental Championship (discontinued)
