titles.epitaph: Held by Kurt Angle at the September 2006 restart, vacated when Angle pursued the World title, then won by Scott Steiner over Raven in a tournament final. Ultimate Warrior took the belt from Steiner at Fallout 2007 and, per the fed's own ledger, carried it with him to ICWC when he moved federations — continuing as the ICWC Intercontinental Championship.

titles.name: UWF World Midget Championship
titles.epitaph: The UWF crowned its first and, on the surviving ledger, only World Midget Champion at the 2007 Ultimate Supercard: Little Beaver, in a four-way dance over Sky Low Low, the Haiti Kid and Lord Littlebrook.

titles.name: UWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the British Bulldogs at the September 2006 restart, then by the Road Warriors, AJ Styles & Christopher Daniels, Owen Hart & Jeff Jarrett (twice), Arn Anderson & Tully Blanchard, and finally Ted DiBiase Jr & Cody Rhodes on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: UWF Television Championship (discontinued)
titles.epitaph: Held by Ravishing Rick Rude at the September 2006 restart, then Macho Man Randy Savage and Curt Hennig, before Rick Rude reclaimed it and carried it to XWF, where Paul Heyman renamed it the North American Heavyweight Championship.

titles.name: UWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Vader at the September 2006 restart, then Sid Vicious, Hulk Hogan, Randy Savage, Roddy Piper, James Storm, Jamie Noble and Harley Race on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: UWF United States Tag Team Championship (discontinued)
titles.epitaph: Named for Demolition at the September 2006 restart. Per both feds' own ledgers, Demolition carried the title with them to XWF, where it continued as the XWF World Tag Team Championship.

titles.name: UWF World Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the September 2006 restart, filled when Sherri Martel defeated the Fabulous Moolah in a tournament final. Trish Stratus, Sherri Martel again, Bull Nakano, Sherri Martel again and finally Beth Phoenix held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: UWF World Women's Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Fabulous Moolah & Mae Young at the September 2006 restart, then Lisa Morretti & Nora Greenwald, Rhonda Singh & Luna Vachon, Trish Stratus & Gail Kim (twice, with Lisa Morretti & Nora Greenwald between), and Awesome Kong & Aja Kong — the last representing ICWC in an interpromotional match — on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: UWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the September 2006 restart, filled by an eight-man tournament Abyss won over Kurt Angle with outside interference from owner Matthew Hopkins and Chyna-Doll. The belt changed hands six more times on the surviving ledger — through Kurt Angle, Brock Lesnar, Sting, Christian Cage (in an elimination chamber over Sting, U.S. Champion Hulk Hogan, Paul Wight, Bill Goldberg and Ric Flair), Kurt Angle again and Ric Flair — before Matthew Hopkins stripped Flair over a real-world dispute involving Vince McMahon and the Stamford Outsiders; the tournament called to fill the vacancy never finished after a riot closed the arena. Randy Orton won the last-recorded reign in a Triple Threat against John Bradshaw Layfield and Flair.

titles.name: UWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Michelle McCool on WAR #7 (8 September 2008), where she retains by disqualification against Candice Michelle. Beth Phoenix won the title outright from McCool's own team in an 8-Diva Tag Team Ladder match at Summer Party (28 September 2008), and is still billed champion on the Sacrifice brand's own later champions list (February 2009). A WAR #16 commentary tease (5 April 2009) separately promises "Beth Phoenix defende [o título] contra Candice Michelle", suggesting Phoenix's reign continued at least that far, though under a title name this document does not itself use.

titles.name: UWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Undertaker at the promotion's own founding (20 June 2008); by Summer Party (28 September 2008), CM Punk is the billed champion, retaining against Undertaker there. No document read records how the title passed between them. This title's own further history after Summer Party is not established -- the promotion's own Sacrifice-era champions list (February 2009) names only a single "UWF Championship" (see that title's own record), and does not separately list a "World" championship, so whether the two were unified, or the World title simply went uncaptured, is unresolved.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The UWF's top belt, restarted at the September 2001 Live and Loud tournament that closed the GIWF and opened the new fed. Its own Quick Facts, as of the 2004 revision, credit Seymour Almasy with the longest reign (138 days) and a three-way tie for most reigns among Danny Jaye, Almasy, and Tsunami Oni; Ruff Ryder's own 0-day reign — champion and ex-champion inside a single SAS — is its shortest. Six Hall of Famers held it before the fed's own last title-history revision; a museum-compiled continuation past that point carries it on through Kenny Mercury and Jamie Shock in 2005 (Shock won it at FANdamonium DOS in May and lost it to Misfit in a three-way at the Regal Rumble in September), then Killer Dude, Misfit, and Clyde, to a final recorded loss at the independently-hosted Sins of the Past, August 2006.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Local NVA Company are its defining team, five reigns, more than any other; the UWF era's own longest reign belongs to the Resurrection (Digital Mortality & Moraless, 84 days). On 5 March 2003, Lyle “In Style” Wile won the belts partnered with a VR T-Shirt — the first inanimate object to hold a UWF title.

titles.name: UWF X Division Championship
titles.epitaph: A new title, restricted to wrestlers under 110 kg, announced by Sacrifice's own GM Mr. Kiz on Sacrifice #1 (24 February 2009); its own inaugural tournament's two semi-finals (Kofi Kingston over Santino Marella; Gregory Helms over Super Crazy) are documented there, but the final between Kingston and Helms was not captured. The Sacrifice brand's own later champions list names Kofi Kingston as champion, consistent with (but not independently confirming) a Kingston win in that final.

titles.name: UWL Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own rules page caps this division at 230 lbs. and under; its Summer Blast '99 results page shows Chris Jericho retaining the belt against Stevie P. with a superplex. No earlier or later UWL document survives naming when the reign began or how it ended.

titles.name: UWL Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own rules page mandates that this belt always be defended in a Falls Count Anywhere, No DQ, hardcore/weapons match; its Summer Blast '99 results page shows Chris Jericho retaining it against Rebel Rouser with a power bomb, the pair brawling through the whole arena. No earlier or later UWL document survives naming when the reign began or how it ended.

titles.name: UWL Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Summer Blast '99 results page shows the Double "A" Express retaining this belt twice in one night — against Shawn Michaels & Triple H, then against Pink & Phoenix (billed the same night as "The Bash Brothers") — under two different names for the same title, "UWL Tag-Team" and "UWL World Tag-Team," the fed's own text never explaining the difference. No earlier or later UWL document survives naming when the reign began or how it ended.

titles.name: UWL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Summer Blast '99 results page shows Ripper retaining this belt against Johnny Hays, submitting him to the Ripp Gripp. No earlier or later UWL document survives naming when the reign began or how it ended.

titles.name: UWL United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own Summer Blast '99 results page shows Frost pinning Stone Cold Steve Austin with the Frostbite to win this belt on 20 June 1999. No earlier document survives naming when Austin's own reign began, and no later document survives naming how Frost's reign ended.

titles.name: UWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served title-history page runs a fully dated chain of fifteen reigns across fourteen holders, from Masked Menace's founding reign (11 January 1997) through Chris Jericho's win on 29 October 1999 — Black Shadow alone holding it twice, in April and again from July to September 1997 — mixing original characters (Moonbeam Kid, Trasher, Big Daddy Cool Zader, Punishing One) with real-wrestler names and gimmicks (Bret Hart, Tommy Dreamer, Chris Jericho). The fed's own Summer Blast '99 results page corroborates one link in the chain from the other side — Psycho defending against Punishing One that night — though its own text breaks off before showing the finish the title ledger independently records. The ledger's own last entry records the title vacant from 1 January 2000, with no further champion attested.

titles.name: UWP Unified World Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt recognized across the coalition's own member federations for whichever woman its own billed champion happened to be.

titles.name: UWP Unified Grand World-Held Championship
titles.epitaph: The coalition's own top prize, recognized across its member federations regardless of which one its billed champion actually wrestled for.

titles.name: UWWA Regional Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 22 May 1997 roster post, growing from two titles (World, Tag Team) on 18 May to four (adding U.S. and Regional) by 22 May, with a World Title Tournament announced for the first eight joiners. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives -- a third party's own account (DUWA, cited not reproduced) confirms the fed closed within a month of this posting, before any tournament or card could be run.

titles.name: UWWA Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 22 May 1997 roster post, growing from two titles (World, Tag Team) on 18 May to four (adding U.S. and Regional) by 22 May, with a World Title Tournament announced for the first eight joiners. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives -- a third party's own account (DUWA, cited not reproduced) confirms the fed closed within a month of this posting, before any tournament or card could be run.

titles.name: UWWA U.S. Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 22 May 1997 roster post, growing from two titles (World, Tag Team) on 18 May to four (adding U.S. and Regional) by 22 May, with a World Title Tournament announced for the first eight joiners. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives -- a third party's own account (DUWA, cited not reproduced) confirms the fed closed within a month of this posting, before any tournament or card could be run.

titles.name: UWWA World Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own 22 May 1997 roster post, growing from two titles (World, Tag Team) on 18 May to four (adding U.S. and Regional) by 22 May, with a World Title Tournament announced for the first eight joiners. No bestowal, holder or result of any kind survives -- a third party's own account (DUWA, cited not reproduced) confirms the fed closed within a month of this posting, before any tournament or card could be run.

titles.name: VCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended twice on the same New Year's Revolution card, kept by the same champion both times.

titles.name: VCW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a tournament on the fed's only surviving card; no champion is named in any document this collection holds.

titles.name: VCW Heavyweight Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding and relaunch paperwork; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: VCW Ironman Championship
titles.epitaph: A title defense thrown out for interference at VCW Pro and rebooked as a steel-cage blowoff.

titles.name: VCW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held alongside the World and Six-Man Tag titles by the same monster heel in 1996.

titles.name: VCW Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by a wrestler the community itself ranked #14 in its own Top 75 of 1995.

titles.name: VCW Six-Man Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held in 1996 by a three-belt monster heel alongside unnamed partners no surviving document identifies.

titles.name: VCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held three times by one man and all at once by another, and defended live against a touring legend in a twelve-man interfederation gauntlet.

titles.name: VCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding and relaunch paperwork; no champion or title match survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: VCW Western States Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at New Year's Revolution after three prior challenges by the same wrestler had come up short.

titles.name: VCW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Held undefeated through eight matches by the same champion, who was left without an opponent when a unification bout fell through.

titles.name: VENUS World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The first of the fed's three planned titles, held from the fed's creation by Karla Starr, the last New ERA Women's Champion, on the belt New ERA's women's division had carried. Its one held match is the first defense, Starr over Foxx at the fed's B1TCHIN' showcase on 30 December 2006.

titles.name: VFWF Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: Recalled by a former handler's own closure testimonial as a title Allen "The Acer" Carter held for the whole of the fed's run ("All Time VFWF Internet Champion"). No dated title match survives in the held record.

titles.name: VFWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, offered as the prize for surviving The Gauntlet; a former handler's own closure testimonial recalls Allen "The Acer" Carter as a former one-time champion. No dated title match survives in the held record.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's lighter-weight singles title, changing hands in an instant reversal on its own 4 October 1997 broadcast.

titles.name: North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary singles title, won in the ring on its own 4 October 1997 broadcast and, by December, held by a different man; how it changed hands is not recorded.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, changing hands twice across its two surviving broadcasts — once in the ring, once by presidential presentation.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own tag team title, called the Hardcore Tag Team Championship in its own earlier recruitment posts and held by Storm Inc. by December 1997.

titles.name: VWA North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Won in a thirty-two-man battle royal at the promotion's first pay-per-view and still in dispute by its second, its full lineage not recovered in this record.

titles.name: VWA North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by the Steiner Brothers from Harlem Heat at the promotion's first pay-per-view; billed as held by Law and Order, whose own claim is not otherwise attested, by the promotion's second.

titles.name: VWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top prize, won in a tainted eight-man tournament final and still on Derek Holmes's shoulder in a sibling federation's own account nearly two years later.

titles.name: VWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by the Travis Brothers from Demolition in a two-out-of-three-falls match at the promotion's first pay-per-view.

titles.name: VWA World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended on a weekly basis under the promotion's own rules; only a single defense survives in this record.

titles.name: VWF 24 Hour Championship
titles.caption: The promotion's top title from its first months, won by Sebastian in a one-night tournament in August 2001 and passed through Kerry Powell, Sebastian again, Jack Spade and Zell Strife to Demonic by December 2001. Scott Starring's title through the summer of 2003, taken by Daniel Sinz on a rope-assisted sunset flip that September; Sinz defended it through Vegas Violence III and Firestorm 10-21-03 before losing it to Yancy "Y2K" Kilpatrick in a 24 Hour/Submission title-for-title match on Firestorm 10-28-03. Kilpatrick's reign ended in vacancy after his death, narrated in-fiction as a plane crash; Thunder Valenkov is already billed as champion by the 12 Days Tournament's own Day Twelve broadcast, retaining against Sonicman on the wing's own Kickoff Card the following January, against The Maquilladora in a ladder match on Firestorm (19 January 2004), and against Lance Voltar in an I Quit match at Ghost Town Blues (19 February 2004).
titles.epitaph: A liberally-defended title, contested in falls-count-anywhere matches and open to challengers from the promotion's own 24 Hour division.

titles.name: RAW-Vegas BlackJack Championship

events.note: Unified with the T3 Title at Ghosts of RAW; the winner became Vegas Heavyweight Champion.
events.title: vwf-vegas-2003-heavyweight

titles.epitaph: The promotion's hardcore title of 2002. Classy Joey Boy had held it since December 2001 apart from one week in Tai Angela's hands, his latest reign running from February 2002, and defended it in a ladder match at Vegas Violence II and a steel cage at Phear Phantastic II; at Ghosts of RAW it was unified with the T3 Title into the Vegas Heavyweight Championship.
titles.notes: Renamed from the BWF Championship on 10 January 2002, when Ric Beauty sold his stake in the BWF back to Rob Beauty on air and Classy Joey Boy continued as champion under the new name.

titles.name: BWF Championship
titles.notes: The title of the Beautiful Wrestling Federation, Ric Beauty's faction inside the VWF, first awarded on 3 October 2001.
titles.epitaph: The belt Ric Beauty created for his Beautiful Wrestling Federation faction, diamond and jewel encrusted, and awarded to Corey Fuller in a match he refereed himself. G-Gangsta took it from Fuller three weeks later; by December it was Classy Joey Boy's, with the faction's new president, Sebastian, demanding it back.

titles.name: VWF Hardcore Championship
titles.caption: A hardcore title Gods Tears proposed to majority owner Kingston Cash on Holiday Havoc II and won at his own off-page GT's Invitational, first billed on New Years Kick Off.
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-rules title of the promotion's final months: Gods Tears proposed it to majority owner Kingston Cash on Holiday Havoc II and was first billed as its champion on New Years Kick Off (19 January 2005), the deciding bout having taken place off the page; its record runs only as far as the surviving broadcasts.

titles.name: VWF Vegas Heavyweight Championship
titles.caption: Classy Joey Boy's long-held title, lost to Randall Crane in a Stretcher match at the wing's own Birthday Bash special; Crane defended it against Classy Joey Boy again at Vegas Violence III before losing it back to him in a No Disqualification match on Firestorm 10-28-03, Classy Joey Boy's third reign. That reign was declared vacant on Firestorm (26 February 2004) after an unseen attacker left the champion hospitalized, co-owner Rob Beauty announcing a Gauntlet tournament to crown his successor.
titles.epitaph: The wing's own top title, defended in falls-count-anywhere and Stretcher-match stipulations across its attested run; its third Classy Joey Boy reign ended in vacancy after an in-storyline attack rather than a defense.

titles.name: RCW Championship
titles.notes: Crowned by the RCW, an invading faction of former outside wrestlers (G-Gangsta, Demonic, Blaze and the Real Deal) inside the VWF in January 2002; the broadcast itself questions whether the VWF recognizes it as an official title.
titles.epitaph: A belt the RCW invaders crowned for themselves rather than one the promotion handed out. G-Gangsta won it in a four-way on 17 January 2002 by outlasting Demonic, Blaze and the Real Deal, then defended it in a Last Man Standing match through three tables and a bloody 2 out of 3 falls brawl through the streets of an old Nevada ghost town that left both men and the referee knocked out.

titles.name: VWF Submission Championship
titles.caption: A new title created for a five-man qualifying tournament run across September 2003; Yancy "Y2K" Kilpatrick won the tournament final at Vegas Violence III to become its first champion, then lost it to Daniel Sinz that November during the wing's own 12 Days Tournament. A challenge from "Maniac" Mike Wolfe at Ghost Town Blues (19 February 2004) ended without a decision when the presumed-dead Kilpatrick reappeared alive mid-match; Sinz retains by default.
titles.epitaph: Crowned by a submission-only qualifying tournament at Vegas Violence III; its first champion also went on to unify it briefly with the promotion's own 24 Hour Championship before losing it during that November's 12 Days Tournament.
titles.note: Qualifiers, in order won: Justin Harper and Johnny Freil (Firestorm 09-12-03); Yancy Kilpatrick, Pandora and Daniel Sinz (Firestorm 09-24-03). Yancy "Y2K" Kilpatrick won the five-man final at Vegas Violence III by submission over Johnny Freil, then lost the title to Daniel Sinz by submission (Millennium Deathlock) on Day Five of the 12 Days Tournament (21 November 2003), after Sinz attacked him with a chair before the bell.

titles.name: VWF Tag Team Championship
titles.caption: First won by Demonic and Blaze in the promotion's Tag Team Title Tournament of October 2001; Dage took Blaze's half in Rage In The Cage, and Triple X won the titles that November. The Rhombus's title, briefly held by Randall Crane and Classy Joey Boy that September before The Rhombus regained it when Classy Joey Boy turned on his own partner, then lost it for good to the Rodeo Boys at Vegas Violence III. The title changed hands again at some undocumented point before the 12 Days Tournament's own Day Twelve, when El Gringo Loco and Jushin Liger GOLD are first billed as champions; they retained against the debuting Fallen Angels on the wing's own Kickoff Card the following January. Loco's own outgoing partner Jushin Liger GOLD then lost his half of the title in a four-way ladder match on Firestorm (19 January 2004), Billy Bones claiming the second belt to form a new pairing with Loco. The new pairing retained without a decision against Hot Property on Firestorm (26 February 2004) after the referee stopped the match over an unidentified man's ringside appearance.
titles.epitaph: A tag title that changed hands off-page between two attested reigns; the surviving record does not show the actual title match. A second, undocumented change of hands followed before the wing's own 12 Days Tournament finale, and a third change split one outgoing pairing's own two belts between two different men in a single ladder match.

titles.name: VWF Triple Threat Championship
titles.notes: Named in the promotion's own 2001 cards as the Triple Threat Title, shortened on air to the T3 Title.
titles.epitaph: A title decided and defended in three-way matches. G-Gangsta won the first one in August 2001 and held it into October, when Zell Strife took it; in November Strife handed the belt to Thomas Rainka, who defended it to the year's end.

titles.name: VXW 24 Hour Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Thunder Valenkov, defended successfully against Robbie Caldwell and, in a match that ended The Maquilladora's own career, at Vegas Violence V, then again against Adam 'The Hype' Jennings on New Years Eve Of Destruction, before losing it to Jennings at Ghost Town Blues inside a Russian Cage Match; Jennings retained the title in a rematch against Valenkov at St Patricks Day Massacre.

titles.name: VXW Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A past championship named only in retrospect at a retiring wrestler's own farewell tribute; The Maquilladora and Classy Joey Boy are both billed as former holders, with no surviving document dating either reign.

titles.name: VXW Spin The Wheel Championship
titles.epitaph: A new title created on the spot at Phear Phantastic 2005, awarded to the first non-champion who pinned another non-champion inside the Rage In The Cage cage match; Damian Payne won it in his own second VXW appearance, pinning Justin Harper with Kagedo's own illegal assistance. Retained in a Table For Two match against Omega on Christmas Comes Early, before losing it to Cobra at Xtreme Machine I in an escapes-only steel cage match and regaining it from Cobra twelve days later at St Patricks Day Massacre.

titles.name: VXW Spin The Wheel Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Its own stipulation is set by a spin of a wheel before every defense; Mike Bisignano won it from Valec Corso through a table at Birthday Bash 2005 and carried it through ladder match defenses at Vegas Violence V and Fear Is Coming II, before losing it to Lark Fenriz inside the Rage In The Cage cage match at Phear Phantastic 2005. Fenriz retained it against Justin Harper on Winter War I after a disqualification reversal, then lost it to Harper on Winter War II inside a triple threat also involving Kagedo. Harper retained the title in a scored Taipei Death Match against Roman Anderson at St Patricks Day Massacre.

titles.name: VXW Submission Championship
titles.epitaph: Stands defunct; Iyasu Saku is remembered on VXW's own broadcasts as its former champion, with no surviving document recording when or how the title stopped being defended.

titles.name: VXW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Hot Property, "All That" Austin Lee and "Hotstuff" Stevie Knight, surviving a draw against Team Brittania, a defense against The Rhombus, and a three-way title match at Vegas Violence V that Team Brittania won by disqualification without taking the belts. Survived a publicly rejected stripping rumor on Setting Sun I and a double-pin, no-decision Tornado Tag Team defense against The O'Malley Brothers on Christmas Comes Early, then a scored Irish Street Fight against the same challengers on New Years Eve Of Destruction, before losing the belts to the O'Malley Brothers at Ghost Town Blues in a Tables Ladders and Chairs match; the O'Malleys retained the titles in their own first defense, against Team Brittania at St Patricks Day Massacre, on a disqualification.

titles.name: W3 Suicidal Championship
titles.epitaph: W3's extreme title. Christian Lee won it in a battle royal on 29 July 2007; Spade took it on 19 August and Darkside on 9 September at the Sin pay-per-view, which is not held. Darkside left it in the ring on 30 September and Hell's Keeper won the vacant belt at Extinction on 7 October.

titles.name: W3 Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Serenity won it in a battle royal on 29 July 2007 and Heather Phoenix took it on 12 August. She defended it through September and lost it to Kristoph Kahn in a three-fall match at Extinction on 7 October.

titles.name: W3 Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at Extinction on 7 October 2007, where Annabelle Sanchez won a four-way elimination to become its first champion. The fed's own Women's Champions page is a blank placeholder.

titles.name: W3 World Championship
titles.epitaph: W3's top title. Its own title page lists Preston Payne, from a battle royal on 29 July 2007, who relinquished it after six days, and then Cody Clark from the four-way of 19 August; the results page of that night calls it the crowning of the first W3 World Champion, which the title page does not. Clark was stripped on 16 September 2007 and Waylon Cash won the vacant belt in the Lion's Den at Extinction on 7 October; the title page, last updated before that, still shows Clark.

titles.name: WAeW North American Title
titles.epitaph: WAeW's own secondary singles championship, a 290-pound weight limit, defended on pay-per-views and on live cards every four to six weeks per the fed's own FAQ. No reign, challenger or defense survives anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: WAeW World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: WAeW's own top singles championship, universal weight limit, defended only on pay-per-views absent the fed head's own say-so. The surviving record catches it mid-tournament: four qualifiers -- Lord Foul the Despiser, "Killer Kid" Brad Slack, Casey Stanfield and The Punisher -- were still cutting promos toward a first champion when the corpus ends, and no reign is attested anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: WAeW World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: WAeW's own tag team championship, universal weight limit, defended only on pay-per-views absent the fed head's own say-so. The surviving record shows an opening tournament round building toward it (the Heartbreakers among the entrants) but no reign or result survives anywhere in the held record.

titles.name: Freedom Championship
titles.epitaph: A Season 1 singles belt created by fiat when the fed's own first tag title was declared defunct, changing hands four times across a single month (Trailboss Mike Dallas, the Maltese Falcon twice, and Bombsquad) before this pull's own read window ends with Falcon still champion.

titles.name: International WAR! Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created in an interfed tag tournament won by DangerZone at CivilWar 1 in June 1995, this title's own record then gaps until Kalifornia Heat, already champions, retained it against the All-Americans in a Texas Death match at the fed's own Dec 1996 supercard.

titles.name: International WAR! Championship
titles.epitaph: WAR!'s original secondary belt, crowned in an inaugural tournament won by Bludgeon days after the promotion's own launch and passed through Johnny Thunder and Butch Williams before Jerry "Goon" Gordon's October 1995 win made him, per the show's own text, the first wrestler to hold two WAR! titles at once; Booster Dunne, Williams again, and "Magnum" Biff McGriff followed across 1996, McGriff winning it off a slow three-count the show's own text calls "tainted... but a victory nonetheless."

titles.name: WAR! Liberty Championship
titles.epitaph: A title born at the Season 2 relaunch opener, when The Mandarin won it from a debuting Joey the Clown (the future DeathJester), then lost it within the week to Jerry "Goon" Gordon's same-week double-title run; a hot-potato stretch followed — Joey the Clown regaining it under his own future ring name, then Sid Starr, then "008" Jim Bondo twice in one night after a retiring Butch Williams signed it over by contract clause — before it settled, by late 1996, on DeathJester and then "Dirty" Doug Simpkins.

titles.name: WAR! Manhattan Championship
titles.epitaph: A borough-named singles title contested through WAR!'s 1999 season, changing hands once in a masked-opponent swerve.

titles.name: National WAR! Championship
titles.epitaph: Born from a 14-man battle royale during the fed's own August 1997 relaunch under new ownership in Manhattan, contested twice in three weeks and still active when the fed's own 'Old War!'/'New War!' rosters reunified that October.

titles.name: WAR! Tag Team Championship (Season 1, defunct)
titles.epitaph: The fed's own first-ever championship, won on its debut card and declared defunct by in-story fiat eleven days later, replaced by the singles Freedom Championship; never contested again.

titles.name: WAR!Lord Championship
titles.epitaph: A title contested through a running succession involving Big Duke, CrocMaster, American Patriot and Robski, the last "regaining" it in a cage match at the fed's own Dec 1996 supercard after an earlier, off-page reign of his own.

titles.name: World WAR! Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A tag title that changed hands at least five times across this pull's own read shows, from the Brotherhood through the Star Smashers, the Aderondac Brothers and Industrial Revolution to the Annihilators, the last won with a moonsault off the roof of a parked van in the WARena parking lot.

titles.name: World WAR! Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize, crowned in a 16-man tournament won by Brutus Noir at the promotion's own second-ever show and changing hands at least nine times since — through Inner City Firmer, Seth Blitzspear, Noir again, Randy Blake, J.R. Death, Stein "Ice" Berg, and Tonnage — before Jason Midnight was crowned via a separate UWC interfed tournament and carried it into the fed's own Dec 1996 supercard.

titles.name: War! Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The War! Heavyweight Championship changed hands on 12 June 2002 when Omega escaped a steel cage ahead of champion Richard Wyngarde to win the title, over interference from Morten Wyngarde at ringside.

titles.name: Manhattan Championship
titles.epitaph: The Manhattan Championship was created on 12 April 2002 and won by Saul Akiva, who beat Jason Charter in the inaugural final. Talon Vickers took the belt from an injured Akiva without a match on 6 May 2002; Akiva had regained it by 12 June 2002, when he beat Talon Vickers to retain it.

titles.name: NWA/NeWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Source: promotions/wccw/archive/newa-world-heavyweight-title-history.html. The NeWA's own introduction page states the hub "share[s] their history" with the real National Wrestling Alliance's own historical World Heavyweight lineage "up until September 1, 1997 when Frans Joule defeated Dan Severn" — the real lineage (Orville Brown through the 1997 champions) is the fed's own claimed kayfabe backstory, not a Museum assertion about the real NWA; only the fed's own post-divergence reigns (1 Sep 1997 onward) are structured in reigns.json. The ledger's own footnote {10} ("defeated Siva in a one match tourney to win the title") is attached to Chris Worrall's own win, dated 25 Nov 1997 — but Siva the Warrior does not become champion until 8 Mar 1998, a full three reigns later; the raw captured HTML carries the same misplaced footnote (not a transcription artifact), so it is recorded here rather than reassigned or silently dropped.
titles.epitaph: WCCW operated under the NeWA hub's own claimed lineage of the real National Wrestling Alliance's World Heavyweight Championship, continuing it in fiction from 1 September 1997 onward under the hub's own champions. Seventeen reigns are recorded from that divergence through the ledger's own last word, 18 December 1999 — Roddy Piper and Dan Severn among them, the real wrestlers staged as the fed's own champions within its own invented history. The full lineage — real and claimed alike — survives verbatim on the fed's own title-history ledger.

titles.name: WCIWF Television Championship
titles.epitaph: The first match ever contested in WCIWF history opened this title's own eight-man tournament; The Great Oni won it in the final, defeating The Jet with a top-rope Savate From the Top on the fed's 24 November 1995 debut card, still champion when the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: WCIWF US Championship
titles.epitaph: An eight-man tournament ran the full length of the fed's debut card, but its own final between Mr. Wonderful and Harley Hatfield ended in a double count-out -- the belt still unclaimed when the surviving record breaks off, with a rematch billed for the following week's card.

titles.name: WCIWF US Tag Team Championship

titles.name: WCIWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Twenty men entered the fed's own opening battle royal for this belt; Jumping Joey Smith outlasted the field, eliminating Barry the Bonecrusher last, to become the WCIWF's first-ever World Champion on its 24 November 1995 debut card, still champion when the surviving record breaks off a week later.

titles.name: WCIWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A seven-team elimination gauntlet on the fed's own debut card doubled as the deciding match for both this belt and the US Tag title; The British Battlers (Jumping Jack Jones and The Brown Bomber) were the last team standing, still champions when the surviving record breaks off.

No dated title-history ledger survives, but the two attestations bracket a single continuous reign.

titles.name: WCOTW World Championship

The fed's own dated 1998 weekly-show logs and PPV recaps otherwise show the belt changing hands repeatedly across its run (among others, HBK, Goldberg, Ravishing Rob Reynolds, Agent-X, Mystik, Buff, and Da Don are each attested as champion at some point). Its own last surviving snapshot (undated, ~2001) names Cold Blooded Mike Bauce champion, with no document recording the change between.

titles.epitaph: Eugene Whifflebottom held it into the promotion's own 2001 run; by Meltdown the belt had passed, off the held record, to Shawn, who carried it (once billed, likely in error, as a separate 'lightweight' title) through the rest of the promotion's own surviving documents.

titles.name: WCWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Dane Rennier won it at Saturday Storm in a multi-stage brawl the promotion's own broadcast narrates only in outline, and was still billed the champion three weeks later.

titles.name: WCWF International Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Nathaniel Duke held it across the whole of the promotion's own held early-2001 run, defending it in a three-way, by disqualification and in a ladder match, until an in-ring explosion left him unable to continue the promotion's own invitational defense format at Total Anarchy 2001 and Jason Myers took the title by default.

titles.name: WCWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Raymond Chandler and Jackson Therapy held it into the promotion's own 2001 run; by British Brawl the belts had passed, off the held record, to Salaok and Quartz's True Evil, whom Derek Frost and Shawn's YB2K1 then dethroned in that card's own tag title match.

titles.name: WCWF Texas Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own surviving documents carry an unresolved contradiction: Ric Landell is billed the reigning Texas Champion at Total Anarchy 2001 (31 Mar), yet Jesse Helms is billed winning 'the WCWF's newest Texas Title' at British Brawl (8 Mar), three weeks earlier by the documents' own dates. Neither document narrates the other; both reigns are recorded as attested rather than resolved.

titles.name: WCWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Insane Cain held it into the promotion's own 2001 run before the title went vacant for reasons the promotion's own surviving documents do not narrate; reinstated by owner Dick Hart, it produced a British Brawl four-corner match that ended in a simultaneous double pinfall, and Raziel Lucifer and JT Savage were ruled joint champions pending a decider the promotion's own surviving documents do not carry.

titles.name: WCWF United States Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: A retired set of belts owner Dick Hart brought back into circulation for one match at Total Anarchy 2001, where Derek Frost and Shawn's YB2K1 won them from Cold Steel.

titles.name: WCWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Raymond Chandler carried it through the whole of the promotion's own held early-2001 run before voluntarily vacating it at Total Anarchy 2001 to open an eight-man tournament; Dan Bonez won that tournament's final over Jason Myers to become the new champion.

titles.name: WCWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Already live when the [DEWF/WCWF] satire subset opens, held by "Hollywood" Hulk Hogan; changed hands twice across the run's nine chapters -- to Shane Douglas via a mid-match contract cash-in, and from Douglas to Nailz by no-show forfeit at the climactic Soul Doubt broadcast.

titles.name: WCWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created and awarded outright to Demolition by owner Ted DiBiase rather than won in a tournament final; the satire subset's own record shows one successful defense, retained by forfeit after an opponent injury.

titles.name: WET World Heavyweight Championship

titles.name: WeWF Americas Championship
titles.epitaph: One of three Continental belts. It changed hands seven times in fourteen weeks, was declared vacant when Frank Steel found himself holding three belts at once, was settled in an eight-man tournament, and ended on a Boston crab at a Supercard — after which the Summer League simply did not carry it.

titles.name: The WeWF Battle Royal
titles.epitaph: The battle royals the WeWF staged in 1991, each with its own winner: the league's first, for $100,000 from Mr. Fujikuchi's Akira Foundation; the Team Challenge Series battle royal; and a sixteen-team Tag Team Battle Royal.

titles.name: WeWF Eurasia Championship
titles.epitaph: One of three Continental belts, held in turn by the Lethal Lemming, “Irish” Mike Flint twice, Destruction, AquaDemon, BudMan and the Millionaire; the last of those won it eight days before the league downsized for the summer and never defended it.

titles.name: The WeWF Iron Man Trophy
titles.epitaph: The trophy of the WeWF's Iron Man Tournament. The Big Kahuna won the first, at the Supercard of 30 April 1991, beating the Romulan Mauler in the final round, and kept it in a four-man round robin at the August Supercard, unbeaten at 3-0.

titles.name: WeWF Six-Man Championship
titles.epitaph: A three-man belt that appears in the record already held: three masked men calling themselves Apocalypse Now beat the Superstars for it in the league's fifteenth turn, and the Down-Under Decking Crew took it off them in the twenty-second — after which the newsdesk's own last word is that the titles were retired and two-thirds of the belts are still in Devastation, Inc.'s hands, because the man who holds the third would not give it up.

titles.name: WeWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Thirteen recorded reigns and eight teams in thirteen months: the Dynamic Machine, the Leaping Lords, the Maniacs, Flint and Steel three times, the Intoxicators, the Law three times, the Highlanders, the Hoosiers twice and RnR — the Law's own third win in February 1992 counted on air, and this ledger's count of their reigns matches the broadcast's exactly.

titles.name: TWIW TV Championship
titles.epitaph: The newsdesk's own singles belt, wrestled for across federation lines: Mr. B held it into 1992 and kept it on a disqualification he was himself the subject of, the Hangman of the IWF took it from him with his own noose on 15 February, and defended it against the UeWF, the WeWF and a bout the championship committee annulled.

titles.name: TWIW TV Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by the newsdesk in March 1992 and settled in a four-round, eight-team tournament drawn from four federations; the Annihilation Alliance won the final over the WeWF's own tag champions with the loser unconscious on the floor from a blowgun dart.

titles.name: WeWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the 1991 Summer League and settled in one night: a sixteen-man tournament in which Bjorn “the Sweedish Pretzel” beat BudMan in an all-Four-Corners final, cleanly enough that both announcers remarked on it — and then held the belt undefeated through five defenses.

titles.name: WeWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: The belt passed through fourteen recorded reigns and ten men between January 1991 and March 1992 — Volcano and Juggernaut inside one turn, then the General four separate times, Frank Steel, DiMadMan, the Big Kahuna, Bjorn “the Sweedish Pretzel” and “Irish” Mike Flint inside a single week in May, and Mr. Roddy, Steelgrave, the Sandman and Metal after it.

titles.name: WFSW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Deferred on the same night its first challengers were announced; already held by Mark "The Crippler" Baker by the promotion's next surviving broadcast, who was still champion, booked into a further defense, when this collection's own record breaks off.

titles.name: WFSW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the promotion's own debut pay-per-view and won there by Harlequin Tragedy in a twenty-man battle royal; he was still champion at the wing's last confirmed defense three months later, and this collection's own record does not reach a title change -- outside sources later call him a former champion, but not on any document served here.

titles.name: WFSW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: First confirmed in the hands of The Returners at the promotion's next-to-last surviving broadcast, who kept the belts through its last; a different federation's own later broadcast billed a separate team as holding this title, a change this collection's own record does not itself capture.

titles.name: WFW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Created at WFW's own first supercard, Summernight Powerslam, and won by Inferno out of a twelve-man battle royal and a count-out final over co-winner Lenny Rose.

titles.name: WFW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands at WFW's own first supercard, Summernight Powerslam, when the Ultimate Fighting Machine pinned champion Johnny "the rebel" Banger.

titles.name: WFW Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Named but never awarded: the promotion's own debut broadcast left it vacant while a taped challenger vowed, on camera, to carry it out of the ring himself.

titles.name: BAD World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: The fed presents this as the title of the old BAD promotion and, until 16 August 2003, held it together with the WFW World Heavyweight Title; that night Shawn Hart, who had just won both, handed it to Diablo to be defended "hardcore style" under falls-count-anywhere, no-disqualification, no-countout rules. No earlier BAD reign is carried onto this title. The fed's own post, headed B.A.D. World Heavyweight Title History (first posted 6 January 2005 and kept up to 2010), repeats the reigns of the unified title before the 16 August 2003 split and dates the later changes a few days after this wing's show rows (Shawn Hart's win over Doc Silver on 20 August 2003, Rat Fink's on 7 September, Felix Red's on 10 December, Minion's on 23 February 2004, Jared Wells's on 22 April) and Minion's vacating on 10 March 2004 at Road to Glory, where this wing's row dates it from the line-up of 27 March; this wing's rows use the dates of the broadcasts and, for the 2007 and 2009 changes, which only the list tells, the list's own dates.
titles.epitaph: Separated from the WFW World Heavyweight Title on 16 August 2003, when Shawn Hart handed it to Diablo. Rat Fink took it from Diablo in Central Park, helped by The American and Fink Bot, and kept it against Psycho in a no-disqualification brawl at Almost Live. Rat Fink kept it against Pulsar at Ghoulish Games, but Felix Red took it from him at Turkey Day Terror on 8 December 2003 with the help of two fans, and won a tag match beside Richard Gideon at Merrython. Felix Red kept it against Psycho at Mind Over Matter on 22 January 2004, and Minion took it from him in a falls-count-anywhere match at Great Expectations on 18 February 2004; the line-up announced at Vox Hiberionacum Part Deux on 27 March says Minion vacated it with a torn ligament. Jared Wells won the vacant title in a four-man falls count anywhere elimination match at the Superbowl of Wrestling on 18 April 2004 and kept it against Mike Lane at BOMB Voyage on 9 June 2004. Jared Wells kept it against Iron Lion at Cherry Blossom Chaos II on 15 August 2004. The fed's own history of the belt has Steve Johnson take it from Wells on 17 April 2007, ending a reign of almost three years, and Wells beat Johnson at Unplugged on 31 December 2009; the fed carried the title into its NGEN relaunch with Wells as champion on 20 January 2010.

titles.name: WFW North American Title
titles.notes: Introduced beside the World Heavyweight Title as the fed's second belt; the Vox Hiberionacum introduction says both resume the lineage of the old NGEN World Heavyweight Title, a claim of the fed's own. While Rat Fink held the stolen belt, the broadcasts went on calling Michael Manson champion. The fed's own post of its North American champions, headed "NGEN/WFW North American Title History" (December 2003, kept up in later years), begins with Michael Manson at Vox Hiberionacum and carries no NGEN reign; like the World title's list, it dates each change a few days after the first post of the broadcast that told it. The same list dates the Psycho change to 26 April 2004, the day the post telling the deciding fall went up; this wing's rows use the date of the first post of the broadcast, 18 April 2004.
titles.epitaph: Won by Michael Manson on 29 March 2003 as the man left unpinned in the three-way final for the World Heavyweight Title. Rat Fink stole the belt in April, and Manson won it back in a ladder match at the first pay-per-view in May. Scotty Michaels took it from Manson in a steel cage at the Spirit of NGEN on 16 August 2003, after Luster struck Manson with a pipe, and kept it against Copycat at Almost Live. Richard Gideon took it from Scotty Michaels in a three-way with Felix Red at Ghoulish Games on 15 November 2003, when Michaels passed out in his figure-four leglock, and kept it against Psycho at Turkey Day Terror on 8 December when Psycho was disqualified for using a fork. Gideon kept it in a three-way against Copycat and Psycho at Great Expectations on 18 February 2004. Psycho took it from Gideon at the Superbowl of Wrestling on 18 April 2004, two falls to one in a match of submissions only, the Four Corners of Hell and a Texas Death Match. Psycho kept it against Rat Fink, Pulsar and El Arco Iris at Cherry Blossom Chaos II on 15 August 2004 and against Golem at Paradise Lost on 20 September 2004.

titles.name: WFW World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: The fed's broadcast says this title and the North American Title "resume and carry on the lineage of the old NGEN World Heavyweight Title" (Vox Hiberionacum, March 2003), and a commentator calls it "descended from both the NGEN & BAD World Heavyweight Titles" (Rage in the Cage). These are the fed's claims; its first champion was crowned in 2003 and no earlier reign is carried onto this title. The fed's own post of its champions, headed "NGEN/WFW World Heavyweight Title History" (December 2003, kept up in later years), begins with Doc Silver at Vox Hiberionacum and carries no NGEN reign; it dates each change a few days after the first post of the broadcast that told it. The same list dates the Michaels, Edmunds and Wylde changes to 31 December 2003, 25 February 2004 and 21 March 2004, a few days after the first posts of the broadcasts that told them (30 December 2003, 18 February 2004 and 10 March 2004), which this wing's rows use. The same list dates the Manson change to 29 April 2004, the day the post telling the ladder match went up; this wing's rows use the date of the first post of the broadcast, 18 April 2004.
titles.epitaph: Created for a fourteen-man tournament that began at the Curt Hennig Memorial Show and ended with a three-way at Vox Hiberionacum on 29 March 2003, where Doc Silver became the first champion. Psycho took it from him in a four-way at the first pay-per-view and Silver escaped a razor-wire cage to win it back three weeks later. Shawn Hart took it from him two falls to one at the Spirit of NGEN on 16 August 2003, winning the last fall, a Last Man Standing match, on the special referee's ten count. Hart kept it against Luster at New World Madness in October 2003 and against Michael Manson in a Chicago street fight at Ghoulish Games, the fed's pay-per-view of 15 November. Scotty Michaels took it from Hart in a Winter Wonderland match in Central Park at Merrython on 30 December 2003, with Luster's help; Sean Edmunds won it from him in a sixty-minute Ironman match at Great Expectations on 18 February 2004, five falls to four; and Alex Wylde, the fed's President, won it from Edmunds at Road to Glory on 10 March 2004. Michael Manson took it from Wylde in a ladder match at the Superbowl of Wrestling on 18 April 2004, with Joey Melton as special referee, and kept it against Richard Gideon at BOMB Voyage on 9 June 2004. Manson kept it against Felix Red at Cherry Blossom Chaos II on 15 August 2004. Manson kept it against El Arco Iris, two falls to one under Lucha rules, at Guerra Interminable on 3 November 2004.

titles.name: WGC World Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced as a first-round tournament bracket on WGC's own mock card; no result or champion survives, and no evidence survives that the fed ever actually ran a show.

titles.name: WHCW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Speed Racer from a previous champion, Dragon, and defended successfully against a rare heavyweight challenger.

titles.name: WHCW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Left vacant before being won in a five-man steel cage elimination match that put two competitors in the hospital.

titles.name: WHCW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated by a former champion under circumstances not attested in this record before Chris Tyler claimed it by presidential decree during an unsanctioned construction-site brawl.

titles.name: WHCW North American Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands when the returning Ultranationalists, disguised as an unfamiliar team, defeated the Sociopaths after a backstage beatdown left the champions battered before the bell.

titles.name: WHCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held five separate times by Adonis Mercury before a promotion-wide contract dispute left him stripped of it, with no successor named in this record.

titles.name: World Hardcore Wrestling United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Retained by "Wildchild" Ryan Decker over Pitbull in a ladder match at February Massacre, following an earlier defense against Hellspawn; this collection's holdings do not trace the lineage before or after.

titles.name: World Hardcore Wrestling World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by "Iron" Mike Austin from Curt X in a steel-cage main event at February Massacre; this collection's holdings do not trace the lineage before or after.

titles.name: World Title
titles.epitaph: WIA’s own top prize is never billed with a fuller name than “the World Title” anywhere in the surviving record, and no reign is ever recorded — the fed’s own January 2003 rankings name six of its ten ranked wrestlers as contenders headed into a “World Title Tourny,” but the tournament’s own bracket, matches, and outcome were never captured, and the ownership handover eleven days later never mentions it again. The belt is real, repeatedly and independently named by the fed’s own staff voice; who if anyone ever won it is not.
titles.notes: Named six times in promotions/wia/archive/rankings-2003-01.html as “World Title” / “World Title Tourny” (Pyro, Steve Jackson, 8 Ball, Jerms, Spastic, Teal Shinto each named a contender or tournament entrant); no other held document names it.

titles.name: WIA Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Corroborated only by its own reigning champion's in-character promo; no title-change document survives from the corpus read this pass.

titles.name: WIA Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested from the wing's own digest; no reign is dated from the document served this pass.

Gangsta New Jack won the fed's own first WICeW Cruiserweight Title in a ten-man battle royal on 4 October 1998; Blizzard held it by the 10 December 1998 championship snapshot, the transition unrecorded.
titles.name: WICeW Cruiserweight Title
titles.notes: An 8 November 1998 card billed a "Cruiserweight Title match" between Kyle Barrows and Blizzard (a two-out-of-three-falls draw) while Gangsta New Jack was still the attested champion -- recorded as billed on that show, not reconciled into this ledger.

titles.epitaph: Volcano won the WICeW European Title from Sean "Iceman" Stevens on 8 November 1998, an upset the broadcast called unpredictable; Kyle Barrows held it by the fed's own 10 December 1998 championship snapshot, the transition between the two unrecorded.
titles.name: WICeW European Title
titles.notes: The fed's own first-ever title match for this belt was billed for an unheld Thursday Night House Show after the 4 October 1998 card (Arch Angel vs. "Superstar" Steve Taylor); its own result is not recorded, and Sean "Iceman" Stevens's own path to holding the belt by 8 November is likewise unrecorded.

titles.epitaph: Berserk won the WICeW Extreme Title from "Mad Man" Max Marshall on 8 November 1998, then lost it to Down South Hustla in a Texas Death Cage rematch of styles less than a month later.
titles.name: WICeW Extreme Title
titles.notes: Max Marshall's own prior reign as this title's holder is referenced only in prose, with no dated ledger surviving for it in this capture.

titles.epitaph: DaLinkwent held the WICeW Internet Title through Black November before Blizzard won it by pinfall on 7 December 1998, ending a match Jupiter interfered in twice.
titles.name: WICeW Internet Title
titles.notes: How and when DaLinkwent first won the title does not survive in this capture; his own retention against Jupiter on 8 November 1998 is the earliest dated evidence of his reign.

titles.epitaph: The Hickerson Brothers won the fed's own first WICeW North American Tag Team Title on 4 October 1998 and held it through a loser-leaves-WICeW defense a month later, before President Gregory Joseph stripped them of it on 12 December 1998.
titles.name: WICeW North American Tag Team Title
titles.notes: President Joseph announced the vacant title would be filled at the fed's next pay-per-view, not itself captured in this holding.

titles.epitaph: Red Dogg won the WICeW Television Title from Gangsta New Jack on 5 December 1998, then successfully defended it against Junior Skaggs one week later.
titles.name: WICeW Television Title
titles.notes: Gangsta New Jack's own prior reign, defended in an 8 November 1998 ladder match against Scorpion, is not entered as its own reign row -- no dated ledger survives for when he first won it.

titles.epitaph: Masta Gangsta was named the fed's own first WICeW United States Heavyweight Champion as runner-up of the 4 October 1998 World Heavyweight Title battle royal; TRU held the belt by 8 November 1998, and it sat vacant by the 10 December 1998 championship snapshot.
titles.name: WICeW United States Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: How and when TRU won the title from Masta Gangsta is not recorded; TRU's own bio card lists the title with no date, and his own successful defense against Sabre on 8 November 1998 is the only dated corroboration on file. How and when the belt went vacant by 10 December is likewise unrecorded.

titles.epitaph: Max A. Million won the WICeW World Heavyweight Title in the fed's own first-ever battle royal on 4 October 1998, then lost it a month later to "Superstar" Steve Taylor, the second and last champion this capture records.
titles.name: WICeW World Heavyweight Title
titles.notes: The ledger's own two entries (4 Oct 1998, 8 Nov 1998) are both structured, each linked to its own dated show; no reign after Steve Taylor's own survives in this capture.

titles.epitaph: The Demon Knights already held the WICeW World Tag Team Title when this capture's own record opens, retaining it via disqualification on 4 October 1998; Original Gangstaz held it by the 10 December 1998 championship snapshot, the transition unrecorded.
titles.name: WICeW World Tag Team Title
titles.notes: Original Gangstaz is billed defeating Nuclear Disaster the same night as the 10 December 1998 snapshot, but no card in this capture shows the Demon Knights actually losing the belt.

titles.name: WIF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Tony "Falcon" Silver holds it through mid-1997, defending it against the dethroned former World Champion Barbwire in a no-DQ, no-time-limit match whose loser must say "I respect you" to the winner.

titles.name: WIF Internet Championship
titles.epitaph: Dark Ninja won it from Tony "Falcon" Silver in spring 1996 (outside this wing's own served window); Roundhouse holds it by June 1997 before losing a title-implicated match to Falcon via outside interference.

titles.name: WIF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The High Fliers (Superfly Dan & Eagle Andy) held it in 1996, outside this wing's own served window. Search & Destroy hold it by mid-1997, billing themselves as four-time champions in their own open challenge.

titles.name: WIF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Dark Ninja held it in spring 1996 (a former champion by that October, outside this wing's own served window); a rookie, Barbwire, holds it by June 1997 before Lancaster Bomber wins it from him in "a classic encounter."

titles.name: Rising Star Championship
titles.epitaph: Eric Scott became the first Rising Star Champion at Fusion 1.2 on 20 October 2002, submitting Marcus Christian with the All-Star Leglock in a three-way that also carried Jerome Marko, then retained the title at Fusion 1.5 on 20 November 2002 by forcing Jesse Ewiak's submission.

titles.name: WILD World Championship
titles.epitaph: Spikyjim became the first WILD World Champion at Fusion 1.2 on 20 October 2002, pinning Eddie Drysdale in a three-way that also carried his own tag partner, Travis Lagrange.

titles.name: Wildside Championship
titles.epitaph: Neige Thirteen became the first Wildside Champion at Fusion 1.2 on 20 October 2002, pinning Jaime Roberts in a three-way that also carried Rick Hanson.

titles.name: WIW International Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's second most prestigious title; its first challengers were drawn from a bucket on the promotion's first-ever broadcast.

titles.name: WIW Superpro Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as a title for wrestlers willing to put it all on the line; its first challengers were drawn from a bucket on the promotion's first-ever broadcast.

titles.name: WIW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by an eight-team tournament at the promotion's first-ever broadcast, its final unresolved when the broadcast ended.

titles.name: WIW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the promotion's working man's title, defended almost every card; its first challengers were drawn from a bucket on the promotion's first-ever broadcast.

titles.name: WIW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Created by a 20-man over-the-top battle royal at the promotion's first-ever broadcast, named its top prize by the promotion's own founding post.

titles.name: WIW:NG Hardcore Title
titles.notes: Reign list and footnotes from the fed's own Hardcore Title history, captured 31 August 2002; its champions list of 29 November 2002 also names Da D'Mon.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own history opens the Hardcore Title on 4 June 1999 when Larry Wood beat Rey Mysterio Jr. in a hardcore match, and lists 51 reigns to Da D'Mon's, won from Larry Stone on 23 July 2002. Raven held it from 29 November 1999 to 13 January 2000, and Trauma and RaZeR were declared co-champions after escaping the Wrestlefest II junkyard together on 9 June 2002.

titles.name: WIW:NG Intercontinental Title
titles.notes: Reign list and footnotes from the fed's own Intercontinental Title history, captured 31 August 2002; later holder from its champions list of 29 November 2002.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own history opens the Intercontinental Title on 17 May 1999 with The Punisher and lists 46 reigns to Chris Storm's of 26 July 2002, among them three by Jack Death and three by Shane Slade. The End won it in a Wrestlefest II cage match on 9 June 2002 and lost it to Storm on 26 July. The November 2002 champions list names Golden Hammer.

titles.name: WIW:NG Tag Team Titles
titles.notes: Holders from the fed's own Showdown results pages and its champions list of 29 November 2002; the titles' own history page is not held.
titles.epitaph: Its history page is not held. J Woods and Shorty the Pimp, the Renegades, won it on 19 July 2002 and defended it against Crazy Cooper and Gladiator on 23 July; a Heavy Metal title match was booked for Last Man Standing, and the November 2002 champions list names Project X.

titles.name: WIW:NG Television Title
titles.notes: Reign list and footnotes from the fed's own Television Title history, captured 31 August 2002; later holder from its champions list of 29 November 2002.
titles.epitaph: Introduced on 31 January 2000 when Benshaw beat Eric Austin, the Television Title was retired after Chris Storm's reign of July 2000 and revived on 1 December 2000 in a fatal four way. The fed's own history lists 29 reigns to Christian Niels's of 18 August 2002, among them Angelo Deville's of 13 to 27 May 2002 and Bryan Statis's of 30 July to 18 August. The November 2002 champions list names Johnny Fame.

titles.name: WIW:NG United States Title
titles.notes: Holders from the fed's own Wrestlefest II and Showdown results pages and its champions list of 29 November 2002; the title's own history page is not held.
titles.epitaph: Its history page is not held; the fed's own cards and champions list give five holders. Erik Erratic carried it into Wrestlefest II, where Shane Slade won it in a Last Man Standing match on 9 June 2002; Larry Stone took it from Ripcord in a title versus title match on 19 July 2002; and the November 2002 champions list names Shorty the Pimp.

titles.name: WIW:NG World Title
titles.notes: Reign list and footnotes from the fed's own World Title history, captured 27 August 2002; later holder from its champions list of 29 November 2002.
titles.epitaph: The fed's own history opens the World Title on 17 May 1999, when Tap Out won a battle royal to become its first champion, and lists 36 reigns across its on-and-off eras to The End's of 18 August 2002. Michael J was its first three-time champion, forfeiting his third reign the next card; Shane Slade won it three times in 2002 and lost the last on 18 August. The November 2002 champions list names Chris Storm.

titles.name: WIW:NG XWO World Title
titles.notes: Named on the fed's own Wrestlefest II results page, served under this wing.
titles.epitaph: Contested at Wrestlefest II on 9 June 2002 in a four-man elimination match with special guest referee Zero, which Erik Erratic won from champion Krazy Kris, The End and Masked Magician. Erratic then met e.T.o. for both world titles the same night in a unification match, which e.T.o. won.

titles.name: WIWO Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag team championship during its 1999 revival.

titles.name: WIWO Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A championship left vacant during the promotion's 1999 revival after a televised title match ran out of time before a fall.

titles.name: WIWO United States Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's secondary singles championship during its 1999 revival.

titles.name: WIWO Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top championship during its 1999 revival, contested on the road to the promotion's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: WLC Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a same-night tournament at the federation's own first pay-per-view.

titles.name: WLC Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: A mid-card singles title contested in a tournament before the promotion's own January 1999 relaunch of its weekly broadcast.

titles.name: WLC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top title, won through a tournament and defended in a chaotic four-way match that ended without a clean finish.

titles.name: WLW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Samhain's belt as of the held record's Achievement Awards -- the corpus never narrates how or when he won it.
titles.notes: First title held by this wing's own registry -- the first time this collection can name a WLW World Heavyweight Champion at all.

titles.name: WLW Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested across a two-month, sixteen-man tournament that opened with the promotion's own 10 September 2002 debut card, the title was won by “The Flyking” Will Geddings in a Quadruple Threat match on 22 October 2002; the broadcast that crowned him does not survive in this wing's own held record, but the promotion's own 25 October press conference and 13 December Wrestlebowl V broadcast both confirm the win and Geddings' first defense, a Chicago street fight against Brody Thunder, which he won.

titles.name: WLW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for Wrestlebowl V, 13 December 2002, and decided in a falls-count-anywhere match among four men where the winner had to pin all three opponents; “Redemption” Justin Slayne became the first champion by pinning K.C. Hagen, Eric Cooper and Carl Lumski at once after knocking all three off the top rope through a table.

titles.name: WLW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for the promotion's 10 September 2002 debut card and decided in a three-fall gauntlet match; when the ring went dark and the belts vanished from a ringside casket, the WLW's own administration named Brett Young and The Suicide Kid, one wrestler from each of the two remaining teams, its first champions.

titles.name: WMW Ace Superior Championship
titles.epitaph: This belt was created by a decision rather than a match. The fed’s own account is that the first act of a new Commissioner, Donovan Merlot, was to strip Jeff Hardkore of the Hardcore Title and hand him the Cruiserweight Championship — a belt the same page heads Ace Superior Championship. Three names sit in one paragraph for what the record shows as a single reign, beginning 16 May 2003 and unbroken at the last capture. The Hardcore title Hardkore is stripped of here is its own separate registry row (wmw-hardcore), chained forward to this one by an on-air rename rather than by this belt inheriting its history.
titles.notes: The fed’s own champions page uses three names for this belt in one paragraph — Ace Superior Championship as the heading, and the Hardcore Title and Cruiserweight Championship in the sentence beneath it. All three are recorded as written.

titles.name: WMW Great Lakes Championship
titles.epitaph: The Great Lakes Championship was Wrestling Midwest’s own top belt, named for the region the fed billed itself the best in. Sub-Beast was its first champion, on 28 February 2003; the champions page's own longest-reign line credits Dess with an undated two-month, two-defence reign somewhere before Tami Weber's own turn with the belt, which ended when Dess took it back on 13 June 2003. Two of the four reigns the record names are undated on one side or both.

titles.name: WMW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Matrix was already the Hardcore Champion when the surviving record opens, retaining it against Outlaw Biker at Ides of March. He no-showed his own title defense at High Stakes a month later — a 180-minute, multi-man Invitational the fed's own commentary explains it would run start-to-finish rather than on the clock — and Jeff Hardkore won the vacant match by pinning Johnny Blayze through a table. Commissioner Donovan Merlot renamed the belt Ace Superior three weeks later, on 16 May 2003, with Hardkore still champion; the fed's own champions page treats that as a new title's own first reign rather than a continuation.

events.title: wmw-ace-superior
events.note: Commissioner Donovan Merlot renamed the belt Ace Superior (also called the Cruiserweight Championship in the same breath) on 16 May 2003, per the fed's own champions page; Benny Tyler's own Blood Factory commentary a week later still has to explain the new name to her broadcast partners, crediting Brad Johnson with wanting something "unique, different" for WMW.

titles.notes: The fed's own champions page opens the renamed title's own ledger at 16 May 2003 and does not credit it with Matrix's or Jeff Hardkore's earlier reigns under the Hardcore name; those are recorded here instead, chained forward to the rename.

titles.name: WMW Midwest Championship
titles.epitaph: Fury won the Midwest Championship when it was new, on 28 March 2003, lost it to Myst inside a month, and spent weeks earning his way back to a triple threat at High Stakes to take it again on 25 April. The fed’s own champions page tells that story in a paragraph and records one successful defence after it.

titles.name: WMW Shoot Championship
titles.epitaph: The Shoot Championship began with Cy Cowart on 28 February 2003 and ran three weeks. The champions page's own longest-reign line ties Matrix with Jeff Hardkore at four weeks each, though only Hardkore's own reign — two defences, ending 6 June 2003 — can be placed in the lineage; Matrix's own reign of the same length is attested but not dated. Maxx Spartan took the belt from Garvin in a glass plate match in his own first Riot, and was still carrying it a week later when the fed's champions page was last written.
titles.notes: The champions page’s own longest-reign line reads “Matrix/Jeff Hardkore (4 weeks)”, naming a holder the page records no reign for. Matrix is not given a reign row here; the line is recorded as the fed wrote it.

titles.name: WMW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Lance Steele and Ryan Scott were the first Tag Team Champions, from High Stakes on 25 April 2003 until Blood Factory on 23 May. The Dream Team — Noah Hanson and Johnny Blayze — beat them there, and the fed’s own champions page notes that no team had beaten Steele and Scott in a title match before.

titles.name: IGA Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Myranda "The Cat" Steele through every one of its own served defenses, against opponents from Sakuya Mistuhara and Alex Vale's own six-woman brawl to a solo challenge from Mizz Da Meaner.

titles.name: MEW Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Angel until a March 2002 broadcast, where Lost Warrior beat her for it with a falling neckbreaker.

titles.name: USW Women's Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice in the surviving record, ending with a champion still holding it as of the league's own last dated bulletin.

titles.name: WoPW King of Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A hardcore-rules championship contested amid the promotion's own season-long faction war.

titles.name: WoPW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's tag team championship, defended against a rotating cast of challengers through the spring of 1999.

titles.name: World Champion of Portugal
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by João Félix from the federation's own founding roster; no document read this pass records how the title was won.

titles.name: ACW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Decided for the first time in a multi-man ladder match at the promotion's own debut pay-per-view.

titles.name: ACWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands three times in 1999, from a returning former champion through a masked impostor's own reveal to a son's own change of heart.

titles.name: IGA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's top title, first decided in a round robin at its first pay-per-view, The Battle for Fort Knox, where Matt Allen beat Mark Davenport in the deciding match. Todd Bishop took it from Allen in a scaffold match at Requiem for Pain on 31 October 2001 and held it through the year's end.

titles.name: MEW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Sabbertooth by March 2002, who kept it against a challenge from Steve Anderson after the challenger was counted unable to answer the referee.

titles.name: CPW World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands nineteen times across seven years, ending in a five-way match the same month the IWF itself closed.

titles.name: EWWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Stolen outright from a defending champion mid-match, then claimed by a self-proclaimed successor before the belt itself was stolen a second time.

titles.name: NAWC World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a lumberjack final at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, then changed hands twice more within the month.

titles.name: SHVF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: First contested in an eight-fighter single-elimination tournament at the promotion's own second event, and still held by that tournament's own winner at the close of the promotion's first year.

titles.name: SWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once on the promotion's own opening card, when its owner turned special referee screwed his own hand-picked champion.

titles.name: STW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands fourteen times before a triple-unified champion carried it, the Unified Double Crown, and the World Light-Heavyweight title together into STW's own closure.

titles.name: TWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship. Billed three-time champion Billy Joe McCallister lost it to his former Pain Incorporated partner Q-Ball at the promotion's own 26 January 1999 pay-per-view; a later broadcast recounts Q-Ball dropping the belt to the mat, vacating it, and quitting the promotion, and it remained vacant through the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: USW World Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Ran nine traced reigns before the record breaks off with a champion still holding it as of the league's own last dated bulletin.

titles.name: WWO World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Declared vacant after a chaotic four-way brawl the previous month, then decided in a 28-man tournament culminating at the promotion's own Tournament of Gods.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top singles title, already contested by the time this record's held documents begin (an off-panel 27 November 1997 tournament, per the fed's own title history) and still active as the held record ends. Changes hands three times across the read supercards -- Magnus Colby to the Gambler at Spring Slams, the Gambler to EMT at Brawl For It All -- with a fourth change (to the Candyman) attested only by the fed's own later roster note, off-panel.

titles.name: STW World Light-Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Retired once, reactivated once, and changed hands some fourteen times before its own last champion unified it with two other titles at once.

titles.name: STW World Light-Heavyweight Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Attested for two reigns before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: ACWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by two singles stars calling themselves Love Muscle, ending a four-month reign by the Alliance of Violence.

titles.name: IGA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: White gold on a black strap with diamonds, the same design as the world title. Forever Unchained, Mark Davenport and Pandemonium, won the first tournament and defended the belts through the end of 2001.

titles.name: MEW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Sabbertooth and Night Hawk before Justin Tyme and Masked Man 2000, billed together as Flying Tyme, won it from them in March 2002.

titles.name: CPW World Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: Changed hands sixteen times across five years, ending with the York Brothers the same month the IWF itself closed.

titles.name: EWWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended twice by the same champions, the second challenge ending in the challengers' own in-storyline arrest.

titles.name: TWL World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the pairing of Torture and XeRo entering 1999.
