The promotion's own president declared the titles vacant at its 26 January 1999 pay-per-view after Torture failed to appear for a scheduled defense and had XeRo assaulted and suspended on the same card; the tag team Sex Sells won the vacant championship in a title-deciding ladder match on the promotion's own 21 February 1999 broadcast and were still billed champions at the end of the surviving record.

titles.name: USW World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Changed hands seven times, ending with a champion still holding the belts as of the league's own last dated bulletin.

titles.name: WOW Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four titles announced in the fed's own founding press release (25 July 1998), to be decided in a future event; no result document survives in the held record.

titles.name: WOW Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four titles announced in the fed's own founding press release (25 July 1998), to be decided in a future event; no result document survives in the held record.

titles.name: WOW Master of the Ring Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles announced in the fed's own founding press release (25 July 1998), to be decided in a future event; no result document survives in the held record.

titles.name: WOW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: One of four titles announced in the fed's own founding press release (25 July 1998), to be decided in a future event; no result document survives in the held record.

titles.name: WOW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced in the fed's own founding press release (25 July 1998) to be decided in a Battle Royal at the Georgia Dome; no result document survives in the held record.

titles.name: WOW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Taken from the Prophet by Jeremy "Roadkill" Thranton at WrestleFest '97.

titles.name: WPCW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Awesome Starr Brothers as of the fed's own founding announcement.

titles.name: WPCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Vicious as of the fed's own founding announcement.

titles.name: WPCW Unified Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Metal Melatia as of the fed's own founding announcement.

titles.name: WPCW U.S. Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by "Franchise" Richards as of the fed's own founding announcement.

titles.name: WPCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Michael Robinson as of the fed's own founding announcement; no title match survives in the held record.

titles.name: WPWF Extreme Title
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the operator's 11 April 1997 relaunch notice, to be decided by a tournament of Extreme-rules matches (Death Matches, Barbed Wire Matches) and defended only in such matches.
titles.notes: No results card postdating the relaunch survives in the held record — results-free; no reign is minted.

titles.name: WPWF Television Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the WPWF's own founding recruitment ads (26-27 March 1997) as the third original championship; dropped from the title list in the 11 April relaunch notice.
titles.notes: No title change is recorded on either served results card — results-free; no reign is minted.

titles.name: WPWF Unified American Title
titles.epitaph: Introduced in the operator's 11 April 1997 relaunch notice as the fed's own American championship, to be decided by tournament.
titles.notes: No results card postdating the relaunch survives in the held record — results-free; no reign is minted.

titles.name: WPWF World Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the WPWF's own founding recruitment ads (26-27 March 1997) as one of three original championships; the operator's 11 April relaunch notice rebuilt it as a Battle Royal prize under an unchanged name.
titles.notes: No title change is recorded on either served results card (Battle of the Titans, We Ain't Role Models) — results-free; no reign is minted.

titles.name: WPWF World Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the WPWF's own founding recruitment ads (26-27 March 1997) and carried unchanged through the 11 April relaunch notice, which rebuilt it as a tournament prize.
titles.notes: No title change is recorded on either served results card — results-free; no reign is minted.

titles.name: Wrestlebowl Championship
titles.epitaph: A traveling championship the WLW's own broadcast traces through four prior editions at other promotions and venues (Pasadena, the Pontiac Silverdome, Australia and New York) before hosting its fifth at Wrestlebowl V, 13 December 2002; Corey Irons won it there from defending champion Joshua Barnes in a three-way elimination match, with help from a masked interloper's cane.

titles.name: WSW Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Two rival Hardcore titles were unified and retired in one cage battle royal at Retribution, its last champion, Nova Johnson, handing the belt itself to Kano backstage that June as a gesture, never revived as a defended championship in the promotion's 2002 run.

titles.name: WSW Interstate Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded at Retribution when Mr. Ed beat “Stunning” Steve Southward to become the last WSW Intercontinental Champion and the first Interstate Champion, the title changed hands twice more that summer before the promotion's own broadcasts left its final holder in dispute.

titles.name: WSW Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Rukus The Luv Train when Western States Wrestling's 2002 run opens, the title changed hands once, to Knuckles at Retribution, and survived a Summer Showdown draw with Kendo Nakamura undecided.

titles.name: WSW North American Championship
titles.epitaph: Retired as a defended championship at Retribution, when Krim'nal became its last champion; the promotion's own 2004 return still called him “the last North American Champion before the shutdown,” unbeaten for it across its whole 2002 run.

titles.name: WSW Pacific Northwest Championship
titles.epitaph: Founded at Retribution when Dean King beat Diablo in the WSW European Championship's own final match, the title passed to Jason Reynolds that July and stayed with him, unbeaten, for the rest of the promotion's 2002 run.

titles.name: WSW Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated when its holders, Ionik, announced their in-storyline departure at Retribution, the New Midnight Express won and held it for the rest of the promotion's 2002 run.

titles.name: WSW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Already held by Nemesis, its second-most-prestigious title in the promotion's own words, when Western States Wrestling's 2002 run opens, it changed hands twice: to “Kid Dynamic” that June and to Kano that July, who defended it for the rest of that run.

titles.name: WSW Championship
titles.notes: Reigns 1-5 are narrated, undated, on the promotion's own August 8, 2002 broadcast; no exact date for any of them survives.
titles.epitaph: Wrestling's own top prize named on Western States Wrestling's broadcasts, its early lineage narrated on the promotion's own August 2002 video package: Thug Life won it first in a six-man elimination match, and it passed through The Mutt, Donovan Astros, Alternativ and “Electric” Evan Sky before “Superstar” Sean Southward's own long reign, defended without loss through every show of its 2002 run.

titles.name: WTWF North American Belt
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own sole surviving founding pitch (29 September 1997, reposted five times), alongside an eleven-position staff roster and a two-show weekly schedule. No card was ever posted, so no bestowal, holder or result survives.

titles.name: WTWF Tag-Team Titles
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own sole surviving founding pitch (29 September 1997, reposted five times), alongside an eleven-position staff roster and a two-show weekly schedule. No card was ever posted, so no bestowal, holder or result survives.

titles.name: WTWF Television Title
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own sole surviving founding pitch (29 September 1997, reposted five times), alongside an eleven-position staff roster and a two-show weekly schedule. No card was ever posted, so no bestowal, holder or result survives.

titles.name: WTWF World Belt
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own sole surviving founding pitch (29 September 1997, reposted five times), alongside an eleven-position staff roster and a two-show weekly schedule. No card was ever posted, so no bestowal, holder or result survives.

titles.name: WU One Shot Championship
titles.epitaph: Called the Contender Championship at its start (Chad Vargas was the first Contender champion at See No Evil), then the One Shot Championship: Skull Daze, Twilight Rayn, Troy Gafgen and CJ Gates held it from October to December 2008. Five defences earned a World title shot; the only cash-in on record is Skull Daze's, helped by four defences the owner awarded him.
titles.notes: The fed's page lists the first reign under the Contender name; the two names are taken as one belt because the page heads the list One Shot.

titles.name: WU Short Circuit Championship
titles.epitaph: David Gunn was the first Short Circuit champion at See No Evil; Porter MaCleod took it at The Bleeding on 19 October 2008 and the belt became the Prime Time Championship, once he had brought a belt from another federation and had it made official.
titles.notes: The Bleeding's own commentary says 'it's still the Short Circuit championship... but it will become the Prime Time championship'; the Rankings page of 21 October lists a Prime Time champion.

titles.name: WU World Championship
titles.epitaph: Requiem won the first World title at See No Evil on 14 September 2008, beating DLS and Drake Daniels; the fed's own history page lists no defence and no loss.

A singles championship of NCW/WWA's own 1997–98 predecessor era, referenced directly in the promotion's own broadcast voice as early as 12 December 1997 (the winner of the CWC Northeast Heavyweight tournament billed as "probably the number one contender") but never staged for or defended within any show read so far. Its first confirmed holder is museum-compiled from a single announcer line: Darken is credited as CWC National Champion (alongside the New England and National/Northeast Tag titles) on 9 May 1998, with no won-date, prior challenger, or staged match surviving in the held record.
titles.name: CWC National Championship

titles.epitaph: A tag title of NCW's own predecessor era, already held by Darken and Steihl (the Overlords of the Dark) on the fed's own served card of 9 January 1998 — no won-date or prior challenger is recoverable, and no title defense survives in the held record.
titles.name: CWC National Tag Team Championship

titles.epitaph: Minted for an 8-man single-elimination tournament staged at the RIC Athletic Complex in Providence, Rhode Island, across two shows (20 and 27 Feb 1998) — Johnny Blaze wins the inaugural championship, submitting House of Pain's Zack Crockett in the final.
titles.name: CWC Rhode Island Championship

titles.epitaph: The LDA brand's own title, created when the WWA briefly split into three brands (Meltdown/NWC, Fiesta/LDA, and SCWF) in 2004. Jack Griffiths won the first Diablo reign on 17 May 2004, surviving a hectic singles bout against Odium and then four more men in a cage-match final; Odium took the belt back from Griffiths one show later, on 14 June 2004, in a match the fed's own title-history ledger never recorded. The lineage ends with the fed's own words: Odium — "the second Diablo Champion," by his own farewell — left the WWA on 11 August 2004, and five days later the belt was folded into the Extreme Championship's relaunch, never defended again.

events.note: Folded into the WWA Extreme Championship's 16 Aug 2004 relaunch, per that show's own main-event billing ("unified the DIABLO and GenX Titles" / "the NEW and FIRST WWA Extreme Champion"); the last champion had left the fed five days earlier per its own news post.

titles.name: Diablo Championship

titles.epitaph: Opens under "WWA GenX" billing, its first champion "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion crowned 7 March 2003 in a title unification with the Cruiserweight Championship — but Zion already held the Extreme belt itself at that point, having won it solo from an untraced "Rage In A Cage 6" after a brief joint reign with Chance, who in turn had won it back from Enigma in a 2-on-1 handicap match on 6 January 2003; Enigma took the belt clean off Chance on 9 December 2002. Chance's own reign before that loss, and Shaman's own four reigns predating Chance's (billed on-air, December 2002 and again February 2003, as "Four time former WWA Extreme Champion"), remain a genuine, honest gap — no opponents or dates for either survive in the recovered corpus. The belt's own recap prose shifts to "Extreme Championship" branding by early 2004 without a break in the numbered ledger. "Bonafide" James Curzon, Shaman, and Jonathon Winters all held it more than once across the run; the title was folded into the Television Championship on 26 March 2006, "merged with the TV Title" in the ledger's own words, before Eddie Van Dorn and Tarin Ballard closed out the fed's final recovered Extreme-title reigns in 2007.

events.note: The FWA's own Hardcore Championship folded into this belt when Shaman defeated FWA Hardcore Champion The Dehibilitator in a title-unification match three and a half weeks after the rest of the FWA was absorbed into the WWA's own banner at Independence Day Rumble (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-28.html).

titles.name: WWA Extreme Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own numbered ledger (title id 9) traces this belt continuously from an earlier "Gen X Championship" billing to the "Extreme Championship" name, with no break in the sequence — only the champion's own billing changes mid-record.

titles.epitaph: A short-lived 1998 title, crowned via a dedicated tournament (semifinals wwa-1998-12-26, final wwa-1998-12-27) and won outright by New Star. Not confirmed to be the same lineage as the modern wwa-extreme title (whose own epitaph traces its recovered ledger continuously only from 2003's "GenX" billing, with no mention of an earlier belt) — filed as a distinct, likely-discontinued early incarnation rather than merged, absent evidence tying the two.
titles.name: WWA Extreme Hardcore Wrestling Championship

titles.epitaph: Created as "the major title on the Fiesta brand" on 21 July 2003, defended only a handful of times in the surviving record before Mal Somers's reign closes out the fed's own recovered ledger on 26 July 2004.
titles.name: WWA Intercontinental Championship

titles.epitaph: Never tracked on the fed's own title-history ledger, and inconsistently billed by the fed's own broadcasts as the "Light Heavyweight" and "Cruiserweight" Championship in different shows of the same era (Eddie Van Dorn — same man, same weight, same hometown billing — defends it as "Cruiserweight" on 4 March 2002 and loses it as "Light Heavyweight" on 15 April 2002, then immediately calls himself "the Cruiserweight champion" in the very next breath as the new champion — the same belt, not two). The surviving record opens on Tuesday Showdown, 22 February 2000, where the reigning champion Mystique lost it to Denrol in a lumberjack-style main event after Denrol swapped places with a disguised Pitt Viper — the show's own commentary crowned the win as making Denrol the WWA's first-ever Grand Slam Champion, not the belt's own first titleholder. "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion was champion by the earliest served 2002 shows; Eddie Van Dorn won it from him off-panel before 25 February 2002 and held it through a 4 March 2002 defense, before Trent LeBeaux (wrestling as Tracer Bullet under his own registered ring name) beat him for it in the 15 April 2002 Monday Night Meltdown main event. Grunge took it from LeBeaux on 12 August 2002, the belt's own last confirmed change in the recovered record. Ramsey Kaine stole it from Grunge with a cheated rollup on 23 September 2002, then no-showed his own next defense; the fed restarted the match as a straight bout between the two men who did turn up, and EkoSyde beat Grunge for it on 7 October 2002. EkoSyde -- unmasked on-air as Enigma, who also held the WWA Extreme Championship at the same time -- lost it in a 2-on-1 handicap match on 6 January 2003, where the referee, unable to award a single champion, named Chance and "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion joint champions of both belts at once -- the belt's own last change directly staged in the recovered record. A later show (10 February 2003) refers back to Jimmi Zion having won the belt outright from Chance at an untraced "Rage In A Cage 6," ending the joint reign; that PPV itself was never captured, so the win is reconstructed from the later show's own retrospective billing rather than a staged title change. The belt's own end is dated precisely, even though its middle stretch isn't: Commissioner Raine retired it on-air on 8 March 2003's Fiesta, unifying it with the Extreme Championship into the new WWA GenX Championship, with Zion's own unified reign dated a day earlier in the fed's own ledger. One clean pre-2000 change is now recovered: Jak "The Boil" Lancer lost the title to Griffin (wrestling masked as "Lone Wolf") in an I Quit match on wwa-1998-11-08 — Lancer's own preceding win date remains unrecovered.

events.note: Retired on-air by Commissioner Raine and unified with the Extreme Championship into the new WWA GenX Championship.
events.title: wwa-extreme

titles.name: WWA World Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.note: Recovered from show text (e.g. archive/2000-02-22.html, archive/2002-01-28.html, archive/2002-04-15.html), not WWA's own titles.php ledger — the only title in this shard sourced that way. Other served shows (1998-08-21, 1999-04-24, 1999-06-25, 1999-08-13, among others) reference this same belt by name with other apparent pre-2000 holders (Jak "The Boil" Lancer, Griffin, Nik Segier); it also keeps getting referenced under the "Cruiserweight" billing across a large share of the rest of the 2002 corpus (archive/2002-06-17.html onward through at least 2002-12-21.html). A fuller lineage on both ends is real, evidenced, and not yet reconstructed; flagged for a future dedicated pass rather than guessed at here.

titles.epitaph: A developmental title for the fed's own newer talent, active from at least 1999 and repeatedly retired and reinstated across the surviving record — "the Rookie Ring is retired, once again" reads one of its own ledger entries, followed months later by a full relaunch. Mal Somers's win over Barrett Sinclair at Birthday Brawl 2002 closes out the fed's final recovered reign.
titles.name: WWA Rookie Championship

titles.epitaph: The fed's own numbered ledger for this belt runs continuously from an early "European Championship" naming (its first tournament winner, The Psycho, crowned 12 April 2003) through 4 March 2004, when Rocky Adams's win is recorded, in the fed's own words, as making him "the last ever EWA Champion and the first ever SCWF Champion" — the same night the European Wrestling Alliance closed and the Squared Circle Wrestling Federation launched from its ashes. Armaan took the belt from Adams on 21 March 2004, carrying the first SCWF Championship into the brand's later absorption back under the unified WWA banner.
titles.name: SCWF Championship
titles.notes: The fed's own numbered ledger (title id 7) traces this belt continuously from an earlier "European Championship" billing to the "SCWF Championship" name, with no break in the sequence — only the champion's own billing changes mid-record. Its earliest surviving row (Desolation, stripped of a pre-existing reign "while still holding the championship" upon his promotion to the WWA roster) predates the belt's own numbered start and carries a corrupted source date; no WWA-side win is recorded for that reign, so it is not counted among these rows.

titles.epitaph: Contested from the fed's earliest recovered years under the New York City Championship name — a New York City Title tournament crowns Randy Cross champion at the RIC Athletic Complex on 21 November 1997, and its own served card explicitly bills the belt as "the New York City Title" straight through Johnny Blaze's own steel-cage title win a fortnight later. WWA's own later title-history ledger folds this same lineage into the "WWA Television Championship" retroactively, dating Cross's own tournament win to 14 November 1997 — a week earlier than the served card's own internal dateline ("Friday, November 21, 1997"), and the served show is preferred here as the stronger primary source (see the reign's own note). From there the belt passed through dozens of hands across the surviving record to the 2008 rebuild; Nicholas Adams's own bio credits him with four reigns, more than any other champion in the title's history, and the belt saw multi-time runs for Mantis, Shaman, and Vik Ventressa.

events.note: The FWA's own Television Championship folded into this belt when Lyle Wile defeated FWA Television Champion Chad Goodman in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble, the same FWA-absorption card (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

titles.name: WWA Television Championship

titles.epitaph: A secondary singles title running alongside the World Heavyweight Championship from the fed's own earliest recovered years, contested under the New England Championship name in WWA's own NCW predecessor era — Johnny Blaze wins it in an over-the-top battle royal the served card bills as "the CWC New England Championship Title" on 2 January 1998, the same event WWA's own later title-history ledger folds into "WWA United States Championship" retroactively, and is billed "the New England Champion" on the fed's own served card of 9 January 1998. From Blaze's ledger-tracked win the title ran on, held across long runs by Steihl, Tracer Bullet (three times), and Grunge, whose 6 June 2003 – 30 November 2003 reign is credited in his own bio page as the longest in the title's history.

events.note: The FWA's own North American Championship folded into this belt when Buck Floyd defeated WWA United States Champion Shawn Cage in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble, the same FWA-absorption card (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

titles.name: WWA United States Championship

titles.epitaph: Crowned at WWA's own 12/12/97 founding tournament, when Mark Lynch outlasted the field to become the fed's first champion — a tournament the served card itself bills throughout as "the CWC Northeast Heavyweight Championship," WWA's own later title-history ledger folding it into "WWA Championship" retroactively from this exact reign. From Lynch's own coronation the belt changed hands dozens of times across WWA's continuous run, carried by four-time champion Tracer Bullet, two-time champions Damian Thorne, Craven Moore, and Armaan, and a seven-month reign for Ian Tense rivaled only by Nik Segier's own early run. The fed's own last recovered capture (September 2010) leaves Trendkiller as champion, having just outlasted RJ Stone, Jack Griffiths, Chris Bagwell, and Jaymz Watkins inside the Ultimate Glory match.

events.note: The FWA's own World Heavyweight Championship folded into this belt when Jim Black, arriving from the FWA, defeated WWA World Heavyweight Champion Nik Segier in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble — the same card that saw the FWA absorbed into the WWA's own banner (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html; data/frontier.json's FWA (Colosseum/Loge/2603) row).

titles.name: WWA World Heavyweight Championship

titles.epitaph: Defended across dozens of pairings from 1998 onward, including four-time champions The Veteranz and a run for The Franchise Players (Tracer Bullet and Denrol). The fed's own title history has the front office retire the belt on 1 May 2003; it was revived exactly one month later, on 1 June 2003, when Havoc defeated X-Corp for the reinstated title, and continued changing hands for years afterward.

events.note: The fed's own ledger: "Matt Warr, in his infinte wisdom retires the WWA World Tag Team Titles." Revived one month later, 1 June 2003, when Havoc defeated X-Corp for the reinstated title.

titles.name: WWA World Tag Team Championship
WWA International Championship
titles.epitaph: Rosco Riggins held it through 2001, keeping it in a ladder match at Spring Fling and against Rizer by submission on WWA Live of 21 September 2001, and was still champion on the roster of 23 September 2001.

titles.name: WWA North American Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended under hardcore rules. William Karnes kept it against both Untouchables at One Night Only and had lost it by early September 2001; Bill Bartlett, billed its new champion on WWA Live of 21 September 2001, kept it against Jayson Carter that night.

titles.name: WWA Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The Blonde Brigade held it until the Frat beat them at One Night Only in August 2001; Crimestarter Jim and Xavier Stone of the PTA took it from the Frat in a three-way with Mark Haley and the Fallen Angel on WWA Live of 21 September 2001.

titles.name: WWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's top title. Bedrock held it through the summer of 2001, beating Crimestarter Jim and Xavier Stone together in a three-way at One Night Only, and was still champion on the roster of 23 September 2001.

titles.name: WWC Cruiserweight Champion
titles.epitaph: The Cruiserweight Championship sits VACANT on WWC's own title ledger with the rest of the fed's eight belts, in a promotion whose roster page reads "NONE AS OF YET" in every capture on file — no cruiserweight, or wrestler of any weight class, was ever signed to contest it (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html; promotions/wwc-council/archive/roster.html).

titles.name: WWC European Champion
titles.epitaph: A belt on a card that never ran. The European Championship is billed VACANT on WWC's own Titles & Champions page, the fed's whole surviving title ledger, alongside all seven other championships — the site's roster page names no wrestler at any point in the capture to have won it (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html).

titles.name: WWC Hardcore Champion
titles.epitaph: The Hardcore Championship is one more line on WWC's own title ledger, billed VACANT alongside every other belt the fed named for itself — the surviving capture shows no card, no result, and no roster entry that could ever have put a name against it (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html).

titles.name: WWC North American Champion
titles.epitaph: Second on WWC's own title ledger and, like every belt on it, never awarded. The North American Championship is billed VACANT in the fed's only surviving Titles & Champions capture, unchanged across the whole eight-year Wayback record held for this site — no wrestler ever registered to contest it (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html).

titles.name: WWC Stable Title
titles.epitaph: The last of WWC's eight named championships, billed VACANT with the rest. The roster page's own "Stables" section lists none, and no stable appears anywhere else in the eight documents this promotion survives on (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html; promotions/wwc-council/archive/roster.html).

titles.name: WWC Tag Team Champions
titles.epitaph: WWC's Tag Team Championship is billed VACANT the same as its six singles belts and its Stable Title. The roster page's own "Tag Teams" section lists none — the fed's whole surviving record shows no team ever formed to be crowned (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html; promotions/wwc-council/archive/roster.html).

titles.name: WWC Television Champion
titles.epitaph: Billed VACANT on WWC's own Titles & Champions page like every other belt the fed listed. The Television Championship never had a card to be defended on: the site's own Cards page names three show slots and fills none of them (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html; promotions/wwc-council/archive/cards.html).

titles.name: WWC Universal Champion
titles.epitaph: The top belt of a fed that never crowned anyone. WWC's own Titles & Champions page — the whole of what survives of it — bills the Universal Championship VACANT from the site's earliest surviving capture (2 August 2001) to its last (29 August 2009); the roster it would have been defended on never filled with a single wrestler across that span (promotions/wwc-council/archive/titles-and-champions.html; promotions/wwc-council/archive/roster.html).

titles.name: WWC United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held but not defended in the one document this wing has served so far.

titles.name: WWC Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own World title, defended and retained in its own debut broadcast.

titles.name: W.W.C.F. Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Robbie "Boston" Cooper going into the fed's first house card, the strap passed to Tecker there and survived a disqualification challenge before "The Fantasy" Brett Young won it by manager interference on the fed's second recorded house-show date, the last title change in the surviving record.

titles.name: W.W.C.F. World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top prize changed hands four times across two January 1996 newsletters, running through five recorded reigns -- Masked Mayhem lost it, regained it, and lost it again -- with The Executioner recognized as champion when the surviving record breaks off, an upcoming title defense against The Hitman still unresolved in-corpus.

titles.name: WWE Chaos Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title History page runs an undated, numbered twelve-reign ledger, now structured in full: Jay Taylor (four reigns), Rick Esteban, Bassel Noori ("B", twice), DJ Finch (twice), and Eli Jimenez (twice) all hold it in turn, with Tony Lozon's own single reign the only other name on the list.

titles.name: WWE Chaos Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served Title History page runs an undated, numbered ten-reign ledger for its own tag titles. "Night and Day" (Bassel Noori and Jay Taylor) and "DS Inc." (Josh Render and Greg Martus) each hold the belts three times over; "The Rednecks" name is held by two different pairings in turn (DJ Finch with Tony Lozon, then DJ Finch with Brandon Walsh); Nick Clyne and Ben Galster ("703"), DJ Finch and Ryan Bronkama, and Jay Taylor and Tony Lozon each hold it once. No exact dates survive on the ledger page itself; the fed's own served 5 January 2005 broadcast independently confirms the ledger's own last-recorded pairing, DJ Finch and Brandon Walsh, still champions at that date.

titles.name: WWEF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles belt defended twice on held cards in the same week, retained both times.

titles.name: WWEF Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's second singles belt, defended and retained twice on held cards within three days of each other.

titles.name: WWEF Lightweight Championship
titles.epitaph: A singles belt for its lighter wrestlers, retained on the twenty-one-match card of 1 May 2002.

titles.name: WWEF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: The federation's tag-team championship, retained on the card of 4 May 2002 against a group-affiliated challenging team.

titles.name: WWEF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: A second singles belt held alongside the Lightweight Championship by one wrestler, retained on the card of 3 May 2002.

titles.name: World Wrestling E-Federation Championship
titles.epitaph: Its senior championship, carried through every held card of May 2002 by the same wrestler, defended in singles, three-way and cage matches without changing hands.

titles.name: WWFL Cage Belt
titles.epitaph: Winnable only inside a steel cage; stripped from a holder by the fed's own president in February 1998 and won back through a tournament before changing hands again in a post-match ambush at the fed's own annual flagship event.

titles.name: WWFL Cruiserweight Belt
titles.epitaph: The fed's own light-weight belt, held by a future WWFL headliner before passing through a fire-breathing champion on its way to one of the promotion's own rising stars.

titles.name: WWFL Intercontinental Belt
titles.epitaph: Changed hands twice around the fed's own December 1997 pay-per-view before settling into one of the promotion's longest-held reigns, its holder's own broadcasts calling it the longest in WWFL history.

titles.name: WWFL Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The fed's own only tag championship, changing hands once in the collection's own held record on the strength of a returning team's own comeback win.

titles.name: WWFL Television Championship
titles.epitaph: A belt the fed introduced into its own 1998 record after its original six; held by its own reigning wrestler through the last held WWFL broadcast.

titles.name: WWFL United States Belt
titles.epitaph: Named in the fed's own complete rulebook; no roster, card, or champion survives in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: WWFL World Heavyweight Belt
titles.epitaph: Named first among six belts in the fed's own complete rulebook (1 Dec 1997); two reigns are now on record from the fed's own 1998 broadcasts, with a further title change referenced but not yet confirmed to a servable standard.

titles.name: WWO Cruiserweight Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-cruiserweight.html.
titles.epitaph: Created for a division the WWO's own ledger records as thin from the start — one undated first reign credited to "Solid Rock" Rusty Bowman is the belt's whole early history. Its one dated match is its last: "Problem Child" Chris Stringer beat Andrew "Flash" Tucker in the finals of the WWO's own cruiserweight tournament, Atlantic City, 5 May 2001. The ledger's own notes record what happened next in two steps — the belt itself was converted into the Television Championship for a lack of competition in the division, and six weeks later, on 18 June 2001, that Television Championship was converted again into the International People's Title.

titles.name: WWO European Commonwealth Championship
titles.notes: First recognised on the WWO's Spotlight broadcast of 27 April 2002 in San Francisco.
titles.epitaph: Recognised by the WWO's president on the Spotlight of 27 April 2002 with Nathaniel Knowitall as its champion and a title defence ordered for the same night. Matt Cole won it from him there, then threw the belt into the crowd. Two reigns on record, both begun that night.

titles.name: WWO Extreme Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-extreme.html. The ledger's own two entries for American Eagle and Christopher Stonebreaker carry a date conflict the source itself never explains — recorded as printed, not resequenced.
titles.epitaph: Formed by merging the ERW Television Title into the WWO's own championship picture once the two promotions came together, and unified away again within a year: the ledger runs Christopher Stonebreaker's own first reign against Derrick Michaels through American Eagle, Jack "Tower of Terror" Harper, "Big Daddy" Justin Fischer, Vader X and "Prime Time" Phill Massacre — vacated once along the way by Fischer's own departure from the federation — before its own notes record it merged into the International People's Championship. The Extreme Title's own life, start to finish, spans less than a year and a half of the fed's own held record.

titles.name: WWO International People's Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-international-peoples.html.
titles.epitaph: Absorbed the WWO Extreme Championship's own lineage into itself in a title-unifying match, then ran nine more reigns before the federation's first closure: Tyrant, Ultimate Thrasher, Darkness, Night's Harbinger, "Latin Lightning" Al Perez, "Blockbuster" Johnny Detson and "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian each held it in turn. Detson took it from Perez in Atlanta on 22 July 1999 and lost it to Sebastian in Salt Lake City that November — the ledger's own last recorded change before the belt goes dark for the mid-era gap. Along the way it was held up once after "Prime Time" Phill Massacre was fired from the federation, and Ultimate Thrasher's own reign ended not in a loss but in his failure to appear and defend it. The revived WWO revived the belt itself sideways rather than head-on: its own Cruiserweight Championship, reintroduced by tournament in May 2001, was converted into this title on 18 June 2001 with "Problem Child" Chris Stringer's own cruiserweight reign carrying over — Stringer is still defending it, by countout over Ultimate Thrasher, at the 24 August 2001 Superstar Showcase.

titles.name: WWO International People's Tag Team Titles
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-ip-tag-team.html. Every reign but the belt's own origin is undated in the source; each is still its own reigns.json row, dated "unknown" per the museum's own honest-gap convention.
titles.epitaph: Won first by Rocky Johnson and Rusty Bowman in a battle royal, the WWO's own International People's Tag Team Titles passed from Continental Connection through the World Leaders, the Bionic Team and Thunderbolts — vacated once when Thunderbolts lost a member to a departure from the federation and sat on hiatus — before Uncivil Disobedience simply stole the belts and declared themselves champions. The ledger's own last word on them: the federation closed with Precious Moments recognized as its final holders.

titles.name: WWO Hardcore Championship
titles.notes: Billed on both surviving March 2002 cards.
titles.epitaph: Rammstein was billed as holder on both surviving March 2002 cards and kept it against Steel Face in a hardcore match on 31 March. One reign on record.

titles.name: WWO Intercontinental Championship
titles.notes: Contested at Easter Extravaganza, 31 March 2002.
titles.epitaph: Iron Face carried it into Easter Extravaganza on 31 March 2002 and lost it there to Mick Williams in a three-way that also included Joe. Two reigns on record.

titles.name: WWO Lightweight Championship
titles.notes: Billed on both surviving March 2002 cards.
titles.epitaph: Billed on Mick Williams on 20 March 2002 and on Chris Callahan eleven days later, when Callahan kept it in a ladder match against John Harris; the record does not show how it changed hands. Two reigns on record.

titles.name: WWO World Championship
titles.notes: Contested on the promotion's Wednesday Night War of 20 March 2002.
titles.epitaph: Jimmy Rage was billed as champion when Ray Scott beat him for it on Wednesday Night War, 20 March 2002, and Scott kept it eleven days later in a Hell in the Cell match against Jim Masters at Easter Extravaganza. Two reigns on record.

titles.name: WWO Six-Man Tag Team Title
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-six-man-tag.html. Every reign but Fire and Ice's own is undated in the source; each is still its own reigns.json row, dated "unknown" per the museum's own honest-gap convention.
titles.epitaph: A short-lived belt: the Lords of the Ring's own undated first reign gave way to Fire and Ice on 23 June 1997, then Aristocracy that July, then Hell's Gate that November — three title changes inside five months. The ledger's own notes say the title was retired outright once Hell's Gate left the WWO, and nothing in the held record revives it.

titles.name: WWO Television Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-television.html.
titles.epitaph: Absorbed the WWO Cruiserweight Championship's own lineage in 1999, then changed hands five times in ten months: "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian took it from Night Stalker in Manchester, Apex took it from Sebastian in Orlando, Latex Lex took it from Apex in Roanoke, Dark Soul took it from Lex in Huntington, and "Smooth as Silk" Miguel Quesada took it from Dark Soul in Salt Lake City on 25 November 1999 — the same night, by the ledger's own dating, the International People's Championship also changed hands. The belt's own earlier history records a Lancaster Bomber reign ended by his own firing and a Wuzho reign forfeited when its holder was arrested in Mexico. Quesada is the ledger's own last word: the federation closed with him still champion.

titles.name: WWO Title of the Americas
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-of-the-americas.html.
titles.epitaph: A newly created title with exactly one recorded holder: Papa Legba eliminated Steve Dumars from the ring to win it in Washington, D.C. on 18 June 2001, and the ledger's own "Quick Facts" table still had him champion as of its own 1 December 2001 count, 166 days into the only reign this belt is known to have had.

titles.name: WWO United States Championship
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-united-states.html.
titles.epitaph: Ran through a tournament final to crown its first champion, The Heckler, and passed through King $$$ Perfect and Andros before Lord Keeblor won it from "Prime Time" Michael Fulton in Auckland on 1 October 1997 — the first of two reigns the ledger credits him with. Underground Kingpin's own two reigns bracket a CJ Gesner title win in between, and "The Prodigy" Tracy Hudson took the belt from "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian in Atlanta on 22 July 1999 before losing it back in the same city, to Lord Keeblor a second time, on 17 March 2000. The ledger's own notes record the federation closing on that same day.

titles.name: WWO World Title
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-world.html.
titles.epitaph: The WWO's top belt, run through a tournament to crown King $$$ Perfect after its own earliest history and on through Tony Tobis, "Ravashing" Ric Studd and "The Master and Ruler of the World" before Randy Bryson won a tournament final on 1 May 1997 after the previous champion's retirement. Andros, Zac Schneider, Iron, Bellamy and Lord Robert d'Artois traded it through 1997 and 1998 — Bellamy's own reign ending in a cage match billed as the Valentine's Day Massacre — before Fury took it and held it 369 days, the longest total reign the ledger's own "Quick Facts" table records, ending only when Fury was forced to retire from professional wrestling. Ultimate Thrasher and a wrestler billed as Roundhouse then traded it five times across 1999 alone, before "Mr. Ratings" Warren Hayes took it in a battle royal on 15 January 2000, knocking out Mike Sebastian to end it — the ledger's own last recorded champion. The held record then goes dark: by the time the revived WWO's Superstar Showcase resumes coverage on 24 August 2001, Tyrone "Purple" Hayes is already champion, defending against Steve Dumars, and nothing the museum holds explains how the belt passed from Warren Hayes to him.

titles.name: WWO World Tag Team Titles
titles.notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-world-tag-team.html.
titles.epitaph: The WWO's own busiest championship by the ledger's own count — the Business Men, World Leaders, Lethal Weapons and Mean Mason/DOC traded it four times inside eleven days in December 1997 alone, and World Leaders' own three total reigns lead every team the ledger names. Uncivil Disobedience won it from Don't You Wish You Were Us in Los Angeles on 21 October 1998, and by 2001 the belts had passed to Physicians Advocating Innovative Neoprocedures, who took them from Vegas Connection in Washington, D.C. on 18 June 2001 and lost them back to the same team in Milwaukee just six weeks later, on 29 July 2001 — the ledger's own last recorded change. The federation's own notes name Thunderstorm, an earlier holder, as "the final WWO tag team champions of 2000," leaving the 2001 Vegas Connection/P.A.I.N. exchanges as a coda the notes themselves never reconcile against that claim.

titles.name: BSCW Women's Heavyweight Title
titles.epitaph: Carrying BSCW's own name into WWP's ring, the belt was gifted to Talia Wichzini as WWP launched, following her own run as a prior champion under BSCW's banner.

titles.name: WWP World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside the Women's Heavyweight Title in WWP's own founding FAQ; no holder or defense survives in this collection's own record.

titles.name: WWWA American Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside the promotion's other two titles in its own founding handbook, but never contested in any surviving document.

titles.name: WWWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Announced alongside the promotion's other two titles in its own founding handbook, but never contested in any surviving document.

titles.name: WWWA Unified World Championship
titles.epitaph: Never awarded: its own sixteen-man tournament reached the final four before the promotion folded without running the pay-per-view meant to crown a first champion.

titles.name: WWWA Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacated by a champion's sudden retirement, handed to a new champion by decree, then lost to a masked challenger who turned out to be a returning wrestler.

titles.name: WWWA Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Created for an eight-man parking garage battle royal and successfully defended in a boiler room brawl two weeks later.

titles.name: WWWA World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Razor for the whole of this record without a single defense shown; still his when the record ends.

titles.name: WWWA World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once in this record, when a distracted referee missed a successful cover and a rival stable's own cover counted instead.

titles.name: WWWCW Alliance Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a five-man stable-war survival match between the Wolf Pack and the Foundation at Alliance Armageddon, resolved when a masked interloper unmasks as a roster member to hand the Foundation the win.

titles.name: WWWCW Extreme Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced at Hog Wild 97 via a five-man Chicken Coop weapons match, its debut and only recorded reign in this collection's holdings.

titles.name: WWWCW Heavyweight Tag-Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by the Twin Sisters (Crazy Phill & Lunatic Larry), who retain it against The Graveyard by disqualification at Hog Wild 97 -- the same show on which The Graveyard and a third wrestler are announced to have quit the fed.
titles.notes: No won-date for the Twin Sisters' own reign survives.

titles.name: WWWCW Intercontinental Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Changes hands at Hog Wild 97 after outside interference from both the Wolf Pack and the Foundation.

titles.name: WWWCW United States Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Awarded to War Dog on the same night he lost the Intercontinental title match, per the fed's own on-air ruling at On Your Screen -- an unusual mechanic recorded as the fed's own writing staged it.

titles.name: WWWCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Godfather, who retains it against Masked Judge by double disqualification at Hog Wild 97 when a stable war interrupts the match.
titles.notes: No won-date for Godfather's own reign survives; the double-DQ result is a defense, not a title change.

titles.name: WWWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned three days after WrestlePania, at Saturday ShootOut (30 March 1997): Head Hunter #1 won a 16-man over-the-top battle royal, becoming the fed's first multi-belt holder.
titles.notes: First held by Head Hunter #1, now minted as a real-wrestler portrayal.

titles.name: WWWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a single-night, best-of-three-falls tournament at the fed's own inaugural WrestlePania, 27 March 1997, with Stone Cold Steve Austin winning an Iron Man final over Mr. Perfect.
titles.notes: First held by Stone Cold Steve Austin, now minted as a real-wrestler portrayal.

titles.name: WWWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned the same night as the World Championship, at WrestlePania (27 March 1997): the Head Hunters won a six-team, best-of-three-falls tournament final over Randy Savage and Sting in a specially-ruled Death Match (three straight pinfalls).
titles.notes: First held by the Head Hunters, now minted as real-wrestler portrayals.

titles.name: Xbrand World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested vacant in a six-way Royal Championship Brawl on X-Brand's own debut show; interference from non-entrants Duff Man and Dias Ferreira voided the match, and incoming General Manager The Game suspended the championship on the spot. No reign of record survives in this wing's own captures.

titles.name: XBWL North American Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own entry-level singles title, which every new member is expected to win before advancing further.

titles.name: XBWL World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: The promotion's own top championship, which a wrestler must first hold the International or Hardcore title before challenging for.

titles.name: XCHW Cruiserweight Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in XCHW's own founding application (17 August 1997); no reign or card survives in the held record.

titles.name: XCHW Tag Team Title
titles.epitaph: The fourth title named in XCHW's own founding application (17 August 1997), conditional there on the fed recruiting "enough tag teams"; no reign or card survives in the held record.

titles.name: XCHW U.S. Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in XCHW's own founding application (17 August 1997); no reign or card survives in the held record.

titles.name: XCHW World Title
titles.epitaph: One of four titles named in XCHW's own founding application (17 August 1997); no reign or card survives in the held record.

titles.name: XCW IC Title
titles.epitaph: Held by the fed's own champion LOCO across both its runs, per his own year-end campaign post.
titles.notes: Reign dated only to "the past year" (1997) by the champion's own retrospective; no show script survives for the actual title change.

titles.name: XCW World Title
titles.epitaph: The fed's own top title, held by champion LOCO per his own year-end campaign post; a World Title Tournament to crown a (further, or the same) champion opens the surviving December relaunch card.
titles.notes: Reign dated only to "the past year" (1997); the tournament that opens Monday Night Madness (22 Dec 1997) may represent a subsequent vacancy -- not adjudicated.

titles.name: XCW Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Won by Randy Orton from Orlando Jordan at the wing's own 11 October 2004 Clash Of The Titans, still champion at this wing's own record's end; the belt changed hands at least three further times earlier in this wing's own 2003 partition (Goldberg, Taz, Jeff Jarrett attested) without a fully reconstructed chain.

titles.name: XCW United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Dean Malenko as of the fed's 7 December 1997 broadcast, named there by a debuting Taz as the only champion "worth a damn" on the roster.

titles.name: XCW World Championship
titles.epitaph: Held by Sting across both of the fed's own surviving 1997 broadcasts, retaining against Davey Boy Smith by disqualification on 17 November and facing a title challenge laid down by a debuting Taz on 7 December.

titles.name: XCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Introduced by a single-elimination tournament beginning at the wing's own 17 July 2003 Superclash I; its first champions are not attested in this wing's own surviving record. Al Snow and Bob Holly won the title on the wing's own 7 October 2004 Wednesday Night Warfare and were still champions at this wing's own record's end.

titles.name: XCWF Championship
titles.epitaph: Crowned in a sixteen-man Royal Rumble on Total HaVok, the fed's own debut show under its new name, when Da Masta outlasted the field. It changed hands thirteen more times across the fed's own life — twice to Al Magz, twice to Kamikazi, twice to Royce Mathers, twice to Mark Estep, twice to Zac Moore — and once by fiat, handed from Kamikazi to Al Magz in Fayetteville rather than lost in a ring. Menace was still holding it when the surviving record ends.

titles.name: XCWF Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Born at ResurreXtion in a four-way ladder match that opened with three men colliding in midair before it even properly started, and closed with Freak climbing past a tornado DDT'd Justin Pearce to unhook the belt. It is the fed's own richest lineage — twenty reigns in eleven months, three of them changing hands in a single week between Bayamon and Cancun, and three more on one Cancun night alone. Royce Mathers was its last champion the ledger records, crowned in Richmond in July 2002.

titles.name: XCWF Intercontinental Championship

events.title: xcwf-interunited
events.note: Menace, Intercontinental Champion since 28 April 2002, won the InterUnited Championship's own inaugural match on this date; the InterUnited title-history page names its own first match a unification bout, and this is the reign that carries forward.

titles.epitaph: Won first by Da Masta on Total HaVok, and carried by Mimic into a two-out-of-three-falls ladder match at Desperation that Kamikazi took in the deciding fall after a masked ally shoved the champion from the ladder. Menace won it in a tournament final in Cancun and carried it into the InterUnited Championship's own creation two months later; PTC's own dated profile of the fed names a different Intercontinental Champion for the week before that, a disagreement the surviving record does not resolve.

titles.name: XCWF InterUnited Championship
titles.epitaph: Created to unify the United States and Intercontinental Championships, won first by Menace in a match the ledger's own key calls a unification bout against Brian Arson. Al Magz took it from him in Indianapolis on the fed's own last recorded show date.

titles.name: XCWF Junior Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Born at ResurreXtion, where Lil Guido beat Jake Simmons with the Bullet to become the first champion. Shawn Boyd and Colby Newsome traded it three times in five spring weeks in 2002, and Talus won it vacant in Indianapolis, the last champion the ledger records.

titles.name: XCWF N.E.W. Championship
titles.epitaph: A single reign survives in the ledger: Shawn Kain won the title vacant in Indianapolis on 25 August 2002, the last date the surviving record carries for the fed at all.

titles.name: XCWF Tag Team Championships
titles.epitaph: Held first by the Immature Playaz and defended, vacated and re-vacated across thirteen reigns — a team named Total HaVok shares its own name with the fed's March pay-per-view, a Tag Team Turmoil Match crowned Shannon York and Unfitt Survivor after the belts went dark, and Predator once held them as a solo champion after beating Donovan Simmons in the straps' own first singles defense. Big 'N' Bad were the fed's last champions the ledger records, having already held the belts once before that summer.

titles.name: XCWF United States Championship
titles.notes: The XCWF InterUnited Championship's own title-history page names this belt as one of the two it unified — but its own last recorded champion, Rage (won 26 May 2002), is not the InterUnited belt's own first champion, Menace, and the ledger records no reign between them. The unification fact stands; how this belt's own lineage actually reached it does not.
titles.epitaph: Won first by Mark Massacre in Ames, Iowa, and changed hands nine times — once, in Nashville, the same night twice over, when Al Magz handed it to Freak and won it back before the night was through. Al Magz beat Sumo for it in a hardcore brawl at ResurreXtion; Stryder won the vacant belt from Ninja at Desperation on a Raven Storm run-in. Rage was its last champion the ledger records; the belt was later folded into the InterUnited Championship, though the ledger does not show how it got there from him.

titles.name: XCWF Women's Championship
titles.epitaph: Won first by Victoria Vengeance in Chicago in December 2001, and defended seven times across the fed's own women's division. Tessa Windsor and Tasha Evans traded it twice apiece in a single month that summer, and Tessa Windsor was the last champion the ledger records.

titles.name: XHCW TransAtlantic Championship
titles.epitaph: Pico Flush lost it to Adam Simon in a Texas Death Match at Retribution, 7 January 2002. Simon lost it to Brad Jones in a three-way Falls Count Anywhere Match at the Silverdome, 2 February 2002. Jones lost or vacated the title in a match no surviving document records; by Affliction, 28 April 2002, it stood vacant for an eight-man tournament, which Vincent Lyons won by beating Fear in the final. Lyons lost the title in turn, undocumented, to a radically changed Ramsus Palantiri, who dropped it to the mat himself at the opening of Hardcore Harvest, 24 October 2002, declaring it beneath him. No document shows anyone taking it up afterward.

titles.name: XHCW World Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The Dehibilitator held it from around November 2001, defending it past Retribution the following January in a Last Man Standing win over James Loyal, then over Midnight Rider, over 2Short and Scotty Fitzpatrick together, and over Midnight Rider again in a screwjob First Blood finish. Nailz beat him for it in a Roofed Glass Cage Match at Unleashed, 16 March 2002, retained it over The Scorpio, and survived a Scaffold Match against The Dehibilitator at Affliction, 28 April 2002, that ended without a pinfall when The Dehibilitator fell through a broken railing. Reverend Death took the title from Nailz in a match no surviving document records, and carried it past Hardcore Harvest, 24 October 2002, in an Xtreme Tables, Ladders and Chairs win over Micheal Graves.

titles.name: XHCW World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: "Sadistic" Steve Liermann held it into November 2001. The Juice took it from him at Awakening, 26 November 2001, and carried it past Retribution the following January with the debuting stable Absolute Power's help. Adam Simon won it from him at Unleashed, 16 March 2002, with Ramsus Palantiri's help. Brad Jones won it from Simon at Affliction, 28 April 2002, with a Sharpshooter and Steve Liermann's own help. Vincent Lyons then took the title from Jones in a match no surviving document records, and lost it in turn to Duff Man at Hardcore Harvest, 24 October 2002, when Steve Liermann's own betrayal — a bat shot — turned the match Duff Man's way; Lyons wrestled that night under a new mask, "Aftermath."

titles.name: XHCW World Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: 2Short lost it to Kletus Casady in a Cage Match at Retribution, 7 January 2002. Chris Cage won it from Casady in a Weapons Match twelve days later and defended it through the winter. Ramsus Palantiri took the title from him in a match no surviving document records, held it past Unleashed and a 30 March Steel Cage main event, then lost it back to Cage, again undocumented. Cage's second reign ended at Hardcore Harvest, 24 October 2002, when a mystery opponent, revealed as a new challenger, Spiral, appeared already holding his belt.

titles.name: XHCW World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Jolted and Frost lost it to John Sebastion and Scotty Fitzpatrick in a Double Dog Collar Match at Retribution, 7 January 2002, after the promotion's own president made the match a title match on the spot; Sebastion and Fitzpatrick kept it once more by simply leaving the arena with the belts. Adam Simon and 2Short, billed as "Short and Long," won it from them in a Weapons Match at Counterstrike, 9 February 2002, and never defended it again on any surviving card; it stood vacant by Hardcore Harvest, where Moose and Anthony Dolarhyde won a four-way dance for it, 24 October 2002, with their manager Paul Wade's own interference.

titles.name: XHCW World Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Chris Jacobson lost it to Moose at the Metrodome, 13 January 2002. Moose lost it to "Sadistic" Steve Liermann in Counterstrike's own "Final Battleground Match," 9 February 2002. Liermann defended it into the spring before losing a "Career vs. Title" match to Duff Man at Affliction, 28 April 2002. Duff Man lost the title to Kryptonic in a match no surviving document records, and Kryptonic lost it in turn to Fudgey McGlone at Hardcore Harvest, 24 October 2002.

titles.name: Xplosion Championship
titles.epitaph: SWWE Fed's own Xplosion brand championship. Rated Xtreme is billed by the promotion's own commentary as "the first-ever champion in SWWE Fed history," holding it through the 29 April 2007 card before losing it to Lashley in a triple threat also involving Eira at Unsurrender. A separate, undated line on the promotion's own 4 March 2007 card calls a wrestler billed as ".:Hardy:."

titles.name: XPW Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Contested in a cage match on 30 July 1999, its most recent title change on record.

titles.name: XPW US Championship
titles.epitaph: Held as of the promotion's own August 1999 newsletter; no title-change document survives.

titles.name: Xtreme Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as held by Rated Xtreme and Felix619 (together, Rated-X) on the promotion's own 29 April 2007 card; no defense or title change survives in the documents read this pass.

titles.name: Cruiserweight Championship
titles.notes: Source: promotions/xuw/archive/vortex6.html (XUW Vortex #6, 31 Jan 2002).
titles.epitaph: The shortest-lived name the eight belts carried — five reigns from Hurrisakie's opening hold to CK's, the one that ended it. At XUW Vortex #6, Mister Webster renamed the belt on-air as the XUW Television Championship the moment CK won it from Hodgo, and the same reign continues there under the new name.

events.title: xuw-television
events.note: Renamed on-air at XUW Vortex #6 the moment CK won it from Hodgo — Mister Webster: “I am changing this belt from the Cruiserweight Title, to the XUW TV TITLE!”

titles.name: Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: Twelve reigns recorded exact to the day, from the Lurchardor's opening 27-day hold to Raven X's as the source's own last snapshot; DDT is the only two-time holder the ledger names.

titles.name: Hermit Championship
titles.epitaph: The shortest of the eight belts' own ledgers — three reigns only, Severson's own twice, the second closing the title out for good: the source's own record states plainly that the belt was retired at that reign's own close.

events.note: The fed's own title-history ledger states the belt retired at the close of Severson's second reign; no exact date for the reign's own close survives.

titles.name: Intercontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: The busiest chain among the eight belts' own founding-era table, its final recorded change putting Numark on top as of the source's own last snapshot; two separate stretches sit vacant on the fed's own record, once for twelve days and once for twenty-four, with no holder named for either.

titles.name: Submission Championship
titles.epitaph: LanceStormDBC's own opening 73-day reign is the longest the belt's founding-era table records; Jack “the Ripper” Nobbledy's second reign is its last, champion as of the source's own final September 2002 snapshot.

titles.name: Television Championship
titles.epitaph: Continues the Cruiserweight Championship's own lineage — CK won the Cruiserweight belt from Hodgo at XUW Vortex #6, and Mister Webster announced, on the spot, “I am changing this belt from the Cruiserweight Title, to the XUW TV TITLE!” Thirty-plus changes follow at a breakneck pace before MV Pete's own reign closes the belt out for good — the source's own record calls him the “Final Television Champion” and states plainly that the belt was retired at his reign's own close.

events.note: The fed's own title-history ledger (champions.shtml / champions_retired.htm) names MV Pete the "Final Television Champion" and states the belt retired at the close of his reign; a later served show (XUW Road Rage III, Aug 2003) records a further change to Saij, a discrepancy the ledger's own retirement claim doesn't resolve.

titles.name: World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Nine holders across the fed's own surviving run, opening on Lopen's tournament win and last recorded changing hands to Sidhe Nimh at the source's own final September 2002 snapshot. The fed's own two ledger pages carry no prose at all — only a title, a holder, and exact dates, reign after reign.

titles.name: World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Dante & Woof Woof's own opening reign gives way to nine further changes of hands, the Boomer Sooners' own second reign the last the source's own snapshot records — the same Boomer Sooners who briefly gave way to an ad hoc, unbranded pairing of Kata & Sheri along the way.

titles.name: XUDF North American Championship
titles.epitaph: One of the two belts XUW's own developmental territory kept for itself — a North American Championship whose complete lineage survives in the XUDF's own champions ledger, from Doughboy's founding run through the vacancy the last capture leaves standing.

titles.name: XUDF U.S. Championship
titles.epitaph: The XUDF's own second singles belt, a U.S. Championship handed across the developmental roster for over a year — its complete lineage survives in the territory's own champions ledger, ending on Nurse Wretched's reign, still open at the final capture.

titles.name: XWF Extreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once in the surviving record, in an outdoor buried-alive match voted the promotion's own greatest match of all time.

titles.name: XWF Submission Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once in the surviving record, unified onto the same night's World title change in a triple-threat ankle-breaker match.

titles.name: XWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Changed hands once in the surviving record, in a triple-threat ankle-breaker match that put both the World and Submission titles on the line at once.

titles.name: Hardcore Title
titles.epitaph: The XWF's hardcore championship, named on all four of the fed's own title pages and held by nobody. The fed's own current-champions page records the belt VACANT with no number-one contender, and its title-histories page carries the heading PREVIOUS HOLDERS with nothing under it: no reign of this championship survives, and the record does not show one ever being decided.
titles.notes: Receipts: promotions/xwf-2001/archive/current-champions.html; also named on the fed's own unserved rankings and title-histories pages.

titles.name: Tag Team Titles
titles.epitaph: The XWF's tag team championships, named on all four of the fed's own title pages and held by nobody — the fed's own tag team roster page is an empty grid, so no team existed to contest them. The fed's own current-champions page records the belt VACANT with no number-one contender, and its title-histories page carries the heading PREVIOUS HOLDERS with nothing under it: no reign of this championship survives, and the record does not show one ever being decided.
titles.notes: Receipts: promotions/xwf-2001/archive/current-champions.html; also named on the fed's own unserved rankings and title-histories pages (geocities.com/nupes/ranks.html, /hist.html) and its own empty tag team roster (geocities.com/nupes/tagrost.html) — all three read for this accession, none served.

titles.name: TV Title
titles.epitaph: The XWF's television championship, and the one belt its surviving card was actually going to decide: the Monday Night Massacre battle royal promised to crown the Television Champion, and no result of it survives. The fed's own current-champions page records the belt VACANT with no number-one contender, and its title-histories page carries the heading PREVIOUS HOLDERS with nothing under it: no reign of this championship survives, and the record does not show one ever being decided.
titles.notes: Receipts: promotions/xwf-2001/archive/current-champions.html and promotions/xwf-2001/archive/monday-night-massacre-card.html; also named on the fed's own unserved rankings and title-histories pages.

titles.name: World Title
titles.epitaph: The XWF's top championship, named on all four of the fed's own title pages and held by nobody. The fed's own current-champions page records the belt VACANT with no number-one contender, and its title-histories page carries the heading PREVIOUS HOLDERS with nothing under it: no reign of this championship survives, and the record does not show one ever being decided.
titles.notes: Receipts: promotions/xwf-2001/archive/current-champions.html (the served current-champions page) and the fed's own unserved rankings and title-histories pages. "World Title" is the fed's own rankings/histories styling; its champions page styles the holder "World Champion."

titles.name: XWF Canadian Championship
titles.epitaph: Defended in a 'Canadian Rules' match on the Massacre of 8 December 2008. 1 reign is filed, from the page that bills its holder.

titles.name: XWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed on the Rage in the Cage page of 4 October 2009, where Chasm beats Nick Ryan for it, and on the Devastation card as a triple threat. 1 reign is filed, from the page that bills its holder.

titles.name: XWF Hart Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed only as a card line, 'Hart Title Standard Match', on the Columbia card of 8 October 2009, and in the funeral page's talk of a 'Hart Title hunt'. No holder is filed: no page held names who held it, or when.

titles.name: XWF International Championship
titles.epitaph: A title decided in numbered rounds on the Massacres of 12 January to 2 February 2009 (Rounds 1 to 4); no page held names the final or its winner. No holder is filed: no page held names who held it, or when.

titles.name: XWF Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as the Tag Team Titles on the Devastation card and in Nick Ryan's 'freshly won tag team gold' on 1 December 2008. Famine of the Vile's homepage of February 2009 lists two reigns of his, one with Scott Young and one with Nick Ryan, with no dates; no reign is filed.

titles.name: XWF Universal Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed in the Heaven & Hell Universal title match of Rage in the Cage (4 October 2009), in the Universal Title Tournament of August and September 2010, and on the X-Mas Xtreme build of December 2008. 2 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder.

titles.name: XWF United States Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed on the Anarchy card of 18 September 2009 and the cards of October 2009; Jensen Kent shows a redesigned United States belt on 26 August 2010. 2 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder.

titles.name: XWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed on the World/US title cage match of Rage in the Cage (4 October 2009), where the winner takes the World title and the loser the US title, and in the 2010 Universal Title Tournament page that has Zach Rizza as World Champion. 2 reigns are filed, each from a page that bills its holder.

titles.name: XWF Xtreme Championship
titles.epitaph: Billed as 'Xtreme Title #1 Contender Match' on the Columbia card of 8 October 2009; the fed's Belts folder holds a picture of it. Famine of the Vile's homepage of February 2009 lists two reigns of his, with no dates; no reign is filed.

titles.name: XWF Tag Team Championship
titles.notes: Attested once, from another promotion's announce desk: at New Era the commentary calls the Monte Brisas Outlaws "the tag team champions" while reporting that C.R. had just laid them out backstage.
titles.epitaph: One line of commentary on an interfed supercard is the whole of what survives of this championship. The Monte Brisas Outlaws held it in April 2003, and the sentence that says so is a sentence about them lying unconscious in their own dressing room. No title change, no earlier holder and no defence of it was ever captured.

titles.name: XWF Cruiserweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Established when Rob Van Dam won a Cruiserweight Battle Royal, last eliminating Lance Storm. Dynamite Kid and then Lance Storm held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: XWF X-Treme Divas Championship
titles.epitaph: Established when Natalya Neidhart won a six-woman elimination match over Madusa Miceli, Layla, Torrie Wilson, Candice Michelle, Maria Kinellis and Lacey Von Erich, last forcing Miceli to submit to the Camel Clutch — the only recorded champion on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: XWF North American Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Established for Ravishing Rick Rude at the January 2008 launch when GM Paul Heyman judged the UWF Television Championship's own name a poor fit for XWF and renamed the lineage Rude brought over. Vader and then Rude again held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: XWF World Tag Team Championship
titles.epitaph: Named for Demolition at the January 2008 launch — the same Demolition who, per both feds' own ledgers, carried the UWF United States Tag Team Championship over from UWF. Cactus Jack & Kevin Sullivan, Demolition again, Raven & Vampiro and finally Harlem Heat held it on the surviving ledger.

titles.name: XWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Vacant at the January 2008 brand-extension launch, filled when Samoa Joe won a King of the Mountain reverse-ladder match. Big Show and finally Brock Lesnar (in a Triple Threat over Big Show and Rob Van Dam) held it on the surviving ledger, before Lesnar's reign was unified into the ICWC World Heavyweight Championship at ICWC Capital Combat (2009).

events.title: icwc-world
events.note: Edge defeated XWF Champion Brock Lesnar and #1 contender Hulk Hogan in a Triple Threat Match at ICWC Capital Combat (2009) to unify both World Championships under the ICWC banner, per ICWC's own served title-history ledger.

titles.name: XWF World Heavyweight Championship
titles.notes: Every fact held about this belt comes from one night on another promotion's card: Primetime Central's own New Era of 20 April 2003. The fed's own championship pages were never captured.
titles.epitaph: The belt left the federation to be defended. Primetime Central put it on its own New Era supercard on 20 April 2003 and gave it a no-disqualification match, and what followed was six men on one: the champion, C.R., was jumped before the bell, put through a table by the number one contender, dragged upright by the tag team champions and set up for a splash from the top rope. He moved, and pinned the challenger. The announce desk was still promising an XWF programme that would settle it when the broadcast handed off to the next match. Nothing held names an earlier champion, and nothing held says what happened to the belt afterwards.

titles.name: CPW Young Blood Challenge Title
titles.epitaph: Attested for two reigns before the surviving record breaks off.

titles.name: ZWF Eurocontinental Championship
titles.epitaph: Chris Jericho's own second Summerslam title, defended the same night as his Light Heavyweight loss: he retained against Booker T, reversing a near-fall Bookend into a Bulldog and a Lionsault. The fed's own commentary names the belt "the Eurocontinental title"; the same broadcast separately introduces Booker T carrying "both Eurpean Title and Intercontinental Title," a wording the served text never reconciles.

titles.name: ZWF Hardcore Championship
titles.epitaph: The Rock carried the belt into ZWF Summerslam with no surviving record of how he won it, and retained it there against Supernova in a weapons brawl, winning with a second Rock Bottom through a table. The fed's own home page separately credits The Undertaker with a later Hardcore reign, its own origin equally unrecorded.

titles.name: ZWF Light Heavyweight Championship
titles.epitaph: Chris Jericho carried the belt into ZWF Summerslam with no surviving record of how he won it; Lita took it from him there, reversing a top-rope Lionsault into a rollup for the pin.

titles.name: ZWF TV Championship
titles.epitaph: X-Pac carried the belt into ZWF Summerslam with no surviving record of how he won it, and lost it there to Jeff Hardy in a Triple Threat also involving Zero, pinned by the Swanton Bomb after Hardy put Zero through a table. The fed's own home page separately credits The Undertaker with a later TV reign, its own origin — and the transition from Hardy's own Summerslam-won title — equally unrecorded.

titles.name: ZWF World Championship
titles.epitaph: The fed's own served World Title page runs a "Last 5 title changes" ledger across five reigns from 1 July to 12 August 2002: Brock Lesnar filled a vacancy by defeating Jerry Lynn by default, The Undertaker beat Lesnar eighteen days later, Sting beat Undertaker, the belt sat vacant again until Jerry Lynn beat Lesnar to reclaim it, and Undertaker beat Lynn for his second reign — the fed's own current champion as of its latest content. A served Summerslam broadcast separately stages Undertaker defending the belt in a steel cage against Triple H, winning clean before Sting attacks him after the bell and drapes the title over him — an echo of the ledger's own Sting reign, never explicitly confirmed as the same event.
